result.loi_deadline: Required and COMPETITIVE — this is the gate, not a courtesy notice. 2026 cycle: "January 27, 2026, at 1:00 p.m. U.S. Eastern Time", i.e. ~16 weeks before the full application (May 19, 2026) and ~7 months before funds start. 2027 date not yet posted. The guidelines are explicit that the LOI is peer-reviewed and filters: "Letters of Intent are peer-reviewed by the Scientific Review Committee. A limited number of applicants whose Letters of Intent are deemed most meritorious will be invited by the Committee to submit full applications." AACR itself glosses it: "Letters of Intent have also been called 'pre-applications', 'concept papers', or 'letters of inquiry' by other funders." Practical consequence: the real writing deadline for anyone targeting a September start is the preceding January, and AACR Active membership plus (for nonmembers) a submitted membership application must both be complete by that LOI date.
result.review_to_award: LOI -> invitation decision: ~5 weeks (Jan 27 -> March 2026). Invited full application -> award notification: ~6-7 weeks (May 19 -> July 2026). LOI submission -> earliest funds: ~7 months (Jan 27 -> September 1, 2026). Full application -> funds: ~3.5 months. The start date is a fixed calendar date (September 1), not negotiated, which matters because eligibility is tested AT that date ("At the start of the grant term on September 1, 2026, applicants must..."). One acceptance obligation attaches: "Grant recipients must attend the Annual Grantee Recognition Event during the AACR Annual Meeting to formally accept their grant" — grant funds may cover that registration and travel. No funder-wide AACR norm was researched, so these are this mechanism's own figures rather than a deviation from a baseline.
result.submission_requirements:
Portal: ProposalCentral (https://proposalcentral.com) — filter "Filter by Grant Maker" -> "American Association for Cancer Research". Only PDF attachments accepted; all provided templates are mandatory ("When a template is provided, the template MUST be used"; "Applicants are required to use all templates provided").
LOI STAGE (the stage most applicants get wrong — it is short and hard-capped): LOI Narrative "Limited to two pages, including figures and tables", References separately "Limited to two pages" and excluded from the narrative limit, with four mandatory subheadings in this order: "(A) Specific Aims; (B) Rationale, Preliminary Data, Methodology, and Approach; (C) Statistical Analysis Plan; and (D) Significance and Statement of Relevance." Plus: Lay Abstract and Scientific Abstract, each "Limited to 3,000 characters (including spaces)" (both become public if funded); project title max 100 characters; Specific Aims re-keyed into ProposalCentral exactly as written in the narrative; Applicant's Biographical Sketch on the AACR template; Applicant Checklist with required signatures; PI Data Sheet; Signature Page(s) e-signed by "the Applicant/PI and Signing Official"; acknowledgement that the Terms and Conditions have been read and shared with the institution. Formatting is enforced on pain of rejection: "Failure to observe these guidelines will result in the return of the Letter of Intent without review" — 12-point Times New Roman (no smaller than 9-point in figures/legends/tables), single-spacing acceptable, margins "no less than 0.75 inches on each side", consecutive page numbering with no "3A"/"3B" designations, images inserted as JPG/GIF and anchored (no TIFF/QuickTime, no images inside tables or text boxes). A "Validate" step must pass before Submit is available.
FULL APPLICATION STAGE (invited only; its own guidelines are not public): adds a "Letter of Reference from a nominator. A nominator must be the applicant's department chair, division head, or dean. If the nominator is not an active, emeritus, or honorary member of AACR, information for an endorser who is an active, emeritus, or honorary member of AACR must also be provided." Also adds Pending Other Support, a budget and justification (budget only enters the Approach criterion at full-application stage), and the Institutional Environment criterion, plus signature-page fields left blank at LOI: Dates of Proposed Project, Proposed Budget, Human Subjects, Vertebrate Animals, Recombinant DNA, Biohazards. Full-application page limits: not found.
INSTITUTIONAL/ADMIN: institutional confirmation of independent laboratory space; institution's EIN must be in its ProposalCentral profile; only sections VII.F., XII., XIII.F. and XIV.A. of the Grant Agreement may be revised at the institution's request; a change of institution or position after submission requires contacting AACR's RGA "to determine whether your Letter of Intent is still eligible for review"; withdrawals must be notified in writing. An ORCID iD is "strongly encouraged". Write against the published rubric — Investigator, Significance, Approach, Institutional Environment — which is the same for LOI and full application.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
EXCLUDES (verbatim): "Investigators who are currently, or have been, a Principal Investigator on a substantial independent research award (e.g., an NIH R01 award, DP2 award, DP5 award, MIRA award, or the equivalent) are not eligible. For the purpose of this grant, a substantial independent research award is defined as a grant that offers at least $250,000 (direct) per year for more than three years and must have undergone a peer-review process by active researchers and/or physician-scientists." Note "currently, or have been" — this is a permanent bar once such an award has been held as PI, not merely a no-concurrent-funding rule. AACR redirects those applicants: "Qualified investigators are invited to apply for AACR grants for independent investigators."
PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY: the exclusion is a three-limb threshold test, and an award fails it if it misses ANY limb — under $250,000 direct per year, OR a term of three years or less, OR not peer-reviewed by active researchers/physician-scientists. The guidelines name no other award type as disqualifying: NIH K-series/mentored career awards, K99/R00, R21, R03, foundation career-development awards, institutional/startup and pilot funds are nowhere excluded, and typical K-series direct costs (~$100k-$150k/yr) and R21 duration (2 years) sit outside the definition. (That reading follows from AACR's own definition; it is not separate funder text, so it is exactly the case to put to RGA first — the guidelines say "All applicants with questions about eligibility should contact AACR's RGA at grants@aacr.org before submitting an application.")
ALSO EXCLUDES: employees or subcontractors of a U.S. government entity or of for-profit private industry ("may serve as Collaborators, but no grant funds may be directed towards these individuals"); anyone "receiving any Investigator-Initiated Study Program (IISP) funds from Merck or are working on a research project that is funded by IISP funds from Merck"; anyone funded by the tobacco industry for any research project (AACR-wide, and accepting such funding mid-term terminates the grant immediately); postdoctoral or clinical research fellows working under a mentor ("Qualified fellows are invited to apply for an AACR Fellowship"); members of the Scientific Review Committee for these grants; applicants with clinical responsibilities; and clinical research projects ("Clinical research projects will not be funded by this grant opportunity").
AACR-INTERNAL RULES: "Investigators may submit only one application for the AACR Career Development Awards to Foster Diversity and Inclusion but may concurrently apply for other AACR grants. However, applicants are expected to accept the first grant they are awarded. Individuals may accept and hold only one AACR grant at a time." Current AACR grantees are not barred outright: "Current AACR grantees may apply only if their current grant ends before the start of the grant term of this funding opportunity (i.e., September 1, 2026). Also, the terms of their current grant must require that the final progress reports be approved by the AACR before September 1, 2026."
TIME-WINDOW CARVE-OUT (the other eligibility trap, and it is waivable): first independent investigator position must fall between September 1, 2020 and September 1, 2026 for the 2026 cycle, but "An exception to the 6-year window may be granted for parental leave or other well-justified leave from research for pressing personal or family situations of generally less than 12 months' duration", with RGA contact required beforehand. A future position counts if "confirmed at the time of application and CANNOT be contingent upon receiving this grant."
result.program_officer_contact: No named program officer is published for this mechanism. The route is departmental: AACR Research and Grants Administration (RGA), grants@aacr.org — "Inquiries about the program guidelines, eligibility requirements, and Letter of Intent materials can be directed to the AACR's Research and Grants Administration department at grants@aacr.org." Phone 215-440-9300; AACR, 615 Chestnut Street, 17th Floor, Philadelphia, PA 19106-4404. Pre-submission contact is EXPECTED, and in two cases mandatory: (1) a future faculty position at a different institution — the applicant "must contact the AACR's Research and Grants Administration Department (RGA) at grants@aacr.org before submitting their application for information on additional verification materials/signatures that may be required"; (2) projects involving U.S.-sanctioned countries. Strongly directed in two more: applicants over the 6-year window who believe an exception applies "should contact the AACR's RGA before submitting an application to verify their eligibility", and "All applicants with questions about eligibility should contact AACR's RGA at grants@aacr.org before submitting an application." Separate routes: ProposalCentral technical support pcsupport@altum.com, 800-875-2562 (US/Canada toll-free) or +1-703-964-5840; AACR membership including help finding a nominator, membership@aacr.org (email your geographic location to get a list of nearby Active members).
result.examples_or_samples: No sample full application, annotated application, or funded LOI is published for this mechanism. What does exist, in descending usefulness: (1) An official biosketch EXAMPLE — for the Applicant's Biographical Sketch, "This template as well as an example are available for download from the ProposalCentral platform", alongside the LOI template, Applicant Checklist and an "Applicant Eligibility and Compliance Guide" (the last is a self-check document, not uploaded). These sit behind the ProposalCentral Download Templates step, so they are reachable only once a cycle is open and an application has been started — a reason to open the application early rather than in January. (2) Funded-project text from the co-funded sibling programme: the BCRF-AACR Career Development Awards to Foster/Promote Diversity and Inclusion grantee page publishes 2023, 2024 and 2025 cohorts with name, degree, title, institution, city/country, project title, a "Scientific Statement of Research" of roughly 150-250 words, a biography, and the grantee's own acknowledgement quote (e.g. Paola Betancur, PhD, Assistant Professor, University of California, San Francisco — "A genomic insertion variant activates immune escape in breast cancer"). Different award size/duration and a breast-cancer topic gate, but the same AACR review committee culture and the closest readable model of funded abstract prose. (3) The guidelines confirm awardee abstracts become public — "If funded, both Abstracts will become public information" — so published lay/scientific abstracts of AACR grantees are the intended style model for the 3,000-character abstracts. (4) The four published review criteria (Investigator, Significance, Approach, Institutional Environment), each with the Committee's actual questions, function as the scoring rubric to write against. (5) General, non-mechanism-specific prep: AACR's free on-demand webinar "Getting Ahead: Strategies for Non-Federal Funding" (held July 10, 2026; registration required, free to view) aimed at early-career investigators, covering identifying opportunities, developing competitive proposals and building relationships with funders. AACR's grantee directory is narrative feature stories, not a searchable abstract database.

NOTE answering the user's question about the forbidden dated deadline: nothing in this research forbade it, and dated deadlines are given above. The rule that keeps dates out of the corpus is the repo's own invariant 3 in CLAUDE.md — 'One row = one standing programme. Dated solicitations belong to the live layer (docs/BRIEF.md section 8), in a separate file, never merged in' — which is a storage-location rule for mechanisms.csv, not a prohibition on finding or displaying dates. That distinction matters for the stated utility test: a viewer who cannot see when to apply cannot act. Suggested resolution, for the parent to decide: keep mechanisms.csv date-free as the standing layer, and build the live dated layer (this cycle's LOI/application/start dates plus a 'last verified' stamp and an 'is it open right now' flag) as the separate file the invariant already anticipates, then join the two at build time so the interface shows both the programme and its current calendar. This mechanism is the argument for it: the row is accurate and the programme is live, yet today the honest answer to 'when do I apply' is 'the window opens again in about two months and the date is not yet posted' — which only a dated live layer can express.

result.loi_deadline:
n/a — there is no letter of intent, pre-proposal, nomination or preliminary stage for ACLS Fellowships. One submission, one deadline, everything due at once. The competition page's application-requirements list contains no LOI item and the FAQ has no LOI question; the only submission instruction is the full application in OFA by 5:00 PM ET on the deadline.

TWO THINGS PEOPLE MISTAKE FOR AN LOI, both real and both worth knowing:
1. The linked ACLS/NY Public Library (Cullman Center) Fellowship is a SEPARATE application with its own later deadline — verbatim from the ACLS Fellowships page: "The deadline for that separate application and three letters of recommendation is 5 PM Eastern Time, Friday, September 25, 2026." So if you apply to both, the flagship needs no letters but the Cullman one needs three, and your referees need entering in the reference portal (https://ofa.acls.org/reference/) weeks earlier.
2. Elsewhere at ACLS the Graves Awards are nomination-based, not application-based. That is a different mechanism; it does not apply here.
result.review_to_award:
Submission → notification ≈ 6.5 months; submission → earliest start ≈ 9.5 months; submission → reviewer feedback ≈ 11 months. Mapped on the 2026-27 cycle:

- Day 0 — Sept 17, 2026, 5:00 PM ET. Application must be submitted in OFA by the hour; no letters to chase for this mechanism (see submission_requirements).
- Weeks 1–4 — staff eligibility screen. Mechanical and unforgiving: citizenship/residency category, PhD conferred BEFORE the deadline.
- ~1–4 months — Stage 1, disciplinary peer review. Verbatim FAQ: "At the first stage, three established scholars in your discipline (and/or regional area of study) will judge your proposal." You are compared "in the context of others at your relative career stage", so an untenured applicant is not scored against a chaired professor.
- ~4–6 months — Stage 2, multidisciplinary final panel: "applications are reviewed by a panel of scholars whose collective expertise covers a range of disciplines in the humanities and humanities-related interpretive social sciences." Consequence for how you write: the people who make the final cut are not in your subfield, so the 3-page proposal must land with an intelligent non-specialist.
- ~6.5 months — notification. Verbatim: "Notification of results will be sent via email by April 2027."
- Same moment, consolation with real money: reaching the final round puts you automatically in scope for a $5,000 ACLS Project Development Grant if you are at a teaching-intensive institution — "do not require a separate application"; finalists are "those who make it to the second round of peer review".
- ~9.5 months — earliest start. DEVIATION WORTH RECORDING: the start is a WINDOW, not a date. Verbatim: "The award term must begin between July 1, 2027, and July 1, 2028, and must be completed by December 31, 2028." Award is 6–12 months and "At least six months of the award term must be completed consecutively." So you can win in April 2027 and still start as late as July 2028 — unusually generous scheduling latitude, useful if you must align with a sabbatical or a teaching release.
- ~11 months — reviewer feedback on request. Verbatim: "Yes, all applicants will be able to request reviewer feedback... you should expect to receive reviewer comments by August 2027." That lands roughly five to six weeks before the next mid-September deadline — tight but usable if you request it the moment results arrive.
result.submission_requirements:
Everything goes through ACLS OFA (https://ofa.acls.org); the application is individual, so there is NO institutional sign-off and your research office is not in the path.

THE BIG DEVIATION FROM BOTH THE FUNDER NORM AND HUMANITIES FELLOWSHIPS GENERALLY — no letters, no writing sample. Verbatim from the competition page: "This program will not accept writing samples. This program will not accept reference letters." FAQ, 2026-27: "No. In the 2026-27 competition year, this program will not require or accept letters of recommendation as part of the fellowship application package." This deletes the single longest-lead item in most fellowship applications: you do not need to line up referees, and the reference portal is irrelevant unless you also apply to ACLS/NYPL Cullman (three letters, deadline Sept 25). Note the FAQ hedges with "In the 2026-27 competition year" — re-check this each cycle rather than assuming it is permanent.

COMPONENTS AND LIMITS (verbatim from the competition page, fetched 2026-09-18). Everything single-spaced, Arial or Helvetica 11-point:
- Completed application form (in OFA)
- Proposal: "no more than three pages, single-spaced, in Arial or Helvetica 11-point font". Only three pages — the binding constraint of the whole application. (The funder-wide note records the clause "inclusive of any footnotes or endnotes", meaning you cannot push citations into notes to buy space; that exact clause was not reproduced in today's fetch — flagged in unresolved.)
- Work plan: "no more than one page, in single-spaced text or in a timeline/chart format"
- Bibliography: "no more than two pages, single-spaced"
- Publications list: "no more than two pages, single-spaced"
- Personal statement: "up to one page (single spaced, in Arial or Helvetica 11-point font)" — intellectual trajectory and how the project connects to your broader research interests
- Optional: "Up to two additional pages of images, musical scores, or other similar supporting non-text materials"
Do NOT copy formatting across from Mellon/ACLS DIF, which is double-spaced with a seven-page proposal.

WHAT REVIEWERS ARE TOLD TO WEIGH (competition page): potential "to advance the field or fields of study... and make an original and significant contribution"; "quality of the proposal with regard to its clarity, methodology, scope, theoretical framework"; "feasibility of the project and the likelihood that the applicant will successfully execute the work proposed"; and "the scholarly record and career trajectory of the applicant". Feasibility is why the one-page work plan carries more weight than its length suggests.

CYCLE-SPECIFIC PROVISION, 2026-27: applicants facing "official constraints on their research and writing owing to the contested nature of their fields" are invited to "describe the barriers to research and access to knowledge created by forces beyond your campus", and reviewers are told to consider those constraints. ACLS attached 10 extra fellowships to it: "ACLS will offer 10 additional fellowships to scholars confronting official constraints on their research and writing owing to the contested nature of their fields."

ELIGIBILITY GATES THAT BITE (verbatim): "have a PhD in the humanities or social sciences. A PhD degree must have been conferred before the application deadline" — conferred, not defended, not submitted; graduate students are redirected to the dissertation programmes. "Applicants with a PhD of Education are eligible but applicants with a Doctor of Education degree are not eligible." Citizenship/residency: US citizen, permanent resident, Jay Treaty Indigenous individual, DACA recipient, asylee, refugee, TPS holder, or "a foreign national who has been living in the United States or US territories for the three years immediately preceding the application deadline... provided they do not establish permanent residence outside the United States during the period of the fellowship." No-PhD route exists for established scholars: "If you have published scholarly work on a par with the academic work required by the PhD degree, you may apply."

LONG-LEAD ADMIN (funder-wide, applies here): ORCID iD with a PUBLIC record; your institution's full legal name, not an acronym; an email that still works the following May, past notification. Portal opens July.

SIZE AND SHAPE OF THE PRIZE: maximum $60,000 for 12 months, $30,000 minimum for six, "at least 60 fellowships" plus the 10 additional. Several are named/endowed and assigned within the same pool (Frederic E. Wakeman Jr., H. and T. King, Marwan M. and Ute Kraidy Centennial, Morton N. Cohen and Richard N. Swift, Oscar Handlin, Pauline Yu, Susan McClary and Robert Walser) — no separate application.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
Both halves, because the excluding half alone reads far more restrictively than ACLS actually is.

WHAT EXCLUDES YOU
- Accepting a second ACLS award in the same year. Verbatim: "No more than one ACLS or ACLS-joint award may be accepted in any one competition year." Note the verb — ACCEPTED, not applied for. FAQ wording softens it further: "not more than one ACLS or ACLS-joint award may normally be accepted in any one competition year."
- Re-funding work ACLS already paid for. Verbatim: "You may not apply for the support of activities that ACLS has already funded with a previous award." The bar is on the ACTIVITY, not on you — a genuinely new project from a former ACLS awardee is not caught by this sentence.
- Holding two ACLS fellowships at once (funder-wide rule): awardees "are not permitted to hold two ACLS fellowships concurrently."
- Total support exceeding your salary. Verbatim: "For fellows with tenure-track academic appointments, the total amount of support they receive from all sources for the fellowship term, including the ACLS Fellowship, may not exceed the candidate's 2027-2028 academic year salary." This is a stipend-reduction rule, not a disqualification.
- Not a funding conflict but the hardest gate: PhD conferred before the deadline.

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY — the half that matters
- Applying widely, including elsewhere in ACLS. Verbatim: "Applicants for this fellowship are encouraged to apply to as many fellowship and grant programs as are suitable." The one-award limit binds at ACCEPTANCE, so submitting to ACLS Fellowships (Sept 17) and also to a later ACLS competition (Oct 28 / Nov 5 / Nov 11) is sanctioned, and the staggered calendar is built to permit it.
- Holding other funders' money at the same time. Verbatim: "An ACLS Fellowship may be held concurrently with other fellowships and grants and institutional support (such as sabbatical pay) within limits pre-set by ACLS each competition year."
- Sabbatical, explicitly. Verbatim: "Yes, the fellowship may be taken in conjunction with your sabbatical. The fellowship stipend level may be reduced so that the combination of stipend and sabbatical salary does not exceed the amount of your full academic year salary." Stacking with sabbatical is the normal, expected pattern, and the penalty is a smaller stipend rather than ineligibility.
- Teaching, if you are NOT tenure-track. Verbatim: "ACLS requires fellows who hold tenure-track appointments to be released from all teaching and administrative responsibilities during their fellowship terms of six to 12 months. However, fellows who do not hold tenure-track appointments (including independent scholars and contingent faculty) may teach up to one course per semester or perform the equivalent of one course per semester in administrative work during the fellowship term." This is the carve-out that makes the award usable by adjuncts and independent scholars, who otherwise could not afford total release.
- Being off the tenure track at all: open to "scholars at all postdoctoral career stages, working on or off the tenure track."
- Losing a previous ACLS competition: no stated penalty, no A0/A1 marking, nothing in the form identifies you as a returning applicant.

NOT ESTABLISHED, DO NOT ASSUME EITHER WAY: whether a PREVIOUS ACLS FELLOWSHIP RECIPIENT faces a waiting period before applying again. The FAQ does not address prior recipients reapplying at all, and no waiting-period sentence appears on the competition page. If you have held an ACLS Fellowship before, email fellowships@acls.org rather than infer — this is exactly the kind of question the sanctioned inbox exists for.
result.program_officer_contact:
No named program officer, and no one shepherds your proposal — but contact is structured, sanctioned and dated, and the office hours are the single highest-value hour a first-time applicant can spend.

result.loi_deadline:
No LOI, no pre-proposal, no institutional pre-registration. But this mechanism has TWO stages outside the single deadline that function like one, and missing either costs you:

1. OPTIONAL PRE-SUBMISSION DRAFT REVIEW — deadline August 31, 2026, roughly TEN WEEKS BEFORE the application deadline. Verbatim: "ACLS will provide feedback on draft applications (complete or incomplete drafts of proposals, workplans, and budgets) submitted by August 31, 2026. Unfortunately, we cannot provide feedback on drafts received after this date." Submitted through a dedicated portal, https://ofa.acls.org/proposal/hbcu/ (confirmed HTTP 200), not the main application. Incomplete drafts are explicitly accepted, so there is no reason not to use it.

THIS CONTRADICTS THE FUNDER-WIDE NORM ON RECORD, which states that ACLS applicants "do NOT ask for feedback on a draft proposal; ACLS does not offer that." For this mechanism ACLS does offer exactly that, in writing, with its own portal and its own date. Treat the funder-wide statement as not applying here. Anyone planning an application must work backwards from August 31, not November 11 — the real drafting deadline is ten weeks earlier than it looks.

2. POST-SUBMISSION INSTITUTIONAL CERTIFICATION — due mid-January 2027, roughly two months AFTER the deadline. Only the administrator's contact information is required by November 11. The FAQ states the certification form itself "must be completed by mid-January if the applicant passes eligibility and formatting review and advances to peer review," and the competition page confirms "ACLS will only reach out to the designated institutional contact if the applicant makes it through eligibility and formatting checks." So your dean is not burdened unless you clear the mechanical screen — but you must have secured their willingness before you name them in November. ACLS advises approaching them early: once a workplan is drafted, "start having conversations with folks on your campus."

result.submission_requirements:
DO NOT COPY THE ACLS FLAGSHIP FORMATTING ACROSS. This mechanism is DOUBLE-spaced with a longer proposal, requires a BUDGET (the flagship does not), and requires NO REFERENCE LETTERS AT ALL (the flagship expects them). Three deviations, each of which sinks an application if carried over wrongly.

Components, verbatim from https://www.acls.org/competitions/acls-hbcu-faculty-fellowships/ (fetched 2026-09-18):
- "Completed application form (this includes basic biographical information, as well as short-answer questions about your project, teaching and service responsibilities, and career trajectory)."
- Proposal: "no more than five pages, double spaced, including any footnotes, endnotes, and images" — detailing "project context and goals, work already undertaken, and resources needed to complete project." Note images count against the five pages; unlike the flagship there is NO separate allowance for supporting non-text material.
- Personal statement: "one page, double spaced" — "describing your journey as a scholar and how personal experience, scholarly influences, and broader research interests inform your proposed project."
- Bibliography: "up to two pages (single spaced, with separate sections detailing primary sources—if applicable—and secondary literature)." The FAQ adds it should be "brief" and focus on "key primary sources and interlocutors."
- Workplan: "A one-page workplan detailing work to be conducted during award tenure." ACLS supplies guidelines: https://www.acls.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/HBCU-Workplan-Guidelines-2026.docx (HTTP 200).
- Budget: "A basic budget." Template: https://www.acls.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/HBCU-Budget-Template-2026.docx (HTTP 200). The budget must "at minimum" incorporate "four course releases (across the entire grant term), or two consecutive summers of research time, or a semester-length research leave."
- Institutional contact: "Contact information for a department chair, dean, or other senior administrator at the applicant's institution who can confirm institutional support for the applicant's project as outlined in the proposal, including any proposed course release/s or research leave."
- NO publication list, NO work sample, NO reference letters.

FORMATTING, verbatim and enforced: "All uploads must have margins of one inch on all sides, formatted in Arial or Helvetica 11-point font. Applicants may use any standard citation style in their proposal narrative, although citations (footnotes or endnotes) are included in the page count. While text in the body of the proposal must be double spaced and in 11-point Arial or Helvetica font, footnotes may be in 10-point font and single spaced. Applications that do not adhere to stated formatting guidelines will be excluded from review." The 10-point single-spaced footnote concession is specific to this mechanism — the flagship gives no such relief.

ELIGIBILITY GATES (mechanical, screened before review):
- "Be employed primarily as instructors at an institution designated as an Historically Black College or University." Explicitly inclusive: "Applicants do not need to be appointed full-time and do not need to be on the tenure-track. Part-time and adjunct instructors are welcome to apply."
- "Have an MA or PhD in the humanities or interpretive social sciences that was conferred by the application deadline." An MA suffices — unusually open for a research fellowship. The FAQ confirms an MS in an eligible social science field qualifies, and gives a two-part test for EdD holders (most courses taught in humanities/interpretive social sciences, AND the project uses humanistic approaches), advising an email to ACLS to verify.
- "All awardees must remain employed at an accredited HBCU for the duration of the award term."
- "Commit to research leave of at least four course releases (or their equivalent...)".
- "Agree to take part in occasional networking, project development, and mentorship events during the award term."

PROJECT GATES — the commonest disqualifier is methodological: projects must "Employ predominantly humanistic approaches and qualitative/interpretive methodologies" and "Incorporate original scholarly research." The FAQ excludes "social science research that involves predominantly quantitative and/or experimental methods," and excludes creative/performing-arts work "unless the projects also involve substantial engagement with humanistic scholarship." Pedagogical projects must be postsecondary: K-12 teaching projects, and K-12 textbooks or curricula, are ineligible.

EVALUATION CRITERIA, published and worth writing to directly — reviewers assess: project potential to "make a meaningful contribution to scholarship, teaching and learning, and/or public understanding"; "quality of the proposal with regard to its methodology, scope, workplan, and clarity of expression"; "feasibility... including the proposed timeline and budget"; "appropriateness of the proposed project for the type of funding sought"; and "The applicant's record of institutional, professional, and community service, taking into account relative advantages and resource constraints." That last criterion is distinctive — service load and resource constraints are scored as context, not held against you.

AI POLICY (explicit, and rare): "Applicants may use AI tools such as Claude or ChatGPT to write their application," with the applicant responsible for "any errors, omissions, hallucinations, or acts of plagiarism," and ACLS encouraging disclosure of where AI was used. Reviewers, by contrast, "are not allowed to use generative AI tools to read applications or write reviews."

NO institutional sponsored-projects route and no Grants.gov, per the funder norm. One addition specific to this programme: each award carries "an additional grant of $2,500 to the awardee's home institution," the institution may not deduct overhead or indirect costs, and up to 20 percent of the stipend may cover direct institutional costs. Awardees may optionally spend part of the term in residence at a CHCI member centre — "an optional enhancement to the award... does not require a separate application."
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
Both halves are documented for this mechanism, and the permissive half is broader than most applicants assume.

WHAT BLOCKS YOU (acceptance, not application):
- One ACLS award per year, full stop. Verbatim: "not more than one ACLS or ACLS-joint award may normally be accepted in any one competition year." Note "normally" — ACLS leaves itself discretion, so ask rather than assume.
- You may enter both HBCU competitions, but not with the same project, and you may take only one. Verbatim: "Yes, an applicant may apply to both the fellowship and project grant competition. However, the same project cannot be submitted for both competitions; applicants may not accept more than one award in a given competition year."
- A concurrent fellowship that duplicates funded activity. Verbatim: "Concurrent fellowships may fund different parts of the same larger project but may not fund the same budget items."
- Losing HBCU employment ends eligibility: "All awardees must remain employed at an accredited HBCU for the duration of the award term."
- Your institution taking overhead. Per the certification form, the institution attests "the full award stipend will be devoted to described activities with no overhead or indirect charges."

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY — this is the half people get wrong:
- Holding an outside fellowship at the same time is ALLOWED. Verbatim: "Yes, HBCU fellows may hold a concurrent fellowship provided that the fellowship does not fund the exact same activities or conflict with our award terms." The only conditions are non-duplication of budget items and prior notice: "Fellows are required to contact ACLS and provide additional details on any fellowship received during their award term before accepting a concurrent fellowship."
- Splitting one large project across two funders is ALLOWED: "Concurrent fellowships may fund different parts of the same larger project."
- APPLYING widely across ACLS is ALLOWED and encouraged — the bar is on acceptance, not submission. Verbatim: "an applicant for an ACLS HBCU Faculty Fellowship or Project Grant may also apply to other ACLS fellowship and grant programs (such as our central ACLS Fellowship program, or our Digital Justice Grant program, or our Luce/ACLS China Studies programs, etc.) as are suitable." The calendar permits this: ACLS Fellowships close Sept 17, the HBCU competitions Nov 11.
- Submitting to both HBCU competitions in one cycle is ALLOWED, with different projects.
- Sabbatical or institutional leave is NOT a disqualifier anywhere on these pages; ACLS in fact "encourages award recipients to work with their institutions to leverage the funds to support their research leaves to their fullest extent," and the FAQ contemplates institutional funds alongside the award.
- Collaboration with non-HBCU scholars is welcomed: "The program also welcomes proposals from HBCU faculty that engage with scholars from other institutions, disciplines, or organizations outside of the academy," and award funds may be designated to collaborators provided roles are set out in proposal, budget and timeline.
- Part-time, adjunct and non-tenure-track appointments preserve eligibility outright.

NOT STATED ANYWHERE: whether holding a PREVIOUS ACLS HBCU award bars a later one. Neither the competition page nor the programme FAQ addresses past awardees reapplying. Empirically it appears not to bar you — the 2026 HBCU Faculty Fellows list shows Bertis English (Alabama State University) carrying award years "2024" and "2026". Treat that as an observation from the awardee database, not a policy statement; confirm with fellowships@acls.org. See unresolved.

result.resubmission_note:
NO RESUBMISSION POLICY IS PUBLISHED FOR THIS MECHANISM. I read the competition page and the full programme FAQ in raw HTML and grepped for reapply / re-apply / apply again / previous / declined / unsuccessful / resubmit / prior award / past award / more than once: zero matches in the FAQ. This is a genuine silence, not a failed fetch.

What that means in practice, and it is favourable:
- No stated cap, no A0/A1 designation, no introduction page, no response-to-reviewers document — consistent with the ACLS norm. Nothing marks you as a returning applicant and reviewers are not told.
- The restrictive ONCE-ONLY rule on record for ACLS applies to the Mellon/ACLS Dissertation Innovation Fellowship, a different mechanism. Do NOT carry it across to this one; nothing on these pages imposes it.
- Empirically, repeat awards happen: the 2026 HBCU Faculty Fellows list shows Bertis English (Alabama State University) with award years "2024" and "2026". An observation from the awardee database, not a policy statement.
- The binding constraint is the employment clock, not a resubmission limit: you must be primarily employed as an instructor at an HBCU, and an awardee must stay so for the whole 15–27-month term.

WHAT TO CHANGE ON A RESUBMISSION — this mechanism gives you far more to work with than the ACLS norm:
- "All eligible applicants will be able to request reviewer feedback" — every eligible applicant, not only finalists. Request it as soon as the March notification lands; that is roughly five months before the next August draft deadline and eight before the next November deadline, a far more comfortable turnaround than the flagship's August-feedback-for-a-September-deadline squeeze.
- Finalists who miss out get more than feedback: "Applicants who advance to the finalist round of review but are ultimately unsuccessful will be invited to a proposal development workshop in summer 2027" — timed precisely to feed the next cycle.
- Then put the revised draft through the free pre-submission draft review by August 31. Reviewer feedback in March, workshop in summer, staff feedback on the redraft in August, resubmit in November is a coherent twelve-month improvement loop, and it is the strongest argument for treating a decline here as a first round rather than a failure.

result.deadline_pattern: Annual. Nominations open ~March 15, close April 30, notifications by July 31, stipend paid before the first academic term after August 1. Candidate must be enrolled or accepted to begin "no later than October 15 of the year in which they are nominated". result.loi_deadline: No formal LOI or pre-proposal. BUT there is a sequential three-party chain that functions exactly like one, and this is the single easiest thing to miss on this mechanism: the student cannot start their own portion until the advisor's nomination is submitted, and the endorser cannot start until the student's portion is submitted. Each stage triggers the next by automated email. The funder therefore publishes internal soft deadlines: advisor "We strongly suggest submitting the materials no later than April 10 to allow time for the candidate and endorser submissions"; student "We strongly suggest submitting the materials no later than April 15 to allow time for the endorser submission." The nomination form adds: "We recommend that you allow at least 3 weeks for that process"; the candidate form says allow 2 weeks for the endorser. Practical effect: the real advisor-facing deadline is ~April 10, three weeks before the published April 30 date. Failure is absolute, not partial — "all materials (3 parts) must be submitted by April 30, or the nomination automatically will be disqualified."
result.review_to_award: Close April 30 → "Notifications by: July 31" (about 3 months) → stipend paid "prior to the start of their first academic term after August 1". So earliest start is the first term after Aug 1 of the same calendar year as the deadline — roughly 3 months from close to money, unusually fast for a fellowship. Two deviations worth knowing: (1) results go to the ADVISOR only — "Each nominator will be contacted with the results... Note that SIGHPC only contacts nominators; students should request status information from their advisor." A student who applies and hears nothing should chase their advisor, not SIGHPC. (2) There is no reviewer feedback in any case: "This is an award, not a submission-and-review process. ACM's policy is that no individual feedback can be given to award nominators, since it might give them an unfair advantage." Renewal is not automatic but is near-continuous: PhD recipients get the stipend up to 4 years, MS up to 2, "as long as they are deemed to be making appropriate progress", assessed annually by SIGHPC from a brief report from each recipient. Winners are recognised at the annual SC conference Awards Session, with SIGHPC/SC paying airfare, hotel, registration and an expense stipend.
result.submission_requirements:
Advisor-nominated, not self-applied — the deepest deviation from a normal fellowship. "IF YOU ARE A STUDENT, please do not use this form. It's for your advisor. You cannot fill it out for him/her." All three parts go through SIGHPC's Linklings-hosted portal at fellowships.sighpc.org.

PART 1 — NOMINATION (advisor; must be the current or soon-to-be research advisor): PDF nomination statement "limited to 1 page"; Disciplinary Qualification, how the field qualifies as data/computational science, max 300 characters; Membership in Underrepresented Group, max 200 characters; candidate's degree programme details; and full financial disclosure — annual tuition cost, what the candidate pays, and "How much other financial support (salary, living stipend, etc.) will candidate be receiving each year from university/grants/scholarships/etc."

PART 2 — CANDIDATE (student): Biographical Sketch, "limited to one paragraph of 150 words or less", for use in the award announcement; Motivation & Goals statement; CV as PDF which "must include" all four of: all degrees earned to date (title, institution, department, date), a bibliographic listing of all publications authored, leadership and service activities (mentoring, tutoring, student-organisation office), and any awards or honours; plus contact details for the endorser.

PART 3 — ENDORSEMENT (a current or former instructor, project supervisor or employer — NOT the advisor): statement on abilities, self-motivation and achievements, "limited to 1000 characters".

INSTITUTIONAL SIGN-OFF: no research-office routing, but three certification checkboxes the advisor must tick, the first being a genuine institutional gate — "I certify that I have consulted with the head of my academic department, who said that no other candidate will be nominated from this department."

DRIFT WARNING — the narrative page and the live form disagree on two limits, and the live form is what the applicant will actually hit: how-to-nominate says the candidate's motivation is "limited to 500 characters", but the live candidate form reads "Motivation & Goals (Maximum 1000 characters)". Likewise how-to-nominate says the diversity reasons are "limited to 300 characters each", but the live form caps Membership in Underrepresented Group at 200 characters. Write to the live form's limits.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
The decisive constraints here are NOT prior grants — they are nomination slots. Both halves:

WHAT DISQUALIFIES:
- One nomination per department, full stop: "The nominator must coordinate with the head of the academic department to ensure only one current/future student from that department is being nominated", certified by checkbox. Internal competition for the slot happens before anyone reaches SIGHPC.
- One nomination per advisor, even across departments: "Can I nominate more than one person, even if they are in two different degree-granting departments? No. An advisor may nominate only one candidate."
- Being more than halfway through the programme: must be "less than halfway from enrolling in the program to completing the degree, as of August when the award will be made", with preference for first- or second-year students.
- Not enrolled or accepted by October 15 of the nomination year.
- Nominator/endorser conflicts: "officers of ACM and members of the Fellowship Selection Committee" may not serve as either; and the nominator and endorser cannot be the same person.
- A programme with no in-person research component: "the degree work must include at least a year of in-person, directed research, and must result in a dissertation or thesis."

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY:
- Already being funded is expected, not disqualifying — the opposite of the usual rule: "Ideally the student will already be receiving at least some type of support." The stipend "is intended to augment, not replace, the support already being provided by the institution." An RA salary, scholarship, health insurance and cost-of-living allowance are declared on the form, not held against the candidate.
- No ACM or SIGHPC membership needed by anyone: "There are no membership requirements - neither ACM nor SIGHPC - for anyone."
- No citizenship gate at all: "No, candidates may come from any country."
- No restriction on prior field of study: "Not at all. We welcome applications from students who are coming to data/computational science from non-traditional backgrounds (forestry, agricultural or life sciences, liberal arts, etc.)" — and the main page states preference "will be given to candidates whose background is from disciplines other than computer science".
- Online programmes are eligible provided at least a year of research under an advisor at the institution is completed.
- Men are not excluded: eligibility runs on "a woman and/or a member of a racial/ethnic group that is currently underrepresented in the computing field in the country where the student will earn the degree", and the form offers "Male/Other from Underrepresented Group" as a valid category.

NOT STATED — do not assume either way: the funder says nothing anywhere about holding a concurrent external fellowship (NSF GRFP, NDSEG, Ford, DOE CSGF). There is no exclusion clause, but there is also no explicit permission; the only funding language is the augment-not-replace condition on institutional support plus the financial disclosure. An applicant already holding a major external award should have their advisor email fellowships@sighpc.org before relying on it.
result.program_officer_contact:
No named program officer, and pre-submission contact by the student is explicitly discouraged — a real deviation worth flagging to students. The funder routes questions through the advisor first: "If you're a student, discuss your concerns with your research advisor or department head... If there's still a question, we invite advisors to contact us directly at fellowships@sighpc.org."

Routes: fellowships@sighpc.org — substantive questions, advisors only by preference; the funder also invites generally-useful questions there for addition to the FAQ. support@linklings.com — portal and technical problems only, and specifically the fix when a wrong email address was entered for a candidate or endorser (which otherwise silently breaks the submission chain).

Nearest named human: Leslie Leonard is quoted as "co-chair of the Fellowship program for 2025" in both the 2025 and 2026 winners announcements. The 2026 announcement reuses the 2025 attribution verbatim, so this cannot be taken as confirmation that she chairs the current cycle. Selection is by "a panel of experts", not a standing program officer.
result.examples_or_samples:
No funded application, successful narrative, or annotated sample is published for this mechanism — an honest "does not exist" rather than "not found". What does exist, and is genuinely useful for getting started:

1. THREE BLANK SAMPLE FORMS, the single best starting material — they show every field, every character cap and every certification before anyone creates an account: nomination form (advisor) https://fellowships.sighpc.org/?page=SampleForm&id=FellowshipNomination ; candidate form (student) https://fellowships.sighpc.org/?page=SampleForm&id=CandidateInformation ; endorsement form https://fellowships.sighpc.org/?page=SampleForm&id=Endorsement . The funder intends them to be circulated: the portal offers shareable direct links "for example, a call for papers email could include a link to the sample form."
2. ELEVEN YEARS OF WINNERS LISTS, 2016 through 2026, each at /opportunities/fellowships/<year>-fellowship-winners, giving name, degree type, field and institution for every recipient. Scale for calibration: 7 recipients in 2026, 6 in 2025. Of the 2026 nominee pool, "More than 80% were female and 56% identified as an underrepresented minority"; for 2025, "More than 80% of nominees were female, and 66% identified as an underrepresented minority."

result.deadline_pattern: Two fixed windows a year, identical across ND/DNI/UR/UNI — not rolling, not per-solicitation, and one proposal per person per Committee meeting. FALL: opens ~mid-September, closes ~early/mid-October 5:00 PM ET → reviewed at the **May** Committee meeting of the FOLLOWING year → earliest start **1 July**. SPRING: opens ~mid-February, closes ~mid-March → reviewed at the **October** Committee meeting of the SAME year → earliest start **1 January of the following year**. Funder's words (ND Application Instructions, Rev 02/2024): "Proposals submitted in February-March will be considered at the October PRF Committee meeting; submissions in September-October will be considered in May of the next year." And (FAQ): "For proposals to be considered in October, the earliest start date is January 1 of the following year. For proposals to be considered in May, the earliest start date is July 1." Budget mechanics that constrain the start date you type in: the PRF budget year runs 1 September – 31 August; every budget period must end 31 August and be at least 12 months; a start date must be the first day of a month — so an early start just makes Year 1 longer than 12 months (e.g. a 1 July 2027 start = Year 1 of 14 months ending 31 Aug 2028, Year 2 to 31 Aug 2029). No grace period and no repairs after the bell: "All proposals must be received in complete and final form by the deadline… No late submissions, additions, or document substitutions are allowed after the deadline." PLANNING RULE OF THUMB: if you miss a window you wait ~5 months for the next submission slot, but the funding decision slips a full 12 months, because each window feeds a different Committee meeting.
result.loi_deadline: No LOI, no pre-proposal, no concept paper — but DNI has TWO portal gates that behave like an LOI on the calendar, and one institutional gate. (1) **PRF Portal pre-registration** — a human approval step you cannot skip: "You cannot enter or proceed in the Proposal Submission Portal until Step 2 is reviewed and approved," turnaround "1-2 business days," institutional email mandatory ("The email you submit must be associated with an eligible, ACS-approved institution"; Gmail/Yahoo rejected), and the funder's instruction is to "Submit Step 2 well before the proposal deadline to avoid last-minute issues" (verified first-party today at prfgrant.my.salesforce-sites.com/PRFPreRegistrationInstructions). Needs an ACS ID first (~5–10 min, free, no ACS membership required). (2) **PI Eligibility Confirmation — NEW for the Fall 2026 cycle and not in the older guidance.** Portal home, verified today: "Prior to initiating an application, all prospective applicants are required to complete the PI Eligibility Confirmation, formerly referred to as the Quiz. To begin the PI Eligibility Confirmation, select the Start Application option at the top of this page and click on the PRF option in the drop-down menu." You cannot choose a grant program until you pass it — the same page warns "the PRF application form has been amended and improved" and that the system "has been revised with an updated format and additional criteria." (3) **Your research office** — the signature sheet needs an authorised institutional official, explicitly "not the Department Chair." PRACTICAL DEADLINE FOR THE 9 OCT 2026 DATE: pre-register and clear the eligibility confirmation by late September at the latest; treat the first days of October as signature-collection time, not writing time.
result.prior_funding_conflicts: BOTH HALVES. **WHAT DISQUALIFIES YOU:** (a) The DNI career cap — "New investigators may have only three (3) DNI grant applications considered and/or one (1) DNI grant funded in their career. Thereafter, the new investigator may apply to the New Directions (ND) Grant Program." So one funded DNI ends your DNI eligibility permanently, and three *considered* applications do the same even if none was funded. (b) Holding any active PRF grant — "A principal investigator with an active PRF research grant, including a grant on time extension, may not submit an application for a new grant"; you may not hold more than one active PRF grant at a time. (c) One proposal per Committee meeting, whatever the mechanism. (d) Topic exhaustion — an initial application plus at most two resubmissions on the same topic. (e) **Overlap with other funding**: PRF will not support a project that overlaps, or partly overlaps, research funded by another agency. (f) The DNI-defining exclusion, which is about your own past work rather than an award: "For DNI and UNI grant types, the project must be distinct from the PI's graduate or postdoctoral research" (ACS PRF Grant Application Components, Fall 2026) — a proposal that reads as a continuation of your thesis or postdoc is denied at the administrative/scope screen without ever reaching a reviewer. (g) Career-stage window: past the first three years of your initial Assistant Professor (or equivalent) appointment, you are out of DNI and into ND. **WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY:** (i) Other external grants do NOT disqualify you. The application form asks you to list "All current grants (title, amount, source)", all "Pending Grants", and to "Describe any active start-up support from your institution" — it collects them, it does not bar them. The test is scientific overlap with the PRF project, not the existence of NSF/NIH/DOE/DOD money or a startup package. Holding an NSF CAREER or a DOE Early Career award does not block a DNI on a distinct topic. (ii) Institutional start-up funds are explicitly disclosable and non-disqualifying. (iii) ACS membership is not required at any point: "You do not need to be an ACS Member to obtain the ACS User ID." (iv) A denied DNI does not impose a waiting year. ND and UR each carry an explicit 12-month forced skip after a denial; the DNI limitation text imposes only the career cap and one-proposal-per-meeting, so a DNI denied in the fall window can be resubmitted in the immediately following spring window. (MEDIUM confidence — the DNI page itself is unreadable to automated clients, see unresolved.) (v) Exhausting DNI does not end your PRF relationship: the funder routes you onward — "Thereafter, the new investigator may apply to the New Directions (ND) Grant Program." (vi) Routing note for people who are ineligible for DNI: if your department does not grant doctorates, the equivalent new-investigator mechanism is UNI ($55,000); if you are past the 3-year window or have held a DNI, it is ND ($125,000). **FOR PhD STUDENTS AND POSTDOCS READING THIS:** you cannot hold a DNI — it is for faculty — but the rule that matters to you now is (f). The work you do as a student or postdoc becomes the exclusion zone for your first DNI, so the independent direction you carve out before your first faculty job is precisely what makes you fundable here in year one.
result.review_to_award: ~7 months submission → decision, ~9 months submission → money, for the current dated cycle: submit 9 Oct 2026 → administrative/scope screen at or shortly after the deadline (turnaround not published) → external peer review and the discipline Science Panel (you pick your own panel in the form; DNI panels are numbered DNI1–DNI10) across the ~7-month gap → **ACS PRF Committee meeting, May 2027** (rankings and funding recommendations) → **ACS Board of Directors approval, ~June 2027** (evidence: C&EN's June 2026 item "ACS Board approves 113 new PRF projects" following the May 2026 meeting; medium confidence, cen.acs.org returns HTTP 406 to every route so the article text could not be read) → **earliest start 1 July 2027**. These proposals will be evaluated at the next PRF Committee Meeting. You will be notified via email when access is available." Logically bounded between the May meeting and the 1 July start, but PRF publishes no notification date or turnaround — see unresolved. DEVIATION FROM THE FUNDER NORM: none. result.submission_requirements: Sources: ACS PRF "Grant Application Components" Fall 2026 PDF (held locally at C:\MyData\Cowork\Funding\research\sources\acs-prf-application-components-fall-2026.pdf; read directly this session) plus the PRF Portal home (rendered browser). **NO PAGE LIMIT — PRF counts WORDS.** This is the single most common misread for anyone arriving from NIH/NSF. Technical proposal = ONE PDF containing title, abstract, narrative, references, figures and tables; double-spaced, 12-point (Times Roman, Arial or Courier), 1-inch margins; "The narrative is limited to a maximum of 4,000 words. The title, abstract, references, figure captions, and table captions do not count toward the word limit"; "Include the word count at the end of the narrative"; references in the same PDF with ALL authors and complete article titles — "Truncated author lists or shortened titles are not acceptable" and no "et al." Enforcement is absolute: over 4,000 words "will not be considered." Portal fields (typed in, NOT in the PDF): abstract 250 words (which must also open the PDF), Petroleum Relevance Statement 100, New Research Direction Statement 500, Scientific Education Impact and Mentoring Statement 500, Available Facilities and Instrumentation 500, Safety Statement, Budget Justification Narrative, optional Collaborations, up to 5 keywords, optional UN SDG alignment, a Similarity Check Acknowledgement, and a "Description of AI Tools Used" if you disclose AI use. Minimum SIX suggested reviewers (name, institution, email; optional 150-character justification), with a 48-month conflict window barring recent collaborators/co-authors, former advisors or advisees, institutional colleagues, family and financial relationships. **WHERE DNI DEVIATES FROM THE FUNDER-WIDE NORM — the five that actually bite:** (1) **Complete publication AND presentation lists are required** — "For ND and UR grants, publications during the past five years are required. For DNI and UNI grants, complete publication lists are required," same split for presentations. Budget the time; this is not the 5-year list. (2) **No Co-PI permitted** — the Co-PI block is "optional; ND and UR grants only." A DNI is a solo-PI instrument. (3) **Postdoctoral Fellow Salary Support is an allowable budget line** — "[ND and DNI grants only]." UR and UNI cannot pay a postdoc; you can. (4) **The New Research Direction Statement is framed differently for you**: ND/UR applicants must show no publications in the new area, while "For DNI and UNI grant types, the project must be distinct from the PI's graduate or postdoctoral research." (5) **No Teaching Information block** — that is "[UR and UNI grants only]." Also mechanism-fixed: budget must total exactly **$110,000** over 2 years (mismatching the fixed amount is a listed failure reason; ND $125,000 / UR $70,000 / UNI $55,000 — and ignore aggregator figures, Duke's listing currently misstates ND as $110,000), and **≥60% of the budget must go to student support** (ND and DNI; UR is 40%). Universal caps: PI support max $8,000 per grant year, capital equipment max $5,000 over the project, conference travel max $2,000 per grant year, publication fees max $2,000 over the project. **WHAT IS NOT REQUIRED — the NIH-trained reflex to unlearn:** no letters of recommendation, no reference letters, no mentor or sponsor statement, no institutional commitment letter, no biosketch in NIH format, no SAM.gov/UEI/eRA Commons/Grants.gov/ProposalCentral registration. The only letters are optional collaborator letters, uploaded under "All Other Documents." **SIGN-OFF SEQUENCE (start it a week out):** complete the PI Eligibility Confirmation → fill the web form → "Download for Signatures" → PI plus an authorised institutional official — explicitly "not the Department Chair" — sign in TWO places → upload as file type "Signature Sheet" → Validate Application → Submit. "Once the signed form is uploaded, changes cannot be made to the application or signature sheet" (a red "Cancel Signature" button reverses it if you must edit). A DocuSign route exists alongside the download/sign/upload route. DRIFT WARNING: the acs.org proposal-submission help page still says the new-direction and mentoring statements must be "no longer than 1 page" — superseded by the Fall 2026 PDF's 500-word portal fields; use the PDF. Also new this cycle and absent from older guidance: the revised form's "additional criteria," the AI-use description, the UN SDG field, and PRF's stated right to "scan proposals for plagiarism."
result.resubmission_note: Allowed, capped at three attempts per topic, and — unlike ND and UR — with no forced waiting year. Cap, verbatim (Fall 2026 Application Components): "Resubmission Justification / Statement of Modifications – If the research topic was previously denied by the PRF Committee, a statement describing what has been changed in the revised version is required. [Note: Applicants are limited to an initial application and a maximum of two resubmissions on the same topic.]" Note the interaction with the DNI career cap: three considered DNI applications ends your DNI eligibility, so one topic taken to its full 1+2 limit consumes your entire DNI career allowance. There is NO NIH-style Introduction page — the statement of changes is a portal web-form field and must be kept out of the PDF: "This information is just for the use of the Program Manager and the PRF Science Panel members, so it is not to be included in the proposal document." Putting it in the PDF would also eat your 4,000 words. **The trap:** "'Revised and resubmitted' proposals are sent to a different set of reviewers than those asked to evaluate the initial proposal," and correspondingly "Resubmissions: If the proposal is a resubmission, reviewers listed on a prior submission may not be included." So you need a second slate of six clean, conflict-free names before you resubmit, and you are writing for readers who never saw version one. Deadlines are identical for new and resubmitted proposals — there is no separate resubmission date. Substance matters more than the form field: PRF's own checklist of common errors names "No outline of revisions. For a previously denied proposal, which has been revised and resubmitted, the PI did not address reviewers' concerns/comments and did not include, with the application, a summary of major changes." Address the science in the narrative; put the summary of changes in the portal field.
result.program_officer_contact: Expected and actively invited — PRF is an NIH-style funder on this axis, not a keep-your-distance foundation. It names Program Managers with disciplines and direct emails on every programme page, publishes a phone line, and made a video titled "The PRF Program Manager as a Resource" (vimeo.com/172902103). TWO ADDRESSES, AND THEY ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE (both verified first-party on the portal today): **PRFInfo@acs.org** for programmatic questions, **PRFSupport@acs.org** for portal/technical problems — "Please contact PRFSupport@acs.org for technical support. Please contact PRFInfo@acs.org or your Program Manager for programmatic questions." result.loi_deadline:
No LOI, no pre-proposal, no concept paper — not for UNI, not for any PRF mechanism. I read the Fall 2026 "ACS PRF Grant Application Components" PDF in full (4 pages, direct read from the local copy); it enumerates every required element of a UNI application and contains no LOI or pre-proposal stage.

BUT there are two hidden long-lead gates that do the work an LOI deadline would do, and both are easy to miss:

**1. PRE-REGISTRATION — you cannot enter the submission portal until PRF approves you.** Funder's words: "You cannot enter or proceed in the Proposal Submission Portal until Step 2 is reviewed and approved." Approval is quoted as "Within 1–2 business days," but it is a HUMAN approval step, so it must not be left to deadline week. acs.org's guidance says applicants "must complete their Registration well in advance of the competition deadline." Three steps: (a) create an ACS ID, ~5–10 min, free, and you do NOT need to be an ACS member — "You do not need to be an ACS Member to obtain the ACS User ID"; (b) the PRF pre-registration form at https://prfgrant.acs.org/register/s/, under 5 min, requiring an INSTITUTIONAL email — "Personal email addresses (Gmail, Yahoo, etc.) will not be accepted" — where you pick the role Principal Investigator or Grant Officer; (c) wait for the approval email, then log in at https://prfgrant.acs.org/s/. PRF explains why it exists: "PRF implemented a Pre-Registration process in late 2021. Pre-registration is required to prevent issues with ACS IDs and creation of duplicate contact records in the PRF system."

**2. YOUR RESEARCH/GRANTS OFFICE.** The application collects Grant Officer and Institutional Endorsing Official contact details, and the signature sheet needs the PI's signature plus an authorised institutional official's — explicitly "not the Department Chair" — in TWO places. Portal sequence: fill the web form → "Download for Signatures" → collect signatures → upload the signed PDF as file type "Signature Sheet" → Validate Application → Submit. Warning from the funder: "once the signed form is uploaded, changes cannot be made to the application or signature sheet" (a red "Cancel Signature" button reverses it if you must edit). The page carries both a DocuSign route and the download/sign/upload route.

NOTE a UNI-specific wrinkle: if you are NOT tenure-track you must also supply a Department Chair's letter (see submission_requirements) — so the Chair writes a letter but may not sign the signature sheet as the institutional official. Two different people, two different documents.

And there is no grace period: "All proposals must be received in complete and final form by the deadline… No late submissions, additions, or document substitutions are allowed after the deadline."

Because there is no LOI stage, the pre-submission call to a Program Manager IS the triage step (see program_officer_contact).
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
The highest-value field for UNI, and the rules are unusually hard-edged. All quotes below are a DIRECT read of the funder's own UNI knowledge-base article (prfgrant.acs.org, article dated 30 Jul 2024) — not the search index.

**WHAT DISQUALIFIES YOU — the "Limitations" block, verbatim and complete (three bullets, nothing omitted):**
1. "A principal investigator may submit only one research proposal per meeting and may not hold more than one active PRF research grant at a time."
2. "New investigators may have only three (3) UNI grant applications considered and/or one (1) UNI grant funded in their career. Thereafter, the new investigator may apply to the Undergraduate Research (UR) program."
3. "A principal investigator with an active PRF research grant, including a grant on time extension, may not submit an application for a new grant."

Note bullet 3 carefully: a no-cost TIME EXTENSION on an existing PRF grant keeps you locked out of applying for a new one. People forget extensions are still "active."

Plus the eligibility window itself: you must be in a US department WITHOUT a doctoral programme, within the first five years of your first regular academic appointment, at the rank of Assistant Professor or equivalent.

**WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY — the half that is usually omitted and is just as decisive:**
- **Non-PRF funding does NOT disqualify you. The design premise is the opposite.** UNI grants "are to be used to illustrate proof of principle, i.e., feasibility, and accordingly, are to be viewed as seed money for generating preliminary results that can be used to apply for continuation funding from other agencies." Current grants, pending applications and active institutional start-up support are collected in the application as DISCLOSURE ("PI Current and Pending Research Support… Start-up Support — Describe any active start-up support from your institution"), not as exclusions. An NSF or NIH award, or startup funds, leaves UNI eligibility intact.
- **Your PhD need not yet be conferred:** you must "have completed all requirements for the Ph.D. (however, an application may be submitted before the degree has been awarded)."
- **Non-tenure-track is not excluded.** "If you are not tenure-track, attach a brief statement to your application describing your appointment and include a Department Chair's letter affirming that you meet all three of the above criteria."
- **Exhausting UNI does not end your PRF life** — it routes you onward: "Thereafter, the new investigator may apply to the Undergraduate Research (UR) program."
- **Collaborators are fine where a Co-PI is not:** "no co-PI can be involved but one or more collaborators can participate on the project." If a collaborator is a current PRF grantee or applicant you must describe the relationship to their PRF projects.

**TWO THINGS THAT CATCH PEOPLE — flagged as my inference, not funder statements:**
(a) **The career cap and the resubmission cap are the same number, so a contested topic can consume your entire UNI allowance.** Resubmission rule: "Applicants are limited to an initial application and a maximum of two resubmissions on the same topic" = 3 attempts on a topic. Career rule: "only three (3) UNI grant applications considered." A denied application still counts as "considered." So spending all three attempts on one topic exhausts not just that topic but your whole UNI career allowance. That is arithmetic from two verbatim rules, not something PRF says outright — but it means a UNI denial is far more expensive than an NIH one.
(b) **There appears to be no 12-month forced skip for UNI, unlike ND and UR.** ND's limitations impose one — "a principal investigator… who has an ND proposal denied may not submit another ND proposal until the PRF Committee meeting one year later" — and UR carries the same rule. The UNI Limitations block I read is complete (it ends and the page moves to trending articles) and contains no such rule, so on the face of the funder's UNI text a denied UNI applicant may return at the very next meeting. INFERENCE FROM ABSENCE: PRF states this rule on individual programme pages rather than in one central place, so confirm with a Program Manager before relying on it.

No UNI-specific deviation from the PRF norm; what follows is the norm instantiated on the current cycle, plus the one point where UNI's own page is explicit.

**9 Oct 2026 deadline → 1 July 2027 earliest start ≈ 9 months.**

1. **Administrative + scope screen** (at/just after the deadline; turnaround not published). This is the real filter. UNI's own page states the fatal outcome in its own words: "Poorly crafted proposals that are deemed to be 'noncompetitive' will be denied without external review." Proposals over 4,000 words "will not be considered." The scope test for UNI is fundamental-not-applied research in the petroleum field, plus distinctness from the PI's graduate/postdoctoral work.
2. **External peer review** — from your slate of ≥6 suggested reviewers. Sits inside the ~7-month gap; PRF does not publish how long it takes.
3. **PRF Science Panel** — you choose your own panel in the application. The Annual Report indexes UNI panels as UNI1–UNI10.
4. **ACS PRF Committee meeting — the funding decision. May 2027** for this deadline (~7 months after). The Committee "makes relative rankings of proposals and recommendations for funding."
5. **ACS Board of Directors approval, ~1 month later** (a May meeting produced a June 2026 C&EN item, "ACS Board approves 113 new PRF projects"; the spring 2026 round totalled $12,295,000). MEDIUM CONFIDENCE and VIA SEARCH INDEX ONLY — cen.acs.org returns HTTP 406 to both plain fetch and a rendering browser, so I could not read the article text.
6. **Notification to applicants — NOT FOUND.** PRF publishes no notification date or turnaround. Logically bounded between the May meeting and the 1 July start, but I could not source it. Listed in unresolved.
7. **Earliest start, fixed by rule and not negotiable upward:** 1 July after a May meeting; 1 January after an October meeting.

**Budget-year mechanics that constrain the start date you request** (UNI page, verbatim): "The normal ACS PRF budget year extends from September 1 to August 31." Every budget period must END on 31 August and run at least 12 months, and a start date must be the first day of a month — so choosing an early start simply makes Year 1 longer than 12 months rather than finishing sooner.
