SPECIAL FELLOW BUDGET INTERNALS. The $75,000/yr award and $70,000/yr minimum to the awardee come from the CDP web page and the existing corpus row. The indirect-cost cap (5%, up to $3,500/yr for Fellow), the prohibition on lab/equipment/travel/tuition spending, and the no-carry-forward rule are quoted from the Fellow document and are presumed but NOT verified for Special Fellow.

THE 'OTHER GRANTS/AWARDS' DOLLAR THRESHOLD FOR SPECIAL FELLOW. The rule is a value comparison against the award itself; the Fellow document words it 'compared to the Fellow Award'. The Special Fellow threshold is presumably the Special Fellow award value, but the exact wording is unverified.

THE INDEPENDENCE / STATUS-CHANGE RULE FOR SPECIAL FELLOW. The Fellow document bars awardees from holding the award as independent faculty within the first year of funding. The Special Fellow award is explicitly intended to make the awardee 'competitive for an independent position by the end of the award', so this rule is very likely written differently. Do not transfer the Fellow wording.
THE CDP PEER-REVIEW PANEL MONTH. Not published in the 2026-2027 guidelines (TRP publishes March 2027; CDP does not). The stale website FAQ implies January. Unconfirmed.

SPONSOR AND PER-LAB CAPS ARE INCONSISTENTLY STATED. The Fellow PDF says a Sponsor may sponsor one Fellow and one Special Fellow in their own lab (plus a co-mentoring expansion); the CDP web page says up to two Fellow and two Special Fellow applications per Sponsor with no more than 4 total Fellows and Special Fellows in any lab. The page's cap is pegged to 'July 1 of the upcoming year', a date the current PDF contradicts. Confirm with the mailbox before a lab submits multiple candidates.

WEBSEARCH WAS UNAVAILABLE. This session had exhausted its 200-call web search budget before I began, and web.archive.org is blocked by the harness, so I could not cross-check via a search index or recover the Special Fellow PDF from an archived snapshot. bloodcancerunited.org returns HTTP 403 to a plain fetch; every page here was read through the rendering browser. These are tooling facts and none of them implies anything about the programme's status.

CORPUS GAP SPOTTED IN PASSING, not part of this mechanism: the Blood Cancer United portal landing page lists an 'HCL2030 Initiative' run with the Hairy Cell Leukemia Foundation, with subcategories 'Laboratory to Clinical Research Grants' and 'Collaborative Team Grants'. It does not appear in the briefing's mechanism list and may be missing from the corpus.

result.program_name: Computational Science Graduate Fellowship (DOE CSGF)
result.funder: U.S. Department of Energy — Office of Science (co-funded with NNSA; administered by the Krell Institute)
result.next_deadline:
NEXT CYCLE (2027-2028): application opens "late October 2026". Funder's own words on the application landing page, checked 2026-09-18: "The 2027-2028 application will be available late October 2026; if you would like to be notified by email, click here." The closing date for that cycle is NOT yet published — expect mid-January 2027 by pattern, but no 2027 date is on the site, so do not print one.

LAST CONFIRMED DATED DEADLINE (2026-2027 cycle, now closed), verified two independent ways: (a) FAQ — "The application deadline is Thursday, January 15, 2026."; (b) the official recruitment poster PDF — "Applications Due 1.15.2026".

ROLLING SUPPORTING-DOCUMENT DEADLINES for that same cycle, which sit AFTER the application deadline and are the thing applicants miss: "Krell Institute will continue to accept reference letters through January 22, 2026 and transcripts until January 31, 2026."

RECURRING PATTERN, in the funder's own words: the open period is "October-through-January"; "The annual DOE CSGF application process typically begins each fall and concludes the following spring when formal acceptance is required of those selected." So the stable shape is: opens late October → application due mid-January → letters +1 week → transcripts +~2 weeks → notification late April → fellowship starts 1 September.

DRIFT NOTE: as of 2026-09-18 the FAQ page still displayed the closed 2026-27 cycle's dates (fall 2026 / Jan 15, 2026 / Sept 1, 2026) while the application page had already rolled to announce the 2027-28 opening. Re-check the FAQ after late October 2026 — it is the page that carries the dated deadline, and it updates when the application opens.
result.deadline_pattern: Annual, single round. Opens late October; full application due mid-January (Jan 15, 2026 for the 2026-27 cycle); reference letters accepted ~1 week past the deadline (Jan 22, 2026); official transcripts ~2 weeks past (Jan 31, 2026); notification by late April; fellowship begins September 1. No second cycle, no rolling submission, no per-topic target dates — none of the DOE SC Open Call's three-layer deadline machinery applies here.
result.loi_deadline:
Not applicable — there is no letter of intent, pre-application or white paper for CSGF. This is a major deviation from the DOE SC norm: the SC Open Call's PAMS pre-application / encourage-discourage gate does not exist for this fellowship. It is a single-stage direct application by the student.

The nearest analogue to a staged timeline runs in the opposite direction: instead of a gate BEFORE the deadline, CSGF grants a grace window AFTER it for third-party documents (letters +1 week, transcripts +2 weeks). The applicant's own "Final Submission" is still hard-dated: "It is the applicant's responsibility to final submit by the stated deadline."

One optional pre-step worth flagging: a "Notify me when the DOE CSGF application opens" email signup at https://www.krellinst.org/doecsgf/reqappl/ — the practical substitute for an LOI, since the open window is only ~11 weeks.
result.review_to_award:
Differs completely from the DOE SC funder-wide norm (no Grants.gov timestamp, no 10 CFR 605.10 six-month clock, no negotiated start, no Contracting Officer, no FedConnect).

Fixed annual arc, quoted from the FAQ for the 2026-27 cycle:
- Submission: Thursday, January 15, 2026.
- Supporting docs close: letters January 22, 2026; transcripts January 31, 2026. Explicit relief if a fall transcript is late — "If the fall term report isn't available until after the January 31, 2026 transcript deadline, we will still accept your application and consider it complete."
- Notification: "For studies beginning in fall 2026, we will notify you by late April 2026." That is roughly 14 weeks from the application deadline.
- Formal acceptance: "concludes the following spring when formal acceptance is required of those selected to comprise the newest class of fellows."
- Earliest start: "For those considering whether to apply for this next class of awards, the fellowship start date will be September 1, 2026." About 7.5 months from the application deadline.

Two conditions clear only between notification and start: the department chair must certify the teaching waiver "ahead of the start of the fellowship period", and a selected fellow plus their PhD advisor "will be asked to sign and return the POS to Krell" — with a NEW program of study required if the fellow enrolls at a different university than the one used in the application.

Renewal is annual, not automatic: "Fellows must renew their appointment each year by submitting an online application" demonstrating academic progress, progress through the approved POS coursework, and DOE-relevant research. Renewable up to four years.

Review criteria/process: no published panel structure, scoring rubric, reviewer counts or feedback mechanism was found on the funder's pages. CSGF does NOT release reviewer comments — there is no PAMS "View Reviews" equivalent. Unsuccessful applicants get nothing back, and materials are destroyed: "All applications from unfunded students are destroyed after the selection and award acceptance period."
result.submission_requirements:
PORTAL — the single biggest deviation. CSGF does NOT use Grants.gov or PAMS. Applications go through the Krell Institute's own secure online system at https://www.krellinst.org/csgf/how-apply/apply-now. Consequently NONE of the DOE SC long-lead registrations apply: no SAM.gov, no UEI, no EIN, no Grants.gov AOR, no PAMS account, no FedConnect, no FSRS, no institutional/AOR sign-off at submission. The student applies as an individual. The DOE SC format baseline (single assembled machine-readable PDF, 15-20 page narratives, ≤50-character filenames, SF-424) is likewise irrelevant.

PICK A TRACK — applicants apply to ONE of two: Science & Engineering, or Mathematics/Computer Science. "Whereas individuals interested in the fellowship's Science & Engineering Track must have a specific science or engineering application for their research, Math/CS Track candidates are expected to focus on fundamental research into enabling technologies that are broadly relevant to science and engineering applications of interest to the DOE." Math/CS requires a doctorate in applied mathematics, statistics, computer science, computer engineering or computational science "in one of these departments or their academic equivalent," with a departmental exception for quantum-information-systems algorithm/software researchers enrolled in a science or engineering field. QIS students are warned to choose deliberately: design/control-of-QIS research belongs in Science & Engineering; algorithms/software for QIS belongs in Math/CS.

STRUCTURE — "Both are composed of 16 individual sections which can be completed in any order and over multiple visits to the secure online portal," with a built-in checklist and reference/transcript status tracking. Work is saved between sessions; the application locks at "Final Submission" within the "Review for Final Submission" section, after which you can still chase references and check status.

PROGRAM OF STUDY (POS) — the signature requirement and the one with no analogue anywhere else in DOE SC. Prepared "with your graduate advisor's assistance." It must give "a solid background in (1) a scientific or engineering discipline, (2) mathematics and statistics and (3) computer science and computer engineering," plus "A course that introduces the concept of high-performance computing ... may be taken from any department with a preference given to those in computer science." Volume: "Two courses (semester system) or three courses (quarter system) are required for each POS discipline area, with the exception of just one course required within the high-performance computing section." Your major field sits in one of the three areas and "they also must attain high marks in the other two to demonstrate that their POS has sufficient breadth." Math/CS applicants get no relief — the science/engineering coursework is still required, and "POS courses from computer science or computer engineering departments must be listed under Computer Science and Computer Engineering and cannot be listed as Science & Engineering Applications." Applicants without a graduate advisor yet: "Please assemble a POS for your top-choice institution"; if no graduate advisor is available, "please have your current undergraduate advisor review your proposed POS." Up to half the listed courses may be taken in the year immediately preceding the fellowship.

THREE LETTERS OF REFERENCE — "list three individuals who can speak to your character, qualifications and accomplishments in the context of the DOE CSGF application." The system emails each a token-based upload link. Chasing them is on you: "It is your responsibility to ensure timely submission and we encourage you to follow up with each contact directly once you have initiated notification via the online system." Due one week after the application (Jan 22, 2026 for that cycle).

OFFICIAL TRANSCRIPTS — from every institution listed, "including your current fall transcript if applicable." Must come from the registrar: "Official transcripts must be sent directly from the university, either by mail or through an e-transcript system. The latter is preferred when the option exists. Transcripts sent by an applicant will not be accepted regardless of delivery method."

POST-SUBMISSION — confirmation email within 24 hours ("If you do not receive an email within 24 hours please contact us"). Lawful permanent residents are then asked for Green Card images: "Krell staff will contact you to request a copy of the front and back of your Green Card via secure submission."

NOT FOUND on any funder page read: GRE requirement, essay word/page limits, or a research-proposal page limit. The detailed component specs live inside the authenticated application system, whose "comprehensive FAQ within the online system" is "accessible during the October-through-January open period" only.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
The decisive gate is CAREER STAGE, not prior awards — but there is one hard concurrent-funding rule.

WHAT DISQUALIFIES:
1. Concurrent federal fellowship. FAQ, verbatim: "I have another fellowship. Does this make me ineligible for the DOE CSGF?" — "You can apply, but you may have to give up your current fellowship if you receive a DOE CSGF offer. The DOE CSGF cannot be accepted concurrently with another federal fellowship." Read carefully: holding an NSF GRFP, NDSEG, SMART or similar does NOT bar you from APPLYING; it forces a choice at the offer stage. Apply to both, decide in April.
2. Being too far along. "Second-year or beyond graduate students" are ineligible, and the measured test is: "At time of application, you cannot have completed more than one year of full-time graduate work toward your Ph.D." Eligibility is "Measured at the time of application."
3. Concurrent professional doctorate — "Students pursuing a concurrent professional doctoral degree, (e.g., dual enrollment as a(n) M.D./Ph.D., J.D./Ph.D., D.V.M./Ph.D., etc.)".
4. Not a US citizen or lawful permanent resident. "I'm a foreign student studying in the U.S. under a student (F1) visa. Am I eligible?" — "No."
5. A master's student who intends to stay put: a current master's student "MUST enroll at a different institution for Ph.D. studies to begin the fall term coincident with the start of DOE CSGF funding."

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY — the half applicants usually cannot find:
1. Non-service awards are fine, and may be held concurrently: "Fellows may accept scholarships, prizes and other payments (including veteran's benefits) that do not require a service." The operative distinction is service obligation, not source.
2. Teaching assistantships are permitted with prior approval, not banned: "the Krell Institute must approve in advance additional graduate responsibilities, such as a teaching assistantship." Separately, "The fellow's department must waive any teaching requirements beyond one term," and where a department mandates teaching, "Your department must certify that no more than one term of teaching, grading or other departmental support activity is required of you, or that any requirements beyond one term will be waived" — certified by the department chairperson before the fellowship starts. So a departmental teaching requirement does not disqualify you; it triggers a certification.
3. Holding a master's degree does not disqualify: "Having a master's degree does not affect your application to the fellowship as long as you plan to attend a different university for your doctoral studies." A master's in a DIFFERENT field is likewise fine.
4. Time out of school preserves eligibility: "You are eligible as long as you will start a Ph.D. program by the time the fellowship would begin." And for the master's-then-industry path: "Yes, you are eligible as long as it has been at least two years since you earned your master's degree."
5. Graduate work that is not PhD work does not necessarily burn the clock — the test is full-time graduate work "toward your Ph.D.," and the FAQ invites edge cases to contact the program.
6. Field ambiguity is not a bar: "If you feel your area of study doesn't fit these categories but does emphasize high-performance computing, we encourage you to apply and convince reviewers that your work can be properly represented as computational science."
7. Not yet admitted / not yet chosen a university is fine — apply with a top-choice POS and resubmit a POS later if you enroll elsewhere.

NOT FOUND: any lifetime cap on attempts, any stated waiting period, any re-application limit, or any bar on prior DOE support. The ECRP-style three-competition lifetime cap does NOT apply to CSGF.
result.resubmission_note:
No published resubmission policy, and none of the DOE SC resubmission machinery applies — there is no SF-424 Field 8, no New/Renewal/Revision choice, no "substantially revised in light of merit reviewer comments" rule, and no PAMS withdrawal mechanism.

Practical reality for a re-applicant: because the eligibility window is measured at time of application and closes once you have completed more than one year of full-time graduate work toward the PhD, most applicants get at most TWO shots — typically as a senior undergraduate and again as a first-year graduate student. Re-application is not prohibited anywhere on the funder's pages, but the stage gate, not a resubmission rule, is what limits attempts.

Anyone re-applying does so blind: CSGF releases no reviewer feedback, and "All applications from unfunded students are destroyed after the selection and award acceptance period." There is no summary statement to revise against, so a second attempt should be rebuilt from the guidance rather than patched.

Within a single cycle, the application is editable up to "Final Submission," after which no further changes can be made — though references and transcripts continue to flow in and status remains viewable.
result.program_officer_contact:
NO named DOE program manager, and no program-officer culture — the sharpest contrast with DOE SC grants, where contacting the named subprogram contact is "strongly encouraged" or outright mandatory. CSGF has been "managed by the Krell Institute since 1997"; DOE funds it, Krell runs it. Krell does not publish individual staff names, emails or topic assignments on the CSGF pages, and no mailto address appears anywhere on the program site (homepage, how-to-apply, apply-now, contact, FAQ, eligibility all checked). There is no pre-submission scientific conversation to have, no fit conversation that shapes a topic, and no encourage/discourage decision.

CONTACT ROUTE (the only published channels):
- Web contact form: https://www.krellinst.org/csgf/contact — "Please complete the form below to submit your request or inquiry to the Krell Institute. Your message will be directed to the appropriate staff member for a timely response."
- Phone: (515) 956-3696
- Mail: Krell Institute, 1609 Golden Aspen Drive, Suite 101, Ames, Iowa 50010

IS CONTACT EXPECTED? Not in general — but it IS explicitly invited in three specific situations, and these are the questions worth asking:
1. Track choice, especially QIS. Math/CS track page: "Please contact Krell Institute staff with related questions prior to submitting an application." This is the one genuine pre-submission judgement call in the whole application.
2. Eligibility edge cases — the FAQ repeatedly routes to "contact us with specific questions," specifically for the second-year question and the "in graduate school a few years but haven't started my PhD" case.
3. Changing university preferences after submission: "Please contact the DOE CSGF to provide an update to university selections after your application has been submitted."
Plus operational: no confirmation email within 24 hours of submitting.

THE REAL GUIDANCE CHANNEL, and it is time-boxed: the substantive help lives inside the application system, not on the public site. "one should refer to the comprehensive FAQ within the online system — accessible during the October-through-January open period — for a more extensive review of topics related to the DOE CSGF application and its various components. Most individual areas of the application also link to section-relevant guidance." Actionable consequence: open an application account early in the window purely to read the internal FAQ and per-section guidance, even if you are nowhere near ready to write.

WHO TO TALK TO INSTEAD, since there is no program officer: your prospective PhD advisor (required anyway — they co-build the POS and must sign it if you win), your department chair (must certify the teaching waiver), and current or former CSGF fellows, who are individually listed with university and field at https://www.krellinst.org/csgf/fellows/list/by-program-year and by university and practicum location. The alumni directory is likewise browsable by cohort year and current location — a practical way to find someone at your own institution or target lab.
result.examples_or_samples:
No funded application texts and no annotated sample essays are published, and the usual DOE routes do NOT work here — the PAMS Public Award Search, the ECRP abstract PDFs and the SC topical award lists all cover SC grants and cooperative agreements, not this Krell-administered fellowship. Nothing on CSGF appears there. Note also that unfunded applications are destroyed after each cycle, so there is no archive to FOIA.

What DOES exist, in order of usefulness to an applicant:

1. A WORKED SAMPLE PROGRAM OF STUDY — by far the highest-value artifact, since the POS is the requirement with no analogue elsewhere and the one most likely to be built wrong. An actual filled-in "Sample DOE CSGF Program of Study - Semester System" table sits on https://www.krellinst.org/csgf/about-doe-csgf/program-study, showing course numbers, titles, credit hours and terms grouped under the four required headings: Science and Engineering Applications (Chem 8130 Reactions in Molecular Organic Chemistry, 3S; Chem 8960 Molecular Spectroscopy, 3S), Mathematics and Statistics (Math 8170 Functional Analysis; Math 8500 Advanced Numerical Analysis), High-Performance Computing (CS 6140 Applications of Parallel Computers), and Computer Science and Computer Engineering (CS 5505 Data Visualization, 4S; CS 6030 Advanced Algorithms). Map your own institution's catalogue onto this shape before writing anything else.

2. FUNDED FELLOWS' RESEARCH ABSTRACTS — the Annual Program Review Fellows' Poster Session & Abstracts page, https://www.krellinst.org/csgf/conf/2026/fellows-poster-session-abstracts, plus the Program Review presentations at /csgf/conf/2026/pres and past reviews at /csgf/conf/past-program-reviews. This is the closest thing to reading what successful CSGF research looks like in the fellows' own words.

3. THE FELLOWS AND ALUMNI DIRECTORIES — https://www.krellinst.org/csgf/fellows/list/by-program-year (also by university and by practicum location), and alumni by cohort year, university, practicum location and current location. Use these to identify who at your university or target lab has won, then ask them directly; with no reviewer feedback and no program officer, a current fellow is the best available source of tacit knowledge.

4. DEIXIS, THE DOE CSGF ANNUAL — https://www.krellinst.org/csgf/outreach/deixis-magazine — "highlights the diverse research and professional experiences of program fellows and alumni," downloadable by year ("click on an individual image to download that year's file"), print copies on request. Long-form profiles of what fellows actually do, including practicum work.

5. PRACTICUM MATERIAL — https://www.krellinst.org/csgf/doe-lab-practicum/practicum-experiences (browsable by location) plus per-lab pages for all ~21 sites (Argonne, Berkeley, Livermore, Los Alamos, Oak Ridge, Sandia, SLAC, PPPL and others). Since the 12-week DOE lab practicum is mandatory, showing awareness of a specific lab's work is a cheap credibility win.

6. RECRUITMENT POSTER PDF — https://www.krellinst.org/doecsgf/images/website/CSGF2026-27_RecruitmentPoster.pdf — one page with benefits and the dated deadline; useful for circulating to a group.

7. SCIENCE IN PARALLEL PODCAST — https://www.krellinst.org/csgf/outreach/science-in-parallel — interviews with fellows and computational scientists.

8. Scale context for calibrating expectations: the 36th class (announced 17 June 2026) comprised "Twenty-nine new Ph.D. students." An applicant-pool figure or acceptance rate is not published.

The programme page reads "The application process for 2027 Cottrell Scholar Awards is closed" and the RCSA Awards Calendar still shows "Apply by July 1, 2026". What carries the date is the funder's own year-free standing wording in the Proposals FAQ: "The July 1 deadline is firm; late proposals cannot be accepted." — RCSA states the rule as a fixed calendar date, not as a per-cycle announcement. The cycle that just closed was 1 July 2026, confirmed verbatim in RCSA's own instructions PDF: "Deadline: Wednesday, July 1, 2026 at 11:00 PM MST". Expect the submission portal to open early April 2027 (funder: "The online submission portal is expected to open in early April 2026" for the closed cycle) and decisions by roughly 15 February 2028. TIME-ZONE TRAP (arithmetic on the funder's stated MST, RCSA being in Tucson AZ which stays on MST year-round): 11 PM MST on 1 July = 11 PM Pacific on 1 July, but 2:00 AM Eastern on 2 July. WHO IT IS FOR IN THAT CYCLE: the funder's rule is "You may apply in the third academic year of your first tenure-track position", and for the 1 July 2026 cycle that meant a first tenure-track start "anytime during calendar year 2023". Applying the same three-year offset, the 1 July 2027 cycle is the year for people who started their first tenure-track position in calendar year 2024 — derived from the stated rule, not separately posted.
result.deadline_pattern: Annual, single fixed date, no rolling or multi-round structure. Proposals due 1 July at 11:00 PM MST; portal opens ~early April (about 3 months of open window); decisions announced by ~15 February of the following calendar year. NAMING CONVENTION THAT CONFUSES PEOPLE: RCSA names a cohort for the year it is announced, one year ahead of the year you submit. Proposals due 1 July 2026 = the "2027 Cottrell Scholar Awards" (RCSA's instructions PDF is titled "Submission of Cottrell Scholar 2027 Proposals" and carries the July 2026 deadline). So a page saying "2027 applications are closed" in late 2026 means the July 2026 deadline has passed — it does not mean a 2027 cycle has been cancelled. Related fixed dates on the same calendar, useful for planning: the Cottrell Scholar Conference runs 8-10 July 2026 and 7-9 July 2027 (awardees must attend at least two during the award).
result.loi_deadline: No letter of intent or pre-proposal stage exists. But three real pre-stages sit in front of the 1 July date and each can cost you the cycle if missed: (1) INSTITUTIONAL AOR ROUTING — mandatory and gating. Funder: "Proposals cannot be submitted to RCSA without institutional approval by the AOR." You enter your Authorized Organizational Representative's name and email in the portal, they get a link, review, approve, and only then does it reach RCSA. RCSA's own instructions warn: "Even though the deadline is July 1, 2026 at 11:00 pm MST, you must route your application through your institution's Office of Sponsored Projects for the Authorized Organizational Representative's approval. Don't forget to check with them on their deadlines for processing your application." Your effective personal deadline is your sponsored-projects office's internal one, typically 3-10 working days earlier. (2) ELIGIBILITY-EXTENSION REQUEST — if your tenure clock stopped (parental leave, medical, other approved delay) you must file RCSA's extension request form before applying off-cohort: https://app.smartsheet.com/b/form/789c3fb4270e4e808c1cf5332b315746. (3) PORTAL REGISTRATION AND ORCID SYNC in PRISM (https://prism.omni.rescorp.org) — the application form only unfolds after you pass an in-portal eligibility questionnaire ("Answer the eligibility questions. If you are eligible, the remaining pages of the application will appear."), and your profile must carry ORCID, degrees, employment history and a title/prefix that cannot be added later from inside the form. RCSA moved to this new system around October 2025, so a pre-2025 RCSA login will not work — register fresh or reset the password.
result.review_to_award: About 7.5 months from deadline to notification: submit 1 July, "Award decisions for the 2027 cohort will be announced by February 15, 2027." Earliest project start date: NOT FOUND — RCSA does not publish a stated start date or notice-to-start interval for this mechanism. THE STRUCTURAL FACT WORTH MORE THAN THE TIMELINE: review is two-stage and the EDUCATION plan is the gate, not the research plan. Funder: "Applications that conform to guidelines are screened by RCSA Program Directors to assess the quality of the educational plan. Submissions with excellent educational plans then advance to review by external research experts and the members of the Cottrell Scholar Selection Committee." A superb research plan attached to a weak educational plan is screened out before any external scientist reads the science. Final step: "Award recommendations are made by the Cottrell Scholar Selection Committee and approved by the RCSA Board of Directors." External reviewers are drawn partly from your own suggested list but not only from it. Reviewer comments are generally not released: "Not typically. Reviewer comments are confidential. At the program directors' discretion, some comments may be provided." Post-award admin (from RCSA's Managing Your Grant page): annual report due 30 days after each anniversary date, final report 60 days after grant end; no-cost extensions (6 or 12 months) must be requested at least 60 days before the termination date; unspent amounts under $300 need not be refunded.
result.submission_requirements: Three-year proposal. Components and limits, all funder-stated, with the deviations called out. NO BUDGET AT ALL — the biggest deviation from every federal norm: "No budget justification or budget pages are required." Nine required elements: title + five keywords + abstract stating how you will become an outstanding teacher-scholar; research plan; educational plan; academic citizenship statement; letter of support from department head, Dean or Provost; a two-page reference list COMBINED across research and education; a list of 10 suggested reviewers; publications from the last five years (explicitly "no abstracts, talks, or conference proceedings"); AOR approval and final submission. PAGE LIMITS: research plan 4 pages (statement of the problem / significance / plan of procedure). Educational plan is three separately-headed sections — problem+significance+plan of procedure 3 pages, assessment plan 1 page, courses taught 1 page — "combined into one PDF of no more than five pages". Academic citizenship statement 1 page. Letter of support "limited to two pages". Collaboration letters 1 page each, NSF format. FORMATTING IS AN ELIGIBILITY SCREEN, not a style note: "Arial 11 point or greater is required for a proposal to be eligible for review", with 0.5" margins. REVIEWER LIST — the most unusual requirement: "Provide the complete names, titles, complete addresses, and email addresses of at least 10 potential reviewers. At least eight reviewers should be 'outsiders,' along with a minimum of two 'insiders.'" An outsider is someone with whom you have had no substantive personal or professional contact; you must label each one and note your relationship ("Ph.D. mentor", "never met", "met once at a meeting"); RCSA advises listing at least five outside reviewers from US or Canadian institutions and warns that omitting scientists you cite "may signal an incomplete understanding of the field". You may email a program director privately to name people the proposal should NOT go to. LETTERS: the chair/dean/provost letter must endorse the EDUCATIONAL proposal specifically and say why you are the right person to lead it — not a generic research endorsement. Research collaboration letters are required whenever the work relies on skills or equipment outside your lab, and "must not include commentary on the proposal or applicant"; education collaboration letters only when the collaborator is at another institution. SCOPE RULES: the research must advance fundamental knowledge in chemistry, physics or astronomy; applied work qualifies only if it clearly advances fundamental knowledge; and a proposal whose research component is itself science-education research is not accepted. Undergraduate research mentoring should not be the centre of the education plan ("Because all faculty are expected to mentor undergraduates in their labs, undergraduate research activities should not be the central component of your educational proposal"). ALLOWABLE COSTS: most direct costs — equipment, supplies, student and postdoc salaries, graduate tuition and fees, conference travel. NOT allowable: indirect costs, academic-year faculty salaries, routine administrative expenses, books/journals, visa costs, construction/renovation; summer salary only for faculty in non-doctoral departments. Applying also commits you to maintaining "a safe, harassment-free research environment". Awardees must attend at least two Cottrell Scholar Conferences during the award (travel charged to the award; hotel and meals covered by RCSA).
result.prior_funding_conflicts: BOTH HALVES, and for this mechanism the surprise is that prior FUNDING is not the problem — prior EMPLOYMENT is. WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (explicit, and unusually generous): holding other grants is not a conflict and is treated as a positive. Funder, verbatim: "Existing research funding does not negatively influence evaluation of Cottrell Scholar applicants, rather existing funding and prior independent publications are viewed as positive indications of the potential of the applicant and the proposed research plan." No exclusion is stated anywhere against NSF CAREER, NIH, DOE Early Career, Packard, Sloan, Beckman or any concurrent award — hold them and apply. The only funding-side constraint is at the level of specific aims, not awards: "the research application could be thematically connected to other proposals or ongoing projects, but it must have specific aims distinct from applications submitted to other foundations or funding agencies", and proposed work "should highlight new innovative directions distinct from currently funded or pending projects". You may propose either a project already underway or a brand-new one: "We ask you for your 'best' project or research idea(s)." Also preserving: tenure-clock stops. Parental leave, medical circumstances and other approved delays earn an eligibility extension that shifts you to the next cycle rather than removing you — funder's worked examples: "Because your tenure clock stopped, you are eligible to apply in 2027" and "Yes, parental leave qualifies for an eligibility extension." And there are no institutional caps: "There are no institutional limits. Multiple eligible faculty may apply, and multiple awards may be made within the same department." WHAT MAKES YOU INELIGIBLE (all employment- or attempt-based): (1) Any earlier tenure-track appointment anywhere — "No. Holding any prior tenure-track position makes you ineligible." This is absolute and catches people who moved institutions; a second tenure-track job does not reset the clock. (2) Being outside the designated cohort year — you must be in the third academic year of your first tenure-track position (calendar-2023 starts for the July 2026 cycle), absent an approved extension. (3) ONE LIFETIME ATTEMPT — "No. You may only apply once for a Cottrell Scholar Award." (4) Primary appointment outside chemistry, physics or astronomy (biochemistry/biophysics count), or in a school of medicine or engineering without a joint or courtesy appointment in an eligible department; the department must grant bachelor's or graduate degrees in the discipline; US and Canadian institutions only. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: because you get exactly one shot in exactly one year, the decision is not "am I eligible" but "is this the year my education plan is ready" — and you cannot defer it by choice, only by an approved clock stop.
result.resubmission_note: There is no resubmission. Funder, verbatim: "No. You may only apply once for a Cottrell Scholar Award." A declined application cannot be revised and resubmitted in a later cycle, and there is no second eligibility window — the one eligible year is the third academic year of the first tenure-track appointment. Reviewer feedback to improve a future attempt is generally unavailable ("Reviewer comments are confidential. At the program directors' discretion, some comments may be provided"). The only thing that moves the attempt is an approved tenure-clock extension, which shifts the single attempt to the following cycle rather than granting an extra one. Consolation route after the award, not after a decline: Cottrell Scholars become eligible for follow-on "Cottrell Plus" awards (SEED, STAR, IMPACT, FRED, Regional Meeting Awards), but only if they attend two Cottrell Scholar Conferences during the award period.
result.program_officer_contact: Named, single, and pre-submission contact is explicitly invited. Silvia Ronco, Senior Program Director — sronco@rescorp.org — is the programme's named Program Director on both the award page and the Cottrell Scholars landing page. RCSA names two situations where you are told to contact her BEFORE applying: (1) appointment fit — "If your primary appointment is outside our core disciplines, contact Senior Program Director Silvia Ronco to discuss your situation and confirm your eligibility"; (2) research fit — "If unclear whether a particular research area fits programmatic guidelines, contact Senior Program Director Silvia Ronco." Also "Please consult with a program director on eligibility issues", and you may email a program director to flag reviewers who should not receive your proposal. General programme mailbox: awards@rescorp.org (RCSA-wide: contactus@rescorp.org). STRUCTURED PRE-SUBMISSION SUPPORT: RCSA runs virtual Cottrell Scholar Office Hours for applicants each spring — in 2026, two sessions on Thursday 14 May (9-10 a.m. Pacific) and Friday 15 May (11 a.m.-noon Pacific), registration closing 6 May, with a short presentation on the programme, the selection process and "tips for effective proposal preparation" followed by live Q&A with Ronco. Run in flipped-classroom format with a required prereading deck (link in examples field). Expect the equivalent in May 2027, roughly six to seven weeks before the deadline; watch https://rescorp.org/news/cottrell-scholar-awards/ for the announcement. Postal: Research Corporation for Science Advancement, 4703 E. Camp Lowell Drive, Suite 201, Tucson AZ 85712.
result.examples_or_samples: Unusually good for a private foundation — RCSA publishes actual excerpts of funded applications. (1) FIVE COMPLETE SUCCESSFUL EDUCATIONAL PROPOSALS, posted as PDFs on the award page under "Examples of Educational Proposals", each on RCSA letterhead headed "Cottrell Scholar Award Application / EDUCATIONAL PROPOSAL" (verified by opening them): Jeanine Amacher, Chemistry, Western Washington University — https://rescorp.org/wp-content/uploads/CS2021Amacher.pdf ; Rachel Bezanson, Astronomy, University of Pittsburgh — https://rescorp.org/wp-content/uploads/CS2021Bezanson.pdf ; Thomas Gianetti, Chemistry, University of Arizona — https://rescorp.org/wp-content/uploads/CS2021Gianetti.pdf ; Christopher Hendon, Chemistry, University of Oregon — https://rescorp.org/wp-content/uploads/CS2021Hendon.pdf ; Alexandra Velian, Chemistry, University of Washington — https://rescorp.org/wp-content/uploads/CS_2021_Velian.pdf . Reading a cohort page is the fastest way to calibrate scope and the research/education balance. (3) RCSA'S OWN APPLICANT PREREADING DECK, "Cottrell Scholar Awards" — the flipped-classroom prereading for office hours, covering the programme, goals, selection process and proposal-preparation tips: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1PnNCOrp4qgns1J9YUtmuoMDcJ8P4Cb4u/edit (publicly reachable). (4) PORTAL WALKTHROUGH with screenshots, step by step through PRISM: https://rescorp.org/wp-content/uploads/Submitting-Cottrell-Scholar-2027-Proposals.pdf . NSF 26-503 publishes NO review timeline ("Information on NSF's proposal processing and review procedures is available on the Overview of the NSF Proposal and Award Process page"). So the numbers below are MEASURED from NSF's own award records via the NSF Award Search API (fundProgramName=SFS), not funder-published policy — treat as observed practice.

MEASURED, FY2026 competition (target date 3 April 2026), 44 awards:
• Award dates cluster **27 July – 13 August 2026**; 13 of the 14 Scholarship Track awards are all dated **27 July 2026**.
• Start dates: 1 Aug 2026 (20 awards), 1 Sep 2026 (16), 15 Aug 2026 (5), 1 Oct 2026 (1), 1 Jul 2026 (2).
• **Target date → award ≈ 16 weeks (~3.8 months). Target date → money ≈ 4–6 months.**
• Examples: Vanderbilt $2,449,463 (awarded 27 Jul 2026, start 1 Aug 2026); Arizona State $1,728,720 (same); Univ. of Rhode Island $1,407,449 (awarded 27 Jul, start 1 Sep); George Mason $500,000 Innovation (awarded 7 Aug, start 1 Sep). One outlier ran much faster: Old Dominion Univ. Research Foundation $2,499,867, awarded 15 May 2026, start 1 Jul 2026 — ~6 weeks.

This is FASTER than the NSF-wide norm you supplied ("up to six months" to notification, 6–9 months to money). An applicant planning a cohort start can realistically assume an August/September start in the same calendar year as an April target date.

DEVIATION IN THE REVIEW MECHANICS: the solicitation names a broader set than the NSF norm — "Proposals… will be reviewed by Ad hoc Review and/or Panel Review, Internal NSF Review, or Site Visit Review" and, separately, "Panel Reviews and pre-award site visits." **Pre-award site visits are explicitly contemplated for this program**, which most NSF education solicitations do not do; budget calendar time for one. Otherwise standard: "After a proposal passes an initial compliance check, it will be reviewed by an NSF Program Officer. In most cases, three or more external experts will also review it (either as ad hoc reviewers, panelists or both)." Standard NSB merit criteria (Intellectual Merit, Broader Impacts); no solicitation-specific review criteria are added.

Scholarship Track awards must be three years in duration; Innovation Track up to three years.

NOT FOUND: the deadline→award interval for the July-deadline (FY2027) competition. The 21 July 2026 deadline had produced no awards as of 2026-09-18, which is consistent with FY2027 money; I did not find a published statement of when that round decides, and I am not extrapolating from the April-target round because the two feed different fiscal years.
result.submission_requirements:
PORTAL: Research.gov or Grants.gov, per the NSF norm — EXCEPT "All collaborative proposals submitted as separate submissions from multiple organizations must be submitted via Research.gov." Institutional AOR submits; individuals cannot self-submit. Standard long-lead items apply (SAM.gov/UEI ~90 days, NSF ID, Research.gov PI role, SciENcv for biosketch and Current & Pending Support).

PAGE LIMITS: NSF 26-503 states NO page-limit overrides, so PAPPG defaults govern in full — Project Description 15 pages (Results from Prior NSF Support up to 5 pages inside it), Project Summary 1 page in three boxes, Budget Justification 5 pages, SciENcv biosketch (no page limit since 20 May 2024), Mentoring Plan 1 page, DMSP via the Research.gov webform. The solicitation gives no separate allowance for its extra required content, so the five mandated Scholarship Track narrative elements all compete for the same 15 pages — that is the real squeeze on this mechanism.

DEVIATIONS AND ADDITIONS (solicitation's own words: "The following requirements are in addition to the requirements included in PAPPG. Proposals that do not include all required components or are not compliant with other PAPPG requirements may be returned without review."):

1. **Title prefix is mandatory** — "Titles must be short and informative and begin with 'CyberAI SFS:' for the Scholarship Track and with 'CyberAI Innovation:' for the Innovation Track."
2. **Evaluation Plan** — required for both tracks: expected outcomes and corresponding metrics, formative AND summative assessment, and a timeline for assessment and reporting. Critical constraint: **"The evaluator may not serve as PI, co-PI, or Senior Personnel on the project."** Evaluations must be attached to annual and final reports.
3. **Mentoring Plan for Graduate Students** — required, citing PAPPG II.D.2.i(i). Note this is broader than the "postdocs only" norm: PAPPG 24-1 verbatim requires it for "each proposal that requests funding to support postdoctoral scholars or graduate students", "In no more than one page", uploaded under "Mentoring Plan" in supplementary documentation, and "Mentoring activities… will be evaluated under the Broader Impacts review criterion." Since the Scholarship Track funds graduate students by design, this is effectively always required.
4. **Results from Prior NSF Support** — required (PAPPG II.D.2.d).
5. **Supplementary Documentation** — "may include evidence of ABET cybersecurity accreditation, National Center of Academic Excellence (NCAE) designation or an equivalent certificate in cybersecurity education or research."
6. **Scholarship Track Project Summary** must additionally "indicate either AI or Cyber as the focus area and include a description of the corresponding academic program; the research, engagement, and scholarship activities at the proposing institution; and the expected number and degrees of CyberAI SFS scholarship recipients" — inside the standard one page.
7. **Scholarship Track Project Description must contain five named elements**: (a) Evidence of a Strong Program in AI or Cybersecurity; (b) Recruitment and Selection of CyberAI SFS Scholars (recruitment plan, selection criteria, onboarding, student counseling; scholars "must agree to undergo the required background investigation"; "CyberAI SFS Scholarships are awarded based on merit, not financial need"); (c) SFS Scholar Mentoring and Cohort Activities; (d) Internship Requirements and Service Obligation; (e) Institutional Responsibility and Project Management Plan (an eight-item list covering eligibility verification, progress tracking, counseling, OPM coordination, employment monitoring, Forgivable Loan Promissory Notes, repayment determination and collection).
8. **Additional eligibility evidence** — "a proposing institution must provide clearly documented evidence of a strong existing program in AI or cybersecurity", e.g. ABET or NCAE designation, or equivalent evidence in the narrative.
9. **Cost sharing prohibited** — "Inclusion of voluntary committed cost sharing is prohibited." No institutional match needed.
10. **Budget mechanics that trip people up**: Scholarship Track budget duration "must be three years"; max $2,500,000 (Scholarship) / $500,000 (Innovation, at $100,000–$200,000 per year). Stipends ($27,000/yr undergraduate, $37,000/yr graduate), tuition, education-related fees and the $6,000/yr professional allowance **"must be listed as Participant Support Costs in the NSF proposal budget (Line F on the NSF budget form and Field E on the Grants.gov budget)"**. Up to $12,000 per student per year may be requested in other direct-cost categories, and must be justified. "Detailed explanation of the use of the $6,000 professional allowance is not needed." Tuition "should reflect the average tuition that would be applied to a similar student without an SFS scholarship", assessed against the U.S. Dept. of Education College Affordability and Transparency Center; after a negotiated net cost the institution "must exempt SFS scholars from paying any tuition and fees unless such charges are optional or refundable." "Support for an individual student must not exceed three years."
11. **PI eligibility is narrower than NSF's default** — as of submission, every PI/co-PI/senior-key person must hold "a tenured or tenure-track position, or a primary, full-time, paid appointment in a research, administration, or teaching position" at a US-based campus of an eligible organization. "Individuals with primary appointments at for-profit non-academic organizations or at overseas branch campuses of U.S. institutions of higher education are not eligible."
12. **No letters of intent, no preliminary proposal, and the solicitation requires no letters of collaboration or commitment.**

STUDENT-SIDE REQUIREMENTS (the layer that matters for the graduate_predoc/undergraduate audience): there is no NSF application at all. A student applies to a funded campus programme. To be eligible a student must "(1) be a citizen or lawful permanent resident of the United States; (2) demonstrate a commitment to a career in AI or cybersecurity; and (3) be a full-time student in a coherent formal program that focuses on AI or cybersecurity at an awardee institution" with sophomore standing (associate's), junior/senior standing (bachelor's), enrolled in a master's, or enrolled in a research-based doctoral program. Community-college sophomores get one year only, and only where a formal articulation agreement with a four-year institution exists. Students must be able to meet criteria for federal employment and obtain a security clearance if required, must complete qualified summer internships during the scholarship, and must serve in a qualifying government organization for at least the scholarship's length.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
Both halves. The disqualifiers here are institutional and mostly about TIMING, not permanent bars — and the preserving carve-outs are unusually generous.

WHAT BLOCKS YOU
• **The 14-month rule (the big one).** Verbatim: "Institutions with an active CyberAI SFS scholarship project must wait until they are within 14 months of the current award's expected end date before submitting a new proposal." An institution mid-award simply cannot submit a new Scholarship Track proposal. This is a hard date-arithmetic gate, and since the competition is annual, missing the window by a month costs a full year.
• **One Scholarship Track proposal per institution per competition** — "each performing organization is limited to one (1) proposal submitted for the same competition date." Add: "Each institutional office of research may have internal processes used to select proposals for submission to the Scholarship Track" — i.e. there is an internal campus competition before NSF ever sees it, which is the real first deadline for a would-be PI.
• **One Scholarship Track proposal per person per competition** — "an individual must not participate as PI, Co-PI, or Senior Personnel on more than one (1) proposal submitted for the same competition date." Senior Personnel counts, so lending your name to a colleague's proposal spends your slot.
• **Two Innovation Track proposals per person per rolling 12 months** — "an individual must not participate as PI, Co-PI, or Senior Personnel on more than two (2) proposals submitted within any 12-month period."
• **One accomplishment-based renewal, ever** — "An institution can only submit one accomplishment-based renewal proposal."
• **Appointment-based PI bar** — primary appointment at a for-profit non-academic organization, or at an overseas branch campus of a US institution, makes you ineligible regardless of funding history.
• **Students**: "Support for an individual student must not exceed three years." Citizenship/LPR is absolute. A scholar who fails the academic or service requirement must repay the U.S. Treasury or have the award converted to a prorated student loan.

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY
• **The Innovation Track has no organizational limit at all** — "There is no restriction for the Innovation Track." So an institution frozen out of the Scholarship Track by the 14-month rule can still submit Innovation Track proposals, and as many as it likes. For an early-career PI at an incumbent SFS campus, this is the open door: the Innovation Track (max $500,000, $100K–$200K/yr, up to 3 years) is also open to two-year colleges and community colleges as lead applicants in their own right, and to non-profit non-academic organizations (museums, observatories, research laboratories, professional societies) — none of which can lead a Scholarship Track proposal.
• **The 14-month rule is a timing bar, not a permanent one.** An active award does not disqualify forever — only until you are inside 14 months of its expected end date. Renewal is the expected path, not an exception.
• **Prior SFS funding is not a competitive penalty — the pools are separated.** Verbatim: "NSF will consider proposals from institutions that have not previously participated in the CyberAI SFS Program separately from proposals from renewing institutions." A first-time institution is not competing head-to-head with twenty-year incumbents, and an incumbent is not penalised for incumbency. Institutions that previously supported scholars "will normally submit a traditional renewal."
• **Community colleges keep a route into the Scholarship Track** as sub-awardees of a partnering four-year institution.
• **No cost sharing** — "Inclusion of voluntary committed cost sharing is prohibited," so lack of institutional matching funds is never a bar.
• **Students: taking SFS does not foreclose a PhD.** 45 CFR 620.4(a)(1) permits deferral of the Commitment Phase for "Enrollment in a program of study or engagement in approved professional activity that would contribute to further professional development and/or cybersecurity workforce readiness" — also for FMLA-qualifying conditions, military call-up, and "other exceptional circumstances". Apply in writing through the SFS program office before the Commitment Phase expires.
• **Students: an academic career satisfies the service obligation.** Qualifying service includes work "as an educator in the field of cybersecurity at a qualified institution of higher education" (45 CFR 620.2), alongside federal executive agencies, Congress, interstate agencies, state/local/Tribal government, and government-affiliated non-profits considered critical infrastructure. A PhD student worried that SFS forces them out of academia should know this.
• **Service timing is generous**: the Commitment Phase begins when the Scholarship Phase ends; the recipient "must begin such employment within 18 months and it must be completed… within 5 years from the date that the Commitment Phase begins."

NOT FOUND (flagged rather than guessed): whether a student may hold an SFS scholarship concurrently with another federal scholarship or fellowship (DoD SMART, NSF GRFP, etc.). NSF 26-503 is silent and 45 CFR 620 is silent. The campus programme decides; ask the campus PI.

result.resubmission_note:
NSF has no resubmission object at all (no A1, no cap, no window, no Introduction to Resubmission), and NSF 26-503 adds no resubmission section. The NSF-wide PAPPG rules govern: "A declined proposal may be resubmitted, but only after it has undergone substantial revision"; "The Foundation will treat the revised proposal as a new proposal"; "A resubmitted proposal that has not clearly taken into account the major comments or concerns resulting from the prior NSF review may be returned without review."

What that means HERE specifically:
• **The per-competition limits are the real cap.** A declined Scholarship Track institution cannot try again until the next annual competition date (third Tuesday in July), because only one proposal per organization per competition date is allowed. So a decline costs a full year. The Innovation Track is far more forgiving: no organizational limit, and an individual may be on two proposals per rolling 12 months, so a declined Innovation proposal can be reworked and resubmitted at the next April target date — or, because it is a target and not a deadline, submitted off-cycle and rolled into the next round.
• **There is no rebuttal space.** Because NSF treats the resubmission as a new proposal, work the panel's concerns into the Project Description narrative itself — and note the 15 pages are already crowded here by the five mandated Scholarship Track elements.
• **Talk to the programme first.** sfs@nsf.gov / CyberAI@nsf.gov; NSF explicitly sanctions the post-declination conversation ("Regardless of whether your proposal is selected for funding, you should continue to stay in contact with your program officer").
• **Renewal ≠ resubmission, and renewals are reviewed in a separate pool** — "NSF will consider proposals from institutions that have not previously participated in the CyberAI SFS Program separately from proposals from renewing institutions." A traditional renewal is the normal route for an incumbent; the accomplishment-based renewal is a one-time-only option requiring prior consultation with sfs@nsf.gov. Both must evidence (1) the current project's achievements including employment statistics, faculty development, integration of research and education, mentoring of non-SFS institutions, partnerships, outreach, curricular innovations; and (2) "development of innovative and potentially transformative interdisciplinary approaches."
• **Formal reconsideration** (process, not science) follows the NSF-wide route: request to the AD/Office Head within 90 days of declination, answered within 45 days; appeal to the Deputy Director within 60 days, answered within 30; that decision is final.
• Compliance failures are the cheap way to lose: "Proposals that do not include all required components or are not compliant with other PAPPG requirements may be returned without review." Common traps on this mechanism specifically: missing the mandatory "CyberAI SFS:" / "CyberAI Innovation:" title prefix, an evaluator who is also PI/co-PI/Senior Personnel, a Scholarship Track budget that is not exactly three years, and stipends/tuition booked outside Participant Support Costs (Line F).

result.loi_deadline: No DAAD letter of intent or pre-proposal: a single complete submission through the DAAD Portal ("MOVE"). However, applicants at a DAAD Partner University face a campus pre-selection stage with its own earlier internal deadline, set by the university, not by DAAD: "At a DAAD Partner University: contact your DAAD campus coordinator and follow the application guidelines for your university's pre-selection. Please note that your university may have an earlier internal deadline." Three carve-outs make this stage narrower than it first looks: (1) it applies to the FALL deadline only — "there is no partner university pre-selection in the spring"; (2) it "does not apply to those who are applying for funding bet. 2-6 months or to performing/visual artists" — i.e. all postdocs (capped at 6 months) and short-stay doctoral applicants are exempt; (3) missing it is not disqualifying — "If you miss your university's deadline, you may follow the general application guidelines", and the FAQ asks directly whether a partner-university student who missed the internal deadline or prefers not to go through their university "can apply directly to the DAAD New York office", answering "Yes." Partner-university internal deadlines are not published centrally — the campus coordinator directory is the only route to them.
result.review_to_award: Acknowledgement of receipt arrives through the portal roughly two months after close: "You will receive an acknowledgement letter through the portal 8 weeks after the deadline." Decisions: "Results will be announced through the portal at the beginning of April (fall deadline) and at the beginning of September (spring deadline)." Earliest start is set by the round, not by the applicant: 30.10.2026 deadline → "Start of funding from June 1st, 2027"; 30.04.2027 deadline → "Start of funding from October 1st, 2027". So the working timeline for the next deadline is ~5 months submission-to-notification and ~7 months submission-to-earliest-start, with a hard rule that "The funding must begin in 2027." Review is by "An independent selection committee consisting of specialist scientists"; the committee — not the applicant — fixes the actual funding period: "The funding period will be determined by the selection committee during the selection process, taking your work schedule into account." No feedback is provided: "Application decisions will not be accompanied with an explanation." The scholarship cannot be extended.
result.submission_requirements: THE CRITICAL DEVIATION: DAAD North America publishes its own checklist that overrides the head-office/portal instructions, and the page limits genuinely differ. Verbatim: "These guidelines are region specific for North American applicants only. You will find that some details on the application portal and the DAAD Bonn website will differ from this document, such as the maximum number of pages for application documents; the instructions on this checklist supersede any conflicting information potentially found elsewhere." Where they conflict — research proposal: max 5 pages (North America) vs "max. 10 pages in total" (Bonn record); publications list: "max. 5 pages, if applicable" (North America) vs "max. 10 pages; mandatory for postdocs" (Bonn). A US applicant following the Bonn page writes double the allowed proposal length. North America also instructs applicants to drop one Bonn item outright: "Please disregard the following requirement on our head office's website: Other documents you think might be of relevance to your application." Unchanged across both: CV in tabular form max 3 pages; letter of motivation 1-2 pages answering "What do you hope to gain from your project in Germany (personally, professionally, for your career)?". Full component list: online application; CV; publications list; motivation letter; research proposal (discussed in advance with the German adviser, plus a description of previous research work); schedule of planned research work; proof of admission to doctoral studies (may be supplied later if admission comes before funding starts); a letter confirming supervision from the academic host in Germany that "refers to the applicant's proposal and confirms that the host institute will provide a workplace"; a separate "Declaration from the scientific supervisor in Germany on safety-relevant and ethical aspects of the research project" (dual-use DOCX form); all university degree certificates with final grades; transcripts of ALL post-secondary study with individual grades and an explanation of the grading system; and the DAAD Sprachnachweis language evaluation form — required even from applicants with no German at all, who must submit it anyway marked "No knowledge of German" ("Please note that German is not a requirement for the Research Grant"). REFERENCES — lighter than US norms: only ONE letter, and the applicant may handle it: "One signed reference form from a university professor in your major field may be either submitted by post or uploaded directly to the application portal by the applicant." DAAD recommends referees use the DAAD reference form (the "referee's report" on the portal); there is no separate referee deadline or referee portal account. "We prefer letters from North American professors. If it is absolutely impossible, you may submit a letter from an employer or non-academic person." If the deadline falls on a Sunday or public holiday, a posted reference "must be postmarked by the following Monday/business day", but the online materials must still be in by the deadline itself. NO institutional sign-off, budget, or sponsored-projects route — the applicant is the applicant of record and submits directly, unless they opt into the partner-university pre-selection. Formatting: "We do not have specific format requirements... a font that's not too small (min 10 point, 12 pt is usually the most comfortable)... If you feel you have explained things well and clearly in less space, going under the limit is always okay." Incomplete applications are rejected unread, and the portal only exists during the open window.
result.prior_funding_conflicts: DAAD answers this mechanism-by-mechanism, and the two halves fall on opposite sides of the same programme family. WHAT DISQUALIFIES: a previous DAAD long-term award of the same kind. Verbatim FAQ: "Can I receive a graduate scholarship more than once? This depends on which DAAD scholarship you've received previously: Study Scholarships for Graduates of All Disciplines: No. Research Grants – One-Year Grants: No. Research Grants – Short-Term Grants: Yes. You can receive one grant per 12-month period." Reinforced by the funder-wide rule that "It is not possible to combine several study or research scholarships (with a funding period of at least 7 months) within one educational period" — an educational period ending with the Bachelor's, Master's, Diplom, state exam or doctorate. Concurrent funding is barred outright: "If you are already funded by the DAAD, another German funding organization or another state agency in Germany, you cannot receive a scholarship from the DAAD at the same time", and "An Erasmus scholarship is not compatible with a full DAAD scholarship." Two non-funding disqualifiers sit alongside these and catch people just as often: "Your application cannot be considered, if you have been resident in Germany for longer than 15 months at the application deadline", and "You cannot apply if you are doing your entire doctorate at a German university." WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY — the half an applicant most needs: a prior SHORT-TERM DAAD Research Grant does not burn the mechanism, capped only at one grant per rolling 12-month period; the ≥7-month combination bar simply does not reach awards under 7 months, so a 2-6 month stay leaves the door open. "Specialist and language courses (e.g. university summer courses) and internships can be combined with all other types of scholarships" — a DAAD summer language course or internship costs nothing in eligibility. Outside funding is not automatically fatal, only offset above a floor: employment or external scholarship income is credited against the stipend only beyond "EUR 603 gross per month". And a former LONG-term grantee is not cut off from DAAD altogether, merely redirected to a different door: Re-invitation Grants exist precisely for "Former holders of DAAD research grants or study scholarships who were funded for a period of over six months", while Research Stays for University Academics, Study Visits for Academics, and Re-invitation Grants each allow repeat awards, generally "no more than once every three years". NOTE FOR THE ROW: mechanisms.csv currently records prior_funding_exclusion as "none" — that is incorrect and should be updated.

The one explicit invitation to make contact is a narrow eligibility edge case: German citizens applying from North America are told they must have lived abroad 10 years or held strong ties for five, and "Please call our office to make sure you are eligible." Institutional route: DAAD Regional Office New York, 871 United Nations Plaza, New York, NY 10017, +1 (212) 758-3223, daad.newyork@daad.de, plus a web contact form at daad.org/en/find-funding/contact-form/. What DAAD does give an applicant to start from: (1) the North America Application Checklist for Research Grants in Germany, the single authoritative document for US/Canadian applicants and the one that supersedes Bonn — https://www.daad.org/files/2023/03/Research_Checklist_26-27.pdf (PDF, ~121 KB, marked "Updated 2025"); (2) the Declaration from the Scientific Supervisor in Germany, a required fill-in form — https://www.daad.org/files/2023/03/a436_zusatz_betreuungszusage_dual-use.docx; (3) the Sprachnachweis / DAAD German language evaluation form, required even with no German — https://www.daad.org/files/2022/09/Sprachnachweis_Formular_NEU.pdf; (4) the DAAD reference form ("referee's report"), available on the DAAD Portal; (5) the Research Grants FAQ, which is the closest thing to written coaching — it covers proposal length, formatting, reference handling and repeat eligibility: https://www.daad.org/en/find-funding/faq/faq-study-scholarship-and-research-grants/; (6) portal walkthroughs at meindaad.de ("Registering in the portal", "Applying in the portal", "Manual for personal funding"). Because a confirmed German host is a mandatory component and the hardest one to produce cold, DAAD points applicants to GERiT – German Research Institutions and the Research in Germany site for identifying a supervisor and institute, and notes DAAD lecturers in many countries are available for questions. For actual past successful applications, the realistic route is the named campus coordinator at a DAAD Partner University, since campus fellowship offices hold their own pre-selection files.
result.resubmission_note: Not established, and the distinction matters: every published DAAD rule I found governs how often you may RECEIVE a grant, not whether a rejected applicant may apply again in a later round. Nothing on the programme record, the US country page or the FAQ bars reapplication after a rejection, and nothing authorises it either — so this should be recorded as unknown rather than inferred in either direction. Two facts do bear on it. First, a resubmission cannot be informed by reviewer feedback: "Application decisions will not be accompanied with an explanation" / "Please note that no reasons for decisions will be given." Second, the twice-yearly cycle means a rejected fall applicant would face the spring deadline ~6 months later, but the spring round has no partner-university pre-selection and a later funding start, so the two routes are not interchangeable. No letter of intent is submitted to Damon Runyon. The gate is INSTITUTIONAL NOMINATION, and for the Clinical Investigator Award only (no other Damon Runyon program has it).

Funder's words: "Each applicant must be nominated by their institution. Applications will only be accepted from institutions that have been invited to submit them by the Foundation (See list). Three (3) nominations per institution, including its affiliated schools, will be accepted." The overview page carries a banner: "NOTICE: Institutional nominations have been reinstated. Please review carefully." — i.e. this requirement lapsed and is back, so guidance written during the lapse is wrong.

STEP 1 — AM I EVEN ELIGIBLE TO BE NOMINATED? Check the invited institutions PDF: https://www.damonrunyon.org/sites/default/files/2026-06/CIA%20Invited%20Institutions%20UPDATED%20-%20JUNE%202026.pdf (verified live 2026-09-18; 12 pages, updated June 2026, organized by state). I counted 45 state-level headings (44 states + District of Columbia) and roughly 150 top-level institutions; THE PDF STATES NO TOTAL, so those counts are mine, not the funder's. Note the structure: affiliated schools and cancer centers are listed indented under a parent institution, and the three nominations are shared across the parent "including its affiliated schools" — so a large university and its medical school and its comprehensive cancer center compete against each other for the same three slots. If your institution is not on the list, you cannot apply at all.

STEP 2 — WIN THE INTERNAL COMPETITION. Three slots means your research development / limited-submission office runs an internal selection. That internal deadline is typically ~2-3 months before the funder deadline, i.e. roughly October-November 2026 for the January 19, 2027 deadline — meaning it is happening NOW or has just passed as of 2026-09-18. Internal packages are usually short (an LOI of a few pages plus an NIH biosketch). This is the single highest-value thing a first-time CIA applicant can do.

result.submission_requirements:
Portal: ProposalCentral (Altum) only — "No hard copies or emailed applications will be accepted." Register a free applicant account and complete your Professional Profile before October 2026, then search "Damon Runyon Clinical Investigator Award" and click Apply Now. Portal support: pcsupport@altum.com, 800.875.2562 (US/Canada) or +1.703.964.5840, 8:30am-5:00pm ET Mon-Fri.

FORMAT NORM (funder-wide, applies here): single-spaced, 12-point type, at least 0.5-inch margins; figures, tables and legends count INSIDE the proposal page limit; references are excluded and must give full titles.

PAGE LIMITS SPECIFIC TO THIS MECHANISM:
- Applicant's Research Proposal: 5 pages, "including figures, tables and legends"; "A list of references is not included in the 5-page limit."
- Mentor's Proposal for Training: "no longer than three pages" — and "If there are two Mentors, submit only one Proposal for Training, no longer than four pages." (Note this is LONGER than the fellowships' 2-page sponsor training plan.) It must include "a statement of the number of hours they will commit to the investigator's training each week" and a description of institutional courses/training programs for clinical investigators.
- Personal Statement: one page.
- Summary of Research Form: "not to exceed one page. This should match the Abstracts tab."

TWO REFERENCE LETTERS — HARD SUBMIT-GATE (not a courtesy). "Applicants must have two letters of recommendation submitted through Proposal Central by referees using their own letterhead. The letters should be from qualified individuals (other than your Mentor)..." Recommended sources are named: "residency program and/or fellowship training period." The Foundation warns: "The quality and depth of these letters will be pivotal in deciding the applicant's suitability." And the gate: "All reference letters must be submitted on or before the application deadline. Applicants will NOT be able to submit their application unless all reference letters are uploaded to the portal." You enter referee emails in the application; ProposalCentral emails them a letter-upload link. ASK REFEREES 4-6 WEEKS OUT AND CHASE THEM — an unuploaded letter means the Submit button does not work, on the day.

CIA-SPECIFIC COMPONENTS THAT DO NOT EXIST IN THE OTHER DAMON RUNYON PROGRAMS — these are the ones that need other people and therefore lead time:
- Application Cover Sheet with all required signatures (ink or electronic) — route to your grants office early.
- The At-a-Glance Form.
- The Research Experience Information Sheet.
- LETTER OF COMMITMENT, endorsed by BOTH the Dean or Center Director AND the Head/Chair of the Department. It must: identify the applicant as their nominee; confirm the applicant's and Mentor's academic appointments; address the applicant's status in securing a tenure-track or equivalent faculty position ("This appointment must not be contingent upon the applicant securing funding."); "state the institution's willingness to support the applicant's research efforts and guarantee 80% protected time"; address commitment to the applicant's development including the start-up package; and "detail the laboratory and office space allotted to the applicant. If the applicant is not occupying the space at the time of the application, please provide a timeline of when this will occur." Two senior signatures plus space and effort guarantees — start this 6-8 weeks out.
- The Applicant's Appointment Letter (and Reappointment Letter, if applicable) stating position title, description of start-up package, and term of appointment.
- If seeking relief from the 80% research-effort rule, a DEPARTMENT CHAIR WAIVER REQUEST: the Committee may consider "a very modest reduction of 80% protected time if their Department Chair can provide a compelling reason... what percentage of effort will be guaranteed, and what safeguards will be put in place".
- MENTOR PACKAGE (this is a mentored award despite being a faculty award): Mentor's Letter of Support (must "describe independence of applicant from the Mentor"), Mentor's NIH Biosketch, Mentor's Current and Pending Funding — and "If there are two Mentors, each Mentor must submit a Letter of Support, Biosketch, and Funding."

APPLICANT NARRATIVE SET (differs from other programs' shapes):
- Applicant's Letter outlining "long-term vision and goals in the field of clinical cancer investigation and their future commitment to clinical/patient research."
- Personal Statement, one page: what they expect to gain from the award; optional personal background/challenges.
- NIH Biosketch (current NIH format).
- Full Bibliography: applicant's name highlighted in every entry; original peer-reviewed articles "listed separately and first with hyperlinks", then reviews/chapters/editorials. "Do not include presentations, abstracts, 'in preparation' or 'under review' articles."
- Most Important Publications: "up to five", each with a 1-2 sentence annotation on importance and the applicant's role. (Contrast: Rachleff Innovation wants exactly three bolded.)
- Accomplishments: "list and describe three most important professional accomplishments."
- Other Sources of Funding: all current and pending plus start-up, "Include the specific aims of each grant, the total amount of each grant as well as the amount received each year, and confirmation that there is no scientific or budgetary overlap". Useful relief: "Please note, we do not request a budget or a budget justification at the time of application."
- If applicable, up to three Collaboration Letters — flagged in capitals as "(NOT REFERENCE LETTERS)". The funder-wide norm is one page each; the CIA page does not restate a length (see unresolved).
- If resubmitting, a Resubmission Summary of Changes (see resubmission_note).

CROWDING RULES THAT CAN BLOCK YOU EVEN WHEN ELIGIBLE: "Only one application will be accepted from a Mentor (Co-Mentor) per review session." And "No more than two Damon Runyon Clinical Investigators will be funded to work with the same Mentor at any given time (including Co-Mentors)." Plus three nominations per institution. Confirm with your Mentor early that they are not backing someone else this cycle.

WHAT DISQUALIFIES YOU:

Note "holding OR AWARDED" — an R01 awarded but not yet started still disqualifies.
