result.deadline_pattern:
Annual, single round, three fixed rule-based stages. All times are midday CEST, not end of day.

- Round opens: ~1 February (2026 instance: "The 2026 application round will be open on 1 February 2026").
- Stage 1, pre-application: 1 April, 12:00 midday CEST, annually. Verbatim: "The deadline for completing the pre-application is 1 April at 12:00 midday CEST annually."
- Reference letters (all three, submitted by the referees themselves): 1 April, 12:00 midday CEST — the SAME deadline as the pre-application, not the full application. Verbatim: "Referee submission of reference letters: 1 April 2026, 12:00 midday CEST." This is the most commonly missed item in the whole mechanism.
- Pre-application outcome: mid-June ("Pre-application decisions: Mid June"; the prose elsewhere says "by the end of June" — plan for mid-to-late June).
- Stage 2, full application (invited candidates only): ~15 July, 12:00 midday CEST (see the 12-vs-15 July conflict recorded under next_deadline).
- Stage 3, interviews: mid-November (2026 instance: 17 or 18 November 2026).
- Results to applicants: within a week of the interview, and in any case "By 27 November", under embargo.
- Press release: December.

Recommended working back-date, from EMBO itself: activate referees at least 4 weeks before the 1 April deadline — i.e. by ~1 March. Verbatim: "We strongly recommend that you complete/activate your referee details at least 4 weeks prior to the deadline to allow referees enough time to submit their letters."

One internal inconsistency worth knowing as a drift signal: the eligibility bullet list in the 2026 guidelines PDF says "Applicants must be available to attend a virtual interview (on 17 or 18 November 2025)" — the year is a leftover typo; the timeline table and committee guidelines both say 2026.
result.loi_deadline:
1 April, 12:00 midday CEST, annually (next dated instance 1 April 2027). Next full-application deadline for those invited: ~15 July, 12:00 midday CEST — about 3.5 months later.

This is a genuine two-stage competition, not a courtesy LOI. Verbatim: "Applications to the EMBO Young Investigator Programme are accepted annually in a two-stage process"; "The EMBO Young Investigator Programme application uses a two-stage online application process. Pre-applications are evaluated, and a subset is invited to the full application." Roughly 50 of the pre-applicants are invited to Stage 2: "Following pre-screening, approximately 50 applicants will be invited to submit a full application and attend an interview."

The pre-application is where almost all attrition happens. EMBO funds "approximately 25 EMBO Young Investigators annually" and states "The success rate of being selected is ~12%", which implies roughly 200+ pre-applications a year, ~50 invited, ~25 funded — i.e. about a 1-in-4 cut at the pre-application stage and about 1-in-2 thereafter. Effort spent on the pre-application is where the competition is actually decided.

What the pre-application already demands (this is NOT a light-touch LOI): an online form; a downloadable offline Word form uploaded as PDF; three reference letters submitted independently by the referees by the same 1 April deadline; an ORCID ID; and a 2,000-character summary of ongoing research. Applications missing any of the three letters are dead: "Applications that do not have all 3 letters of reference by the application deadline are considered incomplete" and "Applications with less than 3 reference letters are considered 'incomplete' and will not pass to the next stage."

Useful carry-forward, stated by EMBO: "The first two pages of the Young Investigator Programme full application offline form are almost identical to the Young Investigator Programme pre-application offline form; we, therefore, advise you to keep a copy of the pre-application form, so that you can copy and update the relevant information should you reach the final selection stage."

No changes are possible after the pre-application deadline: "no further changes (adding any extra information on papers and grants) can be made to your application after the deadline", and separately "no changes can be made to the form after clicking this button ['form complete']". Receipt is confirmed within a week of 1 April.
result.review_to_award:
Roughly 8 months from pre-application to result; roughly 4.5 months from the full application.

Stage-by-stage, from EMBO's timeline and committee guidelines:
- 1 April: pre-application and all three reference letters due. Confirmation of receipt within one week — "Within a week after the pre-application deadline on 1 April, applicants will receive confirmation that your pre-application has been received and is complete."
- April-May: office eligibility screen, then pre-screening by the Young Investigator Committee. "Each application is independently evaluated by four committee members." Committee scores are due back to the office by 31 May 2026 in the 2026 instance.
- Mid-June (~2.5 months): pre-application outcome to ALL applicants by email; ~50 invited to Stage 2. The timeline table says "Mid June"; the prose says "We expect to share this information by the end of June". Plan for mid-to-late June.
- ~15 July: full application due.
- July-November: each full application goes to ONE EMBO Member with subject expertise for confidential external review — "Each application is sent to one EMBO Member" — assessing "the candidates' standing in the field and the feasibility of their proposed work". The applicant may exclude up to three EMBO Members for conflict of interest.
- 17-18 November (~7.5 months from Stage 1): hybrid panel interview. Committee on-site in Heidelberg, Germany; candidate joins remotely by Zoom. Two parallel sub-panels of 5 committee members, each interviewing ~25 candidates. Format: 10-minute research talk + 10 minutes Q&A. A backup video of the presentation must be submitted in advance in case of connection failure, in which case the candidate dials in by phone for the Q&A.
- Within one week of the interview: outcome by email. "All candidates are informed of the outcome of their application by email within a week of the interview."
- By 27 November: results to applicants, under embargo. December: press release. Total ~8 months from 1 April.

EARLIEST START / WHAT ARRIVES WHEN: this is a network-membership and career-development award, not a research grant, so there is no grant start date in the usual sense. Support runs four years. The cash component is small and deliberately delayed: "EMBO Young Investigators receive a financial award of 15,000 euros in their second year" — i.e. the money lands roughly two years after the pre-application deadline. (The corpus row currently records the amount as "unspecified"; the benefits page gives it explicitly as EUR 15,000 in year 2.) The substantive value is in the non-cash benefits: annual network meeting, mentorship by an EMBO Member, EMBO Lab Leadership Courses, access to EMBL Core Facilities, an annual course for the lab's PhD students, travel grants for the group leader and lab members, conference-organising grants, and vacancy posting.

HARD MID-PROCESS GATE, easy to miss: the last-author publication requirement is tested at INTERVIEW date, not application date. A paper may be "in submission" on 1 April, but "The status must be changed to 'accepted' by the interview date", and "Failing to provide this before the interview will lead to exclusion from the selection process." An editor's acceptance email forwarded to yip@embo.org suffices. So a candidate invited in June with nothing accepted has roughly five months to land an acceptance or be excluded.
result.submission_requirements:
WHO THIS IS FOR — the gate that decides everything else. Postdocs are explicitly excluded: "Are postdocs eligible to apply for the Young Investigator Programme? A: No, postdocs are not eligible to apply. You must be a group leader for at least 1 year." The clock runs on lab-start date, not PhD date: "we only consider the number of years since starting your independent lab/group (less than four years and more than one)" and "There is no age limit". The lab must sit in an EMBC Member State, Associate Member State (India, Singapore) or a cooperation-agreement territory (Chile, Taiwan, and for the 2026 round Japan via named JST programmes). A European national working outside those locations is ineligible: "No, only applicants (of any nationality) working at an institute/university in locations and programmes listed on page 3 are eligible to apply." The United States is not on the list — consistent with the existing row's geographic-gate note; the only US connection is that the 2026 committee chair, Giles Oldroyd, is US-based.

TIMING ADVICE FROM EMBO ITSELF — the most useful sentence in the whole document set for deciding WHICH YEAR to apply: "We have had successful applicants within the first 1.5 - 2 years of starting their group, but usually successful applicants are within 3 - 4 years since the start of their own lab. The success rate of being selected is ~12%, so having a relevant publication record coming from the independent group is highly favourable, but not the only criterion considered by the committee." Read plainly: apply late in the window, not early, unless your independent-lab output is already strong.

STAGE 1 — PRE-APPLICATION. Online form: basic CV data; short summary of ongoing research, 2,000 characters including spaces; details of three referees; ORCID ID (register at https://orcid.org/register if you lack one — ORCID is a listed component for YIP, not merely requested); and a PDF of the completed offline form. Then the step people forget: "Please do not forget to click 'form complete' to submit your application." An application left un-clicked shows status "Submission open" and does not enter the round.

Offline (Word) pre-application form, downloadable before you register: sections are Curriculum vitae (independent group leader position(s) with mm/yyyy dates, postdoctoral research, research training/PhD, education, other positions), a field for "the reasons for remaining at / returning to a former supervisor's institute", "Other relevant information", and a structured Publications block broken into Manuscripts in submission / Publications arising from your independent research group / from postdoctoral work / from PhD work / from other work / Other publications.

Formatting, verbatim: "The form should be completed in Helvetica or Arial font, size 10; The margins should not be altered; The form should be saved in PDF format for upload via the online system... colour highlighting, table view or any other formatting is not acceptable."

CV rules: reverse chronological, month and year for start/end dates, matching the online form; include the start date of your independent lab, and for re-applicants "please ensure that the date is congruent with the previous application" (the committee checks). "Other relevant information" takes CV gaps, community/mentorship/outreach work, recent awards — "Please keep it short" — and is also where you summarise any eligibility extension the office has already approved.

Publication rules: compact format as in The EMBO Journal; own name in bold; own lab members italicised; sorted into the prescribed headings; explain a former supervisor's contribution on any independent-group paper. Excluded from the list: papers in preparation, non-English papers, last-author reviews, conference abstracts. No metrics at all — "Applicants must not indicate the journal impact factor or any other metrics such as H-index, number of citations, etc" (EMBO is a DORA signatory).

The eligibility publication itself: at least one last-author primary research paper accepted or published in an international peer-reviewed journal from the independent lab. "In submission" is accepted at 1 April but must be "accepted" by interview date. A last-author preprint counts only with public in-depth peer reviews from a recognised service (Peer Community In, eLife, Review Commons) on a recognised server (arXiv, bioRxiv, medRxiv, Zenodo); informal comments and individual highlights do not count. Co-corresponding authorship does not qualify by default — "Co-corresponding authorship does not fulfil the 'last author' requirement by default" — and first-plus-co-corresponding is a flat no; both cases require writing to the office first.

REFERENCE LETTERS — three, due 1 April, and the mechanics catch people out. "References from three scientists (preferably former supervisors)". You enter referee details and "activate" them; the system then emails each referee a personal form link. You cannot see the letters, only their status, "listed under the link to the application form on the EMBO application system, HOME tab". There is NO upload: "Please inform your referees that there will be no option for document upload in the online system or sending via email... Referees shall follow the steps explained in the form and paste their letter text in the provided field." Reference letters sent by email are not accepted. Tell your referees this in advance — EMBO carries an FAQ entry solely because referees submit an empty form expecting to attach a PDF (the office will reactivate the form if asked). A referee who cannot deliver can be swapped: deactivate, edit, reactivate, which fires a fresh request. You may submit your own form before the letters arrive, but all three must land by 1 April.

STAGE 2 — FULL APPLICATION (invited only). Additional online items: a list of your grants, a list of your lab members, a short description of your institute. Offline full-application form: CV and complete publication list again (updatable since 1 April), with your three best publications underlined; a summary plus a short justification for each of the three best papers, max 1,000 characters including spaces each ("In theory, you can use any three papers, as long as you justify why you chose them. However, it is generally advisable to include first/last author research papers"); and a research vision "no longer than two pages" describing the lab's themes and future directions — "Any figures are included in the page count", figures inserted by copy/paste or drag-and-drop because "the 'insert' menu is not available in protected forms", references may go on an additional page.

INTERVIEW MATERIAL: 10-minute talk, 10-minute Q&A, plus a mandatory backup video submitted in advance. EMBO's own suggested structure: do not recount your whole career, only the steps that contextualise the research; introduce ongoing projects and results; outlook and future plans; and any grant or publication updates since the full application.

HOW IT DEVIATES FROM THE FUNDER-WIDE NORM: no institutional sign-off of any kind — no AOR, no host-institute form (unlike Installation Grants), no portal beyond the individual's own registration. The applicant is the only signatory. Three reference letters are due at the PRE-application, which is earlier than most readers assume. And the framing sentence the committee is given, which should drive the whole application, is: "Committee members are reminded that the candidate is not applying for a research grant. Instead, the potential to become a future leader in research is being evaluated."

AI DISCLOSURE: "EMBO acknowledges the value of using Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, as well as human feedback, in the preparation of funding applications. Applicants are fully and solely responsible for the originality and accuracy of their applications."
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
EMBO inverts the NIH pattern: for YIP, prior and current funding is a REQUIREMENT and a scored criterion, not a disqualifier. Nothing in the published eligibility criteria excludes an applicant on the basis of any grant held — not ERC, not HFSP, not a national group-leader award, not an EMBO Installation Grant.

WHAT PRESERVES OR CREATES ELIGIBILITY (the half usually omitted):

1. Holding substantial funding is expected. Verbatim: "Applicants are expected to have obtained sufficient funding to run their laboratory (consumables, lab space, salary for themselves and their staff). The Young Investigator Programme funding is not intended to replace core funding." And the eligibility page: "Candidates are expected to have obtained sufficient funding to run their independent research group." A well-funded applicant is a stronger applicant, not a conflicted one.

2. There is no minimum and no ceiling. Verbatim FAQ: "How much funding is considered necessary to be able to eligible to apply? A: There is no minimum requirement for the amount of funding you receive, as long as you can fully support your independent group (consumables, lab space, salary for you and your staff)."

3. Funding is an explicit scoring criterion at both stages: "Group size and funding sources: Are the number and the expertise of laboratory members and the available funds sufficient to undertake the described research?" Under-funding is the risk here, not over-funding.

4. Grants must be DISCLOSED, and disclosure is a listed component. The complete application includes a "List of grants and pending grant applications"; the Stage 2 online form adds "a list of your grants". Disclosure is for assessment of independence and capacity, not for exclusion. Financial independence is itself a criterion: "Is the candidate financially independent? Is the candidate able to apply for grants in their own name and report directly to funding agencies?"

5. Prior EMBO Global Investigator Network funding explicitly PRESERVES YIP eligibility. Verbatim from the eligibility page: "However, as an EMBO Global Investigator you can still apply to the YIP if you meet its eligibility criteria." The FAQ repeats it: "as a successful Global Investigator Network awardee, you can still apply to be a YI if you fulfil the eligibility criteria."

6. Applying to YIP and GIN in the same year is expressly permitted and expressly harmless. Verbatim: "Candidates who are applying to the EMBO Young Investigator Programme (YIP) can also apply to the EMBO Global Investigator Network in the same year if they meet the eligibility criteria, for which a separate application is required. Applying to both programmes in parallel does not affect your chances in either programme (the committees and EMBO offices are different). If you are invited for interviews by both, you only have to attend the Global Investigator Network interviews if you are not selected for the YIP."

7. Named JST funding CREATES eligibility for Japan-based PIs who would otherwise fail the geographic gate. Verbatim: "For the application round 2026, PIs or Co-PIs funded by the following programmes of the Japan Science and Technology Agency (JST) at the time of the pre-application deadline until January 2027 or beyond are eligible to apply: ASPIRE, FOREST, ERATO, CREST, PRESTO, ACT-X." (For ERATO: "current Research Director or Group Leader".) This is time-limited to the 2026 round as published and must be re-checked for 2027.

WHAT ACTUALLY MAKES SOMEONE INELIGIBLE (none of it is prior funding):

a. Being an existing EMBO Young Investigator closes the GIN door permanently — a one-way ratchet, and the only true prior-award exclusion in this family. Verbatim: "Please note that once you are selected as an EMBO Young Investigator, you cannot apply to the Global Investigator Network in the future." Practical consequence for anyone eligible for both: GIN after YIP is impossible, YIP after GIN is fine. If you might want both over a career, the ordering matters.

b. Having already been interviewed twice. "Candidates can re-apply as many times as they fulfil eligibility criteria, but only once more after having been interviewed (i.e. candidates can only attend two interviews)."

c. Falling outside the group-leader window (at least 1, less than 4 years at the pre-application deadline; for the 2026 round, lab started no earlier than 1 January 2022 and no later than 1 April 2025).

d. Location outside the EMBC/associate/cooperation list.

e. No accepted last-author paper by interview date.

ELIGIBILITY EXTENSIONS (these preserve eligibility for people who would otherwise be time-barred): "For candidates who have given birth, the eligibility limit is automatically extended by one year per child" — automatic, no application needed. For parental leave without giving birth, the extension is "the actual time taken off; or three months per child, if during the parental leave period the candidate's partner worked at least 80% FTE (full-time equivalent), whichever is longer." Illness, other care responsibilities, extended military service and clinical-scientist circumstances are case-by-case and require contacting the office BEFORE applying. COVID is explicitly excluded: "no special provision will be made for lab closures during the COVID-19 pandemic." Any approved extension should then be summarised briefly in the "Other relevant information" CV field.
result.program_officer_contact:
CONTACT ROUTE: yip@embo.org — one shared programme mailbox covering both the Young Investigator Programme and Installation Grants. Named staff listed on the YIP pages: Gerlind Wallon, Programme Head, +49 6221 8891 112; Roberto Efraín Díaz, Senior Programme Officer, +49 6221 8891 110; Grace Denny, Programme Officer, +49 6221 8891 211. (The general email on the page is JavaScript-obfuscated; yip@embo.org is the address printed throughout both guideline PDFs.)

PRE-SUBMISSION CONTACT IS EXPECTED, AND IN SEVERAL CASES REQUIRED. EMBO asks you to read first — "Should you have questions regarding your application, please first consult the FAQ section in this document. If your question is not answered, please contact the EMBO Young Investigator Programme Office (yip@embo.org)" — and then to write BEFORE applying in these situations:
- Any eligibility extension for illness, extended military service, care responsibilities or other exceptional circumstances: "If you feel your circumstances warrant an extension of the eligibility period, please contact the EMBO Young Investigator Programme Office (yip@embo.org) for advice before applying." (Extensions for giving birth are automatic and need no email.)
- Senior author who is not the literal last author: "Please contact the EMBO Young Investigator Programme Office and describe your contribution to the manuscript, as well as the contributions of other senior authors and an explanation of how the author division took place."
- Co-corresponding authorship you want counted as last authorship: "Please write to the EMBO Young Investigator Programme Office explaining your exact contribution to the paper compared to those from the last author."
- First-plus-co-corresponding author: the answer is "No. But if you feel there is more to the situation, please write to us providing a link to the paper in question, an explanation of how the author division took place and a detailed contribution of the first/last and corresponding authors on the paper."
- A paper accepted but not yet online at 1 April: "Please send the acceptance letter from the editor together with the manuscript to the EMBO Young Investigator Programme Office (yip@embo.org)."
Note the pattern: EMBO wants the specific evidence in the first email (the link, the contribution breakdown, the editor's letter), not an open-ended question.

ROUTINE OPERATIONAL CONTACT, also via the same mailbox: re-sending a referee invitation that went to spam ("First ask your referee to check their spam folder. If they do not see the email, please email yip@embo.org and we will re-send"); reopening a referee's accidentally-submitted blank form ("Yes, we will reactivate their form and re-send them an email containing the link"); recycling a reference letter for a re-application; and an application stuck at "Submission open" after you clicked "form complete".

CONTACTING COMMITTEE MEMBERS IS FORBIDDEN AND DISQUALIFYING. The YIP Selection page carries the disqualification clause in full — verbatim: "Please do not contact the committee members directly. Personally contacting YIP committee members for application advice/feedback can be interpreted as attempting to influence selection results and will disqualify your application." The guidelines PDF repeats the prohibition: "Please do not contact any committee members directly for feedback. Any requests should be addressed to the EMBO Young Investigator Programme Office only (yip@embo.org)." (Note: this corrects a common assumption that only the Installation Grants guidelines carry the disqualification wording — YIP does too.)

This matters because EMBO PUBLISHES the committee. The 2026 Young Investigator Committee is named on page 3-4 of both PDFs: Giles Oldroyd (USA, Chair), Corinne Houart (UK), Urs Jenal (CH), Gaëlle Legube (FR), Jan Löwe (UK), Jean-Christophe Marine (BE), Eric Miska (UK), Jacques Neefjes (NL), Nina Papavasiliou (DE), Irmgard Sinning (DE), Sara Wickström (DE). The legitimate use of knowing who reviews is the reverse of lobbying: at Stage 2 you may exclude reviewers. "Applicants will have the option to exclude three EMBO Members from the evaluation process to eliminate any potential conflicts of interest" / "Candidates can exclude up to three specific EMBO Members from the process."

FEEDBACK AFTER REJECTION — asymmetric, and it should shape strategy. Nothing after the pre-screen: "No feedback will be given following the pre-selection stage due to the high number of applications each committee member has to review." But feedback IS given after an unsuccessful interview: "the committee will provide feedback following an unsuccessful interview and the EMBO Office will forward the comments to the candidates." Reaching interview therefore has consolation value that failing the pre-screen does not — and since a rejected interviewee also retains exactly one more attempt, the interview-stage rejection is the one that can be learned from.
result.examples_or_samples:
There is no EMBO equivalent of NIH RePORTER, and EMBO publishes no sample YIP applications and no reviewer comments. But for THIS mechanism there are four genuinely useful substitutes, and one of them is the reviewers' own scoring rubric.

1. THE SCORING RUBRIC — read this before writing a word. The EMBO Young Investigator Programme Committee guidelines PDF (https://www.embo.org/documents/YIP/YIP_committee_guidelines.pdf) is the document handed to reviewers, and it prints the 1-5 scale verbatim: "5. Outstanding: A highly mature and independent scientist; a demonstrable leader in their field and related areas; clearly original in thinking, with a compelling and ambitious research vision. / 4. Excellent: A mature and independent scientist; clear evidence of leadership within their field; strong indications of original thinking and a well-defined research vision. / 3. Very good: Evidence of emerging scientific maturity and leadership; some indications of original thinking and an emerging research vision. / 2. Good: Limited evidence of scientific maturity and leadership; originality and research vision are not yet sufficiently developed. / 1. Non-competitive: Insufficient scientific maturity and leadership; lacks originality and a coherent research vision." Note what is being scored: maturity, leadership, originality, vision — not project feasibility. Paired with the instruction "Committee members are reminded that the candidate is not applying for a research grant. Instead, the potential to become a future leader in research is being evaluated", this is a clearer guide to what wins than any sample application would be.

2. PER-AWARDEE LISTS OF ACTUAL WINNERS — the EMBO Annual Report "Facts & Figures" PDFs, at https://www.embo.org/about-embo/resources/annual-reports/. The 2025 edition (https://www.embo.org/documents/facts_figures/EMBO_annual_report_2025-facts_figures.pdf, verified live, 64 pages) lists every EMBO Young Investigator selected that year from around page 40 as a three-column table: Name | Institute | Research Interest, each research interest phrased in a single line — exactly the register EMBO's own 2,000-character summary field expects. Verified real rows include Sebastian Baumgarten (Institut Pasteur, Paris, FR), Merav Cohen (National Centre for Biological Sciences, Bangalore, IN), Tom Deegan (Institute of Genetics and Cancer, University of Edinburgh, UK) and Alexis André Jourdain (University of Lausanne, CH). The same file carries Installation Grantees and Global Investigators, EMBO Young Investigator Lecture listings, and application/award/success-rate tables broken down by year and gender. Prior years: 2024 at .../EMBO_annual_report_2024-facts_figures.pdf, and 2020-2023 at https://www.embo.org/documents/news/facts_figures/EMBO_facts_figures_20XX.pdf. Reading two or three consecutive years shows which institutes and which kinds of profile actually get selected.

3. MODEL RESEARCH SUMMARIES — https://people.embo.org (live, HTTP 200; ~3,149 people). Filter by community type "Young Investigator" to browse current and former YIs; profiles carry institution, country, award year, a research title, a short plain-language research summary, keywords and subject areas. These short summaries are effectively worked examples for the 2,000-character "short summary of ongoing research" field. Hub page: https://www.embo.org/the-embo-communities/embo-young-investigator-network/find-a-young-investigator-installation-grantee-or-global-investigator/. Note the live filter set offers Young Investigator and Global Investigator but no separate Installation Grantee facet.

4. THE ACTUAL FORM, BEFORE YOU COMMIT — the pre-application Word form downloads without registering, from https://embo.org/documents/YIP/YIP_preapplication_form.docx (verified, 83 KB, Jan 2026). It shows the exact CV table structure (independent group leader positions, postdoctoral research, research training, education, other positions), the "reasons for remaining at / returning to a former supervisor's institute" prompt, the "Other relevant information" field, and the six-way publication breakdown. Combined with registering early at the portal (http://applications.embo.org/01/register.php?reg=P0M8) to see the online form, this is the cheapest possible reconnaissance.

DO NOT PROMISE: no published sample EMBO YIP applications; no reviewer reports, scores or rankings released to applicants at any stage; no feedback at all after the pre-screen (feedback exists only after an unsuccessful interview, routed through the office). The EMBO Fellows Network (https://fellowsnetwork.embo.org/) is members-only and not a public archive.

I could not check whether any university research office publishes a successful EMBO YIP application: this session's web-search budget was exhausted. Everything above came from direct fetches of embo.org pages and PDFs, not from a search index.
result.resubmission_note:
Unlimited applications, maximum TWO interviews. Verbatim from the eligibility page: "Candidates can re-apply as many times as they fulfil eligibility criteria, but only once more after having been interviewed (i.e. candidates can only attend two interviews)." The FAQ states the applicant-facing version: "If you were rejected after an interview, you may re-apply once more. Previous rejection does not have any impact on the success of the following applications." The application page repeats it: "For re-applicants: one may reapply as many times as one fulfils eligibility criteria, but may be invited to the interview only twice."

Read carefully, this is generous at the pre-screen and strict at the interview. Failing the pre-screen costs you nothing — you may try again every year you remain inside the group-leader window. Reaching an interview and failing spends one of exactly two interview slots. Since the eligibility window is only three-and-a-bit years wide, most people get two or three shots at most before ageing out regardless.

Combined with EMBO's own timing advice ("usually successful applicants are within 3 - 4 years since the start of their own lab"), the sensible pacing for someone with a thin independent record is to let the record build rather than burn the window early — but an early pre-screen rejection carries no penalty and no feedback, so there is nothing to learn from it either.

CONSISTENCY CHECK ON RE-APPLICATION: EMBO cross-checks your dates against the earlier file. "For re-applicant: please ensure that the date [of the start of your independent laboratory] is congruent with the previous application."

RECYCLING REFERENCE LETTERS — documented and officially sanctioned. Verbatim: "If you are re-applying to the Programme and wish to re-use the previous letters of reference, please fill out the name and postal address of the referee in the form but enter yip@embo.org into the email field. This way the EMBO Young Investigator Programme Office will receive the reference letter request and the letter from your most recent application will be added to your application." The FAQ adds the caution that matters operationally: "Please remember that this is a manual process, so the references will not appear as complete immediately" — so do not panic at an incomplete status, but do start it well before 1 April. The same trick is the sanctioned answer to "can I submit a letter on my referee's behalf" (you cannot; use the yip@embo.org email-field route instead).

CROSS-PROGRAMME CONSEQUENCE OF SUCCESS, not failure: winning YIP permanently bars you from the Global Investigator Network ("once you are selected as an EMBO Young Investigator, you cannot apply to the Global Investigator Network in the future"), while winning GIN leaves YIP open. Anyone eligible for both should think about order before applying.

result.program_name: Early Career Program (ECP) Award (formerly Young Investigator Program)
result.funder: Army Research Office (ARO), within DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory (ARL); contracting through US Army Contracting Command — Aberdeen Proving Ground, Research Triangle Park Division
result.next_deadline: 20 November 2027 — but read what that date is. There is NO annual ECP competition deadline. ECP lives inside a single standing Broad Agency Announcement, W911NF-23-S-0001, whose cover page reads "21 November 2022 - 20 November 2027". The BAA states: "Proposals may be submitted at any time while this BAA is open." And: "Proposals will be considered until and including the closing date of this announcement (see cover page of this announcement for opening/closing dates). Proposals submitted after the closing date will not be considered by the Government under this announcement." Corroborated independently by the Grants.gov API (opportunity id 344592): openDate 11/21/2022, responseDate 11/20/2027, archiveDate 12/20/2027, oppStatus "posted" (i.e. still open as checked 2026-09-18). Also corroborated per-topic: every ARL BAA research topic rendered on ARL's topic portal carries "Closing Date: Nov 20, 2027". So the actionable answer for an applicant today is: you can submit tomorrow, or any day for the next ~14 months; the only hard date is 20 Nov 2027, after which a successor BAA would be expected (not established — see unresolved).
result.deadline_pattern: Continuous/rolling against a 5-year standing BAA, not an annual cycle. Practical consequence specific to ECP, and worth flagging to applicants: ECP eligibility is measured "at the time of application" (fewer than five years in a tenure-track position), and because submission timing is entirely applicant-controlled, someone approaching the five-year boundary can choose their own submission date rather than waiting for a cycle — the usual "I missed this year's deadline, so I age out" failure mode does not apply here. (That is an implication of the two quoted rules, not a statement ARO makes.) One genuine timing constraint exists but is set by the topic, not the calendar: an ECP proposal must be written against a live ARO research topic, and individual topics carry their own Published Date and can be added or retired during the BAA's life.
result.loi_deadline: No LOI or pre-proposal exists, and no date attaches to the optional stage. A whitepaper stage exists and is strongly pushed but is explicitly optional: "A whitepaper is not required to submit a proposal." The BAA's recommended three-step sequence is: (1) "Conduct a preliminary inquiry with an ARL TPOC", (2) "Submit a Whitepaper to an ARL TPOC for review", (3) "Submit a Full Proposal". Whitepaper specifics: no prescribed format, "not expected to exceed five (5) total pages", single PDF, emailed directly to the named topic TPOC (not through Grants.gov), and must carry the whitepaper title, submitter name and organization, the research topic name, the topic ID number, and the TPOC name. Turnaround: the TPOC "will provide a response with either 'encouraged to submit a proposal' or 'not encouraged to submit a proposal'" — no stated response time. Critically, a discouraging answer does not close the door: "all proposals submitted under the terms and conditions cited in this BAA will be reviewed regardless of the recommendation received from the ARL TPOC, or lack of submission of a whitepaper." Because there is no deadline, the whitepaper does not compress the timeline the way a dated LOI does — it is a free, low-cost triage step, and its stated purpose is "to minimize the labor and cost associated with the production of detailed proposals that have very little chance of being selected for funding."
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
The honest finding is that this mechanism has essentially no prior-funding exclusion — which is itself the high-value fact, because applicants coming from an NIH K-award mental model will assume one exists. Both halves, from a full-text scan of the BAA:

WHAT DISQUALIFIES YOU — nothing about your award history. The sole eligibility gate is status and citizenship: "open to U.S. citizens, U.S. Nationals, or Lawful Permanent Residents of the U.S. who have held a tenure-track position at a U.S. institution of higher education for fewer than five years at the time of application." A search of the BAA for ineligible / not eligible / previously received / prior award / only one / may not receive returns no investigator-level prior-award bar anywhere; every "ineligible" hit is organizational and contractual (unpaid federal tax liability, corporate felony conviction in the preceding 24 months, or failure to furnish cost/pricing data under FAR 15.403-3). Holding an existing ARO, NSF, NIH, DOE or other federal grant is not disqualifying, and neither is having held one before.

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY — the BAA affirmatively protects concurrent submission elsewhere: the technical proposal must state "The names of other federal, state, local agencies, or other parties receiving the proposal and/or funding the proposed effort. If none, state so. Concurrent or later submission of the proposal to other organizations will not prejudice its review by ARL if ARL is kept informed of the situation." So you may shop the same project to NSF and ARO simultaneously provided you disclose. Disclosure is nonetheless mandatory and broad: "all current and pending research support, as defined by Section 223 of the Fiscal Year (FY) 2021 National Defense Authorization Act, must be disclosed at the time of proposal submission, for all covered individuals," and "All project support from whatever source must be listed. The list must include all projects requiring a portion of the PI's and other key personnel's time, even if they receive no salary support from the project(s)."

TWO REAL CAVEATS, neither an eligibility bar. (1) Undisclosed or adverse funding relationships bite at a different stage: every grant/cooperative-agreement proposal recommended for award goes through the Army Research Risk Assessment Program, whose risk matrix weighs "participation in foreign talent programs; denied entity list affiliation or association; funding sources to include conflict of interest or conflict of commitment, or funding from a strategic competitor; and foreign influence..." The BAA adds "Nationality or citizenship is not a factor in the risk assessment." So foreign funding is a risk-assessment input, not an eligibility rule. (2) A duplicative-effort restriction exists but does not apply to the ECP grant path — it is attached to Other Transactions ("The research covered under this instrument cannot be duplicative of research being conducted under an existing DoD program"), and ECP awards are made as grants to the institution.

A separate non-obvious constraint: the award is institutional, not personal — "Any resulting award will be made to the institution, not to the investigator" — so it does not travel with you automatically if you move.
result.program_officer_contact:
There is no single ECP program officer. Contact is routed through the named Technical Point of Contact (TPOC) for the ARO research topic your proposal targets, and pre-submission contact is strongly and repeatedly urged — this is the "who to talk to" answer and it is the most consequential procedural fact about this mechanism.

ROUTE 1 (the one that matters). Browse the ARL BAA topic database, find an ARO topic matching your science, and email its named POC. The portal is at https://cftste.experience.crmforce.mil/arlext/s/arl-opportunities (the old path https://arl.devcom.army.mil/opportunities/arl-baa/ 301-redirects there). It held 79 topics when checked on 2026-09-18, searchable and filterable by Discipline, Opportunity Type, ARL Office of Responsibility (filter to "Army Research Office (ARO)"), Topic Audience, and Funding Category (ECP is basic research, so 6.1). Each topic card shows a named "Topic POC(s)" — observed examples: Norman W. Manning on ARL-BAA-0107 "Academic Applied and Advanced Innovation"; Matthew W. Glasscott, PhD on ARL-BAA-0119 "Advanced Energy Materials Program". NOTE A DISCREPANCY: the BAA claims "The TPOC names, telephone numbers, and email addresses are listed with each research Topic at the ARL BAA topics website," but the current portal's rendered list view exposes names only — a DOM scan found zero email addresses and zero mailto links. Contact details appear to live in the portal's "DOWNLOAD ALL BAA TOPICS AS PDF" file ("All Topics Document for ARL BAA.pdf", 100 pages), which I did not download. Budget an extra step to obtain the address.

ECP-specific instruction, quoted: "As is the case for all other award types, discussions with the cognizant ARO TPOC identified for a given topic is strongly recommended before submission of a whitepaper or proposal."

Why it is worth doing, in ARO's own framing: "ARL receives several hundred research proposals annually and is able to provide support for only a limited number of the proposals received... ARL TPOCs are available to discuss the general need for the type of research effort contemplated and availability of funding before an interested applicant expends extensive effort in preparing a whitepaper or full proposal." Caveat quoted: "The Government will not be obligated by any discussion that arises out of preliminary inquiries."

ROUTE 2 (no TPOC identified). Use the ARL Contact Us form, https://arl.devcom.army.mil/contact-us/ (redirects to https://cftste.experience.crmforce.mil/arlext/s/contact-us), selecting "BAA Inquiry" from the drop-down; put "BAA Whitepaper Submission" plus the topic name and topic ID in the subject line.

ROUTE 3 (administrative / business, not scientific). Kia S. McCormick, Procurement Analyst, US Army Contracting Command–APG RTP Division, (919) 549-4281, per the Grants.gov listing; the listed contact email field is the ARL contact form rather than an address. Mailbox usarmy.rtp.devcom-arl.mbx.baa@army.mil is for email proposal submission (contracts/OTs only) and for proposal withdrawal requests — not for assistance-instrument proposals and not the right door for scientific questions.
result.examples_or_samples:
No ARO-published sample ECP application, annotated example, or awardee showcase page was found. Four real substitutes, in descending usefulness:

1. THE REVIEWER'S OWN SCORING SHEET — the strongest "get started" material and better than a sample proposal for calibration. ARO Form 16, "Proposal Evaluation Form," is publicly downloadable at https://arl.devcom.army.mil/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2022/09/baa-form-aro16.pdf. It is a 2-page fillable PDF (image-based, so its labels do not extract as text, but its AcroForm field names are unambiguous): Proposal No, Title, PI, Institution, Evaluator; a free-text "Tech Eval" and a separate "Relevance" narrative; a/b/c/n ratings on Objective, Methods, Qualify(ications) and Reason; an Overall scale of a-plus / a / a-minus / b / c; "Technical merit" and "relevance" ratings; and a binary "recommend accept" / "recommend decline" with comments and date signed. Writing to that sheet is the closest thing to seeing a funded application.

2. THE ACTUAL PROPOSAL TEMPLATES — every required section ships as a downloadable form from https://arl.devcom.army.mil/resources/baa-forms/: Publicly Releasable Project Abstract, Table of Contents, Project Description, Biographical Sketch, Bibliography, Current and Pending Support, Facilities/Equipment/Other Resources, ARO Form 51 (cover page), ARO Form 52/52A (proprietary-information preference), ARO Form 99 (summary budget), ARO Form 56 (budget/cost instructions), ARO Form 95 (certifications), SF 424 (R&R), R&R Senior/Key Person Profile, R&R Other Project Information, DD Form 1861, ARRP Privacy Act Statement.

3. REAL FUNDED ECP AWARDS via USAspending — verified working. A keyword search on "EARLY CAREER PROGRAM" restricted to CFDA 12.431 (assistance types 02/03/04/05) returns e.g. award W911NF2410315, The Pennsylvania State University, 2024-09-06 to 2027-09-05, $329,844, "NEW START GRANT - EARLY CAREER PROGRAM: RIFLES: RAPID INFORMATION FUSION THROUGH LEARNING EFFECTIVE CLOSURES." Note the $329,844 over three years sits just under the $360k cap, and note the honest limitation: only this one ARO record surfaced, because most ARO ECP awards are not labelled "Early Career Program" in the free-text description field, so this route under-counts badly. (Beware: a broader Army-wide search returns many DOE "Nuclear Energy University Programs — Distinguished Early Career Program" awards, a different programme entirely.)

4. DTIC — the route ARO itself names, but CURRENTLY OFFLINE. The BAA says a funded grant's abstract "will be posted to a searchable website available to the general public to meet the requirements of Section 8123 of the DoD Appropriations Act, 2015. The website address is https://www.dtic.mil/." As checked 2026-09-18, DTIC's public search returns: "DTIC Public Search is offline while we enhance the capability. It will be back online soon." This is a tooling/availability fact about DTIC today, not a statement that abstracts stopped being published. Retry later; meanwhile use USAspending.
result.submission_requirements:
Where ECP DEVIATES from the ordinary ARO Single Investigator proposal, there is essentially one deviation, and it is decisive.

THE ECP-SPECIFIC REQUIREMENT — an institutional supporting letter, and the BAA makes clear it is graded, not a formality: "The proposal is submitted by the institution where the individual is employed. The proposal must include a supporting letter, both through official channels in the institution where the individual is employed... The supporting letter must be from the individual's Department Chairperson, Dean, Supervisor, or other official who speaks for the institution, and should address support for, and commitment to, the applicant. Strong institution support for the applicant is essential. Evidence of this support can include the applicant's salary, release time from administrative responsibilities, the purchase of equipment, support for the applicant's graduate students, any cost sharing, any start-up funding, etc. The proposal must support the institution's views that the individual is an outstanding investigator, and the institution is making a long-term commitment to the proposal and the research. Any resulting award will be made to the institution, not to the investigator." That letter is load-bearing because ECP carries a fourth review criterion the other award types do not: alongside the three standard criteria (scientific/technical merit; potential contributions to the Army mission; qualifications of the PI), ECP proposals are also judged on "Long-term commitment by the institution of higher education to the early career investigator and the proposed research." Practical read: a generic chair letter is a scored weakness; the letter should enumerate dollars, space, teaching relief and student support.

A SECOND, EASILY-MISSED ECP CLAUSE — non-tenure-track institutions are not excluded, but must opt in explicitly in the text: "Faculty at an institution of higher education which does not designate a faculty appointment as 'tenure track' are eligible if that fact is so indicated in the proposal, and the supporting letter from the institute states that the faculty member submitting the proposal will be considered for a permanent appointment."

OTHERWISE IDENTICAL TO THE FUNDER NORM — ECP "must follow the format set forth in Section II.D.2 (Application and Submission Information) of this BAA." That means: submission through Grants.gov Workspace (mandatory for grants and cooperative agreements; the email mailbox is only for contracts and OTs); SF 424 (R&R) cover page (a proposal is not processed without a signed cover page or SF 424 (R&R)); a prescribed Table of Contents with lettered section paging; ARO Form 52 or 52A disclosure preference; R&R Other Project Information; a publicly releasable Project Abstract on ARO's form, "no longer than one (1) page (maximum 4,000 characters)" and marked releasable; Project Description covering background/objectives/approach/level of effort plus four unusual mandatory statements — other agencies receiving the proposal, environmental impact, use of Class I/II ozone-depleting substances, and government-furnished support requested; Biographical Sketch "limited to three (3) pages per investigator," with up to five closely related and five other publications, four years of collaborators, and each investigator's own advisors and advisees (used for reviewer conflict screening); Bibliography; Current and Pending Support; Facilities/Equipment/Other Resources; budget on ARO Form 99 per year plus cumulative, with a signed summary page and per-year justification ("There is no page limitation for budget proposals or budget justifications"); plus Title IX demographic collection in an appendix.

PAGE LIMITS — note the absence. No overall page limit is stated for the ECP technical proposal. The only stated limits are the 1-page/4,000-character abstract, the 3-page-per-investigator biosketch, the 5-page optional whitepaper, and explicitly no limit on budget material. Do not assume an NSF-style 15-page cap.

REGISTRATION LEAD TIME — SAM.gov registration, a Unique Entity Identifier and a CAGE Code are required; the BAA warns SAM/D&B steps can take "three to five business days or as long as four weeks if all steps are not completed in a timely manner," and advises uploading "at least two days before any established deadline."
result.review_to_award:
No published timeline — and I checked the full BAA text rather than assuming. ARO states neither a review duration, a notification date, nor an earliest start date, which follows logically from having no submission deadline: with rolling intake there is no cohort to notify. What IS documented is the sequence, which lets an applicant infer that this is not fast:

(1) Initial internal screen on scientific merit, Army relevance and expected fund availability — "Proposals not considered having sufficient scientific merit or relevance to the Army's needs, or those in areas for which funds are not expected to be available, may not receive further review." (2) External peer review by "highly qualified subject matter experts, both Government employees and non-Government employees"; an applicant may restrict review to Government employees only, but the BAA warns "to do so may prevent review of the proposal by other qualified experts in the field." (3) Absolute, not comparative, scoring: "Each proposal will be evaluated based on the evaluation criteria... rather than against other proposals for research in the same general area. Each evaluated proposal will receive a recommendation of 'select' or 'do not select'." (4) Cost realism and funds-availability analysis. (5) A mandatory Army Research Risk Assessment (ARRP) on all Senior/Key personnel — this step applies to every grant or cooperative agreement recommended for award and is a real, often-overlooked source of delay between "selected" and "awarded."

START DATE — applicant-proposed but not guaranteed, and fixed only at the end: "Specification of a desired starting date for the project is important and helpful; however, requested effective dates cannot be guaranteed." At notification, "Applicants whose proposals are recommended for award may be contacted by a Contract/Grant Specialist to discuss additional information required for award... The anticipated start date will be determined at that time." And the warning that the call is not money: "The notification email is not an authorization to commit or expend funds. The Government is not obligated to provide any funding until a Government Contracting/Grants/Agreements Officer signs the award document."

WEAK EMPIRICAL ANCHOR, offered as such and not as a funder statement: the one identifiable funded ECP award (W911NF-24-1-0315, Penn State) has a period of performance 2024-09-06 to 2027-09-05 — a start at the very start of a federal fiscal year boundary, consistent with award timing being driven by fiscal-year funds availability. One data point; do not generalise. For comparison within the same BAA, ARO's STIR mechanism does carry a hard performance rule ("Research must be completed within nine (9) months of award"), showing ARO states durations when it has them — its silence on ECP review timing is real silence, not an extraction failure.
result.resubmission_note: Not addressed anywhere in the BAA — a full-text search for resubmit / resubmission / revised proposal / declined / debrief / feedback returns nothing, so there is no stated resubmission limit, no cooling-off period, and no promised reviewer feedback or debrief for an unsuccessful ECP proposal. What can be said from the text, rather than inferred loosely: because "Proposals may be submitted at any time while this BAA is open" and each proposal is scored on its own merits "rather than against other proposals," nothing on the face of the BAA bars resubmitting a revised proposal, and there is no annual cycle to wait for. Separately and more concretely, a discouraging whitepaper verdict does not block a full proposal: "all proposals submitted under the terms and conditions cited in this BAA will be reviewed regardless of the recommendation received from the ARL TPOC, or lack of submission of a whitepaper." An applicant wanting certainty on resubmission should ask the topic TPOC, since ARO has not published a rule. Withdrawal, by contrast, is documented: "Requests to withdraw a proposal shall be directed to usarmy.rtp.devcom-arl.mbx.baa@army.mil."
unresolved: Whether a successor BAA will follow W911NF-23-S-0001 after 20 Nov 2027, and whether ECP will carry over into it. Not stated anywhere; the current BAA itself succeeded two earlier BAAs (W911NF-17-S-0002 and W911NF-17-S-0003), so succession is the historical pattern — but that is inference, not a published commitment, and I am not recording it as a finding.

TPOC email addresses and phone numbers. The BAA asserts they are listed with each topic, but the live topic portal's rendered list view shows POC NAMES ONLY — a DOM scan returned zero email addresses and zero mailto links across the displayed topics. The addresses are most likely inside the portal's 100-page 'All Topics Document for ARL BAA.pdf' (https://cftste.experience.crmforce.mil/arlext/s/baa-download), which I did not download. Unverified either way.
Review-to-award duration, notification timing, and earliest start date. Genuinely not published for ECP; confirmed absent from a full-text scan of the BAA, not merely un-found.
Resubmission policy for an unsuccessful ECP proposal, and whether any reviewer feedback or debrief is provided. Entirely absent from the BAA.

Selectivity: number of ECP awards made per year and success rate. The BAA gives no ECP-specific figure. The Grants.gov listing's numberOfAwards=2000 covers the ENTIRE ARL BAA across all mechanisms and must not be read as an ECP figure.
Whether ARO publishes an ECP awardee list or news announcements naming recipients. ARL's own site search is JavaScript-driven and returned nothing to a plain fetch; not established either way.
An ARO-published sample or annotated ECP application. None found; ARO Form 16 and the section templates are substitutes, not samples.

TOOLING NOTE, not a finding: WebSearch was unavailable for this task (session budget of 200 calls already exhausted before I started), so no search index was used at all. Everything above comes from the funder's own BAA PDF and pages plus the Grants.gov and USAspending APIs, which is a stronger provenance than a search index, but it means I could not sweep for third-party writeups (university research-development office guides, ECP awardee blog posts) that might carry practitioner detail on review timing or success rates.

TOOLING NOTE, not a finding: ARL's topic list and contact form now live on a Salesforce Lightning portal (cftste.experience.crmforce.mil) that returns only a 'CSS Error' shell to a plain fetch; it required a rendering browser. Any future re-check of this row must use a browser, or it will falsely appear that the topic list is gone.

TOOLING NOTE, not a finding: DTIC public search is offline as of 2026-09-18 ('DTIC Public Search is offline while we enhance the capability'). This says nothing about whether funded abstracts are still being posted there.
