result.next_deadline:
**Tuesday— no: Wednesday 28 July 2027, by 5 p.m. submitting organization's local time.** That is the next open competition as of 2026-09-18; the 2026 round (22 July 2026) has closed.

Verbatim from NSF's CAREER page "Upcoming due dates" block (fetched directly 2026-09-18; page "Last updated: September 10, 2026"): "Full proposal / 2027 / July 28 2027 / - Deadline date / Fourth Wednesday in July, Annually Thereafter / Due by 5pm submitting organization's local time".

Three things make this date safe to publish rather than hedge:
1. It is a **Deadline Date** in NSF's three-way taxonomy, not a target date. Solicitation NSF 22-586: "Program Officers will be instructed to not accept any CAREER proposal after the deadline, unless there was a technical problem with the proposal submission... supported by documentation from Research.gov or Grants.gov at the time of submission and prior to the deadline. A possible slowdown of Research.gov or Grants.gov due to volume is not a valid reason for an extension." FAQ: "NSF Program Officers are not authorized to grant extensions of the CAREER deadline."
2. **Submitting organization's local time, not Eastern.** A West Coast PI genuinely has until 5 p.m. Pacific.
3. **One date for the whole agency.** Revision notes: "Only one annual deadline applies to all CAREER submissions, regardless of Directorate." No directorate variation, unlike GRFP.

Status check for drift: the programme's Updates page carries only three items — 8 July 2026 (webinar materials/FAQ), 15 June 2026 (contacts), 17 Dec 2019 (CAREER/PECASE info). **No cancellation, postponement, suspension or supersession notice.** NSF 22-586 remains in force (published 13 April 2022, last updated 10 September 2026). Contrast with MRI, where NSF skipped FY2026 outright — nothing of that kind exists for CAREER.
result.deadline_pattern:
**Fourth Wednesday in July, annually.** Verbatim on both NSF's programme page and in NSF 22-586: "Fourth Wednesday in July, Annually Thereafter", "due by 5 p.m. submitting organization's local time".

Instances: 27 Jul 2022 (first under 22-586) · 26 Jul 2023 · 24 Jul 2024 · 23 Jul 2025 · **22 Jul 2026 (closed)** · **28 Jul 2027 (next, published by NSF)** · 26 Jul 2028 (*computed from the rule, NOT published by NSF — label it as derived if displayed*).

The rule itself has moved once, which is the argument for publishing rule + dated snapshot rather than either alone. NSF 22-586 revision notes, verbatim: "Deadline changed to the 4th Wednesday of July at 5:00 p.m. local time. Changed from the 4th Monday of July." (The predecessor solicitation was NSF 20-525.)

No LOI date, no pre-proposal date, no separate reference-letter date. The July deadline is the only NSF-facing date in the cycle. The dates that actually bind earlier are institutional: your sponsored projects office's internal deadline (typically 3–10 business days before), and the Departmental Letter, which needs weeks of lead time from your department head.
result.loi_deadline:
Not applicable — there is none. NSF 22-586, Due Dates section, verbatim: **"Preliminary Proposal Submission: Not required"**. No letter of intent, no pre-proposal, no concept outline. The full proposal is the only submission, and everything must be in it: "You will not be allowed to submit these letters after the submission deadline, so plan in advance."

The practical substitutes for an LOI stage, which an applicant should treat as real milestones:
- **Departmental Letter** (mandatory, see submission_requirements) — your department head must certify your eligibility and describe how they will mentor you. Allow 4–6 weeks; this is the item most likely to be late, and its absence is an automatic return without review.
- **Program Officer conversation** — not required but strongly expected, and it is the de facto scoping stage, because "some programs do not accept CAREER proposals" (see program_officer_contact).
- **Institutional internal deadline** — the AOR submits, not you.
- **Long-lead account plumbing** — the solicitation itself sets CAREER-specific lead times: new organizations should start SAM registration "at least five weeks in advance"; PIs without an NSF ID (or who have not signed in for a while) "at least three weeks in advance."
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
**Both halves matter, and the preserving half is much larger than applicants assume. CAREER is gated on RANK AND TENURE, not on your funding history.**

=== WHAT DISQUALIFIES YOU ===

**1. A prior CAREER award — and only a CAREER award.** Eligibility list, verbatim: "Have not previously received a CAREER award." FAQ: "You may not submit a CAREER proposal if you already have received a CAREER award." This is the single funding-history disqualifier in the whole mechanism.

**2. Having used three reviewed attempts.** "a Principal Investigator may not participate in more than three CAREER competitions."

**3. Rank/tenure status as of the deadline date** (not funding, but this is where people actually fail). All must be true **as of the annual deadline**: hold a doctoral degree in an NSF-supported field; be engaged in NSF-supported research; "Hold at least a 50% tenure-track (or tenure-track-equivalent) position as an assistant professor (or equivalent title)"; "Be untenured". Then, in capitals in the solicitation: **"NO EXEMPTIONS FROM THESE ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA WILL BE GRANTED."**
- Associate professors are out regardless of funding or tenure: "Faculty members who are Associate Professors or in equivalent appointments, with or without tenure, are not eligible." FAQ: "No. An associate professor (with or without tenure) is not eligible."
- Adjuncts are out: "Faculty members who hold Adjunct Faculty or equivalent appointments are not eligible."
- Degree conferred, not defended: "No. You are not eligible unless you receive the official, dated diploma, by the proposal deadline."

**4. RUI is mutually exclusive with CAREER** (an under-known conflict). FAQ, verbatim: "No. You must choose between submitting a proposal to the RUI or to the CAREER program solicitation. You may not include the additional Certificate of RUI Eligibility or the RUI Impact Statement on a CAREER proposal."

**5. Overlap with your own live submissions.** Returned without review if "The proposed work duplicates, or is substantially similar to, a proposal already under consideration by NSF from the same submitter."

**6. PECASE double-dip** (honorific only): "persons who have received PECASE awards through other agencies may be eligible for CAREER, [but] they are not eligible to be nominated by NSF for another PECASE award."

=== WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY ===

**1. THE key sentence.** Parenthetical inside the eligibility list, verbatim: **"(Prior or concurrent Federal support for other types of awards for non-duplicative research does not preclude eligibility.)"** FAQ expands it: "Yes. You may submit a CAREER proposal if you have NSF or other Federal awards. What you propose to do as part of your CAREER proposal should not overlap what you have been funded to do by NSF or any other agency." So a live NSF standard grant, an NIH R01, a DOE or DOD award, a CRII — none of them touch your CAREER eligibility. **There is no NIH-style K/R01 interaction here.** The only constraint is non-duplication of scope.

**2. No time-since-PhD clock at all.** "Yes, if you satisfy all the eligibility criteria. CAREER eligibility is not limited by time from degree or years in a tenure track appointment." (Asked by someone 6 years past the doctorate.) The window is defined solely by pre-tenure assistant-professor status — which can be much longer or shorter than the 5–10 years typical of other early-career schemes.

**3. Prior tenure elsewhere is irrelevant.** "Previous employment in a tenured position does not affect eligibility."

**4. Tenure already notified, effective in the fall → still eligible this year.** "Your status on the proposal submission deadline date is used to determine eligibility. If your tenure and promotion is effective after the proposal submission deadline date, and you meet the other eligibility requirements, you are eligible to apply." This buys a genuine final attempt for many people.

**5. No citizenship requirement.** "Yes. You may apply if you are employed at an eligible U.S. organization and meet the other CAREER eligibility requirements." (PECASE nomination separately requires US citizen/national/permanent resident.)

**6. An NSF postdoctoral fellowship does not disqualify** — it only triggers a Results from Prior NSF Support section.

**7. Non-traditional employers qualify.** Museums, observatories, research labs: "Yes, but you must hold at least a 50% tenure-track or tenure-track-equivalent appointment... The non-degree granting organization... must be non-profit and located in the United States." Two-year and community colleges: "Yes, as long as your appointment meets the CAREER eligibility requirements." Non-tenure-track appointments can qualify via tenure-track equivalency — (1) continuing appointment expected to last the five years, (2) substantial research and educational responsibilities, (3) project relates to career goals and the department's mission — but the Departmental Letter must then "clearly and convincingly demonstrate" it.

**8. Unreviewed attempts are free.** "Proposals that are not reviewed (i.e., are withdrawn before review or are returned without review) do not count toward the three-competition limit." You get three *reviewed* shots.

**9. A concurrent non-CAREER NSF proposal is fine** if genuinely distinct: "Yes, but only if the research is substantially different." (Talk to the PO if both go to the same program.)
result.review_to_award:
**NSF's own CAREER commitment — verbatim from the CAREER FAQ (NSF 22-100), section C:** "Most proposers will be notified within six months of submission. If you have not received notification of a decision on your proposal within six months of its submission, you can contact the program or division to which your proposal was assigned to inquire about the status of your proposal."

From a fourth-Wednesday-in-July deadline that puts **notification at roughly late January**. This matches the NSF-wide six-month norm, so no deviation on the decision step.

**Where CAREER deviates in practice is the gap between notification and money.** Observed, not policy — NSF Award Search API sample taken 2026-09-18 (n = 49 distinct awards whose titles begin "CAREER:" with start dates in calendar 2026, i.e. the July 2025 competition):
- **Award/obligation dates** cluster March–August 2026, peaking May–July.
- **Project start dates** cluster June–September 2026, peaking July (17 of 49); 13 in September, 8 each in June and August.

So the realistic arc from a late-July deadline is: decision ≈ 6 months (late Jan) → signed award ≈ 8–12 months → **project start typically the following summer, ≈ 11–14 months after submission.** Budget your bridge funding for about a year. *This is a partial API sample, not the full population, and NSF publishes no CAREER-specific award-date or start-date commitment — present it as observed practice, never as a rule.*

Other CAREER-specific timing facts:
- Start dates are negotiable with the Program Officer and normally fall on the first of a month (NSF-wide practice).
- Notification mechanics, verbatim: "Notification of the award is made to the submitting organization by a Grants Officer in the Division of Grants and Agreements. Organizations whose proposals are declined will be advised as promptly as possible by the cognizant NSF Program... Verbatim copies of reviews, not including the identity of the reviewer, will be provided automatically to the Principal Investigator."
- Scale: "Estimated Number of Awards: 500 per year", "Anticipated Funding Amount: $250,000,000" (approximate, includes continuing increments).
- Award size: minimum $400,000 over 5 years including indirect costs; **minimum $500,000 for BIO, ENG and OPP**. CISE states expected content instead of a floor: "one month of PI salary per year, one graduate student per year, and two trips per year." Voluntary committed cost sharing is prohibited.
- Everything else follows the NSF review arc unchanged — compliance check, ad hoc and/or panel review, PO recommendation, Division Director concurrence, DGA decision within ~30 days of the recommendation.
result.submission_requirements:
**Standard PAPPG 24-1 applies; these are the CAREER-specific deviations. Two of them cause automatic return without review.**

**THE TWO AUTOMATIC KILLERS.** NSF lists exactly two CAREER-specific return-without-review grounds: "Co-principal investigator(s) listed on the cover page" and "Departmental Letter is missing (be sure to put the letter in the Supplementary Documents section, not the Single Copy Documents section)."

**1. DEPARTMENTAL LETTER — mandatory, 2 pages, and it is reviewed.** "a proposal submitted without this Letter will be returned without review". One and only one letter, from the PI's department head or equivalent; in joint appointments "signed by both department heads". "The Departmental Letter should be no more than 2 pages in length and include the department head's name and title below the signature." It counts toward the science: "which will be included as part of the consideration of the overall merits of the proposal." Required elements:
 (a) a statement that the PI is eligible — and for non-tenure-track faculty it "must clearly and convincingly demonstrate how the faculty member satisfies all the requirements of tenure-track equivalency";
 (b) that the CAREER research and education activities "are supported by and advance the educational and research goals of the department and the organization, and that the department is committed to the support and professional development of the PI";
 (c) the relationship between the project, the PI's career goals and the department's mission, **and** "the ways in which the department head (or equivalent) will ensure the appropriate mentoring of the PI... throughout the period of the award and beyond."
 Critical framing most people get wrong: **"Note that the Department Letter should not be construed as a Letter of Support for the PI and should address only the items listed above."** It is not a reference letter and must not read like one. FAQ: "Eligibility for the CAREER award is certified by the Departmental letter. The Department Head is responsible for verifying that all eligibility requirements are met."

**2. NO CO-PIs, ANYWHERE.** "No co-PIs are permitted on the Cover Sheet." "Proposals submitted with co-principal investigators will be returned without review." Collaborators go in senior/key personnel, consultants, or subawards — "commensurate with their limited role."

**3. TITLE PREFIX.** "The project title must begin with 'CAREER:' and follow with an informative title." (This is also what makes the funded-award search work — see examples.)

**4. PROJECT DESCRIPTION — 15 pages, but with mandated content.** Five required elements: the research project (with preliminary data where appropriate, objectives, methods, expected significance); "the proposed educational activities and their intended impact"; "how the research and educational activities are integrated or synergistic"; "other broader impacts, besides the education activities"; and "results of prior NSF support, if applicable." Results from Prior is capped at 5 pages inside the 15. "Visual materials, including charts, graphs, maps, photographs, and other pictorial presentations are included in the 15-page limitation." **No URLs**: "the Project Description must be self-contained and... URLs must not be used." Research and education need not be separate sections: "The research and educational activities do not need to be addressed separately if the relationship between the two is such that the presentation of the integrated project is better served by interspersing the two."
 Calibration, verbatim: "While excellence in both education and research is expected, activity of an intensity that leads to an unreasonable workload is not... teaching additional courses or taking on additional duties is not expected."

**5. RESULTS FROM PRIOR NSF SUPPORT is triggered far more broadly than people expect** — and NSF lists a missing one among common CAREER non-compliance causes. FAQ: "You must include a 'Results from Prior Support' section whenever you have served as a PI or co-PI on any NSF grant active in the past five years. This includes postdoctoral fellowships, conferences, EAGER or RAPID grants, and equipment grants such as Major Research Instrumentation (MRI). If you have received more than one prior award (excluding amendments), you need only report on the award that is most closely related to the CAREER proposal."

**6. NO APPENDICES.** "No appendices are permitted."

**7. LETTERS — what is and is not allowed.** Letters of collaboration must use NSF's single-sentence template ("If the proposal submitted by Dr. [name] entitled [title] is selected for funding by the NSF, it is my intent to collaborate and/or commit resources as detailed in the Project Description or the Facilities, Equipment or Other Resources section of the proposal."); "Departure from this format may result in the proposal being returned without review." Place them in Supplementary Documents **after** the departmental letter. And flatly: **"letters of recommendation for the PI or other letters of support for the project are not permitted."**
 → So, unlike NIH career awards: **no reference letters, no sponsor/mentor statement, no mentor's training plan.** The Departmental Letter is the only external letter, and it is institutional certification, not a reference.

**8. PECASE SINGLE-COPY DOCUMENT (optional, costs nothing).** Upload a statement reading: "I wish to be considered for the PECASE honorary award." If you become eligible only after the award is made, you can add it later via an Interim Project Report in Research.gov. PECASE is honorary and carries no extra NSF funds; up to 26 NSF nominees a year, drawn only from recent CAREER awardees.

**9. BUDGET.** Budget Justification "maximum of five pages". Minimums as above ($400K; $500K in BIO/ENG/OPP). Cost sharing prohibited. NSF pushes you toward the floor: "Many programs and Directorates prefer to make more awards by funding CAREER proposals closer to the minimum award size." Academic-year salary is allowed but conditional — discuss with the PO first.

**10. CAREER GETS ITS OWN EXTRA-LEAD-TIME WARNING.** NSF's Supplementary Proposal Submission Timeline (April 2026) says submit 3 business days early via Research.gov / 5 via Grants.gov, then singles this mechanism out: "extra days are recommended for some programs such as the Faculty Early Career Development Program (CAREER) due to the large number of expected CAREER proposal submissions leading up to and on the deadline date." Solicitation adds: new organizations start SAM "at least five weeks in advance"; new/dormant NSF IDs "at least three weeks in advance"; NSF account reconciliation "can take up to three days."

**11. FIXES ARE FREE BEFORE THE DEADLINE, NOT AFTER.** Proposal file updates "will be automatically accepted only if submitted prior to the CAREER deadline." After it, only technical/print problems, only with your PO's approval.

**12. Otherwise standard PAPPG 24-1:** SciENcv biosketch (Common Form v.2024-1, no page limit since 20 May 2024), SciENcv Current & Pending (Other) Support, COA spreadsheet, Synergistic Activities 1 page, Data Management and Sharing Plan now a Research.gov webform (from 27 April 2026, no PDF uploads), Mentoring Plan 1 page if postdocs are supported, Project Summary 1 page in three boxes. AOR submits — no self-submission. Research.gov or Grants.gov both accepted.
result.program_officer_contact:
**Yes — named contacts exist, and pre-submission contact is explicitly encouraged in the solicitation itself.** There are two distinct routes, and you usually want both.

**A. Your disciplinary Program Officer** — the one who will actually handle your proposal. Solicitation, verbatim: **"Proposers are also encouraged to contact the appropriate NSF Program Officer when preparing a submission, as some programs do not accept CAREER proposals."** That trailing clause is the single highest-value reason to call: some NSF programs do not take CAREER proposals at all, and you cannot tell from outside. FAQ: "Your primary contact is a Program Officer in a division or program that is closest to your area of research."

**B. Division/Directorate CAREER contacts** — a published, named list (page dated 15 June 2026), which the solicitation designates as the official route: "General inquiries regarding this program should be made to: Division CAREER contacts listed on the CAREER web page." The current list:

**C. Programme-level catch-all:** nsf-ccc@nsf.gov, (703) 292-5111 ("Faculty Early Career program").

**WHEN AND WHAT TO ASK — NSF tells you directly.** Contact is expected during planning, not deadline week, and the solicitation names three specific occasions:
1. **Scope/home** — is this in your program, and does your program even take CAREER proposals? Also for cross-disciplinary work: "You are strongly encouraged to contact the Program Officer(s) most closely related to the subject matter when preparing a cross-disciplinary proposal."
2. **Budget** — "Before preparing a CAREER proposal, PIs are strongly encouraged to contact their disciplinary Program Officer or the appropriate CAREER contact to discuss budget requests for their proposed CAREER activities, and typical funding levels for their discipline." Also required reading before requesting academic-year salary: "you should contact your disciplinary Program Officer to discuss your individual case."
3. **Readiness / which of your three attempts to spend** — "You might discuss your readiness and your career development to date with your Department Chair, your mentor, or an NSF Program Officer."
Plus: if you plan a CAREER proposal and another proposal to the same NSF program, "please contact the appropriate Program Officer to discuss your individual case"; and if a submission problem hits, get documentation before the deadline.

**D. The low-friction alternative to cold-emailing — NSF runs a CAREER webinar season every spring.** In 2026: CAREER Program Informational Webinars (29 April and 19 May), CAREER Proposal Submission Logistics Webinar (25 June), plus directorate-level sessions — ENG CMMI CAREER webinar (6 May), ENG CBET Early-Career Faculty Workshop (6 May), Engineering Education Research CAREER webinar (16 June), MPS Materials Research open hour on CAREER (8 June), BIO virtual office hour (21 May). These are group Q&A with the same POs. They recur each spring ahead of the July deadline — watch https://www.nsf.gov/events from about March.

Note on rotators: many NSF POs serve temporary terms, so verify a name against the current contacts page (dated 15 June 2026) rather than an older solicitation.
result.examples_or_samples:
**1. The best route, and it works because of a CAREER formatting rule.** Every CAREER title "must begin with 'CAREER:'", so a title-only search for that string in NSF Award Search returns the funded population with public abstracts, award amounts, dates, institutions and the signing Program Officer. NSF's own CAREER page publishes exactly this pre-built query under "Awards made through this program — Browse projects funded by this program":
https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/search-results?AwardTitleOnly=true&BooleanElement=All&BooleanRef=All&Keyword=CAREER%3A&sortBy=date
Filter to your division and the last 2–3 years. Read 15–20 abstracts: they tell you what the program actually funds, what it actually pays, and whom to email. NSF instructs you to do this for budget calibration — "Proposers should also review the list of recent CAREER awards made in their discipline for guidance on average award size" — and for programme-finding: "You may also search on keywords in the NSF Award Search tool to find funded research projects in areas related to your project. The search results indicate the NSF program(s) supporting those projects and names of Program Officers managing those projects."

**2. NSF's own closest thing to a worked example — the CAREER webinar decks (free, current, mechanism-specific):**
- Programme/solicitation walkthrough: "NSF CAREER Program: NSF 22-586 Webinar Slides" (29 Apr 2026) — https://nsf-gov-resources.nsf.gov/files/CAREER_NSF_22-586_Program_29Apr26_508.pdf
- Submission logistics, including a live demo of building a CAREER proposal in Research.gov: https://nsf-gov-resources.nsf.gov/files/CAREER-06-2026-webinar.pdf (25 Jun 2026). Described as "a review of the system-related requirements in the NSF Supplementary Proposal Submission Timeline Guidance, a demo of how to prepare an NSF CAREER proposal in Research.gov, and a Q&A session." The recording is posted on the Research.gov homepage after each event.

**3. Practice environment, no risk:** the Research.gov Proposal Preparation Demo Site — build a mock CAREER proposal end to end, including uploading a biosketch and Current & Pending, before touching the real one.

**4. Full funded CAREER proposals: FOIA only.** Awarded proposals are released on request with personal and proprietary information removed; start at https://www.nsf.gov/policies/foia. Weeks to months. Reviews, panel summaries and review analyses are FOIA-exempt — you will only ever see reviews of your own proposals, released to you through Research.gov after the decision.

**5. The fastest realistic route to reading a real funded CAREER narrative: your own institution.** Many university research development offices and libraries keep internal collections of successful CAREER proposals for their own faculty — CAREER is the most commonly collected type, because departments have a direct stake in their assistant professors winning them. Ask the research development office directly rather than assuming none exists. (Community practice, not an NSF claim.)

**6. Set expectations honestly: unlike GRFP, there is NO public archive of successful CAREER narratives.** There is no CAREER equivalent of the Alex Lang GRFP essay collection or MIT CommLab's annotated GRFP examples. Anyone looking for a downloadable model CAREER Project Description will not find one from NSF or from a stable community source — the abstracts plus an institutional sample collection are the realistic substitutes.

**7. Supporting sources:** NSF Public Access Repository (NSF-PAR) for publications from funded CAREER awards; USAspending.gov for the money side; the CAREER FAQ (NSF 22-100) for 40+ worked edge cases on eligibility, budget and submission.
result.resubmission_note:
**Allowed. But NSF has no "resubmission" object — a declined CAREER proposal returns as a brand-new proposal in the next annual competition, to a possibly different panel, with no space to rebut the prior reviews.** Structurally the opposite of NIH: no A1, no Introduction to Resubmission, no time window.

**The CAREER-specific cap:** "a Principal Investigator may not participate in more than three CAREER competitions." One proposal per competition: "You may submit only one CAREER proposal per year."

**The carve-out that should drive strategy, verbatim:** "Proposals that are not reviewed (i.e., are withdrawn before review or are returned without review) do not count toward the three-competition limit." So you get **three *reviewed* attempts**. Withdrawing before review costs you a year but not an attempt; and a compliance return likewise costs a year but not an attempt. Under PAPPG you may withdraw "at any time before a funding recommendation is made by the cognizant NSF Program Officer."

**The trap on the way back in.** The CAREER solicitation lists as its own return-without-review ground: "The proposal was previously declined and was not revised to take into account the major comments from the prior NSF review." PAPPG: "A declined proposal may be resubmitted, but only after it has undergone substantial revision," and "The Foundation will treat the revised proposal as a new proposal, subject to the standard review procedures." Because there is no rebuttal section and no appendices are permitted, experienced applicants (a) call the Program Officer to find out what the panel actually meant — NSF sanctions the post-declination conversation — and (b) fold the responses into the Project Description narrative itself.

**Timing your three shots.** Eligibility ends at tenure or promotion to associate, so the three reviewed attempts must fit inside the pre-tenure window — but note the two extensions above: there is no time-since-PhD limit, and a tenure decision effective *after* the July deadline still leaves you eligible that year. NSF deliberately declines to prescribe when to spend an attempt: "The most important consideration is whether you are ready to write a proposal with an innovative research idea, and an education plan, aligned with the mission of your department or organization."

**Concurrent submissions.** A CAREER plus a regular NSF proposal in the same year is fine "only if the research is substantially different. NSF may return without review a second proposal on a closely related research topic." Never submit duplicate CAREER proposals to multiple programs; instead designate more than one program on one cover sheet.

**Formal reconsideration** (about process, not science, and rarely used): request from the Assistant Director/Office Head within 90 days of the declination; answer within 45 days; appeal to the Deputy Director within 60 days, answered within 30; that decision is final.

K43 is a PAR with its own custom single annual date, so the standard K calendar does not apply and there is no June or October fallback — it is one shot per year, and missing it costs a full twelve months. The functionally equivalent early step is not a form but a conversation: the NOFO says "Prospective applicants are strongly encouraged to contact the FIC Scientific/Research contact prior to preparing an application to discuss their eligibility" — for K43 this is close to mandatory in practice, because the eligibility rules (LMIC citizenship, one year in post, two-mentor structure, prior-award exclusions counting non-NIH funders) are where applications die.
result.review_to_award: Published in the NOFO's own Key Dates table, so this is mechanism-specific rather than inferred from NIH cycle norms. For the December 3, 2026 due date, both PARs list: "Scientific Merit Review: March 2027"; "Advisory Council Review: May 2027"; "Earliest Start Date: July 2027". That is roughly 3 months submission-to-review, 5 months to council, and about 7 months from submission to earliest possible project start — a single annual track rather than the three-cycle NIH norm, and slightly faster council-to-start than the norm's Cycle III. Score release and summary statement follow NIH-wide practice (scores posted in eRA Commons within days of the March meeting; summary statement typically within about a month). Just-in-Time sits between council and award and is required at least 60 days before the proposed start date — i.e. by roughly early May 2027 for a July 2027 start, which for an LMIC institution means IRB/IEC approvals and other-support documents should be in motion well before council. Two timing caveats specific to this cycle: (1) NIH's emergency review modifications (NOT-OD-26-114 — reduced discussion rates, three-tier outcomes, simplified summary statements) are announced only through the January 2027 council round, so whether they reach this NOFO's March 2027 review / May 2027 council is not yet announced; (2) with one due date a year, the practical cost of a misstep is a 12-month slip, not a 4-month one.
result.submission_requirements:
Standard NIH machinery applies (Grants.gov / ASSIST / S2S, eRA Commons, AOR submission, no error-correction window, ORCID + SciENcv Common Forms). Recorded here are the K43-SPECIFIC DEVIATIONS:

1. PICK THE RIGHT NOFO OF TWO. PAR-24-296 = "Not Allowed: Only accepting applications that do not propose clinical trials. Applicants may propose to gain experience in a clinical trial led by a mentor/co-mentor as part of research career development." PAR-24-295 = for applicants proposing to lead an independent clinical trial, feasibility study or separate ancillary trial; only mechanistic trials are supported, and trials of safety, tolerability, clinical efficacy, effectiveness or clinical management are excluded. PAR-24-295 additionally requires at least one human subjects study record on the PHS Human Subjects and Clinical Trials Information form (or a Delayed Onset record). Applying under the wrong one is a withdrawal, not a correctable error.

2. TWO PRIMARY MENTORS — the single biggest structural deviation from a domestic K. Fogarty FAQ, verbatim: "Applicants are required to have two primary mentors: one primary mentor at the LMIC applicant institution and one primary mentor at the collaborating U.S. institution." A US collaborating institution and mentor must therefore be lined up months before submission.

3. REFERENCE LETTERS ARE A SEPARATE SUBMISSION CHANNEL AND A HARD GATE. NOFO verbatim: "Candidates must carefully follow the SF424 (R&R) Application Guide, including the time period for when reference letters will be accepted. Applications lacking the appropriate required reference letters will not be reviewed. This is a separate process from submitting an application electronically. Reference letters are submitted directly through the eRA Commons Submit Referee Information link and not through Grants.gov." The review criteria ask whether "the reference letters from at least three well-established scientists address the candidate's potential for becoming an independent researcher" — so at least three, from referees other than the mentors, submitted by the referees themselves in eRA Commons.

4. PAGE-LIMIT DEVIATION: "Institutional Commitment to Candidate's Research Career Development is limited to two pages" — double the one page in the NIH-wide K page-limit table. Other K page limits (Candidate Information and Goals 12 pages, Specific Aims 1, mentor plans and statements 6, letters of support 6, RCR 1) are not restated as modified in Section IV.

5. EFFORT: "Candidates are required to commit a minimum of 75% of full-time professional effort (i.e., a minimum of 9 person-months or 30 hours per week) to their career development and research training" (FAQ; the NOFO states the same 75% / 9 person-months).

6. BUDGET AND PERIOD: "The NIH will contribute up to $100,000 per year toward the salary of the career award recipient" and "up to $40,000 per year toward the research development costs"; "The total project period should be a minimum of 3 years and may not exceed 5 years."

7. TIME-IN-POST GATE: the applicant "must hold an academic junior faculty position or research scientist appointment at the LMIC applicant institution and must have been in this position for at least one year at the time the application is submitted." Junior faculty = "entry to mid-level academic or research scientist positions, including but not limited to instructors, lecturers, and assistant professors. Usually these are institutionally funded positions, not grant supported positions."

8. THE APPLICANT ORGANIZATION IS THE LMIC INSTITUTION, NOT THE US PARTNER. That institution must itself hold SAM.gov/UEI, Grants.gov and eRA Commons registrations and must supply the AOR who submits. For a foreign institution registering for the first time, NIH's six-week guidance is a floor, not a target — this is the most common way a K43 misses a once-a-year deadline.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
Both halves, quoted verbatim, and the wording is identical in PAR-24-296 and PAR-24-295 (corroborated by two independent fetches).

DISQUALIFYING: "Current and former PDs/PIs (including Multiple PDs/PIs) on NIH research project (R01), program project (P01), research training (D43), or center (P50) grants, or Project Leads of program project (P01) or center (P50) grants, other major individual career development awards (e.g., K01, K07, K08, K22, K23, K25, K76, K99/R00), or the equivalent to these grants/awards (including non-NIH equivalent grants/awards from other research funding organizations) are not eligible."

PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY: "Current and former PDs/PIs (including Multiple PDs/PIs) of an NIH Small Grant (R03), Exploratory/Developmental Grant (R21/R33), Planning Grant (R34/U34), Dissertation Award (R36), or SBIR/STTR (R41, R42, R43, R44) remain eligible, as do PD/PIs of Transition Scholar (K38) awards and individuals appointed to institutional K programs (K12, KL2)." Fogarty's FAQ restates the safe half plainly: "Individuals who are or have been the PD/PI (including Multiple PDs/PIs) on exploratory/developmental grants -- like the NIH's Small Grant (R03) and Exploratory/Developmental Grant (R21) -- remain eligible."

THE CLAUSE THAT CATCHES LMIC APPLICANTS: the exclusion explicitly reaches beyond NIH. FAQ verbatim: "Individuals who are or have been the PD/PI (including Multiple PD/PI) of a multi-year R01-equivalent independent research grant from an external research funding (not just the NIH) organization and awarded by the application due date are not eligible." So a multi-year independent research grant from Wellcome, EDCTP, a national research council, a major foundation, or similar counts as an R01-equivalent and disqualifies — while a domestically funded small or exploratory grant, an institutional K12/KL2 appointment, or a K38 does not. Two practical readings that follow from the text: the test is being PD/PI of an R01-equivalent, so co-investigator or trainee roles on large grants do not disqualify; and the trigger is an award held "by the application due date", so a pending R01-equivalent application is not itself disqualifying. Because "equivalent" is a judgement call about a non-NIH award, this is precisely the question the NOFO wants raised with the FIC program officer before writing — "strongly encouraged to contact the FIC Scientific/Research contact prior to preparing an application to discuss their eligibility."

Allowed, under the ordinary NIH rules — Fogarty's FAQ answers the question directly ("Yes, you can") and points to the NIH/AHRQ Application Submission/Resubmission Policy at NOT-OD-18-197. result.deadline_pattern:
Annual, and unusually rigid by federal standards: one national deadline for the whole 380-award programme, no rolling window, no second call.

The shape: competition opens ~February → single application deadline mid-September at 5:00 PM Eastern → peer review Oct-Nov → peer-review notification December → embassy/commission/FFSB selection December-May → final notification January-June → grants begin June onward. So you apply roughly 9-12 months before you would travel, and the academic year in the award title (e.g. "2027-2028") is the year you would GO, not the year you apply.

Two structural quirks a first-timer misses:
1. Recommendation letters are due at the SAME instant as the application, not after: "Recommendations must be submitted by September 15, 2026, 5:00 PM EDT (UTC-4:00)." The recommender instructions are blunt about it: "The recommendation/evaluation system will close on this deadline. This means you will not be able to submit your letter after this date and time. Exceptions will not be granted."
2. The invitation letter is the ONLY component with a later deadline — a 10-day extension to 25 September 2026. "If your invitation is expected to arrive after the application deadline, you should submit your application without the letter. You will be able to upload your invitation letter to your application via the Application Status page until the deadline above."

IEA awards break the single-deadline pattern entirely with three staggered dates (Sept / Nov / Feb) — "Refer to IEA page for award-specific deadline dates; all applications due at 5:00 PM Eastern Time."
result.loi_deadline:
No LOI, pre-proposal, white paper, or encourage/discourage stage exists anywhere in this mechanism — a genuine structural difference from DOE SC. The published timeline goes straight from "competition opens" (February) to the application deadline (September) with nothing in between.

The functional analogue, and the thing that actually behaves like a gated pre-stage, is the LETTER OF INVITATION from the proposed host abroad. Its deadline is 25 September 2026, 5:00 PM EDT — ten days AFTER the application itself. Awards fall into four states, quoted: "An invitation letter is required: You must submit an invitation letter. An invitation letter is preferred: You are encouraged to obtain and submit an invitation letter. An invitation letter is optional: You may submit an invitation letter. An invitation letter should not be sought: There will not be a place to upload an invitation."

Where it is required it is a hard eligibility gate: "For awards where the invitation is required: If your letter(s) are not submitted by this extended deadline, your application will become ineligible and will not proceed in the review and selection process." Where it is not: "If an invitation is not required, your application will proceed in the review process with or without an invitation."

Practically this is the long-lead item, because securing it means cold-contacting a foreign institution months ahead. "It is the applicant's responsibility to contact potential hosts." Host rules: "Appropriate hosts might include a non-profit organization, artist residency, studio collective, governmental agency, museum, professional association, cultural organization, K-12 institution, university, college, language institute, research institute, laboratory, think tank or foundation. For-profit organizations may not serve as hosts." And "Local organizations operated by citizens of the host country are preferred over U.S. institutions abroad."
result.review_to_award: Submission → immediate confirmation email from scholars@iie.org → IIE eligibility/completeness screen (Sept-Oct) → discipline-based peer review (October-November) → first notification, recommended/not recommended (December, ~3 months) → Embassy or binational Commission + U.S. Department of State + Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board selection, all three must approve (December-May) → final notification (January-June, ~4-9 months) → grants begin June onward (~9-12+ months from submission). Deviates from the federal norm chiefly in having two notifications rather than one, a foreign-government body in the decision chain, and no published decision-by date. Quoted: "This phase of the review process normally requires several months"; "All three entities must approve selection decisions before candidates can be notified"; "Please note decisions are not communicated by phone." Selected candidates must then submit "a Medical History and Examination Report before their grants."
result.submission_requirements: Individual application direct to IIE at https://apply.iie.org/fusc2027 — no SAM.gov, UEI, Grants.gov, AOR or institutional sign-off, and no U.S. institutional affiliation required. Format for all documents: single-spaced, 12-point, 1-inch margins, PDF or Word. Project Statement "3-5 pages"; CV "Up to 6 pages" (Distinguished Scholar "up to 8 pages"); TWO recommendations, "Up to 3 pages" each, due at the application deadline itself; four character-capped short essays (Country Selection 2,000; Why Fulbright 1,500; Cultural Preparation 2,000; Teaching Preparation 1,500). Research/Teaching-Research add a bibliography "Up to 3 pages"; Teaching/Teaching-Research add syllabi "Up to 10 pages, total"; arts and journalism add a portfolio; language-required awards add a self-evaluation plus an externally registered evaluator. Invitation letter per award status (required/preferred/optional/not sought), due 25 Sept 2026. IEA deviates: institutional statement up to 2 pages, four different essays, no language requirement. Traps: a recommender "may not also provide the applicant with an invitation letter or foreign language evaluation"; relatives, host-country Embassy/Commission staff, ECA staff, and IIE/CIES board or staff cannot recommend; recommendations are confidential and must be in English; the applicant must register recommenders in the portal before they receive anything; the recommendation system closes at the deadline and "Exceptions will not be granted." All four review criteria must be met — "Applications must at minimum sufficiently address each of the review criteria in order to be recommended or ultimately selected" — including Cultural Preparation, which is scored.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
BOTH HALVES, and the carve-outs are unusually generous.

WHAT BLOCKS YOU
 • The two-year rule: "Recipients of a Fulbright Scholar award are eligible to apply for another award two years after the date of completion of the previous award." Measured from COMPLETION, not from award. For multi-trip awards: "For Flex awards, the two-year period begins at the end of the final segment (trip) in the series."
 • Which prior awards trigger it — an explicit closed list: "Fulbright Scholar awards include: Fulbright U.S. Scholar (including Distinguished Scholar/Chair awards), International Education Administrator Seminar, Fulbright Arctic, and Fulbright Visiting Scholar."
 • A soft but real penalty even after the two years: "Preference for Fulbright Scholar opportunities will be given to candidates who have not previously received a Fulbright Scholar grant."
 • No double-running: "Applicants may be on the Specialist roster, but may not carry out both a U.S. Scholar grant and a Specialist grant simultaneously."
 • Wrong career stage: "Graduate or doctoral students seeking funding to complete their degrees are ineligible. Recent college graduates with limited professional experience are ineligible and should instead apply to the Fulbright U.S. Student Program."
 • Conflict-of-interest employment — ineligible until one year after the engagement ends: U.S. Department of State employees and their "spouses and dependent children" (paid or unpaid, part-time, temporary, consultants, externs, fellows, contract employees — "does not include interns"); also "a current board member or staff of the Institute of International Education or the Council for International Exchange of Scholars; a board member or staff of a Fulbright Commission; a member of the Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board; an Alumni Ambassador for the Fulbright U.S. Scholar Program."
 • Residence abroad: "Applicants who have resided abroad for five or more years in the six-year period preceding the application deadline are ineligible. A period of nine months or more during a calendar year constitutes a full year."
 • Citizenship: "Applicants must hold U.S. citizenship by the application deadline. Permanent residence is not sufficient." Dual nationals may be barred from their other country of nationality — "Individual award descriptions specify whether this is a point of ineligibility."

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the half most readers need)
 • A prior Fulbright U.S. STUDENT award does NOT trigger the two-year rule — it is absent from the closed list above. (It does not help you either: "Experience gained as an undergraduate student does not count toward years of experience for the Fulbright U.S. Scholar Program (including internships and Fulbright U.S. Student Program awards).")
 • Fulbright Specialist, in both directions: "Recipients of a Fulbright Specialist Program grant are not required to adhere to the two-year waiting period before applying for a Fulbright Scholar grant. Likewise, recipients of a Fulbright Scholar grant are not required to adhere to the two-year waiting period before applying for or receiving a Fulbright Specialist Program grant."
 • Being on the roster is fine: "You are eligible to apply to the Fulbright Scholar Program while on the Fulbright Specialist roster."
 • State Dept English Language Fellows are carved out of the employment bar: "This provision does not apply to U.S. Department of State English Language Fellow (EL Fellow) Program fellows."
 • No U.S. institutional affiliation required, so unaffiliated/independent scholars, retired and emeriti faculty are eligible: "The Fulbright U.S. Scholar Program is open to applications from retired and Emeriti faculty."
 • NOTHING in the programme's eligibility rules excludes concurrent or prior NON-Fulbright funding (NSF, NIH, DOE, private foundation). No such bar was found anywhere on the eligibility page.

CAREER-STAGE WINDOWS (these are the de facto eligibility gate for postdocs/early-career): "Early Career Academics: Awards are open to those who have been working in the capacity of a teacher or scholar for no more than seven years." Postdoctoral awards — the funder's own page is internally inconsistent: the award-type section says "within five to seven years of the fellowship start date, as noted in the award description", while the eligibility accordion says "within five years of the fellowship start date, unless otherwise noted on the award description's Award Requirements section." Both defer to the individual award, so the award description governs — check it, do not rely on either number.
result.program_officer_contact: Per-award IIE staff named in each award description ("please contact the IIE staff listed on the award") — start here. Regional desks: subsaharanafrica@iie.org, eastasiapacific@iie.org, europeeurasia@iie.org, middleeastnorthafrica@iie.org, southcentralasia@iie.org, westhem@iie.org, IEA@iie.org, Arctic@iie.org, amazonia@iie.org. General/system and recommender problems: Scholars@iie.org. Review-process queries: FulbrightScholarReview@iie.org (email from the address on your application, with full name and host country). IIE, 1350 Eye St NW, Washington DC 20005, 202.686.4000. Campus route: Fulbright Scholar Liaison Network, 1,600+ liaisons, https://fulbrightscholars.org/liaisons. Live group advising: Office Hours, https://apply.iie.org/portal/office_hours (none scheduled as of 2026-09-18; expect resumption ~Feb 2027). Pre-submission contact with IIE is invited, not mandatory; pre-submission contact with the prospective HOST abroad is effectively unavoidable and is the applicant's own responsibility.
result.examples_or_samples: Funder's own pages (no search index needed). Best: the cycle-specific "Application Writing Clinic for the Fulbright U.S. Scholar 2027-2028 Competition, Part I/II" plus an "Application Walk-Through" in the webinar library, https://fulbrightscholars.org/events/webinars. A real annotated template exists for the host-contact step: https://fulbrightscholars.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/Sample-Invitation-Letter-Email.pdf. Read the recommender guidance yourself for the reviewer's-eye checklist: https://fulbrightscholars.org/sites/default/files/2024-04/FUSC-Recommender-Instructions.pdf (and FUSC-Language-Evaluator-Instructions.pdf). Pick your peer-review committee deliberately via the discipline/specialization list PDF. Find people, not documents, in the Fulbright Scholar Directory (https://fulbrightscholars.org/fulbright-scholar-directory) — 50,000+ alumni searchable by discipline, host institution, country and year, but it shows NO project abstracts or titles; the funder notes "Contact information is not provided within the directory, but most contacts are readily searchable online" and lists former Fulbright Scholars as a networking route. Also Alumni Ambassadors and campus presentations. NOT AVAILABLE anywhere: funded project statements, a sample-application library, or any reviewer feedback — so the best real example is a colleague's or one held by your campus Scholar Liaison.
result.resubmission_note:
Diametrically opposite to DOE SC, and this is the fact most worth telling an applicant.

UNLIMITED REAPPLICATION, CLEAN SLATE: "Applicants may reapply for a future competition and we can work with you to do so. Applications are reviewed individually, on their own merit each year." No attempt cap, no waiting period, no A1 numbering, no introduction page, no requirement to show revision — and no "substantially revised" test of the kind HEP/BER impose at DOE. A previously declined application is simply a new application in the next annual cycle.

BUT NO FEEDBACK AT ALL — the cost of that freedom: "Fulbright program policy does not authorize implementing partners (including IIE) to provide reasons for an application to be not recommended or not selected." You are told only "recommended or not recommended" at the December peer-review notification, and nothing about why, at any stage. So you must diagnose your own failure, which is exactly why the campus Scholar Liaison, the writing clinics and a colleague who has served on a peer-review committee matter more here than at agencies that release reviews.

Note also that failure can happen at two different places with very different meanings: screened out by IIE for ineligibility/incompleteness (fixable, mechanical, and you are notified of this outcome), versus not recommended at peer review (substantive), versus recommended but not selected downstream by the Embassy/Commission/State/FFSB — where the cause may be "available funding, the number of applications received, country priorities" rather than anything about your project. "Not all applications that were recommended in the Peer Review process will be selected for grants." A strong application can lose on country quota; that is a reason to reapply, possibly to a different country, rather than to rewrite from scratch.

The 15 September pattern is strong (2027-28 cycle = 15 Sept 2026) but I did not assert a 2027 date. Re-check ~February 2027 when the cycle opens.

A plain fetch returns HTTP 403 and a rendering browser triggered a file-download dialog rather than a page, so I did not open it. Every prior-funding rule I recorded is quoted from the funder's own eligibility page instead, not from the search index; Chapter 600 may contain further detail on concurrent federal funding, which the programme page does not address at all.

POSTDOC DEGREE-RECENCY INCONSISTENCY ON THE FUNDER'S OWN PAGE: the award-type section says doctorate 'within five to seven years of the fellowship start date, as noted in the award description', while the eligibility accordion says 'within five years of the fellowship start date, unless otherwise noted'. Both defer to the individual award description, so the award governs - but a reader comparing the two sections will see a contradiction. Worth flagging in the corpus rather than resolving, since it is the funder's own text.

PER-AWARD VARIATION IS THE REAL GATE AND IS NOT CAPTURED HERE: 380+ awards across 120+ countries each set their own career-profile eligibility, language requirement, invitation-letter status, host restrictions, duration and start dates. Anything recorded at programme level is a default that an individual award can override. No programme-level row can substitute for reading the specific award description in the Award Search.
