result.deadline_pattern:
Annual, appropriations-permitting, with a spring deadline and a January 1 start.

NIJ's own words on the GRF cadence (GRF FAQ, "When is the notice of funding opportunity for the GRF program typically announced?"): "In most past cycles, the funding opportunity has typically posted in January and been open for at least 90 days. The most recent cycle posted in March and was open for 61 days."

NIJ-wide cadence (nij.ojp.gov/funding): "most notices are released December through May"; the Forthcoming Funding list is "typically posted in the late fall."

Start-date rule that anchors the whole cycle (GRF FAQ): "The earliest possible date that funds could become available is January 1 of the year following submission of an application. This is the official 'start date' of the fellowship grant." And: "The proposed fellowship start date should be no earlier than January 1 of the year following application submission."

So the stable, non-rotting shape of this programme is: NOFO posts winter/early spring → open 60–90 days → deadline spring → decisions within ~6 months → funds available January 1 of the following year. Only the specific day-of-month rots.

Caution on drift: the FY25 cycle broke the "typically January" pattern (posted March 25, 2026, open 61 days), so the January assumption is already weakening. Treat "January–March posting, April–May deadline" as the working window and re-check when NIJ posts.

Two-part deadline every cycle: the Grants.gov SF-424 deadline falls roughly ONE WEEK BEFORE the JustGrants full-application deadline (FY25: May 19 vs May 27). Missing the first one is fatal — "If an applicant fails to submit the SF-424 in Grants.gov by the deadline, they will be unable to submit their application in JustGrants."
result.loi_deadline:
No letter of intent, pre-proposal, or pre-registration stage exists for this mechanism. Nothing in the FY25 NOFO, the GRF FAQ, or the programme overview establishes an LOI.

What occupies the "pre-application" slot instead, and should not be confused with an LOI:

1. PRE-APPLICATION WEBINAR (optional but high-value). FY25: "A webinar on this NOFO will be held on April 15, 2026, at 2 p.m. – 3 p.m. ET. Preregistration is required for all participants." Questions could be submitted in advance to grf@usdoj.gov with the subject "Questions for NIJ FY25 Graduate Research Fellowship Webinar." Roughly 3 weeks after posting, ~5 weeks before the JustGrants deadline. The recording, transcript and slide deck are archived on the opportunity page afterwards.

2. SAM.gov REGISTRATION — the real long-lead item, institution-level, and the closest analogue to NIH's hidden registrations. FY25 Key Dates row: "Recommend beginning process by March 25, 2026, and no later than May 12, 2026" — i.e. NIJ tells you to start it the day the NOFO posts, ~8 weeks out. Registration chain is SAM.gov → Grants.gov → JustGrants. This is handled by the university, not the student.

3. INTERNAL OSP DEADLINE — the deadline that actually binds a PhD student. NIJ FAQ: "Because coordination with their university OSP is necessary, students are encouraged to make contact EARLY to express their intent to submit an application." The student cannot submit; see submission_requirements.
result.review_to_award:
Materially FASTER and simpler than the NIH norm — one review level, no council, no JIT, roughly 7 months submission-to-start.

Stated duration (GRF FAQ): "The application review process, including decision-making and other considerations, may take up to six months."

The arc, with FY25 dates as the worked example:
1. Submission — Grants.gov SF-424 May 19, 2026; JustGrants full application May 27, 2026.
2. Basic Minimum Requirements (BMR) screen — a pass/fail gate BEFORE any peer review. "Applicants whose application fails to meet the BMR are provided notice (including an appropriate point of contact for questions) within a few weeks after the submission due date." So a fatal-omission rejection arrives within weeks, not months.
3. Peer review — "evaluated for technical merit by a peer review panel(s) in accordance with OJP peer review policy and procedures." Panels are organised by topic: in 2023 the 146 applications that reached peer review were sorted into 11 panels (Anthropology, Biology, Chemistry, Corrections, Courts, Crime Prevention, Computer Science and Engineering, General, Juvenile, Policing, Violence and Victimization), "All panels comprised academic faculty with experience mentoring graduate students."
4. Programmatic and financial review — "After the peer review, applications undergo additional programmatic and financial reviews. NIJ staff may reach out to applicants during the programmatic or financial review if a submitted form is incomplete or needs to be updated."
5. Final decision — "All final award decisions will be made by the Director of the National Institute of Justice (NIJ), who may take into account not only peer review ratings and NIJ staff recommendations, but also other factors," including "geographic coverage, strategic priorities, available funding, past performance."
6. Notification — by email in JustGrants to the university's Authorized Representative, Entity Administrator and Application Submitter. Note for students: these are OSP staff, not you. FAQ: "students are encouraged to maintain communication with their OSP." Declines come last: "Applicants not selected for an award will receive notification after all award recipients have been notified."
7. Acceptance — "The Authorized Representative for the entity should accept or decline the award within 45 days of the notification."
8. Earliest start — FY25 Anticipated Period of Performance Start Date: January 1, 2027, i.e. ~7 months after the JustGrants deadline.

FEEDBACK, and it is better than most: "NIJ also provides unsuccessful applicants with a summary of peer reviewer comments." That summary is the raw material for the two-page resubmit response next cycle.

POST-AWARD RELEASE LAG — the trap unique to this mechanism. Being awarded is not being paid. Funds are withheld until NIJ receives and approves: proof the dissertation committee has accepted the topic (and that it is "substantively the same as that proposed in the application"); the final approved IRB package plus Human Subjects Protection form and Privacy Certificate; and, for a student who was part-time at submission, proof of full-time enrolment. "If awarded, no work may begin until the IRB determination and privacy certificate are submitted, reviewed and approved by NIJ." NIJ warns applicants "not to anticipate the availability of fellowship funds." After year one, "each annual funding increment is withheld pending annual demonstration of continued enrollment and adequate progress towards the degree."

No continuation/renewal: "Continuation funding is not available for this program."
result.submission_requirements:
This is DOJ/OJP machinery, not NIH — essentially every element deviates from the NIH norm supplied. Nothing here routes through eRA Commons, ASSIST, or SciENcv-mandated Common Forms.

WHO SUBMITS — the single biggest structural difference from an NIH F31. The INSTITUTION is the applicant, not the student. "The official applicant is the academic institution sponsoring an eligible student." Hard gate: "Applications from students who apply as individuals will be removed from consideration." Route: "Students must contact and seek the assistance of the university's Office of Sponsored Programs, or equivalent office... a representative from the university OSP must complete and submit the full application package online at Grants.gov and JustGrants by the deadline date." The student is nonetheless named PI: "The sponsored student should be listed as PI. If this is not permitted by university policy, the chair or advisor may be listed as PI and the student as co-PI."

TWO-STEP SUBMISSION (both steps mandatory, ~1 week apart):
- Step 1, Grants.gov: submit the SF-424 only, signed by the AOR. Section 8F must list the person who will complete the JustGrants application — JustGrants uses that email to assign the application. NIJ advises submitting the SF-424 "not later than 48 hours before the Grants.gov deadline." Expect four Grants.gov emails within 48 hours (submission receipt, validation receipt, grantor agency retrieval receipt, agency tracking number).
- Step 2, JustGrants: the actual application. Miss step 1 and step 2 is impossible.

PAGE LIMIT — 8 pages, and the carve-outs are generous: "The document should not exceed 8 pages. If included in the main body of the proposal narrative, any tables, charts, figures, and other illustrations do count toward the 8-page limit. Title page, resubmit response (if applicable), table of contents, and any appendices do not count toward the page limit." So bibliography, questionnaires, maps, and the project timeline all sit outside the 8 pages.

FORMATTING — a genuine and pleasant deviation from NIH's Arial-11pt regime: "There are no line spacing, font, or formatting requirements other than the page limit specified in the notice of funding opportunity."

AUTHORSHIP RULE: "The proposal narrative is expected to be the intellectual product of the student. Although the involvement of graduate advisors and others is encouraged in the development of research ideas and in the revision of drafts, the student should be the primary author of the research proposal."

BASIC MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS (BMR) — miss any one and the application never reaches a reviewer: "If NIJ determines that an application does not include these elements, it will not proceed to merit review and will not receive any further consideration." The BMR set is: submitted by an eligible applicant; responsive to scope; Proposal Narrative; Budget Detail Form; Verification of Current Enrollment in a qualifying degree program; Undergraduate and Graduate Transcripts (official or unofficial); Statement of Support; Biosketches/CVs/Resumes for key personnel (defined as the student and the statement-of-support writer).

STATEMENT OF SUPPORT — the classic disqualifier. Written and signed by the dissertation committee chair, or, if there is no committee yet, by "a faculty advisor, department chair, departmental director of graduate studies or individual with similar responsibilities." It must describe current status of the work, outline pending milestones, acknowledge availability to assist with Human Subjects/Privacy compliance, and describe the chair's role monitoring the project and verify the chair "will review and approve all performance reports prior to submission to NIJ." Two traps: (a) "This statement may NOT be submitted independently by the committee chair, but must be included with the entire application package submitted by the university OSP administrator" — there is no NSF-style confidential reference portal; (b) "Failure to include the statement of support at the time of application will disqualify an application."

NO LETTERS OF REFERENCE. Unlike NSF GRFP or NIH F-series, there is no set of recommendation letters. One Statement of Support is it. Separately, "Letters of Support (if applicable)" are required only where the research partners with justice agencies or community organisations — signed by a decision-making authority at each partner, and acknowledging that de-identified data will be archived with NACJD. Submit them "as one separate attachment."

FULL JUSTGRANTS UPLOAD LIST (asterisk = BMR): Proposal Narrative*; budget detail form*; Verification of Current Enrollment*; Undergraduate and Graduate Transcripts*; Statement of Support*; Biosketches/CVs/Resumes*; then Personal Statement (max one page, on academic background, research experience, career goals and the fellowship's role in their trajectory); List of Individuals in the Application (use NIJ's "Proposed Project Staff, Affiliation, and Roles" form); Current and Pending (Other) Support — required for BOTH the student and the statement-of-support writer; Gold Standard Science statement (per E.O. 14303); Research and Evaluation Independence and Integrity Statement; Human Subjects Protection form; Privacy Certificate; Request to Use Incentives or Stipends (if applicable); Data Management, Sharing and Archiving Plan (DMSAP, max 2 pages); Letters of Support (if applicable). Plus web forms: Standard Applicant Information, Proposal Abstract, Priority Consideration Inventory, Financial Management and System of Internal Controls Questionnaire, Agency Funding Priorities Inventory, PI Contact Information. Plus disclosures: Lobbying (SF-LLL if prompted), Disclosure of Duplication in Cost Items, DOJ Certified Standard Assurances, DOJ High-Risk Grantee disclosure, DOJ Certifications.

HSP/PRIVACY FORMS ARE REQUIRED EVEN FOR NON-HUMAN-SUBJECTS WORK: "Yes, these forms are necessary for all NIJ grants." IRB approval is NOT required at application; if you have it, submit it to avoid payment delays.

BIOSKETCH: SciENcv is encouraged, never mandated — "No specific format is required. If using an NIH format, the newer 'NIH Biographical Sketch Common Form' format should be used." The NOFO separately encourages the "NIH Fellowship Biosketch" format for the student, whose Personal Statement field can absorb the one-page personal statement. NIJ also points to the SciENcv "NSF Current and Pending (Other) Support" format. Note the cross-agency oddity: an NIH/NSF form used for a DOJ application.

TITLE PAGE must carry: project title, submission date, funding opportunity number, student contact details, a unique author identifier (ORCID, Researcher ID or Scopus Author ID), name of the enrolled doctoral program, key words. Stating the degree program on the cover page routes you to the right topic panel.

MAIN BODY SECTIONS, which map onto the weighted criteria: Statement of the Problem and Research Questions; Project Design and Implementation; Capabilities and Competencies (student, advisor/chair, academic environment, dissemination track record, management plan); Potential Impact.

APPENDICES (uncapped, outside the 8 pages): bibliography; supplemental tables/charts/questionnaires/maps; and "Project Timeline and Expected Milestones... including: advancement to candidacy (if applicable), the writing of the dissertation, major events in the dissemination plan, and expected dissertation defense date."

REVIEW CRITERIA ARE WEIGHTED AND PUBLISHED — write to these percentages: Statement of the Problem 5%; Project Design and Implementation 40%; Capabilities and Competencies 15%; Potential Impact 25%; Budget 15%. Design and Impact together are 65%: methodology plus a concrete dissemination/practitioner-relevance story outrank the literature review by a wide margin.

BUDGET (FY25/current FAQ figures): up to $60,000/year for up to 3 years, max $180,000. Each year: $41,000 Salary and Fringe (may include health insurance; "may not include support for any person other than the doctoral student"; unused salary cannot be moved to other categories); up to $16,000 Cost of Education Allowance (tuition, fees, university administrative or indirect costs — indirect costs ARE allowed here, and unused balance may spill into Research Expenses, in which case "total Research Expenses may exceed $3,000"); up to $3,000 Research Expenses (supplies, instrument facility time, human-subject compensation, undergraduate RAs, data-collection and conference travel, society membership). Budget in discrete 12-month increments; SF-424 shows cumulative. Project end date may run up to 5 years, but only 3 years of funding within it. Cofunding: NIJ "may account for up to 100% of the total cost" — no match required, but a voluntary match, once approved, "becomes mandatory and subject to audit."

NOTE — these figures CORRECT the existing CSV row, which records "<=$35,000 salary/fringe + <=$12,000 education allowance + <=$3,000 research costs; max total ~$150,000". Current published figures are $41,000 / $16,000 / $3,000 and $180,000. FY24 awards on NIJ's own list reach $180,000.

FY25 SCALE: "Total Amount To Be Awarded Under This Funding Opportunity: $1 million"; "Anticipated Number of Awards: 8"; "Anticipated Award Ceiling: up to $180,000."

NO ERROR-CORRECTION WINDOW, and a narrow technical-failure waiver only: you must have a help-desk tracking number obtained BEFORE the deadline, and must email OJP.ResponseCenter@usdoj.gov within 24 hours of the relevant deadline with a description of the problem, a timeline, the complete application as a manual submission, the UEI, and ticket numbers. Explicitly excluded: "failure to begin the SAM.gov, Grants.gov, or JustGrants registration and application process in sufficient time."
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
The headline: for a PhD student this mechanism is unusually PERMISSIVE about other money. There is no NIH-style K/R01 exclusion, no years-since-degree clock, and no prior-award disqualifier. Almost everything that blocks an application is a paperwork or applicant-type failure, not a funding-history failure.

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (all verbatim or near-verbatim from NIJ):
- Holding other fellowships, grants or stipends: "Yes, a student can receive other awards or stipends. However, any other funding or support must be disclosed (e.g., research or teaching assistantships, positions held under an advisor's grant, other private or government fellowships, grants, stipends). NIJ may seek to avoid duplicative funding, if appropriate." So an NSF GRFP fellow, a departmental TA, or someone paid on an advisor's R01 may apply — disclose everything via the Current and Pending (Other) Support form.
- Outside employment while funded: "NIJ doesn't prohibit fellows from obtaining additional employment," subject to university policy and the expectation of primary effort on the dissertation.
- Non-U.S. citizenship: "The official applicant is the academic institution, not the student. Therefore, the student's citizenship does not affect eligibility." International doctoral students at accredited U.S. institutions are eligible — a rare and important carve-out versus NSF GRFP, NIH F31 and most federal predoc fellowships.
- Any stage of the PhD: "Any student enrolled full-time in a qualifying research doctorate program and proposing a relevant dissertation topic may apply at any stage in their graduate career." No candidacy requirement at application.
- Already started the dissertation: "Doctoral students who have already started their dissertation research are encouraged to apply... Commencing research before submitting an application or while the application is under review does not necessarily impact the likelihood of receiving an award."
- No dissertation committee or unapproved topic yet: permitted at application; a faculty advisor/chair/DGS statement of support substitutes, and committee acceptance becomes a condition of fund release, not of eligibility.
- Part-time enrolment at submission: permitted if the institution submits "an official letter stating that it expects that the student will be enrolled full-time... beginning the academic term in which fellowship activity is proposed to begin" (funds withheld until demonstrated).
- Part-time enrolment DURING the award: "NIJ GRF does not require full-time enrollment during the fellowship term."
- Life events: suspension and no-cost extension available at NIJ's discretion for "child birth, adoption, dependent care, elder care, and serious illness."
- Prior unsuccessful application: reapplication is allowed, with no cap (see resubmission_note).
- Multiple students per university: "Yes, but a separate application must be submitted for each student."
- Holding/being near an existing NIJ award is not itself disqualifying — it triggers a disclosure duty (below).

WHAT DISQUALIFIES OR REMOVES AN APPLICATION:
- The student applying directly: "Applications from students who apply as individuals will be removed from consideration." Must come through the institution's OSP.
- Non-U.S. or unaccredited institution: "The applicant will be a degree-granting academic institution in the United States or its territories... fully accredited by one of the regional institutional accreditation agencies recognized by the U.S. Secretary of Education."
- FIELD EXCLUSION, and this is NEW relative to the existing CSV row: "Humanities and Visual and Performing Arts degree programs are not eligible." Eligibility is keyed to the NCSES Survey of Earned Doctorates research-doctorate list and CIP taxonomy (ncses.nsf.gov/pubs/nsf25349/table/A-1 and /A-4). FAQ: "If your degree or field of study does appear on these lists as appropriate (i.e., not classified under Humanities or Visual and Performing Arts), then it is eligible. If it is not listed and you are in doubt, please contact the OJP Response Center... for a determination of eligibility." A criminology/sociology/psychology/forensic-science PhD is fine; an English or art-history PhD is not, whatever the crime relevance.
- Missing Statement of Support: "Failure to include the statement of support at the time of application will disqualify an application."
- Any missing BMR element: "it will not proceed to merit review and will not receive any further consideration."
- Topic outside scope. For FY 2026 the scope has NARROWED sharply: "Applicants for FY 2026 must demonstrate relevance of their dissertation research to (1) supporting law enforcement operations, (2) combating violent crime, (3) protecting American children, or (4) supporting American victims of trafficking and sexual assault." The FY25 NOFO's eligibility text likewise reads "preventing and controlling crime, protecting the border, enforcing the law, promoting public safety, and preventing or reducing crime." Both are markedly narrower than the wording still on the GRF overview page (dated October 1, 2024): "preventing and controlling crime, advancing knowledge of victimization and effective victim services, or ensuring the fair and impartial administration of criminal or juvenile justice." Victimisation/victim-services and procedural-fairness framings that passed in earlier cycles may no longer fit. Treat the FAQ's FY2026 four priorities as governing until the FY26 NOFO posts.

DISCLOSURE DUTIES THAT FUNCTION LIKE SOFT CONFLICTS:
- Current and Pending (Other) Support: "A list of currently active grants or fellowships supporting the student, as well as a list of all pending grant or fellowship proposals the student has submitted and the dates that funding would be active" — required for the student AND the statement-of-support writer.
- Existing NIJ awards must be named: "a description contextualizing the proposed doctoral work relative to, or within, any other work being conducted under an existing NIJ award, which must be specifically identified."
- Disclosure of Duplication in Cost Items: "the applicant must disclose if it has any pending applications for federal funding, including pending applications for subawards of federal funds, for the same project and the same budget items included in this proposal."

POST-AWARD RESTRICTIONS: funds are non-transferable — "Fellowship stipend funds may be used to support only the originally reviewed and awarded GRF fellow and are not transferable to any other student" (though an RA may be paid from Research Expenses). Funds may be drawn "only while the student is actively enrolled in the doctoral degree program and is carrying out research for the dissertation identified in the applicant's funding application," and the approved topic "must remain substantively similar to that initially proposed." No continuation funding.
result.program_officer_contact:
NO NAMED PROGRAM OFFICER, and pre-submission contact does NOT work the way it does at NIH. Do not plan an NIH-style "email the PO with your Specific Aims" conversation — there is no equivalent here, and NIJ says so.

THE ROUTES THAT EXIST:
- OJP Response Center — the general contact of record. Phone 800-851-3420, or 202-353-5556 (TTY, hearing-impaired only). Email OJP.ResponseCenter@usdoj.gov. Hours 9:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m. ET, Monday–Friday. FAQ: "During the open funding opportunity period, please contact the OJP Response Center." This is also the address for the one substantive pre-submission question NIJ will answer: whether an unlisted degree programme is eligible — "If it is not listed and you are in doubt, please contact the OJP Response Center... for a determination of eligibility."
- grf@usdoj.gov — a GRF-specific address used in the FY25 cycle for advance webinar questions. Whether it is monitored outside an open solicitation is not established.
- Pre-application webinar — the real substitute for PO contact, and the highest-value hour available. FY25: April 15, 2026, 2–3 p.m. ET, preregistration required, questions accepted in advance by email. Recording, transcript and slides are archived on the opportunity page and remain readable after the cycle closes.
- JustGrants Service Desk — 833-872-5175, JustGrants.Support@usdoj.gov. Grants.gov Customer Support — 800-518-4726 or 606-545-5035, support@grants.gov, 24/7 except federal holidays. SAM.gov Help Desk (Federal Service Desk), 8:00 a.m.–8:00 p.m. ET weekdays. These are technical, not programmatic.

WHAT NIJ WILL NOT DO — quoted, because it sets expectations:
- Will not pre-clear your topic: "We cannot determine the eligibility of a specific research topic until reviewing the full proposal."
- Will not discuss the review while it runs: "NIJ staff are not authorized to provide information on peer review scores or comment on programmatic, risk, or budget/financial reviews while the merit review is in progress."

WHO TO ACTUALLY TALK TO — for a PhD student the three relationships that decide this application are internal, not federal:
1. Your university's Office of Sponsored Programs (or equivalent). They are the applicant of record and the only party who can submit. NIJ: "students are encouraged to make contact EARLY to express their intent to submit an application." Their internal deadline, plus SAM.gov/Grants.gov/JustGrants registration state, is your real constraint. They also receive the award and decline notices — students hear the outcome through OSP, not directly.
2. Your dissertation committee chair (or, absent a committee, your faculty advisor, department chair, or director of graduate studies). They write the one Statement of Support, whose absence is fatal, and they must commit to reviewing and approving all performance reports. They also need a biosketch and a Current and Pending (Other) Support form of their own — brief them early.
3. After a non-award, NIJ's summary of peer reviewer comments. That document, not a conversation, is the feedback channel, and it is what the two-page resubmit response must answer.
result.resubmission_note:
UNLIMITED reapplication — markedly more permissive than NIH's single-A1 rule. No cap, no 37-month window, no "must be substantially different" test.

NIJ's own words (GRF FAQ, "Can an applicant institution reapply for a doctoral student who does not receive an award?"): "Yes. In this case, a 'resubmit response' statement should be included with the proposal narrative. This statement should include the title and submission date of the earlier application, and describe any changes made to the proposal in response to prior peer review comments."

The FY25 NOFO specifies the mechanics: the Resubmit Response is placed in the Proposal Narrative document, is "no more than two pages," and does NOT count against the 8-page limit. It must address "(1) the title, submission date, and NIJ-assigned application number of the previous application, and (2) a brief summary of revisions to the application, including responses to previous feedback received from NIJ."

So the resubmission loop is: apply → if unsuccessful, NIJ sends "a summary of peer reviewer comments" → revise → reapply next cycle with a 2-page resubmit response keyed to those comments. Keep the NIJ-assigned application number from the prior submission; you will need it.

Practical notes:
- The resubmit response is free real estate: two extra pages outside the page limit, and the only place to demonstrate responsiveness to review. Applicants who omit it lose that signal.
- Because the applicant of record is the institution, the reapplication is formally the university's, filed for the same student — OSP must run the whole two-step submission again.
- Watch the moving scope. A proposal that was in-scope in an earlier cycle may be out-of-scope for FY2026, whose four priorities are narrower (see prior_funding_conflicts). A resubmission may need reframing toward law enforcement operations, violent crime, protecting children, or trafficking/sexual-assault victims, not merely polishing.
- Timing: cycles are annual, so a resubmission costs roughly a year, and the start date moves to January 1 of the year after the new submission.
- No appeal process for a non-award is published for this mechanism.
result.examples_or_samples:
Strong for outputs and abstracts; there is NO public repository of funded GRF applications. NIJ publishes no sample application or annotated form set for this mechanism — nothing equivalent to NIAID's or NIA's sample-application collections. The closest routes, in decreasing directness:

1. PAST AND PRESENT FELLOWS — the single best starting point. https://nij.ojp.gov/funding/fellowships/graduate-research-fellowship-program-past-and-present-fellows — a table of GRF fellows from 2000 to 2024 (300+ fellows), giving fiscal year, award number, fellow name, university, dissertation/project title and dollar amount, with many project titles hyperlinked to abstracts and final reports. Reading 20 titles in your subfield tells you precisely what NIJ funds and at what scope. Sample entries: "Talley Bettens, GEORGE MASON UNIVERSITY — Schoolhouse interrogations and confessions: Perspectives from principals and students ($120,741)"; "Zeyu Tang, CARNEGIE MELLON UNIVERSITY — Procedural and Structural Justice Through Causal Understanding, Component Decoupling, and Relation Characterization ($60,000)"; "Jisoo Cho, CITY UNIVERSITY OF NEW YORK/JOHN JAY COLLEGE — Facility Exposure and Crime in New York City Streets: A Latent Profile Analysis Approach ($37,158)". The spread of amounts is itself instructive: not everyone requests the ceiling.

2. PUBLICATIONS BY FELLOWS — https://nij.ojp.gov/funding/fellowships/graduate-fellowship-program-publications — 19 pages of peer-reviewed articles, dissertations and standards produced by GRF fellows, filtered to subtopic "NIJ Graduate Fellowships." Shows the range NIJ actually funds, from forensic chemistry and DNA to policing and school violence: e.g. "Femur loading during gait in newly walking children" (Journal of Biomechanics, Dec 2025); "A Comparative Study of Mass and Non-Mass School Shootings in the United States" (Journal of School Violence, Oct 2025); "Mixed signals from prison? Postsecondary vocational credentials, race, and postrelease employment" (Criminology, Jul 2025); "PartialEdit: Identifying Partial Deepfakes in the Era of Neural Speech Editing" (Aug 2025).

3. FUNDED-AWARD ABSTRACTS — NIJ's awards database, https://nij.ojp.gov/funding/awards/list?combine=graduate+research+fellowship — award titles, institutions, amounts and award numbers with abstracts. Recent FY2024 GRF awards include "A Combined Molecular Analysis of Pollen Utilizing Lipid Profiling & DNA Barcoding for Plant Species Identification: A Forensic Application" (University of Central Florida, $120,000, 15PNIJ-24-GG-01571-RESS) and "A Multi-Method Genetic, Craniometric, and Isotopic Approach to Estimating Geographic Origin of Unidentified Latinx Remains" (Texas State University, $180,000, 15PNIJ-24-GG-01578-RESS).

4. THE PRE-APPLICATION WEBINAR ARCHIVE — the nearest thing to coaching. The FY25 opportunity page (https://nij.ojp.gov/funding/opportunities/o-nij-2025-172575) carries the April 15, 2026 webinar recording, slide presentation and transcript. NIJ's NOFO update note: "NIJ hosted a pre-application webinar on April 15, 2026. A recording, transcript, and the slide presentation are available."

5. THE NOFO ITSELF AS A TEMPLATE — https://www.ojp.gov/funding/opportunities/O-NIJ-2025-172575.pdf. Unusually, the FY25 NOFO contains worked budget-narrative language with fill-in-the-blank phrasing for student effort, academic vs summer months, fringe rates and conference travel. It is effectively a budget-narrative sample. It also carries the weighted review criteria, which function as a scoring rubric to write against.

6. NIJ FORMS — the "Proposed Project Staff, Affiliation, and Roles" form (List of Individuals in the Application) is provided on the NIJ website; biosketch and current-and-pending formats via SciENcv (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sciencv/).

7. GENERAL OJP GUIDANCE, not GRF-specific — the OJP Grant Application Resource Guide (referenced throughout the NOFO) and the JustGrants Application Submission Training webpage. Note the precedence rule: "If this NOFO requires something different from any guidance provided in the Application Resource Guide, the difference will be noted in this NOFO and the applicant should follow the guidance in this NOFO."

WHERE TO FIND MORE / ADJACENT MECHANISMS for the same population, all on the same NIJ nav: W.E.B. Du Bois Program (https://nij.ojp.gov/funding/fellowships/web-du-bois-program); NIJ Research Assistantship Program (https://nij.ojp.gov/funding/nijs-research-assistantship-program); the NIJ–NSF INTERN opportunity for graduate students (https://nij.ojp.gov/funding/fellowship-programs/nij-and-nsf-invite-graduate-students-broaden-their-horizons-through-criminal-justice-research); NIJ Challenge Program; LEADS.

Per house rules: items 1, 2, 4 and the fellows/publications listings above were read in a rendering browser on nij.ojp.gov (the site's funding listings are JS-filtered and return empty to a plain fetch). Item 3 and the FY25 NOFO PDF were retrieved by direct fetch and the PDF text extracted locally.

Nobody can enter the cycle here — the fellowships page carries the banner "The Letter of Intent (LOI) Deadline for the 2027 Cycle has now passed. (b) NEXT ENTRY POINT for a new applicant (award year 2028): **not posted yet.** As of 18 Sep 2026 the HFSP fellowships page still shows only the AY2027 cycle and carries no AY2028 dates. Do not treat the following as published dates — it is the fixed annual shape, which has held every year: portal opens mid-March 2027; LOI must be INITIATED (open + save the title page to get a 7-digit LOI ID) around 5 May 2027; LOI SUBMITTED around 12 May 2027; invited Full Proposal around 24 September 2027; outcome end of March 2028; fellowship activated between 1 April 2028 and 1 January 2029. result.deadline_pattern:
One round per year, no rolling submission. Verbatim: "There is one application round per year for the HFSP postdoctoral fellowships." Recurring shape (safe to state without a year): portal opens mid-March → LOI ID by ~5 May → LOI submitted ~12 May → LOI outcome mid-to-end August → invited Full Proposal ~24 September → outcome end of March → activation window 1 April to 1 January following. Every deadline 9:00 am US Eastern.

Two cycle-anchored dates move each year and silently gate eligibility, so they must be re-read every cycle rather than carried over: (1) the PhD conferral cut-off is pinned to the FULL PROPOSAL date, not the LOI — for AY2027, "applicants whose doctoral degree was conferred prior to 24 September 2023 are not eligible"; (2) the already-at-the-host-lab rule — "Applicants who are already working at their proposed host institution are eligible ONLY if they have arrived on or after 1 April 2026" (i.e. ~12 months before the activation window opens).
result.loi_deadline:
Mandatory, and it is a TWO-STEP deadline a week apart — this is where first-timers lose the cycle. AY2027 dates, verbatim from the guidelines:

- "5 May 2026: Deadline to initiate the Letter of Intent (LOI) by opening and saving the online form to obtain a 7-digit LOI ID by 9:00 am (09:00, Eastern US Time)"
- "12 May 2026: Submission of Letter of Intent by 9:00 am (09:00, Eastern US Time) via ProposalCentral"

Initiating is not a formality: "To be eligible, applicants must initiate their Letter of Intent in ProposalCentral by opening and saving the online form to obtain a 7-digit LOI ID by 5 May 2026, at the latest." Miss the initiation date and the submission date is unusable.

Gap to the full application: the invited Full Proposal is ~4.5 months after the LOI (12 May → 24 September). Only invited applicants proceed — "Applicants will be contacted by HFSP if they are invited to progress to this stage."

Portal opens ~2 months before LOI initiation (12 March 2026 for AY2027), which is the window HFSP intends you to use for the scope/eligibility email and the webinars.
result.review_to_award: LOI 12 May 2026 → LOI outcome "before the end of August 2026" (~3.5 months). Invited Full Proposal 24 Sep 2026 → external scientific reviewers, then Review Committee assessment, then the Review Committee meeting (funder norm: early February) → notification "once internal HFSP formalities are complete (usually towards the end of March 2027)" (~6 months from full proposal, ~10.5 months from LOI). Earliest start ~1 week after notification: "Successful applicants must begin (activate) their fellowship between 1 April 2027 and 1 January 2028" — so LOI to latest possible start is ~20 months, and the fellow chooses the start date inside that 9-month window. Term fixed at 36 months, non-renewable, 100% FTE. No CDF-specific deviation from the funder-wide arc — CDF and LTF run on one timetable through the same Fellowship Review Committee.
result.submission_requirements:
Deviations from the funder-wide norm first, then the mechanism specifics.

DEVIATIONS WORTH FLAGGING:
1. CDF is a SEPARATE portal opportunity from LTF, not a checkbox inside one form. Verbatim from the ProposalCentral LOI instructions: "click the 'Apply Now' button on the category you wish to apply for (e.g. Cross-Disciplinary Fellowship (D) or Long-Term Fellowship (E))." Choose wrong and you are in the wrong competition.
2. The funder-wide "no signatures at LOI stage" is true for research grants but NOT exactly true for fellowships — the APPLICANT self-signs their own LOI: "you must sign your Letter of Intent by typing your full name in the 'Applicant (Your Name)' field and clicking 'Sign'. You DO NOT need to upload any handwritten or digital signatures for this. No one else is required to sign your application at this stage." Host supervisor and institution sign nothing at LOI and cannot even see it: "They will not have access to the application at this stage."
3. New for AY2027 — an AI-use declaration: generative AI "should only be used to improve readability and language of the application, not for creating content. Applicants are requested to disclose their use of AI... HFSPO reserves the right to check the use of AI tools with appropriate software."
4. The publication rule TIGHTENS between stages. A preprint counts at LOI but not at Full Proposal: at LOI a lead-author manuscript "available online in a recognized open-access (OA) preprint repository AND submitted to a peer-reviewed journal" qualifies; "At the Full Proposal stage, option (iv) is no longer valid." Someone eligible in May can be ineligible in September if the paper has not been accepted by then.

LOI (all typed into ProposalCentral text boxes; character counts include spaces and punctuation):
- Research plan summary "up to 3000 characters, including spaces" — background, aims, central hypotheses, experimental approach, expected outcomes.
- "THREE key references" — exactly three.
- Title; personal data incl. ORCID; short CV; proposed host institution and supervisor(s) with intended arrival date; disclosure of any previous or current collaboration with the proposed supervisor(s); PhD thesis title+abstract plus any previous postdoc project abstracts; full publication list plus the mandatory "Additional Information on Publications" template (downloaded in Section 10 of the portal).
- Confirmation the host supervisor(s) know of and support the application (they get an automated email).
- "No other documents are required at the Letter of Intent stage."

FULL PROPOSAL (invited only) — character limits: Summary carried over ("please refrain from changing this"); Background and significance 3,000; Specific aims 8,000; Experimental design 6,000; Bibliography up to 15 references; how the project differs from the applicant's previous work 2,500; why it is at the leading edge of life sciences 4,000; why the host lab is a good fit 2,000; public summary 2,400.

LETTERS AND SIGN-OFF (the long-lead items — all are other people's work):
- Host supervisor recommendation letter on HFSP's template: brief career/research summary, up to 10 relevant publications, an explicit statement that the plan "is a new direction for their lab" and a significant change from the applicant's prior work, why the lab suits HFSP's mission, and a mentorship plan. "If a candidate has two host supervisors, BOTH must provide their information and a letter of recommendation."
- "Reference letters from TWO additional referees" — written into the portal template, "no more than 3000 characters (including spaces)" each.
- E-signatures from applicant, host supervisor(s) AND the designated host institution official. Hard gate: "the proposal cannot be submitted until all signatures have been registered", and "BEFORE the applicant can submit their Full Proposal: the host supervisor(s) and referees must have submitted their sections, AND the host supervisor(s) and the host institution official must have signed."

WHAT DOES NOT EXIST ANYWHERE IN THIS SYSTEM: no budget, no budget justification, no biosketch, no data-management plan, no facilities section, no uploaded PDF at all for fellowships (the research-grant research plan is the only upload in the whole HFSP system). Beware second-hand summaries that claim a budget or three referees — the guidelines say two referees plus the supervisor(s), and no budget.

PORTAL MECHANICS: account activation and password links "expire 24 hours after being sent"; session drops after 20 minutes idle, so "prepare all the texts for the scientific elements offline before copying and pasting them into the system"; use a personal email "valid during the entire review process AND for the entire funding period", not an institutional one; run "Validate" often, and note that unstarred fields are not listed by it but may still be required.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
Both halves. The short version: almost nothing in your funding history disqualifies you — the binding constraints are one HFSP fellowship per lifetime, one application per year, and a rule about what you may hold CONCURRENTLY once the award starts, which is not an eligibility bar at application time.

WHAT DISQUALIFIES:
- A previous HFSP postdoctoral fellowship. Verbatim: "An HFSP postdoctoral fellowship may only be held once." Non-renewable: "The HFSP Fellowship is awarded for 3 years (36 months). It cannot be renewed."
- Applying twice in one round. Verbatim: "In one year, each applicant may submit only one Letter of Intent for an HFSP postdoctoral fellowship (Long-Term Fellowship or Cross-Disciplinary Fellowship)". You cannot hedge LTF and CDF in the same cycle — pick one before 5 May.
- Concurrent salary once the fellowship is active: "HFSP Fellows cannot concurrently hold an HFSP Fellowship and another paid employment position (i.e., a position supported by a salary) or another paid fellowship from another organization." Also "HFSP Fellows must devote themselves entirely to their research project in the host institution and may not engage in any other paid activity without prior agreement by HFSPO."
- An indirect one people miss: your chosen host supervisor is a rationed slot. "each host supervisor may only endorse ONE applicant per year" and "Applicants must ensure that the host supervisor(s) do NOT endorse another HFSP Fellowship application in this year's application round." That conversation is a competitive negotiation, not a formality, and must happen before the LOI.

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the half applicants get wrong):
- Holding or having held another funder's fellowship or grant does NOT bar you from applying. The AY2027 guidelines contain no list of disqualifying prior awards and no exclusion for current fellowship holders — the concurrency rule sits in Section 6 (conditions of award), i.e. it bites at activation, not at application. Note: a widely-summarised claim that current postdoc-fellowship holders "are not eligible to apply" is NOT in HFSP's text; I checked the guidelines directly and it is not there.
- Topping up is allowed: "the HFSP living allowance can be supplemented from other sources (e.g., from a host supervisor's grant or from institutional funds), for instance to reach the salary requirements of the host institution."
- Research grants are allowed alongside: "HFSP Fellows may apply for and hold additional research grants to assist their conduct of the fellowship research project as presented in their successful HFSP application. However, those funds must not be used as the fellows' salary."
- Rejection does not burn you: "Unsuccessful applicants may reapply in subsequent years, provided they still meet all eligibility requirements."
- The 36-month post-PhD clock can be stopped for "illness, parental leave (childcare), providing full-time care for an immediate family member, military or civil service" — but NOT for "unemployment, volunteer work, paid/unpaid internships, or any form of employment (scientific or otherwise)." Exemptions must be settled by email BEFORE initiating the LOI.
- You may pause the award later: fellows may defer for up to 24 months after completing at least one year, to move to a different lab or to conduct research in a new country, with prior HFSPO approval.
- Your supervisor's HFSP history is not a conflict: "the proposed supervisor may simultaneously mentor HFSP Fellows from previous award years, and/or be part of an HFSP Research Grant team."
- A doctorate is not required at application: "A completed doctoral degree is not required at the time of application" (must be completed before starting, and before 31 December 2027 for AY2027).

NOT A FUNDING RULE BUT THE SAME KIND OF TRAP — the relationship bars: you cannot apply to work with a host supervisor who is a "former scientific collaborator", "former research supervisor", "or with whom they have worked or published", and you are ineligible if you will have spent more than 12 months working with that supervisor by activation, "regardless of any change of institution by the host supervisor."
result.program_officer_contact:
No program officer in the NIH sense — no assigned PO, no portfolio to match, no draft review. One central mailbox, staffed by HFSP's own scientists: **fellow@hfsp.org** (fellowships; grant@hfsp.org is the grants mailbox and the wrong address for CDF). Postal/HQ: 12 Quai Saint Jean, 67000 Strasbourg, France.

Pre-submission contact is EXPECTED and explicitly invited, and for CDF it is the single highest-value move available, because scope is what kills applications:
- Scope: "In cases of doubt, applicants can contact the HFSP Fellowship Office (fellow@hfsp.org) to request general feedback about the alignment of their proposed project with the objectives and scope of HFSP-funded research."
- Eligibility generally: "For questions on the eligibility criteria listed below, please contact the Fellowship Office (fellow@hfsp.org)."
- Dual nationality / host country edge cases: "In case of doubt, applicants should contact the HFSP Fellowship Office."
- Unusual publication records: "Applicants with queries regarding the eligibility of their publication record should contact fellow@hfsp.org to check."
- MANDATORY and time-critical — career-interruption exemptions: "Applicants wishing to obtain an exemption must contact fellow@hfsp.org with details of their interruption periods (dates, reasons) to discuss the possibility of an exemption BEFORE initiating their Letter of Intent." Miss this and the exemption is not available to you that cycle.

WHAT THEY WILL NOT DO: read or comment on a draft. There is no mechanism for it, and reviewers and Review Committee members are barred from any contact with applicants.

THE REAL SUBSTITUTE — staff-run webinars in the window between the portal opening and the LOI deadline. For AY2027: two sessions on 25 March 2026, 09:00 and 16:00 CET, free but "Registration mandatory", run by Carolyn Johnson (HFSP Senior Scientific Officer) and Guntram Bauer (HFSP Chief Scientific Officer) with two fellowship awardees on the panel — named on the AY2027 event page as Samuel Miravet-Verde and Sandra Reinert. Recorded to HFSP's YouTube (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8A-v-tlb-w), so the recording is usable even after the cycle. Expect the equivalent late-March webinar each year.

TIMING NORM: ask scope and eligibility questions BEFORE initiating the LOI (so, before ~5 May). After submission there is nothing to ask and nothing to negotiate — allowances are set by HFSP's own table.

Portal/technical problems go elsewhere, not to HFSP: pcsupport@altum.com, 1-800-875-2562 (US/Canada) or 1-703-964-5840 (international), 8:30 am-5:00 pm US Eastern, Mon-Fri.
result.examples_or_samples:
HFSP publishes NO sample applications, and the old FAQ item "Are there examples of successful HFSP fellowship applications?" now 404s (https://www.hfsp.org/node/44336) though search indexes still serve the dead link. What actually exists, ranked by usefulness to someone starting from nothing:

1. FUNDED ABSTRACTS, FILTERABLE TO CDF — the closest thing to a model. https://www.hfsp.org/awardees/awards is a database of every award 1990-2026, filterable by Program (Cross Disciplinary Fellowships is its own filter value, separate from Long-Term Fellowships), award year, country and nationality, with the note "NB: years are award years". Each entry shows project title, awardee, nationality, host institution and an expandable abstract. HFSP itself points applicants here as the scope test: "Prospective fellowship applicants are encouraged to read about previous HFSP Fellows for examples of the broad scope of projects that have been funded by HFSP in the past."

2. THE SCORING SHEET YOU WILL BE MARKED ON — and it has CDF-specific lines at every band, which is unusually concrete. "HFSP Fellowships 2027 - Assessment criteria and scoring guide for reviewers" (PDF on hfsp.org). Reviewers score 1-10 in 0.5 steps; "Scores of 7 and above are fundable"; the host-lab criterion is rated yes/no/maybe rather than scored. CDF-specific criteria include "Does the proposal combine life sciences and non-life sciences in a unique way?" and "Is the non-life science background of the candidate likely to boost progress in the life sciences?" The failure bands are equally explicit — a 5.0-6.5 CDF is one where "unclear whether the non-life science background of the applicant would have an impact on the biological question asked", and a sub-3.0 is one where "unique experiences and training of applicant are not necessary for or integrated into the project". Read this before drafting, not after.

3. THE BEGINNER'S HANDBOOK — the 21-page "Fellowship Primer" by an HFSP program director, https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/Communications/PRIMER.pdf. Verified live and on-target: "The primer is written for PhD students who have little experience in dealing with funding organizations and who plan on attempting their first fellowship proposal for postdoctoral support." Covers when to apply relative to the thesis defence, how to identify funders, how to approach them.

4. "The Art of Grantsmanship" by Jacob (Jack) Kraicer, former HFSP Director of Research Grants (https://www.hfsp.org/node/5761); HFSP invites copying and reuse. The primer explicitly recommends it as the companion piece.

5. THE ANTI-EXAMPLES — Section 2.2 "What HFSP does not support" is a checklist of rejections: purely applied work (clinical/pharmaceutical focus, drug targets, diagnosis or treatment, applied engineering/biotech/nanotech, "development of novel methods that do not aim to answer a basic biological question", agricultural/environmental problem-solving); "purely observational or descriptive projects, including systematic screening approaches and data collection studies"; "proposals that are an obvious next step in the field"; and for fellowships specifically, projects that are "an obvious next step in the ongoing research of the host laboratory" or "a close continuation--the next logical step--of the applicant's work in their PhD or previous postdoctoral projects". For-profit hosts are ineligible (collaborations allowed).

6. LIVE HUMANS — the webinar recordings put two current awardees on camera answering application questions (AY2027 panel: Samuel Miravet-Verde, Sandra Reinert). Since the awards archive is searchable by name and shows institutions, approaching a recent CDF awardee in your own field is the realistic route to seeing a real application; no university research office or public repository was found hosting a complete funded HFSP fellowship application.

7. Round-level context: newly awarded page https://www.hfsp.org/awardees/newly-awarded and fellowship round announcements (e.g. "Fellowships awarded to 55 pioneering postdoctoral scientists from 26 nations").
result.resubmission_note:
No resubmission track at all — no A1, no introduction page, no response-to-reviewers, no re-review within a cycle. You re-enter the next annual competition as a brand-new applicant, starting again at the LOI. Verbatim from the AY2027 guidelines: "Unsuccessful applicants may re-apply in the next competition year, provided they still meet the eligibility criteria. Application guidelines and criteria may be subject to change each year."

Two consequences that bite:
- Reaching the Full Proposal stage buys you nothing next year. Per HFSP's fellowship FAQ: "If you were successful at the Letter of Intent stage in a previous year but were rejected at the Full Proposal stage, you must submit another Letter of Intent the following year if you wish to apply again... success at the Letter of Intent stage in one year does not guarantee success in the following year."
- The window, not a cap, limits your attempts. No maximum number of applications is published, but the 36-month post-PhD clock (measured to the FULL PROPOSAL date) gives most people only 2-3 shots, and the date moves each year — re-check it every cycle rather than assuming last year's cut-off.

FEEDBACK you can actually build on is stage-dependent: HFSP does not give feedback to applicants rejected at LOI (volume), but applicants who were invited to submit a Full Proposal and then rejected do receive feedback. So a rejected LOI leaves you guessing — which is precisely why the pre-LOI scope email to fellow@hfsp.org and the assessment-criteria PDF matter so much for this mechanism.

Eligibility criteria also drift year to year (AY2027 alone refined host-country/nationality rules, lead-author publication rules, and the "what HFSP does not support" list, and added an AI-use declaration), so a re-application is a re-read, not a re-send.

result.loi_deadline:
Mandatory, and it is a TWO-STEP deadline — this is the single most common way first-timers lose a cycle.

AY2027 (closed): initiate by **5 May 2026, 9:00 am ET**; submit by **12 May 2026, 9:00 am ET**. Verbatim: "To be eligible, applicants must initiate their Letter of Intent in ProposalCentral by opening and saving the online form to obtain a 7-digit LOI ID by 5 May 2026, at the latest. The completed Letter of Intent must then be submitted by 12 May 2026."

"Initiation" = create a ProposalCentral account, open the LTF application, press Save on Section 1 (Title Page), then refresh and confirm a 7-digit LOI ID has appeared under "Proposal Identifiers". If you have not done this by the initiation deadline you cannot submit at all, however finished your text is.

LEAD TIME RELATIVE TO FULL APPLICATION: LOI initiation sits 7 days before LOI submission (the Research Grant equivalent is 9 days — this is a mechanism-level deviation). LOI submission sits **~4.5 months** before the invited Full Proposal (12 May → 24 Sep 2026). The LOI is a genuine cull, not a formality: only invited applicants proceed ("Applicants will be contacted by HFSP if they are invited to progress to this stage").

Account-timing trap, verbatim from the ProposalCentral LOI instructions: "Links sent to your email address to activate your account or to retrieve your login details will expire 24 hours after being sent." Also advised there: use a personal email, not an institutional one — "Please make sure to use an email address that will be valid during the entire review process AND for the entire funding period".
result.deadline_pattern:
Fixed annual cycle, one round per year, same shape every year; award years are named for the year the money starts, so the "2027" competition ran through calendar 2026. All times 9:00 am US Eastern (new for AY2027 — the guidelines list "The time of day for all deadlines is now 9:00 am (09:00, Eastern US Time)" under RECENT CHANGES).

LTF annual shape (safe to state without a year): portal opens mid-March → LOI ID by ~5 May → LOI submitted ~12 May → LOI outcome mid-to-end August → invited Full Proposal ~24 September → award notification end of March → fellowship activates between 1 April and 1 January following.

Guidelines verbatim: "There is one application round per year for the HFSP postdoctoral fellowships." Website: "There is only one competition per year for HFSP Fellowships."
result.review_to_award:
Full elapsed time LOI → money is about 11 months minimum; LOI → first notification about 3.5 months.

- LOI (12 May 2026) → LOI outcome: "Applicants will be notified before the end of August 2026 as to whether their Letter of Intent was selected or not for submission of a Full Proposal." Website is slightly looser: notification "between mid-August and end of August". ≈ 3.5 months.
- LOI outcome (end Aug) → Full Proposal (24 Sep 2026): only ~4 weeks to assemble the full proposal, including two referee letters and the host supervisor's recommendation. This is the real time squeeze in this mechanism — the referees and supervisor must be lined up before you know you are invited.
- Full Proposal (24 Sep 2026) → award notification: "Applicants who were invited to submit a Full Proposal are notified of the outcome of their fellowship application once internal HFSP formalities are complete (usually towards the end of March 2027)." ≈ 6 months.
- Notification (end March 2027) → earliest start: "Fellows must begin their fellowship between 1 April 2027 and 1 January 2028." So the earliest start is within days of notification, and the latest is ~9 months after. Award is "3 years (36 months). It cannot be renewed."

Review mechanics for this mechanism (guidelines §5): "All Letters of Intent will be assessed for eligibility, and all eligible LOIs are then assessed by Review Committee members. The highest scoring LOI applicants are then invited to submit a full proposal. All full proposals are assessed by external scientific reviewers who have expertise in the topics of the proposed research and these reviews, alongside the full proposal, are then assessed by Review Committee members. Proposals are then discussed and ranked at the Review Committee meeting."

Scoring bar you are judged against (AY2027 reviewer scoring guide, verified verbatim): "Review Committee members should use the whole scale of scores from 1 to 10, in steps of 0.5, according to the criteria listed below. Scores of 7 and above are fundable." Three criteria: Excellence of the proposed research plan; Excellence of the applicant; Host laboratory and host supervisor (the last rated "yes/no/maybe", not scored). Band definitions are explicitly LTF-specific — 9.0–10.0 "Specific for LTFs: significantly different from previous work"; 7.0–8.5 "Specific for LTFs: distinct from previous work, but conceptually similar"; 5.0–6.5 (non-fundable) "Specific for LTFs: largely based on previous work with few novel aspects"; 3.0–4.5 "Specific for LTFs: mainly a continuation of previous work". Distance from your own PhD/postdoc work is literally the axis that moves you across the fundable line.

Deferral after award: "Fellows may interrupt ('defer') HFSPO support for up to two years (24 months). Deferrals can be made after having completed at least one year of the HFSP Fellowship in the proposed host laboratory." Third year is portable: fellows "may choose to continue to work in the same host laboratory, to return to their or their spouse's/partner's home country, or to move to another HFSPO member country."

result.prior_funding_conflicts:
HFSP publishes no NIH-style list of disqualifying awards. The binding constraints are (i) a once-in-a-lifetime rule, (ii) an at-activation exclusivity rule, and (iii) a one-application-per-year rule. Crucially, almost nothing blocks you at APPLICATION time — the conflicts bite only on activation.

WHAT DISQUALIFIES / BLOCKS:
- Having already held one: "An HFSP postdoctoral fellowship may only be held once." (Verbatim, guidelines §3.1.)
- At activation, other salary or fellowship: "HFSP Fellows cannot concurrently hold an HFSP Fellowship and another paid employment position (i.e., a position supported by a salary) or another paid fellowship from another organization."
- Any other paid work: "HFSP Fellows must devote themselves entirely to their research project in the host institution and may not engage in any other paid activity without prior agreement by HFSPO."
- Hedging across HFSP schemes: "In one year, each applicant may submit only one Letter of Intent for an HFSP postdoctoral fellowship (Long-Term Fellowship or Cross-Disciplinary Fellowship)." You cannot run LTF and CDF in the same round.
- Your prospective PI's slot: "any host supervisor can endorse only ONE fellowship application (LOI) per competition year." If another postdoc has already claimed that supervisor's endorsement, you are out — verbatim duty on you: "Applicants must ensure that the host supervisor(s) do NOT endorse another HFSP Fellowship application in this year's application round." Settle this before you write anything.
- Note the real gates for LTF are not prior awards at all: the 36-month post-PhD clock, the mobility rules, and the prior-relationship bar on the host supervisor (no former collaborators/supervisors, and ineligible if >12 months already worked with them).

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the half applicants most often get wrong):
- Holding or applying for other fellowships right now is FINE. Verbatim FAQ: "Candidates can apply for the HFSP fellowship even if they have other financial support. However, if you are awarded the HFSP fellowship, the other support will have to be terminated prior to the start of the HFSP fellowship." So you may run HFSP in parallel with EMBO, Marie Skłodowska-Curie, NIH F32, etc., and only choose at activation.
- Top-ups are allowed: "the HFSP living allowance can be supplemented from other sources (e.g., from a host supervisor's grant or from institutional funds), for instance to reach the salary requirements of the host institution." A host lab or institution adding money to meet local salary floors does not breach the exclusivity rule.
- Research grants alongside the fellowship are allowed: "HFSP Fellows may apply for and hold additional research grants to assist their conduct of the fellowship research project as presented in their successful HFSP application. However, those funds must not be used as the fellows' salary." The line is salary, not funding.
- Your host supervisor's own HFSP money does NOT block you: "the proposed supervisor may simultaneously mentor HFSP Fellows from previous award years, and/or be part of an HFSP Research Grant team."
- Being already in the host lab is survivable: "Applicants who are already working at their proposed host institution are eligible ONLY if they have arrived on or after 1 April 2026" (AY2027 wording; shifts with the cycle), and the fellowship "must be activated within 12 months after their arrival".
- No doctorate in hand yet is fine: "A completed doctoral degree is not required at the time of application" — only before starting, and before 31 December 2027 (AY2027 wording).
- Career interruptions stop the 36-month clock: "illness, parental leave (childcare), providing full-time care for an immediate family member, military or civil service" may be exempted — but you must clear it first: applicants "must contact fellow@hfsp.org with details of their interruption periods (dates, reasons) to discuss the possibility of an exemption BEFORE initiating their Letter of Intent." Explicitly NOT exemptable: "unemployment, volunteer work, paid/unpaid internships, or any form of employment (scientific or otherwise)."
- Rejection is not a bar: "Unsuccessful applicants may reapply in subsequent years, provided they still meet all eligibility requirements."
- After award, you can pause or move: deferral up to 24 months after the first year, and a portable third year (same lab, home country, or another HFSPO member country) with prior HFSPO approval.

No program officer in the NIH sense — no assigned PO, no portfolio contact, no pre-submission concept call, and no one who will read your draft. Contact is a central office mailbox staffed by HFSP's own scientists.

- Programme contact: **fellow@hfsp.org** (Fellowships Office). Postal/phone from the AY2027 guidelines footer: HFSP, 12 Quai Saint Jean, 67000 Strasbourg, France; +33 6 63 13 04 80 or +33 7 43 44 41 16.

The fellowships page also lists https://proposalcentral.com/inforequest.asp and +1 703 964 5840.

PRE-SUBMISSION CONTACT IS EXPECTED, and for this mechanism it is the highest-value move available, because scope kills applications:
- Front matter of the guidelines: "If applicants are unsure of their eligibility or the relevance of their proposed research project, they should contact the Fellowships Office at fellow@hfsp.org."
- Scope check: "In cases of doubt, applicants can contact the HFSP Fellowship Office (fellow@hfsp.org) to request general feedback about the alignment of their proposed project with the objectives and scope of HFSP-funded research."
- REQUIRED, not optional, for career-interruption exemptions: applicants "must contact fellow@hfsp.org... BEFORE initiating their Letter of Intent."
- Publication-record edge cases: "Applicants with queries regarding the eligibility of their publication record should contact fellow@hfsp.org to check."
- Dual nationality / host country edge cases: "In case of doubt, applicants should contact the HFSP Fellowship Office."
- HFSP asks you to read first: "For questions about the HFSP Fellowships, please first read the Application Guidelines (above), then contact the Fellowships Office."

WHAT REPLACES THE PROGRAM OFFICER: staff-run webinars in the window between portal opening and the LOI deadline. For AY2027: "We are hosting two Fellowships Webinars on the 25th of March, 2026. Carolyn Johnson (HFSP Senior Scientific Officer) and Guntram Bauer (HFSP Chief Scientific Officer) provide insights into HFSP's expectations for frontier science, application rules and guidelines, and how to develop a compelling Letter of Intent." Expect the equivalent webinar in ~March 2027 for AY2028.

FEEDBACK after the fact: "we cannot provide feedback to unsuccessful applicants at the Letter of Intent stage due to the volume of applications that we receive. However, unsuccessful applicants that were invited to submit a Full Proposal will receive feedback."
result.examples_or_samples:
HFSP publishes NO sample applications — and the old FAQ item that pointed at them is gone: https://www.hfsp.org/node/44336 returns 404 (verified 18 Sep 2026), though search indexes still serve the link. What genuinely exists, in descending order of usefulness to an LTF applicant:

1. **Funded abstracts, filterable to LTF specifically** — https://www.hfsp.org/awardees/awards. Verified live; the filter list includes "Long-Term Fellowships - LTF" as its own option alongside Award year ("NB: years are award years"), Country and Nationality, and each entry expands to an **Abstract**. This is the closest thing to a model of what HFSP rewards in this mechanism, and it is the scope test HFSP itself points applicants to: "Prospective fellowship applicants are encouraged to read about previous HFSP Fellows for examples of the broad scope of projects that have been funded by HFSP in the past." Also https://www.hfsp.org/awardees/newly-awarded and the awardees map https://www.hfsp.org/awardees/awardees-map.

2. **The Fellowship Primer** — https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/Communications/PRIMER.pdf (verified live, 3.5 MB). Written by an HFSP program director explicitly for this audience: "The primer is written for PhD students who have little experience in dealing with funding organizations and who plan on attempting their first fellowship proposal for postdoctoral support." It covers identifying funders, approaching them, and organising proposal material. This is the single best "how do I start" document for a first-time LTF applicant.

3. **The reviewer scoring guide** — https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/Sciences/fellows/2027/HFSP%20Fellowships%202027%20-%20Assessment%20criteria%20and%20scoring%20guide%20for%20reviewers.pdf (verified, text extracted). Not a sample, but better: the exact rubric, with explicit LTF-vs-CDF band language, so you can self-score a draft against the 7.0 fundable line before you submit.

4. **"The Art of Grantsmanship"**, Jacob (Jack) Kraicer, former HFSP Director of Research Grants — https://www.hfsp.org/node/5761 (verified HTTP 200). HFSP invites copying and reuse.

5. **The webinar recording** — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8A-v-tlb-w — includes two HFSP fellowship awardees talking through their applications, plus HFSP's own account of what a compelling LOI looks like.

6. **NOT FOUND**: any university research office or public repository hosting a complete funded HFSP LTF Letter of Intent or Full Proposal. Individual fellows sometimes share theirs privately; the realistic route to seeing a real LTF application is to identify a fellow in the awards archive (filter Program = LTF, pick a recent year and your field) and ask them directly, or approach an awardee panellist from the webinars.
result.resubmission_note:
No NIH-style resubmission track: no A1, no Introduction page, no response-to-reviewers, no re-review within a cycle. You re-enter the next annual competition as a fresh application, starting again at the Letter of Intent.

Verbatim (guidelines §3.1): "Unsuccessful applicants may reapply in subsequent years, provided they still meet all eligibility requirements." And §4.1: "Unsuccessful applicants may re-apply in the next competition year, provided they still meet the eligibility criteria. Application guidelines and criteria may be subject to change each year."

Success at LOI stage does not carry over — a previous invitation to Full Proposal buys you nothing next year; you must submit a new LOI.

No cap on attempts is published, but the 36-month post-PhD window (degree conferred no more than 3 years before the Full Proposal deadline) limits most people to 2–3 tries in practice, and career-interruption exemptions are the only way to widen it.

What you get to build a resubmission on is asymmetric: a rejected LOI buys you nothing ("we cannot provide feedback to unsuccessful applicants at the Letter of Intent stage due to the volume of applications that we receive"), while a rejected Full Proposal does ("unsuccessful applicants that were invited to submit a Full Proposal will receive feedback"). Practical implication: if you were cut at LOI, diagnose it yourself against the published scoring bands — most LOI-stage failures are scope (project too applied, too clinical, too descriptive, or too close to your PhD/the host lab's existing work) rather than quality, and fellow@hfsp.org will give a scope read before you re-initiate.
