result.loi_deadline:
Yes, and it is a TWO-STEP deadline — this is the single most common way first-timers lose a cycle.

Step 1 — INITIATE (get the 7-digit LOI ID), 9 days before the real deadline. Verbatim: "It is essential to initiate the Letter of Intent as soon as the team has seriously decided to submit a letter of intent, but by 17 March 2026 the latest. Please note that this deadline is not mentioned on the application site." HFSP flags its own site's silence on this. Mechanically it is trivial — "the PI just needs to save the 'title page', first page of the online application form. A seven-digit identifier will appear below the left-hand menu" — but miss it and the cycle is gone. Also: "Compulsory initiation of a letter of Intent (by obtaining a 7-digit LOI ID)". The site states the initiation step "is mandatory even for those re-applying from previous years."

Step 2 — SUBMIT the LOI: 26 March 2026, 9:00 AM Eastern (AY2027). "The Letter of Intent must be submitted by 26 March 2026."

Relative to the full application: the LOI precedes the invited full proposal by about 5.5 months (26 March -> 10 September). Only invited teams write a full proposal; the full proposal is invitation-only and cannot be entered cold.

Long-lead items behind the LOI date (funder-wide HFSP machinery, confirmed to apply here): every team member — not just the PI — needs their own ProposalCentral account with a completed Professional Profile, registered "at least 48 hours before this deadline"; account activation links "expire after 24 hours"; ORCID is mandatory and "must be completed in the Professional Profile", not in the form. Per the guidelines, "each team member has to enter their own CV information and publications before the submission deadline" — so a slow co-applicant abroad can sink the submission. Team composition stays fluid until the end: "The composition of the team can be modified up to the final submission deadline."

No signatures, no budget and no uploads at LOI stage.
result.deadline_pattern:
Fixed annual cycle, identical shape every year, all times 9:00 am US Eastern. Award years are named for the year the money starts, so the "2027" competition runs through calendar 2026 — the single most common date-reading error with this funder.

Safe to state without a year (research grants, both RG-Program and RG-Early Career): application site opens late January; LOI ID obtained by mid-March; LOI submitted in the last week of March; LOI outcome mid-July; invited full proposal ~10-15 September; review committee meets late January; awards announced end of March; funds start May at the earliest, December at the latest.

One round per year only. There is no rolling or second window for research grants.

Related cadence worth surfacing next to it, because awarded teams graduate into it: "Awarded teams will be eligible to apply for an Accelerator Grant in autumn 2027" — Accelerator site opens early July, deadline ~22 September, awards late March.
result.review_to_award: ~12 months LOI to award; ~14-21 months LOI to first spend. See detail in the review_to_award narrative field above — key mechanism-specific deviations: RG-Early Career is deliberated in a SESSION SEPARATE from RG-Program ("The proposals for RG-Program and for RG-Early Career are discussed in separate sessions"), so it is not ranked against established PIs; funding threshold is "Scores of 7 and above are considered for funding within the limit of funds available"; LOI outcome mid-July (guidelines) vs "early July" (website) — an internal inconsistency in HFSP's own materials; earliest start "May 2027 the earliest, and December 2027, the latest" for the AY2027 round.
result.submission_requirements:
The machinery is near-identical to RG-Program; only eligibility differs. Listing where it deviates from the funder-wide norm and where the norm itself is unusual.

HFSP COUNTS CHARACTERS, NOT PAGES. Everything is typed into ProposalCentral boxes; the research plan is the only uploaded file in the whole system. Limits include spaces and punctuation, and "each subproject section has an upper limit on the character count, and it is impossible to redistribute between the boxes."

LOI (identical for RG-Early Career and RG-Program; from HFSP's "Writing a letter of Intent"): Title max 100 characters; keywords max 10; disciplines max 10; Abstract of overall project 1,200; one subproject box per member at 1,200 each — note "there are four fields in the online form... In teams with five members, the 4th field will have to be shared between two members"; "Frontier science" 1,200; internationality/same-country justification 600; difference from ongoing research 600; key references max 5, 1,200 total. Each member supplies CV, ORCID and up to 10 publications from the last 5 years. No figures, no uploads, no budget, no signatures.

FULL PROPOSAL (invited only): Scientific abstract 2,400; Public abstract 2,400 (must differ); Overview 8,000; Difference to ongoing research 1,500; Interdisciplinarity 1,500; resubmission note if applicable 600. Uploaded research plan, one PDF: "Maximum 30 000 characters including spaces and punctuation in the main text including tables and figure legends but excluding references"; "Type size: Calibri 11-point, text, 1.5 line spacing (references and figure legends can be single spaced)"; "you may include up to 5 figures and/or tables within the text; all combined, these must not exceed two pages"; "The final pdf-file should not exceed 4 Mbytes."

SIGN-OFF — full proposal stage only: "The full proposal must be signed by all the applicants as well as their institutional officials (no signature is required from the financial officials)." "Institutional officials must have 'Edit' access permissions to be able to sign the application online." The institutional official's named institution must match the applicant's exactly or the application cannot be validated. Financial officials do not sign now. Alert your research office early — the guidelines advise applicants "to alert their institutions on the planned international collaboration."

NOT REQUIRED ANYWHERE — the big deviation from US norms: no budget (fixed sum by team size; "no salary support (including summer salaries) can be paid from the grant"), no biosketch, no data-management plan, no facilities section, no letters of reference or support, no mentor/sponsor statement, no preliminary data ("preliminary data are not required").

GATE THAT MISROUTES PEOPLE: "Postdoctoral researchers are not eligible to apply." A postdoc browsing this belongs in the HFSP Long-Term or Cross-Disciplinary Fellowship row, not here. Early Career applicants "must be project leaders directing a research group... full responsibility for the day to day running of their laboratories, and full control of the HFSP funds", and "In cases where the position of the applicant is unclear, written confirmation may be requested from the Head of Department (or equivalent)."

TEAM SHAPE, which is the real submission requirement: 2-4 independent lab heads in different countries; "Teams with all members in one country and teams with more than one member affiliated to the same institution are not eligible (even if a member moves after the LOI submission)"; Principal Applicant's primary lab must be in an HFSPO member country (the USA is one). Watch the collaboration-history trap: "More than three co-publications are very likely seen as proof for an ongoing collaboration and strongly reduce the chance of funding."

Portal: session times out after 20 minutes of inactivity; HFSP advises drafting offline and pasting in. Portal support pcsupport@altum.com, +1-800-875-2562.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
All HFSP-internal. Verbatim from the AY2027 guidelines, sections 3.5 and 3.6.

WHAT DISQUALIFIES YOU
- Holding any HFSP award: "Scientists cannot hold more than one HFSP award at any one time (as Principal Applicants or Co-Applicants, even during a no-cost extension)." And: "Scientists cannot hold or apply for more than one HFSP award (Research Grant, Accelerator Grant or Fellowship) at the same time." Note the scope — a current HFSP fellowship blocks a grant application, and vice versa.
- Recent award years, hard lockout (AY2027 wording): "Awardees from 2023 and 2024 are not eligible to apply as Principal Applicant or Co-Applicant, this also includes Accelerator Grants awarded in 2024 and 2025." This is stricter than the no-double-holding rule — a 2023 grant has already ended by the AY2027 start and still bars you. Combined effect of the two quoted rules: anyone awarded an HFSP grant in 2023-2026 is out of the AY2027 competition. The lockout years roll forward each cycle, so expect 2024/2025 grant awardees and 2025/2026 Accelerator awardees to be barred from AY2028 — projected from the pattern, not yet published.
- Doubling up within a cycle: "No individual may be an applicant on more than one Letter of Intent in the same review cycle. This rule applies to all applicant roles (as Principal Applicant or Co-Applicant) for both RG-Early Career and RG-Program. If a team member appears as applicant on two or more Letters of Intent, these will all be removed from the competition." You cannot hedge Early Career against Program, and one over-committed co-applicant destroys every LOI they appear on — including yours. HFSP puts the policing duty on the PI: "the Principal Applicant must ensure that no team member is a Principal Applicant or Co-Applicant on another proposal... Failure to ensure this will result in all those applications being withdrawn from the competition."
- Recycling a past award: "Applications bearing a strong similarity to previous awards, either in team composition or topic of research, will not be considered eligible."

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY — the half applicants usually never find
- Older awardees can return, conditionally: "Awardees from 2021 and 2022 may apply for a new grant if it starts after closure of the current award (meaning after approval of all final reports), and if the project and team members are different from the current grant." Two live conditions: final reports approved, and a genuinely different team AND project. Disclosure duty attaches — such members "must provide information about the title, the grant reference and the team composition."
- NON-HFSP FUNDING DOES NOT DISQUALIFY ANYONE. There is no NIH-style R01/K interaction here, no cap on concurrent domestic awards, and no bar on holding NIH, NSF, ERC, HHMI or institutional funds. Nothing in the guidelines excludes an applicant for being otherwise well funded. The only constraint is scientific distinctness: projects "must be distinctly different from all team members' other research", HFSP funds "are not intended to replace or supplement current domestic programs", and proposals that are "an obvious next step in the laboratory of one or more applicants" are unlikely to be funded. So other funding is a framing problem, not an eligibility problem — the sole reporting duty is the post-submission overlap update due 15 January.
- Former Career Development Awardees get a geographic carve-out: "As the only exception, former Career Development Awardees can act as Principal Applicants in an HFSP Research Grant irrespective of the location of their laboratories, as long as the team includes at least one Co-Applicant from an HFSP member country." A former CDA holder outside the member-country list can still lead a team.
- Winning here opens the next door rather than closing it: "Awarded teams will be eligible to apply for an Accelerator Grant in autumn 2027."
- Career interruptions extend rather than forfeit the clock: the 5-year-independent and 10-year-post-PhD windows admit "exceptions... for periods of parental leave, compulsory military service or absence for medical conditions, but not for periods of unemployment", and the reviewer handbook confirms "the 10 and 5 year periods... may be extended." List interruptions in the CV "ensuring to provide both start and end date(s) as well as the number of months".
result.program_officer_contact:
grant@hfsp.org — HFSP Grant Office, 12 Quai Saint Jean, 67000 Strasbourg, France. This address is printed in the footer of every page of the application guidelines.

There is NO program officer in the NIH sense: no assigned PO, no portfolio contact, no pre-submission concept call, no relationship to cultivate. The mailbox is staffed by HFSP's own scientists (Secretariat / Scientific Directors) and is the only route.

Pre-submission contact is INVITED but narrow. HFSP asks you to read first: "Please read the guidelines and the document 'Writing a letter of intent' carefully to establish whether your project is clearly in tune with the aims and requirements of the HFSP Research Grant program." Then: "If you have further questions, please contact the HFSP Grant Office: grant@hfsp.org."

Worth asking, because it is where applications die: scope. 10-15% of LOIs are killed purely on scientific scope before any scoring, and HFSP notes that "Each year, a large number of scientifically excellent projects are rejected, even though they fall within the scientific scope of HFSP" on formal eligibility grounds. Eligibility edge cases are explicitly invited — for this mechanism specifically, clinical-service time against the Early Career clock: "In cases where a team member has had a longer period of purely clinical service, applicants should contact the HFSP grant office (grant@hfsp.org)."

Timing norm: ask BEFORE you initiate the LOI (i.e. before mid-March). After submission there is nothing to ask — the budget is a fixed sum by team size and is not negotiated.

What is impossible: nobody will read or comment on your draft, and review-committee members are barred from contact. Verbatim from the reviewer handbook: "Committee members must not give or discuss with applicants or referees any information relating to the results of the review of a specific application, nor must they offer opinions on the chances of success or failure of a specific application after the Review Committees have met. All requests for information relating to applications or the review process should be referred to the Secretariat."

The real substitute for a program officer is HFSP's staff-run webinars in the window between the portal opening and the LOI deadline (Chief Scientific Officer + Senior Scientific Officer, with awardee panellists, free, registration required, recorded to HFSP's YouTube), plus the LOI-submission walkthrough video at https://youtu.be/s9In4HSq7OE, which is linked from the research-grants page. Note: the webinar I could confirm by name and date is the Fellowships one (25 March 2026); a research-grants equivalent is run but I could not pin its date from HFSP's own pages — see unresolved.
result.examples_or_samples:
No sample application is published. HFSP used to have an FAQ item on this and it is now gone — https://www.hfsp.org/node/44336 returns 404 (I confirmed the 404 today; search indexes still serve the old link). Plan around that absence.

BEST AVAILABLE, and it is genuinely good — THE AWARDS ARCHIVE: https://www.hfsp.org/awardees/awards. Confirmed today that "Research Grants - Early Career" is its own selectable programme filter, so you can read only this mechanism's winners rather than the whole HFSP pool. Filters: programme, award year 1990-2026 ("NB: years are award years"), country, nationality. Each entry gives the project title, every team member with nationality and institution, and an expandable abstract — i.e. the funded public abstract. Reading 20 Early Career abstracts is the closest thing to a model of what this committee rewards, and it doubles as your scope test and your team-shape test (you can see how real winning teams distribute countries and disciplines).

ALSO: newly-awarded landing page https://www.hfsp.org/awardees/newly-awarded; the 2025 Research Grant awardee booklet https://www.hfsp.org/bookletRG2025 (confirmed live); "HFSP Science Digest" write-ups of recently awarded projects, linked from the research-grants overview. HFSP itself points applicants at awarded projects as the scope test: "Examples of funded projects indicating the broad scope of HFSP can be found on our website."

HOW YOU WILL BE SCORED — read the reviewer-facing document, which is public and mechanism-specific: "The Peer Review Process", https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/Sciences/Grants/The%20Peer%20Review%20Process.pdf. It contains the 1-10 scale, the "Scores of 7 and above are considered for funding" threshold, the instruction that Early Career is judged in its own session, and the standing instruction to favour applicants "truly in the early stages of their careers". This is more useful than a sample proposal.

HOW TO WRITE THE LOI: "Writing a letter of Intent", https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/Sciences/Grants/Writing%20a%20letter%20of%20Intent.pdf — box-by-box, with the character limits and HFSP's own warnings about what reads as "solid but not of a 'Frontier' character."

CAVEAT on one commonly-cited resource: "The Art of Grantsmanship" (https://www.hfsp.org/node/5761) by Jack Kraicer, former HFSP Director of Research Grants, is hosted by HFSP and free to copy — but it is dated 5 May 1997 and is general advice, stating it is "relevant to most peer-reviewed research grant applications to most granting agencies." It is NOT an HFSP sample or an annotated HFSP application. (The HFSP "Fellowship Primer", PRIMER.pdf, is live but written for fellowship applicants — wrong mechanism for this row.)

NOT FOUND: any university research office or public repository hosting a complete funded HFSP LOI or full proposal. The realistic route to seeing a real one is to approach a named Early Career awardee from the archive, or an awardee panellist from the webinars — individual awardees do share privately.
result.resubmission_note:
There is no NIH-style resubmission track: no A1, no mandatory Introduction, no response-to-reviewers document, no second look within a cycle. HFSP is explicit that it cannot re-review: "Given the program structure, it is impossible for us to reconvene the Committee for a second round of assessments each year."

What actually happens: you re-enter the next annual competition as a fresh application, starting again at the LOI. Obtaining a new LOI ID "is mandatory even for those re-applying from previous years."

The only formal trace of resubmission is at full-proposal stage: "Applicants are also asked to complete a resubmission section if applicable (Max. 600 characters)" on the Title Page — a 600-character note, the nearest thing HFSP has to an introduction page.

What bites instead of a resubmission rule is the eligibility machinery in prior_funding_conflicts — the one-LOI-per-cycle rule and the strong-similarity bar. Practical implication: a rejected Early Career team usually changes something real (team composition or the project's angle) rather than resubmitting the same LOI. And the Early Career clock is the true cap on attempts — 5 years independent / 10 years post-PhD gives most people only a few shots, though parental leave, military service and medical absence extend it.

FEEDBACK you can actually build on, verbatim: LOI stage — "Upon request applicants are informed of the assessment in general terms and the reason(s) that the project was not retained for a full proposal. For applications discussed by the Selection Committee, the Secretariat prepares brief comments based on the comments by committee members and makes these available to the applicants." Full proposal — "All applicants are informed of the result. Based on the written comments by the RC members, the reports of the mail reviewers and the discussion, the Secretariat prepares a summary of the issues raised by the RC and makes these available to the applicants." So a rejected LOI buys you a general-terms explanation and you must ASK for it; a rejected full proposal buys you real reviewer substance automatically.

result.loi_deadline:
No LOI, no pre-proposal, no nomination, no letter of intent of any kind. But there IS a mandatory gating step that functions like one, and missing it is the most common way to lose the cycle:

**ARC ELIGIBILITY QUESTIONNAIRE — available from September 15, 2026; no stated deadline of its own, but it must be cleared before you can touch the application.** It is a binary eligibility screen, not a merit review — nothing is scored and nothing is rejected on science. FAQ [C1], verbatim: "Your first step will be to verify your eligibility by completing an initial questionnaire, which will be available starting on September 15, 2026. If you are deemed eligible, you will be able to inspect the application prompts, formatting guidelines and instructions in the ARC website, and download a PDF version if you wish. Although you will not be able to begin to fill in the required information until the application opens on November 3, 2026, we encourage you to begin to prepare it in advance."

Three consequences worth planning around:
1. Clearing it early buys you seven weeks (Sept 15 → Nov 3) of drafting against the real prompts.
2. It unlocks the redacted example applications (see examples field) — the single biggest reason to do it now.
3. It sets your significant-articles requirement. The Components doc: "Based on the information you provided in the Eligibility Questionnaire, you are required to cite and describe either 3 or 5 of your most significant research articles."

INSTITUTION-ELIGIBILITY REQUEST — the other pre-window action, with a real deadline. If your institution is not on HHMI's eligible list, FAQ [B8] verbatim: "please write to FHS@hhmi.org after September 15, 2026. We will evaluate your institution for potential inclusion on the list and notify you before the application window opens on November 3, 2026." So that request must go in during the Sept 15 – early-Oct window; leaving it until November is too late.

ORCID iD is required before you can even create the ARC account. Components doc, verbatim: "Prior to creating an account, all users will need to have an ORCID identifier."
result.deadline_pattern:
Biennial, one-shot fixed windows — there is no recurring due-date grid. Each competition opens at a published date/time (9:00 AM ET) and closes at a published date/time (11:59 PM ET); between windows there is no route to apply, and HHMI accepts no unsolicited applications.

From the 2028 cycle onward FHS is no longer a standalone competition: the FAQ header states verbatim that "The Freeman Hrabowski Scholars and Hanna H. Gray Fellows Programs will select scientists through a single, combined competition, opening November 3, 2026. (Applicant review is specific to career stage.)" One application portal, one deadline, one review pipeline; the career stage you are at determines which programme you are reviewed for. FAQ [E2] confirms postdocs and faculty do not compete head-to-head: "Our selection process is carefully designed to weigh the merits, accomplishments, and potential relative to others in a similar career stage."

Planning rule that follows from the shape of this cycle: the window is ~6 weeks and the questionnaire opens ~7 weeks before that, so the trigger for a planning calendar is the questionnaire date (mid-September), not the December deadline.

NEXT COMPETITION AFTER THIS ONE: not published. On a biennial cadence the following FHS/HGF competition would be expected to open in late 2028 for 2030 appointments, but HHMI has published no dates for it and I am not asserting any. If you miss December 15, 2026, the realistic wait is roughly two years — and the 7-year independence clock keeps running, which for many applicants means this cycle is their only shot.
result.review_to_award:
Unusually long — **~8 months to any word at all, ~14 months to a decision, ~17–20 months to money.** Budget for this: you are writing in late 2026 for salary that starts in mid-2028. The full arc is published in both the Applicant Guide and the Components PDF:

- Application close: **December 15, 2026**
- **ALL applicants notified of status: August 2027** (deadline + ~8 months). FAQ [E6], verbatim: "All applicants will be notified of their status in the competition in August 2027. At that time, we will inform semifinalists about the next steps and request additional information." This is total silence for eight months — nothing in between, no acknowledgement of progress.
- Semifinalist leadership interviews: **September and October 2027** (+9–10 months)
- Semifinalist recorded scientific presentations due: **October 2027**
- Finalists notified: **November 2027** (+11 months)
- Finalist scientific interviews: **January 2028** (+13 months)
- Selectees notified: **February 2028** (+14 months)
- Acceptance letters due: **two weeks after notification**
- **Appointments begin: May 1, 2028 to August 31, 2028** (+17–20 months)

Three stages, per the Applicant Guide verbatim: "1. An initial review of submitted materials identifies semifinalists 2. A semifinalist stage in which applicants submit additional materials and participate in a virtual interview to assess leadership 3. A finalist stage where applicants participate in a second virtual interview, focused on their science".

Interview dates are effectively immovable — FAQ [A9] addresses conflicts with other commitments, and finalists are told who is on their panel (FAQ [E4]: "If you are selected as a finalist, we will disclose the identity of the panel of reviewers participating in your virtual interview") while reviewers assigned to the written application are never disclosed.

Two timing traps that follow from the long arc:
- Your eligible faculty position must start by **May 1, 2028** — inside the notification-to-appointment gap. If you are applying on the strength of an accepted offer, that offer's start date is the binding constraint, and the offer letter is requested at the semifinalist stage (August 2027), not at submission.
- If you win a potentially incompatible award while this runs, August 2027 is the moment to raise it — see prior-funding field.

NOTE ON AI IN REVIEW (new in the 2028 Components doc, verbatim): "AI-assisted tools may be used during application review, including to help assess scientific scope and fit with scientific disciplines that HHMI supports. All applications are read by one or more human reviewers, who are responsible for all final decisions."
result.submission_requirements:
You submit personally through ARC (https://arc.hhmi.org/login). No Grants.gov, no eRA Commons, no sponsored-programs routing, no dean's signature. FAQ [C3], verbatim: "the application needs to be prepared and submitted by the applicant. Institutional officials, grants office staff, and personnel in your lab should not be involved in preparing and submitting the application." FAQ [F1]: "HHMI does not require nominations or evidence of institutional approval at the time you apply."

WHERE THIS DEVIATES HARDEST FROM NIH/NSF HABITS — four things people get wrong:
1. **NO BUDGET.** FAQ [C4], verbatim: "No. All Scholars receive the same HHMI lab budget, regardless of their lab size or research program, and their salary is determined by HHMI's salary scale for lab heads, which is non-negotiable."
2. **NO REFERENCE LETTERS.** FAQ [C8], verbatim: "No. We are not collecting academic letters of recommendation for this competition." (That is FHS. Hanna Gray applicants instead trigger a mentor questionnaire + CV/NIH Biosketch, due January 5, 2027 — three weeks AFTER the applicant deadline.)
3. **NO SPECIFIC AIMS, AND NIH/NSF FORMATTING IS FORBIDDEN.** FAQ [C5], verbatim: "No. NIH or NSF formatting guidelines do not apply, nor does the typical structure used in those types of project-based proposals, based on a set of specific aims. HHMI supports people, not projects." Components doc: "outline the themes, directions, and approaches you will follow to achieve your goals" over "a span of 5-10 years."
4. **NO JOURNAL NAMES ANYWHERE.** Verbatim: "HHMI evaluates scientific merit independently of where work is or will be published. Accordingly, journal names should not appear anywhere in your written materials. This includes references to journals in the context of submission status, revision, or acceptance. Inclusion of journal names is a violation of competition guidelines and will be taken into account in the evaluation of your application." Journal branding inside an uploaded article PDF is fine and needs no redaction.

COMPONENTS AND LIMITS (FHS 2028, from HHMI's own Components PDF):
- **Research Program Description — 5 pages.** Verbatim: "Text, figures, and figure legends must fit within 5 pages in total. The reference list with full citations is not included in this 5-page limit." Single PDF; figures embedded with legends; figure text ≥10-point; single-spaced; ≥0.5-inch margins all sides; **Arial 11-point text, Arial 10-point legends**. Verbatim warning: "If your document does not follow these formatting instructions, your application may not be considered." Cite your significant articles in the body and **highlight those citations in yellow**, and highlight them in the reference list too.
- Research program **structured abstract**: Background 100 words + Goals 100 + Approach 100. Do not repeat it inside the 5 pages — "both elements will be combined when presented to the reviewers."
- **Scientific vision**: three questions, 150 words each (what makes the questions compelling/unique; why you are well-suited; how success transforms the field).
- **Leadership/mentoring narratives: five questions, 400 words each.** Note these are heavily rewritten for 2028 and are experience-based, not philosophy — verbatim: "Specific examples are more useful than broad philosophy or general aspirations." They cover: two leadership lessons incl. coordinating people; a working relationship where your initial approach failed; an experience shaping your commitment to inclusion; a time you advocated for someone else; and a non-conventional aspect of your path plus "a specific area where you are still working to grow as a leader."
- **Prior research accomplishments**: up to 3 records, 250 words each (challenges, significance, your specific contribution). Verbatim: "These research accomplishments need not have resulted in a publication."
- **Significant articles — 3 or 5, set by your questionnaire answers.** Applicant Guide, verbatim: "Five significant articles, if you have 4 or more years of experience as a lab head by the application deadline; or three significant articles, if you have less than 4 years of experience, or have not yet started your lab." First/co-first/corresponding/co-corresponding authorship only. Each needs: full author list, the abstract copied verbatim, PMID (or DOI), the article PDF, and a 250-word significance statement in your own words. Preprints (bioRxiv/arXiv/medRxiv/chemRxiv only) count equally; manuscripts in prep/submission/review/revision/accepted/in press are excluded; no patents, no meeting abstracts, no reviews.
- **Bibliography**: imported via ORCID, then hand-corrected; primary research articles only — no reviews, perspectives, case reports, conference abstracts, books, chapters or patents.
- **Funding record**: verbatim — "Please list all competitive grants and/or fellowships you have received, beginning with your doctoral training period. Do not list non-competitive awards, or graduate or postdoctoral fellowships that were not awarded to you individually, or grants or fellowships in which you are not the PI, Co-PI or Co-Investigator." Having none is explicitly fine: "If you have no grants or fellowships to report, you will check a box." FAQ [B11] confirms a thin awards record is not disqualifying.
- **Professional service activities**: one activity with an impact statement; reviewed internally by HHMI and NOT shown to reviewers.
- Scientific profile: up to 2 disciplines, up to 2 organisms, 6 keywords.
- Optional 100-word explanatory notes for gaps in education/training/employment history.
- Citation format throughout: "Full author list. Title of article. (Year) PMID." DOI for preprints or anything not in PubMed.
- File mechanics: PDFs; HHMI recommends files not exceed **30 MB each** "to avoid errors that may cause your application to show up as incomplete."

DEFERRED TO SEMIFINALIST STAGE (August 2027) — not needed at submission: the accepted/official offer letter for your faculty position (salary and benefits must be redacted; if it lacks the required elements, a supplemental document signed by the department chair), contact information for your **dean and department chair**, and lab-culture/mentoring materials. FAQ [F2]: the chair is asked how the department will support you and to "respect the 20% limit on your professional time," and the dean is "asked to confirm the date of your initial tenure-track appointment."

AFTER THE DEADLINE, NOTHING CHANGES. FAQ [D1], verbatim: "We do not permit changes to any of the components of the application after the deadline, including the bibliography." Only employment-status changes are reportable (and transfers to a different institution are possible under [D4] but not for semifinalists/finalists past certain points).

Accessibility: ADA accommodations for the application process go to Yury Metelski, Senior Director, HR Transformation, metelskiy@hhmi.org.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
The governing answer is FAQ [B13], and it is permissive at application and restrictive at appointment. **Nothing about your current funding makes you ineligible to APPLY.** The conflicts bite only if you are offered a place.

WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the half people miss):
- Holding competitive grants is explicitly fine. FAQ [B13], verbatim: "Yes. However, bear in mind that the terms of some funding arrangements may be inconsistent with HHMI's policies... Research funding through competitive grants (e.g., NIH, NSF) or institutional awards is generally allowed, as permitted by your institution, but the terms must be consistent with HHMI's policies." So an R01, an NSF award, a CAREER, institutional start-up — none of these bar you.
- **Work already funded by active grants belongs in the application.** FAQ [C6], verbatim: "Yes. We are interested in all your current and planned research, regardless of the funding source you use or intend to use to support the research. You may already be supported by institutional funds or extramural grants for the research you describe, and in the future, you may apply for additional support for any of the projects that you describe in your HHMI application, even if you are selected." You do not have to carve HHMI-only projects out of your programme, and winning does not stop you seeking further grants.
- **Continuing outside research funding as a Scholar is allowed.** FAQ [H7], verbatim: "Yes, your host institution may accept funding from other sources, including nonprofit and industry sources, for any of your research activities, provided the arrangements are consistent with HHMI policies."
- **Being a current Hanna Gray Fellow does not bar you** — it is an intended pathway. FAQ [B-FHS10], verbatim: "Yes, we encourage you to apply. You can apply to the Freeman Hrabowski Scholars Program if you are a Fellow in the faculty phase, or if you are in the postdoc phase but have accepted a tenure-track (or tenure-track equivalent) faculty offer at an HHMI-eligible institution at the time of the application and are scheduled to start that position no later than May 1, 2028."
- **No HHMI history required.** FAQ [B10], verbatim: "It does not. We welcome applications from scientists with no previous connection to the HHMI community."
- A thin fellowship/prize record is explicitly not penalised (FAQ [B11]).
- No cap on applicants per lab or institution (FAQ [B12]).

WHAT ACTUALLY CONFLICTS (all at appointment, not application):
- **THE SALARY RULE IS THE ONE THAT BITES.** FAQ [B13], verbatim: "Freeman Hrabowski Scholars may not receive salary support from any source other than HHMI." Scholars become HHMI employees; salary is set on HHMI's lab-head scale (currently $173,000–$291,000 per the Applicant Guide) and is non-negotiable, supplementable by the host institution "only for approved administrative positions" (FAQ [H6]). Clinical compensation cannot top it up — an explicit warning to physician-scientists in highly compensated specialties.
- **But grant-funded salary is usually fixable, not fatal.** FAQ [H8], verbatim: "Not necessarily. Your institution cannot continue to accept any such funds for your salary after your HHMI appointment is effective. However, scholars typically negotiate directly with the granting agency to reallocate grant funds from salary to research operations." This is the practical move: convert salary lines to research operations rather than relinquishing the grant.
- **Federal employment or federal lab space is a hard bar.** Applicant Guide, verbatim: "Note that federal government employment is not compatible with the Freeman Hrabowski Scholars Program or with the Hanna Gray Fellows Program." FAQ [B-FHS7]: if you are a federal employee and/or your principal research location is a federal facility (NIH, USDA, DOE, VA) and you plan to keep it beyond May 1, 2028, you are ineligible — "However, you may apply if you plan to resign from your federal position and vacate federal lab space if you are selected." A federally employed postdoc moving to an eligible institution is fine ([B-FHS8]).
- **No second lab.** FAQ [B-FHS11], verbatim: "No. HHMI does not permit Freeman Hrabowski Scholars to operate a second lab. If you are selected, you must close the second lab prior to being appointed as an HHMI lab head."
- **80/20 time rule**, which can conflict with teaching-heavy appointments (FAQ [H5]: large lecture courses "every semester or quarter are likely to be incompatible").
- Pre-existing IP licences can require renegotiation before appointment (FAQ [J2]); consulting/industry collaboration is allowed under HHMI policy but "a Scholar may not consult for and collaborate with or receive funding from a company at the same time" ([I3]).
- For contrast (the sister programme, not FHS): "Hanna Gray Fellows may not hold other postdoctoral fellowships or mentored K-series grants from NIH." The K-award exclusion is an HGF rule, not an FHS rule.

THE PROCESS, AND WHEN TO RAISE IT: FAQ [B13], verbatim: "If you are offered to join one of our programs, HHMI will review your funding arrangements and identify arrangements that are inconsistent with our policies. If an arrangement cannot be modified to be consistent with HHMI's policies, you may be required to choose between joining our program and maintaining the other arrangement." If you win something potentially incompatible mid-competition, FAQ [B14] gives the timing verbatim: "All applicants will be notified about their status in the competition in August 2027. If you have been awarded a grant or fellowship that you believe will be incompatible with our programs (see question B13), you may write to FHS@hhmi.org at that time and explain your situation... you may decide to accept the award while the competition is underway, but be aware that if the award is indeed incompatible with HHMI's policies, you might have to relinquish it before you are appointed as a Fellow or Scholar." Practical reading: take the other award, and sort out compatibility in August 2027.

SEPARATE CLOCK CARVE-OUT (not funding, but the other thing worth asking about): FAQ [B15] allows exceptions to the 7-year window (December 15, 2019 – December 15, 2026) for "military service, and family or medical leave," but only where these "resulted in either an official leave from employment during the eligibility window, or an official approval of a tenure-clock extension during the eligibility window." Requests go to Yury Metelski (metelskiy@hhmi.org) with documentation, from September 15, 2026.
result.program_officer_contact:
**FHS@hhmi.org** — the single programmatic contact. There is no program officer in the NIH sense: no assigned PO, no pre-submission concept review, no scientific advice, no advocate inside the review. Applicant Guide, verbatim: "All inquiries and other correspondence regarding HHMI's Freeman Hrabowski Scholars and Hanna Gray Fellows Programs should be directed to FHS@hhmi.org, or alternatively, to: Freeman Hrabowski Scholars and Hanna Gray Fellows Programs, Howard Hughes Medical Institute, 4000 Jones Bridge Road, Chevy Chase, MD 20815-6789."

Other routes:
- **ARCsupport@hhmi.org** — portal/technical problems only (this is the address printed in HHMI's own 2028 Components PDF).
- **metelskiy@hhmi.org** (Yury Metelski, Senior Director, HR Transformation) — ADA accommodations for the application process, and requests to extend the 7-year eligibility window.
- Institution-eligibility requests for THIS cycle go to FHS@hhmi.org, not to a general mailbox (FAQ [B8]).

Pre-submission contact is NOT expected and is not a relationship-building exercise — it is for eligibility and process only.

WHAT THEY WILL ANSWER:
- Whether a specific position counts as post-training. FAQ [B-FHS2], verbatim: "If you are unsure if your current or former position meets this definition, contact us at FHS@hhmi.org, and we will answer your questions."
- Whether your institution can be added to the eligible list, with a promised answer before November 3, 2026 ([B8]).
- Whether a leave qualifies for a clock exception ([B15]).
- Whether another award is compatible — but raise this in **August 2027**, not now ([B14]).
- Residual eligibility questions after the questionnaire ([B1]).

WHAT THEY WILL NOT DO:
- Pre-screen your science. Judge scope yourself against FAQ [A1] and hhmi.org/programs/science-we-support. [A1] rules out "clinical research that is primarily focused on patient outcomes" and translational work solely focused on that.
- Give any feedback, score or comment, ever. FAQ [E7], verbatim: "No. Regardless of the outcome, you will not receive any written comments or scores on applications submitted for this competition."
- Name your reviewers, or honour exclusion requests except "in extraordinary circumstances" ([E4], [E5]). Finalists do learn their interview panel.

WHO TO ACTUALLY TALK TO INSTEAD — this is where the real guidance lives:
1. **Your institution's foundation relations / research development office.** Several universities run internal HHMI feedback committees with internal deadlines weeks ahead of HHMI's; they also often hold prior-year HHMI applications from their own faculty.
2. **Your dean and department chair — early.** They are formally contacted at the semifinalist stage and will be asked to commit to the 20% non-research cap and to describe departmental support ([F2]). If your teaching load breaches 80/20, that negotiation has to happen with them, not with HHMI ([H5]).
3. **If your institutional leadership is discouraging you**, note FAQ [F3] exists precisely for that case — HHMI "strongly encourage[s] all HHMI-eligible institutions to allow eligible faculty" to apply. Do not let a nervous research office be the reason you skip it.
4. **Current HHMI Scholars/Fellows/Investigators at your institution** — identified by name and institution in HHMI cohort news releases.
5. HHMI's own applicant webinars ("Becoming an HHMI Scientist (for Potential Program Applicants)", on HHMI's YouTube channel) plus the FAQ + Applicant Guide + Components PDFs, which together are effectively the missing PO conversation.
result.resubmission_note:
Unlimited reapplication, actively encouraged — but there is no "resubmission" in the NIH sense. No A1, no Introduction page, no response to reviewers, no resubmission flag, and nothing to respond to because HHMI never releases critiques.

FAQ [B9], verbatim: "Yes. There is no limit to the number of times you can apply, and we encourage you to reapply as long as you continue to meet the eligibility requirements for the program you are applying to. A number of current Hanna Gray Fellows and Freeman Hrabowski Scholars applied multiple times before being selected."

No feedback of any kind. FAQ [E7], verbatim: "No. Regardless of the outcome, you will not receive any written comments or scores on applications submitted for this competition." No summary statement, no percentile, no score. A returning applicant is reviewed as a first-time applicant — no credit and no penalty for having applied before.

**THE REAL LIMIT IS THE CLOCK CROSSED WITH THE CADENCE, NOT A RESUBMISSION RULE.** FHS requires ≤7 years in any independent post-training position as of the deadline, and the competition is biennial. So "reapply next round" means roughly two years later with two years burned off a seven-year window — most eligible faculty get two or three attempts at most, and anyone already 5+ years into independence is on their last. Weigh that against the ~17–20 month arc from deadline to appointment: the decision to apply in a given cycle is close to irreversible.

The one lever: FAQ [B15]'s clock exceptions for military service or family/medical leave, which must have produced an official employment leave or an approved tenure-clock extension DURING the window (December 15, 2019 – December 15, 2026). Leaves before your first independent position do not count. Ask about this early, from September 15, 2026, via metelskiy@hhmi.org with documentation.

Also note (sister-programme rule, for anyone moving between the two): current postdoctoral Hanna Gray Fellows who want the new 2028 terms must reapply, be selected, and forfeit the remainder of their existing fellowship (FAQ [B-HGF6]).
result.examples_or_samples:
**The best FHS material is redacted real applications inside ARC, and you only see them after clearing the eligibility questionnaire.** This is the strongest argument for registering now rather than in November.

FAQ [C5], verbatim: "The organization and format we expect are described in detail alongside the application materials and instructions, which you will be able to preview here by September 15. Once you begin to complete your application in HHMI's Application and Review Channel (ARC) website, after you verify you are eligible (see question B1), you will also be able to review examples from previous competitions. Note that these examples include redactions and might follow different formatting requirements, so they are shared only for general guidance."

The Components doc repeats it and adds a caveat: "You may consult the example applications from prior competitions for general guidance of what we are looking for" / "Note that the example applications from the Freeman Hrabowski Scholars applications followed different format specifications and should be consulted only for general guidance and not formatting." Read them for argument and altitude, not layout.

ACTION, in order:
1. Get an ORCID iD if you lack one (required before ARC registration).
2. Register at https://arc.hhmi.org/register and complete the eligibility questionnaire (live since September 15, 2026).
3. Read the prior-competition examples and download the PDF of the application prompts.
4. Draft against the real prompts through October; the form itself opens November 3.

result.prior_funding_conflicts:
THE CONFLICT BITES AT ACTIVATION, NOT AT APPLICATION — and that distinction is the whole value of this field. Holding an NSF GRFP or an NIH F31 right now does NOT make you ineligible to apply.

WHAT BLOCKS YOU (concurrent holding only):
• FAQ [B9], verbatim: "The Gilliam award cannot be held concurrently with another extramurally funded fellowship (e.g., NSF GRFP or NIH F31). If awarded, a Fellow would need to relinquish the other award to accept the Gilliam Fellowship. Alternatively, they may defer activation of the Gilliam award by one year."
• FAQ [E3], verbatim: "During the fellowship term, Fellows may not receive funds from other extramurally funded fellowships, scholarships, or similar awards (such as NSF GRFP or NIH F31). If you hold another fellowship at the time of selection, you would need to relinquish it before activating the Gilliam award, or defer Gilliam activation by one year."
• Applicant Guide, Fellow-Specific Terms, verbatim: "During the fellowship term, you are not permitted to receive funds from other extramurally funded fellowships, scholarships, or similar awards."

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY:
• The one-year deferral is the designed escape hatch — you can win Gilliam, spend year one on your GRFP/F31, then start Gilliam. FAQ [E2], verbatim: "An initial, one-year deferral is allowed and must be approved by HHMI at the time of award notification." Guide: you and your advisor "are expected to participate fully in HHMI programming even if you defer activation of the award."
• YOUR ADVISOR'S GRANTS ARE NOT A CONFLICT — they are a requirement. The advisor must submit "A list of your PhD advisor's current research support, specifying the support that will fund your project for the duration of your time in the PhD program." Gilliam money cannot touch research costs at all: FAQ [E6], verbatim: "Gilliam grant funds cover stipend, professional development, and institutional costs only. Research costs (including consumable supplies and equipment) are the responsibility of the thesis advisor." [E7]: no indirect costs. So Gilliam never displaces an R01 — it assumes one.
• An advisor who already has or had a Gilliam Fellow is fine. FAQ [B11], verbatim: "If my advisor currently has or previously had a Gilliam Fellow in their lab, can I still apply? Yes." Webinar deck: "Advisors who are current or former Gilliam advisors can apply again."
• No cap per lab or institution. FAQ [B12]: "No. If multiple students from the same lab apply, a complete application for each student is required, including separate, complete and distinct thesis advisor materials customized for each applicant."
• No prior HHMI affiliation needed. Guide + FAQ [D2], verbatim: "We encourage applications from individuals of all backgrounds, experiences, and perspectives and from institutions not previously affiliated with HHMI." Webinar deck records 29 new awardee institutions since 2022.
• Qualifying-exam/candidacy status is irrelevant ([B10]); transcripts are not required ("academic transcripts are not required"); departmental affiliation does not matter ([B16]); MD-PhD/DVM-PhD dual-degree students are eligible ([B15]); adjunct advisors qualify if they are the permanent full-time PhD advisor ([B13]).

BOUNDARY HHMI HAS NOT DRAWN (ask before assuming): the FAQ names only NSF GRFP and NIH F31 as examples of a blocking award. It does not say whether an NIH T32 training-grant appointment, an institutional/departmental fellowship, a diversity supplement, or a foreign government scholarship counts as an "extramurally funded fellowship, scholarship, or similar award." This is the single most likely place for an applicant to get it wrong — write to gilliam@hhmi.org.
result.review_to_award:
SUBMISSION → NOTIFICATION → START, from HHMI's own 2027 pages: October 27, 2026 (close) → "Award Notification: Summer 2027" (roughly 8–9 months) → "Fellowship Terms Begin: September 1, 2027" (roughly 10 months). FAQ [D5], verbatim: "Award notifications are expected in Summer 2027. Fellowship terms begin September 1, 2027."

HOW THIS DEVIATES FROM THE FUNDER NORM — Gilliam is HHMI's FASTEST and SIMPLEST arc. It is a SINGLE-STAGE review: no eligibility pre-window, no semifinalist tier, no interview, no recorded video presentation, no symposium. FAQ [D1], verbatim and complete: "Each application will be evaluated by HHMI with advice from external scientists." Compare FHS/HGF (three stages, two virtual interviews, a 15-minute recorded presentation, ~14 months to notification and 17–20 months to start) and Investigator (~16 months to announcement). Nothing is asked of you between submitting and hearing back.

NO FEEDBACK, EVER. FAQ [D6], verbatim: "No. Due to the volume of applications, HHMI is unable to provide individual feedback." Applicant Guide, verbatim: "HHMI is unable to provide feedback on applications." There are no scores, percentiles or summary statements.

WHAT THE CLOCK LOOKS LIKE AFTER YOU WIN — budget for it now, because your advisor is signing up too. The award runs up to three consecutive years, "typically covering years 3–5 of the PhD" ([E1]). The advisor must complete a year-long HHMI mentorship development course: "monthly online interactive webinars from October 2027 through March 2028 and one in-person workshop in Spring 2028," arranged and paid for by HHMI; an advisor who cannot attend may request a one-year delay to 2028–2029 "even if you have graduated," and an advisor who completed the course within the last two years may retake it or nominate a faculty colleague ([E5]). You must attend the Gilliam Annual Meeting; HHMI pays travel and accommodation. A Gilliam PhD Fellow may afterwards apply for four more years as a Gilliam Postdoc Fellow — not automatic, an internal competition, with roughly 40 postdoc fellows anticipated per year ([F1], [F2]).
result.submission_requirements:
DEVIATION HEADLINE: this is a PAIRED application. You are the lead applicant, but roughly half the package is written by your PhD advisor, and none of it routes through a grants office. FAQ [C2], verbatim: "The student, thesis advisor, and additional reference submit their materials directly via the ARC system. Institutional grants offices are not involved in preparing or submitting Gilliam applications."

HOW TO START (webinar deck, verbatim steps): "Starting September 1, access the Gilliam application by visiting the Gilliam Fellows Program webpage (hhmi.org/programs/gilliam-fellows)" → "Login or create an account for HHMI's Application and Review Channel (ARC)" → "Complete the brief, eligibility questionnaire" → "Add contact info for your PhD Advisor and Reference" → "Submit all materials, including those from your Advisor and Reference, by October 27, 2026 at 11:59pm ET." The live entry point HHMI links from the programme page is https://arc.hhmi.org/applicant/application/gilliam2027/home (it returns an ARC error shell to a logged-out fetch — it needs a session; register at https://arc.hhmi.org/register, and per the funder-wide norm you need an ORCID iD before you can create the account).

STUDENT COMPONENTS (six):
1. Eligibility information and educational history — "academic transcripts are not required."
2. "A list of up to 5 of your contributions to science, which can include primary research articles, presentations, and participation in organized activities that advance excellence and inclusion in science."
3. PhD RESEARCH OVERVIEW — 3 PAGES MAXIMUM, the hardest constraint in the package. Verbatim: "An overview of your PhD research written so that a scientist outside of your field understands your project. The maximum length of this document is three pages, including text and figures. This document must be written by you, not your PhD advisor." Citations go in a SEPARATE uploaded document and do not count ([C7]). Figures DO count ([C8]). FAQ [C7], verbatim: "the 3-page limit is intentional. Gilliam applications are reviewed by scientists, but likely not by experts in your specific field… A shorter, well-crafted overview will serve your application better than a longer, highly technical one."
4. Leadership prompt responses — "specific experiences that have shaped your commitment to advancing excellence and inclusion in science, what those experiences have taught you about yourself as an emerging leader, and how you are putting those lessons into action in your research environment."
5. Career statement — goals, plan for pursuing them during the PhD "including your advisor's role in your development," and how the fellowship supports your growth.
6. JOINT CONFLICT-RESOLUTION STATEMENT — "Written together with your PhD advisor, a joint statement on conflict resolution strategies that you will use during your time together as a student-advisor pair." This has no analogue in any other HHMI competition and requires a real conversation with your advisor; start it early.

ADVISOR COMPONENTS (six, submitted by the advisor in ARC): academic background, training, contributions to science, relevant primary research articles, and "a list of their prior trainees and career outcomes"; current research support naming what will fund your project for the rest of your PhD; a LETTER OF SUPPORT, LIMIT 2 PAGES (promise as a scientist, commitment to a research career, leadership potential, "your areas for growth," and passion for advancing excellence and inclusion); a healthy-research-environment statement; and a MENTORING PLAN covering current lab culture and how it is sustained, how the lab will support your success "including any areas to be further developed," how they will support your professional goals, "Their role in preparing your PhD research overview," and their interest in the required HHMI mentorship development course.

REFERENCE (one, not the advisor): "someone other than your PhD advisor who is familiar with you as a scientist (e.g., a former research mentor or a member of your PhD thesis committee)" — a co-advisor MAY serve ([C6]); a co-advisor may NOT be added as a second advisor ([C4]).

FORMATTING RULE THAT DISQUALIFIES BY HABIT — NO JOURNAL NAMES ANYWHERE. Guide + FAQ [C9], verbatim: "please do not reference journal names in any part of your application materials — whether citing published papers or referring to manuscripts that are in preparation, submission, revision, accepted, or in press at a peer-reviewed journal. This includes references to journals in the context of your contributions to science, citations for your PhD research overview, and your advisor's relevant research articles." Citation format, verbatim: "Full author list. Title of article. (Year) PMID. For preprints and journal articles not indexed on PubMed, use a DOI." FAQ [D4]: "HHMI does not consider journal names at any stage of the selection process… Reviewers are instructed not to consider journal names in their evaluation."

NOT REQUIRED (unlike most fellowships): transcripts, GRE, institutional sign-off, dean's letter, nomination, co-advisor, a second reference, or a specific-aims page.

EVALUATION CRITERIA, verbatim from the Guide: "Your scientific creativity and clarity in communicating your research"; "Your commitment to a career in scientific research"; "Your and your advisor's demonstrated and ongoing commitment to advancing excellence and inclusion in science through your experiences, perspectives, and plans for fostering inclusive research environments."

SCALE (HHMI's own 2027 information-session deck): "80 ANTICIPATED AWARDS FOR 2027 — Largest cohort in program history"; "531 FELLOWS & ALUMNI IN THE COMMUNITY, 2004–Present"; 77 institutions hosted Gilliam Fellows 2022–2025.

ROW CORRECTION FOR data/mechanisms.csv (typical_award_size currently reads "exact stipend not stated on current page"): the 2027 Applicant Guide states it exactly — "$65,000 per year for up to three years," comprising "Your PhD stipend of $50,000," "A discretionary allowance of $5,000" (professional development, conferences, dependent care, non-elective medical/dental/vision/mental-health services, up to $1,000/yr toward food or housing, and computing equipment), and "An institutional allowance of $10,000 to offset additional institutional costs… such as tuition, university-sponsored health insurance coverage, and fees." Paid to the student's graduate institution.

PRE-SUBMISSION CONTACT IS NOT EXPECTED and will not get your science vetted. FAQ [B2], verbatim: "Can I submit an abstract of my research in advance of application if I am unsure whether my project is eligible? We do not provide specific determinations about research eligibility for potential applicants outside of the application review process." Judge scope yourself against hhmi.org/programs/science-we-support plus FAQ [A1], which rules OUT: "clinical research that is primarily focused on patient outcomes; medical and translational research that is solely focused on pharmacological, diagnostic or therapeutic advancements; epidemiology research, or research on health disparities or healthcare services; applied biotechnological or agricultural research; environmental or climate science research; observational studies in ecology or animal behavior; and computational or theoretical research that is not grounded in actual biological data collected experimentally."

GILLIAM-SPECIFIC HARD LINE — DEVIATION WORTH KNOWING: where FHS/HGF operates a documented eligibility-clock exception route (military/family/medical leave, via Yury Metelski), Gilliam does not. FAQ [B3], in full, verbatim: "Does the program make exceptions to eligibility criteria? WHO TO ACTUALLY TALK TO, IN ORDER — this matters more here than in any other HHMI competition:
1. YOUR PhD ADVISOR, FIRST AND IMMEDIATELY. They are a co-applicant, not a referee: six components, a 2-page letter, a mentoring plan, a trainee-outcomes list, and — if you win — a year-long mentorship course (monthly webinars Oct 2027–Mar 2028 plus an in-person workshop in Spring 2028). result.resubmission_note:
REAPPLICATION IS ALLOWED AND UNPENALISED, BUT THE PhD CLOCK USUALLY GIVES YOU AT MOST TWO SHOTS. FAQ [B8], verbatim: "Can previous applicants re-apply? Yes, as long as they still meet all other eligibility criteria — in particular, they must not be beyond their third year of graduate school. Returning applicants are reviewed and evaluated the same as first-time applicants."

There is no "resubmission" in the NIH sense: no A1 designation, no Introduction page, no response-to-reviewers, nothing to respond to — because HHMI releases no critiques ([D6], verbatim: "Due to the volume of applications, HHMI is unable to provide individual feedback"). A returning application is simply a fresh application, neither credited nor penalised for the earlier attempt.

WHAT THE CLOCK ACTUALLY ALLOWS: you must be "in your second or third year of a PhD program as of October 27, 2026" ([B7]: "Students must be in their second or third year of their PhD program as of the application close date"). So a second-year applying in the 2027 competition can apply once more as a third-year in the 2028 competition; a third-year applying now has exactly one attempt. And there is no relief valve — FAQ [B3], in full: "Does the program make exceptions to eligibility criteria? No." Years count from programme entry, not lab entry, and changing labs does not reset them ([B7]). If you are a third-year this year, treat October 27, 2026 as your only date.

TWO POINTS OF CAUTION ON DRIFT: (a) the FAQ is explicitly a living document during the window ("This document may be updated periodically during the application submission window. Last updated: August 17, 2026") — re-read it in the final week; (b) the 2027 Gilliam FAQ says NOTHING about post-deadline edits or deadline extensions. The corresponding FHS/HGF rules ("We do not permit changes to any of the components of the application after the deadline, including the bibliography"; extensions "considered only under exceptional circumstances") are from a DIFFERENT competition's FAQ and I did not find them restated for Gilliam. Do not rely on HHMI practice being uniform here — treat 11:59 PM ET on October 27 as final and unamendable, and ask gilliam@hhmi.org if you need otherwise.

Biennial, single fixed one-shot window; no recurring grid, no rolling submission, no unsolicited applications between windows. From the 2028 cycle onward, Hanna Gray Fellows and Freeman Hrabowski Scholars are selected through ONE combined competition with a single application and a single deadline — HGF page, verbatim: "Beginning with the 2028 competition — opening November 3, 2026 — the Hanna H. Gray Fellows and Freeman Hrabowski Scholars Programs will select scientists through a single, combined competition. (Applicant review is specific to career stage.)"

Window shape for 2028: questionnaire opens T-3 months (Sept 15, 2026), application opens T-6 weeks (Nov 3, 2026), closes Dec 15, 2026. Deadline extensions are effectively unavailable — FAQ [C2], verbatim: "Deadline extensions will be considered only under exceptional circumstances."

result.prior_funding_conflicts:
THE HEADLINE: holding other money does NOT block you from APPLYING. It can block you from ACCEPTING. HHMI adjudicates the conflict at offer stage, not at application stage — so a conflicting award is never a reason to skip the competition.

WHAT DISQUALIFIES (at appointment, not application):
 • Other postdoctoral fellowships and NIH mentored K-series awards. FAQ [B13], verbatim: "Hanna Gray Fellows may not hold other postdoctoral fellowships or mentored K-series grants from NIH." This is the single most important line for the target applicant — an NIH K99 phase, a K01/K08/K23, or a competing private postdoc fellowship (Damon Runyon, Jane Coffin Childs, HFSP, Life Sciences Research Foundation) is the thing that collides.
 • Federal government employment. Applicant Guide, verbatim: "Note that federal government employment is not compatible with the Freeman Hrabowski Scholars Program or with the Hanna Gray Fellows Program." FAQ [B-HGF5] is blunter — a postdoc employed by the US federal government is answered "No", you must be at an HHMI-eligible institution at the time of application.
 • Being a current Hanna Gray Fellow under the old terms. FAQ [B-HGF6]: to move to the new programme you must re-apply, be selected, AND "forfeit the remainder of your current fellowship and be reappointed under the new program terms."
 • Downstream warning for the faculty phase: Freeman Hrabowski Scholars "may not receive salary support from any source other than HHMI" ([B13]). That constraint does not bind you as a Fellow, but it will when you convert.

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the half applicants never get told):
 • Holding non-HHMI funding is fine to apply with. FAQ [B13] question is "I currently receive or expect to receive funding from non-HHMI sources. Am I eligible to apply?" — the answer opens with a flat "Yes."
 • Competitive research grants survive. Verbatim: "Research funding through competitive grants (e.g., NIH, NSF) or institutional awards is generally allowed, as permitted by your institution, but the terms must be consistent with HHMI's policies."
 • The conflict is resolved only if you win. Verbatim: "If you are offered to join one of our programs, HHMI will review your funding arrangements and identify arrangements that are inconsistent with our policies. If an arrangement cannot be modified to be consistent with HHMI's policies, you may be required to choose between joining our program and maintaining the other arrangement." Note "cannot be modified" — HHMI negotiates before it forces a choice.
 • You may accept a conflicting award WHILE the competition runs. FAQ [B14], verbatim: "Depending on the timing, you may decide to accept the award while the competition is underway, but be aware that if the award is indeed incompatible with HHMI's policies, you might have to relinquish it before you are appointed as a Fellow or Scholar." The designated moment to raise it is August 2027, when all applicants learn their status — write to FHS@hhmi.org then, not now.
 • Having NO funding record is explicitly not a mark against you. FAQ [B11] asks whether a thin record of fellowships/prizes hurts; HHMI notes there are more outstanding scientists than there are awards to go round. The Components form makes it mechanical: "If you have no grants or fellowships to report, you will check a box to complete this section."
 • Work already funded by someone else can be proposed. FAQ [C6], verbatim: "We are interested in all your current and planned research, regardless of the funding source."
 • No prior HHMI connection needed ([B10]); multiple applicants from one lab allowed with no cap ([B12]).

WHAT YOU MUST DECLARE: a "Funding record" listing all competitive grants/fellowships since doctoral training where you are PI, Co-PI or Co-Investigator. Excluded from the list: non-competitive awards, and any fellowship not awarded to you individually.
result.review_to_award:
A 14-MONTH REVIEW AND A 17-20 MONTH RUNWAY TO MONEY — far longer than NIH's ~9-month submission-to-award and long even by private-foundation standards. Plan salary continuity across two years from the date you submit.

Submission Dec 15, 2026 →
 • Stage 1, ALL applicants notified of status: August 2027 (deadline + ~8 months). Materials reviewed "by scientific experts and experts in inclusive lab leadership." Everyone hears, not just those advancing — this is also the designated moment to raise an incompatible award ([B14]).
 • Semifinalist leadership interview (virtual, on lab leadership and mentoring): September–October 2027 (+9-10 months). FAQ [A9] indicates interview dates are not reschedulable — hold the window.
 • Semifinalist 15-minute recorded video presentation on research accomplishments and future plans, due October 2027. Semifinalists also supply lab-culture materials, dean and department-chair contacts, evidence of doctoral conferral date, and the appointment letter for their FIRST postdoctoral position (confidential information redacted).
 • Finalists notified: November 2027 (+11 months).
 • Finalist scientific interview (virtual, second interview, focused on the science): January 2028 (+13 months).
 • Selectees notified: February 2028 (+14 months). Acceptance letters due two weeks after notification.
 • EARLIEST START / appointment begins: May 1, 2028 to August 31, 2028 (+17 to +20 months).

DEVIATION FROM THE FUNDER NORM: the three-stage interview ladder (leadership interview, then recorded talk, then a science interview) is heavier than the Investigator programme's single symposium, and unlike Gilliam — which has no documented interview stage at all — a Hanna Gray applicant should budget for two live virtual interviews plus a recorded presentation across Sept 2027–Jan 2028.

result.submission_requirements:
WHERE HGF DEVIATES FROM THE FUNDER-WIDE NORM AND FROM ITS SIBLING PROGRAMME:

1. NO REFERENCE LETTERS — ONE MENTOR QUESTIONNAIRE INSTEAD. HGF page, verbatim: "Recommendation Letters: None are required, but your mentor will complete a questionnaire to help us evaluate your readiness for independence." FAQ [C8]: "No. We are not collecting academic letters of recommendation for this competition." You enter the mentor's details in ARC, click "Notify by Email", and ARC sends them their own login; ARC then shows you whether they have submitted. Their questionnaire + CV/NIH Biosketch is due January 5, 2027 — three weeks after your own deadline. Components PDF, verbatim: "We strongly recommend that you inform your mentor prior to this step, and that you discuss your research and career-development plans with them." The mentor is not a referee; they are asked to confirm support and commitment to your training and to comment on your readiness to go independent.

2. RESEARCH PROGRAM DESCRIPTION — 5 PAGES, AND THE FORMATTING IS ENFORCED. Single PDF containing text, figures and figure legends. Verbatim: "Text, figures, and figure legends must fit within 5 pages in total. The reference list with full citations is not included in this 5-page limit." Arial 11-pt text, Arial 10-pt legends, figure text ≥10-pt, single-spaced, minimum 0.5-inch margins all sides, figures embedded with a legend each, file ≤30 MB. Verbatim warning: "If your document does not follow these formatting instructions, your application may not be considered." Highlight in YELLOW the citations to your significant articles, both in the body and in the reference list.

3. DO NOT WRITE IT LIKE AN NIH PROPOSAL. FAQ [C5], verbatim: "No. NIH or NSF formatting guidelines do not apply, nor does the typical structure used in those types of project-based proposals, based on a set of specific aims." Components PDF: "outline the themes, directions, and approaches you will follow" over a 5-10 year horizon; "not at the level of experimental detail typically expected in a research grant proposal to a federal agency." Written for both generalists and specialists.

4. NO JOURNAL NAMES ANYWHERE — a rule with teeth. Verbatim: "Inclusion of journal names is a violation of competition guidelines and will be taken into account in the evaluation of your application." Applies to the research description, references, bibliography, prior-research records, scientific vision and career-development answers, and to submission/revision/acceptance status. Exception: journal branding inside an uploaded article PDF needs no redaction. Citation format: "Full author list. Title of article. (Year) PMID." DOI for preprints or anything not in PubMed.

5. SIGNIFICANT ARTICLES: 1 to 3 (FHS applicants file 3 or 5 — this is the sharpest HGF/FHS divergence). Verbatim: "at least 1 and up to 3 research articles in which you are the first, co-first, corresponding, or co-corresponding author." Must be publicly available as a peer-reviewed article or a preprint on bioRxiv/arXiv/medRxiv/chemRxiv only. Manuscripts in preparation, submission, review, revision, accepted or in press are excluded. No patents, no meeting abstracts, no reviews. Each needs: 250-word significance statement in your own words, full author list in the original order, the abstract copied verbatim, PMID/DOI, and the article PDF (≤30 MB).

6. HGF-ONLY CAREER-DEVELOPMENT SECTION, 150 words each: how you will spend your professional time during the postdoc phase; what steps you have taken or will take to secure a faculty position; whether you have already applied for faculty positions (Yes/No); and "How is your planned research program distinct from that of your postdoctoral mentor?"

7. LEADERSHIP NARRATIVES — five questions, 400 words each. Two leadership lessons (one coordinating multiple people toward a shared goal); a working relationship where your initial approach failed; an experience shaping your commitment to inclusion in science; a time you advocated for someone else; and a non-linear aspect of your own path. Verbatim steer: "Specific examples are more useful than broad philosophy or general aspirations."

8. ALSO REQUIRED: structured abstract (Background / Goals / Approach, 100 words each — do not repeat it inside the 5-page description); scientific vision, three questions at 150 words each; up to 3 prior research accomplishments at 250 words each (publications not required); bibliography imported via ORCID and then hand-corrected to primary research articles only; education, training and employment history; funding record; up to two scientific disciplines, up to two organisms, six keywords. Optional 100-word explanations for gaps — HHMI asks that you NOT include personal medical or confidential information there.

9. NO INSTITUTIONAL ROUTING, AND DELEGATES ARE BARRED. You submit personally; no grants office, no dean's signature at application time. FAQ [C3] is explicit that institutional officials, grants office staff and lab personnel should not be involved in preparing or submitting. Note the HGF/FHS split: the institutional-confirmation step in [F1]/[F2] applies to Freeman Hrabowski semifinalists; for HGF the equivalent is the mentor questionnaire, with dean and chair contacts collected only at semifinalist stage.

10. PHYSICIAN-SCIENTISTS IN CLINICAL TRAINING ARE ELIGIBLE, with an extra document. Clinical residencies must be complete and you must be scheduled into a mentored postdoc at an HHMI-eligible institution by May 1, 2028. You nominate your FUTURE mentor for the questionnaire, and at semifinalist stage supply that position's offer letter specifying title, start date and the mentor's name, title and affiliation, with salary/stipend and benefits redacted.

11. PREREQUISITES BEFORE YOU CAN EVEN REGISTER: an ORCID iD is required to create an ARC account, and your institution must be on HHMI's eligible list (https://www.hhmi.org/programs/eligible-institutions). If it is absent, write to FHS@hhmi.org before the window opens.

12. THE 7-YEAR CLOCK IS COUNTED UNUSUALLY — read this before assuming you are over. Verbatim [B-HGF2]: "All research positions you have held since the start date of your first postdoctoral research training position count towards this 7-year limit, regardless of title, whether in academia, industry or government, in the US or abroad." Gaps between positions count too, "irrespective of length or employment status, except for clinical training periods." But: "the time between the conferral date of your doctoral degree and your first postdoctoral research training appointment does not count toward the 7-year limit." There is no minimum experience ([B-HGF3]). Mentored roles titled Associate Research Scientist, Research Specialist, Project Scientist or Staff Scientist DO count as postdoctoral positions.

13. NOTHING CHANGES AFTER DECEMBER 15. Verbatim [D1]: "We do not permit changes to any of the components of the application after the deadline, including the bibliography." Only employment-status changes are reportable. Uploads are PDFs; HHMI recommends ≤30 MB per file "to avoid errors that may cause your application to show up as incomplete."
