result.resubmission_note:
UNLIMITED RE-APPLICATION, BUT NO "RESUBMISSION" IN THE NIH SENSE — no A1, no Introduction page, no response to reviewers, nothing to mark as a resubmission, and nothing to respond to because HHMI never releases critiques.

FAQ [B9], verbatim: "There is no limit to the number of times you can apply, and we encourage you to reapply as long as you continue to meet the eligibility requirements for the program you are applying to. A number of current Hanna Gray Fellows and Freeman Hrabowski Scholars applied multiple times before being selected."

NO FEEDBACK, EVER. FAQ [E7], verbatim: "Regardless of the outcome, you will not receive any written comments or scores on applications submitted for this competition." No summary statements, no percentile, no scores. A second attempt is therefore a rewrite from your own judgement, not a revision — budget for that.

THE REAL LIMIT IS THE CLOCK AND THE CADENCE, NOT A RULE ABOUT ATTEMPTS: the programme is biennial and the ceiling is 7 years of postdoctoral experience measured at each cycle's deadline, so in practice a postdoc gets two or three attempts at most, and a failed attempt costs two years rather than one review round. Clock extensions exist and are the thing to ask about — [B15] allows exceptions for military service, family or medical leave, but only where these produced an official leave from employment or an official tenure-clock extension during the eligibility window; leaves before your first postdoc, and generic COVID extensions, do not qualify.

TWO ROUTE-CHANGES THAT ARE NOT RESUBMISSIONS AND ARE EASY TO MISS:
 • WIN A FACULTY JOB MID-REVIEW AND YOUR APPLICATION CAN CONVERT. FAQ [D3] confirms an HGF applicant who obtains a tenure-track position while under review can be considered for the Freeman Hrabowski Scholars Program instead — provided the position is at an HHMI-eligible institution and meets FHS criteria, and you notify HHMI if selected as a semifinalist. The combined competition makes this a conversion, not a new application.
 • CHANGE LAB OR INSTITUTION MID-REVIEW. FAQ [D2] permits switching postdoc mentor and/or institution while under review, provided it happens before semifinalists are notified and the new institution is HHMI-eligible. Verbatim: "Transfers are not permitted for semi-finalists between the semi-finalist stage and the selection stage."

Current Hanna Gray Fellows on the old terms who want the new ones must re-apply, be selected, and forfeit the remainder of their existing fellowship ([B-HGF6]).

result.deadline_pattern: ANNUAL, FEBRUARY ONLY — one shot per year, no spring/fall alternation. Confirmed on CFF's Academic Funding Opportunities list ("Harry Shwachman Clinical Investigator Award — Deadline: February"). It shares this February-only slot with the LeRoy Matthews Physician-Scientist Award and both Clinical Fellowship Award tracks (Education and Training; Research) — all of which ran to 25 February 2026. RFA-to-deadline lead time: ~12 weeks (published 4 December 2025 for 25 February 2026). WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: the basic-science family (Research Grant, Pilot & Feasibility, Postdoctoral Fellowship and their Path-to-a-Cure variants) runs TWICE a year, in May and December, so a slip there costs 6 months. Here a missed February costs a full 12 months, and the mechanism is aimed at a transition window — fellowship-to-faculty — that does not wait. The practical consequence: for a February deadline you want the mentor conversation and the Program Officer conversation happening in October-November, working from the prior cycle's Policies and Guidelines, because the current RFA will not exist until December.
result.loi_deadline: Not applicable — no LOI, no pre-proposal, no invite-only filter. The Policies and Guidelines answer the Letter of Intent line of the Key Dates table with the words "Not applicable to this RFA", and the strings "Letter of Intent" and "LOI" appear nowhere else in the document. This is a one-stage, full-application-only mechanism. THIS IS A REAL DEVIATION AND IT CUTS BOTH WAYS: CFF's clinical track (Clinical Research Award, Clinical Pilot and Feasibility Award) gates full applications behind an LOI approved ~4.5 months ahead, where only ~35% of investigators are invited on. Shwachman has no such gate — nobody screens your idea before you commit, there is no cheap early signal, and you write the whole package (10-page research plan, 5-page training plan, four reference letters, two mentor-supplied uploads) on the first pass. The substitute for the missing LOI is the Program Officer conversation: Elizabeth Yu, Ph.D. (eyu@cff.org). Treat that email as the LOI you do not get to submit.
result.review_to_award: FASTER THAN THE CFF NORM — this is the mechanism's main scheduling advantage, and it changes what you must have ready. Verbatim Key Dates from the 2026 RFA: "Published: December 4, 2025 / Application Deadline: February 25, 2026 at 5:00 PM (Eastern) / Committee Review: May 2026 / Applicant Notification: Late May 2026 / Earliest Project Start: July 1, 2026." That is ~3 months deadline-to-notification and ~4.2 months deadline-to-start. COMPARE THE FUNDER NORM: basic-science Research Grants ran 12 May 2026 → notification September 2026 → start 1 November 2026 (4.0 months / 5.6 months); CFF's own umbrella figure is that review "can take anywhere from four to eight months from application submission to notification depending on the RFA." Shwachman sits at the fast end of that range. THREE CONSEQUENCES: (1) Notification lands in the SAME MONTH as committee review — there is essentially no gap between the panel meeting and the answer, so do not expect a quiet interval to prepare. (2) Start is only ~5 weeks after notification, so IRB/IACUC/IBC approvals and the institution's W-9 and 501(c)(3) letter must be cleared with GCMA during the March-May review wait, NOT after you hear — CFF withholds payment until those are on file. (3) A February deadline with a 1 July start maps cleanly onto an academic-year faculty appointment, which matters because fellows may apply but "funding will only be considered if they will hold a faculty-level appointment at the time of the award." Review is by the PTP committee (fellowships and physician-scientist career awards). Applicants are notified by GCMA with anonymized reviewer critiques — the summary-statement analogue.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
BOTH HALVES. The headline: this RFA names NO prior-funding disqualifier at all — no K, no R01, no other-CFF-award bar. The real gates are stage, effort and institution type.

WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (verbatim, and unusually generous):
- OTHER SALARY SUPPORT IS FINE: "Supplementation of salary from other sources is allowable." Holding other salary money does not disqualify you.
- NIH K AWARDS ARE NOT BARRED. The words "K08", "K23", "R01", "concurrent", "simultaneous" and "previously funded" do not appear in the document. The only stage signal is a norm, not a rule: "Successful applicants are typically pre-NIH K-award and need strong mentorship to establish themselves as independent CF researchers." Read that carefully — this award sits BEFORE the K on the ladder, inverting the usual NIH K→R01 logic. Holding a K does not make you ineligible; it makes you probably past the intended stage, which is a fit question for the Program Officer, not an eligibility bar.
- SENIOR FELLOWS MAY APPLY, not only faculty: "Junior faculty and senior fellows are eligible to apply."
- THE PROFILE THEY WANT: "In general, a successful candidate has: (i) previous relevant research training; (ii) expertise in a related research technique; and (iii) presentation or publication record that demonstrates research competence and productivity during fellowship (and beyond, if applicable)."

WHAT DISQUALIFIES (verbatim):
- FOR-PROFIT, FLATLY: "Applicants must be from a non-profit or academic institution; for-profit entities are not eligible to apply." DEVIATION: funder-wide, for-profit applicants merely have to clear eligibility with the PO first; here they are barred outright.
- NO FACULTY APPOINTMENT AT START: "Fellows may submit applications; however, funding will only be considered if they will hold a faculty-level appointment at the time of the award." You can apply in February as a fellow, but you must be faculty by 1 July or the money does not come.
- UNDER 70% RESEARCH EFFORT: "A minimum of 70% of the applicant's time must be devoted to research." WITH AN EXPLICIT WAIVER ROUTE: "Subspecialties that require a substantial commitment to clinical service (>30%) may be accommodated with a lower research commitment on a case-by-case basis at the discretion of the Program Officer." For a clinically busy applicant this single sentence is the difference between having an application and not having one — and it is only available by asking.

CITIZENSHIP — TWO CFF SOURCES CONTRADICT EACH OTHER, FLAGGING FOR ANY INTERNATIONAL APPLICANT: the award's web page states "U.S. citizenship or permanent resident status is required" (read live 2026-09-18, and this is what the existing CSV row records). The Policies and Guidelines eligibility section says the opposite: "Candidates may be either U.S. citizens, permanent residents, or non-U.S. citizens. International applicants must have the ability to obtain the appropriate visas, as applicable." The PDF bullet may be CFF's cross-mechanism boilerplate while the page carries the mechanism-specific restriction, but I could not resolve which governs. An international applicant must confirm with Elizabeth Yu (eyu@cff.org) BEFORE investing in a package. See `unresolved`.

FUNDER-WIDE CEILINGS, NOT RESTATED HERE: CFF's $168,000/yr combined-support rule is written against "Multiple CF Foundation Research Grants held by a single investigator", and the >$200,000/yr combined CFF direct-cost rule requiring prior PO approval likewise appears in the Research Grant guidelines. Neither is repeated in the Shwachman P&G. If you already hold CFF money, ask whether they bind this award — do not assume either way.
result.program_officer_contact:
NAMED CONTACTS, AND PRE-SUBMISSION CONTACT IS EXPECTED — with one situation where it is the ONLY route to being eligible at all.

WHO:
- Elizabeth Yu, Ph.D. — eyu@cff.org — scientific and programmatic questions, career-development awards. This is your first email.
- Erik Warnke, CFF GCMA Office — ewarnke@cff.org, 301-841-2614 — technical AND content questions on the application itself.
- General / don't know who — grants@cff.org. GCMA Office, Cystic Fibrosis Foundation, 4550 Montgomery Ave., Suite 1100 N, Bethesda, MD 20814; 800-FIGHT-CF / 301-841-2614.
- Any requested deviation from the guidelines, funder-wide: Program Officer Dara Riva — driva@cff.org — approval required BEFORE submitting.
NOTE: the award's own "For More Information" block lists ONLY the general grants@cff.org route and the GCMA street address — the named officers come from Section XII of the Policies and Guidelines, which is why first-timers reading only the web page never find a person to write to.

MANDATORY FOR THIS MECHANISM: the sub-70%-effort accommodation exists only "on a case-by-case basis at the discretion of the Program Officer." If you are a clinical subspecialist who cannot protect 70% research time, you do not have an application until you have had that conversation.

WHEN: before you write, not after. The RFA publishes only ~12 weeks before the deadline, so the useful window for a February deadline is OCTOBER-NOVEMBER, working from the prior cycle's Policies and Guidelines — which change little year to year on everything except priority topics.

WHAT TO ACTUALLY ASK: (a) Does my effort split clear the 70% bar, or do I need the accommodation? (b) Am I at the right rung — the RFA says successful applicants are "typically pre-NIH K-award," so if I hold a K or am about to, is Shwachman still the fit, or is LeRoy Matthews / K-Boost the right door? (c) I am a non-US citizen — the web page and the Policies and Guidelines disagree on whether I am eligible; which governs? (d) I already hold CFF funding — do the $168k/$200k combined-support ceilings apply to this award? (e) My mentor is early in their own career — is that survivable, given that "Letters of Support and Reference are weighted heavily in the review" and the mentor must upload their own list of previous fellows and their CFF track record? (f) Will I hold a faculty appointment by 1 July — does my pending offer letter suffice?
result.submission_requirements:
SAME AS FUNDER NORM: awards.cff.org only, 5:00 p.m. ET; pre-register profile/institution/contacts/title ≥2 weeks ahead; the PI's "Submit to Authorized Institution Official for Acceptance" click is NOT submission — your AIO must enter initials on the ASSURANCE STATEMENT(S) tab and click "Submit to CFF" before 5 p.m. ET; Times New Roman 12 or Arial 11, margins no less than half an inch, single-sided; uploads compiled into one PDF, check via "Application Full Print"; portal character limits of 2,000 characters (Lay Abstract, Scientific Abstract, Project Alignment) and 3,000 (Relevance to CFF mission).

WHERE THIS AWARD DEVIATES — the five things that will catch you:

1. RESEARCH PLAN IS TEN PAGES: "Page limit: Ten (10) single-sided pages, not including the Literature Cited." Between the Research Grant's 12 and the Pilot & Feasibility's 6. Funder-wide enforcement: "Applications exceeding this page limit will not be reviewed." Figures must live INSIDE the plan at ≥11 pt; appendix figures "will NOT be reviewed."

2. A TRAINING PLAN — A WHOLE SECOND DOCUMENT THAT DOES NOT EXIST IN THE RESEARCH-GRANT FAMILY. "Do not exceed five (5) pages." Content spec: "This section should clearly indicate plans for developing the applicant's successful career in CF research," and "It should be clear to reviewers how gaps in prior education or training will be filled to ensure this project can be completed adequately and awardees are appropriately placed to accomplish the next step of their long-term career plan at the end of this award." Budget 15 pages of writing, not 10.

3. FOUR REFERENCE LETTERS WITH ASSIGNED ROLES, AND THEY DECIDE THE OUTCOME: "Letters of Support and Reference are weighted heavily in the review. At least four (4) Letters of Support/Reference are required as follows: [i] The Mentor(s) of the clinical fellowship training... must include a description of CF-specific and other training the applicant received while working under the Mentor's direction. [ii] The Research Mentor(s) for this award – The letter should clearly describe the role the research mentor will play in facilitating the applicant's growth in CF... A clear commitment to the applicant and ensuring their development into an independent investigator in this research space is essential. [iii] The CF Center Director(s) at the applicant (or nearby) institution, if s/he is not the Mentor. [iv] The Chair of the applicant's Department at the applicant institution – The letter should clearly describe the institution's commitment to the professional growth of the applicant." AND THE ANTI-SHORTCUT CLAUSE: "If a letter from any one referee listed above fulfills two of the required roles, additional letters from references who can speak to the applicant's scientific and clinical abilities, interests, and potential to become an independent investigator must be provided to meet the minimum requirement of four (4) letters." You cannot get to four by having one person wear two hats. Note item [iii]: if there is no CF Center Director at your institution, a nearby one is explicitly acceptable.

4. TWO UPLOADS YOUR MENTOR MUST WRITE, NOT YOU: "Mentor's Results of Past and Current CFF/CFFT Support - (upload)" and "Mentor's List of Previous Fellows - (upload)". Your mentor's track record of producing independent investigators is itself scored evidence. This is a substantial ask of a busy senior person and it is the item most likely to be outstanding the week of the deadline.

5. THE REFEREE TIMING TRAP, WHICH IS FATAL HERE BECAUSE FOUR PEOPLE MUST ACT: invite referees via the REFERENCES tab; they Accept/Decline by email. "The applicant should inform Referees to submit the letters at least one (1) week prior to the application deadline... Once the application has been submitted, no documents can be added." Letters must not be password-protected or encrypted (it breaks PDF assembly), and you cannot see them. Four referees plus two mentor documents plus an AIO countersignature means SIX other people must act before you can submit.

FULL REQUIRED-UPLOAD CHECKLIST (verbatim): "Biographical Sketches for Key Personnel - (upload)"; "Mentor's Results of Past and Current CFF/CFFT Support - (upload)"; "Other Support (NIH Format) - (upload)"; "Facilities Available - (upload, if applicable)"; "Budget Justification - (upload)"; "Research Plan - (upload, if applicable)"; "Data Safety Monitoring Plan"; "Mentor's List of Previous Fellows - (upload)"; "Training Plan - (upload)"; "Critique Response – (upload)"; "Appendices (upload, if applicable)". Biosketch: "Do not exceed five (5) pages per person."

BUDGET TERMS: "This award provides support for three years at a level of up to $133,000 in direct costs per year (indirect costs are not allowable)." "Funds may be used to support up to $100,000 in personnel costs, including awardee or other research staff working on the proposed project, and up to $33,000 per year may be requested for supplies, travel, minor equipment, etc." Note "personnel costs," not "applicant salary" — the $100k may cover other staff on the project. Salary cap: "In accordance with National Institutes of Health (NIH) policy, salary requests may not use an institutional base salary in excess of the current federal salary cap (FY 2025) of $225,700."
result.resubmission_note:
ALLOWED, WITH NO NUMERIC CAP STATED FOR THIS AWARD — a genuine deviation worth knowing. The Shwachman Policies and Guidelines impose no two-cycle limit. Compare the Research Grant and Pilot & Feasibility rule, which is hard: "Applications that have not been funded in two review cycles will not be accepted for further consideration by CF Foundation," and the Clinical Research Award's "have not been discussed in two review meetings" version. Neither appears here. The only stated condition is that you must answer the reviewers: applicants "must address reviewer critiques in order to resubmit their applications during future application cycles."

WHAT YOU MUST DO, AND IT IS NOT THE NIH PATTERN — three mandatory steps:
1. FLAG IT in the portal: "In order to resubmit unfunded applications during future application cycles, applicants must indicate that the application is a resubmission."
2. UPLOAD A CRITIQUE RESPONSE — a separate item on the upload checklist ("Critique Response – (upload)"), with a downloadable template inside awards.cff.org: "If the application is a resubmission of a previously declined application, please provide a point-by-point response to the prior reviews. There is no page limit to your responses, but please be concise and succinct." NOTE THE TWO DIFFERENCES FROM NIH: it is a SEPARATE UPLOAD, not an Introduction page inside the research plan, and it is UNLIMITED in length rather than one page. There is no NIH-style "Introduction to Resubmission."
3. VISIBLY REVISE THE SCIENCE: "If the application is a resubmission of an earlier one, revisions must be clearly indicated by a change in font, bolded or underlined. The CF Foundation will not review resubmissions that have not been revised." And: "In addition to providing the response to critiques, the research plan must also be revised and clearly marked to show changes from the previous submission. Research plans that are not clearly revised may not be reviewed." A cosmetic resubmission is rejected without review.

TIMING: no calendar expiry is stated. Because the award runs once a year in February, a resubmission lands a full 12 months after the original — not the 6 months available in the twice-yearly Research Grant family. Factor that against the fellowship-to-faculty window this award is designed to bridge: one failed attempt can consume the eligibility window itself. The lab-level throughput caps ("Each laboratory (not PI) may submit only one application... per cycle") are written for research grants and do not apply to training awards — funder-wide, "This does not apply to training awards."
result.examples_or_samples:
THERE IS NO PUBLIC ABSTRACT DATABASE — no CFF equivalent of NIH RePORTER; awards.cff.org is login-gated. But for THIS mechanism there is one route that actually isolates it, which is better than the funder-wide situation.

1. EUROPE PMC FULL-TEXT SEARCH ON THE AWARD'S OWN NAME — the single best route, verified live 2026-09-18: 32 records. Papers whose funding or acknowledgement text names this specific award, which means you can read the science that this award actually produced and identify people to email. API: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=%22Harry%20Shwachman%20Clinical%20Investigator%20Award%22&format=json&resultType=core ; browse: https://europepmc.org/search?query=%22Harry%20Shwachman%20Clinical%20Investigator%20Award%22 . Example hits include work on CF-related diabetes technology (Diabetologia 2024, PMID 38995399; Diabetes Care 2024, PMID 37874987) and airway epithelial biology (J Clin Invest 2023, PMID 37581935; JCI Insight 2024, PMID 38888974). CAVEAT: the phrase sits in the funding statement, so the award-holder is whichever co-author holds it — often a junior author on a senior-author paper. Open the funding statement and read who is credited; do not assume it is the first or last author.

2. DO NOT try to filter the big CFF grant list by award ID. GRANT_AGENCY:"Cystic Fibrosis Foundation" returns 3,598 records with IDs like DUNCAN24G0, ESTHER24R0, LUKACS20G0, LI19XX0 (surname + two-digit year + suffix), but CFF publishes no key mapping those suffixes to mechanisms, so mechanism-level filtering by ID is guesswork. Use route 1 instead.

3. THE RFA'S OWN PUBLISHED REVIEWER CHECKLIST — the closest thing to a scoring rubric you will get, and it is free. "Chief causes for assigning low priority scores": "Insufficient information or documentation"; "Inadequate statement of hypothesis, experimental design, methods or analytical approaches"; "Failure of the applicant to demonstrate awareness of and plans for coping with key problems and pitfalls associated with the proposed research"; "Insufficient or improper controls, if applicable."; "Failure of the applicant to describe potential relevance of the proposed study to issues in CF"; "Failure of the applicant to document the necessary skills or training to accomplish the goals of the proposal"; "Failure of the applicant to meet all criteria described in the policy statement for a given award"; "Failure of the applicant to describe career goals as they may be related to a long-term commitment to CF research". The last two are career-award-specific and map directly onto the Training Plan and the four letters — write to this list. Stated review criteria also include "Ability of the proposed plan to develop research and analytical skills of the applicant needed for independence", "The Commitment of the Mentor for the duration of the applicant's development and research plan", and "Institution's commitment and ability to provide opportunities and facilities necessary for research career development related to CF".

4. THE TEMPLATES ARE THE STARTER KIT. Because no sample applications are published, CFF's own scaffolding is what you build from, and it is prescriptive: every uploaded component has a downloadable template inside awards.cff.org (Research Plan, Training Plan, Budget Justification, Biosketch, Other Support, Facilities Available, Mentor's Results of Past and Current CFF/CFFT Support, Mentor's List of Previous Fellows, Critique Response). Before you have an account: the "For Applicants: Our Grants Management System" how-to PDF and a three-part video tutorial series, both at https://www.cff.org/researchers/information-applicants-and-awardees ; and this mechanism's full Policies and Guidelines PDF at https://www.cff.org/media/24576/download?inline .

5. CRITIQUES — YOURS AND YOUR COLLEAGUES'. GCMA returns anonymized reviewer critiques to every applicant; that is the summary-statement analogue and it is not public. The move that works is asking a CF-funded colleague in your division to show you their critiques plus the funded application. I found no university research-office library of published CFF sample applications.

6. INSTITUTIONAL SCALE, NOT ABSTRACTS: ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, CFF EIN 13-1930701, https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/131930701 — Form 990 Schedule I lists grants to organizations with amounts and purpose.

7. BE TOLD WHEN THE DECEMBER RFA DROPS: Funding Opportunities newsletter, https://signup.e2ma.net/signup/1941850/1922653/ .

8. BASE RATES: none published for this award. Only the Clinical Research Award publishes them (~35% invited to full application, ~20% of full applications funded) and those do not transfer to a career award with no LOI stage.

result.program_name: Hertz Fellowship (2027 cycle)
result.next_deadline: **October 30, 2026** — a live, dated deadline for the 2027 cycle (cycle opened August 31, 2026 and is open now as of 2026-09-18). Funder's words, apply page: "The 2027 Fellowship application is now open through October 30, 2026." Timeline table on the same page: "Application Deadline — October 30 2026". News release of Aug 31, 2026: "The Hertz Fellowship application closes on October 30, 2026." NO TIME OF DAY IS PUBLISHED for the application deadline itself — only the recommender deadline carries a clock time (6:00 p.m. Pacific), so treat Oct 30 as end-of-day Pacific but confirm with the fellowship team. Caution: the FAQ is vaguer than the other two pages, saying only "The 2027 Fellowship application will open late August 2026 and close late October 2026." Funding for selected fellows begins fall 2027.
result.deadline_pattern: Annual, single round, no rolling window. Pattern: application opens late August; closes late October (Oct 30 in the 2027 cycle); recommender forms due the following Monday at 6:00 p.m. Pacific; internal preselection in November; Round 1 interviews (Zoom) December–January; Round 2 interviews (in person) February; finalists named February; fellows selected late March, notified April, announced publicly May; funding begins the following fall. Applicants must be first- or second-year PhD students in the fall that funding begins — so the cycle you enter is set by when you will start (or have just started) the PhD, not by when you graduate.
result.loi_deadline: Not applicable — no letter of intent, pre-proposal, or nomination stage. One single application submitted directly by the individual through the Hertz portal (fellowship.hertzfoundation.org/apply). The timeline's "Application Preselection — November 2026" stage is an internal review step, not a separate applicant submission. The FAQ is explicit that no institutional route is needed: "nomination by the school is not required" and "You DO NOT need to be currently enrolled in a participating school." The one thing that functions like a second deadline is the recommender form deadline (see submission_requirements) — it falls AFTER the application closes, deliberately.
result.review_to_award: Roughly six months from close to notification, eleven months to money. From the FAQ, verbatim: "After the application closes in October, applicants who advance beyond pre-selection will be invited to first round interviews (via Zoom). You should hear from us regarding your application status by late November. First round interviews will take place in December and January. Second round interviews (in-person) for select finalists will be conducted in February 2027. Fellows will be selected in late March 2027, notified in April and announced publicly in May 2027. Funding for the selected Hertz Fellows will begin in fall 2027." Also: "The first round of interviewees are selected by mid November." So the applicant-facing checkpoints are: status word by late Nov 2026 → Zoom interview Dec 2026/Jan 2027 → in-person finalist interview Feb 2027 → finalists named Feb 2027 → award notice April 2027 → public announcement May 2027 → earliest start fall 2027. Two interview rounds is the distinctive feature; this is an interview-heavy competition, not a paper-only review.
result.submission_requirements:
Individual online application; no institutional sign-off, no sponsor/mentor statement, no research proposal. Specifics:

REFERENCES — four, and they are FORMS, not letters. "In the application, you will be asked to submit contact information for four individuals that will serve as your 'recommenders.'" Supplemental letters are refused: "Can I submit supplemental letters of recommendation that do not use the Hertz Foundation format? No. All of your references must use our evaluation form that is emailed to them." The recommenders page confirms: "No. We learn more about our applicants through our specific form questions rather than a standard letter." Entering a recommender's name in the portal triggers the email immediately, so entering names early is the lever on timing. The form has a checkbox rubric plus short answers on creativity, initiative, problem-solving, strengths/weaknesses at current stage, and a comparison against peers at the same stage — so pick referees who can speak to scientific knowledge AND give creativity examples ("you will miss an opportunity to demonstrate strength in this area if you use someone who can't speak to this topic").

RECOMMENDER DEADLINE — falls after the application deadline, on purpose: "We provide a buffer between the application deadline (October 30) and the recommender deadline (November 2)." Late reference forms are not accepted: "Only references submitted at the recommender deadline are guaranteed to be included in the files for reviewers. Applications will be reviewed whether or not we have received all the letters." See "unresolved" — the funder's two pages disagree on Nov 1 vs Nov 2.

ESSAYS — limits are advisory, not enforced: "Reviewers are less concerned with the word length and more so about the applicant's ability to adequately address the prompt. Therefore, you may go under or over the suggested length of 250–500 words for the various short essays and 500–1000 words for the Personal Essay." The personal essay is explicitly NOT a research statement: "We want you to reveal your creativity beyond your research. This could be your favorite extracurricular activity, a leadership experience, or anything else that gives us a better sense of what makes you who you are."

NO RESEARCH PROPOSAL — "The fellowship is intended to fund individual students, not a specific project. There is no requirement to submit a proposed research project as part of the application process." You may still summarise past/current research and intended directions.

TRANSCRIPTS — "We accept unofficial transcripts in your initial application. If selected as a finalist, we'll ask you to submit your official transcripts." First-year grad students whose grades are not yet posted submit undergraduate transcripts only. Uploads capped at five megabytes per document; multiple documents allowed.

GRE — optional: "The GRE is optional. We will accept GRE Subject Test scores but do not require them." Foundation code #4366. Scores may arrive after the deadline, but "Initial interview decisions will be made in early November. If we have not received your GRE scores by then, your file will be reviewed without them." Previously sent scores are retained for reapplicants.

MORAL COMMITMENT — all applicants make a non-binding commitment "to make their skills available to the United States in times of national emergency."

CITIZENSHIP PROOF — deferred to interview stage: proof of Application for Citizenship or Permanent Resident card is requested only if you advance to interviews.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
The important half here is what does NOT disqualify you — Hertz is unusually permissive, and applicants who assume the usual "one fellowship only" rule wrongly self-deselect.

WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (explicit): holding or winning another fellowship, scholarship or grant does not cost you the Hertz and you do not have to decline either. Verbatim: "If I am awarded both a Hertz fellowship and a fellowship, scholarship or grant from another institution, do I need to turn down the other offer in order to accept the Hertz fellowship? No, you don't need to turn down the other offer. We coordinate with a variety of institutions, including the National Science Foundation, National Institutes of Health, and the National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate Fellowship, to make sure you can take advantage of both offers and receive the maximum possible compensation. You may also defer your fellowship if you are awarded a grant, such as a Fulbright grant, or a scholarship, such as a Rhodes Scholarship, Churchill Scholarship or Marshall Scholarship." So NSF GRFP, NIH and NDSEG are named as coordinated, not excluded; Fulbright/Rhodes/Churchill/Marshall are deferral grounds, not forfeiture. The coordination is money-positive, not a clawback — benefits page, Option 2, worked NSF example: while the 3-year NSF runs, Hertz pays "Full tuition equivalent and $44,000/nine-month personal stipend"; after NSF ends, "$9,000/year supplemental stipend from Hertz Foundation," renewable annually up to five years. Option 1 (Hertz alone) is "$38,000/nine-month personal stipend" plus "Full tuition equivalent," also up to five years. Both options add "$5,000/year stipend for fellows with dependent children." General rule quoted: "If you receive a fellowship, scholarship, or grant offer from another funding entity, we'll coordinate with that organization or institution to make sure you can take advantage of each offer and receive the maximum possible compensation."

Also preserving eligibility: reapplication after a rejection ("Yes, you can reapply... Numerous reapplicants have been awarded the fellowship"); a standalone Masters not leading to a PhD; a Masters held during gap years; not being enrolled at a participating school yet; not being nominated by your school.

WHAT DISQUALIFIES: the bars are about stage, degree type and location, not prior money. (1) Career stage — you must be a first- or second-year PhD student in fall 2027. Beyond the first year of grad school is a near-bar, not a soft one: "We generally do not award fellowships to students after their first year of graduate school, except in rare cases where the fellowship will make an exceptional difference in the kind, quality, or creativity of the applicant's graduate research. Only a select few individuals beyond the first year have been awarded fellowships in more than 60 years." Such applicants must supply two extra things: "an explanation of the specific circumstances that justify applying outside the standard eligibility window, and a clear articulation of how the Fellowship would provide exceptional leverage." Note the Masters accounting trap: if your Masters was a prerequisite inside a PhD program you were already admitted to, "your Masters years will count toward your graduate years for eligibility purposes." (2) Degree type — "We do not award fellowships to applicants pursuing professional degrees other than a PhD, such as an MD, JD, MBA, DPH, or DVM. However, we will support the PhD portion of an MD/PhD program." MD/PhD students should apply the year before starting the PhD portion, or during its first year. (3) Location and mode — full-time, in-person PhD at a US institution; a PhD abroad is categorically out ("Based on our governance documents, one of the requirements of the Hertz Fellowship is that fellowship schools must be in the United States and we do not have flexibility in that regard"); part-time study cannot be funded. (4) Citizenship — US citizens or permanent residents only.

result.deadline_pattern: Annual, one window per year, no rolling option and no second round. Opens early-to-mid January, closes mid-to-late March. Observed windows, each sourced: 2024 = "January 17 - March 27" (Wayback capture 2024-03-01); 2025 = "3 January - 27 March" (Wayback captures 2025-04-23 and 2025-08-05); current live = "5 January - 13 March" (agu.org, 2026-09-18). The window has drifted earlier and got shorter — roughly 10 weeks in 2024 and 2025, about 9.7 weeks now. Downstream rhythm is fixed regardless of the exact dates: submit in March, award presented at the AGU Annual Meeting the following December, second installment the June after that. So the application-to-first-money gap is about nine months, and an applicant who misses a March deadline waits a full year.
result.loi_deadline: n/a — there is no letter of intent, pre-proposal, or pre-registration stage. AGU's application-package page lists five components and all are due at the single deadline; nothing is staged earlier and no eligibility pre-screen exists. The one item that behaves like a hidden early deadline is the reference letters, and it works in the opposite direction from a normal LOI: recommenders cannot upload until the applicant has submitted. AGU's wording: "Once the application is submitted, recommenders will receive an email containing a link to upload their letter," and "Letters must be submitted by the application deadline in OpenWater, the AGU Online Grants System." Both letters must therefore land by the same mid-March deadline as the application itself, so submitting on the final day leaves referees no time. Submit at least a week or two early and warn both referees before you do.
result.review_to_award: Deviates sharply from the agency norm — money arrives in two installments tied to the AGU meeting calendar, not to a project start date, and there is no negotiated start. Sequence, all from the funder page: applications close mid-March; "Grant recipients will receive payment in two installments. The first installment is presented at AGU's annual meeting" (AGU's Annual Meeting is held in December), so earliest money is roughly nine months after the close; "The second installment is given the following June upon receipt by the Hydrology Section president of a brief progress report," i.e. about fifteen months after the close. The award period is defined off the meeting, not off submission: the recipient must be enrolled in the doctoral program "for the duration of the award (one year from AGU's annual meeting where the award is presented)." Plan for the enrollment requirement to run to roughly December of the year AFTER you apply — a student defending in mid-cycle can fail this. The second installment is conditional, not automatic: the progress report "should not exceed two pages in length" and must cover (a) scientific progress, (b) how the first installment was spent, (c) projected expenditure of the second installment, (d) thesis progress and expected graduation date, and "must contain the signed approval of the faculty research supervisor." NOT FOUND: the notification date. Nothing on AGU's public pages says when applicants hear the outcome between the March close and the December meeting.
result.submission_requirements: Submitted through OpenWater, AGU's online grants system (agu.secure-platform.com); the Horton solicitation page itself is behind an AGU login. Five components, page limits enforced mechanically. (1) EXECUTIVE SUMMARY — dissertation title, problem statement, research objectives, proposed methods and progress to date; "The summary should not exceed two single-spaced pages. Cited references should be included on additional pages" (so references do NOT consume the two pages). (2) STATEMENT OF PURPOSE — why the grant matters to the dissertation, "how it will allow work to be carried out beyond that originally planned, and how it will be budgeted"; "The statement should not exceed one page." (3) DETAILED BUDGET — itemized with estimated costs. Allowable items named by AGU: living costs during field work, laboratory supplies, computer time, field instrumentation, travel to field sites and/or a technical symposium, and books related to the project. "Travel costs must be broken down into transportation, hotel/per diem and registration cost." (4) CV AND TRANSCRIPTS — CV with name, address, email, employment history, degrees, research experience, honors, memberships and community service, PLUS "a complete set of graduate school transcripts." (5) TWO LETTERS OF RECOMMENDATION — one from "the applicant's main faculty research supervisor" and one from "another member of their thesis committee"; letters "must be on official letterhead, signed by the referee, and submitted as a PDF using the following filename format: Applicant Last Name_Referee Last Name," uploaded by the referee in OpenWater by the deadline. WHERE IT DEVIATES: no institutional sign-off, no sponsored-programs route and no PI of record — the PhD student applies directly; no biosketch, no data-management plan, no facilities statement, no formal research plan beyond the two-page summary. The two unusual burdens are the complete graduate transcript set (slow to obtain from a registrar — start early) and the referee filename convention, which the applicant is responsible for communicating: "Applicants are responsible for requesting letters and communicating the following instructions to their recommenders." Enforcement is blunt and stated twice: "AGU will remove excess pages prior sharing with the review committee," and "AGU reserves the right to reject, without review, applications that do not meet all eligibility requirements." Write to the six published review criteria, which are the de facto rubric: importance to advancing knowledge within or across fields; extent to which the activity "suggest[s] and explore[s] creative and original concepts"; clarity of objectives; qualifications of the proposer; how well conceived and organized the activity is; and whether "there is sufficient access to resources."
result.prior_funding_conflicts: BOTH HALVES, and the first half is unusually short. WHAT MAKES YOU INELIGIBLE: AGU publishes NO prior-funding exclusion for this grant. Nothing on the overview page, the application-package page, or the AGU Honors policies page bars an applicant who holds, or has previously held, other research funding — including a previous Horton grant. The bars that do exist are status bars, not funding bars, and AGU lists exactly four: "be an active student member of AGU"; "be enrolled in a doctoral program in hydrology, water resources, or a closely related field such as water resources policy science"; "be enrolled in the program for the duration of the award (one year from AGU's annual meeting where the award is presented)"; and "meet all application submission requirements." All parties must also comply with AGU's professional conduct policy, and selected nominees must disclose misconduct allegations or findings — note that disclosure "does not automatically disqualify you." Separately, AGU's union-wide Honors conflict-of-interest policy bars a narrow set of officeholders from any AGU honor during their term — "AGU President; President-elect; Council Leadership Team; Honors & Recognition Committee members, and full-time AGU staff" — plus donors, co-sponsors, and full-time staff of a co-sponsoring organization; that clause is written for nominated honors and is about office, not money. WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY: (a) Holding a fellowship, assistantship, or other dissertation funding is not merely tolerated, it is the assumed baseline — the required Statement of Purpose must explain "how it will allow work to be carried out beyond that originally planned," i.e. AGU expects an already-funded dissertation and funds the extension. An applicant should therefore describe existing support openly and position Horton as the increment, which is the opposite of the instinct trained by exclusion-heavy federal mechanisms. (b) Holding an AGU travel grant is not excluded either; the AGU Student Travel Grant eligibility list carries no cross-award exclusion — though Horton already includes its own travel allowance ($500 US/Canada, $1,000 international, $500 for virtual participation). (c) A career break does not cost you eligibility: AGU will consider allowances to a career-stage eligibility requirement "for up to two (2) years beyond the eligibility requirement" for childbirth, adoption, personal serious illness, being the primary caregiver of someone with a serious health condition, a qualifying military exigency, COVID-affected work conditions, and "other extenuating circumstances (i.e., economic hardship, other career breaks, etc.)." (d) Citizenship is not a bar in any direction — any nationality may apply, and international applicants receive the larger travel allowance. CAVEAT, stated plainly: "no published exclusion" is a description of AGU's public pages, not a positive funder statement that repeat or concurrent awards are permitted. The full solicitation text inside OpenWater is login-gated and was not read, so it could carry terms the public pages omit. An applicant with a live award overlapping the same work should confirm with researchgrants@agu.org before submitting.
result.program_officer_contact: No named program officer is published for this mechanism. The contact route is a mailbox, printed under "Questions?" on the Horton page: researchgrants@agu.org. Note that AGU runs three separate mailboxes and using the wrong one costs days — researchgrants@agu.org for research grants (this one), grants@agu.org for travel grants, honors@agu.org for the general Honors program. General AGU line: +1 202 462 6900, Monday-Friday 8:30am-6pm ET. PRE-SUBMISSION CONTACT IS NOT EXPECTED and is not part of the process — AGU frames the mailbox as for questions, and there is no stated pre-submission consultation, no concept clearance and no program-officer relationship to build. That is the real deviation from federal mechanisms: the conversation that matters here is not with the funder, it is with the two people who must write letters — your main faculty research supervisor and a second member of your thesis committee. Approach both well before the March deadline. On the science side the grant is run by AGU's Hydrology Section: the second installment is released on a progress report "received by the Hydrology Section president," and the Section's own page lists a Horton committee (chair Marc Schleiss, TU Delft; Antonia Sebastian, UNC; Jing Tao, LBL; Ryan Webb, University of Wyoming; Sara Nowreen, BUET). Do NOT rely on those names — that roster carries 2023/2024 terms on a page whose recipient list stops at 2021 and whose deadline text is two cycles out of date.
result.examples_or_samples: No funder-published sample application, funded proposal, or annotated abstract exists for this mechanism — searched the overview, application-package, past-recipients, Honors policies and Honors resources pages, and AGU's grants portal. What IS available, in descending order of usefulness: (1) THE REVIEW CRITERIA AS A RUBRIC — AGU publishes the six questions reviewers answer (importance to advancing knowledge within or across fields; whether the activity "suggest[s] and explore[s] creative and original concepts"; clarity of objectives; qualifications of the proposer; how well conceived and organized the activity is; sufficient access to resources). Mapping the two-page executive summary onto those six is the closest thing to an annotated model. (2) PAST RECIPIENTS ROSTER, https://www.agu.org/honors/horton-grant/past-recipients — 98 entries, filterable by year received, nominating section, regional affiliation, career stage and career sector, each name linked to an AGU profile; most recent listed year is 2025 (Ryoko Araki; Rachel E Breunig; José Gescilam Sousa Mota Uchôa). Use it to see which subfields and institutions win. (3) THE HYDROLOGY SECTION'S OWN LIST, https://connect.agu.org/hydrology/awards/horton-research-grants — the same award with INSTITUTIONS attached, 1983 through 2021 (e.g. 2021 Anna Marshall, Colorado State; 2020 Hyunglok Kim, Virginia; 2019 David Litwin, Johns Hopkins); longer historical run than the main site, but stale after 2021. (4) BEST ROUTE TO AN ACTUAL SUCCESSFUL ABSTRACT — recipients are recognized at the AGU Annual Meeting and the grant funds travel to present, so awardees' funded work appears in the AGU Annual Meeting abstract archive; take a recipient name and year from either roster and search the meeting abstracts for the project the grant paid for. (5) For a real sample package, ask researchgrants@agu.org, or contact a recent recipient directly — recipients at your own or a nearby institution are the realistic source, since AGU posts nothing.
result.resubmission_note: AGU publishes no resubmission policy for this grant. result.review_to_award:
Submission by invited faculty, then "The application is then put through a rigorous vetting process." There is an interim stage: "If the nominated student is notified that they are being considered for an award, the faculty member must stay engaged to provide all due diligence material and documentation necessary to finalize the award." A formal letter of congratulations will be sent to the award winners, but finalization of the award is contingent upon the faculty member engaging with IBM to complete all required due diligence documentation."

DEVIATION WORTH FLAGGING: the award period begins BEFORE finalization and payment. The fellowship covers the Fall semester of the cycle year, yet recipients are only finalized in 4Q of that same year and "The IBM PhD Fellowship payments are sent to the university no later than the last quarter of the year," with timing that "depends heavily on the engagement of the nominator and the university in returning all documentation expeditiously." Earliest start is therefore the Fall semester of the cycle year, with money arriving late in that period. Funds are "payable to the university or foundation, not directly to the student awardee."
result.submission_requirements:
The student submits nothing: "A student does not submit any nomination or documentation to IBM; only faculty may nominate students. Students are encouraged to provide preparation material to the nominating faculty member." Everything below is entered by the invited faculty advisor into a single portal form.

- Nominee admin data: name, department, academic/professional website, phone, university, country, entry date into the programme, expected graduation date, current completed degree, career goal, and "Visa status if applicable, or U.S. citizen."
- Institutional sign-off here is FINANCIAL, not a research-office approval: "All nominations must include contact information for a university finance administrator for the department (designated in the nomination form by the faculty advisor) who can confirm details for payment." At award stage the institution must also provide "additional documentation, e.g. bank statement, proof of non-profit / charitable organization status, IRS Form W-9/W-8," because awards "are governed by US charitable giving rules and regulations."
- Correspondence channel is constrained: nominating faculty must "use the university domain email address for all correspondence."

Selection criteria, in the funder's words: "overall potential for research excellence, the degree to which their technical interests align with those of the IBM focus areas listed in the call, and their progress to-date, as evidenced by publications and endorsements from their faculty advisor and department head."
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
WHAT MAKES YOU INELIGIBLE: "Students receiving a comparable fellowship or support from another company or institution (does not include academic scholarships) during the same IBM funded academic period are ineligible for an IBM PhD Fellowship. IBM reserves the right to revoke nominee's eligibility and withdraw the funding of the PhD award upon knowledge of such award." Note the second sentence: this is a continuing duty, not just an application-time check — an award accepted later in the funding period can be clawed back. Also categorically ineligible: "IBM employees are not eligible to be nominated for an IBM PhD Fellowship," and students "from U.S. embargoed countries or attending institutions located in U.S. embargoed countries." Separately, "IBM employees, IBM supplemental employees and IBM contractors may not submit IBM PhD Fellowship nominations" — so an IBM-affiliated collaborator cannot be your nominator.

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY:
1. Academic scholarships are carved out by name — the bar applies to comparable fellowship or company/institutional support and "does not include academic scholarships." Departmental and university scholarship support does not disqualify.
2. The bar is scoped in TIME, not in history. It reaches only support held "during the same IBM funded academic period" / "during the IBM PhD Fellowship funding period." A comparable fellowship that has already ended before the IBM funding period begins does not disqualify you. This is the half applicants most often get wrong — prior funding as such is not a bar, concurrent funding is.
3. An IBM internship does not conflict and is encouraged: "The internship is not guaranteed or mandatory, but IBM PhD Fellowship awardees are highly encouraged to apply." "All awardees will have an IBM mentor for the duration of the award period."
4. Citizenship does not gate it: "Must I be a citizen of the country of application to qualify? No."

HIGH-STAKES AMBIGUITY, UNRESOLVED: IBM never says whether a federal or government fellowship (NSF GRFP, NDSEG, DOE CSGF, etc.) counts as "support from another company or institution" or falls under the academic-scholarship carve-out. The funder's own instruction is to ask: "Please contact phdfellow@us.ibm.com with any questions." Anyone holding GRFP-class support should get a written answer before being nominated, given the revocation clause.

ADJACENT CONDITIONS THAT CAN FORFEIT THE AWARD (not prior-funding, but same risk class): "Must be enrolled full-time in a PhD program over the academic year of the award or forfeit the fellowship"; "Must stay in the same program for the duration of the award—no transferring of departments or schools"; "Should be within two years of their estimated graduation date at the time of the nomination."
result.program_officer_contact:
No named program officer. A single administrative mailbox, given three times on the funder's page: phdfellow@us.ibm.com — cited for dual-award questions ("Please contact phdfellow@us.ibm.com with any questions"), for data-privacy inquiries, and as the catch-all: "For questions not addressed here or on the program tab above, send an email to phdfellow@us.ibm.com."

Pre-submission contact is NOT expected in the NIH program-officer sense — there is no scientific contact to pitch an idea to, and the mailbox is administrative. It is, however, the only route by which a faculty member who has not received an invitation can ask about the nomination period, and the only route to resolve the federal-fellowship ambiguity above.

WHO ACTUALLY MATTERS FOR THIS MECHANISM (the real "who to talk to"): (1) your doctoral faculty advisor — the only party who can nominate, and only if invited; (2) your department head — must supply a customised, explicitly non-boilerplate supporting statement; (3) your departmental finance administrator — their contact details are a required form field; (4) any IBM researcher you already collaborate with — the form requires the advisor to enumerate every IBM activity you have engaged in, so an existing IBM relationship is captured and weighed.

You may request a copy of the submitted nomination form from the faculty who submitted the nomination." So a previously-nominated student, or a faculty member in your department who has nominated before, can show you a complete, genuine submission. result.submission_requirements:
Submitted BY THE NOMINATOR, not by the student. Two accepted routes and either alone is sufficient — the online form (Wufoo, linked from the page) OR email of the complete package to the EDS Executive Office. FAQ: "Do I need to send a hard copy of my nomination package in the mail AND email an electronic version? -- NO. We only need to receive the nomination package once, either via email or mail."

Package, in the funder's own list:
1. Online application form
2. "Nominating letter by an EDS member."
3. "Two letters of recommendation from individuals familiar with the student's research and educational credentials. Letters of recommendation cannot be from the nominator."
4. "One-page biographical sketch of the student (including student's mailing address and email address)"
5. "Two-page (maximum) statement by the student describing his or her education and research interests and accomplishments." (The flyer's wording of this bullet also asks for "graduation date".)
6. "One copy of the student's under-graduate and graduate transcripts/grades. Please provide an explanation of the grading system if different from the A-F format."

WHERE IT DEVIATES FROM AGENCY NORMS — the deviations are almost all subtractive, and this is an unusually light package:
- NO institutional sign-off, NO sponsored-projects or grants-office route, NO authorised organisational representative.
- NO budget, NO research plan or proposal, NO publication list, NO biosketch in any agency format.
- NO reference-letter portal: letters may go straight to the office. FAQ: "Can nomination and recommendation letters be sent directly from the individuals writing them? -- YES. Applicants will be advised when letters are received at the EDS Executive Office."
- Only TWO page limits exist in the whole mechanism: 1 page (bio sketch), 2 pages (student statement).
- A CV is an accepted substitute for the bio sketch. FAQ: "Can I submit my resume in place of the one page biographical sketch? -- YES. Just be sure that it is only one page long and includes your mailing and email addresses."
- Components may arrive piecemeal and are acknowledged as they land: "EDS staff will contact you as items from your application package are received." There is no single all-or-nothing upload moment.

BINDING CONDITION THAT IS EASY TO MISS because it sits under Eligibility rather than Submission: the candidate must "continue his/her studies at the current institution with the same faculty advisor for twelve months after receipt of award." A planned lab move, an advisor change, or a defence inside those 12 months breaks eligibility — this is a real constraint for anyone in their final PhD year.

Judging basis (what the statement should actually argue): "Demonstration of his/her significant ability to perform independent research in the fields of electron devices and a proven history of academic excellence." Two criteria only — independent research capability and academic record.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
EXCLUDES (funder's own words, both sentences from the eligibility paragraph):
- "Previous award winners are ineligible."
- "This fellowship cannot be given to a candidate for the same work for which an IEEE Technical Field Award or IEEE Medal was previously received."

PRESERVES — the half an applicant actually needs, and it is broad:
- The IEEE Technical Field Award / Medal bar is WORK-SCOPED, not person-scoped. The operative phrase is "for the same work for which". Holding an IEEE Technical Field Award or Medal for DIFFERENT work does not bar you; only the specific body of work already recognised is out of bounds.
- "Previous award winners" means previous winners of THIS award. The sibling EDS Masters Student Fellowship does NOT bar a later PhD Fellowship, and the funder's own winner lists prove it rather than merely implying it: Nilesh Pandey (Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur) appears as a 2019 EDS Masters Student Fellowship winner and again as a 2022 EDS PhD Student Fellowship winner. The EDS Undergraduate Student Scholarship is likewise a separate award.
- NO exclusion of any kind is published against external or concurrent funding. Nothing bars a candidate holding an NSF GRFP, a university or departmental fellowship, a national/government scholarship, or industry sponsorship. There is no other-support disclosure, no current-and-pending form, and no supplantation or stipend-offset rule anywhere in the published materials. The US$5,000 is an honorarium to the student, not salary support, so it does not interact with an existing stipend line.
- Citizenship is not a bar: open to any nationality, with an explicit global regional spread (Americas / Europe-Middle East-Africa / Asia & Pacific).

OFTEN MISTAKEN FOR A PRIOR-FUNDING RULE, and the corpus row currently overstates it: "Only one candidate can win per educational institution." The funder's word is WIN, not "be nominated". The published text caps winners per institution; it does not on its face cap how many candidates an institution may put forward. The existing row's design_notes reads this as "only one candidate per institution may be put forward each year (de facto limited submission)" — that interpretation is NOT supported by the funder's wording and should be softened or flagged. It is a same-cycle competitive constraint, not an eligibility bar on the individual.

HARD NON-FUNDING GATE THAT DOES ACT LIKE ONE — OFAC, stated on the page: "Although the IEEE Electron Devices Society (EDS) is pleased to invite all individuals and groups in the OFAC embargoed countries to submit nominations for IEEE EDS Awards, the IEEE EDS cannot provide any award monies to members from such countries at this time." Nominations are accepted; the money cannot be paid. A candidate in an embargoed country can win recognition but not the US$5,000.

The only published bar is on previous WINNERS ("Previous award winners are ineligible"), which leaves an unsuccessful candidate free to be re-nominated in a later cycle provided they still meet the eligibility terms: still an IEEE EDS student member at nomination, still pursuing the doctorate full-time, and still able to commit to 12 months at the same institution with the same advisor after the award.

FLAG: treat that re-nomination permission as an INFERENCE from the absence of a stated bar, not as an explicit funder statement. EDS nowhere addresses re-nomination directly. If it matters to a decision, it is a question for the EDS Executive Office.

Practical limit on repeat attempts is the PhD clock rather than a rule: the 12-month same-institution/same-advisor commitment means the realistic window is the middle years of the doctorate, giving most candidates two or three viable cycles at most.
