result.prior_funding_conflicts:
The decisive rules are in the competition-specific FAQ, not on the competition pages. Both halves, verbatim.

=== WHAT DISQUALIFIES OR BLOCKS YOU ===

1. ONE CHINA STUDIES COMPETITION PER YEAR — the rule most likely to cost someone an application. Verbatim: "It depends. Within the Luce/ACLS Program in China Studies, you may apply to only one individual competition per year: the Travel Grant in China Studies, the Early Career—Long-Term Fellowship, or the Early Career—Flexible Fellowship. This restriction applies only within China Studies; it does not prevent you from applying to other ACLS programs in the same year. Keep in mind that if you are selected for more than one ACLS award, you may only accept one, per ACLS's policy against holding multiple ACLS awards concurrently."

2. APPLYING TO BOTH VARIANTS IS NOT REJECTED — IT IS SILENTLY DEMOTED. Verbatim, on both competition pages: "Applicants who apply to both the Early Career—Long-Term and Early Career—Flexible fellowships will only be considered for the Flexible fellowship." So a scholar who hedges by filing both loses the Long-Term award (up to $45,000) and is judged only for the $15,000 Flexible. This is the single most expensive mistake available in this mechanism, and nothing in the process warns you at the time.

3. NO CONCURRENT ACLS AWARDS. Verbatim: "No. You may not hold multiple ACLS fellowships or grants in the same competition year (e.g. China Studies Early Career Fellowships, China Studies Travel Grants, ACLS Fellowships)."

4. TENURE IS A HARD GATE, AND IT IS EARLIER THAN PEOPLE EXPECT. Verbatim: "Applicants who have obtained tenure, or who have submitted tenure materials for review by the application deadline, are not eligible." Submitting your tenure dossier — not receiving tenure — ends eligibility. If your file goes up in autumn 2026, your last chance was the cycle before. The FAQ confirms rank is irrelevant: eligibility turns on tenure status, not on whether you are called assistant or associate professor.

5. PhD CONFERRAL, NOT DEFENCE. Verbatim FAQ: your PhD must have been "officially conferred between January 1, 2018, and November 5, 2026." A successful defence with conferral scheduled after the deadline does NOT qualify — the FAQ answers this case explicitly and says no. This is an eight-year window measured from conferral, so it is more generous than a typical "within N years of PhD" rule, but the endpoint is unforgiving.

6. LONG-TERM ONLY — NO OTHER EMPLOYMENT DURING THE TERM. Verbatim: "During the fellowship period, which must consist of consecutive months, fellows must work full time on the proposed project. They must be on leave from teaching and service and may not accept other employment."

7. FLEXIBLE ONLY — LACK OF TEACHING LOAD IS ITSELF DISQUALIFYING. Verbatim: "Scholars without heavy teaching or service loads are not eligible for the Flexible Fellowship and should apply for the Long-Term Fellowship instead." The form collects the evidence: total anticipated teaching responsibility for the upcoming year as a whole number of classes ("a course load of 3-3 should be entered as a 6"), and an 800-character list of service commitments tagged departmental / institutional / disciplinary.

=== WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY ===

1. OUTSIDE FUNDING IS FINE, BOTH TO HOLD AND TO APPLY FOR IN PARALLEL. Verbatim: "Yes. For Early Career—Long-Term Fellowships, Early Career—Flexible Fellowships, and Travel Grants, awardees may accept other non-ACLS sources of funding. You may apply to these ACLS programs and outside fellowships and grants at the same time." Repeated on both competition pages: "Fellows may accept other sources of non-ACLS funding during the fellowship period."

2. OTHER ACLS COMPETITIONS OUTSIDE CHINA STUDIES REMAIN OPEN IN THE SAME YEAR — stated in the same FAQ answer above ("it does not prevent you from applying to other ACLS programs in the same year"). You may file for ACLS Fellowships (Sept 17) and a China Studies fellowship (Nov 5) in one cycle; you simply cannot accept both.

3. PRIOR ACLS SUPPORT IS DISCLOSED, NOT PENALISED — and prior ACLS-funded work is treated as an ASSET. The Administrative Information screen asks you to "identify all ACLS fellowship programs (if any) to which you have previously applied in the last three years" from a checklist of about twenty programmes. And the Publications List instruction reads: "Publications resulting from your previous research are an important factor in evaluating proposals from applicants. Applicants who have previously conducted research supported by ACLS grants should report all publications resulting from that research." Delivering on a past ACLS award is something to show, not hide. No page states any bar on previous Luce/ACLS awardees reapplying (see unresolved).

4. SABBATICAL SALARY DOES NOT DISQUALIFY YOU — you disclose it. The form's "Sources of Support – Confirmed" field asks you to "List other sources of support (e.g., sabbatical salary, other fellowships and grants) ALREADY CONFIRMED," and a separate "Sources of Support – Applying" field lists what is still pending. The FAQ handles the uncertain case: if sabbatical funding is not yet settled you may estimate the amount or leave it blank and inform ACLS if you are awarded the fellowship. ACLS's stated position on what the money is: "Our policy is that ACLS fellowships provide salary-replacement stipends. Early Career Fellowships stipends may be used for research costs (e.g., travel, access to online archives, conference participation, hiring of research assistance outside of the US or Canada) and living expenses, including childcare or eldercare."

5. NON-US/CANADIAN CITIZENS ARE ELIGIBLE VIA APPOINTMENT. Verbatim: "If you are not a US or Canadian citizen/permanent resident, you must hold a long-term, regular research or teaching appointment with an institution in the United States or Canada." The FAQ then rescues cases people assume are lost: an adjunct or part-time instructor IS eligible if the appointment meets the long-term regular standard and shows an "established pattern of renewal"; an affiliated scholar IS eligible if the affiliation is "a formal, renewable appointment with defined institutional responsibilities" rather than honorary. A new PhD with no appointment is generally NOT eligible unless an appointment is confirmed to begin by the fellowship start date.

6. NO TRAVEL TO CHINA REQUIRED, AND THE GEOGRAPHY IS BROAD. Fieldwork in Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan, Tibet and Xinjiang is supported, research on ethnic minorities within China is welcome, and a project that never leaves North America is eligible if the application "convincingly explain[s] why the use of the sources proposed is appropriate." Write-up of already-completed research qualifies.
result.review_to_award:
Roughly SIX MONTHS from deadline to decision, and about EIGHT MONTHS from deadline to the earliest possible start — slightly faster to decision than the ACLS flagship norm, with a much wider start window.

- Day 0 — November 5, 2026, 5:00 PM ET. Must be in SUBMITTED status; the portal's own words are that the application "must be complete and in SUBMITTED status by 5:00 PM Eastern Time on November 5, 2026."
- Then — eligibility screen against the six mechanical gates above.
- Then — DISCIPLINARY REVIEW WITHIN CHINA STUDIES. This is the real deviation from the ACLS funder norm. The general ACLS arc ends at a multidisciplinary humanities panel that includes no one from your subfield; here the FAQ says instead: "Proposals to the Luce/ACLS Program in China studies are read by experts in China studies from a variety of disciplines in the humanities or interpretive social sciences." Everyone reading you is a China specialist. The cross-disciplinary breadth is WITHIN the area. Practical consequence: write for a China historian who is not a literary scholar, not for a generalist humanist — the opposite of the calibration the ACLS Fellowships process demands. Nothing on any ACLS page describes a two-stage panel for this competition; treat it as one expert review, not the flagship's Stage 1 / Stage 2 structure.
- Notification — NOT PUBLISHED. No ACLS page I fetched states a notification date for this competition, and the competition pages contain no sentence with "notify", "notification", "results" or "announced". Two dated anchors bound it: the public announcement of the previous cohort was published **May 5, 2026** ("American Council of Learned Societies Announces 2026 Luce/ACLS Early Career Fellowships and Travel Grants in China Studies"), and the OFA form asks for a primary email that "should be valid through September 2027". So decisions land in or before early May, about six months out; the email requirement shows ACLS expects to reach you through at least September 2027. Plan on late April / early May and do not quote a date to anyone.
- Earliest start — July 1, 2027, about eight months after the deadline. Verbatim, both variants: "The fellowship period must begin between July 1, 2027, and September 30, 2028."
- LATEST start — September 30, 2028, i.e. a fifteen-month window in which to place the term. This is unusually generous and is the main scheduling advantage of the mechanism. Long-Term: four to nine consecutive months, full time, at $5,000/month ($20,000–$45,000). Flexible: the equivalent of three months at $5,000/month ($15,000), and the months "must [not] run consecutively", so it can be broken across a teaching year.
- After the term — "A final report is required upon completion of the fellowship period," filed in a third portal, https://awardee.acls.org.

SCALE, so you can calibrate: the 2026 cycle awarded "24 fellowships and grants" totalling "$405,000" — six Long-Term, five Flexible, thirteen Travel Grants. ACLS publishes no applicant-pool figure, so the success rate is not computable from public sources. Eleven Early Career fellowships a year, nationally, is the real size of this opportunity.
result.submission_requirements:
Submitted through the ACLS OFA system at https://ofa.acls.org. No Grants.gov, no research office, no institutional sign-off — paid to the individual. Where this mechanism DEVIATES from the ACLS funder-wide norm:

=== DEVIATION 1: NO REFERENCE LETTERS AT ALL ===
The single biggest relief, and easy to miss. Verbatim FAQ: "A reference letter is only required for graduate students applying for a travel grant." Neither Early Career variant requires or accepts letters. You therefore do NOT need to enter referees in the portal early, and https://ofa.acls.org/reference/ is irrelevant to you. The long-lead item that dominates most fellowship timelines is absent here.

=== DEVIATION 2: LIMITS ARE IN WORDS AND DOUBLE-SPACED, NOT PAGES AND SINGLE-SPACED ===
The ACLS flagship uses single-spaced page counts. This mechanism uses word counts, double-spaced. Do not carry formatting across from an ACLS Fellowships draft. Constant with the funder norm: "Use Arial or Helvetica 11-point font" and "Margins must be at least one inch on all sides."

FLEXIBLE — upload set, in the portal's own lettering:
- 1A) Application essay — 1,300 words maximum, double-spaced
- 1B) Work plan — 300 words maximum, double-spaced
- 1C) Optional supporting materials — two pages maximum
- 1D) Bibliography — 1,000 words maximum, double-spaced between entries
- 1E) Applicant's statement — 600 words maximum, double-spaced
- 1F) Publications list — 1,000 words maximum, double-spaced between entries
- No budget: "No budget is required as part of this application."

LONG-TERM — the same, PLUS one extra document, which shifts the lettering:
- 1E) RESUME — "ONE SINGLE-SPACED PAGE MAXIMUM" (the only single-spaced document in the packet)
- 1F) Applicant's statement, 1G) Publications list

So: Long-Term needs a resume, Flexible does not. Everything else is identical. A 1,300-word proposal is SHORT — shorter than most NSF one-pagers in substance — and it "will be the basis of the evaluation of the project."

=== DEVIATION 3: THE ESSAY HAS SIX MANDATORY CONTENT ELEMENTS, LISTED ===
Verbatim, the essay "must include all of the following": the aims of the research project — what it is about and what sources are to be examined; the significance of the topic and the project's contribution to the field of China studies; the intended contribution of the research to existing literature in your discipline; the research design; an assessment of the project's feasibility; the nature of results expected. Plus a conditional: "If you are proposing a project to convert your dissertation into a book, you must explain how the proposed project will expand on or revise the dissertation." In 1,300 words that is roughly 215 words per element. Treat it as a checklist, not a prompt.

The work plan (300 words) must carry a timeline with "rationale for the length of time that is being requested", the people, institutions, archives, libraries and sites to be visited, "including proposed institutional affiliation in China (if any)", and again the dissertation-to-book explanation for recent PhDs.

The applicant's statement (600 words) must describe the intellectual trajectory that brought you here and your future plans; if unaffiliated you "must describe plans for a career in China studies in the United States or Canada", and "It will strengthen the application to mention applications underway for academic positions, including names of institutions." Applicants in non-tenure-track posts "must indicate when their current positions will end."

=== DEVIATION 4: ORCID IS OPTIONAL HERE ===
Contrary to the Mellon/ACLS DIF norm, which requires it. The screen is headed "ORCID iD (Optional)" and reads "ACLS encourages all applicants to provide an ORCID iD as part of their application." Still worth having and still worth making public, but it will not block you.

=== DEVIATION 5: FLEXIBLE COLLECTS TEACHING-LOAD EVIDENCE ===
Two fields exist only to police the "heavy teaching or service loads" gate: anticipated teaching responsibility for the upcoming academic year as a whole number of classes, with the instruction that if you taught a reduced load "due to service, medical/family leave, etc., enter the amount you would have taught if not for those releases"; and an 800-character service list. Long-Term asks the same teaching question for "a normal academic year" instead.

=== PORTAL MECHANICS THAT BITE ===
- "Do not use non-Roman characters in the application form as the system cannot process certain characters." Chinese characters are permitted in the uploaded proposal only — and "please view your PDF after uploading to be sure these characters convert properly." For a China studies application this is the number-one technical failure mode. Upload early, then look at the converted PDF.
- Uploads: .doc, .docx, .txt or .pdf, 10 MB limit, extension required in the filename.
- "You must SAVE each time you leave a screen," and never use the browser back button.
- "Follow text box limits. Excess text may appear on the screen but will not be visible to reviewers" — overflow is silently hidden from the people deciding.
- Dates strictly mm/yyyy; dollar fields digits only, no $ or commas.
- Primary email "should be valid through September 2027".
- Institution name must be picked from an internal database using the full legal name, not an acronym.
- Common Profile (Contact, Professional Background, Education) carries forward within a competition year and from a 2025-26 login, but uploaded documents do not. Keep your own copies.
- "After submitting my proposal, I had an article accepted..." — no updates accepted: "Your application will be evaluated as submitted."
- AI is permitted and the policy is published: "You may use AI tools such as Claude or ChatGPT to write your application. However, you are responsible for any errors, omissions, hallucinations, or acts of plagiarism in your application," with ACLS encouraging you to indicate where and how you used it.

=== EVALUATION CRITERIA, VERBATIM (both variants) ===
"The research design of the project and its potential contribution to the field of China studies"; "The quality of the proposal with regard to its clarity, methodology, scope, theoretical framework, and grounding in the relevant scholarly literature"; "The ability of the applicant to accomplish the proposed research, based on academic training and success of previous research projects"; and — Flexible only — "The feasibility of the plan of work alongside the applicant's ongoing teaching and service responsibilities."

=== SCOPE GATE ===
Humanities or interpretive social sciences only. ACLS defines the latter as fields "such as sociology, psychology, and anthropology as they involve the analysis and interpretation of evidence that is not necessarily quantifiable or experimentation," eligible "only if they employ predominantly humanistic approaches and qualitative/interpretive methodologies." Not funded: creative work, performing arts, textbooks, or translations without scholarly apparatus.

- **JM Chris Chang, "Program Officer of China Studies"** — named on https://www.acls.org/staff/ with exactly that title. Also on the International Programs staff: Laura Mowry, "Program Manager", and Morgan Day, "Program Coordinator". (I did not find individual email addresses published on the staff page and am not inferring any; use the programme inbox.)

- **chinastudies@acls.org** — the mechanism-specific address, NOT the generic fellowships@acls.org. It is printed in plain text inside the OFA form itself: "If you have questions about the application process, please consult the FAQ. If your question is not answered there, please email chinastudies@acls.org." Use this one.

- **ofahelp@acls.org** — portal and technical problems only (the OFA portals page carries an obfuscated contact link; this address is the ACLS-wide technical inbox and is printed on the OFA login page).

- References portal is irrelevant here — no letters are required.

IS PRE-SUBMISSION CONTACT EXPECTED? Not expected, but clearly tolerated and specifically useful for eligibility. The pattern to understand: ACLS does not do NIH-style project consultation, and no one will read your draft. But the eligibility rules for this mechanism are unusually fact-specific, and the FAQ itself is built out of real edge cases — is an adjunct appointment "long-term, regular"? does an honorary affiliation count? what if conferral falls after the deadline? If your situation resembles one of those and the FAQ's answer is not exact, email chinastudies@acls.org. That is the question worth a human.

NO OFFICE HOURS FOR THIS PROGRAMME — a concrete deviation, verified rather than assumed. The funder's own 2026-27 webinars page (https://www.acls.org/resources/2026-27-acls-fellowship-and-grant-webinars/, fetched directly) lists recordings and live office hours for ACLS Fellowships, Luce/ACLS Dissertation Fellowships in American Art, Mellon/ACLS Dissertation Innovation Fellowships, ACLS Digital Justice Grants, and ACLS HBCU Faculty Fellowships and Grants — and lists NOTHING for the Luce/ACLS Program in China Studies. Sessions are "hosted by ACLS program officers and staff," so the format exists; it simply is not offered for this competition in this cycle. Do not wait for one. The substitute is the FAQ plus the 27-page sample application, both unusually complete, plus the inbox.

WHERE THE SCHOLARLY COMMUNITY IS: ACLS convenes China studies scholars at the Association for Asian Studies annual conference (ACLS published a 2026 news item on convening scholars and East Asia National Resource Centers there). That, plus the awardee lists below, is the realistic route to "who to talk to" — a recent fellow in your subfield, not a program officer.

result.resubmission_note:
NO STATED CAP AND NO STATED TIME WINDOW. Nothing on the competition pages, the programme FAQ or the application form bars a declined applicant from returning, and no page limits the number of attempts — unlike Mellon/ACLS DIF, which is once only. There is no introduction page, no response-to-reviewers document, and no A0/A1 marking; the form does not identify you as a returning applicant to reviewers.

The portal will, however, help you mechanically: if you applied in 2025-26 you may use the same login for 2026-27 and carry the Common Profile (Contact, Professional Background, Education) forward, then complete the rest. Uploads do NOT carry forward. Keep your own copies of every document.

The form asks you to "identify all ACLS fellowship programs (if any) to which you have previously applied in the last three years" from a checklist — disclosure on the administrative screen, which is explicitly "for administrative purposes only and will not be shown to reviewers."

THE REAL CONSTRAINT IS NOT A RESUBMISSION RULE — IT IS THE ELIGIBILITY CLOCK, and it is sharper here than at most funders because it can close from two directions at once:
- The PhD window is a fixed eight-year span ending at the deadline. A 2018 PhD is at the far edge of the 2026-27 window; each cycle the opening date advances.
- The tenure gate can close abruptly and early: submitting tenure materials for review ends eligibility, which for a typical tenure-track appointment happens in year six, well before any PhD-date limit bites.
Count your remaining attempts from whichever comes first. For most tenure-track applicants that is the tenure file, not the PhD date.

ONE-SHOT-PER-YEAR DISCIPLINE: because only one China Studies competition may be entered per year, a decline costs a full year within that programme. You can, in the same cycle, apply to a non-China-Studies ACLS competition — the FAQ says so explicitly — so a declined November application can be followed by an ACLS Fellowships application the following September, while the next China Studies attempt waits for November.

WHAT SHOULD CHANGE ON A RESUBMISSION: ACLS asks for no comparison document, so there is no prescribed answer. Whether reviewer feedback is obtainable for THIS competition is unresolved (see unresolved) — do not assume the ACLS Fellowships feedback offer extends here. In its absence the actionable levers are the ones the criteria name: sharper research design and stated contribution to the field of China studies; a publications list that now shows delivery on prior work (the instructions call publications from previous research "an important factor"); and, for Flexible, a work plan whose feasibility alongside your teaching and service is demonstrated rather than asserted.

Ask chinastudies@acls.org, or check the OFA account after submitting. Do not publish an inferred date as fact.

REVIEWER FEEDBACK — unknown for this competition. The ACLS Fellowships process offers feedback on request; the China Studies FAQ, both competition pages and the general ACLS FAQ are silent on it. Do NOT assume it carries over. This matters for resubmission strategy and is the highest-value single question to put to chinastudies@acls.org.

REPEAT AWARDEES — no page states whether a previous Luce/ACLS Early Career fellow may win a second time, or whether a previous Travel Grant recipient may later take an Early Career Fellowship. Only the concurrent-holding bar and the one-China-Studies-application-per-year rule are published. One awardee (Mengyang Zhao) appears in the Flexible list tagged '2019/2025', which suggests repeat support across the programme is at least possible, but that is inference from a listing, not a stated rule.

result.submission_requirements:
Applicant-of-record note: the POSTDOC is the PI ("The Applicant (post-doc fellow) is the Principal Investigator ('PI')"), but the Mentor carries formal obligations under the Grant Agreement and writes a large share of the package. Submission is through the MSCRF/TEDCO online portal only; register once and the account works for every MSCRF programme.

FORMAT (hard gate): "point size 12 Arial font with margins no smaller than one-half (0.5) inch on all sides and uploaded in a PDF format". PDF only — "Only PDF format is acceptable." Enforcement is unforgiving: "Applications that are incomplete, do not meet the format and/or content requirements, exceed specified length limits, are non-responsive to this RFA or are from ineligible Applicants will not be reviewed", and "A complete submission (all sections) cannot exceed the page limit as included for each section or it will be rejected without consideration." Also: "Ensure strict adherence to the page limits. Incompliance with the application requirements will result in disqualification."

PAGE LIMITS: Research Project Summary 1 p; Research Plan 6 pp "including all tables, figures and charts"; Resources and Environment 1 p; Data Sharing and Management Strategy 1 p; Resubmission response 2 pp; Collaboration Plan 2 pp (if applicable); Supporting Literature 3 pp; Biosketches 5 pp each for PI and Mentor, 2 pp each for other key personnel; collaborator letters 1 p each.

DEVIATIONS FROM THE MSCRF NORM — this is where the Fellowship differs:
1. NO INDIRECT COSTS AT ALL. "There are no indirect costs allowed with the Postdoctoral Fellowship program." Every other MSCRF programme allows IDC up to 15% (e.g. Discovery's $350,000 cap "includes both direct and indirect costs"). The Fellowship's $130,000 is direct plus fringe only: "up to $65,000 dollars per year, for up to two years, and will include all direct, and fringe benefit cost not to exceed a total of $130,000." (Annual Report 2025 confirms awards are made at the full $130,000, so the corpus row's "est." on award size can be upgraded to sourced.)
2. THE MENTOR WRITES A THREE-PART SECTION, and it replaces the mentor's reference letter: (a) "Proposed Training Program and Training Environment, not to exceed two (2) pages"; (b) "List of up to five (5) previous Trainees, their current employment and any involvement in stem cell research, not to exceed two (2) pages"; (c) "Evaluation of the Applicant and his/her potential to conduct stem cell research, not to exceed one (1) page. This section covers the Mentor's recommendation for the applicant. A separate recommendation letter from the Mentor is not required." Do not send a separate mentor letter.
3. LETTERS — mandatory and specific: "Letters of support from the Applicant's Mentor and sponsoring institution, company, or organization are mandatory." In the Appendix, "At a minimum, include a Letter of Institutional/Organizational Support as well as two (2) Letters of Recommendation from individuals other than the Mentor describing the qualifications, commitment, and potential of the Applicant in the field of stem cell research." So: 1 institutional letter + 2 non-mentor references + the mentor's embedded evaluation. Institutional approval is not optional and not late-bindable: "institutional approval must be included in the application. This approval must be a letter signed by an authorized administrative officer from the institution."
4. INSTITUTIONAL SIGN-OFF BEFORE SUBMISSION: "Applicant PI must obtain approval from their research/grants administration office before submitting an application."
5. TRAVEL: "Expenses for domestic travel are capped at $5000. International travel is not an allowable expense" — and the FAQ clarifies "$5000 limit is for the entire 2-year period of the award", not per year.
6. OTHER SUPPORT: only the PI files it ("Only the PI is required to submit the 'Other Support' document"), and NIH formatting is rejected — "Other Support must be submitted using the form provided in the application submission portal", not NIH format.
7. NO SECOND-TIER FUNDING for this mechanism (second-tier appears in other MSCRF RFAs; the Fellowship RFA has no such provision).
8. A HEADSHOT of both PI and Mentor is a required upload, for publication if awarded.
9. Salary follows the NIH cap ("Does MSCRF follow the NIH salary cap rule? Yes").

WEB-FORM FIELDS with character limits, drafted before you open the portal: non-confidential project summary 1800 ch (published if awarded), Public Health Impact Statement 500 ch, Bioethics statement 1800 ch, Impact on Biotechnology in Maryland 1800 ch, Translational Potential/Plan 1800 ch, keywords 100 ch, PI expertise 100 ch, primary research focus 500 ch, sought collaborations 500 ch, lab URL. The "Impact on Biotechnology in Maryland" field is a distinctive scored element with no NIH analogue — it asks for new IP, collaborations, jobs and workforce development in Maryland.

REGULATORY: full bioethics section covering cell lines and ISCRO/ESCRO/SCRO review, IRB and IACUC. Approvals need not be in hand at submission but must be produced before any money moves.

MARYLAND CONFINEMENT: "All State-funded stem cell research must be conducted in Maryland." Out-of-state and international collaborators are permitted, but "MSCRF funds may not be used to cover personnel costs of collaborators who are located and/or conduct the work outside the State of Maryland." The award is also non-transferable — if the fellow leaves the Maryland institution, the Mentor cannot substitute another fellow: "The grant cannot be transferred to another individual."
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
SHORT ANSWER: there is NO prior-award bar on this mechanism. Nothing in the FY26 R2 Fellowship RFA or the MSCRF FAQ disqualifies an applicant for having held previous funding — MSCRF's or anyone else's. The only real constraints are a one-application-per-cycle rule and a reporting-compliance rule. Both halves below.

WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the part applicants get wrong):
1. Prior MSCRF funding does NOT disqualify you — it is a SCORED REVIEW CRITERION instead. The RFA's "Prior Submissions/Awards" criterion asks, "If the work was previously funded by the MSCRF, in whole or in part: Did the Investigator make significant scientific progress towards the goals of the previously funded research? Were results ... reported in scientific publications and/or presented at conferences? Did the previously funded research result in new collaborations, inventions or Project-generated resources as proposed in the original application? Did the previous project generate subsequent funding from non-MSCRF sources?" Prior MSCRF money is an asset to be evidenced, not a bar.
2. IMPORTANT NON-TRANSFER OF THE LAUNCH RULE. MSCRF's Launch programme does carry a prior-award bar — FAQ Q1: seasoned investigators may apply "provided they have not received any prior MSCRF awards and don't have any publications or grants related to stem cell research." That rule is Launch-specific. It does NOT apply to the Post-Doctoral Fellowship, and prior stem-cell publications or grants are not disqualifying here. (The corpus row already flags this correctly; confirmed against the primary source.)
3. Holding NIH or other external support is not a bar. Current and pending support must be DISCLOSED ("List Other Support for the PI, including both current and pending support") but no overlap, duplication or relinquishment rule appears anywhere in the RFA or FAQ — there is no MSCRF analogue to the NIH K/R01 interaction.
4. You may appear on any number of other applications in a role other than PI: "you may participate as a co-investigator or collaborator in any number of applications under the RFAs."
5. No citizenship bar interacts with this: "applicant's do not have to be citizens to apply."
6. Resubmission after rejection is explicitly allowed (see resubmission note).

WHAT ACTUALLY MAKES YOU INELIGIBLE:
1. ONE PI APPLICATION PER CYCLE, across the whole fund — not per programme. FAQ Q3: "An individual may only serve as the PI in one application per MSCRF funding cycle." You cannot hedge across two Fellowship projects, or run a Fellowship application alongside another MSCRF application as PI.
2. REPORTING NON-COMPLIANCE — AND IT BINDS THE MENTOR TOO. This is the sharpest trap in the mechanism: "A Principal Investigator and Mentor not in compliance with the reporting obligations under the Post-Doctoral Fellowship Grant shall not be eligible to apply for continued or subsequent MSCRF funding." A prospective mentor who is delinquent on mid-term/final reports from an earlier MSCRF fellowship can sink the fellow's application. Check the mentor's MSCRF reporting standing before drafting.
3. The 3-year post-doctorate window (not a funding rule but the main eligibility gate): "The applicant must have completed the doctoral degree within the past 3 years, unless the applicant had any career breaks or periods of part-time work, for example parental or long-term sick leave." See program-officer field — the extension requires advance approval.
4. Non-Maryland organisations: "Organizations based outside the State of Maryland are not eligible for funding."
5. Non-human stem cell work: "we only fund research directed to human stem cells."
result.resubmission_note: Resubmission is permitted and is a recognised, structured route, not a grey area. A dedicated component is provided for it: "Resubmissions - Limited to two (2) pages. In the event that an Applicant PI's proposal is initially rejected, and the Applicant PI chooses to reapply for Program funding, the Applicant PI must submit a written response to the reviewers' comments including how those comments were addressed in the resubmitted application. Please include an introduction to the revised Application, including the Application Number of the previous MSCRF submission, and a point-by-point response to the prior scientific review." The portal's web form separately asks whether this is a "New application or resubmission and the prior application number(s) for prior MSCRF applications". The response is scored — the review criteria ask "If this was a resubmission, was a written response to the previous reviewers' comments provided, including how those comments were addressed in the resubmitted application?" No cap on the number of resubmissions is stated, and no mandatory waiting period. Because every applicant receives reviewer comments and scores whether funded or not, a declined applicant has the raw material for a resubmission in hand. result.loi_deadline:
Not applicable — NSF 23-603 records Letter of Intent: not required; Preliminary Proposal: not required. There is one full-proposal deadline and nothing before it.

BUT there are two hard external dependencies that function like a pre-deadline stage and are the real reason to start early:
1. **The Sponsoring Scientist Statement (3 pages)** is written by your prospective mentor and sent to you — you upload it as a Supplementary Document. You cannot submit without it, and you cannot write it yourself. Securing a sponsor who agrees to host you is the true first deadline.
2. **Three reference letters** (up to four) must be in Research.gov by the same deadline date — see submission_requirements. Unlike GRFP, there is no earlier separate letter deadline, which cuts both ways: no trap date, but also no buffer.

Practical lead time: approach sponsors and letter writers in July–August for an October deadline.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
This is the field where MSPRF is most often misread. Both halves, verbatim from the solicitation's eligibility list.

WHAT DISQUALIFIES YOU:
- "May not have previously been a principal investigator or co-principal investigator of an NSF award (other than a graduate research fellowship or an award in support of a conference or workshop)"
- "Must not have previously been offered an award by the MSPRF program"
- "May not submit a research plan duplicated in another NSF proposal"
- "May not have held the doctoral degree more than 2 years as of January 1 of the year of the award" (and "Must have a doctoral degree conferred before the postdoctoral appointment start date")
- "Must, at the time of submission, be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, or a legally admitted permanent resident alien of the United States"

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY:
- **An NSF Graduate Research Fellowship (GRFP) does not count against you.** It is carved out by name inside the PI/co-PI exclusion. A GRFP fellow is a completely normal MSPRF applicant.
- **An NSF award "in support of a conference or workshop" does not count against you** — also carved out by name. So having run an NSF-funded workshop or conference does not burn your eligibility.
- **A previously DECLINED MSPRF application does not disqualify you.** The bar is on having "previously been offered an award," not on having applied. With a limit of "one proposal per individual per year," a declined applicant may come back in the next cycle for as long as the 2-year post-PhD window holds — realistically two, occasionally three, attempts.
- **Scope of the exclusion, as written:** it is written against *NSF* awards and against the *PI or co-PI role* only. The solicitation names no non-NSF funder (no NIH, DOE, DOD, Simons, NDSEG, foundation or foreign equivalent), and names no role other than PI/co-PI. Being paid as personnel or as a postdoc on someone else's NSF grant is not a PI/co-PI role. (This is a statement about what the text does and does not say — NSF does not affirmatively write out "other funders are fine," so if your case is borderline, that is exactly the question to put to a program officer, who can answer it in one email.)

CONCURRENT SUPPORT ONCE YOU HOLD IT:
- Research Fellowship option: "Fellows will be expected to devote full time to appropriate scientific research during the appointment period of the fellowship." Research Instructorship option: half time to research, with a "teaching load not to exceed the equivalent of three teaching hours per semester" during the half-time academic years.
- Stipend top-ups by your host are allowed without asking NSF: "Institutions may supplement fellowship stipends without prior approval from the Foundation provided that such is done in accordance with established institutional policies. Supplementation may be given only if there is no requirement for duties in addition to normal fellowship activities." The condition is the operative half — money with strings attached (extra teaching, service) is not permitted supplementation.
- "In exceptional circumstances, proposals for less than full-time postdoctoral support, with reduced stipends, will be considered. Requests for such must be made in the original proposal" — i.e. a reduced-time arrangement has to be built into the application, it cannot be negotiated later.
- Host institution is effectively locked at proposal time: "Changes in the host institution will be approved only under extremely unusual and compelling circumstances," and NSF says plainly that "Securing a position at an institution other than the proposed host institution is not considered an 'extremely unusual and compelling circumstance.'"
result.review_to_award:
Substantially FASTER than the NSF-wide norm, and the notification mechanics differ too.

- Submission → notification: about 3 to 3.5 months. Solicitation: "The selection of Fellows will be made by the National Science Foundation, and proposers may expect to be notified by e-mail in late January or early February." NSF's agency-wide "up to six months" does not apply here; this is a fixed annual competition with a published notification window.
- Notification → earliest start: "The postdoctoral appointment must start between June 1 and October 1 of the year of the award." So for the 21 October 2026 deadline: decision late January / early February 2027, money starting between 1 June and 1 October 2027. Total submission-to-start: roughly 7.5 to 11.5 months.
- Real-world confirmation of that arc: the FY2026 cohort (October 2025 deadline) has award start dates of 10/01/2026 and expiry 09/30/2030 in NSF's awards data — i.e. a 1 October start at the far end of the permitted window, with the 48-month clock running from there.
- Review mechanism: "Proposals submitted in response to this program solicitation will be reviewed by Panel Review" and "will be evaluated by a panel of mathematical scientists." No ad hoc mail review.
- **Major deviation from the NSF norm on feedback:** "No written reviews are generated during the review process for this program, so the proposer will not receive copies of reviews." Instead, "The proposer will receive a summary prepared by the review panel that includes the ratings assigned by individual reviewers." NSF's standard promise of verbatim unattributed reviewer comments does NOT hold for MSPRF. Plan accordingly: if you are declined and intend to try again, the panel summary plus a conversation with a program officer is all the diagnostic information that exists.
- Award duration: 48 months of award, containing 24 months of stipend support (18 academic-year months plus 6 summer months). $5,833/month full-time (≈$70,000/yr) or $2,917 half-time, plus a $50,000 allowance paid "in lump sums of $30,000 and $20,000 in the first and second Fellowship years"; "The total Fellowship amount is $190,000." Confirmed against actual obligations: every FY2026 MSPRF award sampled shows exactly $190,000.
result.submission_requirements:
THE BIGGEST DEVIATION FIRST — **you submit this yourself. There is no sponsored projects office, no AOR, no SAM.gov/UEI chain.** Solicitation: "The Mathematical Sciences Postdoctoral Research Fellowships are awards to individuals, and proposals are submitted directly by the fellowship proposer to NSF," and "Fellowship proposals must be submitted by the Fellowship candidate, not by the Fellowship candidate's current or proposed organizational Sponsored Projects Office (SPO)." Every long-lead institutional item in the NSF-wide picture (SAM registration, UEI, 90-day lead, AOR sign-off, institutional internal deadline) is OFF for this mechanism. What replaces it: "Before starting proposal preparation, a proposer must register as a new individual in Research.gov." Do that registration weeks ahead, not the week of the deadline — it is now the only account that can block you.

SYSTEM: Research.gov only. Grants.gov is not an option for this programme, and the solicitation carries the standard requirement that proposers "prepare and submit all proposals for this program solicitation through use of the NSF Research.gov system." (See unresolved — NSF's own Jan 2025 MSPRF instruction document still walks applicants through a FastLane route.)

REQUIRED DOCUMENTS AND PAGE LIMITS (these override the PAPPG defaults — note how much smaller the core document is):
- **Project Description: 5 pages** — not the PAPPG's 15. This is the single most important deviation to internalise; MSPRF is a short-form proposal.
- **Project Summary: 1 page**, with separate headings for Overview, Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts (missing one heading is a return-without-review trigger agency-wide).
- **Sponsoring Scientist Statement: 3 pages** — a document type that does not exist in the PAPPG at all. Written by your prospective mentor, sent to you, uploaded by you as a Supplementary Document.
- **Data Management Plan: 2 pages.**
- **Biographical Sketch: 3 pages** per the MSPRF instructions (see unresolved — this predates NSF's May 2024 removal of the biosketch page cap).
- **References Cited: no page limit.**
- **Plan for long-term absence: 1 page**, if applicable.

WHAT THE 5-PAGE PROJECT DESCRIPTION MUST CONTAIN (MSPRF-specific list, and it is not just science): "an introduction or background section; a description of past accomplishments; a statement of research objectives, methods, and significance; an explanation of how the fellowship activities will enhance the proposer's career development; a justification of the choice of sponsoring scientist and host institution; and a separate section within the narrative labeled 'Broader Impacts.'" Two of those six — career development and the justification of sponsor/host — are about the *fit*, not the mathematics. In five pages that is a real allocation decision, and it is where weak applications lose: they read as a research statement with a mentor's name attached.

REFERENCE LETTERS:
- "Three reference letters are required to be submitted but up to four reference letters may be submitted."
- "One reference letter should be from the doctoral adviser and the other letters should be from scientists who know the proposer and/or the proposer's research well."
- **"The sponsoring scientist is not allowed to serve as an author of a reference letter, unless the sponsoring scientist is also the proposer's doctoral adviser."** Very commonly missed: your future mentor writes the Statement, not a letter — so you need three *other* people, or your PhD adviser doubling as sponsor.
- Mechanics: you add reference writers inside your proposal ("Add References," entering each writer's information and a unique password); writers then go to Research.gov, choose "Manage Reference Letters" under Fellowships and Opportunities, complete a Rating Sheet, upload the letter and submit both. **Writers must complete a rating sheet, not merely upload a PDF** — tell them that, because a writer who uploads and stops has not submitted.
- Timing: "This reference should be submitted as soon as possible and no later than the deadline date." No earlier letter deadline (unlike GRFP, where letters are due three days before applicants).

SPONSORING SCIENTIST STATEMENT — what your mentor must cover: "the expected availability of the sponsoring scientist for consultation during the requested tenure period; the role that the sponsoring scientist will play in the professional development of the Fellow; the opportunities for training and research at the host institution that will be of particular benefit to the Fellow; the appropriateness of the match between the sponsoring scientist and the Fellow," plus how the sponsor expects to benefit. NSF's guidance for sponsors is explicit that it "should NOT be a letter of recommendation" and should avoid evaluative comparison against other researchers. Send your sponsor the Instructions for Sponsoring Scientists PDF — most have never written one.

FORM MECHANICS THAT TRIP PEOPLE:
- Cover sheet asks for host institution details and the MSPRF programme announcement selection.
- "Do not change the pre-populated DURATION OF TENURE entry. All Fellowships are awarded for 48 months."
- Form B requires a primary two-digit MSC 2010 subject classification code — pick it deliberately, it steers your proposal to a panel section.
- Choose your track in the proposal: Research Fellowship (full-time support for eighteen academic-year months within three years, in intervals no shorter than three consecutive months) vs Research Instructorship (one academic year full-time then two half-time, with teaching capped at three teaching hours per semester in the half-time years).
- Work abroad is possible but pre-approved only: "Approval to do so must be obtained in advance from both the sponsoring scientist and the cognizant NSF program officer."
- Limit: "One proposal per individual per year."
result.resubmission_note:
Allowed, and cheaper than at most funders — but with an unusual information handicap.

- Nothing in NSF 23-603 bars a declined applicant from applying again; the disqualifier is "Must not have previously been offered an award by the MSPRF program," which triggers on an *offer*, not on an application. Combined with "one proposal per individual per year," a declined applicant may reapply in the next cycle, bounded only by the 2-years-post-PhD eligibility window.
- Because the window is short, most people get two realistic shots (an application in the final PhD year and one as a first-year postdoc), sometimes three. Front-load accordingly — the common regret is treating year one as a practice run.
- The NSF-wide framing still applies: a resubmission is a *new* proposal ("A declined proposal may be resubmitted, but only after it has undergone substantial revision"), goes to a fresh panel, and has no rebuttal section.
- THE MSPRF-SPECIFIC HANDICAP: because "No written reviews are generated during the review process for this program," you cannot revise against reviewer comments — they do not exist. All you receive is "a summary prepared by the review panel that includes the ratings assigned by individual reviewers." So the post-declination phone call or email to a program officer is not optional polish here; it is the only channel through which the substance of the panel's reservations can reach you. NSF's own guidance sanctions exactly this: "Regardless of whether your proposal is selected for funding, you should continue to stay in contact with your program officer."
- No formal NSF reconsideration is worth pursuing over a declination on scientific grounds — that track (90 days to request, 45 days for the AD's answer) is about process, not merit.

Systems (not science) questions: Research.gov Help Desk, rgov@nsf.gov / 1-800-381-1532.

WHICH ONE TO WRITE TO: every FY2026 MSPRF award sampled in NSF's awards data lists **Stefaan De Winter** as the managing program officer, so he is the de facto cognizant officer for the competition as a whole; the others are the DMS-area contacts. If your question is about fit within a subfield, the awards data lets you check which officer signed awards like yours before writing.

IS CONTACT EXPECTED? Yes — the NSF-wide norm holds ("Anyone can reach out to an NSF program officer—at any stage of their career, no matter their institution"; PAPPG: "Before formal submission, the proposal may be discussed with appropriate NSF program staff"). There is no concept outline and no ProSPCT step for MSPRF; you simply email.

MECHANISM-SPECIFIC REASON IT MATTERS MORE HERE: with no SPO and no AOR in the loop, there is no institutional research administrator to answer your eligibility and mechanics questions. The program officer and the Research.gov help desk are the entire support structure. The eligibility questions worth asking by email — because they are answerable in one line and cost you nothing — are: (1) does a specific prior NSF role count as PI/co-PI against me; (2) does my degree date fall inside the "no more than 2 years as of January 1 of the year of the award" window; (3) is my proposed topic within DMS's scope or another division's. Questions they will not answer: whether your proposal will be funded, and detailed budget mechanics.

Expect slowness in September–October and write earlier. NSF's own advice: "Don't be discouraged if you don't get a reply initially, and try reaching out again later."
result.examples_or_samples:
Three tiers, as at NSF generally, but with one MSPRF-specific twist that changes what is worth chasing.

1. **Funded abstracts — public, and specific to this programme.** NSF Award Search at https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/ holds the abstract for every MSPRF award. The programme string in NSF's own data is "Workforce (MSPRF) MathSciPDFel". Verified FY2026 examples you can look up directly by award number: 2602438 (Newton Polygons and Higher Quasi-F-Injective Singularities), 2602677 (Coupled Multispecies Systems), 2602095 (Foundations of Positive Geometry), 2602712 (Growth in Corners of Linear Groups), 2602552 (Enumerative Geometry of Hitchin Moduli Spaces), 2602381, 2602147, 2602364, 2602679, 2602112, 2602598, 2602173 — all $190,000, 10/01/2026–09/30/2030. Individual award pages sit at https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/show-award/?AWD_ID=<number>.
   HONEST CAVEAT ON THEIR VALUE: MSPRF abstracts are mostly shared programme boilerplate plus a short project-specific paragraph — thinner than a CAREER abstract. Award 2602438's abstract opens: "This award is made as part of the FY 2026 Mathematical Sciences Postdoctoral Research Fellowships Program. Each of the fellowships supports a research and training project at a host institution in the mathematical sciences, including applications to other disciplines such as Artificial Intelligence and Quantum Information Science, under the mentorship of a sponsoring scientist." Read them for two things rather than for prose models: (a) the *distribution of subfields and host institutions* that actually gets funded, and (b) the current framing — that FY2026 boilerplate naming AI and QIS is the programme telling you where it sees itself.
   Tooling note: the Award Search UI is JavaScript-rendered and returned zero results to a plain fetch; the award facts above were confirmed through NSF's public awards API (https://api.nsf.gov/services/v1/awards.json?fundProgramName=MSPRF), which is the same NSF data in machine-readable form and is the reliable route if you are scripting.

2. **Full funded proposals — FOIA, redacted.** https://www.nsf.gov/policies/foia. Awarded proposals are released on request with personal and proprietary material removed. Slow (weeks to months) and only sensible if you are planning a year ahead.

3. **Reviews and panel summaries — do not exist to obtain here.** This is the MSPRF twist: NSF generates no written reviews for this programme at all, so there is no reviewer text to FOIA, no summary-statement equivalent, and nothing a senior colleague can pass you from their own file beyond the ratings-only panel summary they personally received.

MOST EFFECTIVE ROUTE GIVEN ALL OF THAT — read a real application, not an abstract. Because MSPRF awards go to individuals and the award data names every fellow, you can identify recent MSPRF fellows in your subfield or at your target host by name from Award Search, and ask them directly for their five-page Project Description. Mathematicians in this community share these routinely, and it is the only practical way to see how someone fits background, past work, objectives, career development, sponsor justification and Broader Impacts into five pages. Your prospective sponsoring scientist is the second route — a sponsor who has hosted an MSPRF fellow before has almost certainly kept the file, and has written the Statement before.

Also useful: NSF Public Access Repository (NSF-PAR) for publications produced by MSPRF awards, and USAspending.gov for the money side.

Not found: an NSF-hosted or reliably located annotated *sample* MSPRF application. Nothing equivalent to the community GRFP essay archives turned up for this mechanism (and web search was unavailable to me for this run — see unresolved).
result.deadline_pattern:
Annual, single full-proposal deadline, no LOI, no preliminary proposal, no submission window. Rule as NSF publishes it: "Third Wednesday in October, Annually Thereafter," at 5 p.m. proposer's local time. It is a Deadline Date in NSF's taxonomy (not a target date), so late proposals are not accepted.

Published instance: 21 October 2026. Derived next instance from the rule: 20 October 2027 (derived, not sighted on an NSF page).

Cycle shape, so an applicant can see the whole year at once: submit third Wednesday of October → panel review over the winter → e-mail notification late January / early February → appointment starts between 1 June and 1 October of the award year → 48-month award containing 24 months of support.

For an applicant, the binding constraint is usually not the deadline but the 2-year eligibility window ("May not have held the doctoral degree more than 2 years as of January 1 of the year of the award"), which typically admits two, occasionally three, October cycles across a career.

I found no MSPRF-specific statement on whether the programme retains a 3-page expectation or whether SciENcv is mandatory for this individual-submitter mechanism. Worth one email to a program officer.

Whether the host institution may be the applicant's own PhD institution. The solicitation lists eligible host types and locks the host after award ('Changes in the host institution will be approved only under extremely unusual and compelling circumstances') but I found no sentence requiring the host to differ from the doctoral institution. result.deadline_pattern: Annual, but THE DATE MOVES — do not treat any one year's date as the recurring pattern. Evidence from three consecutive cycles of the same page: 2024 cycle "Application due January 15, 2024" (Internet Archive, Nov 2023); 2026 cycle "All application components are due by no later than Monday, December 1, 2025, at 5 PM Central" (Internet Archive, Jan 2026); 2027 cycle 3 November 2026. So the reliable planning rule is "portal opens August, deadline in the Nov-Jan window, check the date each August", not "deadline is 3 November". NOTE ON THE BRIEF'S FRAMING: nothing in the house rules forbids a dated deadline — the rule forbids a GUESSED date. This one is published, dated, and quoted, so it is reported as a date. The pattern is given alongside it precisely because this mechanism's date drifts, which is exactly the failure mode a bare date would cause a year from now.
result.loi_deadline: No LOI, no pre-proposal, no nomination — the applicant applies directly. But there are three genuine pre-submission steps with their own earlier timing, which is what the LOI question is really protecting against: (1) OPTIONAL MENTORED REVIEW, closes 10 October 2026 — if your institution "has received one or fewer McKnight awards", you may ask to be paired with a previous McKnight awardee at a different institution to review your materials before submission; requests go to jkrogstad@mcknight.org "before October 10, 2026". (2) MANDATORY ADVANCE NOTICE for applicants at institutions that do not use professorial titles — a Dean/Director-of-Research letter must accompany the application AND the program manager must be emailed in advance that it is coming. (3) PARENTAL-LEAVE CLOCK EXTENSION — the FAQ tells anyone seeking one to contact the program manager "immediately" to discuss it before investing time in an application. Also note the reference letters are a POST-submission step in the new system: the applicant submits first, then the portal emails the three referees, who have until 24 November 2026.
result.review_to_award: Roughly seven months from submission to money, with a four-month silence in the middle. Submit 3 Nov 2026 → the review committee "invite[s] approximately 20 finalists to interview" and "Applicants invited to interview will be notified in March 2027" → remote interviews "scheduled soon after" (in the 2024 cycle these were two fixed days, Fri/Sat, in early May) → committee recommends to the Endowment Fund's Board of Directors for final decision → "Awards will start June 1, 2027". Funding is $75,000/yr for three calendar years (2027, 2028, 2029), released against annual financial and scientific reports for the second and third payments. Odds, from the funder's own FAQ: 50-150 applications per round in recent years, ~20 interviewed, up to 10 funded — i.e. roughly a 13-40% interview rate and a 7-20% award rate, unusually good for a prize-style award. The interview round is remote, so no travel cost to budget for.
result.submission_requirements: Short, unusually light on institutional machinery, and materially different from an NIH package. Components, all uploaded in the Fluxx portal: (1) PROPOSAL — "must not exceed four numbered single-spaced pages in 12-point font with 1-inch margins", and the four pages cover "abstract, narrative and figures, but not referenced literature"; it opens with "an abstract of 200 words or less". (2) DIVERSITY & INCLUSION STATEMENT — "a half-page narrative with the same formatting guidelines as the proposal", about action taken "beyond the confines of your lab", with the page explicitly asking for personal experience and specific actions rather than philosophy or planned activities. (3) CV — "should not exceed five pages", with a prescribed header (name, current title, institution/department, ORCID, website) plus education/training, appointments, honours, teaching/mentoring/service, bibliography. (4) LIST OF OTHER SUPPORT — start-up funds first, then external funding NIH-style, with amounts (the page's own example is an R01 at $100k annual direct costs); pending-but-unawarded proposals need not be listed. (5) Titles and links to 5 recent publicly accessible publications, pre-prints allowed. (6) Three references, submitted by the referees themselves after you submit. DEVIATIONS THAT MATTER: there is NO budget in the application at all ("There is no budget required in the application submission"); there is NO institutional signature — the page says of the other-support document "But different from NIH, no signature is required"; no sponsored-programs routing, no chair letter, no mentor/sponsor statement (this is an independent-investigator award, not a K-style mentored one); no co-PIs permitted — the award is singular to one person; and indirect costs are barred ("Funds cannot be used for indirect costs"), which your research office needs to accept before you submit. Pilot data is helpful but not required. One institutional-strategy point: there is no cap on applications per institution, and multiple scholars from one institution can be funded in the same round.
result.prior_funding_conflicts: Both halves, and the permissive half is the surprising one. WHAT DISQUALIFIES YOU (all from one sentence on the apply page): "Applicants to the Scholar Award may not apply in more than two rounds of competition, have already been granted tenure, or hold another award from the McKnight Endowment Fund." Add to that: "A candidate may not apply for both Scholar and Neurobiology of Brain Disorders Award during the same funding cycle"; you must currently hold an Assistant Professor (or equivalent) appointment on the submission date; non-tenure-track titles are out ("Instructor, Research Assistant Professor, Adjunct Assistant Professor" named explicitly); and you must be within five years of first starting at Assistant Professor rank, cumulative across institutions — for this round, "the applicant must not have started serving in the rank of Assistant Professor any earlier than December 1, 2021". The only clock exception is parental leave, documented, added to the clock; the FAQ explicitly refuses Covid/lab-closure extensions. WHAT PRESERVES YOUR ELIGIBILITY — the conflicts here are internal to McKnight, not external. Holding NIH or other federal funding does NOT disqualify you and is not held against you: the FAQ says of overlap with federal funding that "if there is an overlap with federal funding that is not a concern to the committee", and that the committee "often don't consider additional funding mechanisms". Holding an R01 is assumed, not penalised — the other-support instructions use an R01 as their worked example. You may submit a topic that was declined elsewhere or is under review elsewhere; the FAQ answers that question with a plain "Yes". Already having won another major prize (Searle, Pew, Packard, Klingenstein, NIH New Innovator, etc.) is not a strike: "We strive to equally consider those who have won no major awards to those who have already received recognition." Start-up funding is expected and simply disclosed. Being at a non-R1 or liberal-arts institution is explicitly welcomed, as is coming into neuroscience from another discipline. In short: the only prior awards that bar you are McKnight's own, and tenure; everything external is disclosure, not disqualification.
result.program_officer_contact: Named and operationally real: Joel Krogstad, Program Manager, McKnight Endowment Fund for Neuroscience — jkrogstad@mcknight.org. He is the single route for the whole mechanism (application support, portal/login problems, eligibility edge cases). Pre-submission contact is not merely permitted, it is REQUIRED or expected in three named situations: requesting the previous-awardee review pairing (deadline 10 October 2026, open to applicants whose institution has received one or fewer McKnight awards); giving advance notice of the senior-official letter if your institution does not use professorial titles; and discussing a parental-leave extension of the five-year clock, where the FAQ says to reach out "immediately" before investing effort in the application. The scientific side is the McKnight Scholar Awards Review Committee, chaired by Dr Vanessa Ruta, with members including Dr Jennifer Raymond and Dr Marlene Cohen (2026 webinar panel); the committee roster is on the Endowment Fund's leadership page. There is no separate NIH-style scientific program officer to negotiate scope with — the committee sees the application cold.
result.examples_or_samples: Unusually rich for a private foundation, though no full funded application is published. (1) FUNDED PROJECTS — the awardees page carries every Scholar cohort from 1977-1979 to 2026-2028 (49 cohorts, ~255 scholars) with name, institution and funded project title; cohorts from roughly 2018-2020 onward also carry a two-paragraph lay summary of the funded work. These are McKnight-written summaries, not the applicants' own abstracts, but they show precisely what wins: the framing, the scale of question, and the balance of ambition to tractability. https://www.mcknight.org/programs/the-mcknight-endowment-fund-for-neuroscience/scholar-awards/awardees/ (2) RECORDED APPLICANT WEBINAR, recorded 27 August 2026 — the review committee chair (Vanessa Ruta) plus Jennifer Raymond, Marlene Cohen, and past awardee Abigail Person walk through what the committee wants; the page says it is pitched at applicants and development staff with no prior knowledge of the programme. https://vimeo.com/1221866644/da7af369bb (3) THE FAQ IS EFFECTIVELY AN ANNOTATED RUBRIC — it contains a six-point self-check for the narrative (one central scientific question, why an outsider should care, a distinctive viewpoint, the best-case understanding gained, a concrete execution and interpretation plan, evidence your lab can deliver), plus guidance on ambition vs feasibility, how much experimental detail to give, what timeline horizon to write to, what reference letters should say, and how many lead-author papers are expected. https://www.mcknight.org/programs/the-mcknight-endowment-fund-for-neuroscience/scholar-awards/faq/ (4) A LIVE HUMAN READER — the previous-awardee pairing service (request by 10 October 2026) is the closest thing to a worked example: a past winner reads your actual draft. result.resubmission_note: There is no formal resubmission mechanism — no summary statement, no response-to-reviewers, no introduction page. What exists is a hard lifetime cap: an applicant "may not apply in more than two rounds of competition", and since eligibility itself expires five years after you start as Assistant Professor, those two attempts must both fall inside that window. A second attempt is a fresh application, not a revision. The funder gives explicit strategic advice on how to spend the two: apply as soon as you can state a crisp novel idea rather than waiting by default, but use judgement about whether your vision is well enough formed, since waiting a year or two may produce a stronger single shot. Practically this means the two-attempt cap, not the annual deadline, is the real timing constraint for this mechanism — and it is the field most likely to be missed by someone reading only the eligibility blurb.

result.submission_requirements:
All through ACLS OFA (https://ofa.acls.org). No Grants.gov, no sponsored-projects route; paid to the individual. ORCID iD required, public record; transcripts are NOT required.

COMPONENTS (verbatim limits, 2026-27 competition page and FAQ):
- Proposal: "no more than seven pages, double spaced, with one-inch margins, in Arial or Helvetica 11-point font." Must cover research aims, how the fellowship year advances them, the training/workshops/travel needed, the external mentor (named, with how you chose them, or a description of the qualities you will seek), and "how they will measure their own success in the fellowship year."
- Personal statement: "no more than two pages, double spaced" — your "journey as a scholar" at the nexus of personal experience, research interests, and the desire to shift the forms and formats of academic research.
- Work sample: "No more than fifteen pages total, double spaced, with one-inch margins, including any images and footnotes or endnotes, in Arial or Helvetica 11-point font." May be previously published. May be co-authored, but "please allocate some space at the beginning of the sample to describe your role in the project and in authoring the paper."
- Bibliography: "no more than two pages," without annotation.
- Timeline: one page of fellowship-year activity plus a provisional sketch of the post-fellowship trajectory to dissertation completion.
- Optional: "Up to two additional pages of images, musical scores, or other similar supporting non-text materials, without annotation."

DEVIATIONS FROM THE ACLS NORM — these are where people lose applications:
1. DOUBLE-SPACED, 7 pages. The flagship ACLS Fellowships proposal is 3 pages SINGLE-spaced. Do not carry formatting across competitions.
2. THE PUBLISHED SAMPLE PDF IS STALE ON FONT. The 2022 DIF-Sample-Application.pdf says "Times New Roman 11-point font" throughout. The 2026-27 competition page and FAQ both say "Arial or Helvetica 11-point font." Use the live page for formatting; use the PDF only to read the questions.
3. EXACTLY ONE LETTER, and it is constrained: "The letter must come from the applicant's dissertation advisor, or a faculty member eligible to be the advisor." "ACLS does not accept reference letters from dossier services, such as Interfolio or university-based services." Your stored Interfolio letter is useless here.
4. AN INSTITUTIONAL STATEMENT, which is a FORM, not a letter — this is the biggest structural difference from every other ACLS mechanism. From "the applicant's department chair, director of graduate studies, or dean," and "The person submitting the institutional form should not be the same as your reference letter writer." The signer attests that (1) a multi-year institutional award would be paused and resumable, (2) the institution will keep you enrolled and waive tuition and fees, and (3) the institution can "respect and accommodate this exploration of non-traditional approaches to scholarship."
5. FIRST-SUBMITTED-WINS, HARD CAP: "No more than one letter of reference and one institutional statement will be accepted... The first reference letter and the first institutional statement submitted will be the letters on file... another referee attempting to submit a letter for you will be prevented from doing so."
6. REFEREES CANNOT SELF-START: "You MUST ENTER YOUR REFEREES on the Reference Letters page BEFORE they can log in to use the online references system." Separate system at https://ofa.acls.org/reference/ — your login does not work for them.

PROGRESS-TO-DEGREE INTERRUPTIONS: the form carries a 1,000-character field for leave, caregiving or medical interruptions, and instructs that "Your referee should note these circumstances as well in their letter" — coordinate the two.

AI: explicitly permitted for the applicant. "YES. From ACLS's perspective, the use of an AI tool to research or write a proposal is not much different from hiring a professional grant writer or seeking help from a university's grants officer, which has always been allowed." Reviewers are barred from using it.

Both halves, because the excluding half alone would wrongly scare off most funded PhD students.

WHAT DISQUALIFIES OR BLOCKS:
- Concurrency, absolute: "These fellowships may not be held concurrently with any other fellowship or grant."
- During tenure: "Individuals must be enrolled full-time and may not accept teaching or research assistantships, other major fellowships, internships, or similar internal or external awards during fellowship tenure." You must be released "from normal coursework, assistantships, and all teaching responsibilities" for the full 9-12 months.
- Within ACLS: "not more than one ACLS or ACLS-joint award may normally be accepted in any one competition year."
- PRIOR APPLICATIONS ARE THEMSELVES AN ELIGIBILITY GATE — unusual, and the one people miss. Applicants must "Have not previously applied for this fellowship more than once." Two lifetime attempts, enforced at screening, not at review.
- Career-clock gates that bite harder than any funding rule: "Have not advanced to PhD candidacy/ABD status prior to January 1, 2026" and "Intend to complete their dissertation after May 31, 2029." Also ineligible: professional/applied PhDs, non-PhD terminal degrees (EdD, MFA), and PhDs outside humanities/social science departments (business, clinical or counseling psychology, creative or performing arts, education, engineering, filmmaking, law, library and information sciences, life/physical sciences, public administration, public health or medicine, public policy, social work, social welfare).

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY:
- A MULTI-YEAR UNIVERSITY FUNDING PACKAGE DOES NOT DISQUALIFY YOU. This is the headline. The institutional statement exists precisely to reconcile it: the signer attests that if you hold a multi-year institutional award, "this support would be paused for the duration of the fellowship and the applicant would be allowed to retain and resume the remainder of that support in subsequent years," and attests "to the compatibility of the Mellon/ACLS award within the structure of your funding package at your university, and that the award will extend rather than replace that funding." You do not lose a year of your package; you push it back a year.
- Your institution must keep you enrolled and waive tuition and fees, and "Fellowship funds may not be captured by fellows' home institution for the payment of fees or tuition." The stipend is yours, not the bursar's.
- Having NO guaranteed funding is equally fine: "We do not require that your institution provide guaranteed funding during your PhD program."
- A department that requires teaching or an RAship to grant a tuition waiver is a negotiation, not an automatic bar — the FAQ answers this case by restating the release requirement rather than declaring you ineligible. Raise it with your DGS early, since the same person signs the institutional statement.
- ALREADY ABD? Still eligible if recent: "Yes, as long as you advanced to ABD status no earlier than January 1, 2026."
- CITIZENSHIP DOES NOT GATE THIS AWARD: "No, eligibility for this program is not restricted based on citizenship or permanent residency. Any doctoral student who is pursuing a PhD in the humanities or social sciences at degree-granting institutions in the United States is eligible to apply." Rare among US funders and worth flagging to international students.
- APPLYING ELSEWHERE IN THE SAME ACLS CYCLE IS ALLOWED (this resolves the open question in the funder-wide notes): "Yes, an applicant to this fellowship may also apply to as many fellowship programs as are suitable. However, not more than one ACLS or ACLS-joint award may normally be accepted in any one competition year." Apply widely, accept once.

result.resubmission_note:
ONCE ONLY, and enforced at the eligibility screen rather than at review. FAQ, verbatim: "Yes, but unsuccessful applicants may reapply to this program only once." Eligibility bullet, verbatim: "Have not previously applied for this fellowship more than once." Two lifetime attempts, total.

No A0/A1 designation, no introduction page, no response-to-reviewers document, nothing in the form marks you as returning, and reviewers are not told. You rebuild the application from scratch; the portal carries nothing forward, so keep your own copies of every upload.

THE REAL CONSTRAINT IS YOUR OWN CLOCK, NOT THE CAP. Because you must not have advanced to candidacy before January 1, 2026 and must intend to finish after May 31, 2029, a student who applies early and is declined has often aged out of the eligibility window before the second attempt. For most people the second attempt is theoretical. Spend the first one deliberately — and if you are choosing between applying this October with a thin proposal or next October with a strong one, check your ABD date first, because that choice may not be yours.

SEQUENCE THAT MAKES ATTEMPT TWO POSSIBLE: declined in late April 2027 → request reviewer comments immediately, and in any case before the hard cut-off of June 30, 2027 → rewrite over the summer → resubmit late October 2027, if still eligible. The feedback window is the only structured input ACLS gives you, and it closes fast.
