So merit review lands ~5 months after submission (vs the NIH norm of ~4), and earliest start ~9-11 months after submission. Summary statement reaches eRA Commons in the usual window after the study section meets; NIGMS advises contacting the PO "once the summary statement is released."

Review venue is specific and worth knowing in advance: MIRA applications go to dedicated CSR study sections MRAA, MRAB, MRAC, MRAD, MRAE, MRAF, "SEPs as needed" (2026 NIGMS webinar). Rosters: public.csr.nih.gov/StudySections/DBIB/MGG/MRAA, /MBBC/MRAB, /CDB/MRAC, /CDB/MRAD, /MBBC/MRAE, /MGG/MRAF. NIGMS states "Approximately 50% of applications are discussed"; discussed applications get an overall impact score and "no individual criterion scores." Both NOFOs confirm: "Review criteria are not scored individually." Whether the NIH-wide emergency reduction to 30-35% discussed applies to MIRA panels is not addressed in any MIRA document I could verify.
result.submission_requirements:
Same portal machinery as all NIH (Grants.gov via ASSIST / S2S / Workspace, eRA Commons tracking, AOR submits, 5:00 PM local time, no error-correction window). The deviations are large and several are auto-withdrawal traps:

**1. NO SPECIFIC AIMS PAGE — this is the defining MIRA deviation.** PAR-26-121: "This application must not include a Specific Aims attachment; inclusion of this page will lead to administrative withdrawal of the application prior to peer review." PAR-27-032 checklist row: "Specific aims — Do not submit this page. N/A", and among its non-responsiveness criteria: an application that "Includes a specific aims page" or "Uses specific aims or similar designation, including 'aims', in the application (for example, using this language in the abstract or research strategy sections)." The word "aims" is itself disqualifying. NIGMS's stated reason (2026 webinar): "MIRA is intended to fund a broad research program, not a narrow set of experiments."

**2. Research Strategy = 6 pages, with mandated non-standard headings.** PAR-27-032 states it explicitly ("Research strategy — All applications. 6"). PAR-26-121 defers to the Table of Page Limits, whose R35 row is 6 pages (verified in the raw table HTML). "Do not use the standard Research Strategy headings of Significance, Innovation, and Approach." Required structure instead: Background / key gaps; Recent progress by the PD/PI over the past five years; Overview of future research plans. NIGMS's suggested split (2026 webinar): ~1-1.5 pages background, ~1-1.5 pages recent progress, ~3-4 pages future plans. "Do not provide a detailed experimental plan."

**3. Preliminary data are not expected.** "We do not require preliminary data in MIRA for ESIs applications." Feasibility may rest on "preliminary data from their independent laboratory, literature citations, data from other sources, or data generated by the applicant as a graduate student or postdoctoral fellow." And explicitly for ESIs: "early career stage applicants may not have published independently as senior or corresponding authors, and the absence of these publications should not be viewed as a weakness."

**4. ESI ONLY — required Institutional Commitment Letter, and it is a completeness gate.** "You must include a letter of support from your department chair, dean, or other academic unit leader. This letter should describe the institutional commitment to your development as an investigator." "If you do not include this letter, we will consider the application incomplete and will withdraw it." No page limit on this letter. It should cover start-up package, space, salary support commitment, career development, mentoring through promotion and tenure, and "career advancement prospects for non-tenure track applicants." Mentor letters are "not required, not encouraged" except for continuing collaborations. Collaborator letters optional, 1 page each, no biosketches attached.

**5. ESI ONLY — single PD/PI.** "We allow only single PD/PI applications. We will not accept applications with multiple PDs/PIs." (EI/NI MIRA is also effectively single-PI: "PDs/PIs whose only NIGMS research grant(s) is a multi-PD/PI grant(s) are not eligible to apply for a MIRA.")

**6. Biosketch for the PD/PI only** (ESI NOFO: "Only provide a Biographical Sketch for the PD/PI"), SciENcv Common Forms required, personal statement tailored to MIRA and expected to cover mentoring contributions and service to the scientific community beyond institutional duties. No figures or preliminary data in the biosketch.

**7. Other Support / Current and Pending is NOT submitted with the application.** "Do not submit Other Support documentation with your application. We will collect this information as needed after review." NIGMS uses it at JIT to verify the effort floor.

**8. Budget is simplified.** ESI: "Maximum budget per year: $275,000 in direct costs"; "Do not include a detailed budget"; "Do not complete the R&R Subaward form"; cap includes equipment and data-management costs; no inflationary escalation; indirect costs requested on top. EI/NI: "Applications from investigators with existing NIGMS research grants may request up to 750,000 direct costs per year"; "MIRA budgets for New Investigators are typically set at 275,000 in annual direct costs, not including equipment"; modest (~12% average) reductions expected for PIs with ≥$400,000 current annual NIGMS direct costs; equipment requested in Year 1 only. Project period up to 5 years, 12-month budget periods.

**9. Effort floor differs by NOFO and is verified at JIT.** ESI: "at least 51% of their total research effort." EI/NI: "at least 45% of their total research effort." Total research effort spans all institutions where the PI holds an appointment, is expressed in person-months, and excludes teaching and non-research administration.

**10. Mission-fit is a hard screen.** "Applications that fall outside the NIGMS scientific mission will be withdrawn prior to peer review." Multi-site clinical research, Phase I/II/III efficacy trials, dissemination/implementation research, comparative effectiveness and pragmatic trials are not permitted; single-site mechanistic clinical trials are.

**11. Data Management and Sharing Plan required, using NIH's 2026 Pilot DMS Plan format** (2026 NIGMS webinar). Foreign organizations ineligible; applications involving foreign subawards/subcontracts are "deemed noncompliant and will not be considered for funding."

NOTE ON SOURCING: PAR-26-121's full text is no longer published at grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/pa-files/ (that URL 404s — NIH stopped issuing HTML guide files for 2026+ NOFOs). I read its complete text out of NIH's own NIH Guide search index API (search.grants.nih.gov/guide/api/data, doctext field), which is the funder's index, not a third-party one. PAR-27-032 is published only as a PDF; I read the official PDF from grants.gov (attachment "PAR-27-032-Full-Announcement.pdf", version par-27-032-rev7, 54 pages) and confirmed the same dates against the NIGMS MIRA landing page and the grants.gov opportunity record.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
The single highest-stakes field for MIRA, because MIRA is designed to REPLACE your NIGMS portfolio. Both halves, per NOFO:

=== ESI MIRA (PAR-27-032) — who is shut out, who is preserved ===

DISQUALIFIES: not being an NIH-defined ESI. "For this Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO), we limit eligibility to NIH-defined Early Stage Investigators (ESIs)." ESI = "completed their terminal research degree or end of post-graduate clinical training, whichever date is later, within the past 10 years and who has not previously competed successfully as PD/PI for a substantial NIH independent research award." Practical pre-flight check (2026 NIGMS webinar): your eRA Commons profile must read "ESI status = 'Yes'". Also disqualifying: not being an ESI but being a New Investigator (go to PAR-26-121 instead); multiple PD/PIs; foreign organization.

PRESERVES ESI STATUS — NIH's published list of awards you can hold or have held and remain an ESI: "An investigator will retain their Early Stage Investigator status if they receive any of the smaller research grants, training, infrastructure, and career awards that appear on this list." R00, R03, R15, UA5, R16, R21, R25, R90, RL9, RL5, R34, R36, R41, UT1, R42, UT2, R43, U43, R44, U44, R50, R55, R56, R61, RL2, SB1, SC2, SC3, U09, U34, X01, X02; D71, all F fellowships, all K career-development awards, Loan Repayment Awards, R38, D43, T32, T34, T35, T90, TL4; C06, G07, G08, G11, G13, R13, U13, S10, S15, S21, S22, UC6, PC1, PC2, OT1, OT2, OT3, and R&D contracts. The one trap NIH flags: "transitioning to the R33 phase of an R21/R33 or R61/R33 phased award disqualifies PD/PIs from ESI status since R33 is not considered a smaller research grant." So a K99/R00, a K08/K23, an R21, an R15 or an F32 do NOT cost you MIRA eligibility; a prior R01 or an R33 transition does.
ESI status can be extended for life/career events (childbirth, adoption, military service, health, disability, natural disaster, periods of less than full-time effort) — request it before you apply.

ESI-specific NIGMS answers from the FAQ: a K99 holder who has not yet transitioned to independence cannot apply, but an R00 awardee may; an SC1 (SCORE) holder is ineligible, while SC2/SC3 holders may apply; an R15 (AREA) holder is eligible if ESI status is maintained; COBRE junior investigators may apply, with NIGMS-related support terminated on award.

CONCURRENT-REVIEW RULE (ESI): "You may not have other research grants being considered by NIGMS (such as R15, R16, R21, DP2, or additional MIRA applications) under review concurrently, regardless of which application was submitted first." Explicitly PERMITTED concurrently: "An application that is being considered for funding by another NIH Institute or Center" and "An R01 application being considered by NIGMS." Applications pending at NIGMS carry "GM" in the grant number — that is how you tell.

=== ESTABLISHED / NEW INVESTIGATOR MIRA (PAR-26-121) ===

QUALIFYING (this NOFO is largely gated ON prior funding, not off it): "PDs/PIs with at least one NIGMS single-PD/PI R01-equivalent award (defined here as R01, R37, DP1, DP2, and SC1) are eligible to submit a new MIRA application before the end of their eligibility time window." Current MIRA holders may submit a renewal. New Investigators with no NIGMS award may apply if not a project leader on any NIH multi-component award, "except for Research Project Leaders and Pilot Project Leaders of COBRE, IDeA-CTR or NARCH awards."

INELIGIBLE: "PDs/PIs whose only NIGMS research grant(s) is a multi-PD/PI grant(s) are not eligible to apply for a MIRA." ESIs must not use this NOFO.

THE ELIGIBILITY CLOCK — the most missable rule, and it runs off your existing award's end date: "The eligibility for investigators funded with at least one single-PD/PI NIGMS R01 or equivalent award extends to the end of the fiscal year following the one in which the funded single-PD/PI R01 or equivalent award was originally set to expire. For example, if the qualifying R01-equivalent award ends in fiscal year 2025 (October 1, 2024 to September 30, 2025), a MIRA application needs to be submitted before September 30, 2026." For current MIRA holders it is one year longer: "extends to the end of the second fiscal year following the one in which the funded MIRA was originally set to expire." And: "No-cost extensions (NCEs) cannot be used to extend the eligibility time window." Extensions are granted for life events and unanticipated administrative issues, but you must ask "at least 8 weeks before submitting the application."

WHAT A MIRA AWARD KILLS: "All current NIGMS research grants except those listed in Section I will be terminated upon issuance of the MIRA grant." A PI receiving support as a collaborator or subcontractor on someone else's NIGMS R01/R15/R21/R37 "must discontinue such funding." "A PD/PI with a NIGMS K award must discontinue the K award prior to the MIRA start date."

WHAT SURVIVES A MIRA AWARD (the carve-outs — this is the half applicants never find): grants supporting research community resources (e.g. R24, NIGMS National and Regional Resources); Collaborative Program Grant for Multidisciplinary Teams (RM1); Biomedical Technology Optimization and Dissemination (BTOD) RM1; training or workforce development grants (T32, T34, SEPA); multi-site clinical research with patient-recruitment/protocol/community-resource costs; INBRE, COBRE, IDeA-CTRs, SEPA and NARCH; SBIR/STTR; conference grants. On a multi-component grant you "may continue to serve as a Project Leader or multi-PD/PI while maintaining at least 45% effort on the MIRA, but may not receive additional funds from the multi-component grant." BTOD is the one that keeps its money: "may retain BTOD funding but must use it exclusively for late-stage technology optimization and dissemination efforts," with ≥45% MIRA effort plus 3 person-months on BTOD (or 1 person-month as a TOP/community-engagement lead). And crucially for anyone with a mentored award from elsewhere in NIH: "A PD/PI with a K award from another NIH institute and Center may receive a MIRA but must reduce effort on the K award to be less than the effort committed to the MIRA (measured in person-months)." Non-NIGMS funding generally is untouched — MIRA consolidates your NIGMS portfolio, not your NIH portfolio.

CONCURRENT-REVIEW RULE (EI/NI): "a PD/PI may not have a MIRA application and another NIGMS research project grant application (e.g., R01, R15, R21, and R37) pending review at the same time. An application is pending review until its summary statement is issued." Exempted from that bar: the same list above (R24-type resource grants, RM1, BTOD, training/workforce, multi-site clinical research, INBRE/COBRE/IDeA-CTR/SEPA/NARCH, SBIR/STTR conference).
result.program_officer_contact:
Yes — named contacts exist, and pre-submission contact is not merely welcomed but effectively expected, with a specific format and a specific lead time. This is stronger and more prescriptive than the NIH-wide norm.

NAMED PROGRAM OFFICERS (from the NIGMS MIRA landing page):
- Established / New Investigator MIRA (PAR-26-121): Ashley Barnes, Ph.D. and Baishali Maskeri, Ph.D. — NIGMS_EINIMIRA@nigms.nih.gov
- ESI MIRA (PAR-27-032): Michelle R. Bond, Ph.D. and Dimitrios Vatakis, Ph.D. — NIGMS-ESIMIRA@nigms.nih.gov

BETTER ROUTE THAN THE GROUP MAILBOX — a named PO in your science: NIGMS Contacts by Research Area, https://www.nigms.nih.gov/about/Pages/contactbyarea. Its own opening line: "NIGMS encourages all potential applicants to talk to a program officer before preparing and submitting an application. Find contact information for the program officer overseeing grants in your scientific area of interest, desired training program, or capacity building initiative below." It lists name, email and a bio link per area across the four NIGMS divisions (Biophysics/Biomedical Technology/Computational Biosciences; Genetics and Molecular, Cellular and Developmental Biology; Pharmacology, Physiology and Biological Chemistry; Research Capacity Building).

WHEN: "We recommend contacting a program officer at least six weeks before the application due date" (ESI MIRA FAQ). The 2026 webinar repeats it: "Contact Scientific/Research Staff at least 6 weeks prior to submission for advice on the suitability of the proposed research for NIGMS," and "Please contact a NIGMS program director in your area of research BEFORE you submit your application." For the Oct 2, 2026 ESI deadline that six-week mark was ~August 21, 2026 — already past, so anyone aiming at Oct 2 should write today and expect a thin conversation, or target Feb 3, 2027 and write by ~December 23, 2026. For the Jan 27, 2027 EI/NI deadline, write by ~December 16, 2026.

HOW — and this differs from the NIH house style: because MIRA forbids a Specific Aims page, the attachment you send is NOT an aims page. ESI MIRA FAQ: "Select one NIGMS program officer whose interests best align with your research and contact that person by email, providing a one-page summary of the proposed MIRA research program." And a rule people break: "Please do not contact multiple staff members at the same time." One PO, one email, one page.

WHAT TO ASK: PAR-26-121 tells you the primary question — "Potential applicants are strongly encouraged to confer with the NIGMS program official managing their qualifying award(s) or relevant research portfolio(s)... before submitting a MIRA application" and "strongly encouraged to contact NIGMS program staff to discuss the possible alignment of their proposed research program to the NIGMS mission before applying," because "Applications that fall outside the NIGMS scientific mission will be withdrawn prior to peer review." So: is my program inside the NIGMS mission; which of the two NOFOs am I in; does my eligibility clock still have room; do my current/pending awards create an overlap problem. The ESI NOFO also says outright: "Discuss any potential situations with a program officer" about concurrent review.

ONE HARD-DATED PO ACTION: extending the MIRA eligibility time window (EI/NI) requires contacting a Section VII Scientific/Research Contact "at least 8 weeks before submitting the application."
result.resubmission_note:
MIRA REVOKES THE NIH-WIDE A1 RIGHT. This is the sharpest deviation from NIH norm in the whole record, and it inverts the usual advice.

PAR-26-121: "A resubmission (A1) application is not allowed; however, a PD/PI may submit a new MIRA application as long as they are eligible." Repeated twice more: "Resubmissions are not allowed."
PAR-27-032: "This NOFO does not allow resubmissions. A PD/PI may submit a new application to this NOFO after an unsuccessful attempt as long as the PD/PI remains eligible as an ESI and the summary statement from the prior application has been issued."
ESI MIRA FAQ, plainly: "If my application for MIRA is not funded, will I be able to prepare a resubmission? No, but if you are still eligible, you may submit a new application for the next receipt date."

Practical consequences:
- There is no Introduction-to-Resubmission page and no obligation (or opportunity) to respond point-by-point to the summary statement. You rewrite as a new A0.
- Your gating constraint is the eligibility clock, not the one-A1 rule: for ESIs, whether you are still an ESI at the next receipt date; for EI/NI, whether you are still inside the fiscal-year window keyed to your qualifying award's original end date. Each failed attempt burns one of a finite number of cycles.
- You must wait for the summary statement before resubmitting: the new application cannot be submitted "before issuance of the summary statement from the review of an overlapping new (A0)... application." With merit review ~5 months out and the two due dates ~4-6 months apart, a failed ESI October application realistically targets the following October, not the next February.
- Renewals (EI/NI only): "If a MIRA renewal application is unsuccessful, the grant will terminate at the end of its approved project period." "Any MIRA application submitted after a prior renewal's pending review must be a new application. However, if a renewal application is withdrawn prior to peer review, another renewal can be submitted in its place." A withdrawal before review is therefore materially better than a bad score.
- Post-submission preliminary-data updates: the NIH one-page update with preliminary data is offered for Type 1 R01/R21/R03, which does not include R35, and MIRA does not expect preliminary data in the first place. Do not plan on it.

Existing CSV row currently carries resubmission_allowed = "unspecified" and an empty resubmission_policy; both are now establishable as "no" / "no A1; new application only, while still eligible."
result.examples_or_samples:
Honest answer: there is NO funded-application sample library for MIRA, and I verified that rather than assuming it. NIH's own curated index (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/samples-applications-and-documents) lists sample collections from NIAID, NCI (four collections), NHGRI, NIA, NIDCD only, covering R01, R03, R15, R21, R33, R37, R50, K, F, U01, G11, SBIR/STTR — no R35, no MIRA, and no NIGMS collection at all. NIGMS publishes no sample-applications page (the plausible URLs 404). So a MIRA applicant cannot read a funded MIRA application the way a K99 applicant can. What exists instead, in descending order of usefulness:

1. **NIGMS's own 2026 ESI MIRA webinar — the closest thing to an annotated sample.** Slides: https://www.nigms.nih.gov/sites/nigms/files/2026-07/MIRA%20for%20ESIs_2026%20Webinar.pdf (26 slides, delivered July 15, 2026 by Marc Rigas and Michelle Bond). Video: https://youtu.be/64AEQ-zBPkM. It gives the page-by-page allocation NIGMS wants inside the 6 pages (~1-1.5 background and gaps, ~1-1.5 recent progress, ~3-4 future plans), the component checklist, the budget rules, the study-section list, and the review considerations verbatim. This is the document to read first.

2. **The ESI MIRA FAQ's four framing questions** (https://www.nigms.nih.gov/Research/mechanisms/MIRA/Pages/faqs-esi-mira) — NIGMS's own outline of what a strong MIRA narrative answers: "Why is the field I am working in important?"; "What are the key questions I think need to be answered... in the next five years?"; "What general strategies will I use... what sorts of alternative approaches might I try?"; "Why am I the right person to do this work?" Plus the instruction to "Keep the narrative at a high-level and focus on how the outcomes... will impact the field." For a mechanism with no sample applications, this is the skeleton.

3. **The NOFO review-criteria sections as a reverse outline.** PAR-27-032's "Context for reviewers" and its NOFO-specific criteria questions ("Are the topics of the research program substantial and suitable for long-term study?", "Is the proposed research program's scope and ambition adequate to address the scientific questions asked?", "Does the PD/PI show promise as a mentor of scientific trainees?") are what the panel is literally asked. Writing to them is the substitute for reading someone else's funded copy.

4. **NIH RePORTER for funded abstracts** (reporter.nih.gov; advanced search reporter.nih.gov/advanced-search). Verified live this session via the RePORTER API: 3,286 NIGMS R35 project records for FY2025. Filter agency = NIGMS, activity code = R35 to read hundreds of funded MIRA abstracts and public-health-relevance statements, with PI, institution, study section and award amount. Note the genre difference — MIRA abstracts describe a program, not aims, so they read differently from R01 abstracts and are a fair model for your own abstract. RePORTER holds no full applications; complete contents require a FOIA request to NIGMS.

5. **RePORTER Matchmaker** (reporter.nih.gov/matchmaker) — paste your draft program summary to surface similar funded NIGMS work, the program officials behind it, and the review panels. Useful precisely because MIRA asks you to pick one PO by scientific area.

6. **The MIRA Eligibility Decision Tree PDF** — https://www.nigms.nih.gov/sites/nigms/files/migrated/mira-eligibility-decision-tree-01-2023.pdf (linked from the NIGMS MIRA page; dated January 2023, so check it against the current NOFOs before relying on it).

7. **The six MIRA study-section rosters at CSR**, which tell you who actually reads it: MRAA public.csr.nih.gov/StudySections/DBIB/MGG/MRAA; MRAB /DBIB/MBBC/MRAB; MRAC /DBIB/CDB/MRAC; MRAD /DBIB/CDB/MRAD; MRAE /DBIB/MBBC/MRAE; MRAF /DBIB/MGG/MRAF. All six verified reachable.

8. **NIH's Annotated Form Set** (grants.nih.gov/grants/ElectronicReceipt/files/) for field-by-field form mechanics — generic, not MIRA-specific.

result.prior_funding_conflicts:
The binding test is not "what have you been funded for" — it is **"are you still non-independent?"** Prior funding matters only insofar as it makes you independent.

WHAT DISQUALIFIES YOU:
1. Being independent at the time of application. All four must be true of you, per RFA-RM-27-004: "Research direction requires mentor approval"; "Research is mainly supported through another investigator's funding"; "No institutionally assigned research space"; "Cannot apply for an NIH R01 without a special institutional waiver or exception." Fail any one and you are ineligible.
2. Degree timing outside the window. "The PD/PI must complete their terminal doctoral degree or post-graduate clinical training between May 1, 2025, and September 30, 2027." The transcript date governs. Clinical training includes residency and fellowship.
3. Excess prior postdoc, narrowly defined: "The PD/PI must not have more than 12 months of postdoctoral training after an earlier, non-terminal doctoral degree. This applies only to individuals with multiple doctoral degrees."
4. Holding a K award concurrently: "A PD/PI cannot hold both simultaneously; if awarded the DP5, the K award must be relinquished."
5. Overlapping applications pending: no new (A0) application "submitted before issuance of the summary statement from the review of an overlapping" application.

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the half applicants get wrong):
1. **Mentored fellowships do not disqualify you.** NOFO, verbatim: "mentored fellowships, such as an NIH F31/F32 or NSF Graduate Research Fellowship, do not make an applicant ineligible." Being on an F31, F32 or a GRFP is affirmative evidence of non-independence, not a conflict.
2. **You may apply for a K and a DP5 in the same season.** "The PD/PI may apply for both a K award and DP5 simultaneously, but the projects must not overlap scientifically." Only holding both is barred.
3. **Becoming independent after you submit does not kill the application.** "The PD/PI may become independent before the award starts and still remain eligible" (guide: "you may become functionally independent after you submit your application and retain eligibility").
4. **The promised faculty position may be contingent and need not be permanent.** "The position does not have to be permanent or tenure-track. The position may depend on receiving this award."
5. **U.S. citizenship is not required** — the institution must confirm the visa covers the full project period. Only the institution must be U.S.-based.
6. **Institutional start-up or other independent funding is not an automatic bar** — but it must be disclosed and explained: the Facilities & Other Resources section requires "If the PD/PI has other funding, explain how the Early Independence Award will affect that support."
7. **A normal postdoc after your terminal degree is not itself the disqualifier** — the 12-month postdoc rule only bites for people with multiple doctoral degrees. The real constraint is the degree-date window.
8. **Failing once does not lock you out.** FAQ: "You may apply as often as you wish as long as you meet the eligibility requirements and a host institution is willing to submit the application on your behalf."

One-line version for an interface: *if you are still working under a mentor, still on someone else's grant or a mentored fellowship, have no lab space of your own, and finished (or will finish) your PhD or clinical training inside the stated ~2.5-year window, you are the target — a fellowship is a qualification here, not a conflict.*
result.program_officer_contact:
Yes — a named officer and a central mailbox, and pre-submission contact is expected. But the route DEVIATES sharply from the NIH norm.

Named contact (Common Fund DP5 funding-opportunity table): **Becky Miller, Ph.D. — earlyindependence@mail.nih.gov — 301-594-9979**.
NOFO Section VII Scientific/Research Contact: Office of the Director (OD), **EarlyIndependence@od.nih.gov**. The NOFO says: "We encourage inquiries concerning this funding opportunity and welcome the opportunity to answer questions from potential applicants" and "Questions should be sent to EarlyIndependence@od.nih.gov."
Financial/Grants Management: NIDCR, deeranotifications@nidcr.nih.gov.
Peer Review: no named contact in advance — "Examine your eRA Commons account for review assignment and contact information (information appears two weeks after the submission due date)."

HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM NORMAL NIH PO PRACTICE — this matters:
- There is no IC to court and no PO to match to your science. The PHS Assignment Request Form instruction is explicit: "do not request an assignment to a particular review panel (integrated review group) or awarding component (NIH Institute or Center). All applications are automatically received as 'Office of the Director' applications and reviewed by a single Special Emphasis Panel convened by the Center for Scientific Review." So the standard advice — RePORTER Matchmaker to find your IC's PO, cover letter requesting a study section — does **not** apply. Use the central mailbox.
- The main pre-submission channel is the **pre-application webinar**, not a one-to-one call. NOFO: "NIH program staff will hold a pre-application webinar to explain the program and answer questions about the application and review process." The FY2027 webinar was held July 13, 2026, 2–3:30 pm ET, about two weeks after the NOFO posted and two months before the deadline; slides and recording stay online.
- The Assignment Request Form is still where you name conflicts: "List the names and affiliations of significant collaborators so the Scientific Review Officer knows who is in conflict with the application and should not review it."
- Your other essential contact is internal, not at NIH: because of the two-per-institution cap and because the institution must write a substantial part of the application, the department chair / dean / research office is a co-author of your submission, not just a signatory. Talk to them first.
result.review_to_award:
Slower than the NIH norm, and the arc is fixed by the NOFO rather than by cycle.

From RFA-RM-27-004 Key Dates: application due September 10, 2026 → **Scientific Merit Review March 2027** → **Advisory Council Review May 2027** → **Earliest Start Date July 2027**. Identical shape one cycle earlier (due September 6, 2024 → review March 2025 → council May 2025 → start July 2025).

So, measured from submission: ~6 months to peer review (the NIH norm is ~4), ~8 months to council, ~10 months to earliest start. The council is the **Council of Councils**, not an IC advisory council.

Review mechanics that deviate from a standard study section:
- A single CSR-convened **Special Emphasis Panel** reviews all DP5 applications, in two phases. Phase I is a mail review: three assigned reviewers matched to the subject area assess independently, with no group discussion. Phase II is "a broad-based editorial panel" of scientists deliberately **not** matched to topic area. "Typically, half of applications are chosen for discussion."
- Scoring is non-standard: panel members score privately, raw scores 1 (best) to 9 (worst), and "overall impact scores of 10-90" are produced by multiplying the average by 10.
- Scores: "within three business days" through eRA Commons. Summary statement: "available within 30 days of the review" — faster and more predictable than the NIH-wide norm.
- **No interview.** Applicants are not interviewed; the interview stage that existed in earlier cycles was removed by NOT-RM-18-018.
- Funding odds, from the NOFO itself: "The NIH Common Fund expects to spend about $5.7 million to fund about 10 awards in FY 2027." The prior cycle committed "approximately $5 million to support approximately 12-13 awards in FY 2025" — so fewer, larger awards.
- A condition after award, unusual and worth knowing before you apply: "NIH will conduct a site visit near the end of the first year to assess progress and confirm institutional support and independence. If support is insufficient, NIH may take corrective action, including reducing or terminating funding."
- Caveat: NIH's current emergency review modifications (reducing discussion to 30–35% and simplifying summary statements) are written for standard CSR meetings; the Common Fund page still describes the usual ~half-discussed DP5 practice. Whether the modifications reach this Special Emphasis Panel is not stated on either page.

The existing mechanisms.csv row says $250,000 direct/yr, and so does the Common Fund application-process guide page (reviewed July 13, 2026) — both are now stale. Modular budget form; up to five years.

1. ONE PD/PI, ONE BIOSKETCH. "Applications can have only one PD/PI. Multiple PD/PIs are not allowed. Only the PD/PI may be listed as Senior/Key Personnel and submit a biosketch." Hard failure mode: "Inclusion of other personnel or collaborator biosketches anywhere in the application will result in your application being administratively withdrawn." Collaborators send letters of support only — never biosketches.

2. LETTERS OF REFERENCE — 3 to 5, and they are NOT letters of support. "Letters of reference are required. The PD/PI must arrange for 3 to 5 letters… If fewer than 3 are submitted, the application is incomplete and will not be reviewed." Referees submit directly at https://public.era.nih.gov/commonsplus/public/reference/submitReferenceLetter.era (no eRA Commons account needed for the referee; the applicant must have one). Window for the last cycle: "Letters may be submitted between August 10 and September 10, 2026, by 5:00 PM local time" — i.e. local time of the *referee*, and "Late letters are not accepted." You never see them. You must give each referee your eRA Commons user ID, your last name exactly as in Commons, and the opportunity number. Two pages or less each, addressing "scientific, leadership, mentoring, and management skills." NIH's own selection advice: "It may not be best to choose referees based primarily on their official position, such as your departmental chair or institutional dean." You are responsible for chasing them — monitor status in Commons.

3. THE INSTITUTION WRITES A LARGE PIECE. Facilities & Other Resources has **no page limit** but a mandatory structure — Candidate Selection Process, Position Details, Institutional Resources Commitment, Institutional Commitment to Career Development — and "Address every item below or the application may be withdrawn for noncompliance," using the given headings and numbering. It must confirm the PD/PI "will hold an independent research position by September 30, 2027," signed by "the department head and institutional business official." NIH's guidance: "Try to avoid boilerplate language that isn't tailored to the candidate." "Institutional commitment… will be given considerable attention during the review and selection process."

4. PAGE LIMITS — same numbers as the NIH-wide table, but with mandated internal structure. Specific Aims **1 page**, and it must carry three headings: "Research Objectives," "Institutional Support," "Early Independence Rationale." Research Strategy **12 pages** ("The essay is limited to twelve pages"), organised under ten required numbered headings: rationale for omitting/abbreviating the postdoc; evidence you are not yet independent; personal/career development plan; evidence of training ability and leadership; host institution interactions; research challenge; approach; innovation; relationship to previous work; timeline. Project Summary/Abstract 30 lines, Project Narrative 3 sentences, as NIH-wide. "Preliminary data are optional, not required."

5. SCIENCE AREA DESIGNATION — a DP5-only field. Enter a one-digit code plus abbreviation in the SF424 Agency Routing Identifier (field 4b) from: 1 CB Chemical Biology, 2 CTR Clinical and Translational Research, 3 IDI Infectious Diseases and Immunology, 4 IE Instrumentation and Engineering, 5 MCB Molecular and Cellular Biology, 6 NS Neuroscience, 7 HIB High-Throughput and Integrative Biology, 8 BCB Bioinformatics and Computational Biology. Optional second area after a semicolon. It must ALSO appear at the top of the Research Strategy essay. It steers reviewer assignment only and "does not affect an application's funding potential."

6. NO ASSIGNMENT REQUEST. Do not request an IC or a review panel (see program_officer_contact).

7. EFFORT COMMITMENT, stated in the application: 9.6 person-months (80%) per year on the project in years 1–2; 9.6 person-months per year on independent research generally in years 3–5. Clinicians may keep enough clinical duty to maintain credentials.

8. Data Management and Sharing Plan required regardless of budget. Clinical trial optional.

9. NO LATE APPLICATIONS AT ALL, and no error-correction grace: "There is no deadline extension to correct for errors in the application, so all errors must be corrected by the submission deadline." Your institution's internal deadline lands days-to-weeks earlier.
result.resubmission_note:
No resubmissions — but you can re-enter as a new application, which is the distinction that matters.

FAQ, verbatim: "If my application is not funded, will I have an opportunity to revise and resubmit? Resubmission applications (A1) are not allowed." Corroborated structurally by the NOFO Key Dates, where the "Renewal / Resubmission / Revision (as allowed)" column reads "Not Applicable" — only New applications are accepted.

But: "If I am not successful this year, may I reapply next year? Yes." and "You may apply as often as you wish as long as you meet the eligibility requirements and a host institution is willing to submit the application on your behalf." So the practical limit is your eligibility window (the degree-date range moves each cycle, so most people get only one or two shots) and your institution's willingness to spend one of its two slots on you again.

Consequences of the A0-only rule: there is no Introduction page responding to the summary statement, and no A1 suffix. A repeat application is reviewed cold as new. NIH's overlap rule still binds: no new (A0) application "submitted before issuance of the summary statement from the review of an overlapping new (A0) or resubmission (A1) application" — with the September-due/March-review/30-days-to-summary-statement arc, the previous cycle's summary statement arrives around April, comfortably before the next September date.

One institution may submit more than one application "provided that each application is scientifically distinct," subject to the two-per-institution cap.

Not soliciting applications at this time." and Application Due Date "August 19, 2027 (estimated)". (Caution: a summarising fetch of the same RFA returned "August 18, 2026" as the due date — that is the expiration date. The due date is August 17, 2026, confirmed in raw HTML and independently in FAQ #10: "Application Due Date | August 17, 2026".)

HARD RULE, deviates from the NIH norm: "No late applications will be accepted for this Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO)." FAQ #3 closes the usual NIH carve-out too: "Can I receive a submission extension if serving as an NIH peer reviewer or in an NIH Advisory Group? No extensions will be given, and late applications will not be accepted."

DP2 does NOT use NIH standard due dates. It is a single annual receipt date and the Renewal/Resubmission/Revision and AIDS columns of the Key Dates table both read "Not Applicable".
result.deadline_pattern: One receipt date per year, mid-to-late August. Observed: FY2027 cycle due Aug 17, 2026; FY2028 cycle forecast Aug 19, 2027 (NIH's estimate). Rhythm around it, from the FY2027 cycle: RFA posted June 26 (~7.5 weeks before the deadline) → application window opens July 17 (~4.5 weeks before) → pre-application webinar July 6, 3–4:30 pm ET (~6 weeks before) → due Aug 17, 5:00 PM local time of the applicant organisation → NOFO expires Aug 18. Practical planning consequence: the RFA text does not exist until late June, so a spring-start applicant works from the prior year's RFA plus the posted sample applications, and the institutional research-office internal deadline (typically 3–5 business days earlier, i.e. ~Aug 10–12) is the real one. Because no late applications are accepted at all, the usual "submit 2–3 days early to fix errors" advice is not optional here.
result.loi_deadline: Not applicable — no LOI stage exists. FAQ #4 verbatim: "Is a letter of intent (LOI) required to apply for this award? Letters of intent are not required or accepted." Confirmed structurally: the string "Letter of Intent" does not appear anywhere in the full text of RFA-RM-27-002, and the Key Dates table carries no LOI row. There is also no pre-proposal, nomination or institutional-limit stage: "There is no limit to the number of applications an institution may submit, but individuals may submit only one application as PD/PI in response to this NOFO."
result.review_to_award:
Published DP2 timeline for the Aug 17, 2026 cycle (FAQ #10 "What is the competition timeline?", cross-checked against RFA-RM-27-002 Key Dates): Earliest Submission July 17, 2026 | Application Due August 17, 2026 | Scientific Merit Review March 2027 | Council of Councils Review May 2027 | Award Notifications July 2027 | Earliest Project Start Date July 2027.

DEVIATIONS FROM THE NIH NORM: submission-to-review is ~7 months, not ~4; notification and earliest start coincide in July, ~11 months out, not ~9; and the second level is the Council of Councils (NIH OD's own council, not an IC council), which "votes en bloc for concurrence with the first level review recommendations", is "not tasked with reviewing the applications for scientific or technical merit and is not asked to provide recommendations on which applications should be funded."

FIRST-LEVEL REVIEW IS TWO-PHASE, NOT A STUDY SECTION. All applications go to one CSR-convened Special Emphasis Panel; "reviewers change from year to year." Phase I: three "mail" reviewers, assigned from the two broad science areas you designate in the Agency Routing Identifier field, who "submit independent assessments electronically and do not discuss the applications with other reviewers." Phase II: "an editorial panel composed of scientists from an array of scientific backgrounds", three members per application, "not matched by area of expertise", who use the Phase I critiques to select what gets discussed — "Typically, only about 17-20% of applications are chosen for discussion" (against the NIH-wide ~50%, or 30–35% under the current emergency modifications).

SCORING: panel members score 1–9, the SRO averages and multiplies by 10, so "A discussed application can have an overall impact score of 10 (best) to 90 (worst)." Explicitly: "because applications are responding to a Request for Applications (RFA), the scores are not percentiled, which makes their interpretation difficult"; "there is no strict cutoff or pay line for funding"; "NIH staff cannot disclose where an impact score falls relative to other application scores." NIH also warns "These scores should not be compared to a regular R01 study section review."

FEEDBACK: overall impact score to eRA Commons "within three business days" of the meeting; summary statement "within 30 days of the review." Not-discussed applications still receive a summary statement carrying the mail reviewers' critiques, without editorial-panel comments.

SCALE AND ODDS: "NIH intends to commit approximately $23 million for approximately 30 awards in FY 2027"; FAQ #12: "The success rate of New Innovator Award applications for fiscal years 2021-2025 is 9%."

JIT and Notice of Award follow NIH norms, with the Resource Sharing Plan specifically deferred to JIT for this NOFO.
result.submission_requirements:
Submitted by the institution's AOR through Grants.gov (ASSIST / S2S / Workspace) and tracked in eRA Commons, as NIH-wide. Everything below is where DP2 DEVIATES.

THE APPLICATION IS AN ESSAY, NOT A RESEARCH PLAN. "Specific Aims: DO NOT USE." Research Strategy is "structured as an essay", "limited to ten pages" (the DP2 line in NIH's page-limits table), and "Presenting the proposed research as a series of specific aims is discouraged, and a detailed experimental plan should not be included." "Preliminary data are allowed but not required." Write "at a level appropriate for reviewers who are broadly knowledgeable but may not be experts in the research area" — literally true, since Phase II reviewers are deliberately not matched to your field.

SIX REQUIRED HEADED SECTIONS, IN ORDER, inside the ten pages: (1) Project science areas; (2) Project Description — must "State prominently that to comply with instructions in the funding opportunity, a detailed experimental plan and extensive preliminary data are not being provided"; (3) Innovativeness — including what you will do "if these approaches are not successful"; (4) Investigator qualifications — "evidence to support your claim of innovativeness and creativity in your prior research... personal qualities and experiences [that] demonstrate your inclination to question paradigms"; (5) Suitability for the New Innovator Award — "Explain why the planned research is uniquely suited to the New Innovator Award rather than a more 'traditional' grant mechanism"; (6) Statement of research effort commitment — an explicit statement committing "a minimum of three person-months (25%)".

EVERYTHING COUNTS AGAINST THE TEN PAGES: "Bibliography & References Cited: DO NOT USE" — "Any bibliographic citations provided must fit within the ten-page limit"; "Figures and illustrations may be included but must also fit within the ten-page limit." (NIH-wide, References Cited is a separate uncapped attachment; not here.)

NOT ALLOWED / DO NOT USE: "Letters of Support: DO NOT USE. Letters of Support are not allowed"; "Letters of collaboration will not be accepted" (collaborators go in the essay text and are listed on the PHS Assignment Request Form); Senior/Key Person Biographical Sketches other than the PD/PI ("Only the PD/PI may submit a Biographical Sketch"); additional Senior/Key Person profiles; Equipment; Consortium/Contractual Arrangements; Progress Report Publication List; Multiple PD/PI Leadership Plan. Appendix: "No publications or other material, with the exception of blank questionnaires or blank surveys."

NO BUDGET: "A detailed budget and other budget forms are not required and will not be accepted." You enter the flat total — "the total direct costs for the 5-year project period of the award is $2,375,000" — in Total Federal Funds Requested. Indirect costs "determined at the time of award and should not be included."

STILL REQUIRED: Facilities & Other Resources, "1-page maximum"; Current and Pending Support "from all sources and effort devoted to each project in person months"; Data Management and Sharing Plan on the NIH DMS Plan Format Page; Project Summary 30 lines and Narrative 3 sentences (NIH-wide); PHS Human Subjects and Clinical Trials Information; PHS Assignment Request Form. Resource Sharing Plan is deferred: "expected as Just in Time information if an award is being considered."

SINGLE PI ONLY: "Only single PD/PI applications are allowed. Applications with multiple PD(s)/PI(s) will not be accepted."

TWO CHOICES THAT SILENTLY DETERMINE YOUR REVIEWERS: the primary and secondary science areas entered in the SF424 "Agency Routing Identifier" field decide Phase I mail-reviewer assignment. Getting these wrong is a self-inflicted mismatch that no cover letter fixes.

ERA COMMONS HOUSEKEEPING IS A DISQUALIFIER: "If an applicant is not identified as an ESI in the eRA Commons, it may result in the application not being reviewed. Applicants are responsible for reviewing and/or updating their degree information in their eRA Commons account in a timely fashion." An ESI-extension request (childbirth, family care, illness, disaster, clinical loan repayment) "may take several weeks for the review process, so applicants should plan accordingly."

POST-SUBMISSION MATERIALS ARE NEARLY CLOSED, deviating from the NIH-wide one-page preliminary-data update: "Only documents to inform of unforeseen events, such as natural disasters, that substantially affect the ability to execute the proposed research will be accepted. No publication updates will be allowed as post-submission material."

The NIH-wide long-lead registrations still apply in full (SAM.gov/UEI, eRA Commons with a PI role, Grants.gov, ORCID linked to the Commons profile, SciENcv-generated Common Forms). Note the Common Fund's own application-process page is stale on this point — it still instructs applicants to obtain a DUNS number via fedgov.dnb.com, which UEI replaced in 2022. Follow grants.nih.gov, not that page, for registration.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
Both halves, in the funder's own words.

WHAT DISQUALIFIES YOU
- You must meet the ESI definition at submission: "a PD/PI who has completed their terminal research degree or end of post-graduate clinical training, whichever date is later, within the past 10 years and who has not previously competed successfully as PD/PI for a substantial NIH independent research award."
- A past R01 is permanent, not a current-holdings test. FAQ #14: "Am I still eligible if I had an R01 several years ago but have no R01 now? No, if you were ever the Principal Investigator (PI) or one of multiple PIs of an awarded R01 (or other substantial NIH grant) that was reviewed with you as a PI, you are not eligible to apply."
- Phased awards are the trap. FAQ #16: "recipients of an R21/R33 or R61/R33 Phased Innovation Award, that combine the review of the R21/R61 and R33 phases of the award, lose their ESI status and are not eligible". NIH's rule behind it: "for phased awards, the activity code of both phases must be listed on this page for a PD/PI to retain ESI status" — R33 is not on the list, so the combined-review version kills eligibility even though a standalone R21 does not.
- A pending award that lands first kills it: "If a pending grant becomes active prior to the New Innovator Award, and the grant mechanism is not on the list of smaller NIH grants and awards that maintain ESI status, then the applicant is no longer eligible to receive the New Innovator Award." FAQ #19 restates it: the award "will not be awarded if you receive an NIH R01 or other substantial NIH grant before the New Innovator Award is made."
- Winning it ends ESI status going forward. FAQ #21: "the NIH Director's New Innovator Award is equivalent to an R01 and removes your Early Stage Investigator status."
- Position and place: "Applicants must hold an independent research position at a domestic (U.S.) institution by September 1, 2027" (i.e. Sept 1 of the award fiscal year). "An 'independent research position' is a position that automatically confers eligibility to the investigator (based on institutional policy) to apply for R01 grants with appropriate institutional commitment of facilities." Foreign organizations and non-domestic components are not eligible.

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY — the half applicants most often get wrong
- K awards do not disqualify you. FAQ #13: "Yes, you are eligible to apply... if you are or have been the PD/PI of a career development (K) award, as long as you meet the other eligibility criteria." That includes K99/R00 (R00 is on the retained-ESI list).
- A standalone R21 does not disqualify you. FAQ #16: "a Principal Investigator of an R21 or other allowable research grant... does not affect Early Stage Investigator (ESI) status."
- NIH's full retained-ESI list ("An investigator will retain their Early Stage Investigator status if they receive any of the smaller research grants, training, infrastructure, and career awards that appear on this list"): R00, R03, R15/UA5, R16, R21, R25/R90/RL9/RL5, R34, R36, R41/UT1, R42/UT2, R43/U43, R44/U44, R50, R55, R56, R61, RL2, SB1, SC2/SC3, U09, U34, X01, X02; D71, all F fellowships, all individual and institutional K awards, Loan Repayment Awards, R38, D43/T32/T34/T35/T90/TL4; C06, G07, G08, G11, G13, G20, R13/U13, S10, S15, S21, S22, UC6; PC1, PC2, OT1, OT2, OT3, and R&D Contracts.
- Inheriting someone else's R01 preserves ESI. FAQ #15: "Yes, you would still be considered an Early Stage Investigator if you were not the submitting Principal Investigator."
- Non-NIH money of any size is irrelevant. FAQ #23: "you are eligible if you have support from sources other than NIH, have never been the Principal Investigator on any NIH grants that would disqualify you..."
- You may have an R01 — or an ESI MIRA R35 — application pending at the same time. RFA: "Applicants may submit or have an NIH R01 or other grant application (including an ESI MIRA R35 application) pending concurrently with their NIH Director's New Innovator Award application, but scientific overlap is not allowed per NIH policy." FAQ #22: "You may either submit applications for different projects concurrently or submit the same project again after receiving the summary statement from the first submission."
- No citizenship or residency gate at all. FAQ #6: "No, there are no citizenship or residency requirements. Foreign scientists are eligible if they apply from a U.S.-based institution." (Note this contradicts nothing in the existing row but is stronger than most NIH career mechanisms, which require citizen/national/PR.)
- Postdocs are not excluded outright: "Investigators still in training or mentored status (such as postdoctoral fellows) are not eligible to apply unless they have a written commitment from the institution stating they will be in an independent faculty position by September 1... The commitment is certified by the institution's submission of the application." No separate letter is filed — the institution certifies by submitting. FAQ #12 adds that the application "must be submitted by the institution where you will hold an independent position", and "This may be done in advance of your actual appointment date if the receipt deadline is before that date."
- ONGOING OBLIGATION, not eligibility: "Award recipients are required to commit at least three person-months (25%) of their research effort each year."
result.program_officer_contact:
NAMED: Patricia Labosky, Ph.D., NIH Office of the Director — the Contact listed for forecast RFA-RM-28-002 on commonfund.nih.gov/newinnovator/grants, and named in FAQ #9.

EMAIL: NewInnovatorAward@mail.nih.gov (decoded from the Cloudflare-obfuscated mailto in that table). Discrepancy to keep: RFA-RM-27-002 Section VII gives the PLURAL NewInnovatorAwards@mail.nih.gov as both the Scientific/Research Contact and the Financial/Grants Management Contact, under "Office of the Director (OD)", with no individual named and no phone number. Both strings are genuine on their own funder pages; prefer the RFA's plural form for NOFO questions.

PRE-SUBMISSION CONTACT IS NARROWER THAN THE NIH NORM — this is the deviation that matters. FAQ #9 verbatim: "Can someone at NIH review my idea and let me know if it is a good fit for this award? NIH staff cannot provide comments on specific ideas or plans for individual research grant applications. The external review will evaluate the merit of your application. However, questions about the scope and intent of the NIH Director's New Innovator Award should be directed to Dr. Patricia Labosky in the Office of the Director." So the standard NIH move — emailing a one-page Specific Aims for a fit read — does not work here. Ask about scope, intent, eligibility edge cases and mechanics instead. Exception: "For applications involving clinical research, applicants should contact program staff at the appropriate NIH Institute or Center (IC) to assure compliance with IC-specific clinical research policies" (IC contacts listed at commonfund.nih.gov/highrisk/clinical).

THE REAL PRE-SUBMISSION CHANNEL IS THE WEBINAR: "NIH program staff will hold a pre-application webinar to explain the program and answer questions about the application and review process." For the Aug 17, 2026 cycle it ran "July 6, 3-4:30 pm ET", ~6 weeks before the deadline, and "included a question/answer session with prospective applicants"; the recording is embedded and the slides posted at commonfund.nih.gov/newinnovator/webinar. Subscribe to the HRHR listserv (list.nih.gov, list NIH-CommonFund-HRHR) — that is where the late-June RFA posting is announced.

DURING REVIEW: no contact is named until after submission — "Examine your eRA Commons account for review assignment and contact information (information appears two weeks after the submission due date)." The CSR Scientific Review Officer "is the point of contact for all review-related questions and issues"; the SRO cannot discuss funding.

AFTER THE SUMMARY STATEMENT — the highest-value contact window: "If you have any questions about your summary statement, you should reach out to the scientific contact for the New Innovator Award (listed in the funding opportunity). The scientific contact attends the review and may be able to provide more insight into the panel discussion and help clarify some of the comments. You can also ask about the probability of funding and get advice on what to do if your application is outside of the likely pay range." How: "It is best to contact NIH staff by email to schedule a time for a meeting. That gives staff time to read your summary statement and review any notes. And be patient." What does not work: "Contacting NIH staff to 'sell' your application or to express differences in scientific opinion related to the reviewers' comments will not affect the likelihood of funding."

WHO ELSE: the annual HRHR Symposium (commonfund.nih.gov/highrisk/symposium) gathers current HRHR awardees — the practical place to find a DP2 holder willing to read an essay draft; and the eight sample-application PIs are named publicly by NIH.

FAQ #30 verbatim: "Can I revise and resubmit if my application is not funded? Resubmission applications (A1) are not allowed. So the NIH-wide Introduction-to-resubmission page (1 page summarising changes and responding to the summary statement) must NOT appear — referencing the prior review is prohibited. Re-entry is a clean A0 at the next August date, subject to still being an ESI then (the 10-year clock keeps running).

The scientific contact will reach out to eligible applicants directly with more information on the response and the deadline." result.program_name: NIH Institutional Research Training Grant (Ruth L. Kirschstein NRSA T32) — parent NOFO PA-25-168
result.next_deadline: September 25, 2026 — with a large caveat that is the single most important thing on this row. The parent T32 NOFO PA-25-168 publishes its own dated calendar through 2027 (Sep 25, 2026; Jan 25, 2027; May 25, 2027; Sep 25, 2027), and the announcement carries "Expiration Date: May 05, 2028", so these are dated, funder-published, non-rotting dates — not scraped guesses. BUT most NIH ICs do not accept T32 applications on all three cycles. NIH's own standard-due-dates page: "Applicants should check with the relevant Institute or Center (IC), since some do not accept T series applications for all three receipt/review/award cycles." Per the Table of IC-Specific Information (grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/contacts/parent_T32.html): MAY 25 ONLY or May-25-primary — NEI, NIAMS ("May 25 only"), NIBIB, NICHD ("May 25 only"), NIDCD, NIDDK, NIEHS, NINDS, NINR, NIDA (non-AIDS), and NHGRI for NEW applications ("May 25 only (new applications); January 25, May 25, or September 25 (as appropriate for renewal and resubmission applications)"). JANUARY 25 ONLY — NCCIH. NIGMS — "Predoctoral MSTP – Jan 25, May 25, Sept 25; Postdoctoral- January 25", and NIGMS does not take predoctoral T32s through the parent except MSTP. NIAID — "January 25 and Sept 25 for non-AIDS applications". NCI — all three. PRACTICAL READ: Sep 25, 2026 is real and one week out from 2026-09-18, but it is usable only at NCI, NIAID, NHGRI (renewal/resubmission only), NIGMS MSTP and other three-cycle ICs. For the majority of applicants the next usable date is MAY 25, 2027. All due "by 5:00 PM local time of applicant organization."
result.deadline_pattern: Three NIH-standard T-series dates per year — January 25, May 25, September 25 — and uniquely among NIH families the SAME dates apply to all application types. Standard-due-dates table row, verbatim: "T Series D Series All - new, renewal, resubmission, revision | Institutional National Research Service Awards | Other Training Grants | January 25 | May 25 | September 25". There is no +1-month offset for renewal/resubmission/revision as there is for the R and K families. The operative pattern for any individual applicant is the IC's subset of those three dates, not the three themselves.
result.loi_deadline: No letter of intent for the parent T32 (PA-25-168) — Section IV carries no LOI requirement and no LOI date. Two adjacent pre-application steps do bite, though, and are easy to mistake for "no pre-application stage": (1) the NIH ≥$500,000-direct-costs-in-any-year rule — the IC-specific table flags advance-permission letters for NCI, NHGRI, NHLBI, NIA, NIAAA, NIAID, NIAMS, NIBIB, NICHD, NIDCD, NIDDK, NIEHS, NIMH, NINR and ORIP; T32 budgets with stipends, tuition and institutional allowance routinely cross that line, so for many programs there is a de facto ~6-weeks-prior approval step. (2) IC-specific T32 RFAs/PARs outside the parent (e.g. the JSPTPN notice NOT-NS-25-020 referenced on the T32 activity-code page) can set their own LOI requirements and single custom dates; the parent's "no LOI" does not carry over to them.
result.review_to_award: Longer than the NIH R-series norm, and published as dated rows rather than month ranges. From PA-25-168's own Key Dates table: Sep 25, 2026 due → Advisory Council March 2027 → earliest start July 2027 (~10 months). Jan 25, 2027 due → Council July 2027 → earliest start December 2027 (~11 months — the January cycle has the longest lag, worth knowing before choosing a cycle). May 25, 2027 due → Council November 2027 → earliest start April 2028 (~11 months). The completed historical row shows the shape end-to-end: Jan 25, 2025 due → Scientific Merit Review May 07, 2025 → Council July 2025 → earliest start Oct 2025. Two deviations from the funder-wide arc: merit review is given as a SPECIFIC DATE (May 07, Sep 07, Jan 07) rather than the R-series "June–July / Oct–Nov / Feb–Mar" window, consistent with T32s being reviewed by convened training-specific panels rather than the standing CSR study sections the funder-norm arc describes; and the T-series council months (Mar/Jul/Nov) do not line up with the R-series council months (Aug-Oct/Jan/May). Plan ~10–11 months from submission to earliest possible start, and note the award is to the institution, so trainee recruitment for year 1 must be timed to the start date, not the notification.
result.submission_requirements: Institution applies, not the trainee — a faculty Training PD/PI assembles it and the AOR/SO submits via Grants.gov, so the funder-wide "your real deadline is your research office's" rule applies with force. Where T32 DEVIATES from the NIH norm: (1) PAGE LIMITS — Research Training Program Plan 25 pages (vs 12 for R01); Introduction for resubmission 3 pages, not the NIH-wide 1 page; Plan for Instruction in the Responsible Conduct of Research 3 pages; renewal Progress Report "5 pages for a program overview and 1 page for each appointee to the grant". (2) TRAINING DATA TABLES — the defining T32 workload and the thing first-time applicants underestimate. NIH: "All current applications must use FORMS-I data tables." Tables 1–8, with separate consolidated sets for undergraduate and international programs. The NOFO: "Particular attention must be given to the required Training Data Tables," and applicants must "summarize, in the body of the application, key data from the tables." Review criteria single out Training Table 5 and Training Table 8 repeatedly — those two carry disproportionate weight. Blank templates and instructions-plus-samples are at grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/forms-directory/data-tables/forms-i (Blank_Data_Tables_ALL.docx; Consolidated_Training_Tables.docx/.pdf). The eRA Commons xTRACT module "allows applicants, recipients and assistants to create research training tables for progress reports and institutional training grant applications" and supports "T32, TL1, T90/R90, and T15", pre-populating trainee names, characteristics, institutions, grant numbers and subsequent NIH/HHS awards from xTrain appointment data. (3) SENIOR INSTITUTIONAL SIGN-OFF BEYOND THE USUAL AOR — "The application must include a signed letter on institutional letterhead from a President, Provost, Dean or key institutional leader" (max 10 pages), covering scientific rigor, resources, facilities, staff, mentor time, safety and trainee support. This has no analogue in R/F/K applications and needs weeks of lead time inside the university. (4) MANDATORY IC CONSULTATION — "prospective applicants MUST consult the Table of IC-Specific Information, Requirements and Staff Contacts, to make sure that their application is appropriate for the requirements of one of the participating NIH ICs." 24 ICs participate, several with hard program constraints (NCI: "No less than 75% of the trainees per award year must be postdoctoral fellows"; NCCIH: "Maximum annual total direct cost ... may not exceed $400,000 per year"; ORIP: "Restricted to veterinary students and graduate veterinarians only"). (5) MULTIPLE APPLICATIONS ALLOWED — "Applicant organizations may submit more than one application, provided that each application is programmatically distinct." (6) PD/PI — "Any individual(s) with the skills, knowledge, and resources necessary to carry out the proposed research training program"; should be "an established investigator" with "administrative and training experience"; active eRA Commons account required. Notably, PA-25-168 does NOT require the Training PD/PI to hold independent research support. Funder-wide items (SciENcv/Common Forms, ORCID, SAM.gov/eRA/Grants.gov registrations, 5:00 PM local time, no error-correction window) apply unchanged.
result.prior_funding_conflicts: Two levels, and they behave oppositely — this is what makes the field useful. AT THE GRANT (INSTITUTION) LEVEL there is essentially NO prior-funding bar: T32s are explicitly renewable ("Awards for T32 institutional NRSA research training grants may be for project periods up to five years in duration and are renewable"), holding one does not block another, and "Applicant organizations may submit more than one application, provided that each application is programmatically distinct." A department already holding a T32 is a strong applicant for a second, distinct one, not a disqualified one. AT THE TRAINEE (APPOINTEE) LEVEL the gates are real. WHAT DISQUALIFIES: citizenship — an appointee "must be a citizen or a noncitizen national of the United States or have been lawfully admitted for permanent residence" (this bars international students and postdocs from the slot, though not from the lab or the program's non-NRSA positions); concurrency — "An NRSA appointment may not be held concurrently with another Federally sponsored fellowship, traineeship, or similar Federal award that provides a stipend", so you cannot hold an F31 or F32 and a T32 slot at the same time; and part-time work — "All trainees are required to pursue their research training full time, normally defined as 40 hours per week." WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the half applicants usually miss): the concurrency rule bars SIMULTANEOUS stipend-paying federal support, not SEQUENTIAL support — the standard and expected career path is T32 slot first, then convert to an individual F31/F32, or vice versa, relinquishing one as the other starts; prior T32 support does not disqualify you from a later individual NRSA fellowship, nor from later K or R awards; the payback obligation attaches only to postdoctoral support — "Kirschstein-NRSA recipients incur a service payback obligation for the first 12 months of postdoctoral support" — so predoctoral T32 support carries no payback, and postdoctoral payback is discharged by ordinary continued research, research training or teaching ("engaging in health-related research, health-related research training or health-related teaching (or any combination thereof)"), which nearly every continuing academic career satisfies automatically; and non-stipend awards (supplements, travel, small internal grants) do not trigger the concurrency bar. UNVERIFIED IN THIS SESSION — flagging rather than asserting: the existing corpus row states an aggregate NRSA cap of 5 years predoctoral / 3 years postdoctoral counted across institutional (T32) and individual (F) awards combined. PA-25-168 does not state it — its only five-year statement is about the grant's project period, not the trainee — and every NIH Grants Policy Statement chapter-11 URL I tried returned HTTP 404, so I could not source it here. Treat the 5/3 aggregate as carried forward from the existing row, not re-verified.
result.program_officer_contact: Expected, and more load-bearing here than the NIH norm, because the IC decides both whether it accepts your cycle at all and whether your program area fits. The NOFO makes consultation mandatory in its own words: prospective applicants "MUST consult the Table of IC-Specific Information, Requirements and Staff Contacts." That table (https://grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/contacts/parent_T32.html) is the contact route — it lists named scientific contacts for each of the 24 participating ICs, and all ICs strongly encourage contact before submission to discuss fit and requirements. Named examples read off the table: NCI — Susan E. Lim, PhD and Susan N. Perkins, PhD; NEI — Neeraj Agarwal, PhD; NHGRI — Tina Gatlin, PhD (Genomic Sciences), Heather Junkins, MS (Genomic Medicine), Joy Boyer (ELSI); NHLBI — Jane Scott, ScD MSN (Cardiovascular), Xenia J. Tigno, PhD (Lung), Henry Chang, MD (Blood). Section VII (Agency Contacts) of PA-25-168 is the other route, though the section was truncated in the page as fetched. The questions worth asking are T32-specific: does my IC take this cycle; is my program area within your training priorities; what trainee mix do you expect (NCI's 75%-postdoc floor is the kind of thing only a PO will tell you early); is my budget over the $500k threshold that needs advance permission. IMPORTANT ROLE DISTINCTION FOR THE UTILITY TEST: a PhD student or postdoc who wants T32 support does NOT contact an NIH program officer. The T32 is awarded to the institution, and the person who appoints trainees to slots is the Training Program Director at the university — that faculty member is the who-to-talk-to. The NIH PO is the contact for the faculty member writing the grant, not for the person hoping to be funded by it.
result.examples_or_samples: NEGATIVE FINDING, worth recording as such: NIH's own curated samples index (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/samples-applications-and-documents) lists sample applications with summary statements from NIAID, NCI, NHGRI, NIA and NIDCD, but NO T32, T34, T35 or TL1 sample applications. The gold-standard "funded application beside its summary statement" exercise that exists for R01/F/K does not exist for T32 on NIH's index. What does exist, in descending usefulness: (1) SAMPLE COMPLETED DATA TABLES — the closest thing to a worked example of the hardest component, at grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/forms-directory/data-tables/forms-i, which provides both blank templates (Blank_Data_Tables_ALL.docx) and "Training Data Tables, Instructions, and Samples" (Consolidated_Training_Tables.docx/.pdf), plus undergraduate and international variants. Start here. (2) NIH RePORTER (reporter.nih.gov) filtered to activity code T32 — abstracts, institutions, PDs, amounts and resulting publications for every funded T32; this is how you find the programs closest to yours and the people running them. RePORTER Matchmaker returns the program officials behind similar awards with email addresses. (3) FOIA to the funding IC for a complete application — NIH's stated route for full application contents. (4) Annotated form sets at grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/samples-applications-and-documents/annotated-form-sets. (5) FOR A PROSPECTIVE TRAINEE rather than a writer, the practical "example" is the roster of currently funded programs — the T32 activity-code page itself lists 31 currently supported JSPTPN neuroscience training programs with program directors and contact information, which is a directory of people to email.
result.resubmission_note: One resubmission only (A1), within 37 months, per the funder-wide rule — but with two T32-specific differences. First, the Introduction to a resubmission is 3 PAGES, not the NIH-standard 1 page (the page-limits table gives "3 pages" for "all Training (T)" codes) — three times the room to respond to the summary statement, and reviewers expect it used. Second, T-series resubmissions are due on the SAME dates as new applications (January 25 / May 25 / September 25), with no one-month offset — the standard table row reads "All - new, renewal, resubmission, revision". Watch the IC interaction: NHGRI takes new T32s only on May 25 but accepts "January 25, May 25, or September 25 (as appropriate for renewal and resubmission applications)", so a resubmission may have MORE cycles available to it than the original did. Renewals are the common case here rather than the exception, since T32s are renewable five-year awards; a renewal carries the Progress Report at 5 pages plus 1 page per appointee, and the trainee outcomes in Tables 5 and 8 effectively are the renewal's case.
unresolved: AGGREGATE NRSA SUPPORT CAP NOT RE-SOURCED. The existing corpus row asserts 5 years predoctoral / 3 years postdoctoral aggregate across institutional + individual NRSA awards. PA-25-168 does not state it (its only five-year figure is the grant's project period), and three NIH Grants Policy Statement chapter-11 URLs returned HTTP 404. Tooling fact, not a finding — the cap is not contradicted, merely unverified here. Needs a fetch of the Grants Policy Statement via its correct current slug or the NRSA PDF.

xTRACT REQUIRED OR OPTIONAL — NOT ESTABLISHED. era.nih.gov/help-tutorials/xtract/overview.htm describes what xTRACT does and which mechanisms it supports (T32, TL1, T90/R90, T15) but contains no sentence with 'required', 'must', 'optional' or 'mandatory' about its use for T32 applications. era.nih.gov/erahelp/xtract/ returned an empty body to a plain fetch.
