result.program_name: NIH R01 for Early Stage / New Investigators (ESI/NI-flagged R01)
result.next_deadline:
**October 5, 2026** (a Monday — no weekend/holiday rollover), 5:00 PM local time of the applicant organization. This is a real dated deadline, not a pattern: it is printed in the Key Dates of both current Parent R01 NOFOs. PA-25-301 (Clinical Trial Not Allowed) and PA-25-305 (Clinical Trial Required) each list, verbatim, "February 05, 2025; June 05, 2025; October 05, 2025; February 05, 2026; June 05, 2026; October 05, 2026; February 05, 2027; June 05, 2027; October 05, 2027", and both expire January 08, 2028. It is independently corroborated by NIH's standard-due-dates table ("February 5, June 5, October 5" for new R01). After Oct 5, 2026: February 5, 2027, then June 5, 2027, then October 5, 2027.

For an A1 resubmission the next date is **November 5, 2026** (renewal/resubmission/revision R01 = "March 5, July 5, November 5"), then March 5, 2027 and July 5, 2027.

ESI-specific timing that is NOT a deadline but behaves like one: ESI status "will be determined at the time of submission" from your eRA Commons profile, so the profile must be correct BEFORE Oct 5, not after. If you need an ESI-window extension, NIH says you "will receive an email response, within four weeks of receiving all requested information" — so a request made after roughly early September 2026 may not be resolved in time for the October 5 date.
result.deadline_pattern: Three cycles a year, same calendar as any other R01 — the ESI/NI flag does not change a single date. New: February 5 / June 5 / October 5. Renewal, resubmission (A1) and revision: March 5 / July 5 / November 5 (one month later). There is no ESI-only cycle, no ESI-only NOFO, and no ESI-only due date. NOFO instructions override where an IC-specific PAR or RFA sets its own single date. Dates are the funder's permanent published calendar, restated in each Parent R01 NOFO's Key Dates, so they are safe to record as dates rather than only as a pattern.
result.loi_deadline:
Not applicable — no letter of intent and no pre-proposal stage. PA-25-301's Letter of Intent field reads "Not Applicable"; PA-25-305 carries no LOI requirement either. (Caveat: an IC-specific R01 PAR or RFA may impose its own LOI, typically 30 days before the due date — check Section IV of whichever NOFO you actually use.)

The functional equivalent of a pre-proposal stage for an ESI is two things that must happen weeks earlier and are invisible in the NOFO: (1) completing the Education section of the eRA Commons Personal Profile so the ESI flag can be computed, and (2) if the 10-year window has lapsed for a qualifying reason, filing an ESI Extension Request — NIH responds "within four weeks of receiving all requested information", and determinations "are made on a case-by-case basis at the sole discretion of NIH". Neither has a published deadline; both gate whether the application is flagged ESI at all.
result.review_to_award:
Same clock as any R01 — about 9 months submission to earliest start — with one genuine ESI deviation in the middle.

For an October 5, 2026 submission (Cycle III): scientific merit review February–March 2027, Advisory Council May 2027, earliest project start July 2027. PA-25-301's own Key Dates list is consistent with this (its 6th-position entries are Scientific Merit Review March 2027, Advisory Council May 2027, Earliest Start July 2027).

ESI DEVIATIONS, in NIH's own words:
- Review grouping: "When feasible, ESI applications are not interspersed with those of established investigators at the review meeting."
- Summary statements come EARLIER than for everyone else: "Summary statements for ESI R01 applications are prioritized, and when possible, released before summary statements for other applications reviewed in the same meeting. Generally, summary statements will be available no later than 30 days before Council." For an Oct 5, 2026 submission that means a statement in hand by roughly early April 2027 — which is what makes the November 5, 2027 A1 date reachable rather than theoretical.
- Funding: "ESI applications with scores within funding range will be prioritized for funding by the institute or center receiving the application."

CURRENT CAVEAT: the emergency review modifications (NOT-OD-26-114) cover the January 2027 Advisory Council, with prior modifications having applied to the January, May and October 2026 Councils. An October 5, 2026 submission goes to the MAY 2027 Council, which is beyond the announced coverage — whether the 30–35% discussion rate reaches it has not been announced. NOT-OD-26-114 makes no mention of ESI or New Investigators at all, so it does not say whether ESI clustering and prioritized summary statements survive under it.
result.submission_requirements:
The central fact, and the one applicants get wrong: **there is no ESI application.** You apply to an ordinary R01 NOFO and the flag is attached automatically from your eRA Commons profile. Neither Parent R01 NOFO mentions Early Stage or New Investigators anywhere. There is no ESI checkbox, no ESI attachment, no ESI justification to write.

WHERE TO APPLY (verified, current): Parent R01 PA-25-301 "NIH Research Project Grant (Parent R01 Clinical Trial Not Allowed)" or PA-25-305 "(Parent R01 Clinical Trial Required)" — both opened January 5, 2025, both expire January 8, 2028, both accept New, Renewal, Resubmission and Revision. Or any IC-specific R01 NOFO/PAR/RFA.

THE ONLY ESI-SPECIFIC REQUIREMENT, and it sits outside the application package: "Investigators must enter the date of their terminal research degree and/or end of post-graduate clinical training date in the Education section of their eRA Commons Personal Profile for ESI eligibility to be calculated." Then "If the eRA Commons Profile indicates the investigator is considered an ESI, that information will be automatically indicated on any R01 or R01 equivalent grant application submitted", and "ESI status and the End of Eligibility Date will be displayed in the eRA Commons profile." Because "The ESI status of the PD/PI(s), on a R01 equivalent grant application will be determined at the time of submission", an incomplete profile on the due date means an unflagged application, permanently — it cannot be added later.

THE MULTI-PI TRAP (highest-value single sentence for an early-career applicant): "A multiple PD/PI R01 or R01 equivalent grant application will be considered an ESI application only if all Principal Investigators listed are ESIs." Adding one senior co-PI to strengthen the team forfeits ESI treatment for the entire application. This is a structural decision, made months before submission.

EVERYTHING ELSE IS THE STANDARD R01, with no deviation: Research Strategy 12 pages, Specific Aims 1 page, Project Summary/Abstract 30 lines, Project Narrative 3 sentences, Introduction 1 page for a resubmission. PA-25-301: "All page limitations described in the How to Apply- Application Guide and the Table of Page Limits must be followed." Submission is by the institution's AOR/Signing Official through Grants.gov, due "by 5:00 PM local time of applicant organization", with no error-correction window. SciENcv-produced Common Forms and an ORCID linked to eRA Commons apply as they do to every NIH application.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
Both halves matter, and for this mechanism the preserving half is much longer than the disqualifying half. This is an eligibility ENHANCEMENT, not an exclusion — almost every award an early-career person realistically holds leaves ESI status intact.

WHAT PRESERVES ESI — NIH's own framing: "An investigator will retain their Early Stage Investigator status if they receive any of the smaller research grants, training, infrastructure, and career awards that appear on this list." The full published list, by activity code:
- Research grants: R00 (Pathway to Independence research phase), R03, R15/UA5, R16, R21, R25/R90/RL9/RL5, R34, R36, R41/UT1, R42/UT2, R43/U43, R44/U44, R50, R55, R56, R61, RL2, SB1, SC2, SC3, U09, U34, X01, X02.
- Training and mentored career: ALL F awards, ALL K awards (individual and institutional, explicitly including K99), all loan repayment awards, R38, D43, D71, T32, T34, T35, T90, TL4.
- Instrumentation/construction/education/meetings: C06, G07, G08, G11, G13, G20, R13/U13, S10, S15, S21, S22, UC6.
- Other: PC1, PC2, OT1, OT2, OT3, and R&D contracts.
So: a K99/R00, any K, any F, an R21, an R03, an R15, an R34, SBIR/STTR, a training grant, an LRP — none of these end ESI status. A K99/R00 holder is still an ESI.

WHAT ENDS ESI: the definition is the exclusion — an ESI is a PD/PI "who has completed their terminal research degree or end of post-graduate clinical training, whichever date is later, within the past 10 years and who has not previously competed successfully as PD/PI for a substantial NIH independent research award." Anything NOT on the list above is disqualifying: a prior R01, U01, P01, DP1, DP2, R35 (note: MIRA is absent from the list), R37, and comparable substantial independent awards.

THE PHASED-AWARD TRAP: "For phased awards, the activity code of both phases must be listed on this page for a PD/PI to retain ESI status." R33 does NOT appear on the list (R21 and R61 do). Read literally, this means an R21/R33 or R61/R33 phased award would not preserve ESI even though its first phase would. Flagged as a direct consequence of NIH's two quoted rules rather than as NIH's own worked example — worth confirming with the ESI mailbox before relying on it.

THE CLOCK, AND HOW TO STOP IT: the 10 years run from terminal degree or end of post-graduate clinical training, whichever is later. NIH will consider extensions for researchers who "have lapses in their research or research training or have experienced periods of less than full-time effort", specifically for childbirth, medical concerns, disability, family care responsibilities, natural disasters, and active duty military service. Requested through "an ESI Extension Request link found in the Education section of the PI's Personal Profile in eRA Commons"; "determinations are made on a case-by-case basis at the sole discretion of NIH"; response "within four weeks of receiving all requested information."

NEW INVESTIGATOR vs ESI: NI is the broader category (never held a substantial independent award, no time limit); ESI is NI plus inside the 10-year window. The documented payline and review benefits on the ESI policy page are written for ESIs specifically.
result.program_officer_contact:
Pre-submission contact is expected and encouraged, and for an ESI it is closer to mandatory practice than optional — the PO is the only person who will tell you whether your record is competitive for an R01 yet, or whether you should do an R21 first.

ROUTE FOR THIS MECHANISM: PA-25-301 Section VII points to an IC-specific contacts page (https://grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/contacts/IC-specific-information-PA-25-301.html). That page turns out not to list individual program officers by name; it gives each Institute/Center's mission and directs you onward. What it does recommend is the RePORTER Matchmaker Tool — enter "your draft specific aims, abstract, or other scientific text" and select "Similar Program Officials". Its own advice is unusually practical: "Reach out to best matching program officer first, and don't worry if it's not a perfect fit. If they're not the best match, they can direct you to who is."

ESI-SPECIFIC CONTACTS:
- The NIH ESI Extensions page lists a dedicated NIH mailbox for ESI extension and status questions. My fetch tool's email filter redacted the address, so read it directly off grants.nih.gov/policy-and-compliance/policy-topics/early-stage-investigators/extensions rather than taking an address from me.
- eRA Service Desk, 301-402-7469 or 866-504-9552 toll-free, https://www.era.nih.gov/need-help — this is the right contact for the characteristic ESI failure mode, "my profile is complete but no ESI flag or End of Eligibility Date is showing."
- Grants.gov support: 800-518-4726.

WHAT TO ASK A PO AS AN ESI: is my record competitive for an R01 in your IC yet, or should this be an R21/R03 first; does your IC operate an ESI payline extension and roughly where; is the scope right for 5 years; which study section is likely, and does it see ESI applications; should I add a senior co-PI (remember this forfeits the ESI flag) or keep it single-PI. Standard NIH limits apply — POs will not co-write, rewrite or edit sections, will not give detailed experimental design, and cannot promise funding. Timing: at the Specific Aims stage, roughly 2–4 months out, and again after the summary statement before committing to an A1.
result.examples_or_samples:
Honest headline: **no NIH collection is labeled as ESI/NI-flagged R01 samples.** Because the ESI application IS an ordinary R01, you read ordinary R01 samples. The following were checked this session.

BEST — full applications paired with their summary statements:
- **NIAID**, https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/sample-applications — verified live via a rendering browser (the site returns HTTP 403 to a plain fetch, a tooling fact). Eight R01 full applications, each with its summary statement as a downloadable PDF, spanning Forms-C through Forms-H: George Liu (UC San Diego, Forms-H), Emily Troemel (UC San Diego, Forms-G), Vernita Gordon (UT Austin), Monica Gandhi (UCSF), Tom Muir (Princeton), William Faubion (Mayo), Chengwen Li & Richard Samulski (UNC), Mengxi Jiang (UAB). Plus R03, R15, R21, R21/R33, SBIR/STTR, K01/K08/K23, F31, G11, U01. NIAID's words: "Several NIAID investigators have graciously agreed to share their exceptional applications and summary statements as samples to help the research community." Two caveats it states itself: "Although these applications demonstrate good grantsmanship, time has passed since these grant recipients applied. The samples may not reflect the latest format or rules", and use is permitted "for nonprofit educational purposes only". The page also carries a standing banner: "Due to current HHS and NIH restructuring, some content on niaid.nih.gov is not being updated regularly."
- NIAID's mechanism-choice guidance is directly useful to an ESI deciding whether to go for the R01 at all: "R21s are not intended for new investigators, and there is no evidence that they provide a path to an independent research career", and "R03s are not intended for new investigators."
- **NIDCD**, https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/funding/sample-grant-applications — nine R01 full applications, every one with a summary statement (Carney, Cherney & Heinemann, Crane, Froemke, Gifford & Camarata, Lomvardas, McCreery, Sanes, Shera). Also three Early Career Research (ECR) R21 samples with summary statements (Chow, Monson, Walker) — the only explicitly early-career sample set found anywhere, though R21 not R01. NIDCD: "The NIDCD Early Career Research (ECR) R21 Award supports both basic and clinical research from scientists who are beginning to establish an independent research career."
- **NHGRI ELSI**, https://www.genome.gov/Funded-Programs-Projects/ELSI-Research-Program/Sample-Applications-and-Summary-Statements — R01, R03, R21, K01, K99/R00, with summary statements.
- **NCI**, four separate collections: behavioral research https://cancercontrol.cancer.gov/brp/funding/sample-grant-applications (R01/R03/R21), cancer epidemiology https://epi.grants.cancer.gov/funding/grant-application-examples.html (R01/R03/R21/R37), implementation science https://cancercontrol.cancer.gov/is/funding/sample-grant-applications (R01/R21/R37), healthcare delivery https://healthcaredelivery.cancer.gov/funding/samples.html (R01/R03/R21/R50).
- **NIA**, https://www.nia.nih.gov/research/training/sample-applications, plus small business samples at https://www.nia.nih.gov/research/sbir/nia-small-business-sample-applications.
- NIH's index of all of these: https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/samples-applications-and-documents

FOR FUNDED ABSTRACTS AND AIMS AT SCALE: NIH RePORTER (reporter.nih.gov) — abstracts, Specific Aims text, IC, study section, amount, resulting publications; Matchmaker for the "who funds work like mine" question. RePORTER does not hold full applications; those come via a FOIA request to the funding IC.

FOR HOW MANY ESIs ACTUALLY GET FUNDED: NIH Data Book report 304, "R01-Equivalent Investigators, New (Type 1): Number of Early Stage Investigators (ESIs)" (https://report.nih.gov/nihdatabook/report/304) and report 166, "R01-Equivalent Investigators, New (Type 1): Funding Rates, by Career Stage" (https://report.nih.gov/nihdatabook/report/166). Linked from the ESI policy pages; not opened this session.
result.resubmission_note:
Standard NIH rules apply unchanged — one A1 only, within 37 months of the A0, Introduction of 1 page, no overlapping applications under review — with A1 due dates one month after new: November 5, 2026, then March 5, 2027, July 5, 2027. A not-discussed or (under the current modifications) "competitive but not discussed" application is still resubmittable.

THE ESI-SPECIFIC TRAP, which follows directly from NIH's own rule rather than being stated by NIH as a worked example: because "The ESI status of the PD/PI(s), on a R01 equivalent grant application will be determined at the time of submission", ESI status is re-evaluated at the A1, not inherited from the A0. If your End of Eligibility Date (visible in eRA Commons) falls between the two submissions, the A1 is not an ESI application and loses the payline priority and review clustering that the A0 had. An A0 submitted October 5, 2026 gets its summary statement by roughly early April 2027 (NIH prioritizes ESI summary statements to "no later than 30 days before Council") and the A1 date is November 5, 2027 — a 13-month gap in which the window can close. Check the End of Eligibility Date before choosing between an A1 and a fresh A0, and file any extension request early, allowing NIH's stated four weeks to respond.

Second ESI-specific consideration: winning any substantial independent award in the interval — including a different R01 — ends ESI status for the pending A1. Awards on the ESI-preserving list (R21, R03, K, F, R00, etc.) do not.

result.loi_deadline:
FY2027: 19 December 2025 — i.e. roughly 2.5 months BEFORE the full application (4 March 2026), and about 6 weeks after the RFA drops. This is the single most timeline-critical fact for this mechanism.

Funder's words: "A Letter of Intent (LOI) is required for all grant applications. A LOI form is provided in Appendix 8 and must be submitted online or via email to NJCCR at: njccr@doh.nj.gov no later than December 19, 2025."

SECOND GATE, distinct from the LOI and genuinely easy to miss — a mandatory pre-award Technical Assistance session ten days BEFORE the LOI: "A mandatory Pre-award Technical Assistance Session (TA) will be held on December 9, 2025, from 9:00 AM to 11:00 AM. Failure to attend the TA will result in disqualification, and the application will not be considered for funding." And: "All grant applicants that plan to submit a LOI (December 19, 2025) are required to attend the Virtual Technical Assistance (TA) session." No registration needed — it is held on MS Teams and the RFA prints the join link, meeting ID and dial-in.

Practical consequence: the real entry point into this fellowship is roughly a month after the RFA appears, not the March application date. A postdoc who finds the programme in January has already missed it for that cycle.

LOI mechanics: one-page form (RFA Appendix 8), submitted either through an online Microsoft Forms link ("NJCCR LOI Form 2027") or by email to njccr@doh.nj.gov. It asks for grant type, research type, cancer site(s) targeted, PI name and email, any Co-PIs, the institution's grant/fiscal contact, and project title. The form explicitly warns that the PI is the fellow, not the mentor: "[Please make sure this is the PI not the Sponsor/Mentor]".
result.deadline_pattern: Annual, fixed to the New Jersey state fiscal year. One cycle per year: RFA released early November → mandatory TA session early December → mandatory LOI mid-December → full application due the first week of March at 4:00 PM ET → award notice end of June → project start 1 July. Awards are two years but "Multi-year awards are made through one-year contracts", with each year contingent on available funds and satisfactory progress reports.
result.review_to_award: ~3.9 months application-to-notification, then ~2 days to start. Application due 4 March 2026 (4:00 PM) → "Notifications will be issued no later than June 28, 2026, through the SAGE system" → "Notice of Grant Award June 30, 2026" → "Project Start Date July 1, 2026". The start date is pinned to the state fiscal year, not negotiated, so there is effectively no ramp between notification and start. Two-stage review: NJCCR administrative/compliance screen, then an out-of-state scientific peer review panel scoring under NIH scoring guidelines; the Commission then sets funding decisions and may weigh programmatic and geographic-diversity factors among applications of comparable merit. Multi-year awards are issued as successive one-year contracts contingent on funds and progress reports.
result.submission_requirements:
Submitted electronically through SAGE (System for Administering Grants Electronically), NJDOH's portal — "Paper submissions will not be accepted." Portal: https://njdohsage.nj.gov (the RFA also prints https://dohsage.intelligrants.com). SAGE registration is not instant: if the institution already uses SAGE you request an account from a local designated administrator; if it has never used SAGE, contact the NJDOH SAGE Help Desk at njdoh.grants@doh.nj.gov. Start this early — it is an institutional account process, not a self-signup.

Page/word limits (RFA Appendix 7, "Grant Submission Checklist"), Postdoc column:
- Project Description — 1 sentence
- Lay Abstract — 250 words, in plain language for a non-scientist; note it is reused publicly: "If the award is granted, this summary will be used in press releases, public announcements, and various NJCCR publications."
- Proposal Narrative Abstract — 30 lines of text
- Specific Aims — 1 page
- Research Strategy — under 6 pages (covering Significance, Preliminary Studies/Data, Research Design, References, Facilities, Major Equipment)
- Written Response to Reviewer Critiques — if a resubmission

Formatting, enforced on pain of withdrawal: "Applications may be administratively withdrawn by NJCCR if the proposal does not comply with the format requirements (type size/character per inch, lines per page and page limitations)." Minimum 11-point font; font must be Arial, Calibri or Helvetica; minimum 1/2 inch margins; high-contrast text; smaller text allowed only inside figures if legible at 100% zoom.

Fellowship-specific components that deviate from a generic project grant:
- THREE letters of reference: "for the predoc and postdoc applicants, three (3) Letters of Reference from individuals other than the Sponsor is required" — uploaded to the "References" section of the Researcher Profile, not emailed separately. They must come from people other than the mentor, so they need soliciting well before March.
- A Sponsor (mentor) who is a tenured, tenure-track or equivalent scientist at a New Jersey Qualifying Research Institution; Co-Sponsors permitted and encouraged where useful.
- A Sponsor-written personalized training plan, 1–2 pages, co-developed with the fellow. Hard warning: "Submission of identical or substantially similar training plans by a Sponsor is strictly prohibited and may result in removal from funding consideration." A mentor recycling boilerplate across two fellows can sink both.
- An Individual Development Plan (IDP) is "not required" but "strongly encourage[d]".
- NIH-format biosketches (the fellowship biosketch template) for applicant and Sponsor.
- Researcher Qualifications summary.
- One application only: "each applicant shall submit only one well-developed application rather than multiple submissions."
- Multiple fellows may share one Sponsor in a cycle "provided that the Sponsor submits a justification."

Institutional / sign-off attachments (these are on the institution, and are the usual cause of late scrambles): IRS 501(c)(3) determination, annual audit report or audit engagement letter, tax clearance certificate, NJ Charities Registration, organizational letter of support, board of directors/trustees list, proof of nonprofit status, salary policy, budget justification, FFATA certification, disclosures and certifications, additional certifications for research applicants, and suggested reviewers. Travel/telephone/computer-security policies only if the proposal involves those elements.

File naming is prescriptive: each attachment must be prefixed with the grant number, e.g. "COCR27PDF###_Reference form".

Budget specifics for the postdoc award: stipend up to $65,000/yr inclusive of fringe; fringe rate up to 12%; travel up to $1,500/yr with prior NJCCR notification and approval, and "International travel is not allowed"; indirect costs up to 15% inclusive of total budget; supplies/equipment allowed with justification and a quote.

Generative AI: not banned for writing, but the RFA warns PIs "use AI tools at their own risk" citing plagiarism, fabricated citations and falsified information as research misconduct; AI is prohibited for peer reviewers (mirroring NIH NOT-OD-23-149). See RFA Appendix 5.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
This is a fellowship-exclusivity rule, NOT an NIH-style R01/K interaction. There is no prior-K or prior-R01 exclusion here at all. The disqualifier is holding or having accepted ANOTHER postdoctoral fellowship.

WHAT DISQUALIFIES (funder's own words, stated three separate times in the RFA — the redundancy signals they enforce it):
- "Applicants who have already accepted another Postdoctoral Fellowship award are not eligible."
- "Applicants pursuing second fellowship will NOT be supported under this award."
- "Applicants currently holding or who have accepted another postdoctoral fellowship — whether simultaneous or overlapping with any other entity are not eligible to apply."
- Applied across both fellowship mechanisms: "Applicants who have already accepted another Predoctoral and Postdoctoral award are ineligible for NJCCR Fellowship grant."
- Stipend top-ups may not be laundered through another fellowship: "Institutions may supplement stipends; however, such supplements may not come from other full-time fellowship awards or from NJCCR funds."
- Ongoing duty, not just a point-in-time test: "If funding is obtained from another agency, it is the responsibility of the PI and Sponsor to promptly notify the NJCCR" — and for the RFA's own competing-funding case, "If the submitted project has been funded by another organization after submission..." must be reported. Winning a national fellowship between March and July does not quietly coexist with this award; it must be disclosed.

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the half an applicant actually needs):
- Institutional stipend supplementation IS allowed — it simply may not come from another full-time fellowship award or from NJCCR funds. A department topping up to its own postdoc scale is fine.
- Teaching is allowed without seeking permission: "Applicants may serve as a teaching assistant while holding a Postdoctoral Fellowship without special permission."
- Being on a mentor's research grant is not addressed as a bar; the exclusion is written against fellowship awards to the individual, not against the Sponsor's project funding. The binding effort rule is separate: at least 80% of the fellow's time on the cancer research project.
- An alternative route if the fellowship bar catches you: "Postdoctoral Fellows who meet the eligibility criteria may elect to apply for a Pilot Grant if it is the more suitable option." A postdoc already holding another fellowship can therefore still seek NJCCR money via the Pilot Research Grant (up to $100K/2yr) rather than the PRF.
- Co-Sponsors are permitted and encouraged, and multiple fellows may share a Sponsor in one cycle with written justification — so a strong lab is not capped at one applicant.
- Prior UNFUNDED NJCCR applications preserve eligibility and may be resubmitted (see resubmission_note).

Other eligibility gates that are not prior-funding but do exclude: must be at one of ~23 New Jersey Qualifying Research Institutions (RFA Appendix 1); U.S. citizen or permanent resident; PhD/MD/DrPH/DO or equivalent in hand before award activation; no more than five years past the doctorate at the commencement of the fellowship (note: measured at fellowship start, not at submission — "Applicants are ineligible if more than five years have passed since the completion of their doctoral degree... at the commencement of the NJCCR fellowship grant").

result.resubmission_note:
One resubmission permitted, and it is reviewed as a fresh competing application with an explicit penalty for ignoring critiques.

Funder's words: "Applicants may submit one resubmission following an unfunded original application. Unfunded applicants are eligible to resubmit in a future grant cycle; however, only one resubmission per original application is permitted. Resubmitted applications must clearly address all reviewer feedback if provided and will be reviewed as a new, competing proposal. Failure to adequately address previous critiques may negatively impact the overall impact score, even if other review criteria were strong."

Practical notes: the submission checklist includes a "Written Response to Reviewer Critiques (if applicable)" component, so the response is a formal required attachment on a resubmission, not just a narrative gesture. Because the cycle is annual, a resubmission costs a full year — and the five-years-post-doctorate clock is measured at fellowship commencement, so a postdoc near the boundary may age out of eligibility between the original and the resubmission. result.next_deadline:
**THE WINDOW IS OPEN RIGHT NOW. It closes Thursday 15 October 2026, 5 p.m. submitter's local time — 27 days from today (2026-09-18).**

AAPF does not use a Deadline Date; it uses a **Submission Window**, which under PAPPG I means "designated periods of time during which proposals will be accepted for review by NSF" — i.e. you may submit on any day inside it, with no penalty for submitting early and no partial credit for being late.

NSF's own opportunity page, raw HTML fetched 2026-09-18, verbatim: "Upcoming due dates | Full proposal 2026 | August 15 2026 - October 15, 2026 - Window | August 15 - October 15, Annually Thereafter | Due by 5pm submitting organization's local time".

Solicitation NSF 22-621 gives the full published series verbatim: "Submission Window Date(s) (due by 5 p.m. submitting organization's local time): August 15, 2022 - October 24, 2022; August 15, 2023 - October 16, 2023; August 15 - October 15, Annually Thereafter".

DURABLE RULE vs DATED INSTANCE — the rule is "August 15 - October 15, Annually Thereafter"; the instance is 15 Aug – 15 Oct 2026. Next cycle on the rule: 15 Aug 2027 (Sun) – 15 Oct 2027 (Fri). Treat 2027 as a projection off the rule, not a published date.

TIME-OF-DAY NUANCE SPECIFIC TO THIS MECHANISM: the 5 p.m. clock is "submitting organization's local time", but for AAPF the candidate *is* the submitting party — the solicitation states the candidate "serves as his/her own SPO and Authorized Organizational Representative". There is no institutional AOR queue to beat, which removes the usual 3–10 business-day internal deadline. (The local-time reading follows from the individual being the submitter; NSF does not spell that out in so many words.)

DRIFT CHECK, 2026-09-18: the AAPF Updates page (https://www.nsf.gov/funding/opportunities/aapf-nsf-astronomy-astrophysics-postdoctoral-fellowships/updates) carries NO notice — no cancellation, pause, or deadline change. NSF 22-621 is still the live solicitation (page metadata "pubnum: 22-621", no archive flag). Positive evidence the competition is actually running, not just posted: NSF's awards API returns 10 AAPF awards issued May 2026 from the FY2026 cycle (e.g. award 2602368, 07 May 2026, $330,000).
result.loi_deadline:
Not applicable. NSF 22-621 states verbatim: "Letters of Intent: Not required" and "Preliminary Proposal Submission: Not required". There is no pre-proposal, no concept outline, and no staged timeline — the full proposal inside the window is the only submission event.

IMPORTANT ADJACENT POINT, because this is where people assume a hidden second deadline: AAPF requires letters, but **they are not referee-submitted and have no separate due date**. The host institution letter(s) and letters of collaboration are uploaded by the candidate as components of the proposal itself ("Other Documents: The following documents indicated as 'MAY BE REQUIRED' in Research.gov are required components of an AAPF proposal: Host Institution Letter and Letters of Collaboration"). There is no reference-letter portal and no letter-writer deadline — the words "reference letter" do not appear anywhere in the solicitation (verified by grep over the full fetched text; only two occurrences of "referen*" exist, both unrelated). This is the opposite of GRFP, where reference letters are due three days *before* the applicant deadline. Your letters are your own upload, so the real long-lead item is your mentor's and department chair's calendar, not NSF's.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
BOTH HALVES. AAPF has no prior-award exclusion at all in the NIH sense — nothing about having held research funding disqualifies you. The binding limits are a lifetime competition cap and a concurrency rule that bites at tenure, not at application.

**WHAT DISQUALIFIES / CONFLICTS**
1. Lifetime competition cap (verbatim): "Each proposer may submit only one AAPF proposal per annual competition. In addition, a proposer may not participate in more than two AAPF competitions." Two reviewed attempts, ever.
2. Concurrent holding, during tenure (verbatim): "No additional appointment or fellowship may be held during the period of the fellowship." And: "No other remuneration from any source may be accepted during the period of the fellowship without permission from the cognizant NSF Program Officer." You cannot stack AAPF with another named postdoctoral fellowship.
3. No renewal (verbatim): "Fellowships cannot be renewed."
4. Host-institution conflict — an *institutional* exclusion people miss: "National centers, facilities, sites, or institutes funded by other federal agencies, such as NASA or the U.S. Department of Energy, are ineligible as host institutions for the NSF AAPF Program." A NASA-center or DOE-lab host kills an otherwise eligible application. NSF-funded centers and NSF-operated international sites (ALMA, CTIO, Gemini South are named) ARE eligible.
5. The 5-year clock: doctorate "within five (5) years prior to the proposal submission deadline".

**WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY**
1. Withdrawal or return is free (verbatim): "Proposals that are not reviewed (i.e., withdrawn before review or returned without review) do not count toward the two-competition limit." So a withdrawal before review costs you nothing against the cap, while a compliance failure that still gets reviewed does. Under PAPPG you may withdraw "at any time before a funding recommendation is made".
2. Currently holding a postdoc job or another fellowship does NOT bar you from applying. Read the text precisely: the prohibition is on holding another appointment "during the period of the fellowship" / "during the fellowship tenure" — it is a condition of tenure, not a condition of eligibility. You apply while employed, then resolve the overlap if you win.
3. The remuneration bar is waivable, not absolute — "without permission from the cognizant NSF Program Officer" is a live route; ask Louise Edwards rather than assuming a conflict is fatal.
4. Not having the PhD yet is fine: eligible if you "will complete the doctoral degree by 1 October following the proposal deadline". Certification of completion is required before funds are released, not before applying.
5. No prior-NSF-funding exclusion of any kind. Having been funded by NSF, or being on an NSF grant now, is not mentioned as a bar.
6. No institutional cap competing against you (verbatim): "There is no limit on the number of candidates or fellows that an organization may host." You are not competing against colleagues for an institutional slot, and there is no internal nomination round.
7. Multiple hosts are allowed — you may hold it "concurrently or sequentially at more than one institution", with a host letter from each.
result.review_to_award:
**Materially faster and far more predictable than the NSF six-month norm — this is a fixed annual calendar, not a rolling queue.**

- Submission closes 15 October.
- Notification (verbatim): "Successful proposers will be notified on or about 1 February following the proposal submission deadline." That is roughly 3.5 months from the window close, against NSF's agency-wide "up to six months". Because the window is fixed and annual, you know the answer date before you apply.
- Award issuance runs later than notification, and has slipped: NSF's awards API shows FY2025 AAPF awards issued 12–13 March 2025, and FY2026 awards issued 07–21 May 2026. So notification ≈1 Feb, paperwork and the Division of Grants and Agreements action follow by roughly 6–14 weeks. The March→May shift is observed from award records, not NSF policy — plausibly the FY2026 appropriations lapse, but I did not find NSF saying so.
- After notification (verbatim): successful proposers "will be contacted by NSF and asked to provide additional information, such as completing acceptance forms and starting certificates, before starting their fellowship tenure."
- Latest possible start (verbatim): "Fellowship tenure must begin on or before 1 October following the proposal submission deadline." So the outer envelope is submit 15 Oct 2026 → know by ~1 Feb 2027 → must be started by 1 Oct 2027. A start date is requested on the Cover Sheet, so you can propose earlier.
- Tenure shape: up to 36 months of support at $110,000/yr, but "The total duration of the fellowship may not exceed 48 months" — the 36 months of money can be spread across a 48-month envelope, and "Interruptions in tenure of up to 12 months or extensions without additional cost to NSF require approval of the cognizant NSF Program Officer." Paid leave including parental/family leave is accommodated but "cannot be used to increase the level of the Fellow's salary support beyond 36 months."

PLANNING CONSEQUENCE for a final-year PhD student: the 15 Oct 2026 window aligns with a 1 Feb 2027 answer and a start up to 1 Oct 2027 — it slots cleanly against the standard US astronomy postdoc job cycle rather than against it.
result.submission_requirements:
**The single biggest deviation: YOU submit, not your institution.** Verbatim: "Fellowship proposals must be submitted by the Fellowship candidate, not by the Fellowship candidate's current or proposed organizational Sponsored Projects Office (SPO). The Fellowship candidate serves as his/her own SPO and Authorized Organizational Representative (AOR)… the Fellowship candidate, serving as the SPO/AOR must electronically sign and submit the proposal using the Sign and Submit button in Research.gov." Every piece of the funder-wide "your research office submits, allow 3–10 business days internally" advice is void here.

**REGISTRATION (do this first, it is the real long-lead item)**: "Before starting proposal preparation, the proposer must be registered as an individual." Register as an *unaffiliated individual* at https://www.research.gov/accountmgmt/assets/welcomeunaffiliated.html. Grants.gov is also accepted, but "if submitting via Grants.gov, you must also obtain an NSF ID in Research.gov." Set-up path: "Prepare New Full Proposal" → select "I am a Postdoctoral Scholar (Postdoctoral Fellowship Proposals)" → search this solicitation in Step 1. You are auto-designated PI.

**DEVIATIONS FROM THE PAPPG NORM (the solicitation takes precedence where they conflict):**
- **Project Description: 10 pages, not 15.** "must be no more than ten (10) single-spaced pages in length". Must contain three things: a research AND education plan "articulated to a level of detail suitable for an NSF grant proposal"; "a detailed justification for the choice of host institution(s)" naming collaborating scientists, educational mentors, facilities and resources; and "a description of the proposer's long term career goals and role of this postdoctoral experience in achieving them." A separate "Broader Impacts" header on its own line is mandatory.
- **Project Summary: 1 page, with an extra requirement** — "The Overview section of the Project Summary must also identify the proposed scientific mentor(s) and the proposed host institution(s)."
- **Title must be prefixed exactly**: "Postdoctoral Fellowship: AAPF:" then your descriptive title.
- **Budget is pre-populated and read-only** ($75,000 stipend + $35,000 fellowship allowance). "An annual budget must be submitted for each of the three years of the fellowship support and the budgets must be identical." Grants.gov users put the stipend on line E.2 and the allowance on E.5 as Participant Support, participants = 1, "No other budget lines should be used."
- **Budget Justification is replaced by a placeholder**: "Upload a document that states 'A Budget Justification is not required for an AAPF proposal'."
- **Postdoctoral Mentoring Plan: omit it.** "A Postdoctoral Mentoring Plan is not applicable to an AAPF proposal and should not be included."
- **Mentor documents: omit them.** "Neither the Biographical Sketch nor the Collaborators and Other Affiliations Information are required for the scientific mentor as part of an AAPF proposal, so please do not include these documents." The mentor is instead named via Personnel Documents → "Add Mentor/Advisor" using their NSF ID or email.
- **Your own COA Table 4 is truncated**: "you may list only the first three (3) co-authors." Tables 1, 2, 3 and 5 are unchanged — a real relief for anyone from a large collaboration.
- **Cover Sheet**: a requested start date is required; duration is pre-populated read-only; Primary Place of Performance = host institution.

**REQUIRED LETTERS — the make-or-break component, and the one with a distinctive tone rule:**
- **Host institution letter from EACH proposed host**, "signed by both the department chair (or equivalent) and the proposed scientific mentor." Must affirm: your proposal "has been read and approved by the proposed scientific mentor(s)"; adequate facilities and support; that your teaching/education plan "is aligned with the institution's educational plans and goals, including a description of how any proposed course or seminar will complement existing curricula"; and that you "will be fully integrated into the educational and research activities of the host institution." It should also discuss the mentor's role in your professional development and the training opportunities available.
- **CRITICAL TONE RULE — this is not a recommendation letter**: "Letters of support will not be considered. A host institution letter should not reflect a letter of support and should make no subjective statements regarding either the proposer or the proposed research and education plan." Give your chair and mentor this sentence verbatim; praise-style letters are the classic AAPF own-goal.
- **Letters of collaboration** are "required from major institutional partners such as educational centers or programs that are critical for conducting the proposed educational activities", signed by both the educational mentor/collaborator and the partner institution's director.

**STILL REQUIRED, INHERITED FROM THE PAPPG**: "Proposals must include all of the required sections of a full research proposal submitted to NSF as specified in Chapter II.C.2 of the PAPPG." So your own Biographical Sketch and Current & Pending (Other) Support via **SciENcv** (Common Form v.2024-1), References Cited, Synergistic Activities, Facilities, and the **Data Management and Sharing Plan** — the last of which is now the Research.gov webform, not a PDF upload, since 27 April 2026. Reviewers are explicitly told to look at it: "reviewers will also be asked to review the Data Management Plan and the Postdoctoral Researcher Mentoring Plan, as appropriate."

**PAGE-LIMIT ENFORCEMENT**: "All page limitations include pictures, figures, tables, graphics, etc." and "Proposals that do not conform to the requirements will not be accepted or will be returned without review." Standard PAPPG fonts/margins apply.

**EXTRA REVIEW CRITERIA beyond Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts**: "Qualifications of the candidate and his/her potential for continued professional growth and leadership in the field; Qualifications and suitability of the proposed host institution(s) and the scientific and educational collaborati[ons]…". The host-choice justification is scored, not decorative. NSF also signals appetite for change of direction: "Proposers are encouraged to approach the fellowships as opportunities to broaden their experience with research that moves beyond their previous research focus."

NOT MENTIONED ANYWHERE IN THE SOLICITATION: SAM.gov, UEI, cost sharing for the individual. See unresolved.
result.resubmission_note:
The NSF-wide rule applies — there is no A1, no rebuttal section, and a resubmission is treated as a brand-new proposal ("A declined proposal may be resubmitted, but only after it has undergone substantial revision"; "The Foundation will treat the revised proposal as a new proposal"; a resubmission that "has not clearly taken into account the major comments or concerns resulting from the prior NSF review may be returned without review").

**BUT AAPF puts a hard ceiling on top of it that the agency-wide rule does not have: "a proposer may not participate in more than two AAPF competitions."** In practice you get one application and one resubmission, lifetime — and the 5-year post-PhD clock usually closes the door anyway. Budget your two shots deliberately rather than firing one off early.

The strategic asymmetry is sharp here: "Proposals that are not reviewed (i.e., withdrawn before review or returned without review) do not count toward the two-competition limit." A withdrawal before review is free; a proposal that goes to review and fails costs you half your lifetime allowance. If you realise in late September that the package is weak, withdrawing is genuinely cheaper than submitting.

Because there is no space to answer reviewers, the working method is the NSF-wide one: get your reviews through Research.gov after the ~1 Feb notification, then talk to the Program Officer about what the panel actually meant before rewriting, and fold the answers into the Project Description narrative itself. With a fixed annual window, a resubmission means the following 15 October.

Formal reconsideration exists but is about process, not science, and is rarely relevant here: request within 90 days of declination, answered within 45 days.
result.program_officer_contact:
**Named, single, and current: Louise O. Edwards — loedward@nsf.gov — 703-292-7597 — NSF Directorate for Mathematical and Physical Sciences (MPS), Division of Astronomical Sciences (AST).**

Confirmed twice on 2026-09-18: in the NSF 22-621 Agency Contacts section ("General inquiries regarding this program should be made to: Louise O. Edwards, telephone: (703) 292-7597, email: loedward@nsf.gov") and independently in the "Program contacts" table on the live opportunity page. The independent confirmation matters because the solicitation carries the standard caveat: "Please note that the program contact information is current at the time of publishing. See program website for any updates to the points of contact." NSF 22-621 dates from 2022, so a stale-rotator risk existed — the live page rules it out.

**Pre-submission contact is expected and explicitly invited.** NSF's own guidance: "Anyone can reach out to an NSF program officer—at any stage of their career, no matter their institution." PAPPG: "Before formal submission, the proposal may be discussed with appropriate NSF program staff."

WHAT IS WORTH ASKING FOR *THIS* MECHANISM SPECIFICALLY — the generic "is this in scope?" question matters less here, because AAPF takes "any area of astronomy or astrophysics" and there is no routing puzzle between divisions. The high-value AAPF questions are instead:
1. **Host eligibility**, before you invest in a relationship — is this specific centre, observatory or non-profit an eligible host? The NASA/DOE exclusion is the trap, and edge cases (joint institutes, NSF-operated international sites) are exactly what the PO can settle in one email.
2. **The concurrency waiver** — if you hold or are offered another fellowship or any other remuneration, the PO is the named authority who can permit it ("without permission from the cognizant NSF Program Officer").
3. **Tenure interruptions and extensions**, which require PO approval, including the up-to-12-month interruption and no-cost extensions.
4. After a declination — what the panel meant, and whether to spend your second and final competition.

Note the timing: contact her now, in the open window, not on 14 October. Also expect the NSF-wide reality — "Don't be discouraged if you don't get a reply initially, and try reaching out again later." Program virtual office hours and webinars are listed at https://www.nsf.gov/events. Research.gov and Grants.gov mechanics go to the help desks instead (Research.gov Help Desk 1-800-673-6188, rgov@nsf.gov) — with no sponsored projects office behind you, that help desk is your submission support.
result.examples_or_samples:
**There is an unusually clean recipe for this mechanism, because AAPF award titles are forced into a fixed prefix.** The solicitation requires every proposal title to begin "Postdoctoral Fellowship: AAPF:", so every funded award is trivially findable.

1. **NSF Award Search — https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/** — search the exact phrase "Postdoctoral Fellowship: AAPF". Every hit is a funded AAPF abstract, with the fellow's name, host institution, amount, dates and cognizant program officer.
2. **Machine-readable route, verified working on 2026-09-18** (no login, returns full abstract text):
   `https://api.nsf.gov/services/v1/awards.json?keyword=%22Postdoctoral+Fellowship%3A+AAPF%22&printFields=id,title,abstractText,date,pdPIName&rpp=25`
   Or pull the whole programme with `fundProgramName="NSF ASTRON & ASTROPHY PSTDC FE"` (NSF program element code **160900**, MPS/AST). This returned 10 FY2026 awards issued May 2026 and FY2025 awards issued March 2025 — a directly usable corpus of recent winning abstracts.
3. **What the abstracts teach you that the solicitation cannot**: each one is written in two registers — a public-facing paragraph and a technical paragraph — and each names a *specific* education/outreach activity tied to the host. A real FY2026 example (award 2602368): a fellow at NRAO pairing ALMA thermophysical mapping of Ceres with outreach "to create engaging, edifying, and friendly astronomical outreach events for the residents" of nearby elder-living facilities. Reading 15–20 of these is the fastest way to calibrate how concrete the Broader Impacts half of an AAPF is expected to be — it is half the proposal, not a paragraph.
4. **Full funded proposals: FOIA only.** NSF releases awarded proposals with personal and proprietary material removed, notifying the institution and PI first; start at https://www.nsf.gov/policies/foia. Weeks to months, but it is the only route to a complete funded AAPF narrative.
5. **Reviews and panel summaries: not obtainable by anyone but the PI** — FOIA-exempt. You see your own through Research.gov after the ~1 Feb notification. There is no AAPF equivalent of an NIH summary-statement library.
6. **Mentor and department first.** Because AAPF requires a host institution letter co-signed by your prospective mentor and their chair, your mentor is very likely to have hosted or reviewed an AAPF before. Asking a recent AAPF fellow (findable by name from step 1 — search your target institution) for their funded Project Description is the fastest practical route, and past fellows in astronomy are generally willing.

CAVEAT: unlike GRFP, which has well-known community archives of successful essays, I could not verify any public archive of successful AAPF Project Descriptions — see unresolved.
result.deadline_pattern: Annual **Submission Window** (not a Deadline Date): "August 15 - October 15, Annually Thereafter", closing at 5 p.m. submitting organization's local time. A two-month window each autumn, with the decision landing "on or about 1 February" following and tenure required to begin "on or before 1 October following the proposal submission deadline." Historical instances published in NSF 22-621: 15 Aug–24 Oct 2022; 15 Aug–16 Oct 2023; then the standing 15 Aug–15 Oct rule. Because it is a window rather than a deadline, submitting in August carries no disadvantage and no advantage — but it does remove the risk of a Research.gov problem on the final afternoon, which matters more than usual here because you are your own AOR with no research office to escalate for you.

Funded ABSTRACTS are fully verified and abundant (see examples field); only full narratives are unconfirmed.
