result.program_name: NSF GOALI - Grant Opportunities for Academic Liaison with Industry
result.next_deadline:
GOALI HAS NO DEADLINE OF ITS OWN — it inherits the host opportunity's. PAPPG 24-1 Ch. II.F.5, verbatim: "GOALI is not a separate program; GOALI proposals must be submitted to an active NSF funding opportunity and must be submitted in accordance with the deadlines specified therein." So the durable rule is: pick the host program first, then the deadline is whatever that solicitation says.

That rule is not a dodge — for an applicant it is usually GOOD news, because the largest GOALI host solicitations are no-deadline. Live dated snapshots, all checked 2026-09-18 on NSF's own solicitation pages (all full proposals due "by 5 p.m. submitting organization's local time"):

1. MPS Chemistry Research Programs, NSF 26-519 (posted 17 Aug 2026; replaces NSF 22-605/22-606) — "Proposals Accepted Anytime" / "Full proposals are accepted anytime starting September 1, 2026." OPEN NOW. Covers nine disciplinary chemistry programs (CAT, SYN, CMI, CSD, CTMC, CMFP, MSN, CLP, CSS). GOALI named explicitly as a welcome special category.
2. MPS Materials Research Programs, NSF 26-521 (posted 17 Aug 2026) — "Proposals Accepted Anytime", with a scheduling tip in the Program Description: submit between 15 June and 15 April, since proposals in that window "may be processed faster than those submitted outside this window due to fiscal year timing." GOALI named as an accepted proposal type.
3. EFRI Wave-Based Computing, NSF 26-524 (posted 17 Aug 2026) — the dated counter-example: mandatory Concept Outline by 19 Nov 2026 (FY2027 cycle) or 16 Nov 2027 (FY2028), then Full Proposal Deadline 11 Feb 2027 / 10 Feb 2028. Solicitation: "NSF GOALI proposals (PAPPG Chapter II.F.5) provide one mechanism for academia-industry collaboration."

NSF's funding search (https://www.nsf.gov/funding/opportunities?query=GOALI) returned 14 CURRENT opportunities naming GOALI on 2026-09-18 — mostly the MPS Chemistry and MPS Materials programs plus EFRI-WBC and SBE's Science of Organizations. Most carry no "next required due date" at all.

Mechanism is demonstrably live: NSF's awards API (keyword=GOALI) returns awards dated through 18 Aug 2026, across CHE (Chemical Catalysis, Chemical Synthesis, Chemical Measurement), CMMI (Advanced Manufacturing, Dynamics & Control, Infrastructure Systems), CBET (Fluid Dynamics, Interfacial Engineering), ECCS (Circuits and Systems) and CISE.
result.deadline_pattern: Inherited, not intrinsic. Three possible shapes depending on host: (a) "Proposals Accepted Anytime" — the common case for the consolidated MPS Chemistry (NSF 26-519) and MPS Materials (NSF 26-521) solicitations that host most GOALI chemistry/materials awards; (b) a hard Full Proposal Deadline, e.g. EFRI-WBC 11 Feb 2027; (c) a Target Date. Time of day follows the NSF norm: 5 p.m. submitting organization's local time. The GOALI supplement route has no deadline at all, only a lead-time rule (see review_to_award).
result.loi_deadline:
No LOI or preliminary proposal is imposed by GOALI itself, and the two biggest hosts impose none either — NSF 26-519 and NSF 26-521 both state "Letters of Intent: Not required" and "Preliminary Proposal Submission: Not required".

Two caveats that function like a pre-stage:
1. GOALI imposes a MANDATORY pre-submission conversation (PAPPG II.F.5): the proposer "must contact the cognizant NSF Program Officer listed in the relevant funding opportunity prior to submission." No form, no date — but it is worded as a requirement, not an encouragement.
2. A host opportunity can add a real gated pre-stage. EFRI-WBC (NSF 26-524) is the live example: "Each prospective Principal Investigator (PI) interested in submitting a proposal to the EFRI Wave-Based Computing solicitation must submit a Concept Outline via email to EFRI2027-2028@nsf.gov by November 19, 2026 for proposal submission for the Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 cycle or by November 16, 2027 for proposal submission for the FY 2028 cycle." That is ~12 weeks before the 11 Feb 2027 full-proposal deadline — a genuine timeline trap for anyone who only reads the full-proposal date.
result.review_to_award:
Full-proposal route: same as the NSF norm (merit review, PO recommendation, DGA decision within ~30 days of the division recommendation, NSF's six-month notification commitment, ~6-9 months to money). Two GOALI-specific deviations:

1. AN EXTRA PRE-AWARD GATE THAT CAN DELAY THE AWARD AFTER IT IS WON. PAPPG II.F.5(a)(iv): "A signed IHE-industry agreement on IP (including publication and patent rights) must be submitted prior to issuance of an award." NSF disclaims any role — "NSF is responsible neither for the agreement reached nor the IP information exchanged between the institution of higher education and the industrial partner." In practice this puts your university tech-transfer/legal office and the company's counsel on the critical path between "recommended for funding" and "award issued". PIs should start the IP conversation at proposal-writing time, not at award time; NSF's own instruction is that partners "should agree in advance as to how intellectual property (IP) rights will be handled."

2. THE SUPPLEMENT ROUTE IS MUCH FASTER AND MAY SKIP EXTERNAL REVIEW ENTIRELY. PAPPG Ch. VI (Supplemental Support): requests "must be signed and submitted by the AOR via use of NSF's electronic systems at least two months prior to the need for the additional funds and must be adequately justified." And decisively: "Program Officers may make decisions regarding whether or not to recommend a small supplement without merit review of the supplemental request. Requests for larger supplements will require external merit review." So adding a GOALI element to an existing award can be a ~2-month PO-level decision rather than a 6-9 month panel cycle. (Honest caveat: that chapter's general framing is about completing "the original scope of work" in "unusual circumstances", while PAPPG II.F.5(b) separately and explicitly authorises GOALI supplements — so confirm scope with the PO, which II.F.5 requires anyway.)

Start dates follow the NSF norm but note PAPPG VI.D.1: "the start date used by NSF is either the 1st or the 15th day of the month."
result.submission_requirements:
Standard PAPPG 24-1 package applies (15-page Project Description, 1-page three-box Project Summary, SciENcv biosketch with no page cap, 2-page DMSP now a Research.gov webform, 5-page budget justification). GOALI ADDS/CHANGES the following — all verbatim from PAPPG 24-1 Ch. II.F.5 unless noted:

ROUTE A — as part of a competitive proposal:
- "At least one industrial co-PI must be listed on the Cover Sheet at the time of submission." (Not a collaborator, not a letter-writer — a co-PI, on the cover sheet, at submission. Cannot be added later.)
- "The IHE-industry interaction should be described in the Project Description".
- GOALI-INDUSTRIAL PI CONFIRMATION LETTER: "A GOALI-Industrial PI Confirmation Letter from the industrial partner that confirms the participation of a co-PI from industry must be submitted with the proposal (if applicable, the letter also must state the degree of industrial participation as well as detail any support that the industry is providing to the institution of higher education). If funds are requested for support of a small business industrial partner, the letter must certify that the small business industry partner meets the small businesses eligibility requirements... All GOALI-related confirmation letters must be uploaded under 'GOALI-Industrial PI Confirmation Letter' in Research.gov. This supplementary documentation will not be counted towards the 15-page Project Description limitation". NOTE: this letter is a real, substantive letter — it is the one place NSF's usual single-sentence Letter-of-Collaboration rule does NOT apply.
- IP AGREEMENT: signed IHE-industry IP agreement (publication and patent rights) required "prior to issuance of an award."
- SINGLE-ORGANIZATION ONLY — a hard deviation from normal NSF practice: "For GOALI collaborative proposals, the proposal must be submitted by a single organization with any collaborators listed as subawards. Collaborative proposals submitted through multiple organizations will not be accepted."
- MANDATORY PRE-SUBMISSION PO CONTACT (see program_officer_contact).
- MECHANICS (from host solicitations, e.g. NSF 26-519): "When submitting, select 'GOALI' as the proposal type. Proposal titles should begin with 'GOALI:' See additional guidance in the PAPPG."

ROUTE B — supplement to an existing NSF award:
"Supplemental funding requests to add GOALI elements to a currently funded NSF research project should be submitted by using the 'Supplemental Funding Request' function in Research.gov. Such requests should include a brief description of the proposed activity, a budget, and a budget justification, in addition to items (ii)-(iv) above. At least one industrial participant must be included in the GOALI activity and must be specified in the GOALI-Industrial PI Confirmation Letter." (i.e. no industrial co-PI on a cover sheet, but the interaction description, confirmation letter and IP agreement all still apply.)

EXTRA REVIEW CRITERIA — write to these, they are additional to Intellectual Merit / Broader Impacts: what new knowledge could lead to innovations addressing societal challenges; "What critical role do the partner(s) bring to the collaboration without which the proposed project cannot be successfully executed?"; anticipated longer-term societal impact; and "What opportunities for industrial experience and training could the proposed GOALI project create for students/postdoctoral scholars/faculty?" Reviewers "may be asked to evaluate the degree and extent to which industry will be involved... and the extent to which students and/or post-doctoral scholars will benefit from the interaction."

MONEY FLOW CONSTRAINT: "The industrial participant cannot use or receive any NSF funds on a GOALI award" except qualifying small businesses; where a small business is funded, "the size of the subaward to the small business partner must not exceed one-third of the total award budget," and "The proposal must disclose any financial interest that the PI, co-PI, other senior/key personnel and/or IHE have in the small business partner and identify appropriate mitigation of any financial conflict of interest."
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
Both halves, because the exclusions here are narrow and the preservations are the actually useful news.

WHAT DISQUALIFIES / BLOCKS:
1. SBIR/STTR interaction (the only true prior-funding bar, and it lands on the COMPANY, not the academic). NSF's GOALI page: "The industrial participant cannot use or receive any NSF funds on a GOALI award, except for small businesses that are not currently funded by the NSF Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) programs and meet these requirements: Must be a small business (fewer than 500 employees) located in the U.S.; At least 50% of the company's equity must be owned by U.S. citizens or permanent residents; All funded work must take place in the U.S. (including work done by consultants and contractors)." So a startup partner currently holding an NSF SBIR/STTR award cannot receive GOALI subaward money. It can still participate as an unfunded partner.
2. Subaward cap: small-business subaward "must not exceed one-third of the total award budget."
3. Undisclosed financial interest: PI/co-PI/senior-key/IHE financial interest in the small business partner must be disclosed and mitigated.
4. HOST-PROGRAM PER-PI PROPOSAL CAPS COUNT GOALI AGAINST YOU — the most-missed item, and it is a pattern across the new consolidated MPS solicitations, not a one-off. NSF 26-519 (Chemistry): "Limit on Number of Proposals per PI or Co-PI: 2... Beginning Sept. 1, 2026, and annually thereafter, no more than two proposals per year may list the same individual as either PI, co-PI or senior/key personnel," applying Sept 1 – Aug 31 across the nine chemistry programs, and "If two proposals list the same individual as PI, co-PI or senior/key personnel, at least one of those proposals must be a multi-investigator or collaborative proposal." Then: "These restrictions also cover the following funding opportunities: Grant Opportunities for Academic Liaison with Industry (GOALI)..." Over the cap: "Any proposals submitted after reaching the two-proposal limit will be returned by NSF without review." NSF 26-521 (Materials) does the same per fiscal year: "This restriction also applies to proposals submitted to the following funding opportunities: Grant Opportunities for Academic Liaison with Industry (GOALI)..."

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY:
1. NO agency-wide prior-funding bar of any kind. There is no NIH-style R01/K interaction, no "you already hold an award so you're out", no career-stage exclusion. GOALI is a proposal TYPE, not a competition with an eligibility gate.
2. HOLDING A CURRENT NSF AWARD IS AN ADVANTAGE, NOT A CONFLICT — it unlocks the cheap route. PAPPG II.F.5(b) exists precisely so you can "add GOALI elements to a currently funded NSF research project" by supplement.
3. SUPPLEMENTS ARE EXEMPT FROM THE PER-PI CAPS. NSF 26-519, listing what is not counted: "The proposal types listed below are not subject to these limitations and may be submitted at any time after consultation with the cognizant NSF program officer: Conferences; Supplemental funding requests to existing grants; EArly-Concept Grants for Exploratory Research (EAGER); Rapid Response Research (RAPID); Research Advanced by Interdisciplinary Science and Engineering (RAISE)." So a GOALI supplement does NOT consume one of your two annual chemistry slots, while a full GOALI proposal does. For an early-career PI with one award already running, that is the single highest-leverage fact in this record.
4. A LARGE INDUSTRY PARTNER RECEIVING NO NSF MONEY IS THE NORMAL CASE, not a disqualification — big-company co-PIs participate unfunded, and no SBIR/STTR test applies to them (that test only gates small businesses seeking subaward funds).
5. Faculty associates are uncapped under NSF 26-521: "There are no such limits for faculty associates, as defined in PAPPG Exhibit II-3.A.2."
6. NSF 26-519 sets "Who May Serve as PI: There are no restrictions or limits" and "Limit on Number of Proposals per Organization: There are no restrictions or limits."
result.program_officer_contact:
Two distinct routes, and you need both.

1. MECHANISM-LEVEL (for "is GOALI the right vehicle?"): NSF's ENG GOALI page, verbatim — "Questions about NSF's GOALI program can be emailed to the lead program director, Prakash Balan (pbalan@nsf.gov)." (https://www.nsf.gov/eng/goali, checked 2026-09-18, live page, not the archived NSF 10-580 synopsis.)

2. PER-PROPOSAL, AND MANDATORY (for "will you take this proposal?"): PAPPG 24-1 II.F.5 — "A proposer interested in submitting a GOALI proposal or a GOALI supplemental funding request to an existing NSF-funded award must contact the cognizant NSF Program Officer listed in the relevant funding opportunity prior to submission."

This is a genuine deviation from the NSF-wide norm. Agency-wide, PO contact is "encouraged" / "may be discussed"; for GOALI it is written as "must contact... prior to submission". Treat it as a required step, not networking. The relevant PO is the one named in the HOST solicitation (each opportunity lists cognizant POs by name and email), not Balan — Balan is the cross-cutting owner of the GOALI mechanism.

Because most GOALI hosts are no-deadline, the PO conversation is effectively the scheduling event: there is no date forcing you, so the exchange that establishes scope-fit is what tells you when to submit. Useful additions: host-program webinars and office hours (EFRI-WBC, for instance, states EFMA "will host a webinar in October 2026 to discuss the EFRI FY 2027/2028 solicitation and to answer questions"), and NSF's general guidance at https://www.nsf.gov/science-matters/nsf-101-5-tips-how-work-nsf-program-officer ("Anyone can reach out to an NSF program officer—at any stage of their career, no matter their institution.").
result.examples_or_samples:
Unusually good for a mechanism with no solicitation of its own, because GOALI awards are tagged and titled.

1. BEST ROUTE — NSF's own pre-built query. The ENG GOALI page links "Recent GOALI awards" to NSF Award Search filtered on PROGRAM REFERENCE CODE 1504 (= GOALI): https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/advancedSearchResult?ProgRefCode=1504&BooleanRef=All&ActiveAwards=true — a durable, funder-maintained list of active GOALI awards. Use ProgRefCode 1504 in NSF Award Search advanced search to reproduce it.
2. TITLE PREFIX MAKES KEYWORD SEARCH WORK — funded GOALI award titles begin "GOALI:" (the solicitations require it: "Proposal titles should begin with 'GOALI:'"). A plain keyword search for GOALI at https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/ returns public abstracts with amount, dates, awardee and the cognizant program officer's name.
3. VERIFIED LIVE 2026-09-18 via NSF's public awards API (https://api.nsf.gov/services/v1/awards.json?keyword=GOALI): awards dated through 18 Aug 2026 at Utah, Michigan, Johns Hopkins, Lehigh, Chicago, Boston College, Minnesota, Ohio State, Iowa State, UCF, Florida, UT Austin and others, spanning Chemical Catalysis, Chemical Synthesis, Chemical Measurement, Advanced Manufacturing, Dynamics & Control, Infrastructure Systems, Fluid Dynamics, Interfacial Engineering, Circuits and Systems and Software & Hardware Foundations. Reading 15-20 of these abstracts is the fastest way to see what an industry-partnered NSF project actually looks like AND to identify the PO to email (step 1 of the mandatory pre-submission contact).
4. FULL FUNDED PROPOSALS — only via FOIA, redacted (NSF-wide route, https://www.nsf.gov/policies/foia). Reviews and panel summaries are FOIA-exempt; you see reviews only of your own proposals, via Research.gov.
5. NO NSF-published annotated GOALI sample narrative was found (see unresolved). The practical substitute is your institution's research development office, which often holds internal copies of funded proposals from your own faculty — worth asking directly. The GOALI-Industrial PI Confirmation Letter in particular has no published template, so ask the PO and your sponsored projects office for the format they have seen accepted.
result.resubmission_note:
Agency-wide NSF rule applies unchanged: a declined GOALI proposal "may be resubmitted, but only after it has undergone substantial revision," is treated as a NEW proposal, and may be returned without review if it "has not clearly taken into account the major comments or concerns resulting from the prior NSF review." No A1 designation, no cap, no window.

MECHANISM-SPECIFIC OVERLAY: the host program's per-PI submission cap is what actually limits you, not a resubmission rule. NSF 26-519 (Chemistry): "Declined proposals can be resubmitted in the same one-year period in which they were submitted, if major revisions are made and the annual submission limit described above has not been exceeded. A resubmitted proposal that has not addressed reviewers' and/or program officers' major comments or concerns may be returned by NSF without review". So a resubmission consumes one of your two annual slots — practical consequence: in a capped host program, a fast weak resubmission costs more than it does at NSF generally. Because there is no rebuttal section anywhere in NSF, work the panel's concerns into the Project Description narrative, and use the mandatory PO contact (which GOALI requires again for the resubmission) to find out what the panel actually meant.
unresolved: No page limit or template is published for the GOALI-Industrial PI Confirmation Letter. PAPPG says only that it is excluded from the 15-page Project Description limit and lists what it must state; it does not cap its length or give a format. Not found on NSF's site.

Whether a CAREER proposal may carry the GOALI designation is not established. CAREER was not among the 14 current GOALI-mentioning opportunities in NSF's funding search, but absence from that index is not proof of exclusion. Would need the CAREER solicitation (NSF 22-586) read directly.

Deadline status of the ENG core programs (CBET, CMMI, ECCS) was NOT individually verified. NSF's ENG division page at https://www.nsf.gov/eng/cmmi states nothing about deadlines or accepted-anytime status, and ENG core programs did not surface in the GOALI keyword search of current opportunities — yet the awards API shows many 2026 GOALI awards flowing through CMMI, CBET and ECCS programs. So GOALI clearly runs through ENG; the specific ENG host opportunities and their dates remain to be pinned down.

NSF 12-513 (named in the existing row as the successor to archived NSF 10-580) returned HTTP 404 at both https://www.nsf.gov/pubs/2012/nsf12513/nsf12513.htm and .jsp. This is a tooling/URL fact, not evidence of termination — GOALI guidance has simply migrated into the PAPPG (Ch. II.F.5) and NSF no longer maintains a standalone GOALI solicitation. Recommend source_url be repointed to https://www.nsf.gov/policies/pappg/24-1/ch-2-proposal-preparation#ch2F5 (primary) with https://www.nsf.gov/eng/goali as the plain-language landing page.

No NSF-published annotated or sample GOALI proposal narrative was found. Only public abstracts (Award Search) and FOIA-redacted full proposals are available; there is no GOALI equivalent of the community GRFP essay archives.

Exact scope boundary for GOALI supplements is ambiguous in NSF's own text: PAPPG II.F.5(b) explicitly authorises supplements to ADD GOALI elements, while the general Supplemental Support section in Ch. VI frames supplements as for completing 'the original scope of work' in 'unusual circumstances'. The chapter itself concedes that for special programs 'the guidance in this section may not be applicable.' Resolve with the cognizant PO.

WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted before research began (200/200 used), so no search index was consulted. Every fact above comes from a direct fetch or rendered browser read of an nsf.gov page or NSF's public awards API — no secondary or third-party sources were used, and no claim here depends on a search index.

result.program_name: NSF Graduate Research Fellowship Program (GRFP)
result.next_deadline:
DATED. FY2027 competition, solicitation NSF 26-526. All times 8:00 p.m. Eastern Time. Verbatim from the solicitation deadline table: "October 19, 2026 Life Sciences / October 20, 2026 Computer and Information Science and Engineering; Materials Research; Psychology; Social Sciences / October 22, 2026 Engineering / October 23, 2026 Chemistry; Geosciences; Mathematical Sciences; Physics and Astronomy".

REFERENCE LETTERS ARE A SEPARATE, EARLIER, SINGLE DEADLINE FOR EVERYONE: "Reference letters are due Friday, October 16 by 8:00 p.m. Eastern time" — 3 days before the earliest applicant deadline, 7 before the latest.

CROSS-CHECKED, and the check mattered. NSF's own applicant fact sheet (GRFP-Applicant-Overview.pdf, slide 7) gives an identical table. TOOLING CAVEAT: a plain fetch of the /funding/opportunities/grfp landing page returned a MISALIGNED table — it inserted a spurious "Full proposal" row against 19 Oct, shifted every field down one row, and produced a non-existent "October 26, 2026" deadline. Solicitation and fact sheet agree; the landing-page rendering is the outlier. Do not source the date table from the landing page.

ON THE DATED-DEADLINE QUESTION: for GRFP the specific dates are load-bearing, not a fragile snapshot. This is a one-week staggered window whose fields are individually dated and whose letter gate falls BEFORE the earliest of them. A pattern-only display ("mid-October, annually") cannot tell a chemist she has 4 more days than a life scientist, and cannot warn either that letters were due the previous Friday. Publish the dates; keep the pattern as the fallback when the cycle turns over.
result.deadline_pattern:
Annual, fixed-deadline (NOT one of NSF's "accepted anytime" core programs). Staggered by Major Field of Study across roughly one week in late October, with a single all-fields reference-letter deadline on the preceding Friday. Fellowship year always begins September 1.

TWO DEVIATIONS FROM THE NSF-WIDE NORM:
1. Time of day is 8:00 p.m. EASTERN Time, not the NSF-standard "5 p.m. submitting organization's local time". GRFP is the stated exception; a West Coast applicant loses 3 hours against the NSF norm they may be used to.
2. NSF has no agency-wide due dates and many core programs have none at all — GRFP is the opposite: one hard annual shot, dated, with no target-date or submission-window flexibility and no late acceptance.

Minor wording inconsistency, non-substantive: the solicitation and references page say "Eastern Time"/"Eastern time"; NSF's fact sheet slide says "8 p.m. Eastern Standard Time". Late October is actually EDT. Plan against 8:00 p.m. ET on the stated date.
result.loi_deadline:
No letter of intent or preliminary proposal exists for GRFP — confirmed absent from NSF 26-526, the how-to-apply page and the FAQ. Note also that NSF's Concept Outline machinery (now email-based since the ProSPCT portal was decommissioned 12 May 2025) does NOT apply here; that route is for research proposals, not GRFP.

BUT THERE IS A DE FACTO EARLIER GATE, and it is the single most-missed item in this mechanism: the REFERENCE LETTER DEADLINE, 16 October 2026, 8:00 p.m. ET. It functions exactly as an LOI deadline would on a timeline — it falls before the application deadline, it is outside the applicant's direct control, and missing it is fatal. Two mechanics make it sharper than it looks:
- "Applicants will be unable to submit applications without the required number of reference letters" (references page) — letters gate SUBMISSION, not just review.
- "At least two letters must be received for your application to be reviewed" (FAQ). You must name three writers; you may list up to five; if more than three arrive "the top three will be considered". So the real floor is 2 received, the requested number is 3, and the buffer strategy is to list 4-5.

Practical consequence for any timeline display: show the letter deadline as the applicant's first hard date, roughly 6-8 weeks after they should have asked their writers.
result.review_to_award:
Faster to notification than the NSF norm, and with a FIXED start date rather than a negotiable one.

- Submission: 19-23 Oct 2026.
- Review: online virtual panel, by Major Field of Study. "Applications are reviewed in broad areas of related disciplines based on the Major Fields of Study selected by the applicant."
- Notification: "NSF Graduate Research Fellowship Program applicants will be notified of the outcomes of their applications by early April of the competition year." NSF's applicant deck: "Spring 2027: Fellowship Offers Announced". So about 5-6 months, comfortably inside NSF's 6-month commitment.
- Accept/decline: "May 2027: Acceptance of Award and Declaration of Tenure/Reserve". Awardees must "accept or decline the Fellowship by the deadline indicated in the award notification letter".
- Money: "September 1, 2027: Fellowship Year Begins". FIXED — unlike a standard NSF award, where start dates are negotiable with the Program Officer and normally the first of a month.
- Full arc: ~10.5 months from submission to first stipend.

TWO DATES THAT SIT OUTSIDE THE REVIEW ARC AND CATCH PEOPLE:
- Withdrawal without penalty: "November 15, 2026: Final withdrawal deadline without penalty" (NSF GRFP program page) — about 3 weeks AFTER submission.
- Enrollment condition on undergraduate applicants: "Undergraduate students must apply for graduate schools and be enrolled by September 1, 2027." Winning the fellowship does not help you get into a PhD program in time; the graduate-admissions cycle runs in parallel and must succeed independently.

None of the standard NSF post-decision machinery applies: no Division of Grants and Agreements business review, no Grants and Agreements Officer signature, no 30-day DGA window — the fellowship goes to the individual, not to an institution via an award instrument.
result.submission_requirements:
GRFP deviates from the NSF/PAPPG norm more sharply than any other NSF mechanism. Almost nothing in the funder-wide profile applies.

WHAT DOES NOT APPLY (all confirmed absent): no AOR or sponsored projects office, no institutional sign-off, no SAM.gov registration, no UEI, no Research.gov organizational role assignment, no SciENcv, no biosketch, no Current and Pending Support, no COA, no budget or budget justification, no Project Summary, no Project Description, no Data Management and Sharing Plan, no Facilities/Equipment, no Mentoring Plan, no SAHF plan. The long-lead institutional items in the NSF profile are simply not on this path — which is why a student can decide to apply in September and still make October.

HOW IT IS SUBMITTED: by the student, directly. "The NSF GRFP is awarded to individuals, and applications are submitted directly by the individual to NSF." Separate applicant module at https://www.research.gov/grfp/Login.do. "To access the module, you will need to create a Research.gov account (if you do not already have one)." The module has a preview feature to verify uploaded documents before submitting.

REQUIRED COMPONENTS (solicitation): "Personal Information; Education, Work and Other Experience; Transcript PDFs; Proposed Field of Study; Proposed Graduate Study and Graduate School Information; Personal, Relevant Background, and Future Goals Statement PDF; and Graduate Research Plan Statement PDF; Names and email addresses of at least three reference letter writers".

PAGE LIMITS: Personal, Relevant Background and Future Goals Statement — 3 pages. Graduate Research Plan Statement — 2 pages. CRITICAL DEVIATION: both limits "include all references, citations, charts, figures, images, and lists of publications and presentations". Under the PAPPG norm References Cited has NO page limit; here your bibliography eats your argument. Budget the citations first.

TRANSCRIPTS: "Official undergraduate transcripts are required. Graduate transcripts may be unofficial if the institution does not provide official transcripts for first year, first academic term graduate students." Ordering officials takes institutional lead time — treat as a long-lead item.

REFERENCE LETTERS: name 3, may list up to 5 and rank them; "If more than three reference letters are received, the top three will be considered"; "Two reference letters must be received by NSF"; "At least two letters must be received for your application to be reviewed"; "Family members cannot be reference writers". Writers submit through the NSF Reference Letter System after an invitation from Rgov-No-Reply@nsf.gov — warn writers to whitelist it. Letter format: max 2 pages, PDF, 11-point Times New Roman, signed and on letterhead where possible.

FORMATTING (applies to the applicant's own PDFs): "Arial (not Arial Narrow), Courier New, or Palatino Linotype in 10-point or larger font; Times New Roman or Computer Modern family, 11-point or larger font"; "Use 1" margins on all sides, with no text inside the 1" margins"; "Use no less than single-spacing (approximately 6 lines per inch)"; "PDF format only".

NSF SUPPLIES TEMPLATES — unusual and worth surfacing to any applicant: Personal Statement template (DOCX) and Research Plan template (DOCX) at nsf-gov-resources.nsf.gov. They give compliant structure, not content.

REVIEW CRITERIA, AND HOW THEY BIND THE WRITING: "two equally weighted NSF Merit Review Criteria: Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts. Evidence of Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts should appear throughout the entire NSF GRFP application package." Merit review considerations include "Demonstrated potential for significant achievement in STEM", "a comprehensive approach to review", and balanced consideration of "Educational and research record, leadership, outreach, service activities, future plans, individual competencies, experiences, and other attributes (e.g., creativity, innovation, perseverance)." Note the criteria attach to the PERSON, not to a project — the research plan is evidence of capability, not a funded work plan.

ACCESSIBILITY: "To request accessibility accommodations, please contact the Program at least three (3) weeks before the application deadline."
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
The binding constraint on GRFP is CAREER STAGE AND PRIOR DEGREES, not prior grant funding. Both halves below are from NSF's own current pages.

DISQUALIFYING:
- Any prior graduate or terminal degree, in ANY field: "Individuals who have earned a master's, doctoral or terminal degree in any field" are ineligible. The FAQ is blunt: "If you have a master's degree, you are not eligible." Note "in any field" — an unrelated prior master's (MBA, MA, MPH) disqualifies just as a STEM one does. NOTE FOR THE ROW: the existing eligibility_notes say ineligible if holding a graduate degree "in a GRFP-eligible field" — that is NARROWER than NSF's current wording and understates the bar. Worth correcting.
- Previously accepted a GRF: applicants must have "Never previously accepted a Graduate Research Fellowship."
- "Declined any previously offered Graduate Research Fellowship by the declination deadline (if applicable)."
- Previously applied while enrolled in a graduate degree program — the graduate-stage attempt is once per lifetime, not once per year.
- Second-year and beyond graduate students.
- Prior enrollment in a graduate degree program beyond the permitted first year.
- Current NSF employees: "Not be a current NSF employee."
- Visa holders; foreign institutions.
- CONCURRENT FEDERAL SUPPORT: "An individual may not accept the Graduate Research Fellowship if the individual accepts or is supported by another federal graduate fellowship." This is a choose-one, not a bar on applying — you may apply for NDSEG, DOE CSGF, NIH F31 and GRFP in the same season and must pick if more than one lands. Mirrors the NDSEG row already in the CSV, which states the same interaction from the other side.

WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the half applicants get wrong, and the higher-value half):
- UNLIMITED ATTEMPTS BEFORE GRADUATE ENROLLMENT. Undergraduate seniors and bachelor's holders with no prior graduate enrollment "have no restrictions on the number of times they can apply before enrolling in a graduate degree-granting program." This is the most under-exploited fact in the mechanism: a senior who applies and misses can apply again in a gap year, and again, at no cost to the one graduate-year attempt.
- NON-DEGREE GRADUATE COURSEWORK DOES NOT BURN ELIGIBILITY: applicants must have "completed less than one academic year in a graduate degree program (according to the institution's academic calendar; non-degree coursework must be clearly identified in the transcript and does not count toward this limit)." Post-bacc and non-degree classes are safe — but the transcript must identify them clearly, so check how your registrar codes them.
- First-year graduate students in their first graduate program retain exactly one application, if "less than one academic year completed according to the institution's academic calendar" at the deadline. Caution: "Summer research activities that are part of the graduate degree program (e.g., research credits) will be counted as graduate activities" — a funded summer before Year 1 can push you over.
- Joint bachelor's-master's students get one application and may choose WHICH year to spend it in: "can apply only once in the final undergraduate OR first graduate year of the joint program."
- WITHDRAWAL PROTECTS THE ATTEMPT: NSF's program page lists "November 15, 2026: Final withdrawal deadline without penalty." Withdraw by then and the attempt is not consumed — so a first-year graduate student who submits a weak application has a three-week escape hatch after the deadline. (Sourcing asymmetry worth noting: the "without penalty" framing appears on the GRFP initiatives page; the solicitation and FAQ describe the Withdrawal option in the module but do not spell out the eligibility consequence.)
- NOT A STATED BAR ANYWHERE: prior NSF REU participation, being paid as an RA on someone else's NSF grant, prior non-federal fellowships (Goldwater, institutional, private), or an honorable mention in a previous GRFP competition. None appears as an exclusion on the eligibility page, the FAQ or NSF 26-526. Record as "no stated exclusion found" rather than as affirmative permission.
result.program_officer_contact:
NO NAMED PROGRAM OFFICER, AND NO PROGRAM EMAIL. This is GRFP's sharpest deviation from NSF's funder-wide norm, and getting it wrong wastes an applicant's time.

NSF's agency-wide posture — "Anyone can reach out to an NSF program officer—at any stage of their career, no matter their institution", every opportunity listing its cognizant POs by name and email — DOES NOT TRANSFER TO GRFP. There is no cognizant PO to email, no one-page-summary convention, no pre-submission scope conversation, because there is no scope question to resolve: you pick a Major Field of Study from a fixed list and the field routes your application.

Every contact route NSF actually publishes for GRFP:
- NSF's own applicant deck, slide titled "Program Contacts", lists exactly three and nothing else: "NSF GRFP – Program Information Website: NSF.gov/grfp"; "NSF GRFP Application Module Website: https://www.research.gov/grfp/Login.do"; "NSF IT Service Desk: https://www.research.gov/research-web/content/contactus".
- Solicitation section VIII: "Please note that the program contact information is current at the time of publishing. See program website (https://www.nsf.gov/grfp) for any updates to the points of contact. If you require assistance with the GRFP module or have any questions about processing applications please contact the NSF Service Desk."
- The GRFP Contact Us page yields only the research.gov contact form, NSF's switchboard (703) 292-5111, and the Alexandria address.
- Accessibility is the one substantive route to the program itself: "To request accessibility accommodations, please contact the Program at least three (3) weeks before the application deadline."

OBSERVED MACHINERY CHANGE: nsfgrfp.org — historically the GRFP Operations Center's own site, the source of the info@nsfgrfp.org address and toll-free line that circulate in older advice — now returns 301 Moved Permanently to https://www.nsf.gov/funding/initiatives/grfp. The Operations Center no longer exists as a separate contact surface on the current web presence. Stated as observed; no NSF statement was found announcing its retirement. Treat any older guidance citing info@nsfgrfp.org as stale.

SO WHO SHOULD AN APPLICANT ACTUALLY TALK TO? Since the funder offers no human route, the useful contacts are all local or peer:
1. Reference writers — the only people with a formal role in your application, and the earliest deadline. Approach 6-8 weeks out.
2. Prospective or current PhD advisor — on the Graduate Research Plan's feasibility and framing.
3. Campus fellowships / research development office — many run GRFP-specific workshops and keep local collections of successful applications.
4. Prior GRFP awardees in your field — findable BY NAME via the public awardee list (see examples field), filtered to your field and institution. This is the substitute for the PO conversation and is more useful here than a PO would be.
result.examples_or_samples:
Unusually well served, but NSF hosts NO sample essays — templates and an awardee roster from NSF, real essays from the community.

FROM NSF (structure and rules):
- Personal Statement template (DOCX): https://nsf-gov-resources.nsf.gov/files/GRFP-Personal-Statement-template.docx
- Graduate Research Plan template (DOCX): https://nsf-gov-resources.nsf.gov/files/GRFP-Graduate-Research-Plan-template.docx
- GRFP Application Fact Sheet, 1 page: https://nsf-gov-resources.nsf.gov/files/GRFP-Application-Onepager.pdf — eligibility, benefits, and the post-submission timeline on one page. The best single handout for someone deciding whether to bother.
- GRFP Applicant Overview deck, 12 slides: https://nsf-gov-resources.nsf.gov/files/GRFP-Applicant-Overview.pdf — carries the dated deadline table (slide 7), an eligible/ineligible decision tree (slide 5), the application package list (slide 6), the merit-review slides (9-10) and Program Contacts (11).
- The applicants/resources page explicitly offers no sample essays, no webinars, no recorded sessions, no annotated applications.

PUBLIC AWARDEE ROSTER — the "who to talk to" engine:
- https://www.research.gov/grfp/AwardeeList.do — awardees and honorable mentions, searchable 1952 through 2026, showing Name, Baccalaureate Institution, Field of Study, and Current Institution ("the institutional affiliation of the applicant at the time of GRFP application submission"). The 2026 list carries 2,597 entries. Filter to your field plus your department and you have a list of named, emailable people who won it recently from where you are standing.

COMMUNITY ARCHIVES (third-party; NSF neither hosts nor endorses these):
- Alex Hunter Lang's collection, https://www.alexhunterlang.com/nsf-fellowship — "These are all the essays of recent winners that I could find online", in a sortable/filterable table, still actively soliciting new submissions. IMPORTANT FILTER: the page warns "Remember the format changed starting in 2014!" — the pre-2014 entries are a different application. Use 2014-onward only.
- MIT Broad Communication Lab CommKit, https://mitcommlab.mit.edu/broad/commkit/nsf-research-proposal/ — two downloadable ANNOTATED research statements from successful GRFP applications ("a research statement that was part of an MIT BE graduate student's successful NSF GRFP application"), plus a companion NSF Personal Statement CommKit. Annotation is what makes these more useful than raw essays.
- Campus fellowships offices frequently hold local collections of successful GRFP applications — ask directly rather than assuming none exists.

CALIBRATION FIGURES (useful for deciding whether to apply, both from NSF's own materials): "Estimated Number of Awards: 1,500" (NSF 26-526) against "~Per Competition 12,000+ Applicants" (NSF infographic) — roughly 12-13%. NOTE FOR THE ROW: selectivity currently reads "~2,000 new fellowships awarded per year (est.); official success rate not published". NSF now publishes an estimate of 1,500 and an applicant count, so both halves of that cell can be upgraded and sourced.

NOT OBTAINABLE: reviewer comments and panel materials. The standard NSF release of verbatim unattributed reviews to the PI has no documented GRFP equivalent — the review-process page is silent on applicant feedback (see unresolved).
result.resubmission_note:
GRFP INVERTS THE NSF-WIDE RESUBMISSION RULE. NSF agency-wide has no resubmission object at all — uncapped, no A1, no window, subject only to "A declined proposal may be resubmitted, but only after it has undergone substantial revision." None of that governs here. GRFP rations attempts by CAREER STAGE, and the ration is absolute.

- Before enrolling in a graduate degree program: UNLIMITED applications. A senior may apply, miss, apply again in a gap year, and again.
- Once enrolled: EXACTLY ONE application, in the first year of the first graduate program, once per lifetime.
- Joint bachelor's-master's students: one application total, spendable in either the final undergraduate or first graduate year.
- Second year and beyond: no application at any quality.

STRATEGIC CONSEQUENCE, and it is the opposite of standard NSF advice: at NSF generally you iterate against panel feedback. Here you cannot. Apply every year you are eligible as an undergraduate or unenrolled bachelor's holder — those attempts are free — and treat the single graduate-year attempt as non-renewable. If the graduate-year application is going out weak, "November 15, 2026: Final withdrawal deadline without penalty" preserves it; a withdrawal is cheap and a spent attempt is not. (This mirrors the CAREER logic in the NSF profile, where withdrawal before review does not count against the three-competition limit — but CAREER gives you three tries and GRFP gives a graduate student one.)

Also absent for GRFP: no PAPPG "substantial revision" requirement, no Introduction to Resubmission, no return-without-review-for-ignoring-prior-comments provision, and no documented formal reconsideration or appeal pathway (the 90-day reconsideration / 60-day appeal chain in the NSF profile attaches to declined PROPOSALS, not to fellowship applications). An applicant reapplying as a senior is submitting a genuinely new application to a new panel with no memory of the last one.
unresolved: INTERRUPTION / RETURNING-STUDENT EXCEPTION — NOT FOUND. Older GRFP guidance carried an exception letting applicants with prior graduate study or a prior master's apply if returning after two or more consecutive years away. It does not appear on the current eligibility page, the FAQ, or NSF 26-526 as fetched; the FAQ instead states flatly 'If you have a master's degree, you are not eligible.' I am NOT asserting NSF removed it — only that it is absent from every current page checked. This is the highest-value item to resolve, because it determines eligibility for career-changers and returning students. Recommend a targeted re-check of NSF 26-526 section IV in a rendering browser.

APPLICANT FEEDBACK — the review-process page does not say whether GRFP applicants receive reviewer comments, and if so how or when. Standard NSF proposals get verbatim unattributed reviews released to the PI; no GRFP equivalent was documented. Unknown, not absent.

NUMBER OF REVIEWERS PER APPLICATION — not published. The solicitation says applications 'will be reviewed online by Panel Review' by disciplinary experts but gives no count, unlike the PAPPG's 'three to ten other persons outside NSF' for proposals.

GRFP PROGRAM EMAIL — none found anywhere on nsf.gov or research.gov. The accessibility line says to 'contact the Program' without naming a route. Older third-party advice citing info@nsfgrfp.org should be treated as stale given the nsfgrfp.org redirect.

WEBINARS / OUTREACH EVENTS — could not confirm. https://www.nsf.gov/events?query=grfp returned an EMPTY BODY to a plain fetch (JS-rendered listing). This is a tooling fact and NOT evidence that no GRFP webinars are scheduled for the 2026 cycle. Needs a rendering browser. Worth resolving, since with no program officer to email, webinars would be the only direct funder contact.

LANDING-PAGE DEADLINE TABLE MISALIGNMENT — the /funding/opportunities/grfp landing page rendered a shifted deadline table on fetch (spurious 'Full proposal' row, every field displaced by one, phantom 'October 26, 2026'). Source the table from the solicitation or the applicant fact sheet, which agree. Flagged so no downstream pass re-derives the wrong mapping from the recorded source_url.

WITHDRAWAL 'WITHOUT PENALTY' — the 15 Nov 2026 date and the no-penalty framing come from the GRFP initiatives page; the solicitation and FAQ describe the module's Withdrawal option without stating the eligibility consequence. Single-source; worth a confirming quote before it drives advice.

EST vs ET — the fact sheet slide says '8 p.m. Eastern Standard Time' while the solicitation and references page say 'Eastern Time'. Late October is EDT. Non-substantive, but noted because time-of-day is drift-sensitive.

ROW CORRECTIONS SURFACED (data only, no file modified): (a) eligibility_notes say a disqualifying graduate degree must be 'in a GRFP-eligible field' — NSF's current wording is 'a master's, doctoral or terminal degree in any field', which is broader; (b) selectivity says '~2,000 new fellowships awarded per year (est.); official success rate not published' — NSF 26-526 states 'Estimated Number of Awards: 1,500' and NSF's infographic gives '12,000+ Applicants' per competition, so both halves can now be sourced; (c) design_notes cite 'current solicitation NSF 25-547' — the current one is NSF 26-526 (FY2027).

result.program_name: NVIDIA Graduate Fellowship Program
result.next_deadline: Not found as a dated 2027-2028 deadline — NVIDIA has not published one. As of a live render of https://research.nvidia.com/graduate-fellowships on 2026-09-18 the page still describes the cycle that closed for the 2026-2027 fellowship year and carries the banner "Submissions are now CLOSED". The most recent dated cycle, quoted verbatim, is: student deadline "3pm Pacific Time, September 15, 2025" and recommender deadline "the deadline for recommendation letters is 12noon Pacific Time, September 15, 2025" (letters close 3 hours before the student submission). PATTERN TO PLAN AGAINST: annual, single stage, portal opens over the summer and closes mid-September at 3pm Pacific; decisions "emailed by the end of November"; mandatory internship the following summer; the 9-month fellowship year then runs the academic year after the deadline (a September 2025 application funded the 2026-2027 year). PRACTICAL WATCH POINT: the "Submissions are now CLOSED" line on the funder page is itself the apply control — it is an anchor with an empty href in the live DOM, and it becomes the live submission-portal link when a cycle opens, so that one page is the only thing you need to watch. Note the ambiguity: a mid-September 2026 round for AY2027-2028 would have closed days before this check, and the page shows no trace of one — I could not distinguish "round ran and the page reverted to prior-cycle text" from "next round not yet posted" (WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted and web.archive.org is blocked in this environment, so no index or archive cross-check was possible).
result.deadline_pattern: Annual, single-stage, fixed mid-September close at 3pm Pacific (most recently 15 September 2025), with recommendation letters due 12 noon Pacific the same day. Full applicant timeline for one cycle: portal open over the summer → student deadline mid-September (year Y) → committee review ~8 weeks → notification by end of November (Y) → mandatory in-person NVIDIA summer internship, 3-4 months (summer Y+1) → 9-month fellowship year (academic year Y+1 to Y+2). So a student applying in September is being funded roughly a year later and must be able to give NVIDIA the intervening summer in person.
result.loi_deadline: n/a — no letter of intent, pre-proposal, or institutional nomination/limited-submission stage. The student applies directly through NVIDIA's own submission portal and manages the application themselves: "We are using a Submission Portal in which the student manages their own application." The only pre-deadline dependency is the recommenders, whose letters close 3 hours before the student deadline.
result.review_to_award: Submission to notification: about 10 weeks. Review itself is quoted as "The entire review process usually takes about 8 weeks", and "Notifications of final decisions will be emailed by the end of November" from a 15 September deadline. Review body: a committee "headed by our Chief Scientist, Bill Dally ... comprised of over 80 senior technical staff and managers from research and development groups across the company", reviewing "competitively in several review sessions". Notification to earliest money: NOT the following term — this is the field most applicants get wrong. The award year is the 9-month academic year that starts roughly 12 months after the application, and it cannot start until the internship is done: "If selected for an award, a completed internship at NVIDIA is required before the Fellowship award year can begin." For the cycle that closed 15 Sep 2025: notified end of Nov 2025, internship summer 2026, fellowship year 2026-2027, with eligibility requiring the student "should not be expecting to graduate sooner than May/June 2027". Funds are paid to the university, not the student, so add your institution's own gift/fellowship set-up time on top.
result.submission_requirements: Four components, all uploaded by the student to NVIDIA's portal (verbatim from the funder page): (1) "Research summary/thesis proposal - up to 2 pages, plus bibliography (bibliography does not count toward 2 page maximum for proposal). Be sure to include your name at the top of the proposal." Images are allowed but count against the 2 pages: "Yes - images are fine, as long as all your proposal content -- text and images -- fit into the 2-page limit." (2) "Resume/Curriculum Vitae (CV) including contact information". (3) "Professor nomination letters (2 letters minimum (must include one from thesis advisor), up to 3 letters maximum -- OK to have nomination letters from non-professors, as long as you have one from your thesis advisor/professor)." (4) "Confirmation of availability for an in-person summer internship". DEVIATIONS FROM THE USUAL FEDERAL-STYLE NORM: no biosketch, no budget or budget justification, no data-management plan, no institutional/grants-office sign-off at application, no sponsor or mentoring plan beyond the advisor's letter, and no eRA-style routing — but recommenders are invited from inside the portal and their letters close 3 hours early, so the process fails on advisor lateness rather than on paperwork ("it is the student's responsibility to ensure their letters are received into the system"). There is an opt-in extra: "Applicants may choose to opt-in for an internship evaluation outside of the fellowship (in the event the applicant is not chosen for an award.)" Stated evaluation criteria: student quality (letters of recommendation; GPA and achievements), research quality (results to date, the proposal, publication track record), and relevance to NVIDIA ("How your research might influence the design, performance or use of future GPUs"). Competitive bar, quoted: "Our prior fellowship recipients have had track records of multiple publications in top-tier venues of their fields. To be competitive, you should have at least one strong publication." NVIDIA publishes its own "Helpful Hints" on the same page for both the proposal (state your post-PhD vision, say what you have done so far, name the NVIDIA technologies you use, say what you would want to work on during the 3-4 month internship, mention any past NVIDIA internship) and the recommendation letters (pick recommenders who know you, ask in person before sending the portal request, give at least 2 weeks' notice, confirm they received the portal email within 24 hours, remind at 1 week and 3 days out).
result.prior_funding_conflicts: WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (unusually permissive, and all quoted): repeat awards are allowed — "At this time there is no limit on the number of times you can be awarded the NVIDIA Graduate Fellowship Award. Keep in mind you can only receive one per year!"; a current fellow may reapply — "Yes. You can apply each year you are enrolled full-time until the year before you complete your PhD. You can follow the same guidelines and application process as any new applicant."; no institutional or lab cap — "there is no limit per University nor is there a limit per graduate team provided the research is different and interesting to NVIDIA."; a prior NVIDIA internship is an asset, not a conflict (the hints invite "Have you ever interned with NVIDIA before? If so, let us know what you worked on"); outside part-time work is permitted conditionally — allowed "as long as the work is beneficial to the progress of your PhD, you remain full-time enrolled at your institution, and a conflict of interest does not exist between NVIDIA and the other entity". WHAT RESTRICTS: holding another fellowship is neither automatically allowed nor barred, and NVIDIA makes it a conversation, not a rule — "Whether it is OK to combine the NVIDIA fellowship with another fellowship depends on several factors -- please contact the NVIDIA Graduate Fellowship for details on this matter." Two mechanical limits do the real work when stacking (e.g. with NSF GRFP or a departmental fellowship): the award "is based on the individual student's actual costs of stipend, tuition and mandatory fees" and "Amount of the award cannot exceed stipend, tuition, and mandatory fees" — so another award covering the same line items shrinks what NVIDIA can pay rather than adding to it; and "There may also be university-specific restrictions that pertain", so your own institution's stacking policy can bind before NVIDIA's does. Further award-side conditions: "no overhead or indirect costs are charged to the award"; "Awards are not transferable to another student"; "Awards are issued to the university for disbursement, not directly to the student". HARD BARS (not prior-funding but absolute): "Full-time NVIDIA employees and immediate family of NVIDIA employees cannot participate" / "Students may not be immediate family of a current NVIDIA employee". Eligibility-window bars: must have "already completed their first year of PhD level studies (at the time of application)" and must not expect to graduate before the award year ends. No NIH-style prior-award exclusion (no R01/K analogue) exists for this mechanism.
result.program_officer_contact: No named program officer and no fellowship email address is published. Verified directly against the rendered page's DOM on 2026-09-18: zero mailto links and zero @nvidia.com addresses anywhere on https://research.nvidia.com/graduate-fellowships. NVIDIA nonetheless names a contact route twice in its own words — "please contact the NVIDIA Graduate Fellowship for details on this matter" (fellowship stacking) and "If there is any doubt on the conflict of interest, please check with your NVIDIA Fellowship contact" (outside work) — which in practice means the support/contact channel inside the submission portal, available while a cycle is open, and (for current fellows) the NVIDIA person assigned to you. The only published NVIDIA Research email is researchinquiries@nvidia.com, scoped on https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/research/inquiries/ to "all business inquiries relating to NVIDIA Research" — a fallback, not the fellowship desk. PRE-SUBMISSION CONTACT IS NOT EXPECTED: unlike a federal program officer relationship, nothing on the page invites a pre-application conversation, and the decision body is an 80+ person internal committee under Chief Scientist Bill Dally, not a single officer you can lobby. The person to actually talk to before applying is your thesis advisor (their letter is mandatory and letters are "a heavily-weighted component"), plus any NVIDIA researcher you already collaborate with or interned for.
result.examples_or_samples: No funded application, sample proposal, or annotated abstract is published for this mechanism — NVIDIA releases no reviewer comments and no exemplar text, so treat "no public sample" as the answer. What NVIDIA does give you, and explicitly tells you to use as the benchmark: the annual recipient lists. FAQ, verbatim: "We suggest you look at the list of past recipients and see whether your application is comparable. If so, then go ahead and apply and see where your application falls in the review process compared to all the other applications." Those lists are linked from the programme page and carry names and institutions (the 2026 cohort page names 10 recipients — at Stanford (x4), Georgia Tech, USC, UC San Diego, University of Washington, Harvard, UC Berkeley — plus 4 named finalists at TU Darmstadt, MIT, Max Planck Institute for Informatics and Peking University): https://research.nvidia.com/graduate-fellowships/2026, /2025, /2024 and the archive at https://research.nvidia.com/graduate-fellowships/archive (2002-2023). The workable method is to take a named recipient, read their publication record and lab page, and calibrate your own record against it — that is the only route to "what a winning profile looks like".
