result.deadline_pattern:
Annual, single round, no rolling window and no target-date system at all (a total contrast to DOE SC's three-layer rolling/target-date structure). One hard close per year at a stated minute, Eastern time.

Full annual clock, with the FY2027 cycle instantiated:
- Application opens: 3 Aug 2026, 12:01 AM ET
- Application closes: 30 Oct 2026, 5:00 PM ET (HARD)
- De facto personal deadline for references: whenever YOU submit — references must be in BEFORE your submission (see submission_requirements; this is the single biggest timeline trap in this mechanism)
- Panel review: "late January to early February" 2027 (quoted from the Panelists page)
- Awards announced / awardees published: historically July-early September of the FY year — FY2026 on 3 Sept 2026, FY2025 on 5 Aug 2025, FY2024 on 1 July 2024, FY2020 on 15 July 2020. For FY2027 that implies roughly July-September 2027. PATTERN-DERIVED, not published.
- Stipends begin: September ("NDSEG Fellows typically receive their stipend between the 5th and 10th business day of each month during his/her tenure starting in September").

Practical consequence worth telling an applicant plainly: you submit in late October and you will likely not hear until roughly 9-10 months later, weeks before the money would start. Budget your other funding accordingly.
result.loi_deadline:
Not applicable — no letter of intent, no pre-proposal, no white paper, no encourage/discourage step. Single-stage competition. (This is the sharpest structural deviation from the DOE SC machinery in the brief: there is no PAMS-style pre-application layer and no two-portal confusion.)

The only pre-step is a four-question eligibility screener that doubles as account registration, at https://applyndseg.sysplus.com/Eligibility. It asks exactly four things: (1) "Are you a U.S. Citizens, U.S. Dual Citizen, or U.S. National?" (2) "Have you received or will you receive an Undergraduate Degree prior to the Fellowship Period?" (3) "Are you at or near the beginning (within first 2 years) of your Graduate or doctoral study in Science or Engineering?" (4) "Are you applying to or have been accepted to a graduate or doctoral program within the US to begin during the Fellowship period?" It asks NOTHING about prior or current funding.

THE HIDDEN LONG-LEAD ITEM that functions like an LOI deadline: your references must have submitted before you hit submit. "Your references must complete their recommendations BEFORE you submit your application. Therefore, you need to coordinate with your references to ensure that their recommendations are received prior to your intended submission date." Treat "ask your three referees" as a task due 3-4 weeks before 30 Oct 2026, not a week before.

There are no SAM.gov / UEI / Grants.gov / institutional-AOR registrations of any kind — this is an individual-direct application and your university does not sign off. The only registration is your own portal account.
result.review_to_award:
Long and back-loaded; this differs materially from the DOE SC norm of "within six months of receipt".

1. Submission closes 30 Oct 2026, 5 PM ET. No edits ever afterwards: "You will not be able to make any changes after submission. It is up to you to start a new application for consideration. However, you should notify our office if you plan to do this, so we validate and evaluate the correct application." (There is no PAMS-style withdraw-and-resubmit; the fix is a whole new application plus an email to NDSEG.PMO@sysplus.com.)
2. Completeness gate: "If for any reason an application does not contain all of the required elements, it will not be reviewed. It is the applicant's responsibility to ensure the completeness of his or her application." A redaction failure also kills it here: "Failure to follow this guidance will prevent your application from moving forward in the evaluation process."
3. Panel review, late Jan - early Feb 2027: "Panelist review approximately 20 applications via the DoD NDSEG FM Web Application in late January to early February." Panelists are "a panel of academic experts who have doctoral degrees from the science and engineering discipline of the applicant's proposed advanced degree program", drawn from academia, government and industry (doctorate + 5 years, or master's + 10 years). Panel output is a ranked list.
4. Service selection: "Participating DoD agencies will then select final awardees from the top-ranked applicants. Final selection of fellows will be made by AFRL, ARO, ONR, and other sponsoring DoD agencies (if applicable)." So panel rank is necessary but not sufficient — the sponsoring service picks from the top-ranked pool, which is why the awardee list is broken out by agency.
5. Notification: "Systems Plus will notify successful and unsuccessful applicants within 14 days of the official award." Email only. "Fellows must provide their acceptance soon after receiving their award notification." An institutional hard-copy letter is available on request to NDSEG.PMO@sysplus.com.
6. Observed notification/publication dates: 3 Sept 2026 (FY2026), 5 Aug 2025 (FY2025), 1 July 2024 (FY2024), 15 July 2020 (FY2020).
7. Earliest start: September. Tenure is "a maximum of 36 months during 3 consecutive years"; second- and third-year funds are contingent on the institution certifying satisfactory academic progress.

END-TO-END: roughly 9-11 months from the October deadline to notification, with the award starting within weeks of notification. Implied for FY2027: apply Oct 2026 → panel Jan/Feb 2027 → notified ~July-Sept 2027 → stipend starts Sept 2027.

NO FEEDBACK LOOP: nothing on the site offers reviewer comments, scores, or a summary statement to unsuccessful applicants, and applicants are explicitly barred from chasing "the decision/selection status" with DoD. There is no DOE-style "View Reviews" and no NIH-style summary statement. Declined applicants get an email and nothing more.
result.submission_requirements:
Individual-direct, one portal (https://applyndseg.sysplus.com/), no institutional sign-off, no SAM/UEI/Grants.gov. DoD's own burden estimate for the whole package is "12 hours per response" (OMB Control Number 0701-0154, expiration 31 Aug 2028 — useful evidence the collection is authorized to keep running).

THE DEFINING DEVIATION — BLIND REVIEW BY APPLICANT-PERFORMED REDACTION. You upload BOTH a redacted and an original version of the proposal and CV. "Redaction is defined as no inclusion of any identifying information, such as your or any person(s) names, organization/institution names, or specific details that could tie the application back to you and any institution/organization or person. Failure to follow this guidance will prevent your application from moving forward in the evaluation process." Specific guidance: the CV must not name your school ("The CV template just shows you where to put your major and degree, but you should not identify the school"); publications — "You can mention the title but do not mention authors/co-authors and name of the journal"; awards — describe generically, never name the awarding body. Essays must be written de-identified from the start. This is the opposite of the biosketch-and-institutional-prestige model most applicants are trained on.

COMPONENTS:
1. Research Proposal [redacted AND original]. "4 Page Proposal with work cited / 3 Page Proposal Single line space / 1 Page Max Cited Work / Graphics and Charts may be included / 12Pt. Times New Roman Font — a smaller font size may be used for cited work, charts and graphics / Margins should be no less than 0.5". DRIFT TRAP: the legacy ndseg.org requirements page still says "11Pt. Times New Roman" and "1 inch" margins — that page is a stale 2022 artefact; the sysplus figures are current.
2. DoD Strategy Document alignment. The proposal must map to a research area in a current DoD Strategy Document (formerly "BAA"). You enter the document NUMBER (not name) plus the research-area title. Preferred service is optional — you may select one, say your work suits multiple services, or state no preference. Crucially: "You are NOT required to fulfill any of the requirements put forth by the DoD Strategy Documents. You are only using them as reference to align your research and proposal to DoD strategic and scientific research mission, initiatives, and priorities."
3. Two essays, typed into web forms, "no more than 500 words for each essay" — and "the 500-word requirement applies to each essay", not combined. Essay 1: short/long-term professional goals, how they developed, foundation laid, how the fellowship fits. Essay 2: personal story — "personal journey to get where they are today (e.g., 1st to receive PHD, 1st to go to college, worked multiple position while achieving degree...)".
4. Resume/CV [redacted AND original], PDF. A template is provided inside the portal but is optional: "The template on the website is only an example of what elements to put but it is not required to be used."
5. Official transcripts, PDF. "The Department of Defense requires scanned/photographed copies of the official transcripts. Official transcripts typically contain a raised/embossed seal and a signature from a member of the University staff. Unofficial transcripts do not." Multiple master's degrees: combine into one file.
6. References — OPTIONAL THIS CYCLE, up to 3. "Yes, you can submit your application without references. This year's application does not require references." But "highly recommended". Referees should be "an Academic Advisor, Research Advisor, or Internship Supervisor". THEY DO NOT WRITE LETTERS: "Letters on letterhead will NOT be accepted" — they complete a structured Reference Evaluation Form via a system-generated link you trigger (Save, then Send Email), which includes a free-text comments box. References do NOT require redaction this cycle. HARD SEQUENCING RULE: they must submit before you do — "Once you submit your application, your references will no longer be able to submit their recommendations", and the only remedy is to start a fresh application and email the office to disregard the first.
7. Applicant Statement + Disclosure & Release Statement — these pages only unlock once every other element shows "[Saved/Complete]" (not merely "[Saved]").

MECHANICAL: PDF only, each file under ~4MB (the portal cannot handle larger); phone numbers must be '###-###-####' with dashes. No GRE: "No. GRE scores are no longer required for an application."

NOT REQUIRED (and notable by absence): no institutional endorsement, no sponsor/mentor statement, no advisor letter of support, no budget, no biosketch, no data-management plan, no page-limit negotiation route.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
**WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the half applicants usually get wrong — this is a permissive mechanism at the application stage):**
- Holding or having held other fellowships, scholarships or assistantships does NOT bar you from applying. There is no prior-award exclusion anywhere in the eligibility criteria, and the eligibility screener's four questions never mention funding.
- You MAY apply to NDSEG and NSF GRFP (and others) in the same season. The restriction bites only on acceptance.
- Previously declined applicants may reapply, explicitly and without limit or waiting period: "If you complete an application, and are not selected, you can apply again as long as you continue to meet all of the eligibility criteria above." No NIH-style A1 cap, no resubmission cover letter, no introduction page.
- Current graduate students already funded by a departmental TA/RA are eligible, provided they are within the first two years.
- Once a fellow, other compensation is not banned outright: "You may be allowed to engage in a reasonable amount of teaching or similar activities if approved by the DoD." Internships (DoD and non-DoD) are explicitly permitted with prior written approval. The portal has standing request types for "Other Compensation request, Internship, Scholarship".

**WHAT DISQUALIFIES OR FORCES A CHOICE:**
- You cannot draw two fellowship stipends at once: "Fellow **may not** accept simultaneous remuneration from another fellowship, e.g., if an applicant is offered both an NSF and an NDSEG Fellowship, the applicant must choose between the two offers."
- And you cannot sequence your way around it, because there is no convenience deferral: asked how to handle receiving NSF GRFP at the same time as NDSEG, the program answers that the decision is yours but notes "the NDSEG Fellowship Program is non-deferrable." So the classic GRFP manoeuvre — take one, defer the other — is unavailable. NDSEG must be taken now or declined.
- Deferral exists ONLY for three hardship/service grounds, needs prior written approval, and never extends the award: "An NDSEG Fellow may be granted 1 or more deferrals ... and may receive up to 12 months in deferral(s)" for (a) "Fulfilling an active duty military service obligation with the Department of Defense", (b) "Diagnosis of a health condition that prevents fellow from progressing in their academic studies", (c) "Immediate family member requires medical care or assistance from the fellow". "Upon return to the program, the fellow will only be given the remaining time from the original fellowship award time." Internships are expressly not a deferral ground.
- Concurrent earnings above the stipend suspend it: "If you make more that the NDSEG stipend, you will not be eligible to receive your fellowship stipend on the months you are receiving other compensation."
- Non-funding eligibility bars, since they disqualify more people than funding conflicts do: permanent residents are ineligible (citizens, U.S. nationals and dual citizens only); anyone pursuing a medical degree only; anyone not at a U.S. accredited institution; anyone past the first two years of graduate study; and the trap nobody reads — you must have "at least THREE remaining years in your graduate degree program at the time of application", because the award is 36 consecutive months and cannot be deferred or truncated. A third-year PhD student is out even if otherwise stellar. Also: "You must complete your bachelor's degree by the application year" — a current senior finishing next spring does not qualify this cycle.
- Not established either way: whether a former NDSEG awardee may hold a second NDSEG. The site is silent; do not assume.
result.program_officer_contact:
**Pre-submission contact with a program officer is EXPRESSLY FORBIDDEN.** This is the exact inverse of the DOE SC norm and, for anyone trained on NIH/NSF/DOE habits, the most dangerous assumption to carry into NDSEG.

From the DoD Supporting Agencies page: "PLEASE DO NOT CONTACT THE PROGRAM MANAGERS listed in the BAAs for any reason. They are not able to assist you in any way with the NDSEG application or the proposal you are to submit for the NDSEG application. If you require assistance, please work with your advisor(s)."

From the Application FAQ, asked directly whether one may contact DoD personnel about strategy documents, proposal review, or selection status: "Absolutely not. Do *not* reach out to any member of the Department of Defense unless they reach out to you first. This includes not reaching out to email addresses you receive from various forms of social media, including GradCafe and Facebook. They are not going to be able to answer your DOD STRATEGY DOCUMENTS (E.G., BAA/FOA) questions, they will not review your proposal, and they will not provide you any information that has not already been provided to NDSEG Program Office."

THE ONE ROUTE IN — a contractor-run program office, not a scientist:
- DoD NDSEG Program Office, Systems Plus, Inc. — **NDSEG.PMO@sysplus.com**, **(301) 948-4232**, One Research Court, Suite 360, Rockville, MD 20850.
- Service standard, quoted: "Your email to NDSEG.PMO@sysplus.com will receive a response, typically the same day or the next business day." And use the shared box, not individuals: "Directly emailing a member of the NDSEG staff may not get answered quickly."
- No named individual program officer is published for this mechanism anywhere on the site.

WHO ACTUALLY PLAYS THE PM ROLE: your own advisor. The funder says so twice — "If you require assistance, please work with your advisor(s)" and "Your sole point of contact aside from your research & academic advisors is NDSEG.PMO@sysplus.com." The site's own Application Tips lead with "Have an Advisor review your Proposal, Personal Statement/Application". So the pre-submission conversation that DOE routes to a federal PM, NDSEG routes to your thesis advisor and to the shared contractor inbox for procedural questions only.

There is no informational webinar, no office hours, and no proposal-writing session offered for applicants (the NDSEG Mentor programme and the annual Fellows Conference are post-award, for fellows). The only "Upcoming Event" listed is the 2027 Technical Research Exchange, which is "a DoW-invite-only event".
result.examples_or_samples:
No funded application text, no annotated sample proposal, and no abstract library is published for NDSEG — unlike DOE (PAMS public award search, ECRP abstract PDFs) or NIH (RePORTER). There is no NDSEG equivalent. What DOES exist, in descending order of usefulness:

(1) **AWARDEE LISTS BY FISCAL YEAR — the best available signal.** https://ndseg.sysplus.com/NDSEG/awardees/FY2026.aspx tabulates all 102 FY2026 awardees as AGENCY / AWARDEE / DISCIPLINE AREA / GRADUATE INSTITUTION. Because the sponsoring service is named per person, you can read off which service funds which discipline — e.g. ONR taking Electrical Engineering, AI/ML, Aeronautical & Astronautical; ARO taking Materials Science, Chemical Engineering, Quantum Science, Cognitive/Neural/Behavioral; Dept. of the Air Force (AFRL/USSF) taking Physics/Optics, Materials for Extreme Environments, Biotechnology. That is the closest thing to "who does my program manager already fund". FY2025 list at https://ndseg.sysplus.com/NDSEG/awardees/FY2025.aspx.
   Also note the discipline taxonomy has visibly expanded beyond the older published list — "Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning", "Quantum Science", "Biotechnology (Separate from Biosciences)", "Materials Science and Engineering (Includes Materials for Extreme Environments)" now appear as named areas.

(2) **THE DoD STRATEGY DOCUMENTS — the actual source material your proposal must answer to**, all linked from https://ndseg.sysplus.com/NDSEG/About/DoD-Agencies.aspx: National Defense Science and Technology Strategy 2023 (https://media.defense.gov/2023/May/09/2003218877/-1/-1/0/NDSTS-FINAL-WEB-VERSION.PDF); USD(R&E) Strategic Vision and Critical Technology Areas (https://www.cto.mil/usdre-strat-vision-critical-tech-areas/); AF Science & Technology Strategy and AF Operational Imperatives; AFOSR BAA (via Grants.gov); ARL BAA (https://www.arl.army.mil/collaborate-with-us/opportunity/arl-baa); Army MRDC BAA (https://usamraa.health.mil/BAA/); ONR funding opportunities (https://www.nre.navy.mil/work-with-us/funding-opportunities). The FAQ walks through exactly how to extract a usable document number and research-area title, with a worked example: AFOSR number FA9550-19-S-0003, title formed from Competition ID + Competition Title, "RTB 1-8—Remote Sensing".

(3) **Press releases with context and scale** — FY2026: https://ndseg.sysplus.com/NDSEG/News/DoDNDSEG2026NDSEGAwardeesAnnouncement.pdf ("102 outstanding individuals from 61 U.S. universities", "over 5,000 fellowships awarded since its inception"); FY2024: https://ndseg.sysplus.com/NDSEG/images/Forms/2024_NDSEG_FY2024_Awardee_Press_Release.pdf; FY2020: https://ndseg.sysplus.com/NDSEG/images/Forms/FY2020_NDSEG_Fellowship_Awardee_PR.pdf.

(4) **Fellow-voice material** — "NDSEG Professional Development Highlights" (https://ndseg.sysplus.com/NDSEG/images/Forms/NDSEG_Professional_Development_Fellows_Highlights.pdf) and the Fellows Conference poster/technical-presentation award lists (https://ndseg.sysplus.com/NDSEG/images/Forms/NDSEG_Conference_Awards.pdf, .../NDSEG_Conference_Award_Winners.pdf) — awarded research topics in fellows' own framing.

(5) **The portal's own templates** — a redacted-CV template and the Reference Evaluation Form live inside https://applyndseg.sysplus.com/ once you register. They are not on the public site. Registering early (the screener is four questions) is the cheapest way to see the real forms.

(6) **Your department.** Since blind review means institutional prestige is stripped out, the highest-value read is a recent NDSEG fellow's own redacted proposal. With 102 awards across 61 universities each year, most R1 departments have one. There is no official route to anyone else's.
result.resubmission_note:
Reapplication is explicitly permitted and unrestricted, with no waiting period, no attempt cap, no A1 numbering and no introduction page: "If you complete an application, and are not selected, you can apply again as long as you continue to meet all of the eligibility criteria above."

THE BINDING CONSTRAINT IS THE ELIGIBILITY CLOCK, NOT THE RESUBMISSION RULE. Because you must be within the first two years of graduate study AND have "at least THREE remaining years in your graduate degree program at the time of application", a typical PhD student gets at most two or three shots: final undergraduate year (only if the bachelor's completes in the application year), then year 1, then year 2. Miss those and eligibility closes permanently. This is the practical inverse of DOE's Open Call, where unlimited rolling resubmission is possible but substantive revision against reviewer comments is mandatory — here revision is unconstrained but the window slams shut.

You also cannot revise against feedback, because none is given: no reviewer comments, no scores, no summary statement, and contacting DoD about selection is forbidden. A second attempt is rewritten blind, against the DoD Strategy Documents and your advisor's judgement.

WITHIN-CYCLE CORRECTION (the NDSEG analogue of DOE's PAMS withdrawal): there is no withdraw function and no edit after submission. "You will not be able to make any changes after submission. It is up to you to start a new application for consideration. However, you should notify our office if you plan to do this, so we validate and evaluate the correct application." The same remedy applies to the commonest self-inflicted error — submitting before your referees have filed, which locks them out: "please start a new application and inform us to disregard your current application at NDSEG.PMO@sysplus.com."
unresolved: FY2027 notification date and fellowship start date are not published. The July-September notification window and the September stipend start are PATTERN-DERIVED from four observed announcement dates (3 Sept 2026, 5 Aug 2025, 1 July 2024, 15 July 2020) plus the quoted 'starting in September' stipend rule — not a funder statement about FY2027.

Per-cycle selectivity: not found. Only cumulative figures are published ('over 70,000 applications received', 'over 5,000 fellowships awarded' since 1989) plus FY2026's 102 awards from 61 universities. The number of FY2026 or FY2027 applicants is not published, so no cycle acceptance rate can be stated without guessing.
Whether a former NDSEG awardee may receive a second NDSEG fellowship: not addressed anywhere on the funder site. Do not assume either way.

Whether references will remain optional in future cycles. The FAQ scopes it tightly to now — 'This year's application does not require references' and 'references do not require redaction for this year's application' — so this is a per-cycle setting that has already changed once (the legacy 2022 site required three). Re-verify each August.

Review criteria are not published with any weighting or rubric. The only statement is that merit review relies on 'academic records, CV, Essays and research proposals'; the panelist scoring sheet is not public.

No named individual program officer exists for this mechanism; only the contractor shared inbox. Not a gap in research — the funder deliberately publishes no scientist contact and forbids approaching one.

Exact FY2027 stipend for the incoming class: the published $3,600/month ($43,200/yr) is the current posted rate, but the funder states 'Stipend amounts are determined for each Fellowship class by the DoD', so the 2027 class rate is not guaranteed by that figure.

TOOLING FACTS, not findings: the legacy portal https://ndseg.viointegration.com/ could not be fetched (expired TLS certificate); https://basicresearch.defense.gov/Programs/NDSEG/ returned 403; mojeek.com returned 403; Google and DuckDuckGo served bot-verification challenges which were not bypassed. None of this bears on programme status - the programme is demonstrably open and running.

ROUTE DISCLOSURE: this research used the funder's own pages throughout (ndseg.sysplus.com, the administering program office, reached via a pointer on ndseg.org/apply-link). No search index was used for any substantive claim - WebSearch was unavailable (session budget exhausted) and the index fallbacks were blocked.

result.review_to_award: Not found. result.submission_requirements:
Portal: awards.sfn.org ("Apply Now" from the NSP page); an account in SfN's awards system is required. Six required components, quoted/listed by the funder: (1) Resume/CV; (2) Adviser's biosketch; (3) Two-year plan, "500 words maximum"; (4) Professional goals statement, "500 words maximum"; (5) Two letters of recommendation; (6) Unofficial transcripts — undergraduate AND graduate-level for graduate students, graduate-level only for postdoctoral researchers.

Where this DEVIATES from the NIH-style norm this audience will expect: (a) limits are WORD counts (500), not page limits — two short statements, not a Specific Aims/Research Strategy set; (b) no research proposal, no budget or budget justification, and no institutional sign-off / AOR submission is stated anywhere — this is an individual direct application, not one routed through a sponsored-programs office; (c) it asks for the ADVISER'S biosketch, not a written sponsor/mentor statement in the F-series sense, and not the applicant's own biosketch; (d) unofficial transcripts are required even of postdocs, which is unusual at that career stage; (e) two letters of recommendation, versus the three-plus common on NIH fellowships. The practical long-pole items are therefore the adviser's biosketch and the two letter writers — both depend on other people and should be requested in December, before the January open.

Not found: whether the adviser must be one of the two letter writers, who else may write, reference letter submission mechanism/deadline (whether letters are due at the same noon cutoff or later), and any formatting spec. Ask NSP@sfn.org.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
Both halves, stated plainly — and the honest answer is that the exclusion half is empty at the funder.

WHAT DISQUALIFIES: No prior-award or current-funding exclusion appears anywhere on SfN's NSP pages. The eligibility criteria are exhaustively two items, quoted: applicants must be "Citizens of the United States" and "Enrolled in a graduate degree-granting program or postdoctoral fellowship." Nothing about held grants, fellowships, training-grant appointments, or other SfN awards.

WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY: There is no NIH K/R01-style interaction to manage here — NSP is a professional-society training, mentoring and community fellowship (up to $1,500 enrichment funds, meeting travel, membership, a mentoring team), not a salary-or-research-support career-development award, so it does not trigger the concurrent-support rules that govern K awards. Holding an NIH F31 or F32, an NSF GRFP, or a T32 slot is not named as a bar; on the contrary, being "enrolled in ... a postdoctoral fellowship" is itself a qualifying status. Because the benefits are non-salary (enrichment funds and travel, not stipend), they are unlikely to collide with another award's stipend-exclusivity terms — but that reasoning is mine, not SfN's.

IMPORTANT CAVEAT for the corpus: absence of a stated exclusion is NOT the same as an explicit carve-out. This should be recorded as "no prior-funding exclusion published" rather than "prior funding explicitly permitted." An applicant holding another fellowship should confirm with NSP@sfn.org before assuming.

Also unresolved and genuinely high-value for this audience: whether an unsuccessful applicant may reapply in a later cycle, and whether an NSP Associate (the top ~100 applicants beyond the up-to-16 Fellows) may reapply for Fellow status. Since most applicants land in the Associate tier, the reapplication rule is the question most of them will actually have, and SfN does not answer it publicly.
result.program_officer_contact:
No named individual program officer is published. Two institutional routes, both from SfN's own pages:
- NSP@sfn.org — the program contact, published on NSP Central (https://www.sfn.org/nspcentral), together with phone (202) 962-4000. This is the right address for eligibility, reapplication, and application-content questions.
- awards@sfn.org — application-system/portal support, published on awards.sfn.org ("for inquiries about the awards and fellowships system"). Use for login, upload, and submission-mechanics problems.
- SfN HQ: 1121 14th Street NW, Suite 1010, Washington, D.C. 20005; (202) 962-4000 / 1-888-985-9246; general contact form at https://www.sfn.org/contact.

Pre-submission contact is NOT stated as expected or required — there is no "contact program staff before applying" instruction, unlike NIH-style mechanisms. It is optional, and given how much is unpublished (notification timing, reapplication, letter-writer rules), it is worth doing.
result.examples_or_samples:
No sample application, annotated example, successful two-year plan, or funded-abstract library is published for NSP. SfN offers none, and no fellow roster or testimonial page exists on the pages checked. State this as a genuine gap rather than implying materials exist.

Closest usable substitutes, all on SfN's Neuronline platform and explicitly open access — the NSP webinar archive states: "All materials available in this archive are provided open access to the field and are supported by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS)":
- Public NSP webinar collection (program years 2015-16 through 2025-26): https://neuronline.sfn.org/collection/public-nsp-webinars
- NSP Next Gen 2023 collection: https://neuronline.sfn.org/collection/nsp-next-gen-2023 — the two most directly useful sessions for someone drafting the two-year plan and goals statement are "NSP Next Gen 2023: Grant Writing" (https://neuronline.sfn.org/professional-development/nsp-next-gen-2023-grant-writing) and "NSP Next Gen 2023: Funding Opportunities and Strategies" (https://neuronline.sfn.org/professional-development/nsp-next-gen-2023-funding-opportunities-and-strategies)
- NSP Central, the participant portal: https://www.sfn.org/nspcentral — includes the Fellow Enrichment Fund application and instructions, which is the best available evidence of what the $1,500 may be spent on, and mentor/mentee resources showing what the mentoring team actually does. Post-award in orientation, but it shows a prospective applicant what they would be signing up for.
- Main NSP collection: https://neuronline.sfn.org/collection/neuroscience-scholars-program
result.resubmission_note: Not found. SfN publishes no reapplication policy for NSP: nothing on whether an unsuccessful applicant may apply again in a later cycle, nothing on whether an NSP Associate may reapply for Fellow status, and no limit on number of attempts. Given the two-tier structure (up to 16 Fellows; the remaining top 100 eligible applicants become Associates), the Associate-to-Fellow question affects the large majority of applicants and is the single most conspicuous omission from the public materials. Direct applicants to NSP@sfn.org.
unresolved: Exact close date for the 2027 cycle — SfN has published only that the cycle 'will open January 2027'. The close date is not yet posted as of 2026-09-18. Re-check the NSP page in January 2027; the 2026 analogue was Friday, February 13, 12 p.m. EST.
Notification date / review-to-award timeline — not published in any form. No review process, no selection criteria, no announcement date.
Term start date — whether the two-year term begins at the SfN annual meeting is implied by the both-years travel award but never stated.
Reapplication policy — whether unsuccessful applicants may reapply, and whether an NSP Associate may reapply for Fellow status. Affects most applicants; unpublished.
Prior-funding exclusions — none published. Recorded as 'no exclusion stated', NOT as an explicit permission. An applicant holding an F31/F32/GRFP should confirm with NSP@sfn.org.
Letters of recommendation — whether the adviser must be one of the two writers, who else qualifies, how letters are submitted, and whether they are due at the same noon cutoff as the application.
Institutional sign-off — no AOR or sponsored-programs routing is mentioned anywhere; treated as an individual direct application, but never explicitly confirmed as such.
No named individual program officer — only the NSP@sfn.org and awards@sfn.org role addresses.
No sample or annotated application, successful statement, or funded-applicant roster exists publicly for this mechanism.

result.program_name: Non-Academic Research Internships for Graduate Students (INTERN) and Graduate Research Internship Program (GRIP) supplements
result.next_deadline:
NO DEADLINE — rolling, plus one annual target date. Governing DCL NSF 21-013, verbatim: "Supplemental funding requests may be submitted at any time with a target date of April 15th for each Fiscal Year."

DURABLE RULE (publish this): submit any time; April 15 each fiscal year is a TARGET date, not a deadline. In NSF's own taxonomy a target date means late requests are still accepted but may miss that funding round — nothing is refused for lateness.

DATED INSTANCE (as of check date 2026-09-18): the FY2026 target of 15 April 2026 has passed; the next target date is **15 April 2027** (FY2027 runs 1 Oct 2026 – 30 Sep 2027). This is a derived calendar instance of the published recurring rule, not a date NSF prints as "15 April 2027" — NSF's own page shows only "See letter for details."

THE DATE THAT ACTUALLY BINDS is not April 15 at all — it is your internship start date minus the lead time. PAPPG 24-1 VI.E.5: supplemental requests "must be signed and submitted by the AOR via use of NSF's electronic systems at least two months prior to the need for the additional funds." So work backwards from when the student would start, not forwards from April.

NSF 21-013 is confirmed live: its page carries "This document contains information about an active funding opportunity," publication number NSF 21-013, replacing NSF 18-102, last updated 15 January 2026.
result.deadline_pattern:
"Submitted at any time," with an April 15 annual target date in most of the family. INTERN is not one opportunity but a family of eight co-existing Dear Colleague Letters, all listed as current on https://www.nsf.gov/tip/intern, each showing "Next Required Due Date: See letter for details." Due-date text checked in each letter individually:

- INTERN, the parent DCL (NSF 21-013, posted 8 Oct 2020): "may be submitted at any time with a target date of April 15th for each Fiscal Year."
- NSF-AFRL INTERN, Air Force Research Laboratory (NSF 21-029): "any time with a target date of April 15 for each Fiscal Year."
- Geothermal INTERN, with DOE EERE (NSF 23-024): "any time with a target date of April 15 for each Fiscal Year."
- NSF-DEVCOM INTERN, US Army (NSF 24-071): "any time with a target date of June 15 for Fiscal Year 2024 and April 15 for future Fiscal Years."
- Hydrogen INTERN, hydrogen and fuel cell technologies (NSF 24-087): "any time with a target date of June 15 for Fiscal Year 2024 and April 15 for future Fiscal Years."
- NSF-NIBIB/BETA INTERN, biomedical engineering (NSF 24-083): "may be submitted at any time." No target date at all.
- NSF-NIJ INTERN, forensic science and criminal justice (NSF 23-150): "may be submitted at any time." No target date.
- GeoHealth INTERN, GEO (NSF 23-112): "may be submitted at any time." No target date.

Practical consequence worth surfacing to a student: three of the eight have no date of any kind, so for those the only timing constraint is the two-month AOR lead time before the internship starts. This mechanism is the clearest example in the NSF corpus of "you can apply the month you are ready."

DRIFT NOTE: the AFRL letter (NSF 21-029, drafted Dec 2020) still instructs "must be submitted electronically via FastLane." That text is stale — FastLane no longer handles this; the operative system is Research.gov per PAPPG 24-1 VI.E.5 and per the parent DCL NSF 21-013. Do not follow the FastLane sentence.
result.loi_deadline:
No letter of intent, no pre-proposal, no concept outline. But there are three real pre-submission gates that function like one, and missing any of them costs more than a missed LOI would:

1. MANDATORY-IN-PRACTICE PO CONTACT. NSF 21-013: "A PI on an NSF grant should contact his/her cognizant program director prior to submission," and "PIs are encouraged to discuss with the cognizant NSF program director activities that are synergistic with the NSF project scope." Two letters harden "should" into "must": NSF-DEVCOM (24-071) and Hydrogen (24-087) both read "A PI or co-PI on an NSF award must contact his/her cognizant program director prior to submission." GeoHealth (23-112) requires contact "about their intention to submit prior to submitting a supplement request." No stated lead time for the conversation.

2. SIGNED IP AGREEMENT, BEFORE THE MONEY. NSF 21-013: "The NSF awardee and the organization hosting the graduate student must agree in advance as to how intellectual property (IP) rights will be handled. A signed agreement on IP (including publication and patent rights) must be submitted prior to the award of the supplemental funding." This is negotiated between your university's tech-transfer/contracts office and the host company's legal team — the single most common cause of an INTERN start slipping. Start it as soon as the host says yes, not after NSF approves.

3. TWO-MONTH AOR LEAD TIME. PAPPG 24-1 VI.E.5, verbatim: requests "must be signed and submitted by the AOR via use of NSF's electronic systems at least two months prior to the need for the additional funds and must be adequately justified." Caveat recorded honestly: the same section says "Special NSF programs such as Research Experiences for Undergraduates may provide their funding through supplements to other NSF grants. In such instances, the guidance in this section may not be applicable" — so the two months is NSF's default rather than a rule NSF 21-013 restates. Treat it as the planning floor, and add your own institution's internal turnaround on top.

FOR GRFP FELLOWS the pre-submission chain is longer and is the thing students get wrong. Per the GRFP Administrative Guide NSF 25-033: "Fellows should contact their CO for assistance with submitting an INTERN Supplement request. The CO will contact the GRFP Principal Investigator (PI) who will submit the request on the Fellow's behalf." So: Fellow → Coordinating Official at the institution → GRFP PI → AOR → NSF. Four hands before it reaches NSF. Start months out.
result.review_to_award:
Much faster and much less formal than the NSF full-proposal arc — the funder-wide six-month norm does NOT apply here, and quoting it to a student would badly mislead them.

NO EXTERNAL REVIEW. NSF 21-013: "Requests for supplemental funding submitted in response to this DCL will be reviewed internally by NSF Program Officers. All supplements are subject to (a) the availability of funds, and (b) merit review of the supplemental funding request." No ad hoc reviewers, no panel, no panel summary, no six-month clock, no DGA-style published interval. PAPPG 24-1 VI.E.5 confirms the internal route for supplements of this size: "Program Officers may make decisions regarding whether or not to recommend a small supplement without merit review of the supplemental request. Requests for larger supplements will require external merit review." At up to $55,000 an INTERN request sits in the internally-decided band.

NSF PUBLISHES NO SUBMISSION-TO-DECISION INTERVAL FOR THIS MECHANISM. Not found on any of the eight letters or in PAPPG. The only official timing anchor is the requirement to submit "at least two months prior to the need for the additional funds" (PAPPG VI.E.5) — which is NSF telling you how much runway it wants, and is the closest thing to a published turnaround. Do not convert that into a promised decision date; it is a lead-time instruction, not a service standard.

AWARD MECHANICS. There is no new award. PAPPG VI.E.5: "If approved, the NSF Grants and Agreements Officer will amend the award to provide additional funding for the current support period." A Grants and Agreements Officer signs, not the Program Officer. The parent award's end date normally stays put, though PAPPG VI.D notes the end date "may be changed... by approval of a request for supplemental support (up to six additional months in accordance with Section E.4. below)."

EARLIEST START. Governed by the internship, not by an NSF cycle: two months after AOR submission at the earliest, and in practice gated by whichever of the IP agreement, the host's onboarding, or NSF's decision finishes last. Budget realistically for three to four months from "host says yes" to "student starts," with the IP agreement as the usual long pole.

FUNDING RISK IS REAL BUT MODEST. NSF 21-013: "NSF plans to fund up to approximately 260 supplements in each fiscal year starting with FY 2021, depending on the availability of funds"; the TIP page says NSF "supports more than 250 INTERN experiences each year." Requests are explicitly "subject to the availability of funds," so a late-fiscal-year request competes against a drawn-down budget — one practical argument for the April target date over a July request.
result.submission_requirements:
Submitted via Research.gov as a supplemental funding request on an existing award. The student never submits, and neither, formally, does the PI: the PI prepares, the AOR signs and submits (PAPPG 24-1 VI.E.5: "AORs are required to electronically sign the supplemental funding request via the Authorized Organizational Representative Functions in Research.gov").

DEVIATION FROM THE NSF NORM — THIS IS THE HEADLINE. None of the standard full-proposal apparatus appears in NSF 21-013's enumerated component list: no 15-page Project Description, no three-box Project Summary, no SciENcv biographical sketch, no Current and Pending Support, no Data Management and Sharing Plan, no Collaborators and Other Affiliations spreadsheet, no Synergistic Activities, no formatting/typeface rules. The heavy NSF machinery in the funder-wide profile is for proposals; this is an amendment to an award you already hold. Total realistic package: roughly six pages plus a budget.

REQUIRED COMPONENTS, per NSF 21-013 ("Each supplemental funding request must include the INTERN DCL title and DCL number in the summary section of the proposal and include the following components"):
1. A TWO-PAGE SUMMARY describing the internship. It "must include a concise statement from the graduate student describing how the activity will better prepare the graduate student to enter the workforce." The student writes this part in their own voice — the one place in the package that is theirs.
2. A STUDENT RESUME, up to 2 pages: educational preparation institution, major, year of study, summary of graduate coursework completed, professional employment history, publications, other relevant information. ORCID iD encouraged but "submission of the ORCID ID is optional." Note the downstream obligation: "The resume must be included in the PI's annual and final project reports under Special Requirements."
3. A LETTER OF COLLABORATION FROM THE HOST, from "an authorized official at the organization which will host the student," describing the internship and the mentoring the student will receive. Critical clause: "This letter should include a statement confirming that neither the graduate student nor the PI has a financial interest in the organization hosting the internship." Unlike standard NSF letters of collaboration, this one is substantive, not the one-sentence boilerplate form — the usual NSF single-sentence template is wrong here.
4. A LETTER FROM THE PI confirming the student meets the DCL's eligibility requirements, describing "how the proposed internship activity will contribute to the student's graduate education experience and how it may impact time to degree," and describing "activities that are synergistic with the scope of the PI's NSF Grant to be supplemented."
5. A SIGNED IP AGREEMENT between awardee and host covering publication and patent rights, "submitted prior to the award of the supplemental funding." NSF explicitly disclaims involvement: "NSF is responsible neither for the agreement reached nor the IP information exchanged."
6. A BUDGET AND CLEAR JUSTIFICATION for all requested costs.

THE STRING REQUIREMENT. The variant letters require an exact character string in the first sentence of the project summary — e.g. Geothermal INTERN (NSF 23-024): "Each supplemental funding request must include the character string GEOTHERMAL INTERN DCL and the DCL announcement number in the first sentence of the project summary section of the supplement request." Get the string wrong and the request routes to the wrong pot of money. Check your specific letter.

BUDGET RULES (NSF 21-013). Ceiling "$55,000 per student per six-month period." Allowable: travel, tuition and fees, health insurance, additional stipend, temporary relocation. Sub-caps: "Up to $2,500 may be used for the PI or the graduate research fellow's advisor to travel to work with the host organization in co-mentoring the student"; "Up to $2,500 may be used for materials and supplies." Indirect costs allowed at the negotiated rate, inside the ceiling. Explicitly excluded: "Spousal and dependent travel are not supported."

OTHER CONDITIONS. On-site is the default: the internship "will be on-site at the host organization unless a specific exception to this is granted due to extenuating circumstances by the cognizant program officer." Internships are "considered equivalent to traineeships" for IP purposes, and "The National Science Foundation claims no rights to any inventions or writings that might result from its traineeship awards." The awardee must have a harassment policy and "should work with the Host Organization to ensure that the Host Organization also has a policy or code of conduct."
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
The logic here is inverted relative to NIH career awards: prior NSF funding is the ENTRY TICKET, not the disqualifier. There is nothing you can hold that locks you out; there are only things you must hold, and a short list of structural exclusions.

WHAT YOU MUST ALREADY HAVE (the gate):
- An active NSF award. NSF 21-013: "This opportunity is open to PIs (and co-PIs) who are supporting graduate students through an active NSF award." No active award, no INTERN — there is no standalone application, and a student cannot apply on their own behalf.
- The student must be past year one: "To be eligible, graduate students must have completed at least one academic year in their graduate programs (master's or doctoral) and be making satisfactory progress towards the completion of their degrees." First-years are excluded.

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the half applicants get wrong):
- HOLDING A GRFP FELLOWSHIP DOES NOT DISQUALIFY YOU — it is a named, supported route. NSF 21-013's stated goal is to let students "augment their research assistantships or NSF Graduate Research Fellowship Program (GRFP) fellowships with non-academic research internship activities." GRFP Administrative Guide NSF 25-033: "Fellows can be either on Tenure or Reserve while receiving support from INTERN."
- RESERVE STATUS IS AN ADVANTAGE, NOT A PROBLEM. NSF 25-033: "Fellows with Reserve status may be eligible for stipend support through INTERN or other similar supplement requests," and "For Fellows on Reserve, the budget can include stipend at the GRFP level (as specified in the GRFP solicitation), tuition, and required fees." A Reserve-year fellow can be paid a full stipend through INTERN — genuinely useful and little known.
- A PRIOR INTERN SUPPLEMENT DOES NOT DISQUALIFY YOU. NSF 21-013: "Up to two supplemental funding requests may be submitted on a grant per student. This would allow the student up to two internship periods up to six months each (i.e., a maximum of 12 months per student)." You may go twice.
- EPSCoR AND HBCU AWARDS ARE EXPLICITLY WELCOMED: "EPSCoR Research Infrastructure Improvement (RII) and HBCU-Excellence in Research (EiR) awards may apply. Supplement requests are encouraged from any NSF-funded PIs located in EPSCoR-eligible jurisdictions. Eligible requests submitted to the original funding directorate will be considered for EPSCoR co-funding support."
- FOUR DIRECTORATES IMPOSE NOTHING EXTRA: "The Directorate for Engineering (ENG), Directorate for Biological Sciences (BIO), Directorate for Geosciences (GEO) and Directorate for Social, Behavioral and Economic Sciences (SBE) do not have limitations or special conditions."
- Non-federal internships, assistantships and traineeships are separately compatible with a GRFP stipend (NSF 25-033): "Fellows may be permitted to receive additional compensation from one of these if the funding is from a non-federal source or is a component of a benefits package provided to veterans," subject to the institution's own policy.

WHAT ACTUALLY EXCLUDES YOU:
- WHICH DIRECTORATE HOLDS THE PARENT AWARD. CISE: "This opportunity is open only to active awards within the Office of Advanced Cyberinfrastructure (OAC); projects funded by other CISE divisions are not eligible" — and OAC adds "Only doctoral candidates may apply." Most of CISE is shut out; this is the single biggest exclusion in the mechanism. OIA: "open only to active awards within the Research Capacity and Competitiveness Section (RCC)."
- MASTER'S STUDENTS IN SOME UNITS. MPS applies to all divisions, but "In the Divisions of Astronomical Sciences and Mathematical Sciences only doctoral candidates may apply." Same doctoral-only restriction in CISE/OAC.
- FINANCIAL INTEREST IN THE HOST. The host letter must confirm "that neither the graduate student nor the PI has a financial interest in the organization hosting the internship." Interning at your own PI's startup, or your own, is out. Note the deliberate asymmetry: NSF names SBIR/STTR-funded start-ups as desirable hosts — someone else's start-up is encouraged, your own is disqualifying.
- A BUDGET CONSTRAINT THAT IS NOT AN ELIGIBILITY BAR, AND IS ROUTINELY MISREAD AS ONE. NSF 21-013: "Additional stipends are not allowed for GRFP fellows on tenure but a stipend will be considered for fellows on reserve equal to the monthly rate of the GRFP stipend." NSF 25-033: "Fellows on Tenure are not eligible to receive stipend above the regular GRFP stipend. Therefore, an INTERN budget request for Tenure students should not include stipend if the Fellow is receiving a GRFP stipend." A Tenure-year fellow is fully ELIGIBLE for INTERN — they simply cannot double-dip stipend, and can still request travel, tuition and fees, health insurance and relocation.

ROUTING RULE, EASY TO MISS: a GRFP fellow's request is not submitted by the fellow or by their research advisor. NSF 21-013: "GRFP INTERN supplement requests are submitted by the GRFP PI, not by the GRFP fellow or the fellow's research advisor," and "A PI for an active GRFP fellowship (not the GRFP fellow) should contact GRFP regarding specific GRFP requirements before submitting a supplemental funding request on behalf of a GRFP fellow."
result.program_officer_contact:
Named contacts, published per directorate, and pre-submission contact is expected — in two letters, required. This is the most contact-forward mechanism in the NSF set, because the PO decides it alone with no panel.

GENERAL: NSF-INTERN@nsf.gov (the only contact given on https://www.nsf.gov/tip/intern).
GRFP-SPECIFIC: grfpintern@nsf.gov. Per NSF 25-033, this is an escalation route, not the first stop: "If there are additional questions after the Fellow and CO consult, the CO or PI may contact GRFPINTERN@NSF.gov."

NAMED CONTACTS, verbatim from NSF 21-013 (letter dated Oct 2020, last updated 15 Jan 2026):
- TIP: Dr. Tyrslai Williams, tyrwilli@nsf.gov
- ENG: Dr. Prakash G. Balan, pbalan@nsf.gov
- GEO: Dr. Barbara Ransom, bransom@nsf.gov
- SBE: Dr. Josie Miranda, jwmirand@nsf.gov
- OIA/EPSCoR: Dr. Andrea Johnson, andjohns@nsf.gov
- EDU: "GRFP PIs should contact grfpintern@nsf.gov"
- BIO, CISE/OAC, MPS: "The cognizant program officer on the NSF grant."
Staleness caveat: these names are from a 2020 letter. NSF rotators turn over. Verify against the current staff directory before emailing, and fall back to NSF-INTERN@nsf.gov or to the PO named on your own award.

WHO YOU ACTUALLY TALK TO. For most people it is none of the above — it is the Program Officer who manages YOUR parent award. NSF 21-013 routes you there by default, and the NIBIB and NIJ letters say it plainly: "A PI or Co-PI with an NSF award should contact the program director who manages the award prior to submission." That name is on your award notice and in NSF Award Search.

IS CONTACT EXPECTED? Yes, and in two letters it is mandatory. NSF 21-013 uses "should contact... prior to submission"; NSF-DEVCOM (24-071) and Hydrogen (24-087) both use "must contact his/her cognizant program director prior to submission"; GeoHealth (23-112) requires notifying the PO "about their intention to submit." Since the request is "reviewed internally by NSF Program Officers" with no panel, that one conversation is effectively the whole review — an unprepared PO is the failure mode.

WHAT TO ASK: is this host and this project in scope for my award's program? Is the internship sufficiently "synergistic with the NSF project scope" (the DCL's own test)? Is $X the right ask? Are funds still available this fiscal year, or should we target April 15? Will an off-site or hybrid arrangement be granted an exception?

WHO A STUDENT SHOULD TALK TO FIRST — not NSF. On a research grant: your PI, who must agree to submit and must write the eligibility letter. On a GRFP: your institution's GRFP Coordinating Official, per NSF 25-033 ("Fellows should contact their CO for assistance"). Then your sponsored projects office, for the AOR submission and the IP agreement. A student emailing NSF cold has skipped three people who all have to act before NSF ever sees the request.
result.examples_or_samples:
Weakest link in this mechanism, and worth being blunt about: there is no public library of funded INTERN requests, and the usual NSF answer — read funded abstracts in Award Search — largely does not work here.

WHY AWARD SEARCH UNDER-DELIVERS. An approved INTERN request produces no new award record. PAPPG 24-1 VI.E.5: "the NSF Grants and Agreements Officer will amend the award to provide additional funding for the current support period." The supplement is an amendment to the parent award, so what you find in Award Search is the PARENT project's abstract and an increased obligated total — not the two-page internship summary, not the host, not the student. Verified against the NSF awards API (api.nsf.gov/services/v1/awards.json): keyword searches for "INTERN DCL" and "Non-Academic Research Internships" return ordinary parent awards whose abstracts merely contain similar workforce language, not supplement records. Searched, not assumed.

WHAT DOES WORK, in the order a student should try it:
1. YOUR OWN INSTITUTION'S RESEARCH DEVELOPMENT OR GRADUATE SCHOOL OFFICE. This is the highest-yield route and the one most students never try. INTERN is a recurring internal process — the same office shepherds several a year, and typically holds previous successful two-page summaries, host letter templates, PI letter templates and a worked budget. Ask for last year's approved package. For a GRFP fellow the equivalent person is the GRFP Coordinating Official, who is named in NSF 25-033 as the first point of contact anyway.
2. YOUR COGNIZANT PROGRAM OFFICER. With no panel, the PO knows exactly what a fundable request looks like in their program and can say so before you write. Ask what a strong two-page summary looks like for their portfolio.
3. NSF AWARD SEARCH, https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/ — still useful for the narrower question of which PIs and programs in your field hold active awards of the kind that host INTERN students, and which PO signs them. Treat it as a map of who to approach, not as a sample library.
4. NSF-INTERN@nsf.gov for anything the letters do not answer.
5. FOIA (https://www.nsf.gov/policies/foia) is available in principle but a poor fit: it reaches awarded PROPOSALS, and the supplement request is an amendment rather than a proposal, so what you are likely to receive is the parent proposal. Weeks to months. Not worth it for a six-page package.

WHAT IS NOT AVAILABLE: no NSF-published sample INTERN request, no annotated example, no FAQ document, no template — none found on nsf.gov. Internal PO reviews of supplements are not released to anyone but the PI, as with all NSF reviews. There is no community archive comparable to the GRFP successful-essay collections.

SOURCING NOTE: all of the above is from NSF's own pages, NSF's own award API, and PAPPG 24-1. result.resubmission_note:
The NSF resubmission framework in the funder-wide profile does not apply here. PAPPG Chapter IV's rules ("A declined proposal may be resubmitted, but only after it has undergone substantial revision") govern PROPOSALS. A supplemental funding request is not a proposal, and neither NSF 21-013 nor any of the seven variant letters says anything about resubmitting a declined request. Recorded as not found rather than inferred.

WHAT DOES CONSTRAIN REPEAT ATTEMPTS is the count cap, which limits awards rather than attempts. NSF 21-013: "Up to two supplemental funding requests may be submitted on a grant per student. This would allow the student up to two internship periods up to six months each (i.e., a maximum of 12 months per student)."

PRACTICAL READING, flagged as interpretation, not quotation: because the decision is made internally by a single Program Officer with no panel and no written reviews released, there is no review document to respond to and no rebuttal mechanism. A declined request is handled by talking to the PO — which is also why the DCL pushes you to talk to them before submitting. Two of the eight letters make that conversation mandatory. If the decline was for availability of funds rather than merit (both are named as conditions: "subject to (a) the availability of funds, and (b) merit review"), resubmitting early in the next fiscal year, ahead of the April 15 target, is the obvious move.

FORMAL RECONSIDERATION under PAPPG Chapter IV (90 days to request, 45 days for the AD to respond) is written around declined proposals; whether it reaches a declined supplement request is not addressed in any source checked. Not found — do not promise it to an applicant.

result.deadline_pattern:
Two solicitation cycles per year, on a stable and publicly pre-announced calendar — unusually predictable for DOE SC.

Solicitation 1: opens ~mid-February → due ~first week of May, 5:00 PM ET → offer notification ~first three weeks of September → research start window ~early November to ~1 March.
Solicitation 2: opens ~mid-August → due ~first week of November, 5:00 PM ET → offer notification ~first half of April → research start window ~early June to ~early October.

Every deadline is 5:00 PM Eastern and the online system closes at that minute. Award period is 3–12 consecutive months, and the awardee chooses the start date within the published window.

This mechanism does NOT inherit the DOE SC Open Call structure recorded funder-wide: there is no rolling NOFO, no annual 30 September NOFO close, no per-topic "target dates," and no fiscal-year April–September spillover rule. SCGSR runs on its own fixed twice-yearly competition calendar.
result.loi_deadline:
Not applicable — no letter of intent, no pre-application, no white paper, and no encourage/discourage step. This is a single-stage competition, which is a sharp deviation from the DOE SC funder-wide norm where pre-applications go to PAMS and a formal encourage/discourage decision is issued for every one.

There is, however, a de-facto long-lead prerequisite that functions like a pre-stage and is the single most common reason people miss a cycle: **you cannot submit without a named collaborating DOE National Laboratory scientist who co-develops the proposal and submits a letter of support through the system.** The proposal "must be co-developed by the applicant and the DOE scientist in consultation with the applicant's PhD thesis advisor." Securing that person is the real first deadline. The FAQ tells applicants to discuss the request "well in advance with your graduate thesis advisor and collaborating DOE laboratory scientist, and allow adequate time for them to act on the request," and the collaborator-identification page urges applicants to "initiate the conversation with their thesis advisor and the DOE scientist as early as possible."

Second de-facto long-lead item: the PhD candidacy letter must come from your university registrar or department chair and must certify (a) all required coursework completed and (b) a thesis topic officially approved by your PhD committee, with the approval date. Institutional offices are slow; start this early.

No SAM.gov, no UEI, no EIN, no Grants.gov AOR, no PAMS account, no FedConnect, no FSRS — none of the funder-wide long-lead registrations apply, because the student applies as an individual.
result.review_to_award:
Published end-to-end and much more precise than the SC funder-wide "generally within 6 months / no later than 12 months" regulatory language.

For the cycle now open (2026 Solicitation 2): application due 4 Nov 2026 → **Offer Notification Period April 1–16, 2027** (~5 months from deadline) → about one week to accept ("You will be given about a week to decide if you accept the offer of an award") → **earliest start 7 June 2027, latest start 4 October 2027** (~7 months from deadline to earliest possible start; up to ~11 months if you pick a late start).

The just-completed mirror cycle confirms the shape: 2026 Sol 1 due 6 May 2026 → notification 8–21 Sept 2026 (~4 months) → start window 2 Nov 2026 – 1 Mar 2027.

Practical planning number: budget roughly 5 months from submission to hearing, and 7–11 months from submission to actually being at the lab. A student defending within a year of applying is likely to be unable to use the award.

Review is three sequential stages (workshop deck, slide 18): (1) Eligibility and Compliance Review — "Does the application meet all the guidelines?"; (2) Relevance Review — "Alignment with at least one of the SCGSR Priority Research Areas?"; (3) Merit Based Expert Review by external reviewers — "Each application will be reviewed by external subject matter experts based on the established merit review criteria." The site summarises: "Applications will first be subject to an eligibility and compliance review. All eligible and compliant applications will then be reviewed externally by experts." Final selection rests on peer review plus "other program policy factors (e.g. availability of funds, etc.)."

Notification is by email from the DOE Office of Science direct to the applicant.
result.submission_requirements:
PORTAL — the biggest deviation from the funder-wide norm. **Not Grants.gov and not PAMS.** SCGSR uses its own ORAU-hosted online application system. The programme landing page links https://apps.orau.gov/SCGSR/Account/Login; the September 2026 workshop deck prints https://wdts.orau.gov/scgsr/Account/Login — treat these as the same system reached by two host names and start from the link on the live landing page. The student is the applicant of record; there is no institutional submission, no AOR, no sponsored-projects sign-off and no SF-424.

FIVE REQUIRED COMPONENTS (workshop deck, slide 14):
1. All required fields of the online application system — contact, academic, citizenship/LPR status, professional information, plus advisor and collaborating-scientist contact details. A separate "Research Proposal Information" section collects the proposal abstract, proposed start and end dates, host lab, and collaborating scientist details; this does NOT count against the proposal page limit and "does not need to be repeated in the SCGSR research proposal document."
2. Official graduate transcripts — "all Social Security numbers and/or dates of birth redacted or removed." This is a hard kill: applications containing PII "will be deemed non-compliant and will not be considered," and the deck warns they "will be immediately eliminated from the system." Keep your name on it. Unofficial grade reports are rejected.
3. Letter confirming PhD candidacy — from the university registrar OR academic department chair, confirming the applicant has "completed all the required coursework of the PhD program" and has "a PhD thesis topic officially approved by their official PhD thesis committee (include date of approval)."
4. Research proposal — 3 pages maximum (see format below).
5. Two letters of support — from the primary thesis advisor and from the collaborating DOE lab scientist.

PROPOSAL FORMAT (verbatim from the SCGSR Research Proposal Guidelines PDF): PDF only ("designated as 'filename.pdf'"); "Pages must have margins of one inch around the text (top, bottom, left, right), and use a sans serif font (e.g., Calibri, Arial, Helvetica, etc.) 11 points or larger, single-spaced. Page numbers must be indicated in the bottom right margin." Length "is limited to a total of three (3) pages. Any page beyond this limit will not be considered for the review. References do not count towards the three-page limit and can be provided in one (1) separate page." Figures: "Project descriptions may contain embedded figures, but the entire proposal should be legible when printed in black and white ... and the inclusion of figures must not result in exceeding the page limit" — i.e. figures DO count, unlike references. Enforcement is silent truncation: "If a proposal (excluding the 1-page reference section) contains more than three pages, the additional pages will not be included as part of the application."

REQUIRED PROPOSAL ELEMENTS, in order: (a) Proposal Title on the first line, identical to the title entered in the online system; (b) applicant's first and last name; (c) Body covering five numbered items — 1. Overall Goal (problem/fundamental question/critical barrier and why it matters); 2. Background (relation to the doctoral thesis, gaps in current knowledge, prior and preliminary work, and "connections of the proposed SCGSR research to the research activities of the collaborating DOE National Laboratory scientist, and/or how relevant facilities, instrumentation or capabilities ... will uniquely enable the proposed research"); 3. Specific Aims; 4. Approach and expected results (including potential problems and mitigations — "Reviewers should have a clear idea of what exactly you will be doing once you start working at the lab"); 5. Timeline of major tasks, as narrative, bullets or a table. Then 6. References (≤1 page, superscript consecutive numbering, full author list, title, journal, year, volume, pages, DOI; ">8 authors" may use "et al").

LETTERS OF SUPPORT — these are structured FORMS, not free letters, and that detail saves your referees hours. The deck is blunt: "The letters are actually FORMS! ⇒ Tell them: 1) not to spend time preparing a letter!!! 2) not to wait until the last minute!!!" Four prompted topics for the thesis advisor, five to six for the collaborating scientist. Both must give how long and in what capacity they have known you, your preparedness, the importance of the project, and explicit "verification that they have read and approved the applicant's proposed SCGSR research project." Submission is system-only: "Letters of support can only be received through the online application system" — you enter their contact details, the system emails them, they fill the form. You can see receipt status; "It is the applicant's responsibility to remind their graduate thesis advisor and collaborating DOE laboratory scientist that they must submit their individual letters of support before the application deadline." Both scientist and advisor are auto-notified when you upload the proposal.

REVIEW CRITERIA, with published scores (deck slide 23) — write directly to these: **1. Scientific and/or Technical Merit (score 0–6)** — is the research well-conceived with clear understanding of the challenges; is the method and approach appropriate; is the applicant sufficiently prepared; "Are the DOE laboratory resources adequate? If applicable, has the necessary access to a scientific user facility been secured?" **2. Relevance to Graduate Thesis Research and Training (score 0–4)** — potential to make a significant contribution to the PhD thesis; will it enhance training and research skills. Merit is weighted 6:4 over training relevance.

SCOPE TRAPS: SCGSR funds "Hypothesis driven research: Fundamental research (NOT applied research)" and method/instrument development only "when aimed to enable fundamental research, or if it is part of a large fundamental science experiment." Explicitly not supported: exploratory work, human health. The proposal must address the aims of at least one of the ~56 SCGSR Priority Research Areas for the current cycle across six SC programme offices plus Isotope R&D — these are re-published each cycle, so read the current list, not last year's. Separate warning from the deck: using a DOE scientific user facility "If you want to use them: SEPARATE PROPOSAL!!!" — user-facility access is its own application and the merit criteria ask whether you have secured it.

HARD PROCEDURAL RULES: "Only complete applications submitted by the deadline will be considered"; no supplementary materials after the deadline; the system permits placeholder text or blank PDFs while drafting, which you must remember to replace. The workshop advises avoiding AI as decoration in the relevance section: "AI is not a magic term, if included must be in a thoughtful intentional and useful way."
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
WHAT DISQUALIFIES YOU

1. Having already worked at the lab you are proposing. This is the exclusion most people trip over. "Graduate students who are currently conducting research at a DOE laboratory/facility are not eligible to apply to conduct research at the same DOE laboratory/facility, but may apply to conduct their graduate thesis research at a different DOE laboratory/facility." The compliance-review slide operationalises it as "New Research Experience: <3 Months work at the proposed National Lab." The programme is buying you a new environment, not subsidising the one you are in.

2. Re-proposing work already funded by SCGSR. "An application whose SCGSR research proposal has the same scope as that of a previously awarded SCGSR application will not be considered." (The How to Apply page states this more loosely as duplicate proposals from previous award cycles will "NOT be considered" — see resubmission note for the drift risk.)

3. Exceeding the 12-month lifetime ceiling. Multiple awards are allowed "provided that the cumulative total of the award periods for all SCGSR awards do not exceed 12 months."

4. Holding an unfinished SCGSR award at the new start date. "If a current SCGSR Awardee is successful in competing for a new SCGSR award, the Awardee must successfully complete the current award and fulfill all their obligations and award terms and conditions associated with that award before the award start date of the new award to be eligible to receive that award."

5. BES ONLY — a proximity-plus-co-funding test with no analogue elsewhere in DOE SC (deck slide 20, "Can the collaboration happen without SCGSR support?"). University-to-lab distance ≤5 miles: ineligible regardless. Between 5 and 50 miles: ineligible if the PhD advisor and the lab scientist are co-funded on the project the applicant is working on; eligible if they are not. Greater than 50 miles: eligible either way. If you are applying through BES and live near your target lab, check this table before writing anything.

6. Status bars: not a US citizen or lawful permanent resident at time of application; under 18; not yet a PhD candidate — ineligible if the applicant "has not obtained the Ph.D. candidacy with an established thesis project at the time of application"; master's students; not enrolled full-time for the duration of the proposed project; not at an accredited US college or university; or outside the supported fields (physics, chemistry, materials sciences, non-medical biology, mathematics, engineering, computer or computational sciences, select environmental sciences).

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES YOUR ELIGIBILITY — this half matters as much, and applicants routinely self-reject on all four counts

1. Other fellowships do NOT disqualify you. There is no bar on holding NSF GRFP, DOE CSGF, NDSEG, university or departmental support concurrently. The obligation is disclosure, not surrender: "Applicants are required to disclose current sources and levels of graduate student support at the time of applying; awardees will be required to report concurrent other funding sources and expenses incurred during the award period." SCGSR is deliberately "supplemental support for the incremental costs associated with conducting the proposed research project" and sits on top of your existing support. Caveat on amount, not eligibility: the stipend is "up to $3,600" per month and the actual figure is set with consideration of research duration, home location and concurrent federal funding — so other federal money can reduce the payment while leaving you fully eligible.

2. A previous SCGSR award does not bar you. You may hold more than one, subject to the 12-month cumulative cap and a genuinely different scope.

3. Being declined costs you nothing. There is no cap on attempts, no waiting period, no penalty. "You must reapply and submit a new application to the current solicitation."

4. Already working at a DOE lab does not bar you from the programme — only from that lab. You "may apply to conduct their graduate thesis research at a different DOE laboratory/facility."

5. None of the funder-wide DOE SC prior-award machinery applies here. There is no ECRP-style lifetime cap on competitions entered, no "prior winners permanently ineligible" rule, and no programme-policy preference for PIs not previously supported by SC.

WHEN TO CONTACT WHOM. The programme routes newcomers to the programme manager first, not to the labs: "For prospective applicants who do not know where or how to begin identifying a collaborating laboratory scientist, they should first contact the SCGSR program manager" — who will ask about your research interests and, if it aligns with a priority area, "recommend a list of potential laboratory scientists." The DOE Lab POCs page repeats it: students unsure about identifying a collaborator should "first begin with contacting the SCGSR Program Manager." If you already have a target area, the programme manager confirms alignment with the priority research areas and then recommends scientists. If your advisor already collaborates with a lab, you are told to "consult their thesis advisor and the laboratory scientist on opportunities to expand on the existing collaboration."

FINDING THE COLLABORATING SCIENTIST — the deck gives seven routes: author affiliations on relevant papers; your advisor's network; literature searchers refined by institution; the national laboratory websites (https://www.energy.gov/national-laboratories); the SCGSR list of potential collaborating scientists; the SCGSR publications list (find who already hosts SCGSR students); and emailing sc.scgsr@doe.gov or the programme managers directly. Two supporting directories: a non-exhaustive list of roughly 200+ named lab scientists who want SCGSR collaborators, with email, lab, SC programme alignment and a research blurb (static, not filterable); and a page of named POCs with emails at each of the 17 participating labs/facilities (Ames, Argonne, Brookhaven, Fermilab, General Atomics/DIII-D, Idaho, Los Alamos, Berkeley, Livermore, NETL, NREL, Oak Ridge, PNNL, PPPL, SLAC, Sandia, Savannah River, Jefferson Lab).

HOW TO WRITE THE COLD EMAIL — the deck gives a template, which is unusual and worth using verbatim: lab scientists "are very interested in collaborating! However, they get A LOT of spam, so: 1. Use your school's email address 2. Subject: 'Interest in collaborating on a DOE SCGSR project on xxx' (your topic in 3-4 words!) 3. Cc your advisor 4. Brief description of the SCGSR program. (Essential information: No cost to them!) 5. Brief summary of the work you want to do." Then settle six things up front: overlap of interests; whether they have time; instrumentation/expertise available; accessibility and scheduling of equipment or computing; whether specialised adaptations are needed; and whether you must separately apply to use specific user facilities.
