result.examples_or_samples:
Full funded SCGSR proposals are not published. But there is more usable material here than for most mechanisms, and one item is a genuine annotated sample.

1. ANNOTATED BEFORE/AFTER ABSTRACT — the highest-value item, and the closest thing DOE publishes to a worked sample for SCGSR. The Application Assistance Workshop 1 deck (2026 Solicitation 2, 3 September 2026) prints a real applicant abstract on slide 27 ("MDSD Simulation of Impurities in α-Iron") marked up with the reviewer questions it fails to answer — Problem? Approach? Outcomes? Impact? Connect to Priority Areas? Training? Need of lab resources? Connection to thesis? — and then slide 28 gives "A More Polished Version…" rewritten to hit every one, with the BES priority area named explicitly and the need for lab-specific HPC resources made concrete. Reading slides 26–28 side by side teaches the rhetoric of the mechanism faster than anything else available. URL: https://science.osti.gov/-/media/wdts/scgsr/pdf/Workshops/SCGSR-2026-S2---Application-Assistance-Workshop-1.pdf. The same deck carries a reviewer's own words on what separates strong proposals: "The strongest SCGSR proposals outline both sides of the student-Lab relationship in a balanced manner."

2. WHO ACTUALLY GETS FUNDED — the SCGSR Awards and Publications page posts an accepted-offers spreadsheet per cycle; the 2025 Solicitation 2 file (https://science.osti.gov/-/media/wdts/scgsr/excel/WDTS-SCGSR-Offers-Accepted_2025-S2.xlsx) covers 75 graduate students from 27 states. Use it to see which universities, labs and programme offices actually convert.

3. THE PUBLICATION TRAIL — the same page carries a non-exhaustive list of 1,000+ journal articles coauthored by SCGSR awardees, running from 2015 to 2026 and organised by SC programme (ASCR, BES, BER, FES, HEP, NP, IRP, ARDAP). Each entry links the awardee to their cohort, programme, host laboratory and named collaborating scientist, with DOI. The deck recommends this explicitly as a way to find a collaborator — it is effectively a searchable record of which lab scientists have already hosted SCGSR students and what came out of it.

4. RESEARCH HIGHLIGHTS — https://science.osti.gov/wdts/scgsr/SCGSR-Highlights carries 13 funded-project profiles spanning 2017–2024, each with the awardee's name, institution, cohort, host lab and collaborator, a plain-language research summary and the resulting publication. Examples: Aleksei Sorokin (Illinois Institute of Technology, 2024 S1), Henry H. Wong (UCLA, 2022 S2), Robert Underwood (Clemson, 2018 S2).

5. THE SCORED CRITERIA THEMSELVES — DOE publishes the merit review criteria with their point ranges (Scientific/Technical Merit 0–6; Relevance to Graduate Thesis Research and Training 0–4) and the sub-questions reviewers answer. Treat these as the outline of the proposal.

CAUTIONS. There is no DOE sample-proposal library for SCGSR and no published abstracts of funded SCGSR projects (unlike the Early Career Research Program, which posts per-fiscal-year PDFs of funded abstracts — those are a useful stylistic model but a different mechanism, different career stage and different review). Nothing indicates that declined SCGSR applicants receive their reviewer comments; the PAMS "View Reviews" route recorded funder-wide applies to SC grant applications, not to this appointment-based award. The best remaining route to a real narrative is the same as everywhere: ask a senior student in your department or your lab POC to show you a funded one.
result.resubmission_note:
None of the DOE SC funder-wide resubmission machinery applies — no SF-424, no New/Renewal/Revision choice, no PAMS withdrawal mechanism, no "substantially revised in light of merit reviewer comments" bar.

The rule is simply: a declination ends that application, and you start over. "You must reapply and submit a new application to the current solicitation." Applications are not carried forward or automatically reconsidered in a later cycle. There is no cap on the number of attempts, no waiting period, no introduction page and no A-number. Because the programme runs twice a year, a declined applicant can be back in the next competition roughly six months later.

The one hard bar is against re-proposing funded work, not declined work: "An application whose SCGSR research proposal has the same scope as that of a previously awarded SCGSR application will not be considered."

DRIFT RISK worth flagging: the How to Apply page states more loosely that duplicate proposals from previous award cycles will "NOT be considered," which could be read as covering previously *submitted* proposals rather than previously *awarded* ones. The Eligibility page's "previously awarded" wording is the specific and more recent-sounding formulation, and it is consistent with the FAQ's instruction to reapply. A declined applicant reusing their own scope should confirm with the programme manager rather than rely on either page.

Practical consequence: unlike the SC Open Call, you are not required to demonstrate revision against reviewer comments — and since there is no documented release of reviewer comments to SCGSR applicants, you could not do so anyway. Improvement has to come from the published criteria, the workshops and office hours, and conversation with the programme manager and your lab collaborator.
unresolved: Selectivity / success rate — NOT FOUND. DOE publishes awards made (75 accepted offers in 2025 Solicitation 2, 27 states) but does not publish the number of applications received in any cycle, so no success rate can be computed. Do not infer one.

Whether declined SCGSR applicants receive reviewer comments or any written feedback — NOT FOUND on any SCGSR page or in the FAQ. The PAMS 'View Reviews' route recorded funder-wide covers SC grant applications, not this appointment-based award; do not assume it carries over.

Whether an applicant may submit more than one application in a single solicitation cycle, or name more than one host lab / priority research area in one application — NOT FOUND. The FAQ and guidelines describe one collaborating scientist and one host laboratory per application but never state whether multiple applications are permitted.

Exact 2027 Solicitation 1 dates — the Key Dates page gives only 'February 2027 / May 2027 / September 2027 / November 2027 – March 2028' and labels them 'All Dates are tentative'. Treat the months as the pattern, not as dates.

Two different application-portal host names are published concurrently — apps.orau.gov/SCGSR/Account/Login on the programme landing page and wdts.orau.gov/scgsr/Account/Login in the September 2026 workshop deck. Not established whether one redirects to the other or one is stale. Applicants should follow the link on the live landing page.

Annual, on fixed calendar dates that do not move year to year. Cycle: guidelines posted Dec 16 → nomination requests to the 50 university presidents Jan 31 → online system opens Feb 15 → institutional nominations due Mar 15 → full application + all four reference letters due Apr 20, 5:00 pm PT → Advisory Panel review May–Sep → Panel convenes and Board approves Sep → announcement Oct 15 → award period begins Oct 16.

result.loi_deadline:
The gate that replaces an LOI is the presidential nomination, due March 15 — roughly five weeks before the April 20 application deadline.

Mechanics, from the funder: "Every year, the Foundation invites the presidents of 50 universities to nominate two early-career professors each from their institutions." Nominations are "requested in January of each year from the presidents of 50 universities selected by the Advisory Panel. Up to two nominations may be made by the president of each institution." The nomination form "should not include any written comments" — it is an identification form, not an evaluated document. And: "nominees will not be able to access the online application system until they have been identified to the Packard Foundation."

Consequence for timeline planning: the competitive selection you must win first is internal and happens before March 15. The FAQ is explicit that individuals cannot apply directly and directs candidates to "your university's Office of Sponsored Research or Department Chair" for the internal nomination process. Each campus sets its own internal deadline; Packard does not publish these, and none is recorded here.

Optional pre-nomination route: the Foundation runs "Nomination Office Hours" for faculty with eligibility questions — see program_officer_contact.
result.review_to_award:
About six months from application to notification, with the earliest start the day after notification. All dates are fixed rather than approximate.

- Application deadline Apr 20 → review May–Sep: "Fellowship Advisory Panel conducts a detailed review of 100 applications and reference letters." (100 applications = 50 institutions x 2 nominees, so the nominee-stage success rate is 20/100.)
- September: "The Advisory Panel convenes and selects 20 award recommendations, which the Board of Trustees then approves."
- Notification Oct 15: "Foundation announces Packard Fellowship Awards on website." Note this is a public website announcement, not a private notice.
- Earliest start Oct 16: "Pending signed grant agreement, Fellowships award period begins October 16." The FAQ confirms: "The Packard Fellowship grant begins in mid-October of the year the grant is awarded. The Fellowship is a five-year grant."

So: ~6 months submission-to-notification, ~1 day notification-to-start, ~13 months from the internal campus deadline to first funds. No funder-wide norm was established for this funder, so there is no deviation to report against.

MATERIAL CHANGE TO THE AWARD, effective with the cycle now opening — the Foundation announced on 2026-09-10: "Beginning with the 2027 class, each Packard Fellow will receive $1.017 million in unrestricted funding over five years, an increase from the current $875,000 award," and "Fellowship awards will increase incrementally over the following three years, reaching $1.065 million beginning with the 2030 class." Fellow count stays at "approximately 20 Fellows" annually. The existing CSV row's $875,000 is correct for 2026 and earlier but stale for the next cycle a reader would actually apply to.
result.submission_requirements:
Submitted through the Foundation's own system at fellows.packard.org (not a common portal). Nominees cannot access it until the institution has identified them to the Foundation.

1. NOMINATION FORM from the university president — name, contact details, email, departmental affiliation, sponsoring institution, president's name and address. It "should not include any written comments." Due March 15.

2. ONLINE SUBMISSION by the nominee: contact information; departmental and institutional affiliation(s); disciplinary field(s); educational background; professional positions held; honors and awards; "Current external research support"; publications; and the research statement.

3. RESEARCH STATEMENT — the only narrative, and unusually short. It "should describe why the research is important and outline the general goals for the next five years. The statement should also indicate, in general, how funds will be used. This does not need to be a detailed budget and will not be binding on the actual use of funds." Hard limit: "limited to 1,400 words (maximum two pages of text, prepared in 12-point font with 1-inch margins). If there are relevant figures, images or references, please include these separately on a third page." So: 2 pages of text + 1 optional page for figures/references. There is no separate budget, no biosketch form, no data management plan, no institutional budget justification.

4. FOUR LETTERS OF RECOMMENDATION, with a specific and easily-missed composition rule:
   - One from the nominee's department head, describing "first-hand knowledge of the nominee's ability to do creative research." Joint appointments "may submit a single letter signed by both department heads." Emphasis "should be given to information not available in other letters."
   - Three from people OUTSIDE the nominee's university "who are personally familiar with the nominee's work and creative ability."
   - "At least one recommendation must be from a person who has had no supervisory or collaborative contact with the nominee." This rules out your PhD advisor, postdoc PI and co-authors for that slot — plan it early.
   - Letters "should not exceed two pages" in 12-point font with 1-inch margins; uploaded to the system or emailed directly to Foundation staff.
   - "the referee will not have access to the online system until the nominee enters their name and contact information into the system" — the referee chain is blocked until the nominee acts.

5. TIMING TRAP: "All applications and all reference letters are due" by the same April 20, 5:00 pm PT deadline. Letters get no grace period after the application.

INSTITUTIONAL SIGN-OFF: the presidential nomination is the sign-off, and it happens five weeks before the application. Note the award carries an institutional share — of the $175,000 paid each year, "$17,500 is available to the university as compensation for administrative costs," with $157,500 for the Fellow's use.

Deviation worth flagging: this is a notably light application by US standards — one 1,400-word statement and four letters, "few funding restrictions and limited paperwork requirements" in the funder's words. The selection burden sits in the letters and in the internal campus competition, not in the paperwork.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
Both halves, and the headline is that the excluding half is nearly empty.

WHAT DISQUALIFIES — no prior or concurrent award does. Across the eligibility page, the FAQ and the full 2026 Guidelines PDF, the Foundation names no grant, fellowship or award that makes a candidate ineligible. There is no equivalent of the NIH K/R01 interaction here. Holding an NSF CAREER, an NIH award, a DOE Early Career award, a Sloan Research Fellowship or similar is nowhere stated to bar a nomination. "Current external research support" appears only as a DISCLOSURE field on the application form, not as an eligibility test. (Stated as an absence after reading the complete guidelines text, not as a positive funder claim.)

The only funding-related statement is competitive, not categorical: "The Fellowship Program provides support for highly creative researchers early in their careers; faculty members who are well-established and well-funded are less likely to receive the award." Reinforced by scope: "The Foundation emphasizes support for innovative individual research that involves the Fellows, their students, and junior colleagues, rather than extensions or components of large-scale, ongoing research programs." So heavy existing funding is a disadvantage at review, not a bar at the door — and proposing an extension of a large funded programme is the thing actually penalised.

WHAT ACTUALLY EXCLUDES YOU is institution, career stage and research area:
- Institution: "Candidates must be faculty members at one of the 50 Invited Institutions." If your university is not on the list you cannot apply at all, and the FAQ confirms "nominations are only open to those universities." The 50 are named in the guidelines PDF (p.4).
- Career stage: "within the first three years of their faculty careers," defined for the 2026 cycle as initial faculty appointments that "began no earlier than May 31, 2023, and no later than May 31, 2026" — a rolling three-year window that shifts one year each cycle. The 2027 window will be stated in the guidelines posting 2026-12-16; it is not recorded here because Packard has not yet published it.
- Must be "eligible to serve as principal investigators."
- Research area: "Candidates engaged in research in the social sciences will not be considered." Also out of scope: "clinical research, research associated with the design and construction of large national facilities such as accelerators and space stations, and applied research of direct relevance to national security."

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY:
- Citizenship does not matter. "Packard Fellowships are awarded without regard to age, race, national origin, citizenship, religion, gender, sexual orientation, or physical disability." For an international early-career hire at a US invited institution, the faculty appointment is what counts, not a visa or passport. This is the single most under-known eligibility fact for this mechanism.
- Joint appointments are accommodated (single letter signed by both department heads).
- Eligible disciplines are broad: "physics, chemistry, mathematics, biology, astronomy, computer science, earth science, ocean science, and all branches of engineering."

THE REAL CONFLICT an applicant faces is internal, not federal: each president may nominate only two people per year. Your binding competition is a colleague in another department, decided on your own campus before March 15. Optimising your relationship with the research development office matters more here than your grant portfolio does.

A second, high-value target for conversation: the guidelines name all twelve Fellowship Advisory Panel members who actually read the applications — Richard B. Alley (Penn State), Kristi S. Anseth (Colorado Boulder), Erich Jarvis (Rockefeller), Celeste M. Nelson (Princeton), Andrei Y. Okounkov (Columbia), Franklin M. "Lynn" Orr (Stanford), Stephen R. Quake (Stanford), Robert J. Reviewers are senior scientists spanning many fields, not specialists in yours — which is the practical reason the 1,400-word statement must open with why the work matters to a non-specialist. The Foundation publishes NO sample application, annotated example or successful abstract for this mechanism. Verified by reading the whole guidelines PDF, the eligibility page, the FAQ and the program landing page. Substitutes, in order of usefulness:

Because this is a limited submission, that office ran an internal competition every January and holds past internal nomination packets and often the statements of people it went on to nominate. Use it to identify the last two or three cohorts in your discipline at institutions like yours, then read those people's lab pages and the work they published in their fellowship's first two years. That reverse-engineers what a winning statement looked like better than a sample would.

3. ANNUAL CLASS ANNOUNCEMENTS in the funder's newsroom (https://www.packard.org/news/), posted each October 15. I could not retrieve an October 2025 class announcement — /news/page/2/ returns 404 and this session's web-search budget was exhausted, so the archive route beyond the first page is unverified. Not applicable: there is no NIH-style RePORTER equivalent, no public abstract archive, and no funded-application library for this program.

result.loi_deadline:
No LOI and no pre-proposal for this mechanism. Confirmed three ways: (1) neither the Pathway page nor the Call for Nominations PDF nor the Initiator Application Instructions mentions any LOI or pre-proposal; (2) ADA's Current Funding Opportunities table shows an explicit "LOI:" line for the mechanisms that have one (e.g. "Type 1 Diabetes RFA (2026) LOI: April 28, 2026 Full Submission: June 24, 2026"; "Innovative Research for Enhanced Diabetes Prevention and Care in Primary Care Settings LOI: December 4, 2025 Full Submission: February 19, 2026") while the Pathway row shows a single date ("Pathway to Stop Diabetes—2026 May 19, 2026") — a clean negative control on the funder's own page; (3) the projected funding timeline table lists only four events, with no LOI stage.

BUT THE GATE THAT REPLACES IT — do not read "no LOI" as "no earlier stage." Institutional nomination is a hard prerequisite: "candidates will be identified through institutional nominations. Each institution is allowed a maximum of two (2) nominations per grant cycle." ADA sets NO separate earlier nomination deadline — nomination materials ride the same May 19 deadline inside SmartSimple: "Nomination materials must be submitted through SmartSimple... The Association will not accept such materials separately after the application submission deadline. Applications submitted without the appropriate nomination forms are considered incomplete and will be administratively disapproved." The earlier deadline is therefore set by the applicant's own institution, not by ADA (INFERENCE, structurally forced by the 2-per-institution cap and the penalty below — ADA does not publish institutional internal dates).
result.review_to_award:
Long, and lengthening — materially longer than the ~3–4 month turnaround typical of disease-advocacy project grants.

2026 cycle: submission Tue May 19, 2026 → notification Mon Nov 23, 2026 = 188 days (~6.2 months); notification → earliest start Mon Feb 1, 2027 = 70 days; total submission → earliest money = 258 days (~8.5 months).
2025 cycle: Jul 23, 2025 → Nov 17, 2025 = 117 days (~3.9 mo); → start Jan 1, 2026 = 45 days.
2024 cycle: Jul 17, 2024 → Dec 2, 2024 = 138 days (~4.5 mo); → start Jan 1, 2025 = 30 days.

So plan on 4–6 months to a decision and roughly 8–9 months from submission to first funds. Review is by the Pathway Mentor Advisory Group: "Applications will be subjected to confidential scientific review by the Mentor Advisory Group." Notification route: "Notification of the funding decision will be sent directly to the applicant via email... Applicants will be notified of their application's final funding decision only following the conclusion of the review process" — i.e. no interim score or summary-statement release, unlike NIH.

Post-award conditions that affect the real start: IRB/IACUC may be deferred to just-in-time ("If approval is not obtained by the application deadline, a just-in-time submission by the funding start date of the award is acceptable"), but "The Association requires IRB and/or IACUC approval within ninety (90) days of the award letter being sent. Award payments will be held until necessary approvals are received."

Phase 2 is not automatic — it is a second gate: "Phase two support will be approved by the ADA Research Programs team contingent upon adequate progress in phase one, as well as the receipt and approval of documentation verifying that: 1. The candidate has obtained a faculty appointment at an accredited research institution. 2. The institution has agreed to provide adequate laboratory space... and adequate time (75% effort)... 3. The institution provides the candidate with an adequate and protected start-up package."

Minor funder error worth knowing: the Call for Nominations PDF writes "Friday February 1st, 2027"; Feb 1 2027 is a Monday, and the web page correctly says "Monday, February 1, 2027". Treat the web page as authoritative.
result.submission_requirements:
Submitted via SmartSimple (ADA's grant management system, diabetes.us-2.smartsimple.com); "Emails and word processing files submitted outside of SmartSimple will not be accepted." Body of the Application must be ONE combined PDF; "multiple attachments and other formats will not be accepted." Single PI only: "only one person must be specified as the Principal Investigator and Co-Principal Investigators are not permitted for these grants."

WHERE IT DEVIATES MOST FROM THE NORM — the research plan is tiny and the narrative is personal:
- Research Strategy: 4-page maximum, figures included in the limit. Explicitly NOT an NIH-style plan: "The research strategy section is flexible in format and does not require a detailed project plan, description of methods or preliminary data." Must address (a) scientific question(s)/problem(s), (b) approach(es), (c) significance and potential impact, (d) "potential risks and challenges, and how they will be overcome."
- Annotated Publications: 1-page max, exactly 5 references — "your five most impactful publications to date and briefly describe the qualities of these publications that make them notable," demonstrating independence and innovation.
- Essay Questions: 1-page max for ALL THREE answers: (a) what makes the strategy innovative and "uniquely suited for this program rather than a traditional research grant program"; (b) most significant accomplishments and the personal qualities behind them (evidence of "ability to challenge paradigms, identify opportunities and take intellectual risks"); (c) future career plans and "long-term commitment to diabetes research."
- References: optional, 1-page max.
- Open Data and Resource Sharing Plan: 1-page max (or 1-page waiver request, only for Human Subject Protection / Superseding Regulations / Intellectual Property). "the data and resource sharing plan will not impact the application score, it is a requirement for submission."
- Online-only fields (must NOT appear in the PDF): Scientific Abstract 250 words, Lay Abstract 250 words, and a distinctive "Move the Needle" statement, 150-word maximum, on how the research "has the potential to significantly improve the lives of people at risk of diabetes or living with the disease." Avoid non-ASCII symbols — "any non-ASCII symbols will be converted to question marks ('?') upon submission" (write "alpha", not the Greek letter).
- Table of Contents is MANDATORY and numbered page 1: "Applications that do not include a Table of Contents will be administratively disapproved." Use ADA's Initiator ToC template; enter "N/A" rather than leaving a page number blank.
- Nothing extra: "the Association will not accept other materials that are not listed in the Table of Contents. Inclusion of any additional materials will result in administrative disapproval of application."
- Formatting: Arial, Helvetica, Palatino Linotype or Georgia; black; 11 pt or larger; ≤15 characters per inch; ≤6 lines per inch; margins at least one-half inch; single-spacing acceptable; header with last name/first name, footer with page number. "Applications that do not adhere to these formatting requirements will not" be accepted.

THREE LETTERS OF RECOMMENDATION — role-prescribed, not free choice, and they gate submission:
Addressed "Dear Mentor Advisory Group", confidential, uploaded by the referee directly in SmartSimple (applicant enters referee name + email in the Letters of Recommendation tab; referee gets a system link; applicant sees only pending/submitted status). Required roles: (1) Current Mentor — must address ability to advance to independence, ability to innovate and collaborate, and "How the applicant compares to previous trainees (percentile ranking - i.e. in the top 5% of previous trainees)"; (2) Graduate or Medical Training Advisor — potential for significant contributions, innovation/collaboration, same percentile ranking; if not the direct advisor, the writer "must explain their relationship with applicant"; (3) Past or Current Collaborator — potential for significant contributions, ability to innovate and collaborate. Hard stop: "the system will prevent the submission of the application" without all three; "Adding additional letters may cause errors when submitting." Practical warnings from ADA: upload "at least two (2) weeks prior to the submission deadline," and "Due to potential institutional firewall issues, we propose asking your recommenders for a personal email address versus work email address." (Document conflict: the Call for Nominations PDF says letters go "directly through Blackbaud"; the Application Instructions and the SmartSimple Pre-Award FAQ both say SmartSimple, and the live portal is SmartSimple — Blackbaud is a stale reference from ADA's previous system.)

INSTITUTIONAL SIGN-OFF — two separate documents:
(1) A signed Nomination Form (ADA .xlsx template) "certifying that the application has been routed through the usual administrative channels of the sponsoring institution."
(2) An Institutional Nomination Letter inside the Body of the Application PDF, from "Chair of Nominating Committee, Dean of Research, Division Head, etc.", addressed "Dear American Diabetes Association Mentor Advisory Group", and "signed by the institutional representative and co-signed by the Department or Division Head of the applicant." It must: give the rationale for nominating this candidate; certify the full-time position; "ensure that at least 75% of their total time and effort will be allocated to research during the term of this award"; assure academic commitment; and "Outline the institution's plans to support the long-term development of the candidate and specific expectations for the individual's career course."

OTHER COMPONENTS: SciENcv/NIH-format biosketch (collaborator biosketches optional, NIH format, 5-page max); ORCiD iD required; All Sources of Support template; IRB/IACUC approval letter only if already obtained.

EFFORT COMMITMENT: at least 75% of total time on research overall, and "between 75-100% effort towards the Association funded project in phase one and between 50-75% effort towards the Association funded project in phase two."

AI POLICY (effective March 1, 2026 — new, and strict): only "limited, non-substantive tasks" (grammar, formatting, reference management, non-scientific boilerplate). AI "may not be used to draft, edit, or alter any scientific sections of the proposal - including specific aims, research strategy, hypotheses, methodologies, significance, innovation, data, figures, or analytical plans." Any AI use at all requires a formal disclosure "on official institutional letterhead," naming the approved platform and exact sections, "signed by both the PI and Research Officer," appended as the last page of the Research Plan. Modelled on NIH NOT-OD-25-132.

ELIGIBILITY QUIZ: SmartSimple makes you "Complete the eligibility quiz to confirm your eligibility status... Submitted applications that do not meet the eligibility criteria will be administratively disapproved."

Overall: "Application submissions that are incomplete or do not adhere to section page limits will be administratively disapproved." Administrative disapproval is invoked for at least six separate failure modes — ToC missing, extra materials, page limits, formatting, eligibility, missing nomination form.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
THE EXCLUSION (one line, narrow) and THE CARVE-OUT (unusually generous) — both verbatim from the Call for Nominations, Initiator Award Eligibility:

"Initiator award recipients cannot concurrently hold an NIH K99/R00 grant. All other Career Development awards are allowable (unless holding of concurrent awards is prohibited by the other granting agency)."

WHAT THIS MEANS IN PRACTICE:
- DISQUALIFYING: only a concurrent NIH K99/R00. Note "concurrently hold" — the bar is on holding it at the same time, not on ever having applied for one. ADA does not exclude prior K99/R00 applicants, and does not exclude someone who has a pending K99 application.
- EXPLICITLY PRESERVED: every other career-development award — K01, K08, K22, K23, K25, F32, institutional K12/KL2, and non-NIH CDAs (JDRF, Burroughs Wellcome, foundation fellowships). The carve-out is stated affirmatively by ADA, not merely implied by silence.
- THE SECOND-ORDER TRAP: eligibility can be destroyed by the OTHER funder, not by ADA — "unless holding of concurrent awards is prohibited by the other granting agency." Many CDAs impose their own effort or concurrent-support limits. Combined with ADA's 75–100% phase-one effort requirement, the effort arithmetic — not ADA's exclusion list — is what usually blocks a dual hold. Check the other award's terms before assuming ADA's permission is sufficient.

CAREER-STAGE CEILING (functions as an eligibility conflict): "Applicants must currently be in research training positions (i.e. post-doctoral fellowships, research fellowships) and can have no more than seven (7) years of training since their doctoral degree." Taking an independent faculty post before applying moves you out of Initiator and into the sibling Accelerator track.

Also required: MD, PhD, DMD, DO, PharmD, DVM or equivalent; full-time appointment at the sponsoring institution ("Rare exceptions to full-time positions may be granted on a case-by-case basis and must be pre-approved by ADA Research Programs staff prior to application submission"); fellowship position at a university-affiliated or non-profit research institution in the US or US possessions; "permission to work within the U.S., either as U.S. citizens or permanent residents, or with appropriate work visas/permits. Institutional confirmation of permission to work within the U.S. will be required at the time of application submission" — so a work visa is acceptable; this is a work-authorization gate, not a citizenship gate.

THE INSTITUTIONAL CONFLICT THAT MATTERS MOST, AND IS EASIEST TO MISS — you compete against your own colleagues before you compete against the field: "Each institution is allowed a maximum of two (2) nominations per grant cycle: one (1) applicant must be focused on basic science/preclinical research and one (1) applicant must be focused on translational science. Each nomination can be for either of the Pathway Program Award types: Initiator or Accelerator." Two consequences: (a) an Initiator candidate may be squeezed out by a more senior Accelerator candidate from the same institution, because the two award types share the same two slots; (b) "if an institution nominates two (2) applicants with proposed projects covering the same phase of research... one of the submitted applications will be administratively disqualified," and "Nomination of more than the two (2) allowable applicants may result in the administrative disapproval of all nominations from the same institution." Multi-component systems may count as separate institutions: "Individual components of multi-component institutions (e.g., University of California Los Angeles and University of California Berkeley... or Harvard University and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center...) are sufficiently independent to be considered individual institutions. Institutions must have a unique DUNS and/or IPF number to be considered independent." If unclear, ADA invites a direct query: "If there is any uncertainty regarding institutional status for nomination, please contact grantquestions@diabetes.org."

FOR CONTRAST (the sibling track, since postdocs approaching independence often ask): Accelerator applicants "may currently hold independent NIH funding (K, U or R awards, including an initial R01/U01) but must not have applied for (regardless of outcome), or received, an R01/U01 renewal or a second R01/U01 award." Note "regardless of outcome" — merely submitting an R01 renewal ends Accelerator eligibility.
result.program_officer_contact:
No named program officer for this mechanism. The published route is a team mailbox: grantquestions@diabetes.org — "Questions? Please contact Research Programs staff at grantquestions@diabetes.org." (The address is Cloudflare-obfuscated on the live page and renders as "[email protected]" to a plain fetch or to a text scraper; I decoded it from the page's data-cfemail attribute, and it also appears in plaintext three times inside the Call for Nominations PDF, so it is confirmed independently.) Mailing address: ADA National Office, 2451 Crystal Drive, Suite 900, Arlington, VA 22202; 1-800-DIABETES (800-342-2383).

PRE-SUBMISSION CONTACT IS EXPECTED IN TWO SPECIFIC SITUATIONS, both mandatory rather than optional:
- Less-than-full-time appointments: "Rare exceptions to full-time positions may be granted on a case-by-case basis and must be pre-approved by ADA Research Programs staff prior to application submission."
- Institutional-independence questions for the nomination cap: "If there is any uncertainty regarding institutional status for nomination, please contact grantquestions@diabetes.org for clarification."
Also used for portal access problems, post-submission status/contact changes, and if no confirmation email arrives.

There is NO published route for pre-submission scientific consultation on project fit — unlike an NIH program officer, ADA does not offer a "discuss your aims with us" channel for Pathway, and the reviewing body (Mentor Advisory Group) is not contactable.

WHO TO ACTUALLY TALK TO FIRST (the practically important answer): your institution's research development / limited-submissions office, NOT ADA. Because only two nominations per institution are permitted and over-nomination can disqualify every applicant from that institution, the institution must run an internal selection, and its internal deadline is the first real deadline. The nominating signatory is a "Dean of Research, Nominating Committee Chair, Division Chair," co-signed by your Department or Division Head — so the conversation to start is with your department/division head and the research dean's office, ideally as soon as a cycle is announced. (The existence of an internal competition is an INFERENCE forced by ADA's cap and penalty language; ADA does not publish institutional internal deadlines.)

Review body, useful for calibrating who reads the application: the Pathway Mentor Advisory Group, co-chaired by Christopher B. Newgard, PhD (Duke) and Louis H. Philipson, MD, PhD (University of Chicago), with ~24 members spanning basic science through behavioural and health-services research (e.g. Barbara B. Kahn, Rohit N. Kulkarni, Alan R. Saltiel, Sherita Hill Golden, Mary de Groot, Elbert S. Huang, Jill Weissberg-Benchell). Roster is public at the Mentor Advisory Group URL. This is a generalist panel, which is why ADA tells you to write "with a level of detail appropriate for reviewers who are knowledgeable of the field, but who may not be directly involved in the proposed area of research."
result.examples_or_samples:
NO funded application, sample abstract, or annotated example is published for the Initiator Award. ADA releases nothing comparable to an NIH sample-application library. Saying so plainly matters — an applicant should not waste time hunting for one. What DOES exist, in descending order of usefulness:

1. OFFICIAL FILL-IN TEMPLATES (the closest thing to a starter kit, all linked from the Pathway opportunity page under "Application Materials"):
- Sample Institutional Nomination Letter: /sites/dpro/files/2026-01/sample-institution-nomination-letter-template.docx — an actual model letter; hand this to your dean's office, since a non-compliant nomination letter is an administrative-disapproval risk.
- Initiator Table of Contents Template: /sites/dpro/files/2026-01/initiator-table-of-contents-template.docx — mandatory, and the instructions reproduce a worked EXAMPLE ToC showing the exact required section order: 1. Annotated Publications (1 p, 5 refs), 2. Essay Question Responses (1 p), 3. Research Strategy (4 p), 4. References (optional, 1 p), 5. Open Data Sharing Resource Plan (1 p), 6. Nomination Letter, 7. Collaborator Biosketches (optional), 8. Letters of Support, 9. IRB/IACUC approval.
- Nomination Form: /sites/dpro/files/2026-01/pathway-nomination-form.xlsx
- All Sources of Support Template: /sites/dpro/files/2026-01/all-sources-of-support-template.docx
- Open Data and Resource Sharing Plan Waiver Form: /sites/dpro/files/2026-01/open-data-and-resource-sharing-plan-waiver.docx
- SmartSimple Pre-Award FAQ (step-by-step portal walkthrough incl. reference-letter mechanics and troubleshooting): /sites/dpro/files/2026-01/smartsimple-preaward-faq.upated1.2026.pdf

2. FUNDED-PROJECT EXEMPLARS (titles + lay summaries + awardee quotes, on the Pathway landing page) — the best available signal of what wins. 2026 recipients include: Jessie Barra, PhD (Post-Doctoral Fellow, University of Florida Diabetes Institute) "Immune Modeling and Intervention in Type 1 Diabetes Using Engineered Stem Cell-Derived β-Cells"; Sagar Bapat, MD PhD (UCSF) "Living Therapeutics: Development of a novel T cell therapy to enhance thermogenic function of adipose tissue"; Rebecca Voorhees, PhD (Caltech) "Dissecting the role of ER stress in the pathogenesis of diabetes mellitus"; Christina Astley, MD ScD (Harvard/Boston Children's) "Dysglycemia progression in diabetes using continuous glucose monitoring and artificial intelligence"; Marissa Burgermaster, PhD (UT Austin) "Nutri: A Clinic-Cluster Randomized Trial..."; Tinashe Chikowore, MSc PhD (Brigham/Harvard) "Optimizing dietary intake for global diabetes prevention..."; Angela Trude, MS PhD (NYU Steinhardt) "OPT-TEEN: Optimization trial to empower selection of nutritious foods." Note the deliberate basic-to-population spread, mirroring the two-nomination-slot rule. CAVEAT/INFERENCE: ADA does not label which recipients got Initiator vs Accelerator; Barra is the only one listed at postdoctoral rank, so by the eligibility rules she is almost certainly the Initiator awardee — treat as inference, not funder-stated.

3. AWARDEE ROSTER 2014–2025 (~49 names with institution and year) at /research-grants/pathway-stop-diabetes/previous-pathway-awardees — names, institutions and years only; no award type, no titles, no abstracts. Use it to find people at your own or a peer institution who have been through the process and can describe the internal nomination competition. ADA states the program "has successfully propelled 50 scientists into independent faculty positions."

4. FREE EXPERT REVIEW OF YOUR DRAFT — the single most actionable resource, and easy to miss because ADA buries it in a "Researcher Resources" paragraph: the NIDDK-funded National Center for Engagement in Diabetes Research (CEDER) "offers expert guidance, feedback, and collaboration opportunities to support the design, implementation, evaluation, and dissemination of diabetes-related research and programs, including reviewing grant applications. To request a free CEDER consultation and studio services, complete this form." Best suited to community-engaged/clinical/population proposals.

5. REVIEW CRITERIA AS A WRITING CHECKLIST (published, and short enough to write against directly): Principal Investigator — "Proven ability to establish independent research program," "Proven ability for creativity, collaboration, and innovation," "Institutional commitment"; Research Strategy — "Innovation and creativity," "Potential impact for understanding/treatment of diabetes," "Clarity of thought and approach." Framing: "Scientific excellence is the primary benchmark... with an emphasis on the investigator's potential to significantly transform diabetes through translational research ('moving the needle')." The 2026 call adds a stated tilt: "This call for nominations will prioritize translational applications that move knowledge and discovery gained from basic research to its eventual translation into patient and population benefit." Also read the AI policy PDF (/sites/dpro/files/2026-03/ada-Research-Programs-AI-Policy-for-Grants-3-3-26-FINAL.pdf) before drafting — the disclosure requirement needs a Research Officer signature and therefore institutional lead time.
result.resubmission_note: No resubmission policy is published for this mechanism — neither permitted nor prohibited in any of the three governing documents (opportunity page, Call for Nominations, Initiator Application Instructions). There is no resubmission/"A1" category, no introduction-to-resubmission page allowance in the Body of the Application contents, and no response-to-reviewers section in the mandatory Table of Contents — structurally, the application has no place to put one. Given the design (institutional re-nomination required each cycle, hard 7-year post-degree ceiling), a repeat attempt is in practice a fresh nomination competing for one of the institution's two slots, not a formal resubmission. Because ADA "will be notified of their application's final funding decision only following the conclusion of the review process" and releases no critiques or summary statements, there is also no reviewer feedback to respond to. NOT FOUND as an explicit funder statement — do not record as "allowed" or "not allowed"; record as unpublished. The 7-year ceiling is the real constraint on re-trying: a candidate at year 6 has one cycle left, and since the calendar slot drifts by months, that may amount to a single genuine shot. Worth querying grantquestions@diabetes.org directly, as this is a real gap in ADA's published rules.
unresolved: NEXT CYCLE DATES (2027) — not published as of 2026-09-18. The live page still shows the closed 2026 cycle. Because the deadline slot moved Jul 17 2024 -> Jul 23 2025 -> May 19 2026, no date can be projected responsibly. Re-check https://professional.diabetes.org/research-grants/current-funding-opportunities around Jan-Feb 2027.

RESUBMISSION POLICY — genuinely unpublished (not merely unfound). Absent from all three governing documents; the mandatory Table of Contents has no slot for a resubmission introduction. Candidate question for grantquestions@diabetes.org.

SELECTIVITY — no success rate, application count, or number of awards per cycle published anywhere. Only indirect signals: ~49 awardees over 2014-2025 (both tracks combined), 2 nominations per institution per cycle, and recent cohorts of 5-6 per year across BOTH Initiator and Accelerator.

INITIATOR vs ACCELERATOR SPLIT among awardees — ADA never labels which awardee received which track, on either the awardee roster or the recipient profiles. The identification of Jessie Barra (2026) as the likely Initiator awardee is my inference from her postdoctoral rank, not a funder statement.

NUMBER OF INITIATOR AWARDS PER CYCLE — not stated; the two award types share one undifferentiated applicant pool and one Mentor Advisory Group review, so the Initiator-specific hit rate cannot be derived.

INSTITUTIONAL INTERNAL NOMINATION DEADLINES — set by each applicant's institution, months before ADA's deadline; not published by ADA and necessarily institution-specific. The EXISTENCE of an internal competition is a structural inference from the 2-per-institution cap plus the all-nominations-disapproved penalty, not an ADA statement.

DOCUMENT CONFLICT — the Call for Nominations PDF says recommendation letters are submitted 'directly through Blackbaud by the referee' while the Initiator Application Instructions and the SmartSimple Pre-Award FAQ both say SmartSimple. SmartSimple is almost certainly correct (it is the live portal and the majority of documents); Blackbaud appears to be a stale reference to ADA's prior system. Not authoritatively resolved by the funder.

FUNDER DATE TYPO — the Call for Nominations PDF gives 'Friday February 1st, 2027' for the earliest award start; Feb 1 2027 is a Monday, and the web page says 'Monday, February 1, 2027'. Web page treated as authoritative.

2025 CYCLE AWARD-YEAR LABELLING — the landing page heading reads '2025 Pathway Awardees' while every profile beneath is tagged '2026 Pathway to Stop Diabetes Grant Recipient'; the roster page separately lists a 2025 cohort of 6 and no 2021 cohort. ADA's own award-year labelling is internally inconsistent; cohort-year attribution should not be treated as reliable.

STIPEND/SALARY CAP DETAIL — the instructions reference salary 'based on a full-time, 12-month appointment at the PI's' institution; the exact cap language was not fully extracted and lives in the budget section of the Initiator Application Instructions and the Pathway Grant Stipulations PDF.

TOOLING NOTE — this session's WebSearch budget (200/200) was exhausted before any search ran, so every finding above comes from direct fetches of ADA's own pages and PDFs plus Internet Archive snapshots; no search index was used. professional.diabetes.org served a plain curl fetch fine (HTTP 200), but obfuscates the contact email via Cloudflare, so a text-only scrape yields '[email protected]' rather than the real address.

result.program_name: Pew Latin American Fellows Program in the Biomedical Sciences
result.next_deadline:
NOTE ON THE "NO DATED DEADLINE" QUESTION: nothing here forbids a dated deadline. The house rule forbids an INVENTED date, not a sourced one. Where Pew publishes a calendar date I give it verbatim below; where it has not yet published one I say so and give the projection separately, labelled.

STATUS AS OF 2026-09-18: the cycle just closed. The 2027-class deadline was Aug. 19, 2026 — 30 days ago. Pew's own words (To Apply page, still live today): "Applications must be submitted electronically by 5 p.m. ET on Aug. 19, 2026." This is the only Pew biomedical deadline published with a clock time.

WHAT IS PUBLISHED AND DATED (2027 class, verbatim from Pew, useful as the planning template):
- "The application portal opens on June 3, 2026." / "Please email fellowsapp@pewtrusts.org on this date or later for login information."
- "The application deadline is Aug. 19, 2026." (5 p.m. ET)
- Regional committee review + interviews: Sept./Oct. 2026; candidates NOT advancing are notified in that window
- National advisory committee review: November 2026 – March 2027 ("No interviews are conducted during this period of review")
- Notification: April 2027
- Board approval + public announcement: June 2027
- Grant issued to the US sponsoring institution, first payment: August 2027

PROJECTED 2028-CLASS WINDOW (derived from the pattern, NOT published — do not quote as Pew's): portal opens ~first week of June 2027; deadline ~mid-to-late August 2027, 5 p.m. ET.

ACTIONABLE ANSWER TO "WHEN DO I CHECK": the FAQ fact sheet itself states it "was updated in February 2026 to reflect application and award dates for the 2027 class of fellows." So Pew posts the new cycle's dates in FEBRUARY. Check https://www.pew.org/en/research-and-analysis/fact-sheets/2018/04/frequently-asked-questions-about-the-pew-latin-american-fellows-program in February 2027 for the exact 2028 dates. But do not wait for February to start work — see loi_deadline: the binding task starts a year earlier.
result.loi_deadline: Not applicable — no LOI stage exists. The functional equivalent is the sponsor-lab commitment, which Pew's own timeline places in the February–June window BEFORE the portal opens (for the 2027 class: "February 2026 - June 2026"). For the 2028 class that means beginning in roughly February 2027, with the proposal drafted jointly with the sponsor before the ~June 2027 portal opening. Pew warns it "may require a significant time commitment and take several months," and a sponsor "may not commit to more than one applicant per year," so earlier is materially better.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
Pew publishes NO rule about grants or fellowships the APPLICANT already holds for this mechanism. The "Funding from the NIH, other government sources, and project grants from nonprofit associations do not pose a conflict" carve-out is published on the Pew Biomedical Scholars page and is explicitly scoped there — the sentence ends "...with the Pew scholars program." It is NOT restated anywhere on the Latin American Fellows pages. Do not assume it transfers; ask fellowsapp@pewtrusts.org.

WHAT ACTUALLY DISQUALIFIES YOU (all verbatim from Pew, 2027 cycle):
1. PRIOR POSTDOCTORAL TRAINING — the real "prior support" bar. "May not have started any postdoctoral training in the U.S. or in Europe prior to March. 1, 2025." For the 2027 cycle that is ~15 months before the portal opened. This is the single most common disqualifier and it moves forward one year per cycle.
2. DEGREE WINDOW. "Must have been awarded a Ph.D. and/or M.D. degree between June 3, 2021, and Feb. 1, 2027." (Exactly 5 years before portal open, through ~2 months before the award year.)
3. YOUR OWN PhD SUPERVISOR CANNOT BE YOUR SPONSOR. "Applicants will not be considered if they have completed graduate work with their proposed Pew sponsor." / "A sponsor may not be the same person who advised or mentored the applicant during completion of his or her Ph.D. work."
4. SPONSOR-LEVEL CONFLICT. "A proposed sponsor may not commit to more than one applicant per year." Another candidate can lock out your target lab.

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY — the half applicants usually miss:
1. POSTDOC TRAINING OUTSIDE THE US AND EUROPE DOES NOT COUNT. The bar names only "the U.S. or in Europe." Postdoctoral time in Latin America, or elsewhere outside those two regions, is not excluded by the published wording. Confirm your specific case with the program office, but it is not an automatic bar.
2. AN OLDER M.D. IS NEGOTIABLE. "M.D. candidates whose degree was completed prior to June 3, 2021, may contact the program office for a discussion about eligibility." An explicit, published exception route.
3. A NON-LATIN-AMERICAN DEGREE IS A PREFERENCE, NOT A BAR. "Preference is given to applicants who received their undergraduate and graduate degrees from institutions in Latin America. Applicants may have obtained their degrees from institutions outside of Latin America, but preferably not in the U.S." A US PhD weakens you; it does not disqualify you.
4. YOU DO NOT NEED A JOB LINED UP IN LATIN AMERICA. "At the time of application, candidates are not required to have a commitment of a position and laboratory space after the fellowship." Only the later $70,000 return payment requires that.
5. CUBA/VENEZUELA IS A CONVERSATION, NOT A REFUSAL. "Applicants intending to establish a lab in Cuba or Venezuela should contact the program office (fellowsapp@pewtrusts.org) for additional information."
6. THE AWARD IS DESIGNED TO BE STACKED WITH SPONSOR FUNDING — co-funding is mandatory, not a conflict. Pew pays a $30,000 stipend; the sponsor "must commit to providing... Supplemental salary to meet the NIH suggested salary guidelines for postdoctoral fellows" plus two years of medical benefits and a comprehensive training plan. Pew links NIH notice NOT-OD-26-044 as the governing scale (I did not open that notice). No indirect costs are allowed on the Pew grant.
result.program_officer_contact:
PRE-SUBMISSION CONTACT IS EXPECTED, INVITED IN WRITING, AND UNUSUALLY GENEROUS. Treat this as closer to an NIH program officer than a closed-door foundation.

PRIMARY AND ONLY ROUTE: fellowsapp@pewtrusts.org — the program office mailbox. It appears five separate times across Pew's Latin American Fellows pages, each time as an invitation. No named biomedical program officer is listed on the Latin American Fellows pages themselves (the staff names in the funder-level notes — Kara Coleman, Donna Dang, Sarah Kelly — were not re-verified on these pages; use the mailbox).

WHAT THE MAILBOX IS EXPLICITLY OFFERED FOR (Pew's own words):
- Eligibility rulings: "Please reach out to the program office at fellowsapp@pewtrusts.org for further clarification."
- Older M.D. degrees: "may contact the program office for a discussion about eligibility."
- Cuba/Venezuela return plans: "should contact the program office... for additional information."
- SPONSOR MATCHING (highest value, and time-limited): "The program office will assist with the identification of possible laboratories with matching research interests." Offered only "prior to June 3, 2026" — i.e. before the portal opens.
- INTRODUCTIONS TO PAST FELLOWS: "The program's regional committee members are ready and willing to talk with interested candidates. Pew staff can also connect you with current fellows and alumni; email fellowsapp@pewtrusts.org to request an introduction." A funder that will personally broker an introduction to an alumnus in your country is rare — use it.
- Portal credentials: mandatory, and only on/after the opening date.

A BROKEN LINK WORTH KNOWING ABOUT: the FAQ says "seek advice from members of the regional committees... Find regional committee contacts here" — but that link resolves to the To Apply page, which does not list any regional committee members or contacts. I checked the rendered page in full; no accordion or hidden section contains them. So the only working route to the regional committees is to email fellowsapp@pewtrusts.org and ask for the contact for your region.

WHEN TO WRITE: for a 2028 application, February–May 2027 for sponsor help and eligibility rulings; on/after the June 2027 portal-opening date for credentials.

OTHER NAMED PEOPLE (context, not application contacts): Eva Nogales, Ph.D. (UC Berkeley, HHMI) chairs the national advisory committee; the full 12-person committee is published by name and institution on the Program Details page — useful for reading the scientific taste of the panel. Erin Davis, Manager, Communications, 202.540.6677 is the MEDIA contact only; do not route application questions there.

NOT AVAILABLE: Pew does not review draft proposals and there is no concept-check step. Your readers are your sponsor, a past fellow, and your regional committee contact.
result.resubmission_note:
NO PUBLISHED LIMIT ON THE NUMBER OF APPLICATIONS for this mechanism. I read the Program Details page, the To Apply page and the FAQ (web and PDF) in full; none contains a cap. Treat this as UNKNOWN, not as unlimited.

THE CONTRAST IS INFORMATIVE: Pew publishes an explicit cap for its sister programmes — Pew Biomedical Scholars: "May apply to the program a maximum of two times." Nothing equivalent exists for Latin American Fellows. Because Pew clearly knows how to write such a rule and did not write one here, the absence is probably real rather than an oversight — but confirm with fellowsapp@pewtrusts.org before planning a second attempt.

THE BINDING CONSTRAINT IS THE CLOCK, NOT A RESUBMISSION RULE, AND IT IS TIGHTER THAN IT LOOKS. Two rolling gates run against each other:
- Degree awarded between June 3, 2021 and Feb. 1, 2027 (a ~5.7-year window, generous)
- "May not have started any postdoctoral training in the U.S. or in Europe prior to March 1, 2025" (~15 months before the portal opened — brutal)

The second gate is what limits you. Each cycle it advances roughly one year. So if you have already started a US or European postdoc, your eligibility expires within about one or two cycles regardless of any resubmission policy. DERIVED, NOT PUBLISHED: an applicant who began a US postdoc in early 2025 was eligible for the 2027 class but would likely fail the 2028 class's equivalent gate. In practice most candidates get ONE realistic shot, occasionally two.

The candidates with genuine multi-cycle optionality are those still finishing a PhD or doing postdoctoral work outside the US and Europe — for them the degree window governs and two or three cycles may be available.

There is no resubmission machinery in the NIH sense: no summary statement, no response-to-reviewers section, no "what changed" requirement. Pew issues no written critique. A second application is simply a new application. Note also that the sponsor relationship is re-negotiated each time, since "A proposed sponsor may not commit to more than one applicant per year."
result.review_to_award:
TOTAL: ~12 months from submission to first money. ~8 months to a decision. Pew publishes the whole arc by month, which is unusual and lets you plan precisely.

For the 2027 class (Pew's own published timeline, submission Aug. 19, 2026):
- Sept./Oct. 2026 (months 1-2): Regional committee review. Four-plus regional committees composed of FORMER PEW LATIN AMERICAN FELLOWS review applications, invite shortlisted candidates to interview "in person or by video conference," and each "nominates six final candidates from its region to Pew for further consideration." CRITICAL: "Individuals who are not moving to the next round will be notified at this time." You learn you are out roughly 2 months after submitting — far faster than most fellowships.
- November 2026 - March 2027 (months 3-7): National advisory committee review in the US. "No interviews are conducted during this period of review." Twelve named members, chaired by Eva Nogales.
- April 2027 (month ~8): "Applicants are notified of the advisory committee's decisions." 10 fellows selected.
- June 2027 (month ~10): "Pew board of directors approves the 2027 class of fellows and awardees are publicly announced soon after." (The 2026 class was announced June 16, 2026 — the pattern holds.)
- August 2027 (month ~12): "Pew award is granted to the institution of the sponsoring lab in the U.S., and first payment is made." EARLIEST EFFECTIVE START.

WHERE THIS DEVIATES FROM THE PEW BIOMEDICAL NORM — two differences that matter:
1. THIS IS THE ONLY PEW BIOMEDICAL MECHANISM WITH AN INTERVIEW. Pew Scholars and Pew-Stewart have none. Prepare to defend the project and your return-to-Latin-America plan live, in your region, to former fellows, around September-October. Budget for this; it is not mentioned in the application materials list.
2. THIS IS THE ONLY ONE WITH AN EARLY REJECTION NOTICE (Oct.). Scholars candidates wait until April to hear anything.
Otherwise the back half is identical to the Pew family norm: April notification, June board approval and announcement, August money.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: the money arrives ~12 months after you apply and ~18 months after you start looking for a sponsor. Your sponsor must be willing to hold or bridge a postdoc position across that gap — discuss this explicitly when securing the commitment.
result.submission_requirements:
NO INSTITUTIONAL SIGN-OFF, NO NOMINATION, NO INSTITUTIONAL LIMIT. The applicant submits directly. This is the major deviation from Pew Scholars / Pew-Stewart, where a single institutional nominee is chosen in an internal competition months earlier.

ACCESS: there is no self-registration and no public portal URL. "Potential candidates must send an email to the program office at fellowsapp@pewtrusts.org to request login information for the application portal." Requests are honoured on or after the opening date only. "The secure online application contains detailed instructions and an application guide" — the guide is not published publicly and arrives with your credentials.

REQUIRED MATERIALS (verbatim from Pew's 2027 FAQ timeline):
- "Candidate's curriculum vitae (CV)"
- "Statements on intent to further research career in Latin America and most significant scientific contribution" — TWO statements: (a) how you will further your research career in Latin America after the fellowship "and support the development of scientific communities and infrastructure there"; (b) your most significant scientific contribution. Statement (a) is a formal eligibility requirement, not a nicety: "applicants are required to submit a written statement describing how they will further their research career in Latin America."
- "Research proposal"
- "Three letters of reference from individuals familiar with the applicant's work"
- "Sponsor letter of commitment, sponsor's CV and current grant funding the sponsoring PI will have during the award period"

THE SPONSOR PACKAGE IS THE BIG DEVIATION. It is three separate items (commitment letter, CV, and a statement of the PI's grant funding covering the award period) and it is SEPARATE FROM THE THREE REFERENCES. Per the funder-level notes, Pew is emphatic that the sponsor "should not write one of the 3 reference letters listed above" — so you need four people, not three. Your sponsor's funding is audited: the lab must be able to top your $30,000 up to the NIH postdoctoral scale plus two years of benefits.

PAGE LIMITS: NOT PUBLISHED on any current Pew page. The figure in the funder-level notes — a 5-page research proposal, "written by the applicant, but work on with sponsor" — comes from a 2023 Pew program-officer presentation describing the 2024 cycle, i.e. three cycles old and not re-verified by me. Plan around 5 pages but confirm against the application guide you receive with your portal credentials.

REFERENCE-LETTER DEADLINE — THE TRAP. Pew's public pages give only the application deadline. Per the same 2023 Pew deck, LAF reference and sponsor letters were due TWO WEEKS BEFORE the application deadline ("August 2, 2023 Reference and sponsor letters due (2 weeks prior to deadline)"). I could NOT find a published letter deadline for 2027 or 2028 — it is in the application guide. Working assumption: ask your four letter-writers in June, not August.

WHAT PEW LOOKS FOR IN THE SPONSOR LAB (published, and effectively proposal criteria): sufficient funding to supplement the stipend plus benefits; "a strong track record of training postdocs"; "Preference is typically given to sponsoring labs led by senior level faculty, though exceptions are made for junior faculty with a very strong track record and funding"; a comprehensive training plan; and — easy to fail — "The chosen sponsor lab should be one in which the fellow will learn new skills that are not a direct replication of his or her doctoral thesis work." Write the proposal so the discontinuity from your PhD is obvious.

POST-AWARD OBLIGATIONS THAT SHAPE THE APPLICATION: annual progress and financial reports; mandatory attendance at the annual meeting (March or April) in each of the two years plus a third meeting to present; $4,500 travel allowance reserved for that meeting; no indirect costs; 24-month stipend extendable to a 60-month maximum grant period if the sponsor funds the extra years (Pew adds no stipend); the $70,000 return payment requires a confirmed position and lab space in Latin America and "a written request to Pew at least four months prior to the fellowship end date," and is forfeited if you do not return within the 60-month maximum.

There is no Pew RePORTER equivalent and Pew publishes NO funded applications and NO reviewer critiques. What exists instead is better than most foundations offer: ~250-word first-person funded-project abstracts, the sponsor for every past fellow, and direct email addresses.

1. DIRECTORY OF FELLOWS — the primary resource. https://www.pew.org/en/projects/pew-latin-american-fellows/directory-of-latin-fellows
Searchable by keyword, research field, institution, award year, and — uniquely useful here — COUNTRY OF ORIGIN. Each profile carries: title, department, institution, postal address, EMAIL ADDRESS, lab website, research field, award year, country of origin, MENTOR NAME (i.e. the sponsor), a first-person funded-project abstract, and keywords. URL pattern: /directory-of-latin-fellows/<year>/<name-slug>.
Verified example — Bernabé Battista, Ph.D. (2026, Argentina, Harvard Medical School, mentor Monica Colaiácovo, Ph.D.): "I will investigate the molecular mechanisms that govern the accurate segregation of chromosomes during egg and sperm development... The Colaiácovo lab discovered that a pair of proteins that normally cap the ends of chromosomes, called POT1 and POT3, act as novel regulators of late chromosome remodeling... This work could lead to the development of new strategies for minimizing improper chromosome segregation and thereby preventing infertility, miscarriages, and even cancer."
THE HOUSE STYLE IS LEARNABLE FROM THESE: one named mechanism, an explicit hook into the sponsor lab's own prior discovery, a named set of techniques, and a closing human-health payoff sentence. Read ten in your field before drafting.

2. THE DIRECTORY IS ALSO YOUR SPONSOR TARGET LIST. Pew says so outright: use "Sponsors of previous awardees, which can be found in the Latin American fellows directory. Please note that you do not need to be sponsored by a Pew scholar in order to apply." Filter by your country of origin, read which US labs have hosted fellows from your country, and approach them — they have done this before and know the paperwork.

3. CLASS ANNOUNCEMENTS — a whole cohort in one read, each entry giving fellow + sponsor lab + institution + a one-line project summary, and flagging which sponsors are Pew alumni. "Pew Supports 10 Leading Latin American Scientists," June 16, 2026: https://www.pew.org/en/about/news-room/press-releases-and-statements/2026/06/16/pew-supports-10-leading-latin-american-scientists — e.g. "Isabel Barón-Mendoza, Ph.D. / Laboratory of Victoria Abraira, Ph.D., 2019 Pew biomedical scholar / Rutgers University." The 2026 class drew from seven countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Peru, Uruguay). Companion article: "These 36 Scientists Are Leading the Way to Biomedical Discoveries" (June 16, 2026), covering all three Pew biomedical classes together.

4. TALK TO PAST FELLOWS — Pew will broker it. Emails are published on every profile, and Pew states: "Pew staff can also connect you with current fellows and alumni; email fellowsapp@pewtrusts.org to request an introduction." Regional committee members are drawn from former fellows and are "ready and willing to talk with interested candidates."

5. READ THE PANEL. The 12 named national advisory committee members (chair Eva Nogales) are listed with institutions on the Program Details page; several are themselves Latin American-origin senior US scientists. Their published work tells you the scientific register the final stage rewards.

6. ALSO AVAILABLE, NOT OPENED BY ME: "Where in the World Are Pew's Latin American Fellows?" data visualization, March 13, 2026 (https://www.pew.org/en/research-and-analysis/data-visualizations/2026/where-in-the-world-are-pews-latin-american-fellows); the 2027 flyer PDF (https://www.pew.org/-/media/assets/2026/05/nih/2027-pew-latin-american-fellows-flyer.pdf); a program video (April 24, 2023); and "A Ripple Effect on Latin American Science" (2014), the outcomes survey of 1991-2011 fellows that Pew cites for its "about 7 in 10 return" figure.

NOT AVAILABLE ANYWHERE: the application guide (issued only with portal credentials), any annotated sample application, and any reviewer summary statement.

result.loi_deadline:
NO letter of intent or pre-proposal exists AT PEW — but do not read that as "no gate before the full application." There is a mandatory gating stage, it is the highest-attrition stage in the whole process, and it is run by your own institution rather than by Pew, which is why it is invisible on Pew's website.

THE FUNCTIONAL LOI IS YOUR CAMPUS PRE-PROPOSAL. Pew's own words: "Institutions are expected to complete a limited submission competition in order to identify and select one nominee... Interested applicants should submit pre-proposal material to an internal selection committee for consideration." Only ONE nominee per institution goes forward, out of 212 participating institutions.

Two hard dates, in order:
1. INTERNAL CAMPUS DEADLINE — set locally, 6–10 weeks before Pew's. Measured for the 2027 cycle: BU "Tuesday, March 10, 2026 by 11:59 pm ET" (via InfoReady Review); CU Boulder "11:59pm MST April 6, 2026". Projected for the 2028 cycle: February–April 2027.
2. PEW NOMINATION — May 13, 2026 for the 2027 class; projected Wed. May 12, 2027 for 2028. "To nominate a candidate, a member of the internal selection committee must complete an online survey from the Pew program office describing the selection process used by the institution and submit the name and contact information of the chosen applicant by May 13, 2026." Filed BY the institution, not by you.

Then, and only then, ~16 weeks to write the full application (portal opens 2nd Wednesday of June, closes first week of September).

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE PEW DEADLINE: "The individual chosen for the institutional nomination is guaranteed an application to the program." Win your campus competition and you are guaranteed a shot at Pew. Lose it and there is no appeal, no waiver and no direct route — Pew will not accept you. Most candidates who never become Pew scholars are eliminated on their own campus in March, not by the National Advisory Committee in the spring.

DO NOT CONFUSE YOUR CAMPUS'S REQUIREMENTS WITH PEW'S. The internal pre-proposal is a different, much shorter document, and its specs are set locally: CU Boulder 1 page; BU "2-page Project Proposal... References may be included on one additional page" plus a "1-paragraph Self-Assessment Statement" plus "an up-to-date CV (please provide a CV and not a Biosketch)"; Weill Cornell 2 pages plus unlimited references, 12-pt, 1-inch margins, a 30-line abstract, a 1–2 page chair's nomination letter, a biosketch stating the exact first-appointment date, and a 1-page "3 most influential publications"; Dana-Farber/HCC 1–2 pages plus CV plus chair's letter; Stony Brook 3 pages double-spaced.

SECOND ROUTE THAT BYPASSES THE CAMPUS COMPETITION: alumni nomination. Pew separately solicits every Pew alumnus to nominate people. Pew's own words: "Nominees do not participate in the nomination process. Nominees are not guaranteed an automatic application. Nominations are reviewed by a board of Pew alumni and a subset are invited to apply." Weaker than the institutional slot (no guarantee), and you cannot apply for it — but it is a reason to be visible to Pew scholars in your field.

- Submission closes Sept. 3, 2026

Candidates will be notified in April if they have been recommended to the Pew board." Note what you are told in April is that you have been RECOMMENDED — the board has not yet approved.
