FULL ARC FROM THE FIRST ACTIONABLE MOMENT: your campus internal deadline (March 2026) to money in hand (August 2027) is about 17 months. Budget your lab's runway accordingly; this is not a bridge-funding mechanism.

NO INTERVIEW at any stage for Pew Scholars. (Contrast the sister Pew Latin American Fellows program, which does interview via regional committees — that stage does not exist here.)

NO WRITTEN FEEDBACK. Pew issues no summary statement, no score and no critique, whether you succeed or fail. If you are not selected you will not learn why.
result.submission_requirements:
SOURCING CAUTION, STATED UP FRONT: Pew does not publish its application guide. It is emailed only to nominated applicants when the portal opens ("The Pew program office will email grant application portal login information and a detailed application guide directly to all nominated applicants by June 10, 2026"). The component specs below are Pew's own numbers but come from a deck given by Pew's Project Director Kara Coleman, Ph.D. to Boston University on April 5, 2023 describing the 2024 cycle (https://www.bu.edu/foundations/files/2024/07/Pew_BU_2023.pdf). They are three cycles old. Confirm against the guide you receive when the portal opens.

COMPONENTS (per that Pew deck):
- PROJECT PROPOSAL: "6 pages, double-spaced including figures (limit does not include references)". Read that carefully — double-spaced with figures counted inside the limit is roughly 3 single-spaced pages of actual text. This is dramatically shorter than an R01 and is the single most misjudged spec in the application. References are excluded.
- PERSONAL STATEMENTS: "1 paragraph each" against three prompts — (a) "Briefly describe your most significant research contribution to date"; (b) "Highlight the most innovative and novel aspects of your proposed research. Describe a risky or creative approach you might use in pursuit of your goals"; (c) "The program aims to support both the research and the researcher. Please describe how your personal background and past experiences have helped you stand out in your approach to science and your career". (The 2023 cycle also carried a "COVID impact" field; assume it is gone unless your guide shows it.)
- CV INFORMATION: entered as structured portal fields, not uploaded as a document.
- 3 REFERENCE LETTERS: "thesis advisor, postdoc advisor, scientific reference."

STILL CURRENT — CROSS-CONFIRMED: CU Boulder's 2027-cycle internal page reproduces the same three prompts with a character limit, asking for "most significant research (1400 characters max)", "most innovative and novel aspects of research (1400 characters max)", and "how your personal background and/or scientific training has helped you stand out in your approach to science and your career (1400 characters max)". Three cycles on, the personal-statement structure has not drifted; 1,400 characters is about one solid paragraph, which matches Pew's "1 paragraph each". The 6-page proposal limit is the item I would most want re-verified against the current guide.

THE TRAP MOST APPLICANTS MISS — REFERENCE LETTERS ARE DUE TWO WEEKS BEFORE THE APPLICATION DEADLINE, NOT ON IT. Pew's deck states for the 2024 cycle: "August 31, 2023 Pew-Stewart application closes (*reference letters due 2 weeks prior)" and "September 7, 2023 Pew scholar application closes (*reference letters due 2 weeks prior)". Applying that rule to the 2027 cycle puts letters around Aug. 20, 2026. I could NOT find the exact 2027 letter date published — it lives in the application guide issued with portal access. ASK YOUR REFEREES IN JUNE, NOT AUGUST. Your thesis and postdoc advisors will be travelling in August.

INSTITUTIONAL SIGN-OFF: the nomination itself is the institutional act, filed by a member of your internal selection committee via a Pew online survey. There is no separate departmental or chair's sign-off at the Pew stage (your campus may demand a chair's letter at the INTERNAL stage — Weill Cornell and Dana-Farber/HCC both do).

NO sponsor or mentor statement is required — this is an independent-investigator award, not a mentored one. (The sponsor letter requirement belongs to the sister Latin American Fellows program.)

SUBMISSION PATH: a Pew-operated portal with NO self-registration and no public URL. Credentials are emailed directly to nominees. Research administrators get access only by emailing scholarsapp@pewtrusts.org with the applicant cc'd, and only AFTER the portal opens — "No requests will be accepted prior to this date." Emailing in May gets you ignored. I could not establish the portal's software vendor; probes of two candidate hosts returned a generic catch-all page and a refused connection respectively, which establishes nothing either way.

WHAT PEW SAYS A STRONG PROPOSAL LOOKS LIKE — this is the most useful guidance available and it is explicit: "Successful applications should not look like typical R01 grant applications with incremental research steps and safe hypotheses supported by existing data. We support truly out-of-the-box, innovative, early-career science which may accelerate and advance progress to understanding aspects of biomedical research and may not be fundable through other more typical funding mechanisms." Also: "Propose a specific project (not just overall lab vision)"; "Lots of preliminary data isn't necessary, but must outline your experimental details"; "Preprints can be cited and used to show unpublished body of work"; "The third 'scientific reference' letter is very impactful"; "reviewers will be in your field, but may not be experts in your specific scientific niche". And from pew.org: "This program does not fund clinical trials research."

BUDGET RULES THAT SHAPE THE PROPOSAL (verbatim from pew.org):
- CORRECTION TO THE RECORDED ROW: the award is NOT $300,000. Pew's current page states "The current grant level is $306,000; $75,000 per year for a four-year period with a $6,000 travel stipend for travel to the program's annual meeting, disbursed as $1,500 per year. No indirect costs may be applied to the travel supplement." The existing CSV row carries "$300,000 total ($75,000/yr over 4 years) (est.)" at confidence=medium with a note that the amount was not confirmable on the funder's page — it is now confirmable, it is $306,000, and the $300,000 figure (which appears in the 2023 Pew deck) is one cycle stale.
- PI salary capped at "$12,500 per year (including benefits) or $50,000 over the duration of the grant. There are no limits on student or postdoctoral salaries."
- Indirect costs: "Not more than 8 percent ($24,000) of the total award value" — very low; your sponsored-research office should see this early.
- Carryover allowed; one no-cost extension year available with written approval; subawards allowed.
- Effort: "at least 80 percent of their time in work or activities related to the accomplishment of their overall research goals... However, Pew provides flexible support to the general research aims of the scholar and does not require effort reporting."
- Mandatory annual meeting attendance in March or April for all four years, expenses paid; continued funding is contingent on attendance plus acceptable annual narrative and financial reports.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
THIS IS THE FIELD WHERE PEW IS MOST PERMISSIVE AND MOST MISUNDERSTOOD. Almost nothing about your funding portfolio disqualifies you; what disqualifies you is structural and about your APPOINTMENT and your ATTEMPT COUNT.

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (verbatim from pew.org): "Funding from the NIH, other government sources, and project grants from nonprofit associations do not pose a conflict with the Pew scholars program."

Read that carefully, because it is broader than most applicants assume. Holding an R01 does not disqualify you. Holding a K award does not disqualify you. NSF, DOD, DOE, NASA money does not disqualify you. Project grants from disease foundations and nonprofit associations do not disqualify you. There is no R01/K-style interaction rule here at all, and no overlap or supplantation test of the NIH kind. Pew positions itself as funding what those mechanisms will not fund, so a healthy federal portfolio is evidence you are a "successful independent investigator" — which is one of the stated review criteria — rather than a conflict. If you have any doubt about a specific award, Pew asks you to ask: "If you have questions concerning eligibility, please contact Pew Biomedical Programs (scholarsapp@pewtrusts.org) in advance of applying."

WHAT ACTUALLY DISQUALIFIES YOU (all verbatim from pew.org unless noted) — none of it is about prior funding:
1. THE APPOINTMENT CLOCK, which is the binding constraint for nearly everyone. For the 2027 award: "Must not have been appointed as an assistant professor and run an independent lab at any institution prior to June 10, 2023, whether or not such an appointment was on a tenure track." A three-year window, pegged to the portal-opening date. "Time limit stands regardless of changing institutions" — you cannot reset it by moving.
2. APPOINTMENT TITLE. "Appointments such as research assistant professor, adjunct assistant professor, assistant professor research track, visiting professor, or instructor are not eligible." This catches a lot of people who believe they are eligible. You must "run an independent lab and hold a full-time appointment at the rank of assistant professor" as of the application deadline.
3. TWO ATTEMPTS, LIFETIME. "May apply to the program a maximum of two times."
4. SAME-YEAR DOUBLE NOMINATION. "May not be nominated for the Pew Scholars Program and the Pew-Stewart Scholars Program for Cancer Research in the same year." And one individual will not receive both awards.
5. INSTITUTION-SHOPPING IS BLOCKED. "If applicants have appointments at more than one eligible nominating institution or affiliate, they may not reapply in a subsequent year from a different nominating entity."
6. NOT BEING NOMINATED. There is no unsolicited route. Your institution must nominate you, and it may nominate only one person from the 212 participating institutions list.
7. TOPIC. "This program does not fund clinical trials research."

THE CLOCK EXCEPTION IS REAL AND IS THE HIGHEST-VALUE PHONE CALL IN THIS ENTIRE PROCESS. "Time spent in clinical internships, residencies, in work toward board certification, or on parental leave does not count as part of this three-year limit. Candidates who need an exception on the three-year limit should contact Pew's program office to ensure that application reviewers are aware an exception has been given." Pew's own deck adds: "There is flexibility for nominees who have taken family or medical leave during the first 4 years of their appointment. Please contact us for details." This must be arranged BEFORE the nomination, not after — an exception the reviewers do not know about is worth nothing, and your campus committee needs to know too or it will screen you out as ineligible before Pew ever sees you.

WATCH THE DRIFT ON THE CLOCK. The window was temporarily widened from three years to four for COVID ("Eligibility has been adjusted to 4 years due to COVID challenges through the 2025 competition") and has now REVERTED TO THREE YEARS for the 2027 award. If you are working from advice, a mentor's memory, or a campus page written during the COVID years, you may believe you have a year you no longer have. Check the current cycle's page yourself.

NOT FOUND — treat as unknown, not as permitted: Pew's page names no exclusion for holding other private early-career awards (HHMI Freeman Hrabowski, Searle, Packard, Beckman, Rita Allen, Vallee and similar). The carve-out sentence covers government funding and nonprofit project grants but is silent on named private early-career prizes. Silence is not permission. If you hold one, this is exactly the question to put to scholarsapp@pewtrusts.org before your campus nominates you. (For contrast, the sister Latin American Fellows program DOES publish a competing-awards rule — "Cannot hold Pew Latin American Fellowship and other competing awards simultaneously," naming Human Frontiers and LSRF — which shows Pew states such rules when it means them, and did not state one here.)

Email scholarsapp@pewtrusts.org". Prefer the mailbox over an individual's direct line unless you already have a relationship.

PEW INVITES CONTACT IN WRITING, REPEATEDLY — four distinct invitations on the funder's own pages:
1. Eligibility generally: "If you have questions concerning eligibility, please contact Pew Biomedical Programs (scholarsapp@pewtrusts.org) in advance of applying."
2. Clock exceptions: "Candidates who need an exception on the three-year limit should contact Pew's program office to ensure that application reviewers are aware an exception has been given." The single highest-value contact an applicant can make, and it must happen before the nomination.
3. Institutions not on the list of 212: "Institutions that would like to be considered for invitation may contact scholarsapp@pewtrusts.org." If you are at a strong research institution that is not on the list, your research office can ask to be added — this is an invitation, not a long shot.
4. Internal selection design: "For guidance on this process, please contact scholarsapp@pewtrusts.org." Pew runs "Pew office hours (for institutional selection)" and "Pew webinars (for applicants)."

WHEN IN THE CYCLE TO MAKE CONTACT (projected to the 2028 cycle):
- Jan.–Mar. 2027: institutional and research-development questions; ask to be added to the participating list.
- Before the nomination, Apr.–early May 2027: eligibility rulings and clock exceptions. THE CRITICAL WINDOW.
- After the portal opens (projected ~June 9, 2027) ONLY: portal access requests. "No requests will be accepted prior to this date."
- June–Aug. 2027: application-guide mechanics; attend the applicant webinar.

WHAT EXPERIENCED APPLICANTS ACTUALLY ASK: (1) Does my appointment date count, and can I get a documented exception for leave or a clinical track? (2) Is my title eligible — the research/adjunct/instructor exclusions catch many people. (3) Is my project better placed in Scholars or in Pew-Stewart this year? (4) Does my other funding conflict — the published answer is no for government and nonprofit project grants.

WHAT IS *NOT* AVAILABLE, so you do not waste the contact: Pew program officers DO NOT review draft proposals, and there is no pre-proposal or concept-check step at Pew. Scientific triage happens on your own campus and then at the National Advisory Committee. The people to show a draft to are your institution's research development office and, better, a past Pew scholar.

YOUR INSTITUTION WILL BROKER ACCESS — ASK IT TO. Weill Cornell hosted an internal information session for the 2027 cycle featuring Pew's own Donna Dang and Sarah Kelly, with a recording. Ask your research office whether a Pew briefing is scheduled. This is routine, not a favour. Pew also advises institutions to put their own Pew alumni on the internal selection committee, so your campus's past scholars are both the people who will judge you internally and the best-placed people to advise you.
result.examples_or_samples:
There is NO Pew equivalent of NIH RePORTER, and Pew publishes NO full funded applications and NO reviewer summary statements. What exists instead is better than most foundations offer: several hundred lay-written funded-project abstracts, plus unusually direct access to the awardees themselves.

1. THE PEW SCHOLARS DIRECTORY — the primary resource, and the best proxy available for a winning Pew proposal.
https://www.pew.org/en/projects/pew-biomedical-scholars/directory-of-pew-scholars
Every scholar back to 1985 has a profile carrying a ~200-word first-person funded-project description, plus research field, keywords, institution, award year, lab website AND a direct email address. Filterable by keyword, research field, institution, award year, state, and an "Innovation Fund Investigator" flag. URL pattern: /directory-of-pew-scholars/<year>/<name-slug>. The 2026 class has 21 scholars.
Verified example — Corey Allard, Ph.D., Assistant Professor of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School, 2026, corey_allard@hms.harvard.edu, https://allardlab.hms.harvard.edu/ : "My lab will explore how some sea slugs turn to thievery to gain new abilities. Acquiring novel traits is a fundamental feature of evolution, but several lineages of sea slugs adopt an unusual approach to the problem, electing to swipe subcellular structures from their prey... Now, using cutting-edge methods in cell and molecular genetics, biochemistry, and functional imaging, we will identify the ion channels, transporters, receptors, and other molecular machinery... Our work will illuminate a novel form of evolutionary innovation that could lead to new approaches for engineering cells with enhanced metabolic or defensive capabilities."
HOW TO USE IT: read twenty of these in your own field and the house style becomes obvious — one specific mechanism, a named unconventional approach, an explicit payoff sentence at the end, and no incrementalism anywhere. That structure maps directly onto Pew's stated preference for work that would "not be fundable through other more typical funding mechanisms."

2. SISTER DIRECTORIES, same structure, useful for range:
- Pew-Stewart Scholars for Cancer Research: https://www.pew.org/en/projects/pew-stewart-scholars-for-cancer-research/directory-of-stewart-scholars
- Pew Latin American Fellows: https://www.pew.org/en/projects/pew-latin-american-fellows/directory-of-latin-fellows (also lists each fellow's US SPONSOR — the practical way to build a target list of sponsor labs)

3. ANNUAL PRESS RELEASES — a whole class of funded-project summaries in one read, good for seeing the portfolio's breadth quickly. Biomedical scholars are announced each June: "Pew Announces 21 New Biomedical Scholars" (June 16, 2026) and the companion article "These 36 Scientists Are Leading the Way to Biomedical Discoveries" (June 16, 2026). Both are linked from the project page.

4. THE ORAL HISTORY AND ARCHIVES PROJECT — genuinely unusual and underused. Pew's own words: the project "has collected the life stories of more than 200 Pew scholars and produced one of the most extensive biomedical research oral history archives available today in the United States." Launched 1988; "The completed oral histories are archived at the Science History Institute in Philadelphia. Many of the histories are available for viewing and research upon request." This is where you learn how Pew scholars themselves narrate risk-taking and career choices — which is precisely what personal-statement prompts (b) and (c) ask you to do.

5. TALK TO AWARDEES DIRECTLY — the directory publishes their email addresses, and Pew encourages the approach. Also ask your own institution for its past Pew scholars: the Weill Cornell limited-submission page, for instance, lists its nine past recipients with emails. Since Pew advises institutions to seat alumni on the internal selection committee, a past scholar on your campus may well be the person deciding whether you are nominated.

6. INTERNAL INSTITUTIONAL PAGES as a proxy for the application's shape — university limited-submission pages reproduce pre-proposal prompts that mirror Pew's own, and they are public where Pew's guide is not:
- Weill Cornell: https://research.weill.cornell.edu/funding/funding-opportunities/pew-charitable-trusts-pew-biomedical-scholars-program
- Boston University (2027 cycle): https://www.bu.edu/research/2026/01/22/the-pew-charitable-trusts-pew-biomedical-scholars-2027/
- CU Boulder: https://www.colorado.edu/researchinnovation/pew-biomedical-scholars (reproduces the three self-assessment prompts at 1,400 characters each)
Treat these as the institution's requirements, never as Pew's.

7. PEW'S OWN PROGRAM-OFFICER DECK — the closest thing to an annotated guide that exists publicly: "Pew Biomedical Programs Overview," Kara Coleman, Ph.D., Project Director, to Boston University, April 5, 2023. https://www.bu.edu/foundations/files/2024/07/Pew_BU_2023.pdf It carries the component page limits, the personal-statement prompts, the reference-letter timing, the full cycle timeline, and two slides headed "Qualities of a strong application." Three cycles old, so verify specs against your current guide, but the guidance on what Pew wants scientifically is not date-sensitive.

8. GRANT-LEVEL TAX DATA — Pew is a public charity and its IRS Form 990 Schedule I lists grants paid; available via ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer and Candid. Useful for amounts and recipient institutions, useless for scientific content. I did not verify Pew's EIN against an authoritative source, so look it up rather than trusting an aggregator.
result.resubmission_note:
A HARD LIFETIME CAP OF TWO ATTEMPTS, and no resubmission mechanics in the NIH sense at all.

Pew's words: "May apply to the program a maximum of two times. All applicants must be nominated by their institution and must complete the 2027 online application." Dana-Farber/HCC's reproduction of the call puts the same rule as "Candidates may be nominated by their institution only twice."

THE STRUCTURAL POINT THAT MATTERS MOST: a second attempt is NOT a resubmission you control. It is a fresh nomination. Your institution must choose you again, over every other eligible candidate on campus, in a year when it can still nominate only one person. Many second attempts die on campus and never reach Pew at all. Your "two attempts" are therefore two attempts you must win the internal competition to use.

THERE IS NOTHING TO RESUBMIT AGAINST. No introduction page, no response-to-reviewers section, no requirement to mark what changed, and — critically — no summary statement, score or written critique from Pew to react to. The second application is simply a new application. If you are reapplying, your only sources of diagnosis are your campus committee's feedback and any Pew scholar willing to read your draft.

INSTITUTION-SHOPPING IS EXPLICITLY BLOCKED: "If applicants have appointments at more than one eligible nominating institution or affiliate, they may not reapply in a subsequent year from a different nominating entity." And candidates with dual appointments at affiliated institutions can only be nominated from one.

THE ONE GENUINE SECOND BITE IS CROSS-PROGRAM. "May not be nominated for the Pew Scholars Program and the Pew-Stewart Scholars Program for Cancer Research in the same year" — but sequencing is explicitly allowed, per Pew's own deck: "A candidate can be nominated to Pew scholars one year and Pew-Stewart the next." So a cancer-relevant investigator has up to FOUR shots across the two programs (two each), provided the institution nominates them each time and the eligibility clock holds. Note two constraints on that arithmetic: one individual will not receive both awards, and Pew-Stewart draws from a much smaller pool (95 cancer centers vs 212 institutions) with only ~5 awards a year against ~21–22 for Scholars — better odds per applicant are not guaranteed.

THE REAL LIMIT IS THE CLOCK, NOT THE ATTEMPT COUNT. With a three-year eligibility window ("Must not have been appointed as an assistant professor and run an independent lab at any institution prior to June 10, 2023" for the 2027 award), most people physically cannot use two attempts unless they are nominated in their first or second eligible year. If your campus passes you over in your first eligible year, you may have only one attempt left in reality. Plan the first attempt as though it were the only one — and note that the window reverted from four years to three after the COVID adjustment ended with the 2025 competition, so it is tighter now than recent precedent suggests.

result.deadline_pattern:
Three distinct patterns coexist inside this one row — this is the thing most applicants get wrong:
1. **Batched windows with fixed calendar dates** — Pfizer (3 per year: early Jan, late Apr, early Sep) and most Merck MISP therapeutic areas (2–4 competitive reviews per year, dates set per area, republished annually in the Areas of Interest PDF). Merck Immunology states it plainly: "There will be 3 competitive reviews in 2026 by the MISP Review Committee to determine approvals."
2. **Monthly cutoffs** — Merck Ophthalmology, 1st of every month.
3. **Continuous/rolling** — AstraZeneca ESR ("reviewed on a regular basis by Company Review & Evaluation Groups"), Genentech IIS, Merck HIV ("an ongoing competitive process that will be conducted throughout the year"), Gilead self-initiated concepts.
Merck republishes the whole dated schedule each year inside one PDF (the Areas of Interest word list, current version "Updated: February 2026 V4"); Pfizer republishes its schedule as a standalone one-page PDF on cybergrants.com. Both are the authoritative dated source — the HTML programme pages do not carry the dates.
result.loi_required: yes — for Gilead, AstraZeneca and Genentech (formal or de facto). no — for Merck MISP (most areas) and Pfizer, which take a full submission in one step. The stage structure differs by company and is the single biggest timeline variable.
result.loi_deadline:
No LOI has a published calendar date anywhere in this family — LOIs are rolling in every case, and the dated deadline (where one exists) sits on the full submission.

• **Gilead — formal Letter of Interest, then full proposal by invitation.** "For RFP Programs and RFP Topics of Interest: Begin with a Letter of Interest submission, then submit full proposal upon invitation." Self-initiated concepts also start with a Letter of Interest unless pre-invited. Submitted through Gilead OPTICS.
• **AstraZeneca — two documents, two decisions.** Concept proposal first, full protocol only after the proposal clears: "Approval of a proposal does not imply or guarantee approval of a protocol." Budget an extra review round.
• **Genentech — de facto pre-proposal is a conversation, not a document.** Three steps: "1. Discuss Concept with Your MSL... 2. Submit Your Proposal... 3. Submit Final Protocol. If your proposal is approved, you will be notified to submit additional details including a budget and protocol." The guide is blunt: "Potential sponsor-investigators should discuss their concepts with their MSL prior to submission into the portal."
• **Merck MISP — NO LOI for most areas: the first thing you submit is the full protocol.** The standard submission package at the dated deadline is "Protocol, Detailed Budget, Principal Investigator CV". Two softenings: Immunology — "We are requesting full protocols unless discussed beforehand with the MISP chair if acceptable to provide an abbreviated protocol"; and across areas, "Please contact your local Regional Medical Scientific Director (RMSD, US only) or country specific liaison for any guidance pertaining to your specific concept prior to its submission".
• **Pfizer — no LOI stage stated.** One proposal into the ISR portal inside the window.

Timeline consequence: at Merck and Pfizer you must have a finished protocol and costed budget by the deadline; at AZ/Gilead/Genentech you can test the idea cheaply first, but add one to two extra review rounds before any money moves.
result.review_to_award:
**Pfizer — ~14 weeks, and the notification date is published in advance.** Jan 7 → Apr 13; Apr 22 → Jul 27; Sep 9 → Dec 14 (2026). "Our commitment is to review all proposals and communicate decisions by the notification dates below" and "A formal notification regarding the status of your application will be sent on or before the posted notification date." Two documented slippage cases: "studies involving an asset from an inter-company Alliance may require additional time or follow a modified process"; and "For applicants outside of US, the review process may require additional time."

**AstraZeneca — the fastest published turnaround in the family: "Decisions are typically communicated within 45 days of receipt of a complete submission."** Note "complete" — an incomplete package restarts the clock, and AZ will "notify you if additional information is required" during the Proposal in Review state.

**Merck MISP — deadline to committee meeting is short, deadline to written feedback is long.** HIV: submission deadline → Review Committee meeting is ~3–5 weeks (Aug 25 → Sep 9; Nov 17 → Dec 10). But the areas that publish an end-to-end date show ~12–14 weeks: Pneumococcus protocol deadline April 10, 2026 → "Final Comments to Investigator July 1, 2026"; RSV May 1, 2026 → August 7, 2026. Subcutaneous pembrolizumab was ~5 months (Dec 5, 2025 → "End April, 2026").

**GSK (adjacent comparator): "GSK is committed to responding to your proposal within eight weeks from the closing date of the relevant submission period."**

**EARLIEST START — the part that surprises people.** "Approved" is not "funded" anywhere in this family; nothing starts until a contract is executed, and at Genentech three documents must be in place first. Pfizer: "Pfizer support will only be extended upon the execution of an agreement." Merck: "Financial and/or product support is contingent upon full execution by both parties of the research agreement." Genentech, before support can be initiated: "A fully executed IIS agreement... A fully executed IIS safety data exchange agreement... An EC/IRB and/or Health Authority Approval." Realistically add a further contracting-and-IRB period on top of the review clock; the funder pages publish no duration for it (unresolved — see below). If the study needs your own IND, add that too: Genentech requires the sponsor to "submit a IND/CTA and write the final study report and manuscripts".
result.submission_requirements:
**The defining deviation from every federal norm: you are not applying for a grant, you are volunteering to become the regulatory Sponsor.** Genentech states the requirement directly — a sponsor must "Have the scientific, technical and operational capabilities to conduct the study including statistical support" and "Be able to fulfill all regulatory requirements (e.g. submit a IND/CTA and write the final study report and manuscripts) and comply with all relevant laws." That, not page count, is what sinks early-career applications.

**What you actually upload:**
• **Merck MISP** — full protocol on the MISP template, detailed budget on the MISP template, and PI CV with the update date visible in the document. Templates are public downloads (see examples field). Oncology uses its own submission form; non-clinical work has a separate proposal template. No page limit published.
• **AstraZeneca ESR** — the proposal is a structured web form in VCV, not a document. Mandatory attachments: PI CV and budget. Mandatory fields include primary/secondary objectives and endpoints, inclusion/exclusion criteria, hypothesis, rationale, population, sample-size justification/statistics, treatment regimen, blinding, randomisation, study phase — plus operational milestones in months ("Contract Execution to FSI", "FSI to 50% Enrollment", "50% Enrollment to LSI", "LSI to LSLV", "LSLV to FSR"). **At least one planned publication is mandatory** (category, type, date, journal/congress). Two disclosure fields sit in the General Information section: "Have you contacted anyone in AZ?" and "Support from outside AstraZeneca?"
• **Genentech** — portal submission; on submitting you get a Submission ID and a link to a Diversity & Inclusion Questionnaire ("We highly encourage you to complete immediately after submitting"). Protocol and budget come only at stage 3.
• **Pfizer** — everything goes through the ISR portal at www.Pfizer.com/ISR (currently being relaunched). Pfizer's own advice on timing is worth heeding: "Please do not wait until the submission deadline to enter your request into the online portal. Plan to apply early to allow time for clarification questions and to ensure completeness."
• **GSK (adjacent)** — CV via the Files tab; budget breakdown if money is requested.

**Mentor / reference letters — rare, but present where it matters for early-career applicants.** Merck's subcutaneous pembrolizumab guidance is the one explicit case: "The Program encourages less experienced investigators to seek guidance from a mentor prior to submitting IISP proposals. If working with a mentor please also provide their CV where possible, along with a detailed letter from the mentor describing the mentoring plan." No ISS/IIS programme in this family requires reference letters.

**Track record is scored, and Merck says so:** "Please include documentary evidence of successful and timely accrual and publication of investigators' studies in similar indications where possible. Feasibility is carefully considered in our assessment process."

**Institutional sign-off** is not requested at submission by any of the five — but it becomes unavoidable at contracting, because the agreement is institution-to-company. Budgets are tested against a benchmark, not a cap: Genentech "evaluate all funding requests against local fair market value."

**Contrast worth knowing (a sibling mechanism with real page limits):** Gilead's early-career Research Scholars Program does cap length — research abstract "no more than 325 words", research proposal "limited to 5 pages total, not including the bibliography or budget", single-spaced 11pt Arial or larger. ISR/IIS proposals have no published page limit.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
**BOTH HALVES, and they run opposite to NIH intuition.**

**WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the half people assume wrongly).** No ISS/IIS programme in this family publishes any bar based on the applicant's own award history. There is no R01 exclusion, no K-award interaction, no career-stage gate, no "new investigator" carve-out, and no citizenship rule. Merck: the programme is "open to all academic and community-based physicians and researchers worldwide who are interested in conducting their own research." Pfizer: "This global program is open to all researchers who are interested in conducting their own research." Genentech accepts academic medical centres, "Individual investigators / Researchers", collaborative study groups, cooperative groups, healthcare providers and government research institutions. **Holding an R01, a K, a foundation award, or another company's ISS does not disqualify you.** Every published exclusion attaches to the STUDY, not to the person.

**WHAT MAKES YOU INELIGIBLE (all study-level):**
• **Overlap with the company's own trials — or with someone else's ISR.** Pfizer's Internal Medicine areas of interest list out-of-scope work including "Studies overlapping with ongoing Pfizer clinical research or other ISRs" (also excluded there: head-to-head/comparative studies, protocols requesting placebo formulations, paediatric investigations). Merck: "IISP proposals competing with or duplicating any company sponsored trial for Subcutaneous Pembrolizumab will not be supported." This is the real analogue of a prior-funding conflict here, and it is invisible from outside — it is the single strongest reason to talk to an MSL/RMSD before writing.
• **Off-AOI scope.** Merck: "Proposals that are not within the scope of these AOIs may be rejected without further review." Merck Immunology in 2026 would consider only translational studies that are "non-interventional and there is no use of study product or drug supply"; "Proposals for which the primary objectives are translational are outside of the current MISP AOIs" for subcutaneous pembrolizumab.
• **Wrong regulatory stage or wrong country.** Gilead requires the study to occur "after regulatory approval of the product in the country where the study will be conducted." Merck's DOR/ISL: "until further notice only applications from investigators from these two countries [United States and Japan] for work to take place in-country will be accepted," and any approval "would not be final and would be contingent on an eventual approval by the regulatory agency."
• **Wrong company / wrong portal.** Merck's I-DXd (ifinatamab deruxtecan): "Concepts involving I-DXd as monotherapy or in combination with drugs should be submitted through the Daiichi Sankyo portal. Concepts involving the combination of I-DXd and other MSD assets (i.e., pembrolizumab) are not currently being accepted."
• **Money for anything other than running the study.** Genentech: "Funding requests for expenses not associated with the conduct of the study are strictly prohibited." Non-clinical studies and compassionate-use/expanded access are explicitly "not considered investigator-initiated studies" at Genentech and route elsewhere.
• Pfizer obesity currently refuses: investigational products/therapeutics including GLP-1 RA and anti-obesity drugs, Pfizer investigational drugs or pure compounds, retrospective drug-specific analyses, highly invasive studies with ethical concerns, replication of existing studies, and pharmacoeconomic analyses.

**THE MIRROR-IMAGE RULE THAT CATCHES EARLY-CAREER APPLICANTS.** The industry programme that DOES bar prior funding is the early-career one next door, not the ISS/IIS. Gilead's Research Scholars Program (HIV) states: "those who have received substantial NIH research awards, such as being a PI on an R01, P01, or U01, are not Early Stage Investigators", plus "Received your initial faculty appointment within the last 5 years at the time of application", "Have a research mentor with extensive experience in their field", "Be able to devote approximately 50% of professional time to research", and a US citizenship/permanent-residence/valid-visa requirement for the 2-year period. And it routes product studies away: "Proposals utilizing Gilead product(s) are not eligible for funding through the Research Scholars Program. Proposals involving Gilead product(s) should be submitted for review under the Investigator-Sponsored Research Grant Program through the ISR online portal."

**So the decision rule for an early-career applicant:** pre-R01, within 5 years of first faculty appointment, and NOT using company product → the Research Scholars-type early-career programme. Already hold an R01, or your study touches the company's drug at all → the ISR/IIS door is the open one, and your award history is irrelevant to it.

**Caution not sourced to the funder:** industry ISS support (including in-kind study drug) is normally disclosable to your federal sponsor and triggers institutional conflict-of-interest review. None of the five programmes addresses this on their pages — treat it as your institution's question, not the company's.
result.program_officer_contact:
**Yes, and pre-submission contact is expected at four of the five — the company medical-affairs liaison is the de facto program officer.** This is the "who to talk to" answer: it is a person assigned to your region and therapeutic area, not a grants office.

• **Genentech — your Medical Science Liaison (MSL).** "If you have questions or would like to discuss your concept, please reach out to your Medical Science Liaison (MSL)." No MSL yet, or general questions: **usa.iisportal@gene.com**. The MSL role is explicit: "Your MSL can help with pre-approval by discussing your concept with the study review team and providing you with feedback." US-based investigators only; outside the US go to iisportal.roche.com/IISPortal/RochePharma.
• **Merck MISP — named humans, published.** The Contacts page lists a Scientific Leadership & Research Manager per therapeutic area who will "Shepherd your proposal to committee for review" and "Communicate the status of your proposal", with email and phone. General MISP inquiries: **catherine.gauthier@merck.com** (Catherine Gauthier). Pre-submission contact is requested in the funder's own words: "Please contact your local Regional Medical Scientific Director (RMSD, US only) or country specific liaison for any guidance pertaining to your specific concept prior to its submission, to ensure that it falls within the scope and interest of the Investigator Initiated Studies Program (IISP)." Merck also invites out-of-scope ideas through that channel: "Occasionally, we receive proposals out of the AOIs that represent 'out of the box' thinking and are ultimately of great interest. If you believe this may apply for your proposal, please review with your RMSD or appropriate liaison prior to submission." The site is US-only: "Investigators outside of the US... should contact their local MSD office."
• **AstraZeneca — your local market medical representative.** "Please contact your local market medical representative before submission to ensure funding and alignment to strategy." The submission form itself asks "Have you contacted anyone in AZ?", so the contact is recorded and scored.
• **Pfizer — a mailbox, not a person.** **GlobalMedicalGrants@pfizer.com** (programme page) and **ExternalResearch&Grants@Pfizer.com** (the review-cycles PDF). No named officer and no stated expectation of pre-submission contact. Pfizer also runs an alerts list: "Sign up to receive all grant announcements, including Request for Proposal (RFP) postings" — worth joining now, since that is how the 2027 cycle dates and the restored submission link will surface.
• **Gilead — "your local Gilead contact"**; each RFP carries its own email in its description.

If you are early-career and have no MSL/RMSD relationship, that is the first thing to fix — ask your division's clinical research office or a senior colleague who already runs industry-supported studies to make the introduction. Every published route into this mechanism runs through that person.
result.examples_or_samples:
**No company in this family publishes a sample application, a funded abstract, or an annotated example.** Do not go looking for one. Three real substitutes, in order of usefulness:

**1. Read actual funded ISS protocols on ClinicalTrials.gov (verified live, 2026-09-18).** An ISS is registered with the academic institution as lead sponsor and the company as collaborator — that combination is searchable, and since results-posting requirements took effect many of these records carry the full protocol and statistical analysis plan as a downloadable PDF. Verified counts via the ClinicalTrials.gov API: **1,588** studies with a non-industry lead sponsor listing "Merck Sharp & Dohme LLC" as collaborator, of which **625 have results posted**; **1,389** for Pfizer. Verified example with a downloadable protocol: NCT04483544, "Pembrolizumab and Olaparib in Cervical Cancer Patients", lead sponsor Baptist Health South Florida, document "Study Protocol and Statistical Analysis Plan" (Prot_SAP_000.pdf, 798 KB). Other verified examples of the shape: NCT03636503 (Dana-Farber Cancer Institute / Pfizer), NCT02068586 (Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center at Thomas Jefferson University / Pfizer), NCT04919122 (Duke University, with BMS, Exelixis, Merck and Pfizer as collaborators). Query form: clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?filter.advanced=AREA[LeadSponsorClass]OTHER AND AREA[HasResults]true&query.spons=<company>
**2. Merck publishes the blank forms you will actually fill in** — the closest thing to an annotated sample, and free to download without registering: MISP Clinical Protocol Template (.docx), Non-clinical Proposal Template (.docx), Material Transfer Protocol Template (.docx), Clinical Interventional Budget Template (.xlsx, v7 09-MAR-26), Clinical Non-interventional Budget Template (.xlsx, v8 09-MAR-26), Non-Clinical Budget Template (.xlsx, 08APR-2026), MISP Oncology Submission Form (.docx, 03Sep2026), and Translational Studies Data Tiers 2026 (.pdf). All linked from misp-investigator-studies.com/resources.
**3. Field-by-field walkthroughs of the two big portals** — Genentech's "IIS Portal User Guide - Investigator" PDF (screenshot of every required field, gene.com/download/pdf/Genentech-Investigator-Initiated-Study-Portal-User-Guide.pdf) and AstraZeneca's "Overview – How to create and submit an ESR study proposal" infographic PDF (2026 edition), which enumerates all 14 steps and every mandatory field. GSK's "Submitting a Proposal" guide (iss.gsk.com/Documents/Submitting-a-Proposal.pdf) is the same idea for that programme.

Also read the Areas of Interest documents as worked examples of what the company wants: Merck's single Areas of Interest PDF (February 2026 V4, 19 pages) spells out the scientific questions, the exclusions and the dated cycle for every therapeutic area at once; Pfizer splits the same content across six web pages (Oncology, Rare Disease, Vaccines and Antivirals, Inflammation and Immunology, Internal Medicine, Anti-Infectives).
result.resubmission_note: Not found — no resubmission or resubmission-limit policy is published by any of the five programmes. Two adjacent facts that bear on it: Merck describes several areas as a repeating "competitive process" with three or four reviews a year, which implies a rejected protocol can be brought back to a later cycle, but no page says so; and GSK (adjacent) notes a submitted proposal is frozen — "Once the proposal is submitted, it cannot be changed." Ask the MSL/RMSD; this is exactly the kind of thing the liaison answers and the website does not.
unresolved: Pfizer ISR 2027 application windows and notification dates — NOT FOUND. The funder page says the schedule 'will be reposted soon' and the unsolicited-submission link 'will be posted shortly'. The 2026 PDF is still live and is the only dated Pfizer source. This is a tooling-independent fact read off the live page 2026-09-18, not a fetch failure, and it is NOT evidence the programme ended — Pfizer calls it an application-window change and continues to run RFPs with dated deadlines.

Merck MISP 2027 cycle dates — not found; Merck republishes them inside the Areas of Interest PDF, current version February 2026 V4. Areas whose 2026 cycles have closed (Immunology, Pneumococcus, RSV, subcutaneous pembrolizumab) have no posted next date.

Typical award size for ISR/IIS — still not publicly fixed by any of the five companies; budgets are negotiated against 'local fair market value' (Genentech). The existing row's 'amounts not publicly fixed' stands.

Time from approval to executed agreement / earliest study start — no company publishes a duration, only the condition that support follows contract execution (plus, at Genentech, a safety data exchange agreement and IRB/EC or health authority approval).
Resubmission policy — no programme publishes one (see resubmission_note).

Whether concurrent federal funding on the SAME study is permitted, and how in-kind drug supply should be reported to a federal sponsor — not addressed on any of the five funder pages. I did not obtain a citable NIH Other Support quote this run (the NIH Other Support page returned only a general CPOS description), so this is deliberately left as an institutional-COI caution rather than a sourced claim.
Selectivity / success rates — none published by any company.
Named program-officer contacts at Pfizer, AstraZeneca and Gilead — only mailboxes and 'your local contact' routes exist; Merck and Genentech are the exceptions (named managers; assigned MSL).
AstraZeneca ESR dated review-group meeting calendar — not published; only the 45-day decision commitment.

TOOLING NOTE: my WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of this task (200/200), so I located the Merck, AstraZeneca, Genentech and Gilead programme URLs via a DuckDuckGo results page read through the rendering browser. Every substantive claim above was then taken from the funder's own page or the funder's own PDF, not from the search index. Two further tooling facts: pfizer.com had to be read with the rendering browser because a plain fetch redacts email addresses; and all five PDFs (Pfizer cycles, Merck AOI, Genentech guide, AstraZeneca infographic, GSK guide) returned as undecoded binary to a plain fetch and were extracted locally with pdftotext.
result.confidence: medium-high — the Pfizer and Merck dated schedules are high confidence (both quoted from the funder's own live PDF, retrieved 2026-09-18), as are the Genentech, AstraZeneca and Gilead process descriptions (funder pages, same date). Overall confidence is held at medium-high rather than high because this is a FAMILY row: the five companies differ on deadlines, stages, review speed and exclusions, so no single value in these fields is true of the whole row, and each field above is therefore reported per company rather than aggregated.

result.deadline_pattern:
Two cycles per year, May and December, both 5:00 p.m. ET, submitted at awards.cff.org. Each cycle's RFA (with a dated Key Dates table and a revised priority-topic list) publishes ~2 months before the deadline. The recurring cadence is shared with the Research Grant, PTAC Research Grant, PTAC P&F, Postdoctoral Research Fellowship and PTAC Postdoc.

A hard cadence cap makes the practical planning unit one shot per LABORATORY per cycle, not per PI: "Each laboratory (not PI) may submit only one application (research grant or pilot and feasibility award) per cycle (resub vs original). This does not apply to training awards." Plus: "Applicants may only submit for one research grant and one pilot and feasibility award in a 12-month period," and on the live page, only one P&F application in calendar 2026 across both cycles.
result.loi_deadline:
Not applicable. The mechanism's own Policies & Guidelines carries a Letter of Intent section whose entire content is: "IX. Letter of Intent Guidelines — Not applicable to this RFA." This is a single-stage full application.

IMPORTANT CONFUSABLE: the sibling Clinical Pilot and Feasibility Award DOES require an LOI, on a ~4.5-month lead — "Fall: LOI March, full application August / Spring: LOI October, full application February" (currently published: LOI 1 October 2026 → full application 17 February 2027). Applicants routing clinical/interventional work to the wrong P&F variant miss a mandatory gate entirely.
result.review_to_award:
Published verbatim in the mechanism's own Key Dates and General Timeline tables (Spring 2026 cycle, the most recent completed one):
- Published: March 13, 2026
- Full Application Deadline: May 12, 2026
- Committee Review Date: August 2026
- Notification to Applicants: September 2026
- Earliest Project Start Date: November 1, 2026

So for this mechanism: ~3 months deadline-to-committee, ~4 months deadline-to-notification, ~5.6 months deadline-to-earliest-start. The December cycle runs the same shape: 9 Dec 2025 deadline → 1 May 2026 earliest start (~4.7 months). This is faster than CFF's own umbrella hedge ("four to eight months from application submission to notification depending on the RFA"), so plan on the mechanism's table, not the umbrella figure.

Review route: an internal CFF panel first screens every application for alignment with the Section VI priority topics — "Applications focused on high priority research topics will be reviewed by an external committee for technical merit... Applications not focused on high priority research topics may receive a modified and abbreviated review." External review is by the Research and Research Training Committee (RRT), stated explicitly in the Experimental Design instructions. Notification comes from GCMA with anonymized reviewer critiques.

Start-date trap: payment is withheld until IRB/IACUC/IBC approvals and the institution's W-9 + 501(c)(3) (or W-8BEN-E for non-US) are on file with GCMA — "The CF Foundation will not release payments to awardee institutions until these documents are received." Clear compliance paperwork during the ~4-month review wait, not after the award letter.
result.submission_requirements:
Portal is awards.cff.org (CFF's own system; not proposalCentral, not Grants.gov). Formatting is funder-wide: Times New Roman 12 or Arial 11, margins no less than half an inch each side, single-sided, PI name in the header.

WHERE THIS MECHANISM DEVIATES:

1. RESEARCH PLAN = SIX (6) PAGES, the shortest of any CFF non-training mechanism (Postdoc 7, Shwachman 10, Research Grant 12, Clinical Research Award 13). Verbatim: "Page limit: Six (6) single-sided pages, not including the Literature Cited. Applications exceeding this page limit will not be reviewed."
2. PRELIMINARY DATA NOT REQUIRED — the key early-career concession, and the opposite of the Research Grant's expectation: "Preliminary data are not required, however, if provided, will be evaluated in the context of the application."
3. CAREER-GOALS PARAGRAPH IS MANDATORY inside Background and Significance: "describe the relationship of the proposed work to your long-term career goals. Preference will be given to applicants who express an interest in a long-term career in CF-related research."
4. NO MENTORSHIP SECTION: "V. Mentorship Requirements — Not applicable to this RFA" (unlike the training awards).
5. Required subsections a-g: Hypothesis and Specific Aims ("Do not exceed one page"); Background and Significance; Preliminary Results; Experimental Design and Methods; Limitations and Potential Pitfalls; Consultant Arrangements; Literature Cited (excluded from the 6 pages).
6. FIGURES CANNOT BE EXILED to an appendix: "Key figures and legends must be included in the Research Plan and should be of sufficient quality and size (at least 11 pt font)... If uploaded as Appendices, they will NOT be reviewed."

LETTERS OF REFERENCE — the long-lead item that sinks first-timers. Required only if you answer "Yes" to "Are you a junior investigator?" on the GENERAL tab, which then reveals a REFERENCES tab. Three letters: the Chair of the applicant's department (must "indicate the release of sufficient space and facilities for the work described, as well as guarantee the time commitment of the investigator"; if the applicant is currently a fellow it must confirm the pending faculty-level appointment), plus "At least two (2) other individuals familiar with the applicant's scientific interests and abilities." Critically: "Letters of Reference must be submitted prior to submission of the application... The applicant should inform Referees to submit the letters at least one (1) week prior to the application deadline... Once the application has been submitted, no documents can be added." Referees are invited through the tab and Accept/Decline by email; letters must not be password-protected or encrypted (breaks PDF assembly).

OTHER UPLOADS: Biographical Sketch, NIH format, "Do not exceed five (5) pages per person" (dependent faculty must also supply the lab PI's biosketch). Other Support, Facilities Available, Critique Response: no page limit. Results of Past and Current CFF/CFFT Support: past five years, with award #, PI, project title, applicant's title, start/end dates, total amount, results. Letters of Support required for investigators new to CF. Appendices restricted to IRB/IACUC/IBC certifications, signed Letters of Support, and signed Letters of Collaboration from Co-PIs.

PORTAL-ENTERED CHARACTER LIMITS (typed in, not uploaded): Project Alignment to Research Priorities and Expected Outcomes (new in the current RFA; must "Identify up to three specific outcomes"), Lay Abstract, and Scientific Abstract each "no more than 2,000 characters (including spaces)"; Summary of Relevance to CF Foundation mission "no more than 3,000 characters (including spaces)".

BUDGET: up to $50,000/yr + 12% indirect, max 2 years; Year 2 contingent on an approved renewal progress report. NIH salary cap $228,000 (FY2026). Travel capped at $1,500 per person per year. Tuition capped at $10,000 per person per year. Indirect costs NOT allowed on major equipment (>$5,000), computer software, software licenses or tuition. Subcontract indirect only on the first $25,000.

INSTITUTIONAL SIGN-OFF — your click is not submission. You click "Submit to Authorized Institution Official for Acceptance"; status becomes "Pending Authorized Institution Official Acceptance" and the application LOCKS. Your AIO must then open it via My Applications > Pending Authorized Institution Official Acceptance, enter AIO initials on the ASSURANCE STATEMENT(S) tab and click "Submit to CFF" — before 5 p.m. ET. ("Revise AIO" reverts it to Draft.)

TWO-WEEK PRE-REGISTRATION: "We strongly encourage all applicants to pre-register their profile, institution, contacts, and title of their application at least two weeks prior to the application deadline." Register under "Domestic Institution" or "International Institution" — the wrong pick misroutes the application. Domestic applicants verify the institution by EIN/TIN; GCMA needs the W-9 and 501(c)(3). Non-US applicants must file a W-8BEN-E plus a tax equivalency letter (or a letter stating none is available) and may need a CFF International Institution Form under USA Patriot Act / Treasury anti-terrorist-financing rules.

Save at the bottom of every page; return to drafts via "My Applications" > "Draft Applications", NOT via "Funding Opportunities". Uploads are compiled into one PDF — preview with "Application Full Print."
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the half applicants get wrong, and the most valuable thing here):

A PRIOR R01 DOES NOT DISQUALIFY YOU. CFF uses prior funding only to decide which PAPERWORK you file, not whether you may apply. The definition, verbatim: "The CF Foundation defines junior investigator as any individual who has not received a CFF/CFFT Research Grant or NIH equivalent (e.g., R01, R21, R23) as a Principal Investigator AND is within their first five years of their first academic appointment at the level of Assistant Professor or equivalent." The consequence, verbatim: "Investigators who have received a prior CFF/CFFT Research Grant or NIH equivalent, are not required to submit Letters of Reference; however, if they are new to CF research, Letters of Support and/or Collaboration should be provided as uploads in the FULL APPLICATION UPLOADS tab." So prior R01 holders simply skip the three reference letters.

Also preserved: established investigators moving INTO cystic fibrosis are an explicit target ("to support promising new investigators as they establish themselves in research areas relevant to CF"); "An investigator is considered new to CF if they have not previously (1) published in CF or (2) received extramural funding for a CF-focused research project" — such applicants add a letter of support from an established CF collaborator. Non-US applicants and institutions are eligible ("United States residents and applicants from outside the United States are welcome to apply"). For-profit entities "may (under select circumstances) be considered." Training awards do not count against the one-application-per-laboratory-per-cycle cap. Faculty whose appointment depends on a senior investigator ARE eligible, provided they attach the lab PI's biosketch and letter of support.

WHAT BLOCKS YOU:

1. THROUGHPUT CAPS, not award-type exclusions. "Each laboratory (not PI) may submit only one application (research grant or pilot and feasibility award) per cycle (resub vs original). This does not apply to training awards." And "Applicants may only submit for one research grant and one pilot and feasibility award in a 12-month period. Each application must describe a research project that is distinct." And on the live page: "Applicants may submit only one Pilot and Feasibility Award application in 2026 (either the Spring or Fall cycle)." A labmate's submission consumes your lab's slot.
2. THE $200,000 CEILING (needs PO approval, not automatic): "PIs with a combined total of CF Foundation research support exceeding $200,000 per year in direct costs (excluding Research Development Program, National Resource Center, Therapeutic Development Network, and Care Center Awards) with an end date more than six (6) months from the application deadline must receive Program Officer approval before an application will be considered."
3. SCOPE BAR ON CONTINUATIONS — the P&F-specific one: "Applications for continued funding of a project, or long-term support of an investigator, will not be considered through this program. Projects that are an extension of previous work should be submitted through the Research Grant mechanisms." Reinforced in the published low-score list: "Application is a continuation or extension of an existing research project."
4. CAREER-STAGE ROUTING: "Candidates who are clinical fellows should apply to the CF Foundation Clinical Fellowship program"; "Candidates who are postdoctoral fellows should apply to the CF Foundation Postdoctoral Research Fellowship program." Applicants must be independent investigators, i.e. have "completed fellowship training and whose institution allows them to submit applications for research funding as a Principal Investigator."
5. TOPIC ROUTING (the most common fatal error): CFTR protein-function restoration or gene fix/replace work belongs in the Path to a Cure P&F. Human-subjects work is reviewable here ONLY if sampling is minimal-risk (venipuncture, nasal brushings) and samples/data are anonymous; "The CF Foundation Patient Registry and Interventional studies involving human subjects cannot be supported through this program and should instead apply as a Clinical Pilot and Feasibility Award."
6. DOCUMENT FAILURE IS AN ELIGIBILITY FAILURE for dependent faculty: "Failure to provide these materials may result in the application being withdrawn." For-profit applicants who skip the mandatory PO call: "Failure to do so may result in withdrawal of the proposal."

CORRECTION TO THE FUNDER-WIDE BRIEFING: the $168,000 multiple-Research-Grants ceiling ("Multiple CF Foundation Research Grants held by a single investigator will not be permitted... when the total combined funding exceeds $168,000 per year") does NOT appear anywhere in the Pilot & Feasibility Policies & Guidelines — I searched the full extracted text and found no occurrence of "168". Only the $200,000 PO-approval threshold is stated for this mechanism. Do not tell a P&F applicant the $168k cap binds them; flag it as a Research Grant rule and a PO question.
result.resubmission_note:
ALLOWED, capped at two cycles, and the required paperwork is unlike NIH's.

How many, verbatim from Section VII: "Applications that have not been funded in two review cycles will not be accepted for further consideration by the CF Foundation. (Exceptions for one additional resubmission may be considered for tenure-track PIs who are pre-tenure with prior approval from the Program Officer)." In practice: original + one resubmission, with a third attempt only if you are pre-tenure on the tenure track AND cleared it with the PO in advance.

What must change, verbatim: "In order to resubmit unfunded applications during future application cycles, applicants must indicate that the application is a resubmission and clearly address reviewer critiques through a response to reviewers and revisions to the research plan."

Three mandatory, separable actions:
1. FLAG IT as a resubmission in the portal.
2. UPLOAD A CRITIQUE RESPONSE (its own downloadable template, a separate attachment — not part of the research plan, and with no page cap, unlike NIH's one-page Introduction): "If the application is a resubmission of a previously declined application, please provide a point-by-point response to the prior reviews. There is no page limit to your responses, but please be concise and succinct."
3. REVISE THE SCIENCE AND MARK THE CHANGES: "If the application is a resubmission of an earlier one, revisions must be clearly indicated by a change in font, bolded or underlined. The CF Foundation will not review resubmissions that have not been revised." And: "In addition to providing the response to critiques, the research plan must also be revised and clearly marked to show changes from the previous submission. Research plans that are not clearly revised may not be reviewed." A cosmetic resubmission is rejected without review.

No calendar expiry is stated. The binding constraints are the two-cycle count and the throughput caps, so a resubmission normally lands 6 or 12 months later — and because a resubmission counts the same as an original against the one-per-laboratory-per-cycle rule, choosing to resubmit spends the lab's only slot that cycle.

WORTH ASKING THE PO: the P&F wording is "not been funded in two review cycles", whereas the Clinical Research Award says "not been discussed in two review meetings". Since P&F applications off the priority list "may receive a modified and abbreviated review", it is not stated whether an abbreviated/triaged review consumes one of your two cycles. Unresolved — confirm before spending an attempt.

There is NO public abstract database for CFF — no RePORTER/NSF-Award-Search equivalent; awards.cff.org is login-gated and shows only open opportunities and your own applications. Six routes that do work, best first:

1. THE RFA'S OWN REVIEWER CHECKLIST — the highest-value starter material, and specific to this mechanism. Section VII publishes "Chief causes for assigning low priority scores to applications during review": failure to address contemporary CF research priorities; application is a continuation or extension of an existing project; insufficient information or documentation; inadequate statement of hypothesis, experimental design or methods; failure to demonstrate awareness of and plans for coping with key problems and pitfalls; insufficient or improper controls; failure to describe potential relevance to issues in CF; failure to document the necessary skills or training; failure to meet all criteria in the policy statement. Write against this list directly. Source: https://www.cff.org/media/11101/download?inline

2. EUROPE PMC GRANT SEARCH — the closest working proxy for a funded-abstract database. VERIFIED LIVE 2026-09-18 via the REST API: GRANT_AGENCY:"Cystic Fibrosis Foundation" returns 3,598 records; adding the phrase "pilot and feasibility" narrows to 47. Records carry the CFF award ID (SURNAME + two-digit year + code). This identifies who CFF funded, when, and on what, and lets you read the resulting papers — the closest public stand-in for a funded aims page. Browse https://europepmc.org/search?query=GRANT_AGENCY%3A%22Cystic%20Fibrosis%20Foundation%22 ; API https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=GRANT_AGENCY:%22Cystic+Fibrosis+Foundation%22&format=json&resultType=core . PubMed's "Grants and funding" field carries the same data. Caveat: award IDs do not distinguish P&F from Research Grant, so filter by topic and by the $50k/2-year scale.

3. THE TEMPLATES ARE THE REAL STARTER KIT. Because no sample applications are published, CFF's own scaffolding is what you build from, and every uploaded component has a downloadable template inside awards.cff.org: Budget Justification, Research Plan, Biographical Sketches for Key Personnel, Other Support, Facilities Available, Results of Past and Current CFF/CFFT Support, and Critique Response (if resubmission).

4. YOUR OWN AND COLLEAGUES' CRITIQUES. CFF returns anonymized reviewer critiques to every applicant with the notification — the summary-statement analogue. Not public, so the practical move is to ask a CF-funded colleague to show you theirs alongside the funded application. I found no university research-office library of published CFF sample applications.

5. BEFORE YOU HAVE AN ACCOUNT: the "For Applicants: Our Grants Management System" how-to guide PDF and a three-part video tutorial series, both linked from https://www.cff.org/researchers/information-applicants-and-awardees ; plus each mechanism's full Policies & Guidelines PDF. Subscribe to the Funding Opportunities newsletter (https://signup.e2ma.net/signup/1941850/1922653/) to be told the moment the Fall 2026 RFA drops — which is how you get the dated deadline.

6. FORM 990 SCHEDULE I for institution-level scale and distribution (no abstracts): ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, CFF EIN 13-1930701, https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/131930701

BASE RATES: not published for this mechanism. Only the Clinical Research Award publishes figures (~35% of investigators invited to full application, ~20% of full applications funded); do not transfer those to P&F.
