result.prior_funding_conflicts:
PREP has no grant-style prior-award exclusion (no R01/K analogue). What limits eligibility is a CATEGORY CLOCK — cumulative years already spent as a PREP researcher in a given category. Both halves, from the 2022 NOFO §I and §III.3:

WHAT USES UP / BLOCKS ELIGIBILITY:
- Undergraduate: "eligible to collaborate with NIST as PREP researchers for five (5) years in this category."
- Graduate students: "eligible for three (3) years as master's degree seeking students and six (6) years as doctoral degree students."
- Bachelor's / master's degree holders: three (3) and five (5) years respectively — AND "these individuals are not allowed to enroll in a degree seeking program at any university/college in the United States or abroad during their time participating in this category." (So a post-bacc PREP appointment and starting a PhD are mutually exclusive.)
- Post-doctoral fellows: must hold "a doctoral degree for five (5) years or less"; eligible five (5) years in category. Passing the 5-years-post-PhD mark moves you out of this category.
- Senior research fellows: doctoral degree "for more than five (5) years"; eligible five (5) years in category.
- Hard ceiling regardless of category: "individual PREP researcher appointments cannot exceed the period of performance of the governing cooperative agreement."
- Students must be enrolled FULL-TIME at the partner institution; degree holders "must earn the respective degree before beginning the appointment." GPA 3.0 unweighted recommended.
- PREP is salaried employment by the university, so it is not compatible with a fellowship that forbids concurrent full-time salaried employment (the NOFO is silent on this — it is a term of the other fellowship, not of PREP; check the other award's terms).

WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the half that matters):
- The clocks are PER CATEGORY and you get a fresh one when you advance. NOFO: "participating researchers may be considered for the next PREP research category after the years of eligibility are met and degree requirements are fulfilled for the initial category of the appointment. For instance, a postdoctoral fellow may transition to senior research fellow appointment five (5) years after their appointment, subject to the approval of both the recipient and NIST." So prior PREP time as an undergraduate does NOT consume your six years as a doctoral student.
- Mid-appointment movement is expected, not penalised: "PREP researchers are employed by their academic institutions and may, if appropriate, matriculate to another PREP researcher category during their time participating in the program," and recipients "must develop a mechanism to provide career progression for PREP researchers who participate in the program for more than 12 months or matriculate to another PREP category (for example, advancing from a graduate student appointment to a postdoc appointment)."
- Undergraduate and graduate categories: "may request one (1) additional year of eligibility under extenuating circumstances," subject to NIST and recipient approval with compelling evidence.
- A new cooperative agreement re-opens the ceiling: "If a subsequent cooperative agreement is established with a given PREP recipient, the PREP recipient may request to extend a PREP researcher's appointment, up to the maximum eligibility for a given category."
- Citizenship does NOT gate eligibility: "PREP researchers are not required to have U.S. citizenship to participate" — a valid nonimmigrant visa plus work authorisation (E-Verify) is the requirement. Note individual postings may still state a preference (req PREP0005234 lists "U.S. Citizen Preferred" under qualifications).
- Academic affiliates (faculty, research faculty, adjunct, instructors, lecturers): "There is not a term limitation for this category."
- No federal-employment conflict: a PREP researcher is "an Associate working at NIST, who is not a Federal Employee." Corollary to state plainly — "participation as a PREP researcher does not imply consideration for future federal employment," and PREP associates "are generally prohibited from receiving career development and other training offered to federal employees."
result.review_to_award: Individual route — no published review timetable, because it is a hiring process, not a merit review. Measured from live postings: close date to anticipated start is ~2–3.5 months (req 74563 closes 22-Sep-2026, anticipated start 1 Dec 2026; req 74699 closes 29-Sep-2026, anticipated start 27 Dec 2026). Selection is by the NIST sponsor, not a panel — Michigan Tech: "Applicants will submit their resumes to the specific opportunity, and the NIST sponsor will select the PREP Fellow from the list of applicants. The selected PREP Fellow will then be reviewed by the PREP Management Team for confirmation." The schedule risk sits after the offer: "This position requires the successful completion of an NAIS agreement and federal security clearance, as mandated by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Employment is contingent upon approval of these requirements, as determined by NIST." Non-citizens additionally need visa/work authorisation; the NOFO tells institutions to factor in State Department and DHS processing times. Institutional route (2022 NOFO, only published timetable): due 30-Sep-2022 → "NIST expects to complete its review, selection of successful applicants, and award processing by November 2022. NIST expects the earliest start date for awards under this NOFO to be December 2022" — about two months, far faster than the ~9-month NIH norm. Review: "At least three (3) objective reviewers," scored individually not by consensus, ranked by numerical average; the Selecting Official is the NIST PREP Program Manager and "may recommend applications out of rank order based on the selection factors."
result.submission_requirements:
THE BIG DEVIATION: for the individual, essentially none of the funder-wide NIH-style machinery applies. No Grants.gov, no SAM.gov/UEI, no eRA Commons, no ASSIST, no SciENcv, no ORCID requirement, no biosketch, no Specific Aims, no page limits, no budget, no institutional Authorized Organizational Representative, no 5 PM local-time rule. You are applying for a job. Do not route this through your research office.

INDIVIDUAL — what each hub actually asks for:
- CU Boulder (Boulder hub): "To apply, please submit the following materials: Resume or CV; Cover letter addressed to the Search Committee briefly describing your qualifications, professional goals, and specific interest in this position; (optional) Transcripts/Proof of Degree." Plus: "During the application process, you will need to enter contact information for a reference. We will request the letter of recommendation immediately following your application." — so line up one referee before you click submit. And: "Application materials will not be accepted via email. For consideration, applications must be submitted through CU Boulder Jobs."
- UMD (Gaithersburg hub): "To be considered for a position, we ask that you submit a cover letter explaining your qualifications for the position and a curriculum vitae." Allowed types .pdf/.doc/.docx, max file size 8 MB, submitted through the form at prep.umd.edu. Questions to prep@umd.edu.
- Michigan Tech: resume submitted to the specific opportunity; nistprep@mtu.edu.
- Gating facts that are easy to miss: students must be enrolled FULL-TIME at a participating PREP university (FAQ: "PREP researchers who are undergraduate or graduate students are required to be enrolled full-time at a partnering PREP university"); degree holders must have the degree in hand before the appointment begins; you sign a Guest Researcher Agreement and are a NIST associate, not an employee; grad students at a partner university have "their tuition paid for by their NIST sponsor" (undergraduate tuition is not paid); all categories except undergraduates get benefits and relocation assistance.

INSTITUTIONAL (2022 NOFO, if/when a new one posts) — where it deviates from the NIH norm: Project Narrative "limited to twenty-five (25) pages double-spaced, noting the limit of two (2) pages for the Executive Summary"; page limit "includes Cover Page; Table of Contents (if included); Project Narrative with all required information, including figures, graphs, tables, images, and pictures"; "Easy to read font (10-point minimum)"; resumes excluded from the count but "must be a maximum of two (2) pages each"; "Applicants applying to both PREP Boulder and PREP Gaithersburg must submit a separate application for each location"; Grants.gov only, "Paper, Email, and Facsimile (fax) Submissions. Will not be accepted"; no cost sharing. Scoring rubric: Program Approach and Management Plan 0–35, Qualifications and Experience 0–35, Success Metrics 0–20, Match of Budget to Proposed Work 0–10.
result.program_officer_contact:
Pre-submission contact is not just expected — it is close to the whole game, and it is a different person than at NIH. The NIST FAQ is explicit that demand originates inside NIST: "Who can request a PREP researcher? A request should come from a NIST researcher." A posting exists because a specific NIST scientist wants someone.

WHO TO EMAIL, in order of usefulness to a PhD student/postdoc:
1. THE NIST SPONSOR NAMED ON THE POSTING — the decision-maker. UMD publishes the sponsor's name AND @nist.gov address on every job detail page (e.g. PREP0002567, National Fire Research Laboratory, sponsor Rodney Bryant, rodney.bryant@nist.gov). Email them before applying, with a short note and your CV, exactly as you would a prospective postdoc PI. If your interests match a NIST group but no posting exists, this is also how a posting gets created.
2. Hub administrators: prep@umd.edu (Gaithersburg/UMD); recruitprep@colorado.edu and cuprepadmin@colorado.edu, (303) 492-4122 (CU Boulder — posting contact named as Lisa Valencia); nistprep@mtu.edu (Michigan Tech).
3. NIST programme-level: **prep@nist.gov** (listed as the PREP Program Manager contact on both the PREP page and the PREP FAQs, page updated 27 May 2026). PREPGaithersburg@nist.gov appears in the 2022 NOFO.
4. 2022 NOFO §VII contacts, 2022-vintage and possibly stale: Kara Robinson, 202-236-4515, kara.robinson@nist.gov (programmatic/technical, Grants.gov, rules); Dean Iwasaki, 301-975-8449, dean.iwasaki@nist.gov. The current IAAO staff directory (updated 10 Aug 2026) lists Academic Program Managers Kara Belle Arnold, Elaine Lalanne and Cara O'Malley and Deputy Director for Academic Affairs LaKesha Perry, but publishes no emails and no per-programme assignment — so prep@nist.gov is the reliable route.

No SRO, no study section, no summary statement, no post-review PO conversation: none of those roles exist in PREP.
result.examples_or_samples:
There is no NIH-style library of funded applications with summary statements for PREP, and nothing equivalent to RePORTER covers it. Say so plainly rather than sending someone hunting. What does exist, and is genuinely useful:

1. THE LIVE POSTING CORPUS IS THE SAMPLE SET. 200 current PREP positions at prep.umd.edu/SearchJobs/ProfessionalResearchExperienceProgram, each with the research summary, required and preferred qualifications, the NIST group, the NIST sponsor's name and email, salary band and hours. Reading twenty of these teaches the house style faster than any sample application, and filters by category (Undergraduate / Post-baccalaureate / Post-masters / Graduate student / Postdoctoral researcher / Senior researcher / Academic affiliate) and location. Boulder equivalent: jobs.colorado.edu search on "Professional Research Experience Program". Concrete salary anchors for negotiation: UMD postdoc PREP0002567 $82,764–$91,760; CU Boulder req 74699 Postdoctoral Associate $74,000–$108,000, Research Associate $78,000–$135,000.
2. NIST PREP FAQs — nist.gov/iaao/academic-affairs-office/prep/prep-faqs (updated 27 May 2026): pay, tuition, benefits, employer of record, guest-researcher status.
3. The 2022 NOFO itself is the "annotated sample" for an institution: full required-content list, formatting rules and the scoring rubric with point weights.
4. Participant narrative: NIST links a PREP student story from the PREP page ("Stories from PREP Students" → nist.gov/blogs/taking-measure/pokemon-physics-my-journey-perseverance-research). Michigan Tech runs a PREP announcements blog (blogs.mtu.edu/nist-prep/category/announcement/); CU PREP posts researcher news at colorado.edu/program/cuprep.
5. For an institution wanting a funded application's text, there is no public repository — a FOIA request to NIST would be the route. Not verified in this session; flagged in unresolved.
result.resubmission_note:
No resubmission concept exists for individuals, and this is a genuine advantage worth stating to applicants: there is no A0/A1, no 37-month window, no one-resubmission cap, no per-year application limit, and no penalty for an unsuccessful application. If you are not selected for a posting, you apply to the next one — at the same hub or a different partner university — immediately and as often as you like. The only real limits are the category clocks in prior_funding_conflicts.

For institutions, the 2022 NOFO contains no resubmission policy (the word does not appear in that sense). What it does offer: "Unsuccessful applicants will be notified by e-mail and will have the opportunity to receive a debriefing after the opportunity is officially closed. Applicants must request within 10 business days of the email notification to receive a debrief from the program office." That 10-business-day window is the drift-sensitive detail — miss it and the feedback is gone. One selection factor to note when preparing a next attempt: reviewers consider "Whether the project duplicates other projects funded by NIST."
unresolved: Whether NIST will run a new institutional PREP competition in 2027. The 5-year-cycle read (2017 NOFO -> 2022 NOFO -> Dec 2022 awards with up-to-5-year performance) is my inference from grants.gov's archive and the NOFO's own dates, NOT a NIST statement. No forecast record exists on grants.gov as of 2026-09-18.

Current named PREP programme officer. The IAAO staff directory (updated 10 Aug 2026) lists three Academic Program Managers but no emails and no programme assignment; the named contacts I have (Kara Robinson, Dean Iwasaki) come from the 2022 NOFO and may be stale. Kara Robinson and the directory's Kara Belle Arnold may or may not be the same person - not verified, not assumed.

Stipend/salary bands for undergraduate, post-bacc, post-masters and graduate-student PREP categories. Verified figures exist only for postdoc/research-associate postings I opened (UMD $82,764-$91,760; CU Boulder $74,000-$108,000 and $78,000-$135,000). NIST publishes no PREP pay scale; bands are per-posting and per-university.

Whether the Gaithersburg partners other than UMD, Michigan Tech and Montgomery College use close dates or pure rolling postings. JHU (nistprep.engineering.jhu.edu) returned a Cloudflare interstitial (HTTP 403) to a plain fetch - a tooling fact, not evidence about the programme. Georgetown, GWU, Morgan State, Mines and Montgomery College pages were not opened in this session; their links are as listed on NIST's own PREP page.

Whether NIST's published 2022 partner list is current. The NIST page is the authority I used and it was updated 2 September 2026, but several listed institutions were not independently confirmed to be holding live postings today.

Whether a funded PREP institutional application is obtainable by FOIA. Stated as the logical route by analogy with other agencies; NIST publishes no FOIA guidance specific to PREP and I did not verify it.

The Charleston, South Carolina campus. The NOFO and the NIST page both say institutions may apply to support Charleston (administered under PREP Gaithersburg), but no Charleston-specific applicant portal or live posting was found.

result.program_name: RSF Dissertation Research Grants (DRG)
result.next_deadline:
February 2027 — month published, exact DAY not yet posted as of 2026-09-18. RSF's deadlines page says, verbatim and in full: "Dissertation Research Grants / Next deadline: February 2027."

BUT a dated answer IS available as evidence, not as a guess. Every prior round was published with a hard date, in RSF's own words:
- Round 2: "The next deadline will be February 1, 2023"
- Round 3: "The next deadline will be February 1st, 2024"
- Round 4: "The next deadline is 2pm ET on February 4, 2025"
- Round 5: "The next deadline is February 3, 2026, at 2PM ET" — and the DRG RFP page: "Applications will be accepted through February 3, 2026 (2 pm Eastern Time/11 am Pacific Time). Late applications will not be reviewed."
(Rounds 2-4 read from Wayback captures of RSF's own /how-to-apply/application-deadlines page; round 5 from the live RSF RFP page plus captures of the current deadlines page. No third-party or search-index source used anywhere in this record.)

PLAN AGAINST: the first business days of February 2027 — Feb 1-4 — at 2pm ET / 11am PT. Every one of the four published rounds landed in that four-day window (Wed, Thu, Tue, Tue). Treat Feb 1, 2027 (Monday) as your working deadline; do not treat it as published.

WHEN THE DAY APPEARS: RSF still said "The next deadline is expected to be in February 2026" on 13 Sep 2025 and had posted the hard "February 3, 2026, at 2PM ET" by 18 Nov 2025. So the exact day normally goes up in NOVEMBER, roughly 2.5 months out — the same moment the Fluxx portal opens ("The Fluxx application portal will open two months ahead of a deadline"). RSF then trails it twice in its Monthly Bulletin (Nov 2025: "Upcoming Dissertation Research Grants Deadline"; Jan 2026: "Dissertation Research Grants Deadline"), so subscribing at russellsage.org/about/subscribe is the reliable way to catch the date.

CUT-OFF IS ABSOLUTE: "Our deadlines are strict... Any applications submitted after the cut-off time will automatically be deferred to the next round of applications." There is one round a year; missing it costs 12 months.

CAUTION ON THE LIVE RFP: https://www.russellsage.org/apply/grants/dissertation/rfp is still the Feb 3, 2026 round's text (unchanged in captures from Nov 2025, Jan 2026, Jun 2026 and live on 2026-09-18). A student reading it today sees a closed deadline. It will be refreshed for the 2027 round.
result.deadline_pattern:
Annual, ONE round per year, one step, no LOI. Deadline = first business days of February at 2pm ET / 11am PT (Feb 1 2023, Feb 1 2024, Feb 4 2025, Feb 3 2026). Fluxx portal opens ~2 months before (early December). Decisions/announcements mid-May to mid-June. Earliest grant start July 1. Rounds to date: 1st awarded Jun 2022, 2nd May 2023, 3rd May 2024, 4th 18 Jun 2025 (29 awards), 5th 18 Jun 2026 (24 awards). Sixth round = February 2027.

Backwards plan for a Feb 2027 deadline: email programs@rsage.org with an abstract by ~early January (RSF: "reach out at least one month ahead of the deadline"); create the Fluxx account by ~third week of January (see the 5-business-day trap in submission_requirements); watch /news/watch for the "How to Apply - Dissertation Research Grants" webinar, which ran 6 Jan 2026 for the last round.
result.loi_deadline: Not applicable — there is none. RSF FAQ, verbatim: "Do I have to submit a letter of inquiry before applying? No, dissertation research grant applications do not require an initial letter of inquiry." This is the single biggest structural difference from RSF Core Research Grants, which are LOI-gated and run ~8 months. DRG is a direct one-step proposal submission. Nothing is due before the February deadline.
result.review_to_award:
FUNDER-WIDE NORM IS 8 MONTHS (Core, LOI to decision). DRG IS ROUGHLY HALF THAT, but RSF publishes two slightly different numbers and reality has run longer than both:
- Grant Seeker FAQ (DRG block): "Completed applications will be reviewed, and decisions announced within approximately three months of the application deadline."
- Review Process page (early-career track): "The full review process takes about three to four months from a proposal deadline to a final decision."
- DRG RFP (2026 round): "Decisions are expected to be announced in May and grants can start on or after July 1."
- WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED: Feb 3, 2026 deadline → awards announced 18 Jun 2026 (4.5 months); Feb 4, 2025 deadline → announced 18 Jun 2025 (4.5 months). Earlier rounds announced May 2023 and May 2024. So budget 4-5 months, i.e. a mid-May to mid-June answer for a February submission, and do not build a plan that needs money before July.

EARLIEST START: July 1 — published ONLY on the DRG RFP page ("grants can start on or after July 1"), not in the deadlines table, which gives no grant-start column for DRG. Award records carry a Project Date of the announcement month (e.g. Frederick DeVeaux, UCLA, "June 2026").

BETWEEN DECISION AND MONEY (real, and easily underestimated by a student): the grant is paid to the university, not to you — "The grant will be administered by the applicant's university which must act as the fiscal agent. RSF will pay the entire grant within several weeks of receiving the signed grant letter." Before a grant agreement is issued RSF requires written confirmation of IRB approval OR IRB exemption; written confirmation of access to any non-public data; and proof of pre-registration for RCTs. Plus the DRG-specific supervisor letter (below). Start the IRB early — it is the usual bottleneck between "you won" and "you are paid."

REVIEW STAGES AND ODDS: internal staff screen ("Approximately 33-50 percent of the proposals will move to the next stage") → "At least 3-4 peer reviewers will read each proposal. PIs may be asked to respond to reviewer comments in detail before moving forward" → a standing DRG advisory committee that "recommend[s] which proposals to fund or decline." Overall funding rate, RSF's own figure: "about 12-15% for the pipeline and dissertation grants" (vs 8-9% for Core). RSF "expects to approve up to 20 grants" per round; it actually made 29 (2025) and 24 (2026). Everyone who reaches external review gets masked reviewer comments whether funded or not; those screened out internally get none, but "Applicants who do not receive comments may email programs@rsage.org to request feedback from the initial screen."

GRANT TERM: "Projects are limited to one year." Reporting is one final narrative report due 14 months after the start, and — unusually — "No financial reporting is required for dissertation research grants," and "Spending of grant funds is not restricted to a specific grant term... no grant amendment or approval from RSF is required to continue spending after the end date."
result.submission_requirements:
PORTAL: Fluxx only (https://rsf.fluxx.io/user_sessions/new). No Grants.gov, SAM.gov, eRA Commons or ORCID.

*** THE BIGGEST DEVIATION FROM THE FUNDER-WIDE NORM — ACCOUNT APPROVAL IS 5 BUSINESS DAYS, NOT 2 ***
RSF's general Application Requirements page says "**Allow up to 2 business days for a new account to be approved**". The DRG RFP page says something different, twice: "**Allow up to 5 business days for a new account to be approved**" and "*New accounts must be created at least one week before an application deadline. Activating a new account may take up to 5 business days.*" Take the DRG page's number. A first-time applicant who registers in the last week of January for a Feb 1-4 deadline can be locked out. Register by roughly 20 January.
Portal window: "The Fluxx application portal will open two months ahead of a deadline" — so ~early December to the February deadline. Draft expiry: "If a draft application is not electronically submitted by the next applicable deadline, the application will automatically be withdrawn and you will need to restart the process."
Account ownership: "The account must be in the name of the applicant... university administration staff or a student may not submit on behalf of faculty." For DRG the student IS the PI, so the account must be the student's own; a grants administrator may be given access to the record but cannot be the submitting account.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY UPLOADED AT SUBMISSION — ONLY TWO DOCUMENTS. RSF's Fluxx application preview for DRG lists, under "Requested Documents": CV, Proposal. That is the entire upload list.
- Proposal: "Maximum of 5 single-spaced pages (with standard 12-point font and 1-inch margins), excluding (1) references, (2) supporting tables and figures, and (3) appendices like draft survey instruments and interview protocols." The RFP restates it as "A concise single-spaced (5 pages maximum) proposal describing the research; Bibliography does not count towards page limit". (Half the Core proposal's 10 pages; 2 pages under Pipeline's 7.)
- CV: 5 pages max per PI/co-PI.

DELIBERATELY NOT REQUIRED AT SUBMISSION (this is where DRG deviates most from what students assume): NO budget — "a budget is not required at the time of submission. The budget will be finalized with the PI and their university's research office after approval of the grant"; NO letter from the dissertation supervisor; NO letters of reference or support; NO transcript; NO institutional sign-off or research-office routing; NO point-by-point response memo (that is a Core-proposal requirement only). You can submit this alone, from your own account, without your department's involvement.

WHAT THE 5 PAGES MUST DO: "Proposals should briefly outline the rationale of the research, clearly state the question(s) under study, and provide extensive details regarding the research methods, data, measures, and analytic approach to be employed. The proposal should include a brief budget description that explains what RSF funds would cover and what existing sources of support are already secured." Apply the funder-wide allocation rule hard at 5 pages: "The research design (describing the data, methods, analytic plan, etc.) should take up at least 50 percent of the narrative... Discussions of broader impact, fit with RSF goals, investigator qualifications, and requested budget should be brief." Also cite across disciplines — "your application may be reviewed by scholars outside your discipline."
SELECTION SIGNAL, stated only for DRG and Pipeline: "Priority will be given to proposals that will use RSF funds to gather new quantitative or qualitative data, including conducting interviews, field work, and archival work, carrying out experiments, paying study participant incentives, purchasing data not already available to the investigator, etc."

THE FLUXX FORM ITSELF (draft offline from https://www.russellsage.org/sites/default/files/2026-04/DRG_application_04012026.pdf): doctoral-student-in-US-or-US-territory confirmation; ABD confirmation phrased "By the time of the grant start date"; PhD discipline; first-generation-college question; how you heard about the programme; project title; "Project Abstract/Summary: [recommended 1000 characters]"; proposed project start date; consent to be contacted about your career path for 2 years; budget-category checkboxes including "Stipend (max. $7500)"; CONFIRMED and PENDING sources of support (name of organisation and amount); data types used; whether a new dataset results; whether existing data are publicly available and your access plan; whether it is an experiment/RCT and where you will pre-register; qualitative/quantitative/mixed methods.

IF YOU PASS REVIEW — the second wave of documents. RFP: "Conditional on positive external reviews, applicants will be invited to submit: A letter from the dissertation supervisor... A detailed Excel budget, using the RSF budget template; A budget narrative that explains what RSF funds would cover [and which] must also include a timeline that includes the dissertation activities for which funds will be requested and when the dissertation is expected to be completed." Supervisor letter content is prescribed: "The supervisor must document that the dissertation research (a) is the same research that was described in the DRG proposal and (b) has been approved by the dissertation committee. If you are defending your prospectus this Spring after the application deadline, this must be received before funds can be disbursed."

BUDGET RULES WHEN YOU GET THERE: maximum $15,000 (a flat cap — note the corpus row's "Up to $15,000 (est.)" can be hardened to $15,000, sourced); "Projects are limited to one year"; "No indirect costs are allowed"; "The PI can request a stipend up to $7,500" (so at most half can be stipend); RA wages allowed at the higher of state minimum wage or $15.00/hour, but no tuition remission or student fees; participant incentives at the same wage floor; economy travel only, conference travel case-by-case and only if certified unavailable from your institution; no personal computers; two quotes required if a survey firm collects the data. RSF-supported scholars may use the Cornell, Yale or Baruch NYRDC sites without paying an access fee. The Excel budget template published on /apply/tips is labelled "for core research grant proposals only" and the DRG "Sample Budget" is still marked "(coming soon)" — RSF sends the DRG template after approval.

ONE CARVE-OUT IN YOUR FAVOUR: the funder-wide open-data condition does not bind you. Terms & Conditions: "RSF requires that the investigators make their datasets publicly available... Note that this requirement does not apply to RSF's Dissertation Research Grant Program." Likewise the capstone-conference obligation applies to Pipeline and Criminal Justice grantees, not DRG.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
BOTH HALVES, because the "preserves" half is what most students get wrong.

=== WHAT DISQUALIFIES ===
1. A PREVIOUS DRG. "There is a lifetime limit of one dissertation research grant per applicant." Note the limit is on the GRANT, not the application — being declined does not consume it.
2. YOUR OWN PRIOR PUBLICITY ON THE PROJECT. "We do not support projects where the proposed research has already been circulated as a working paper or submitted for publication." This is the quiet killer for economics and political-science students who post job-market papers: a dissertation chapter already on SSRN/NBER/arXiv or under journal review is out of scope as a proposed project.
3. BEING TOO FAR ALONG. "These grants will support all aspects of dissertation research (data collection, data preparation, data analysis, and writing), but they are not intended for students who have completed data collection and propose to spend the entire grant period finishing the dissertation." A pure write-up year will not be funded.
4. SCOPE, not funding status: routine use of public data alone ("RSF does not consider submissions that solely make routine use of publicly-available data, such as the Current Population Survey, American Community Survey, Panel Study of Income Dynamics, National Longitudinal survey of Youth... Only novel uses... particularly ones that link publicly-available data to new data sets or ones that use the restricted versions of these data will be considered"); health or mental-health outcomes and health behaviours; "studies focused on educational processes or curricular issues" — though "RSF does, however, support research that examines the causes and consequences of inequalities in student achievement or educational attainment"; non-US-focused work except rare comparative cases.
5. NOT A TUITION SOURCE. "We do not give scholarships or other types of grants for support of college funding," and tuition remission is an unallowable budget line.

=== WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY ===
1. OTHER FUNDERS' AWARDS DO NOT DISQUALIFY YOU — DISCLOSURE DOES THE WORK. RSF: "Co-funding is encouraged as long as RSF is made aware of existing and/or potential co-funding and requested RSF funds are allocated to budget items that are not covered by other funders. We require that you inform us of your current funding for the proposed research and any pending proposals. We can then confer with the other funding source(s) to avoid duplication." An NSF DDRIG, SSRC/IDRF, Ford, Spencer, departmental fellowship, RA-ship or TA-ship is fine. The Fluxx form asks you to "select all CONFIRMED and PENDING sources of support for the proposed one-year grant period" (external grant, internal or matching grant, fellowship, research assistantship, teaching assistantship, other employment at degree-granting institution, other) and then to describe each by organisation and amount. The only real constraint is no double-charging the same budget line.
2. A DRG DOES NOT BURN YOUR FUTURE RSF EARLY-CAREER ELIGIBILITY. The Sheldon Danziger Pipeline Grants rule reads: "Assistant Professor, Adjunct Assistant Professors and Lecturers who have not received an RSF research grant previously (not including Dissertation Research Grants) are eligible to apply." The parenthetical is the carve-out — taking a DRG now still leaves you eligible for a ~$65,000 Pipeline grant as an assistant professor later. (Core Research Grants state no prior-RSF-funding bar at all; Causal Research on the Criminal Justice System says "Applicants who have received prior RSF funding are eligible to apply.") So the RSF early-career ladder DRG → Pipeline → Core is deliberately open.
3. YOU DO NOT HAVE TO BE ABD ON THE DEADLINE DATE. The eligibility page's "Applicants must be doctoral students who have completed all program requirements except the dissertation" is softened by the Fluxx form, which asks: "**By the time of the grant start date**, will you have completed all requirements of your PhD program aside from the dissertation?" and by the FAQ: "If my dissertation proposal defense occurs after the deadline, am I still eligible to apply? Yes. An applicant may apply for the Dissertation Research Grants ahead of the official approval. If approved for funding, we will require proof of approval prior to releasing any funds." A February applicant with a spring prospectus defence is eligible. If your department has no formal prospectus-approval step at all, RSF invites you to write: "please email programs@rsage.org to see if you or your project is at the appropriate stage for RSF support."
4. NATIONALITY IS IRRELEVANT; THE INSTITUTION MUST BE US. "Eligibility is limited to students at institutions based in the United States. There are no restrictions on nationality." The Fluxx form widens this slightly: "Are you a doctoral student at an institution of higher education in the US or a US territory?" International students at US universities are fully eligible. (The corpus row's citizenship value "other" can be hardened to this.)
5. FACULTY CO-AUTHORSHIP IS ALLOWED. RFP: "Papers that are coauthored with faculty are eligible under this program, but the faculty coauthor is ineligible for funding." Your advisor being on the paper does not sink it; they just cannot draw money.
6. CO-FUNDERS ARE ASSIGNED, NOT APPLIED FOR. In the 2026 round "Six grants are co-funded with the W.E. Upjohn Institute for Employment Research, and the Washington Center for Equitable Growth is providing additional support for four grants" (2025: four Upjohn, three The Policy Academies). There is no separate application — RSF matches projects to partners, so employment/labour and inequality topics have extra capacity behind them.
7. A DECLINED APPLICATION COSTS YOU NOTHING. See resubmission_note.
result.program_officer_contact:
NO NAMED PROGRAM OFFICER, ONE SHARED INBOX — programs@rsage.org — AND CONTACT IS EXPLICITLY INVITED, INCLUDING ONE INVITATION WRITTEN SPECIFICALLY FOR DISSERTATION APPLICANTS.

The DRG-specific invitation, on both the eligibility page and the FAQ: "If your discipline, department, or institution does not use this process to approve dissertation proposals, please email programs@rsage.org to see if you or your project is at the appropriate stage for RSF support." That is RSF telling a student in writing to ask whether they are at the right stage — the most common pre-submission worry for this mechanism.

The general invitations: Tips & Resources — "If you're unsure, please reach out at least one month ahead of the deadline to programs@rsage.org with a short abstract and some details about the research design." FAQ — "If you have questions about the application, budget, or process in general, email us at programs@rsage.org and one of our program staff will respond. Applicants are also encouraged to reach out to program staff in advance to inquire about the fit of their proposed project with current funding priorities."

WHEN: by early January for a February deadline (one month out), i.e. once the Fluxx portal has opened. Not deadline week.
WHAT TO SEND: a short abstract plus the specifics of the research design. Not a draft; not a call request.
WORTH ASKING, for DRG specifically: (1) does my project sit inside a current RSF priority — Behavioral Science and Decision Making in Context, Future of Work, Race Ethnicity and Immigration, Immigration and Immigrant Integration, Social Political and Economic Inequality (unlike Core, DRG does not rotate priorities by round, so all five are in play every February); (2) am I at the right stage, given that I am/am not through my prospectus; (3) my chapter exists as a working paper — does that rule the project out; (4) my design is mostly secondary analysis of ACS/PSID — is the novel-use bar met.
WHY IT PAYS: 50-67% of DRG proposals die at the internal staff screen, and RSF names the three causes — the application "(1) is not perceived to be well-aligned with the Foundation's funding priorities; (2) lacks sufficient detail on the research design, data, and methods to allow reviewers to assess the viability of the project; or (3) is poorly framed or written." Cause (1) is exactly what one email settles.

AFTER A DECLINE: "Applicants who do not receive comments may email programs@rsage.org to request feedback from the initial screen." Few people know this lever exists.
AFTER AN AWARD: a different address — grantsmgt@rsage.org — for "any substantial modification of the research design or deviation from the attached budget."

OTHER LIVE CHANNELS: RSF recorded a mechanism-specific webinar, "How to Apply - Dissertation Research Grants - January 2026" (6 Jan 2026), on https://www.russellsage.org/news/watch — watch it before drafting. General "Best Practices for Grant Writing" sessions ran 11 Feb 2026 and 3 Jun 2026 and are on the same page; the next is 22 Sep 2026, 2:00pm EDT (Zoom registration linked from /apply/tips). A Fluxx instructional video is linked from the deadlines page. No office hours are advertised.

WHO ACTUALLY DECIDES: a standing DRG advisory committee ("Each early career program has a standing advisory committee that reviews all proposal materials"). RSF no longer publishes its membership — the programme page that once listed it (Maria Abascal, Celeste K. Carruthers, Sarah Halpern-Meekin, Alexander Hertel-Fernandez, Heather D. Hill, Shinobu Kitayama, as of Jan 2025) now 404s and the names do not appear anywhere on the current site. Treat that roster as historical, but as a fair indication of the interdisciplinary social-science register the committee reads in. RSF's leadership page names Bruce Western (President) and Program Directors Leana Chatrath, Aixa Cintron-Velez and James Wilson, with no individual emails and no mapping to programmes.
result.resubmission_note:
UNUSUALLY CLEAN FOR THIS MECHANISM — RSF states it outright on the DRG RFP: "An applicant whose proposal is not funded can reapply in a subsequent competition."

Mechanics, and how they differ from NIH habits:
- No A0/A1 counter, no resubmission-specific deadline, no Introduction-to-resubmission page. The funder-wide rule applies: "An applicant may revise an application and submit during a subsequent funding round. However, the application will be processed as a new submission." You simply file again the following February.
- The lifetime cap is on the AWARD, not attempts: "There is a lifetime limit of one dissertation research grant per applicant." Declines do not count against it. No cap on the number of times you may apply and no waiting period is published.
- The real constraint is biographical, not procedural: one round a year, and you must still be pre-defence (ABD by the grant start date) and not yet finished collecting data. For most students that leaves two or three genuine shots.
- You will usually have material to revise with. Anyone whose proposal reached external review receives masked reviewer comments "whether funded or not"; anyone screened out internally can request feedback from programs@rsage.org. Use it — the same reviewers may see you again.
- Mid-review, not after a decline, DRG has its own response-to-reviewers moment: "PIs may be asked to respond to reviewer comments in detail before moving forward." No page limit is published. The Core sample response memos on /apply/tips are the best available model for the register, since RSF publishes none for DRG.
- Distinct from Core: DRG has no "invited resubmission" category, no LOI to restart, and therefore no 2-week deferral lever — the Core deferral rule ("at least 2 weeks before the proposal deadline") is tied to an invited proposal and does not apply here. Miss February and the application is simply not reviewed: "Any applications submitted after the cut-off time will automatically be deferred to the next round of applications."

result.program_name: RSF Visiting Researchers Fellowship (recorded in the row as "RSF Visiting Researchers Fellowship (Visiting Scholars Program)" — but see unresolved: these are TWO separate RSF fellowships with different deadlines, different eligibility and different money, and the existing row has merged them)
result.next_deadline: May 4, 2027, 2pm ET / 11am PT — a real, dated, RSF-published deadline (read from the raw HTML of /apply/application-deadlines, not a search index). The Visiting Researchers table has exactly one row: "September 2027 - June 2028 | May 4, 2027 (2pm ET) | June 2027" — i.e. deadline May 4 2027, decision June 2027, residency between Sept 2027 and Jun 2028. Page footnote: "*ALL applications (LOIs & Proposals) are due by 2pm ET/11am PT". As of today (2026-09-18) this deadline is ~7.5 months out and has NOT passed. Long-lead items that bite: the Fluxx portal is shut until roughly Mar 4, 2027 ("The Fluxx application portal will open two months ahead of a deadline"), and a first-time registrant must "Allow up to 2 business days for a new account to be approved" — so do not register on May 3. Enforcement is absolute: "Any applications submitted after the cut-off time will automatically be deferred to the next round of applications."
result.deadline_pattern: One annual, fixed, published date per residency year — no rolling window and no multiple rounds, unlike RSF's Core grants (Mar/Jul/Oct LOIs). Only ONE forward Visiting Researcher row is published (residency 2027-28), whereas Visiting Scholars publishes two years ahead, so the 2028-29 Visiting Researcher date is not yet knowable — not found, do not extrapolate. PLANNING INSIGHT worth more than the date itself: the Visiting Researcher deadline for a given residency year falls roughly TEN MONTHS AFTER the Visiting Scholars deadline for that SAME residency year. Both the Jun 25, 2026 VS deadline and the May 4, 2027 VR deadline feed the identical Sept 2027–Jun 2028 residency. So Visiting Researcher is the late door into a residency year whose funded door has already closed — if you missed Visiting Scholars for 2027-28, you can still get an RSF office for 2027-28, just without the salary.
result.loi_deadline: Not applicable — there is no LOI or pre-proposal stage. RSF's Visiting Researcher FAQ, verbatim: "Do I need to submit a letter of inquiry prior to applying for a fellowship? No. Letters of inquiry are not required." This is a genuine DEVIATION from the funder-wide norm: RSF's Core Research Grants and MOS Grants are two-stage (LOI -> invited proposal, ~3.2-3.8 months apart, ~15% of LOIs invited). This fellowship is one-step — you submit the full application once, on the published date. Nothing is gated behind an earlier invitation, so the May 4 2027 date is the only date that matters.
result.review_to_award: FASTEST MECHANISM RSF RUNS — a major deviation from the funder norm. RSF: "Selected applicants are typically contacted within 45 days of the application deadline; acceptances cannot be deferred." Arc: apply May 4, 2027 -> notification ~mid-June 2027 (the calendar says decision "June 2027") -> residency begins on or after Sept 1, 2027. That is ~1.5 months to decision and ~4 months to start. Compare within the same funder: Core Research Grants run "about 8 months from an LOI deadline to a final decision" plus ~1.5-2 more months to earliest grant start; the one-step early-career grants (Pipeline/DRG/CRCJS) run "about three to four months from a proposal deadline to a final decision"; and the sibling Visiting Scholars fellowship takes ~6 months to notification (apply late June, "Final decisions are made at the Foundation's November Board meeting and applicants are typically notified of the decisions by mid-December") and ~14 months from application to residency. TWO CONSEQUENCES FOR AN APPLICANT: (1) there is no Board-meeting bottleneck here — no Trustee review, no $75,000 threshold question, because there is no money; (2) "acceptances cannot be deferred" means you must be certain you can actually be in New York in the Sept 2027-Jun 2028 window before you apply. There is no deferral lever at all, unlike an invited Core proposal, which can be deferred if requested "at least 2 weeks before the proposal deadline." If you cannot come, you reapply for a later year.
result.submission_requirements:
Submitted through RSF's own Fluxx instance (https://rsf.fluxx.io) like everything else at RSF; no Grants.gov, SAM.gov, eRA Commons or ORCID. The account "must be in the name of the applicant" — an assistant or admin cannot submit for you. A draft not submitted by the deadline "will automatically be withdrawn and you will need to restart the process."

REQUIRED COMPONENTS (verbatim, /apply/info/requirements, raw HTML) — the entire package is TWO documents:
- "Proposal: Maximum of 5 single-spaced pages (with standard 12-point font and 1-inch margins), excluding (1) up to 2 pages of references and (2) supporting tables and figures. Proposals should outline the basics of the project to be carried out while in residence, how the project is relevant to RSF's program areas, how the residency and interactions with the Foundation's Visiting Scholars and staff would be beneficial to the project, and the expected outcome of the work. The letter should also specify the time period for which the applicant would like to be in residence."
- "CV: 5 pages max"
- "RSF does not accept supplementary application materials, such as papers and recommendations."

WHERE IT DEVIATES FROM THE RSF NORM:
1. NO BUDGET, and no budget narrative, at any stage — unique among RSF mechanisms, because the award carries no money. Core requires a budget + budget narrative + the two-survey-firm quote rule; Pipeline/DRG/CRCJS require one after approval. Here, never.
2. NO LETTERS OF ANY KIND. Explicitly: "Can I submit letters of recommendation and other supporting materials? No. RSF does not accept letters of recommendation or other supporting materials. It selects external reviewers with substantive expertise who consider the individual's demonstrated record of research accomplishment and the merit of the proposed project." No referees to chase, no sponsor/mentor statement, no dissertation-supervisor letter (that is the DRG rule), no institutional sign-off.
3. NO POINT-BY-POINT RESPONSE MEMO — that mandatory Core document exists only because Core has an LOI review stage to answer. Not applicable here.
4. A CONTENT ELEMENT THAT EXISTS NOWHERE ELSE AT RSF: you must argue the *residency* itself, not just the science — "how the residency and interactions with the Foundation's Visiting Scholars and staff would be beneficial to the project" — and you must name your requested dates. Two of the five pages are effectively about fit with the house, not the study.
5. The Core "at least 50 percent of the narrative on research design" allocation rule is NOT stated for this mechanism, and would be wrong advice here given (4).
6. PROJECT-STAGE GATE, RSF's own words on /apply/tips: "Visiting Fellowships support projects after data collection has been completed." This mechanism is for analysis and writing-up. A project still collecting data is in the wrong mechanism, however good it is.
7. Residency obligations are real and enforceable: "Fellows are expected to spend at least 75% of their fellowship period at work at the Foundation's offices. Limited travel for scholarly purposes is naturally anticipated, but extended trips (more than one week) are not allowed during periods when the foundation is open." Term: "visits up to five months, between September 1 and June 30, as space permits. In rare circumstances, visits up to ten months may be considered."
8. NO FLUXX APPLICATION-PREVIEW PDF EXISTS FOR FELLOWSHIPS. RSF publishes blank form previews for Core, Pipeline, DRG and CRCJS only — so unlike a grant applicant, you cannot see the Fluxx form fields before the portal opens in March 2027.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
THIS MECHANISM INVERTS THE USUAL RULE — prior funding from this funder is an ASSET here, not a bar. Both halves:

WHAT PRESERVES / ACTIVELY HELPS ELIGIBILITY (verbatim, /apply/info/eligibility and the FAQ): "Visiting Researchers must be several years beyond the PhD and have a publications record and current research project that is relevant to the Foundation's program areas. Priority will be given to RSF-sponsored grantees and scholars who are seeking to complete existing work, although we welcome applications from scholars carrying out innovative work related to our current program areas." Read that plainly: holding or having held an RSF research grant moves you UP the queue. The archetypal successful applicant is someone finishing the work an earlier RSF grant paid for. Prior non-RSF funding is nowhere mentioned as a problem. There is also no citizenship or institution-location bar stated for this fellowship, and no published cap on the number of Visiting Researcher visits.

WHAT MAKES SOMEONE INELIGIBLE: there is NO published prior-funding exclusion for this mechanism. None. The only hard gates are career-stage and project-stage: "several years beyond the PhD", "a publications record", relevance to RSF's programme areas, and (from /apply/tips) data collection already complete. Space is the real constraint, not prior funding: "the Foundation has one or two available office spaces", awards granted "as space permits".

WHY THIS MATTERS — CONTRAST INSIDE THE SAME FUNDER, so an applicant picks the right door:
- Sheldon Danziger Pipeline Grants EXCLUDE prior RSF grantees: eligible are those "who have not received an RSF research grant previously (not including Dissertation Research Grants)" — note that carve-out, a DRG does NOT burn your Pipeline eligibility. Also: "professors who have previously received RSF funding are eligible to be co-PIs on projects but cannot receive salary support or conference travel funds."
- Dissertation Research Grants: "There is a lifetime limit of one dissertation research grant per applicant."
- Causal Research on the Criminal Justice System explicitly preserves it: "Applicants who have received prior RSF funding are eligible to apply, however we especially encourage applicants who have not previously received RSF support."
- Visiting SCHOLARS (the sibling programme, NOT this one) caps repeats: "Individuals are allowed a maximum of two visits to RSF as a Visiting Scholar. A former visiting scholar may apply for a second fellowship that would begin no earlier than seven years after their first visit. However... first-time applicants, all else equal, receive priority."
So: prior RSF money HELPS you here, is NEUTRAL-but-discouraged at CRCJS, and DISQUALIFIES you at Pipeline. A researcher wrapping up an RSF-funded project should be applying to this, not to Pipeline.

ONE CONCURRENCY RULE, AND A CAUTION ABOUT ITS SCOPE: RSF publishes, in the Visiting SCHOLAR FAQ only, "From the time a scholar accepts the fellowship, they may not apply for a foundation grant that will be considered for funding by the Board while they are in residence. Applications that are submitted for a deadline before accepting the fellowship are eligible for consideration. Likewise, fellows may apply towards the end of their fellowship as long as the application is considered for funding after the fellowship period ends." RSF does NOT restate this in the Visiting Researcher FAQ, and I could not establish whether it binds Visiting Researchers — see unresolved. If you intend to hold a residency and submit a Core LOI in the same window, that is the one question to put to programs@rsage.org before applying.
result.program_officer_contact:
NO NAMED OFFICER FOR THIS MECHANISM — one shared inbox: programs@rsage.org. That address is the only email published anywhere on the eligibility, requirements, FAQ or tips pages. RSF names a President (Bruce Western) and Program Directors (Leana Chatrath, Aixa Cintrón-Vélez, James Wilson) on /about/who-we-are but publishes no individual addresses and no director-to-programme mapping, so there is no one to cultivate and no "my PO" relationship to build — a real difference from NIH/NSF that trips people coming from federal funding.

IS PRE-SUBMISSION CONTACT EXPECTED? Invited in general, but read the small print for THIS mechanism. RSF's standing invitation on /apply/tips is written around research grants, not fellowships: "If you're unsure, please reach out at least one month ahead of the deadline to programs@rsage.org with a short abstract and some details about the research design." The FAQ is broader: "If you have questions about the application, budget, or process in general, email us at programs@rsage.org and one of our program staff will respond. Applicants are also encouraged to reach out to program staff in advance to inquire about the fit of their proposed project with current funding priorities." So contact is welcome and unremarkable, but note that the classic reason to make contact at RSF — settling programme fit before the ~65-75% internal-screen cull on Core LOIs — does not transfer: this fellowship has no LOI and no published screen statistics.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY WORTH ASKING HERE, given what the pages leave open: (1) whether office space is expected to be available at all for your requested window, since the award is explicitly "as space permits" with "one or two available office spaces" — this is the binding constraint and it is not published anywhere; (2) whether a stay longer than five months is realistic for you, since ten months is possible only "in rare circumstances" and RSF's own advice is that a full-year book project "should consider applying to the Foundation's Visiting Scholars Program" instead; (3) whether "several years beyond the PhD" is satisfied in your case, since unlike Visiting Scholars ("at least two years beyond the Ph.D.") RSF publishes no number; (4) the concurrency question above. TIMING: one month ahead of May 4 2027 is early April 2027, which is also about a month after the Fluxx portal opens — not the week of the deadline.

OTHER LIVE CHANNELS: RSF runs grant-writing webinars ("Best Practices for Grant Writing", Sept 22, 2026, 2:00pm EDT, Zoom, linked from /apply/tips), archives recordings at /news/watch/webinars, and posts a Fluxx instructional video from the deadlines page. No office hours are advertised.
result.examples_or_samples:
NOTHING IS PUBLISHED UNDER THE LABEL "VISITING RESEARCHER" — but there is an exact-format proxy, and knowing that is the whole trick here.

1. THE RIGHT PROXY — Visiting Scholar sample proposals. I verified against RSF's own requirements page that the Visiting Scholar and Visiting Researcher application specs are character-for-character the same shape: proposal "Maximum of 5 single-spaced pages... excluding (1) up to 2 pages of references and (2) supporting tables and figures", CV 5 pages max, and the identical sentence "RSF does not accept supplementary application materials, such as papers and recommendations." The two specs differ in exactly one clause — the Visiting Researcher version adds "and interactions with the Foundation's Visiting Scholars and staff" and requires you to "specify the time period for which the applicant would like to be in residence." So these three real funded Visiting Scholar proposals (posted 2026-06) are the correct model to write against, adjusted for that clause:
- https://www.russellsage.org/sites/default/files/2026-06/Barnes_VS_Proposal_OK_06302026.pdf
- https://www.russellsage.org/sites/default/files/2026-06/Kraus_VS_Proposal_OK_06302026.pdf
- https://www.russellsage.org/sites/default/files/2026-06/Logan_VS_Proposal_OK_06302026.pdf
(All three, plus everything below, are linked from https://www.russellsage.org/apply/tips.)

2. WHO HAS ACTUALLY HELD IT — https://www.russellsage.org/fellows/visiting-researchers carries the current roster with project descriptions; at the time of checking it listed a single Visiting Researcher, Daniel S. Nagin, working "on a book that examines bystander intervention and decision-making." One name on the page is itself the most honest selectivity signal available, and it matches "one or two available office spaces." Read it as the register to aim for: an established scholar bringing a finished-data book project.

3. NOT APPLICABLE TO THIS MECHANISM, despite being RSF's famous resource — the reviewer-response corpus. RSF unusually publishes complete Core applications WITH masked reviewer comments and the applicants' response memos (Derenoncourt, Gause, Thomas LOIs, proposals and .docx comment/response files under /sites/default/files/2025-10/), plus sample DRG proposals (/sites/default/files/2025-08/sample_drg_proposals.pdf). These are superb, but they model a two-stage grant with budgets and a response memo — none of which exist here. Do not write a Visiting Researcher proposal off the Core samples.

4. BACKGROUND / FIT EVIDENCE — the grants database at https://www.russellsage.org/research/grants (~2,303 awarded projects, 1994-2026, filterable by discipline, research priority and year) is how you check that your topic actually sits inside a current RSF programme area, which is the stated eligibility test. RSF publishes no reviewer scores and no summary statements for fellowships, and no blank Fluxx form preview exists for fellowships.
result.resubmission_note:
No resubmission policy is published for this fellowship, and the RSF-wide grant machinery does not map onto it. There is no A0/A1 counter, no Introduction page, no invited-resubmission category (that belongs to the Core advisory-committee/Board track), and no published waiting period or cap on how many times you may apply — in contrast to the sibling Visiting Scholars fellowship, which does cap repeats at "a maximum of two visits" with a second beginning "no earlier than seven years after their first visit." The RSF general rule for a declined application is that you simply apply again in a later round and "the application will be processed as a new submission."

THE PRACTICAL POINT, which is not a resubmission rule but functions as one: "acceptances cannot be deferred." An offer is for the residency year you applied for. If you are selected and cannot take it up, you do not bank it — you reapply for a later year, and because only one Visiting Researcher deadline is published at a time, the next date will not yet exist on the calendar. Since the award is unfunded and the binding constraint is office space rather than merit-plus-budget, a decline may reflect space in your requested window as much as the proposal; asking programs@rsage.org about availability before reapplying with different dates is the rational move.

Portal: awards.cff.org, 5:00 p.m. ET. Verbatim, Section VIII: "The CF Foundation reviews applications electronically, and only documents submitted online at http://awards.cff.org will be reviewed."

RESEARCH PLAN — 12 PAGES. Verbatim: "Page limit: Twelve (12) single-sided pages, not including the Literature Cited. Applications exceeding this page limit will not be reviewed." Enforcement is absolute. Inside it: "Hypothesis and Specific Aims... Do not exceed one page." Required subsections: Hypothesis and Specific Aims; Background and Science; Preliminary Results; Experimental Design and Methods; Limitations and Potential Pitfalls; Consultant Arrangements; Literature Cited. Figures must live INSIDE the research plan at 11 pt minimum — if uploaded as appendices they will not be reviewed, so you cannot buy space by exiling them.

FORMAT: Times New Roman 12 or Arial 11; margins no less than half an inch each side; PI name typed in the document header; the supplied template tracks page numbers.

THE DEVIATION THAT MATTERS MOST FOR EARLY-CAREER FACULTY — THREE REFERENCE LETTERS, DUE BEFORE YOU SUBMIT. A "Are you a junior investigator?" question on the GENERAL tab unlocks a REFERENCES tab. CFF's definition, verbatim: "The CF Foundation defines 'junior investigator' as any individual who has not received a CF Foundation Research Grant or NIH equivalent (e.g., R01, R21, R23) as a Principal Investigator AND is within their first five (5) years of their first academic appointment at the level of Assistant Professor or equivalent." Junior investigators must obtain letters from: (1) "The Chair of the Applicant's Department at the Applicant Institution — The letter of reference from the Department Chair should indicate the release of sufficient space and facilities for the work described, as well as guarantee the time commitment of the investigator to the project. If the applicant is currently a fellow, the letter of reference should include confirmation of the pending faculty-level appointment." (2) "At least two (2) other individuals familiar with the applicant's scientific interests and abilities." Verbatim: "Letters of Reference must be submitted prior to submission of the application." You invite referees on the REFERENCES tab and must click "Invite" to trigger the email; they Accept or Decline; you cannot see the letters. Verbatim: "The applicant should inform Referees to submit the letters at least one (1) week prior to the application deadline... Once the application has been submitted, no documents can be added." And: letters "should not be password protected or otherwise encrypted. Such encryption will cause errors in assembling a single-print PDF."

NON-INDEPENDENT APPLICANTS. "Applicants must be independent investigators (an individual that has completed fellowship training and whose institution allows them to submit applications for research funding as a Principal Investigator)." Verbatim: "Applicants whose appointment is dependent on a senior investigator (non-independent faculty positions) must include a biosketch and letter of support from the laboratory PI clearly indicating the affiliation and support for the application. WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY — this is the headline:

Holding an R01/R21/R23 as PI does exactly one thing: it takes you out of the "junior investigator" category, which REMOVES a requirement rather than adding one. Verbatim: "Investigators who have received a prior CFF/CFFT Research Grant or NIH equivalent, are not required to submit Letters of Reference; however, if they are new to CF research, Letters of Support and/or Collaboration should be provided as uploads in the FULL APPLICATION UPLOADS tab." So an established non-CF investigator moving into CF submits a lighter application than a first-time assistant professor.
- A prior CFF/CFFT Research Grant does not bar a further one, subject only to the dollar ceiling below.
- Competing renewals are allowed: "Competing renewals will be accepted during the year prior to project completion but new funding will be issued coincident with the original program end date."
- Investigators established elsewhere but new to CF are explicitly welcomed (they just add Letters of Support/Collaboration).
- Non-US residents and institutions are eligible: "U.S. residents and applicants from outside the U.S. are welcome to apply", subject to USA Patriot Act / US Treasury documentation.

WHAT MAKES YOU INELIGIBLE — the binding constraint is CFF-internal concurrent funding, not outside funding:
- Verbatim: "Multiple CF Foundation Research Grants held by a single investigator will not be permitted for this program when the total combined funding exceeds $168,000 per year. In such cases, the most recent application submitted will be considered administratively ineligible." Note the penalty falls on the NEWEST application — you lose the one you just wrote.
- Verbatim: "PIs with a combined total of CF Foundation research support exceeding $200,000 per year in direct costs (excluding Research Development Program, National Resource Center, Therapeutic Development Network, and Care Center Awards) with an end date more than six (6) months from the application deadline must receive Program Officer approval before an application will be considered." Note the four excluded award types — they do not count toward the ceiling.

"Candidates who are postdoctoral fellows should apply to the CF Foundation Postdoctoral Research Fellowship program." You must be an independent investigator able to submit as PI.

- For-profit applicants must contact the Program Officer to discuss eligibility before beginning an application; failure to do so "may result in withdrawal of the proposal".
- Throughput caps bind independently of any of this: one Research Grant application per calendar year; one application (research grant or P&F) per laboratory per cycle; one research grant plus one P&F per 12 months.

There is no CFF equivalent of NIH RePORTER — no public abstract database for funded CFF Research Grants; awards.cff.org is login-gated and shows only open opportunities and your own applications. (Established by searching CFF's own site, not by a CFF statement to that effect — see unresolved.) Four routes work, best first:

1. THE RFA'S OWN PUBLISHED REVIEWER CHECKLIST — the most mechanism-specific starter material that exists, and it is free and public inside the Policies and Guidelines PDF. Verbatim, Section VII, "Chief causes for assigning low priority scores to applications during review include the following: Failure of the application to address contemporary research priorities in CF; Insufficient information or documentation; Inadequate statement of hypothesis, experimental design, or methods; Failure of the applicant to demonstrate awareness of and plans for coping with key problems and pitfalls associated with the proposed research; Insufficient or improper controls; Failure of the applicant to describe potential relevance of the proposed study to issues in CF; Failure of the applicant to document the necessary skills or training to accomplish the goals of the proposal; Failure of the applicant to meet all of the criteria described in the policy statement for a given award." Note how directly this maps onto the required research-plan subsections — the "Limitations and Potential Pitfalls" section exists because bullet 4 exists. Write to this list.

2. EUROPE PMC GRANT SEARCH — the closest working proxy for a funded-abstract database. Query GRANT_AGENCY:"Cystic Fibrosis Foundation" to see who CFF funded, in what year, on what topic, and read the papers the award produced. Award IDs come back in SURNAME+two-digit-year+code form (e.g. DUNCAN24G0, MCGARRY23Y5). Browse: https://europepmc.org/search?query=GRANT_AGENCY%3A%22Cystic%20Fibrosis%20Foundation%22 ; API: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=GRANT_AGENCY:%22Cystic+Fibrosis+Foundation%22&format=json&resultType=core . PubMed's "Grants and funding" field carries the same data. (Figure of ~3,598 records comes from the briefing, not from a call I made this session.)

Because no sample applications are published, CFF's own scaffolding is what you work from, and it is unusually prescriptive: every uploaded component has a downloadable template inside awards.cff.org — Research Plan, Budget Justification, Biosketch, Other Support, Facilities Available, Results of Past and Current CFF/CFFT Support, Critique Response. Publicly, before you have an account: the Research Grant Policies and Guidelines PDF (https://www.cff.org/media/11116/download?inline), and the "For Applicants: Our Grants Management System" how-to guide plus a three-part video tutorial series, both linked from https://www.cff.org/researchers/information-applicants-and-awardees .

4. COLLEAGUES' CRITIQUES. CFF returns anonymized reviewer critiques to every applicant. They are not public, so the practical move is to ask a CF-funded colleague in your department to show you theirs alongside the funded application. I found no university research-office library of published CFF sample applications.

Institution-level money, no abstracts: ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, CFF EIN 13-1930701, https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/131930701 — Schedule I inside the full 990 filings lists grants to organisations with amounts and purpose.
