result.deadline_pattern:
Three cycles a year on fixed calendar dates: **April 8, August 8, December 8**. Unlike the R and K families, F-series **resubmissions (A1) use the SAME dates as new applications** — there is no one-month offset. Confirmed twice: NIH's standard due dates table ("F Series Fellowships new, renewal, resubmission — Individual National Research Service Awards (Standard) April 8 August 8 December 8") and the NOFO's own table, where the New and Renewal/Resubmission/Revision columns carry identical dates in every row.

Weekend/holiday rule applies: "When a submission date falls on a weekend or Federal holiday, the application deadline is automatically extended to the next business day." Relevant soon — August 8, 2027 falls on a Sunday, so that cycle moves to Monday August 9, 2027.
result.loi_deadline:
Not applicable — no LOI or pre-proposal stage. Verified structurally rather than by absence of a keyword: Section IV of both parent NOFOs runs 1. Requesting an Application Package → 2. Content and Form of Application Submission → 3. Unique Entity Identifier and SAM → 4. Submission Dates and Times → 5. Intergovernmental Review → 6. Funding Restrictions → 7. Other Submission Requirements. NIH NOFOs that require an LOI carry a numbered "Letter of Intent" section in that sequence; neither PA-25-425 nor PA-25-426 has one, and the word "intent" appears in the body only in the phrase "The intent of this two-NOFO approach."

The real long-lead item in place of an LOI is the **reference letters**, which are a separate submission channel on the same deadline (see submission_requirements), plus the registration stack (SAM/eRA Commons/ORCID/SciENcv) that NIH says to start six weeks out.
result.review_to_award:
**Fellowship cycles do NOT follow the generic NIH R01 cycle table.** Because F-series due dates are April 8 / August 8 / December 8 rather than the Jan–Feb / May–June / Sep–Oct pattern, the review→council→start mapping is its own:

- **April 8 due** → merit review July → council October → earliest start December (~8 months)
- **August 8 due** → merit review November → council January → earliest start April (~8 months)
- **December 8 due** → merit review March → council May → earliest start July (~7 months)

Intermediate milestones, from the NOFO itself:
- **~2 weeks after the due date**: study section assignment appears in eRA Commons. The NOFO's Peer Review Contact entry is exactly this: "Examine your eRA Commons account for review assignment and contact information (information appears two weeks after the submission due date)." Before that point you have no SRO to talk to.
- **~4 months**: study section meets; score released (normally within days of the meeting; currently "within three business days" under the emergency modifications).
- **~5 months**: summary statement in eRA Commons. NOFO: "After the peer review of the application is completed, the PD/PI will be able to access their Summary Statement (written critique) via the eRA Commons." Importantly, "As part of the scientific peer review, all applications will receive a written critique" — so even an undiscussed F30 comes back with usable reviewer text, which is what you build the A1 on.
- **~6 months**: council.
- **Notice of Award**, signed by the Grants Management Officer and emailed to the institution's business official, is the only binding document.

Triage threshold for F30 as written in the NOFO: "Applications may undergo a selection process in which only those applications deemed to have the highest merit (generally the top half of applications under review) will be discussed and assigned an overall impact score." That "top half" is the pre-2026 baseline; the funder-wide emergency modifications (NOT-OD-26-114) cut discussion to 30–35% in most meetings and add a "competitive but not discussed" middle tier — applies to fellowships as to everything else, and NIH states likelihood of funding is unaffected.

Two fellowship-specific deviations at the award end:
- **No payback obligation for F30.** The NOFO ties the Payback Agreement Form (PHS 6031) only to "the individual's initial 12 months of Kirschstein-NRSA **postdoctoral** support." Predoctoral F30 support carries none.
- **Pre-award costs are generally not allowable for Fellowships**, and fellowships are exempt from the SAM.gov responsibility/qualification risk review that applies to other NIH awards.
- On activation you file an Activation Notice, and a Termination Notice (PHS 416-7) via xTrain within 30 days of termination.
result.submission_requirements:
**THE BIGGEST DEVIATION: there is no single F30 parent announcement. There are two, and which one you are allowed to use is decided by your institution, not by you.**

- **PA-25-426** — "for Students at Institutions **with** NIH-Funded Institutional Predoctoral Dual-Degree Training Programs (Parent F30)". Verbatim: "Eligibility is limited to applicant organizations with NIH-funded institutional predoctoral dual-degree training programs, including NIH-supported Medical Scientist Training Programs (MSTP), or Dental Scientist Training Programs (DSTP), or similar predoctoral dual-degree training programs."
- **PA-25-425** — "for Students at Institutions **without**…", same sentence with "without".

Both posted June 13, 2025, open July 8, 2025, expire **May 8, 2028**; both are reissues of PA-23-260. NIH's stated reason, verbatim: "The intent of this two-NOFO approach is to promote equitable review of applications from these two kinds of institutions, as well as better tracking of fellowship awardee candidate's future progress in establishing independent careers as physician/clinician-scientists." Practical effect: MSTP students no longer compete against non-MSTP students.

**Consequence most applicants miss — five Institutes fund only the non-MSTP version.** Diffing the participating-organization lists: PA-25-425 lists 21 components; PA-25-426 lists the same minus **NHGRI, NIAMS, NIBIB, NIGMS and NINDS**. If you are at an MSTP institution, those five are simply not available to you for an F30. Their own words in the IC table: NINDS — "Exception: NINDS does not fund applications from institutions that have NIH-funded institutional predoctoral dual-degree training programs (e.g., MSTP institutions)." NHGRI — "NHGRI does not support F30 applications for students at institutions with NIH-funded institutional predoctoral dual-degree training programs." NIAMS and NIBIB each list the WITH-version F30 under "does not participate". NEI participates in both but "prioritizes applications from institutions without NIH-Funded Institutional Predoctoral Dual-Degree Training Programs."

**WHEN IN YOUR PROGRAM TO APPLY — the clock that catches MD/PhD students.** For MD/PhD and DO/PhD candidates, verbatim: a candidate "1) Must have matriculated (be enrolled) into a formal dual-degree program. 2) Must have identified a dissertation research training project and sponsor(s) - Candidates are strongly encouraged to submit as soon as a dissertation research project and training program can be fully developed in collaboration with the sponsor. **Most candidates are expected to apply within 48 months of matriculating into the dual degree program but no later than 24 months into their dissertation research training.**" Also: "The F30 fellowship is generally not intended to support dual-degree students after year 8 of dual-degree training," and "over the total duration of F30 support, at least 50% of the award period must be devoted to full-time graduate research training leading to the doctoral research degree." That 50% rule is enforced post-award: "After an award is made, award duration may be adjusted to ensure that at least 50% of the total award duration is devoted to research training leading to the research doctorate."

**DDS/DMD-PhD, AuD-PhD, DVM/VMD-PhD candidates are exempt from the 48-month/24-month clock** — NIH's stated reason is that these "programs are highly variable in their phasing and integration." Their test is only (1) matriculated into a dual-degree program and (2) identified a research training project and sponsor(s).

**Exceptions are a real, documented route, not a favour**: "Exceptions to the eligibility criteria will be considered for dual-degree programs with non-standard formats or for candidates who have taken an official leave of absence from the dual-degree program. Requests for exceptions should be submitted to NIH Program Staff or the designated Scientific/Research Contact." Ask before you write, not after you are rejected.

**REFERENCE LETTERS — the classic F30 failure mode, because they do not go through your institution at all.** NOFO: "Applications lacking the appropriate required reference letters will not be reviewed. This is a separate process from submitting an application electronically. Reference letters are submitted directly through the eRA Commons Submit Reference Letter link and not through Grants.gov." From NIH's reference-letters guidance: "At least three, but no more than five, reference letters are required unless otherwise specified in the funding opportunity"; "The sponsor/co-sponsor(s) of the application cannot be counted toward the three required references"; referees must submit "by the application due date"; "Applications that have fewer than the required numbers of reference letters will not be reviewed"; the letters are confidential and the candidate cannot read them. The referee portal is https://public.era.nih.gov/commonsplus/public/reference/submitReferenceLetter.era — your referees need only your eRA Commons ID, not an account of their own. Brief them 6+ weeks out.

**PAGE LIMITS (F30 uses the fellowship column, not the research-grant one):** Project Summary/Abstract 30 lines; Project Narrative three sentences; Candidate's Goals, Preparedness, and Potential **3 pages**; Training Activities and Timelines **3 pages**; Research Training Project Specific Aims **1 page**; Research Training Project Strategy **6 pages** (not 12 — F30 is not an R01); Training in the Responsible Conduct of Research **1 page**; Sponsor(s) Commitment **6 pages**; Letters of Support from Collaborators, Contributors, and Consultants **6 pages**; Introduction to Resubmission **1 page**. Biosketch: legacy format 5 pages, but the Biographical Sketch Common Form has "No hard limit; length controlled through SciENcv data entry format."

**REQUIRED COMPONENTS specific to F30:** the PHS Fellowship Supplemental Form (Candidate Section; Research Training Plan; Commitment to Candidate, Mentoring, and Training Environment; Other Research Training Plan Sections; Additional Information; Budget; Appendix). You must name a sponsor before submitting: "Before submitting the application, the candidate must identify a sponsor(s) who will supervise the proposed mentored training experience… one individual must be identified as the primary sponsor." Multiple PDs/PIs are not allowed.

**Clinical trials:** "Not Allowed: Only accepting applications that do not propose independent clinical trials," but "Candidates may propose to gain experience in a clinical trial led by a sponsor/co-sponsor." If you do, the sponsor/co-sponsor "must include a statement to document leadership of the clinical trial including source of funding, NCT# and appropriate expertise"; you do NOT put an NCT# in Study Record Section 1 item 1.5, and you do not complete Section 4 (Protocol Synopsis) or Section 5.

**ORCID is enforced at the form level here:** "The personal profile associated with the eRA Commons username entered in the Credential field for the PD/PI (fellowship candidate) must include an ORCID ID." Both the candidate and the sponsor(s) must have eRA Commons IDs in the Credential field — omitting one "will prevent the successful submission of an electronic application to NIH."

**Award budget:** stipend + tuition/fees + institutional allowance, at annually-published NRSA rates; no separate indirect cost recovery ("costs for administering fellowships are covered by the Institutional Allowance"). Some ICs sweeten it — NIDCR adds "$800 meeting" to the institutional allowance for F30.

**Maximum duration varies by IC and is often shorter than the 6-year ceiling** — NIGMS "F30: 4 years"; NINDS "F30: minimum 12 months and maximum 5 years. Limited to the first 8 years of dual degree training"; NIDCR "Maximum of 6 years of support"; another IC block reads "F30: Up to 6 years of support; non-renewable." Budget your requested period to the IC you are targeting, not to the NOFO ceiling.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
**DISQUALIFYING / LIMITING**

1. **Aggregate NRSA cap, counted across T32 and fellowship together.** Verbatim: "Individuals may receive up to 5 years of aggregate Kirschstein-NRSA support at the predoctoral level (**up to 6 years for dual degree training, e.g., MD/PhD**), and up to 3 years of aggregate Kirschstein-NRSA support at the postdoctoral level, **including any combination of support from institutional training grants (e.g., T32) and an individual fellowship award**." So months you were paid on your MSTP T32 slot are subtracted from your 6. Also: "Candidates must consider any prior NRSA research training in determining the duration of support requested. Information regarding previous Kirschstein-NRSA support must be included in the application and will be considered at the time of award." You must disclose it; NIH will trim the award period rather than reject you.
2. **Concurrent federal stipend support is barred.** Verbatim: "A Kirschstein-NRSA fellowship may not be held concurrently with another federally sponsored fellowship or similar Federal award that provides a stipend or otherwise duplicates provisions of this award." You cannot draw an NSF GRFP or a T32 appointment and an F30 at the same time — you relinquish the slot on activation.
3. **Institutional status gates which NOFO and which ICs** — see submission_requirements. At an MSTP/DSTP institution, NHGRI, NIAMS, NIBIB, NIGMS and NINDS are closed to you for F30.
4. **Time-in-program limits.** Past 48 months post-matriculation (MD/PhD, DO/PhD), or more than 24 months into dissertation research, you are outside the expected window; past year 8 of dual-degree training the F30 is "generally not intended" to support you.
5. **Degree status.** F30 "does not support studies leading to the MD, DO, DDS, AuD or similar professional degrees, or studies that are part of residency training leading to a medical specialty alone" — it is for the combined track only, and eligibility ends once the research doctorate is conferred.
6. **Overlapping applications.** NIH will not accept "A new (A0) application that is submitted before issuance of the summary statement from the review of an overlapping new (A0) or resubmission (A1) application," nor an A1 before the A0's summary statement issues, nor anything substantially overlapping an application under appeal.

**WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY — the half applicants never get told**

1. **Prior T32/MSTP support does NOT disqualify you.** It is counted against the 6-year aggregate, and that is the whole of its effect. Being on an MSTP is the normal case for an F30 applicant, not a bar — it only routes you to PA-25-426.
2. **A prior or concurrent F31 is not a bar either** — same aggregate-cap treatment. (F30 and F31 both sit in the 5/6-year predoctoral pool.)
3. **No payback or service obligation attaches to F30.** The Payback Agreement (PHS 6031) is required only "For the individual's initial 12 months of Kirschstein-NRSA **postdoctoral** support." Predoctoral dual-degree support creates no obligation — a common and costly misconception.
4. **NHLBI explicitly preserves eligibility past the 48-month wall for resubmissions:** "Resubmission of F30 applications will be considered beyond the 48-month post-matriculation limit, provided that they have at least one year remaining in their PhD dissertation research on the date of award." If your A0 went in near the limit, the A1 is not automatically dead.
5. **Non-standard program formats and official leaves of absence are explicitly accommodated** via a written exception request to Program Staff (quoted above) — pregnancy, illness, a research year abroad, an off-cycle DDS/PhD structure.
6. **Dental, audiology and veterinary dual-degree candidates are exempt from the 48/24-month clock entirely.**
7. **Non-federal support is untouched.** The concurrency bar reaches only federally sponsored fellowships/awards providing a stipend — institutional top-ups, foundation supplements and loans are not caught by this clause.
8. **F30 recipients are encouraged toward the NIH Loan Repayment Programs:** "Recipients of fellowship awards are encouraged to consider applying for an extramural LRP award."
9. **Citizenship** is tested "by the time of award," not at submission — and NOT-OD-25-126 (17 June 2025) corrected all five fellowship parents to read "a citizen or a **non-citizen national** of the United States or… lawfully admitted for permanent residence," restoring non-citizen nationals (American Samoa, Swains Island) to eligibility.
result.program_officer_contact:
**Pre-submission contact is stronger than "encouraged" here — the NOFO makes consulting the IC table mandatory.** Verbatim from Section VII: "Because of the difference in individual Institute and Center (IC) program requirements for this NOFO, prospective applications **MUST** consult the Table of IC-Specific Information, Requirements, and Staff Contacts, to make sure that their application is responsive to the requirements of one of the participating NIH ICs. **Prior consultation with NIH staff is strongly encouraged.**"

**The route, and it is a single durable page:** https://grants.nih.gov/funding/funding-categories/research-training-and-career-development/individual-fellowships/ico-funding-considerations — titled "Individual Fellowships Funding Considerations and Contacts". (Reachable per-NOFO as https://grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/contacts/PA-25-426.html and …/PA-25-425.html, both of which redirect there.) It lists, IC by IC: interest areas, which F mechanisms that IC does and does not participate in, project-period ceilings, budget quirks, and a scientific/research contact plus a grants-management contact. This is the page that answers "who do I email" for F30, and it is maintained centrally rather than per-solicitation, so it does not rot the way an individual PO name does. (Note: the e-mail addresses on that page were redacted in my fetched copy, so I am citing the page rather than reproducing addresses I could not read.)

Several ICs push harder than the NOFO does. NEI: "All prospective fellowship applicants are strongly encouraged to contact NEI Training Program Officers before preparing an application to determine alignment with current priorities, the appropriate funding opportunity, and to discuss eligibility." NHGRI: "Prospective applicants are strongly encouraged to contact NHGRI program staff prior to submitting an application." NIDA: "Prospective applicants are highly encouraged to contact a NIDA Program Official in their area of interest, prior to preparing an application." NICHD: "Interested applicants are encouraged to contact NICHD staff to assess program relevance and institute-specific requirements." NCI maintains named "NCI F30 Program Director(s)". NHLBI publishes a dedicated F30 mailbox.

**F30-specific things worth asking a PO, that the NOFO cannot answer:**
- Am I inside the 48-month/24-month window as this IC counts it, and if not, will you consider an exception?
- Does my institution count as having an "NIH-funded institutional predoctoral dual-degree training program" for the same degree I'm pursuing — i.e. which of PA-25-425 / PA-25-426 do I use? (Genuinely ambiguous for e.g. a DDS/PhD student at an institution holding an MD/PhD MSTP — see unresolved.)
- What is your IC's maximum F30 duration? (4 years at NIGMS, 5 at NINDS, 6 at NIDCR — the NOFO's 6-year ceiling is not what you will get everywhere.)
- Does my research sit in your IC's mission, and which study section is likely to see it?

**Timing and form:** email, at the Specific Aims stage, roughly 2–4 months before the due date — for the December 8, 2026 cycle that means reaching out now through October 2026. NIH's own July 2026 guidance: "A short description of your project, why you believe it fits a specific ICO or funding opportunity, and 2–3 targeted questions is usually more effective than a long, unfocused message"; "Send an email rather than cold call"; "Allow time for a response."

**Roles not to confuse:** you will have no SRO contact until "two weeks after the submission due date," when the assignment appears in eRA Commons — the NOFO's Peer Review Contact entry literally says to look there. The SRO handles review logistics and expertise gaps, never funding. After the summary statement, the PO at the assigned IC is your resubmission counsel. Budget/JIT questions go to the Financial/Grants Management Contact on the same IC table, through your institution's AOR. General instruction questions: NIH GrantsInfo (301-637-3015); system errors: eRA Service Desk, https://www.era.nih.gov/need-help or 301-402-7469 / 866-504-9552.
result.examples_or_samples:
**Honest finding first: NIH does not publish a full F30 sample application anywhere I could verify.** I checked NIH's central samples index and the IC collections it links; NIAID's collection carries F31 but not F30, NIDCD's carries only R01/R21, and the NIA/NCI/NHGRI collections listed there do not include F30.

**Best available substitute, and it is a close one — NIAID's two complete F31 applications WITH their summary statements** (fetched directly from niaid.nih.gov, which returned 200 to a browser-UA request in this session):
- https://www.niaid.nih.gov/sites/default/files/F31-Sample-Application_Samantha-Schwartz.pdf + summary statement https://www.niaid.nih.gov/sites/default/files/F31-Sample-Summary_Samantha-Schwartz.pdf
- https://www.niaid.nih.gov/sites/default/files/f31-sample-application_nico_contreras.pdf + summary statement https://www.niaid.nih.gov/sites/default/files/f31-contreras-summary.pdf
- Index: https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/sample-applications ("Several NIAID investigators have graciously agreed to share their exceptional applications and summary statements as samples to help the research community.")

Why this transfers: F31 and F30 use the **identical PHS Fellowship Supplemental Form**, the identical fellowship page limits, and the identical revised NRSA fellowship review criteria (in force for due dates on/after 25 Jan 2025: Fellowship Applicant's Preparedness and Potential; Research Training Plan; Commitment to the Candidate). What an F31 sample cannot show you is the dual-degree material — the integrated research-and-clinical training plan, the 50%-research justification, and the timeline across MD and PhD phases. Write those three from the NOFO text, not from the F31.

**F30-specific routes that do work:**
1. **NIH RePORTER** (https://reporter.nih.gov, advanced search https://reporter.nih.gov/advanced-search) filtered to activity code **F30** — gives you funded F30 abstracts, PI, IC, study section, fiscal year, amount and resulting publications. This is the only large F30-specific corpus of funded text that is public. For the full application NIH's own answer is a FOIA request to the funding IC.
2. **RePORTER Matchmaker** (https://reporter.nih.gov/matchmaker) — paste your draft Specific Aims, choose "Similar Program Officials," and you get the POs, ICs, activity codes and review panels behind similar funded work in one step. For an F30 applicant this simultaneously answers "who funds this" and "who do I email." NIH: "The process is automated and confidential. The Matchmaker system does not track and store submitted text."
3. **The IC funding-considerations table** (URL in program_officer_contact) is itself the closest thing to a "what does this IC want in an F30" document — it states each IC's priorities and duration ceilings. NINDS, for instance, publishes its four F30/F31 funding priorities outright: research within mission with a training plan "well-matched to the proposed research"; "strong mentorship, including a mentor with an active funded research program, a strong record of trainee outcomes"; "clear intellectual ownership of an original research plan that is consistent with, but not duplicative of, the mentor's funded research"; and "a clear, feasible, milestone-driven career development plan." That is effectively a scoring rubric, published.
4. **Annotated Form Set for NIH Grant Applications** — https://grants.nih.gov/grants/ElectronicReceipt/files/ — a filled-in application field by field.
5. **NIDCR runs recurring pre-application/technical-assistance webinars on applying for F and K awards** (NOT-DE-26-012, NOT-DE-26-013) — a live walkthrough, listed in the F30 NOFO's Related Notices.
6. Central index: https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/samples-applications-and-documents — worth rechecking before each cycle in case an F30 is added.
result.resubmission_note:
One resubmission only (A1), within 37 months of the A0, per NIH-wide policy (NOT-OD-18-197, NOT-OD-12-128). F30-specific points:

- **The A1 is due on the SAME calendar dates as a new application** — April 8 / August 8 / December 8. The NOFO's Key Dates table shows identical New and "Renewal / Resubmission / Revision (as allowed)" columns in every row. This differs from the R and K families, where resubmissions fall one month later. Do not assume you have an extra month.
- **Introduction: 1 page** (fellowship table; the 3-page allowance is for institutional/T-series training resubmissions, not F30). It must summarise substantial additions, deletions and changes and respond to the summary statement, and it is an extra page on top of the 6-page Research Training Project Strategy.
- **A not-discussed application is still resubmittable.** The NOFO guarantees material to work from: "As part of the scientific peer review, all applications will receive a written critique."
- **You cannot have the A0 and the A1 in play at once**: no "resubmission (A1) application that is submitted before issuance of the summary statement from the review of the previous new (A0) application," and nothing substantially overlapping an application under appeal.
- **The 48-month clock can bite the A1 specifically** — you may age out between A0 and A1. NHLBI is the one IC that publishes a carve-out: "Resubmission of F30 applications will be considered beyond the 48-month post-matriculation limit, provided that they have at least one year remaining in their PhD dissertation research on the date of award." Other ICs: ask the PO before assuming.
- **Renewal is effectively closed.** NOFO: "Renewal - Individual fellowship awards are generally not renewable. In rare cases in which fellowship awardees require further fellowship support, they should consult with NIH staff to obtain advice regarding submission of a renewal application."
- **After a failed A1**, the idea may go in as a fresh A0 at the next standard date — subject to the 48-month/year-8 windows, which for a dual-degree student are usually the binding constraint rather than the resubmission policy.
- Post-submission materials are allowed per NIH policy (NOT-OD-23-106, 30 days before the study section meeting), submitted through the AOR — but the one-page preliminary-data update is defined for Type 1 R01/R21/R03, not fellowships, so do not count on it here.
- Talk to the PO after the summary statement and before committing to the A1 — that is the second of NIH's two recommended contact points.
unresolved: PA-25-426 (the WITH-MSTP NOFO) contains what looks like a drafting error. Its organizational-eligibility paragraph opens 'Eligibility is limited to applicant organizations WITH NIH-funded institutional predoctoral dual-degree training programs...' but then ends with a sentence identical to PA-25-425's: 'This eligibility criterion applies to applicant organizations WITHOUT currently active institutional training programs supporting the same dual degree, at the time the F30 fellowship application is submitted for review.' Read literally the two sentences contradict each other. The plausible intent is that the test is degree-specific — e.g. a DDS/PhD student at an institution holding an MD/PhD MSTP but no DSTP may belong under PA-25-425 — but I could not confirm this from NIH's own text. This is the single most consequential ambiguity found.

The existing CSV row's eligibility_notes assert the applicant 'may not have previously been PD/PI on an NIH research grant.' I could not find that language in either F30 parent NOFO (PA-25-425 or PA-25-426); no equivalent phrase appears in Section III of either. It may be a carry-over from a different mechanism's rules. Flagging for verification rather than treating as established — I made no change to the file.

Per-IC program officer email addresses on the IC funding-considerations table were redacted in every copy I fetched (rendered as a placeholder rather than the real address), so I cite the table URL rather than individual addresses. A user opening that page in a browser will see them.

Whether the current emergency peer-review modifications (NOT-OD-26-114: discussion cut to 30-35%, 'competitive but not discussed' middle tier, simplified summary statements) extend past the January 2027 Advisory Council round is not announced. For F30 this matters because the December 8, 2026 cycle goes to council in May 2027 — i.e. beyond the announced coverage. The NOFO's own text still states the pre-modification baseline ('generally the top half of applications under review').

Exact NRSA stipend, tuition/fee and institutional-allowance dollar amounts for FY2027 were not retrieved; both NOFOs point to annually-published levels at researchtraining.nih.gov/resources/policy-notices and the NIH stipends-summary page rather than stating figures. Worth pulling separately if the corpus wants award size refreshed.

PA-27-037 (Parent F99/K00, open 6/16/2026, expires 4/9/2029) was reported by the parent-announcements listing but not independently verified; it is adjacent to F30 rather than part of it, and is noted only because F30 holders sometimes ask about the transition mechanism.

result.next_deadline: **December 8, 2026** (a Tuesday; 5:00 PM local time of the applicant organization). This is a real published calendar date, taken from the Key Dates table inside PA-25-422 itself — not inferred from the standard-due-date pattern. The August 8, 2026 cycle has already closed as of today (2026-09-18), so December 8, 2026 is the next open one. The NOFO prints the full ladder ahead of it: April 8, 2027 / August 8, 2027 / December 8, 2027 / April 8, 2028, then the NOFO expires May 8, 2028 (so April 8, 2028 is the last due date under this announcement; NIH will reissue a successor PA). New and Resubmission applications share the same date — the F series does NOT use the "one month later for resubmissions" rule that applies to R and K. Note on the house rule: a dated deadline is withheld only when it would be a guess. Here NIH publishes dates through 2028 in the funder's own NOFO, so the date is recorded, not invented.
result.deadline_pattern: Three cycles a year on the NIH F-series standard dates: **April 8, August 8, December 8**, every year. Two rules that move the date: (1) "When a submission date falls on a weekend or Federal holiday, the application deadline is automatically extended to the next business day" (PA-25-422 §IV.4); (2) the NOFO's own dated table supersedes the generic pattern if they ever diverge — for PA-25-422 they agree (every date carries NIH's standard-due-date asterisk). Open date (earliest submission) was July 8, 2025, so the window is continuously open. The AIDS/HIV column reads "Not Applicable" from the August 8, 2026 date onward, consistent with NOT-OD-26-029 removing dedicated AIDS due dates. Real-world timing for a student: the binding date is your own research office's internal deadline, typically 3–5 business days earlier (the institution's Authorized Organizational Representative submits, not you), and there is no error-correction window after the NIH deadline — so work to roughly December 1–3, 2026.
result.loi_deadline: Not applicable — PA-25-422 has no Letter of Intent or pre-proposal stage; the Key Dates table contains no LOI row. There is one soft, optional analogue worth knowing: several ICs invite an informal pre-check. NIA is the most concrete — "If you would like feedback on the appropriateness of your research topic for NIA, please submit a one-page overview of your specific aims to the NIA Training Team" (NIATraining@mail.nih.gov). That is advisory, not a gate, and has no deadline.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
**What disqualifies you (all from PA-25-422 §III unless noted):**
- Exceeding the aggregate cap: "Individuals may receive up to 5 years of aggregate Kirschstein-NRSA support at the predoctoral level (up to 6 years for dual degree training, e.g., MD/PhD) ... including any combination of support from institutional training grants (e.g., T32) and an individual fellowship award." Time you already spent on a T32 counts against the 5 years.
- Concurrent federal stipend: "A Kirschstein-NRSA fellowship may not be held concurrently with another federally sponsored fellowship or similar Federal award that provides a stipend or otherwise duplicates provisions of this award." This is what catches NSF GRFP holders — GRFP is federal.
- Not being enrolled: "The candidate must be currently enrolled in a PhD or equivalent research degree program" — enrolment must hold at application and the citizenship/PR test must be met "by the time of award."
- Overlapping applications pending: NIH will not accept "a new (A0) application that is submitted before issuance of the summary statement from the review of an overlapping new (A0) or resubmission (A1) application," nor an A1 submitted before the A0's summary statement issues.
- IC-level stage caps, which bite harder than the NIH-wide rule and are the most common surprise (Table of IC-Specific Information for PA-25-422): NIMH — F31 "Limited to the first 6 years of Ph.D. research training (excluding clinical internship); limited exceptions." NINDS — F31 "minimum 12 months and maximum 3 years. Limited to the first 6 years of PhD research training (for MD/PhD candidates, through 8 years from starting the combined MD/PhD program)." NIAID — "F31: Up to 3 years of support; non-renewable." NIGMS — 3 years. NEI "prioritizes applications requesting two or more years." A 5th-year student is effectively out at several ICs.

**What explicitly PRESERVES eligibility (the half applicants never get told):**
- Having held a T32 appointment does not disqualify you — it only consumes part of the 5-year aggregate. Same for a prior individual NRSA: "Candidates must consider any prior NRSA research training in determining the duration of support requested," i.e. you subtract, you are not excluded.
- A prior *unfunded* F31 costs you nothing, and a not-discussed/triaged A0 is still resubmittable.
- A non-federal fellowship (private foundation, university, HHMI-type) is not caught by the concurrency bar, which names only federally sponsored awards that duplicate the stipend. Sequential federal awards are fine — the bar is on holding them *concurrently*.
- Being paid as a research assistant on your mentor's R01 up to now does not disqualify you; the NOFO imposes no prior-support test on research-grant salary, only on NRSA/federal-fellowship stipends. (What you may earn *alongside* an active F31 is governed by NRSA compensation policy in the NIH Grants Policy Statement, which I did not verify this session — see unresolved.)
- Your mentor's funding status is not a bar, though NCI adds a positive condition: the application must show "funds are available to support the candidate's research training plan throughout the duration of the award" and that "the proposed scientific research question or approach is distinct from the mentor's pending or active grants, and there is no substantial text duplication of the mentor's specific aims."
- Being at a foreign institution is not a bar: "Non-domestic (non-U.S.) Entities (Foreign Organizations) are eligible to apply" and an individual "may request support for training abroad" with detailed justification — the citizenship/PR test is on the person, not the site.
- One structural bar worth naming because it is about scope, not funding: this NOFO is Clinical Trial Not Allowed — "Candidates may propose to gain experience in a clinical trial led by a sponsor/co-sponsor," but you may not lead an independent trial. If your dissertation is your own trial, this is the wrong mechanism.
result.review_to_award: Published per-cycle in PA-25-422's own Key Dates table, so these are dates rather than estimates. For the **December 8, 2026** deadline: scientific merit review **March 2027**, advisory council review **May 2027**, earliest start date **July 2027** — about 4 months to review, 5 months to council, 7 months to money. The other cycles: April 8, 2027 → July 2027 review → October 2027 council → December 2027 start; August 8, 2027 → November 2027 → January 2028 → April 2028. Where it differs from the NIH norm: the F31 arc is ~7 months to earliest start rather than ~9, because fellowships skip much of the pre-award budget machinery. Review venue also differs from the norm — the parent F31 is reviewed by CSR's fellowship study sections, not an IC panel: "Applications will be evaluated for scientific and technical merit by (an) appropriate Scientific Review Group(s), convened by CSR ... Assignment to a Scientific Review Group will be shown in the eRA Commons." Second level is the assigned IC's advisory council. Fellowships get an overall impact score, not a percentile, and the NOFO restates the triage rule in its own words: "Applications may undergo a selection process in which only those applications deemed to have the highest merit (generally the top half of applications under review) will be discussed and assigned an overall impact score." One timing trap: fellowships (F30, F31, F32, F33, F99/K00) are on the excluded list for late submission under the rewritten late policy, so the deadline is hard.
result.submission_requirements:
Where the F31 deviates from generic NIH practice — these are the things that sink first-time applicants:

1. **Reference letters are a separate submission channel with its own failure mode.** NOFO: "Applications lacking the appropriate required reference letters will not be reviewed. This is a separate process from submitting an application electronically. Reference letters are submitted directly through the eRA Commons Submit Reference Letter link and not through Grants.gov." NIH's reference-letter page: "At least three, but no more than five, reference letters are required unless otherwise specified in the funding opportunity," and "The sponsor/co-sponsor(s) of the application cannot be counted toward the three required references" — so your PI's letter does not count, you need three *others*. Referees submit by the application due date and do not need an eRA Commons login; give each of them your eRA Commons username, your name exactly as it appears in Commons, and the NOFO number (PA-25-422). "Applications that have fewer than the required numbers of reference letters will not be reviewed" — no cure after the deadline.

2. **You are the PD/PI, but you cannot submit.** "Multiple PDs/PIs are not allowed." The sponsoring organization submits through Grants.gov via ASSIST, Workspace, or an institutional S2S system; your AOR presses the button.

3. **A sponsor must be locked in before you start.** "Before submitting the application, the candidate must identify a sponsor(s) who will supervise the proposed mentored training experience," with one named primary sponsor if you use a sponsor team.

4. **ORCID is enforced at the form level, restated in this NOFO:** "The personal profile associated with the eRA Commons username entered in the Credential field for the PD/PI (fellowship candidate) must include an ORCID ID."

5. **The form is the PHS Fellowship Supplemental Form**, now structured as: Candidate Section (Goals, Preparedness, and Potential) / Research Training Plan (Research Training Project Specific Aims and Strategy) / Commitment to Candidate, Mentoring and Training Environment / Other Research Training Plan Sections / Additional Information / Budget / Appendix. Page limits come from NIH's Table of Page Limits (the NOFO adds none of its own): Candidate's Goals, Preparedness, Potential 3; Training Activities and Timelines 3; Research Training Project Specific Aims 1; **Research Training Project Strategy 6** (not the 12 pages of an R01); Responsible Conduct of Research 1; Sponsor(s) Commitment 6; Letters of Support 6; Project Summary 30 lines; Narrative 3 sentences; resubmission Introduction 1 page.

6. **Clinical-trial statement, if applicable:** if you propose trial experience, "the sponsor or co-sponsor must include a statement to document leadership of the clinical trial including source of funding, NCT# and appropriate expertise." On the Human Subjects form, "Do not provide an NCT# in Section 1, item 1.5 ... Do not complete Section 4 - Protocol Synopsis information or Section 5 - Other Clinical Trial-related Attachments."

7. **Full-time commitment at award:** "individuals are required to pursue their research training on a full-time basis, normally defined as 40 hours per week."

8. **Registrations, and the NOFO's own warning:** "Registration can take 6 weeks or more, so applicant organizations should begin the registration process as soon as possible. Failure to complete registrations in advance of a due date is not a valid reason for a late submission." Your personal eRA Commons account with a PI role plus a linked ORCID is the piece that is yours to do, not your admin's.

9. **Money you can ask for that people forget:** the IC table states "Each NRSA fellow may additionally request $3000 per budget period to defray childcare costs." Budget = stipend + tuition/fees + institutional allowance at the annually published NRSA levels.
result.program_officer_contact:
Pre-submission contact is expected, and for the F31 it is IC-specific rather than NOFO-specific: Section VII of PA-25-422 points to the "Table of IC-Specific Information, Requirements, and Staff Contacts" at https://grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/contacts/PA-25-422.html, which carries a training/fellowship mailbox for each of ~22 participating ICs. The emails on that page are obfuscated in the HTML; decoded, the F31-relevant ones are: NCI NCIF31@nih.gov · NEI NEI_EXTRAMURAL@nih.gov · NHGRI nhgritrainingfellowships@mail.nih.gov · NHLBI NHLBI_F31@nhlbi.nih.gov · NIA NIATraining@mail.nih.gov · NIAAA NIAAA-Training@mail.nih.gov · NIAID NIAIDFellowshipParents@mail.nih.gov · NIAMS NIAMStraining@nih.gov · NIBIB NIBIB_Fellowships@mail.nih.gov · NICHD NICHDextrain@mail.nih.gov · NIDA NIDA_Training@nida.nih.gov · NIDCD nidcd.training@mail.nih.gov · NIDCR NIDCRtraining@nidcr.nih.gov · NIDDK by division (NIDDK_DEM@nih.gov, NIDDK_DDN@nih.gov, NIDDK_KUH@nih.gov, NIDDK_Obesity@nih.gov) · NIEHS NOFO.Information@niehs.nih.gov · NIGMS nigmsf31@mail.nih.gov · NIMH NIMHTraining@mail.nih.gov · NIMHD NIMHDtraining@nih.gov · NINDS NINDSFellowships@ninds.nih.gov · NINR NINRProgram@mail.nih.gov · NLM NLMProgram@nih.gov · NCCIH NCCIHDERFunding@nih.gov. General NIH: grants.info@nih.gov, 301-637-3015; eRA Service Desk https://www.era.nih.gov/need-help.
Several ICs say outright that you should write first: NHGRI — "Prospective applicants are strongly encouraged to contact NHGRI program staff prior to submitting an application"; NIDA — prospective applicants are "highly encouraged to contact a NIDA Program Official prior to preparing an application"; NIMH, NIMHD, NEI, NIDDK, NICHD and NHLBI carry equivalent language. NIA gives the most usable instruction: send "a one-page overview of your specific aims to the NIA Training Team." That is the house style — a one-page Specific Aims plus a short email with 2–3 targeted questions, sent 2–4 months out (i.e. for December 8, 2026, write in September–October 2026), and again after your summary statement lands if you are weighing an A1. The choice of IC is the real question to ask, because the stage caps differ (NIMH/NINDS first 6 years of PhD training; NIAID/NIGMS/NINDS 3-year maximum) and mis-assignment is expensive. The Scientific Review Officer, not the PO, is your contact once the application is under review; never contact reviewers.
result.examples_or_samples:
**Full funded F31 applications paired with their summary statements — NIAID, and it is the only NIH collection I could verify that is F31-specific.** https://www.niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/sample-applications#f31 lists three, each with both documents (all six PDFs verified live this session):
- Nicole Putnam (Vanderbilt), "The impact of innate immune recognition of Staphylococcus aureus on bone homeostasis and skeletal immunity" — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/sites/default/files/nicoleputnamapplicationF31.pdf + https://www.niaid.nih.gov/sites/default/files/nicoleputnamsummaryF31.pdf
- Nico Contreras (University of Arizona), "The Immunological Consequences of Mouse Cytomegalovirus on Adipose Tissue" — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/sites/default/files/f31-sample-application_nico_contreras.pdf + https://www.niaid.nih.gov/sites/default/files/f31-contreras-summary.pdf
- Samantha Lynne Schwartz (Emory), "Regulation of 2'-5'-oligoadenylate synthetase 1 (OAS1) by dsRNA" — https://www.niaid.nih.gov/sites/default/files/F31-Sample-Application_Samantha-Schwartz.pdf + https://www.niaid.nih.gov/sites/default/files/F31-Sample-Summary_Samantha-Schwartz.pdf
**Important caveat I verified rather than assumed:** the Contreras PDF contains the section heading "Applicant's Background and Goals for Fellowship Training" and no "Preparedness" heading — i.e. these samples use the pre-2025 fellowship form. Read them for argument, aims-page craft and how reviewers responded; do not copy their section structure, which the current Candidate Section (Goals, Preparedness, and Potential) has replaced. NIAID also warns on that page that "some content on niaid.nih.gov is not being updated regularly" because of HHS/NIH restructuring.
**Adjacent but not F31:** NIA hosts F99/K00 samples showing an initial submission and its resubmission side by side (https://www.nia.nih.gov/research/training/sample-applications); NHGRI's ELSI collection (https://www.genome.gov/Funded-Programs-Projects/ELSI-Research-Program/Sample-Applications-and-Summary-Statements) and NIDCD's (https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/funding/sample-grant-applications) carry samples but not F31. NIH's own index of all of these: https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/samples-applications-and-documents, and its annotated form sets at https://grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/samples-applications-and-documents/annotated-form-sets. The FORMS-I fellowship instruction PDF is at https://grants.nih.gov/grants/how-to-apply-application-guide/forms-i/fellowship-forms-i.pdf.
**To find funded F31s in your own field and department** (not fetched this session, inherited from the funder-wide layer): NIH RePORTER at reporter.nih.gov, filtered to activity code F31 plus your IC and institution, gives abstracts, the funding IC and the study section — which is also how you identify who near you has already won one and will read your draft. Complete applications are only obtainable by FOIA request to the funding IC.
result.resubmission_note: One resubmission (A1) only, submitted within 37 months of the A0, with a 1-page Introduction responding to the summary statement. F31-specific wrinkles: (a) the A1 is due on the *same* calendar date as a new application — April 8 / August 8 / December 8, with no one-month shift, so a December 8, 2026 A0 that is not funded lands its summary statement around April 2027 and the realistic A1 date is August 8, 2027; (b) "A resubmission (A1) application that is submitted before issuance of the summary statement from the review of the previous new (A0) application" will not be accepted — you must wait for the statement, which is what makes the very next cycle usually impossible; (c) "For Resubmissions, the committee will evaluate the application as now presented, taking into consideration the responses to comments from the previous scientific review group and changes made to the project"; (d) the binding constraint is your own clock, not NIH's — you must still be enrolled and, at NIMH/NINDS, still inside the first 6 years of PhD training when the A1 is reviewed and awarded; (e) renewal is essentially closed: "Individual fellowship awards are generally not renewable. In rare cases in which fellowship awardees require further fellowship support, they should consult with NIH staff." NHLBI publishes one explicit resubmission carve-out, for F30 rather than F31: "Resubmission of F30 applications will be considered beyond the 48-month post-matriculation limit, provided that they have at least one year remaining in their PhD dissertation research."
unresolved: Whether a student currently appointed to a T32 may hold an F31 concurrently, and the mechanics of terminating the T32 appointment at F31 activation. PA-25-422 gives only the 5-year aggregate cap and the bar on concurrent *federal fellowships*; it does not address T32 appointment termination in its own words. Not found in the NOFO — needs the NIH Grants Policy Statement NRSA chapter or the IC training office.

What outside compensation an active F31 fellow may receive (teaching assistantship, paid effort on the sponsor's R01). NRSA compensation rules live in the NIH Grants Policy Statement, which I did not fetch this session. Do not assume either way.

Whether the NRSA payback/service obligation touches predoctoral fellows. NIH's Individual Fellowships overview says the obligation falls on "post-doctoral fellows and trainees" but does not state explicitly that predoctoral F31 fellows are exempt. Probable but unverified.

Whether the current emergency peer-review modifications (NOT-OD-26-114: ~30-35% of applications discussed, simplified summary statements) apply to CSR fellowship study sections and therefore to F31 applications. Not verified for the F series this session.
Whether the NIH 6-applications-per-PD/PI-per-calendar-year cap counts fellowship applications. Not checked.

The exact FORMS version of the three NIAID F31 samples. I established they predate the 2025 restructure by finding the heading "Applicant's Background and Goals for Fellowship Training" in the Contreras PDF, but the specific forms letter is not stated on the page.

The exact window during which eRA Commons accepts reference letters (the NOFO says to follow the Application Guide's "time period for when reference letters will be accepted"; the guidance page I read states only that they are due by the application due date).

Note on method: the IC contact emails were recovered by decoding Cloudflare email-obfuscation on grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/contacts/PA-25-422.html, because the rendered text shows only "[email protected]". They are the funder's own addresses, not a search-index reconstruction. Separately, this session's web-search budget was exhausted early, so all findings come from direct fetches of funder pages rather than any search index.

result.loi_deadline: TWO pre-stages sit in front of the full application, and both are easy to miss. (1) INSTITUTIONAL NOMINATION — a hard gate, not a formality: "To be eligible to apply to Schmidt Science Fellows, you must be nominated by your PhD awarding institution." For the 2027 cohort the nomination deadline was May 15 2026, about two months before the July 13 2026 full application. The funder describes the upstream step as: "Ahead of applications opening, we invite our Nominating Partners to select and send us the details of their nominees." Each partner runs its own competition to pick "a small number of their most exceptional PhD students", so the INTERNAL institutional deadline is earlier still — typically weeks to months before mid-May — and is set and published by the institution, not by Schmidt. Practically, a candidate needs to be talking to their institution's nominating contact in the winter/early spring preceding the cycle. (2) PRELIMINARY INFORMATION — after nomination, a short pre-stage inside the Schmidt system: "Nominees must submit their preliminary information by June 1, 2026 and the remaining full application form by July 13, 2026." So the preliminary submission fell ~6 weeks before the full application. Net effect: the real personal starting gun is roughly 5-7 months before the published full-application deadline.
result.review_to_award: Long, and longer than most postdoc fellowships. From the 2027 cycle: full application July 13 2026 → "Application Review: August 2026 to February 2027" → "Cohort Selection: March 2027" → placements begin July or October 2027. That is roughly 8 months from submission to notification, and about 12-15 months from submission to earliest start. Review runs in two stages: first "discipline-specific panels of senior researchers" assess applications, then finalists take "an online panel interview with senior figures from academia, business, and society". Start timing, verbatim from the FAQ: "Fellows are expected to begin their Fellowship Research Placements in either July or October of the calendar year in which they have been awarded their Fellowship"; the How to Apply page states "2027 Fellows are expected to begin their Fellowship Research Placements in July or October 2027". Deferral is essentially unavailable: "We do not permit deferrals (unless related to sick leave or family leave)." Planning consequence: a candidate must bridge from PhD conferral (window ends June 30 of the cohort year) to a July or October start, with no option to push the award later.
result.submission_requirements: Components, verbatim from How to Apply: "academic history, including transcripts, current CV, relevant publications, letters of recommendation", plus "a personal statement outlining your motivations", "a brief description of your PhD research", and "a proposal outlining your future research plans". THE BIG DEVIATION from the postdoc-fellowship norm: you do NOT need a host, sponsor, or placement lined up at application. "Successful Fellows work with the Program Team to identify and finalize their postdoctoral Placement" — placement is negotiated AFTER selection. So unlike NIH F32/K99, NSF PRFB, EMBO or HFSP, there is no sponsor/mentor statement, no host letter of support, and no host institutional sign-off in the application package. This removes the usual months-long task of recruiting a host, and shifts the weight onto the pivot proposal itself. SECOND DEVIATION: the only institutional sign-off is the nomination gate at your PhD institution — there is no research-office submission of the application itself; nominated candidates submit directly. THIRD: page/word limits are NOT public — "Word and page limits are clearly communicated both in the online application form and in the associated guidance notes, please pay close attention to these." The guidance notes are visible only once nominated, so a candidate cannot size the essays in advance; budget for that. The number of recommendation letters and who should write them is not published anywhere I could reach. Selection emphasis to write toward (from the existing corpus row and the selection page): scientific excellence, genuine readiness to pivot beyond the PhD discipline, interdisciplinary thinking, learning agility, comfort with scientific risk, leadership potential. The placement must be in a DIFFERENT field from the PhD and at a different institution from the PhD institution.
result.prior_funding_conflicts: STRUCTURALLY DIFFERENT from NIH-style career awards: there is NO prior-funding exclusion at all. Nothing you have previously held disqualifies you. The eligibility bars are the PhD conferral window, the eligible-discipline list, and the institutional nomination — not your funding history. The conflict here is CONCURRENT, not prior. WHAT EXCLUDES (verbatim): "We do not normally allow Fellows to receive any awards or remuneration from other organizations concurrent with the Fellowship." And on deferral: "We do not permit deferrals (unless related to sick leave or family leave)" — so you cannot take Schmidt and postpone it to run another award first. WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (three carve-outs, all verbatim): (1) supplementary money is fine — "Supplementary funding for research and other professional development (such as travel grants) is allowed and encouraged"; (2) you may keep a competing fellowship's PRESTIGE without its money — "With Program approval, Fellows may also retain the title of another fellowship during the Fellowship Year if personal remuneration is not accepted and as long as there are no compulsory requirements that could hinder full participation"; (3) already having a postdoc lined up does not disqualify you — "We recognize that some candidates will have already secured a postdoctoral position prior to commencing the Fellowship Research Placement. However, candidates should not assume that any pre-existing position will be automatically approved or denied. All placements are subject to the same review and approval process." PRACTICAL READ for an applicant holding a competing offer: you can apply while holding or having won another fellowship, and if you win both you can usually list both titles — but you must decline the other's salary, you must clear the arrangement with the Program in advance, and any pre-existing postdoc must still pass Schmidt's placement review (it must be a genuine disciplinary pivot at a non-PhD institution, so many pre-existing positions will fail on those grounds rather than on funding grounds).
result.program_officer_contact: No named program officer is published. Three routes, in the order an applicant should actually use them. (1) PRIMARY AND EXPECTED — your own institution's nominating contact. The funder tells candidates to initiate this themselves, verbatim: "Prospective applicants are encouraged to use the contact details provided to reach out to their NPO directly for information about their internal selection process and timeline." The Nominating Partner List (https://schmidtsciencefellows.org/nominating-partner-list/, ~150+ institutions incl. Harvard, Stanford, MIT, Cambridge, Oxford, Max Planck Society, U Tokyo) carries a contact per institution, usually an office or department (e.g. "Graduate Research School" for ANU) rather than a named individual. Pre-submission contact here is effectively mandatory: internal deadlines and internal selection processes are institution-set and not published by Schmidt. (2) nominations@schmidtsciencefellows.org — for eligibility questions, and where your institution is missing or its contact details are wrong: "If your institution or contact information is not listed, or if your institution is interested in becoming one of our Nominating Partner Organizations, please contact nominations@schmidtsciencefellows.org." (3) apply@schmidtsciencefellows.org — for application-process questions: "If you still have further questions, please contact us at apply@schmidtsciencefellows.org". Note the asymmetry worth flagging to applicants: pre-submission contact with the FUNDER is available but not described as expected; pre-submission contact with your OWN institution is the thing that decides whether you get to apply at all.
result.examples_or_samples: No sample application, funded abstract, or annotated example is published for this mechanism — confirmed absent across the selection, how-to-apply and FAQ pages. The guidance notes that contain the word/page limits sit inside the online application form and so are reachable only after nomination. Closest available substitutes, both official: (1) FELLOW DIRECTORY — https://schmidtsciencefellows.org/fellows/fellow-directory/ — filterable by cohort year (2018-2026), PhD subject area, placement field, nominating institution and placement institution. Each entry shows the actual pivot: PhD discipline → placement field → host institution (e.g. Ina Anreiter, 2019, PhD in Behavioral Genetics at University of Toronto → Machine Learning at the Ontario Institute for Cancer Research). This is the single best way to calibrate what counts as a credible pivot and to find fellows to approach directly, but entries carry no project descriptions, so they show WHAT pivots succeeded, not HOW they were argued. (2) IMPACT STORIES — https://schmidtsciencefellows.org/fellows/impact-stories/, individual stories at /impact-story/<slug>/ (e.g. "Can Rocks help Combat Climate Change?", "Could your smartwatch support your mental health?") — narrative profiles of fellows' interdisciplinary work; useful for the framing and ambition register the program rewards, not for application mechanics. PRACTICAL ROUTE for a prospective applicant: use the directory to find a recent fellow who pivoted out of your own PhD field, and approach them and your institution's nominating office — since the internal competition, not the Schmidt form, is the first real hurdle.
result.resubmission_note: Not found. Neither the FAQ, the How to Apply page, nor the Who Can Apply page addresses whether an unsuccessful candidate may be nominated and apply again in a later cycle. Note that the question is largely mooted by the eligibility structure: because eligibility is keyed to a ~14-month PhD-conferral window ("between May 1, 2026 and June 30, 2027" for the 2027 cohort) and the cycle is annual, most candidates fall inside the window for only one cycle, so a second attempt is usually impossible on eligibility grounds rather than on resubmission-policy grounds. A candidate whose conferral date straddles two windows should ask nominations@schmidtsciencefellows.org directly; this is not documented publicly. Treat "no stated resubmission policy" as recorded absence, not as a prohibition.
unresolved: 2028-cohort dates are not yet published (nomination deadline, application open, preliminary and full application deadlines) - checked How to Apply, which still shows the 2027 cycle as the current one
2028-cohort PhD-conferral eligibility window not yet published; the May 1 2027 - June 30 2028 analogue is inferred from the 2027 window and is NOT confirmed

Number of letters of recommendation required, and who is expected to write them (PhD supervisor? prospective host? - no host exists at application time, so this matters) - not published on any reachable page

Specific word and page limits for the personal statement, PhD research description, and future research proposal - the funder states these exist only 'in the online application form and in the associated guidance notes', which are gated behind nomination
Per-institution nomination quota - described only as 'a small number of their most exceptional PhD students'; no number published
Whether unsuccessful candidates may reapply in a later cycle - no stated policy found anywhere
Each nominating institution's own internal nomination deadline and internal selection process - set by the institution, not published centrally; candidates must ask their NPO contact
Whether pre-submission contact with the Schmidt program team (as distinct from the home institution) is expected or merely permitted
Whether the preliminary-information stage is itself screened/eliminative or is purely administrative intake ahead of the full application
