result.review_to_award:
Roughly 4 months submission-to-notification, 7 months submission-to-earliest-start. Measured on the FY24 cycle:
- JustGrants deadline May 30, 2024
- Peer review by OJP panel over the summer
- Notification: "Generally, award notifications are made by the end of the current Federal fiscal year, September 30." (~4 months)
- "Period of Performance Start Date: Not earlier than 01/01/2025" (~7 months after submission)
This is materially faster than NIH's ~9-month submission-to-award arc, and there is no council round — but it is also less predictable, because the whole cycle is pinned to the federal fiscal year rather than to a standing calendar.

THE REVIEW ARC, in NIJ's own terms:
1. Basic minimum requirements screen. OJP screens before peer review for: eligible applicant type; responsiveness to scope; and presence of every required item. Verbatim consequence: "If NIJ determines that an application does not include these elements, it will not proceed to peer review and will not receive any further consideration." This is a hard, unappealable gate and the commonest way a good proposal dies.
2. Merit review by "a peer review panel(s) in accordance with OJP peer review policy and procedures". Weighted criteria, which NIJ publishes and which applicants should treat as the scoring rubric: Statement of the Problem (understanding of the problem) 15%; Project Design and Implementation (quality and technical merit) 50%; Capabilities and Competencies (capabilities, demonstrated productivity and experience of the applicant organization and proposed project staff) 20%; Potential Impact 10%; Budget 5%. Half the score is method.
3. Other review factors beyond merit: "geographic diversity, strategic priorities... available funding, past performance", plus the budget's reasonableness.
4. Risk screen under 2 C.F.R. Part 200 — SAM.gov exclusion check; for anticipated awards over $250,000 (i.e. essentially every Du Bois award), OJP "must review and consider any information about the applicant that appears in the non-public segment of the integrity and performance system accessible through SAM.gov."
5. Decision: "All final award decisions will be made by the Director of the National Institute of Justice (NIJ), who may take into account not only peer review ratings and NIJ staff recommendations, but also other factors as indicated in this section." One named official decides; there is no two-tier council.
6. Applicants do receive feedback — the NOFO's resubmission section requires "responses to previous feedback received from NIJ", which only makes sense if critiques are returned. The NOFO does not state when or in what form.

FY24 scale, for calibration: "Anticipated Total Amount To Be Awarded Under This Solicitation: $2,000,000", against a Fellows nominal minimum of $250,000 and a Scholars nominal minimum of $500,000 — i.e. a pool sized for only a small handful of awards. Number of awards and per-award maximum were both left "To be determined by the number and quality of applications received and funding available."
result.submission_requirements:
TWO-STEP ELECTRONIC SUBMISSION, TWO SEPARATE DEADLINES (the structural thing to internalise):
- Step 1, in Grants.gov by the Grants.gov deadline: SF-424 plus SF-LLL (Disclosure of Lobbying Activities) only. In SF-424 Section 8F you name the person who will complete Step 2. You must select the correct Competition ID — FY24 used C-NIJ-2024-00005-PROD for Scholars and C-NIJ-2024-00006-PROD for Fellows. Choosing the wrong one puts you in the wrong competition.
- Step 2, in JustGrants (JustGrants.usdoj.gov) by the JustGrants deadline, two weeks later: the entire substantive application.
OJP recommends submitting at each step "at least 48 hours prior to" that deadline.

BASIC MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS — missing any one of these means no peer review at all:
- SF-424 and SF-LLL (Grants.gov)
- Proposal Narrative (JustGrants)
- General Mentorship Plan — Scholars category only
- Budget Web-Based Form (budget details plus budget narrative, completed as a web form in JustGrants, not an uploaded spreadsheet)
- Curriculum Vitae/Résumés for Key Personnel — and NIJ defines key personnel very broadly: "all investigators regardless of status (i.e., principal investigator [PI], subaward PI, co-principal investigator [Co-PI], subaward Co-PI, co-investigator [Co-I], subaward Co-I, investigator[I], and subaward-I), senior staff (e.g., project leader/director/manager, senior technical advisor), and any other technical staff (e.g., consultants, statistician, project coordinator, research associate, data coordinator)." Collect the statistician's and the data coordinator's CVs early.

PROPOSAL NARRATIVE — format and page limit, verbatim: "The attached document should be double-spaced, using a standard 12-point size font; have no less than 1-inch margins; and should not exceed 30 numbered pages." Tables, charts and graphs must also use 12-point. Enforcement is soft but real: "If the Proposal Narrative fails to comply with these length restrictions, NIJ may consider such noncompliance in peer review and in final award decisions."
DEVIATION WORTH NOTING: 30 pages DOUBLE-SPACED is roughly 15 single-spaced pages — comparable in substance to an NIH R01's 12-page Research Strategy, not two and a half times it. Do not read "30 pages" as generous.

NOT counted against the 30 pages: Title Page; Resubmit Response; Table of Contents and Figures; Appendices.
Required narrative sections: Statement of the Problem; Project Design and Implementation; Potential Impact; Capabilities and Competencies; Plan for Collecting Performance Measures Data. The title page must carry project title, submission date, funding opportunity number, PI and co-PIs, "Unique author identifier (e.g., ORCID, ResearcherID, Scopus Author ID), if available" (encouraged, NOT mandatory — unlike NIH), keywords, contact details, and "Requests for consideration under 'new investigator and/or priority areas of research'." Fellows must additionally "indicate on the cover page of the program narrative that they are applying to the Fellows category."

SEPARATE ATTACHMENTS beyond the minimum set:
- Data Archiving Plan — a labelled separate file, "one or two pages in length", committing to deposit with the National Archive of Criminal Justice Data (NACJD), covering data, instrumentation, codebooks, programming code, de-identification procedures and the privacy certificate, "and include the level of effort associated with meeting archiving requirements." NIJ-specific; no NIH equivalent.
- Human Subjects Protection documentation
- Privacy Certificate (a DOJ-specific instrument, separate from IRB approval — see NIJ's model privacy certificate guidance)
- Research and Evaluation Independence and Integrity Statement (if proposing research/evaluation — in practice, always here)
- Letters of Support or Commitment, submitted "as one separate attachment", each covering the four points NIJ lists, and each acknowledging NACJD archiving. Hard rule: "Letters of support and commitment must also have wet signatures, e-signatures, or digital signatures; otherwise, they will be considered invalid." A typed name is an invalid letter.
- Consortium/Contractual Agreements; Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (if applicable); Disclosure of Process Related to Executive Compensation (if applicable); Applicant Disclosure of Duplication in Cost Items (JustGrants web form); Applicant Entity Questionnaire; Request to Use Incentives or Stipends (if paying research participants); Project Management Plan and Timeline
- Documentation of "New Investigator" status, if claiming it — see the prior-funding field
- General Mentorship Plan, as an appendix, Scholars only

CATEGORY-SPECIFIC SUBSTANCE:
- Scholars "must propose a mentorship component to the study that goes beyond hiring graduate and undergraduate students as project staff." At award stage NIJ requires mentee CVs, a career development plan, a description of resources, availability of seminars/interaction, training in career skills (grant writing, budget formulation, project management, presentations), and "A statement that at least one peer-reviewed journal article from the project will be first authored by the mentee(s)." Nominally 36+ months, minimum value $500,000.
- Fellows: nominally 24+ months, minimum value $250,000. Fellows must "Be the proposal PI if the project has multiple investigators."
- Anyone applying under Priority Area 1 must supply, in the narrative, a description of the data (case counts, variable descriptions, collection method, format, source, cost of access); a description of the justice phenomenon producing the disparity; "A disparity analysis (using existing data) showing evidence of racial or ethnic disparity"; the intervention and supporting literature; analytic techniques; and "An explicit statement discussing how the proposed research follows the W.E.B. Du Bois Program's tradition of multidisciplinary scientific inquiry." The disparity analysis is a preliminary-data requirement in all but name — budget time for it.
- Two discretionary scoring levers: "special consideration" for methods including "meaningful engagement with the people closest to the subject of study", and "Special consideration will be given to proposals that dedicate at least 15% of the requested project award funding toward implementing such [dissemination] strategies, as demonstrated in the 'Budget Worksheet and Budget Narrative'." That 15% is a concrete, checkable budget target.
- Period of performance "Cannot exceed 60 Months". Maximum federal request $2,000,000.

REGISTRATIONS (the OJP long-lead equivalent, much lighter than NIH's):
- SAM.gov registration required before applying; OJP: "Applicants are encouraged to start the SAM.gov registration or renewal process at least 30 days prior to the application's Grants.gov deadline," and a first-time registration "may take several weeks." Failing to start at least 10 business days out forfeits any technical waiver.
- Grants.gov registration; JustGrants entity onboarding is triggered by the SF-424 ("This email should arrive within 24 hours").
- NOTABLE DEVIATION: "Individuals" are a listed eligible applicant type, and "The SAM.gov registration is not required for a person applying as an 'individual' and not on behalf of a company; state, local, or tribal government; academic institution; or other type of organization. Individuals should obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) and not apply using a social security number." An unaffiliated researcher can genuinely apply in their own name — impossible at NIH.
- Roles: Entity Administrator, Authorized Representative (must approve and submit), Application Submitter. As at NIH, an institutional applicant does not submit for themselves; your research office's internal deadline governs.

LATE SUBMISSION: far harsher than NIH. "OJP will only consider requests to submit an application after the deadline when the applicant can document that a technical issue with a government system prevented submission on time," and the request must reach the NOFO contact "within 24 hours of the [respective] deadline". Explicitly insufficient: failure to register in time, failure to follow instructions, and "Technical issues with the applicant's computer or information technology environment." And "OJP does not automatically approve requests to submit a late application even in the event of technological difficulties." There is no weekend/holiday rollover provision and no error-correction window.

SUPPORT HOURS, worth knowing on deadline day: OJP Response Center 10:00 a.m.-6:00 p.m. ET Mon-Fri, extended "to 8:00 p.m. ET on the solicitation closing date". JustGrants Service Desk 7:00 a.m.-9:00 p.m. ET Mon-Fri. Grants.gov support is 24/7 except federal holidays. Note the JustGrants deadline itself is 8:59 p.m. ET — the help desk closes one minute after the deadline.
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
Both halves, and the headline is that prior funding is NOT a barrier to this programme — it only affects one optional scoring bonus.

WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the larger half here):
- There is NO prior-funding exclusion at the programme level. Nothing in the FY24 NOFO disqualifies an applicant for holding, or having held, NIJ or other federal awards. The gates are career-stage gates, not funding-history gates.
- NIJ goes further and actively recruits the unfunded: for Fellows, "In this funding category, first-time grant recipients are encouraged to apply."
- Multiple applications are allowed: "An applicant may submit more than one application, if each application proposes a different project in response to the solicitation. Also, an entity may be proposed as a subrecipient (subgrantee) in more than one application." No NIH-style per-PI annual cap and no bar on overlapping applications under review.
- A prior NIJ GRADUATE RESEARCH FELLOWSHIP is expressly carved out and preserves even the New Investigator bonus (see below). This is the exact structural analogue of NIH's K-to-R01 carve-out, and it means the intended pipeline — NIJ GRF as a doctoral student, then Du Bois Fellow as an assistant professor — is protected by design.

WHAT ACTUALLY GATES YOU (career status, tied to fixed calendar anchors, not to funding):
- Du Bois FELLOWS (early career): doctorate "awarded an academic or research doctorate terminal degree within seven years of December 31, 2023"; must "Not have been awarded tenure by December 31, 2023"; must "Be the proposal PI if the project has multiple investigators." Tenure, not funding, is the disqualifier.
- Du Bois SCHOLARS (advanced): doctorate "awarded... at least seven years prior to December 31, 2023". The seven-year line sorts applicants between the two categories; nobody is excluded from the programme by it, they are routed.
- Note both anchors are FIXED DATES pegged to the fiscal year, not rolling "years since degree". They will move in any new NOFO. Career interruptions: the FY24 NOFO states no extension or relief provision for family leave, illness or military service — a gap NIH would normally cover. Do not assume one exists.

WHERE PRIOR FUNDING GENUINELY BITES — the "New Investigator/Early Career Opportunity". This is a separate, optional special consideration in award decisions, available on top of either category, and its third criterion is a prior-funding test:
- "Hold a non-tenured assistant professor appointment at an accredited institution of higher education in the United States or an equivalent full-time staff scientist position at a research institution in the United States."
- "Have completed a terminal degree or post-graduate clinical training within the six (6) years prior to September 30, 2024."
- "Have never previously received NIJ funding as a PI on a research project with the exception of Graduate Research Fellows."
So: any previous NIJ award held AS PI on a research project kills the bonus; being a co-I or subaward investigator does not; and a prior NIJ Graduate Research Fellowship explicitly does not. Non-NIJ funding (NSF, NIH, foundation) is not mentioned and so does not appear to count against it.

TWO CLOCKS, EASILY CONFLATED — this is the trap. The Fellows clock is SEVEN years to December 31, 2023. The New Investigator clock is SIX years to September 30, 2024. They are different lengths and different anchor dates. A researcher can be a valid Du Bois Fellow and still be too far past degree to claim the New Investigator bonus. Check both separately.

CLAIMING IT IS AN ACTIVE STEP, not automatic. You must flag it on the title page ("the applicant should identify that it is submitting a New Investigator/Early Career proposal on the title page of the application") AND file a separate attachment: "Documentation of 'New Investigator' status", which must state when the doctorate or post-graduate clinical training was completed; contain "a statement corroborating that they have not received previous NIJ funding as a PI on a research award (except for GRF grantees)"; and provide "verification that the investigator currently holds a non-tenured assistant professor appointment at an accredited institution of higher education in the United States or an equivalent full-time staff scientist position at a research institution in the United States." An eligible applicant who simply forgets the attachment forfeits the benefit silently.

ONE ORGANISATIONAL RESTRICTION, unrelated to the individual: "Federal agencies are not eligible to apply." And on multi-party projects, "only one entity may be the applicant... Any others must be proposed as subrecipients (subgrantees)", with "The applicant is expected to conduct the preponderance of the work proposed."
result.program_officer_contact:
NO NAMED PROGRAM OFFICER, AND PRE-SUBMISSION CONTACT IS NOT THE NORM. This is the sharpest cultural deviation from NIH in the whole record and the thing most likely to mislead someone who has only ever applied to NIH.

The FY24 NOFO's Agency Contact Information section names no scientist, no program manager, no division. It routes everything to a shared help desk, verbatim: "For assistance with the requirements of this solicitation, contact the OJP Response Center by phone at 800-851-3420 or 301-240-6310 (TTY for hearing-impaired callers only) or email grants@ncjrs.gov. The OJP Response Center operates from 10:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Eastern Time (ET) Monday-Friday and from 10:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET on the solicitation closing date." A search of the whole solicitation for programmatic-contact language returns only this route.

There is no NIJ equivalent of RePORTER Matchmaker, no IC program-officer directory, no published "contact a PO at the idea stage" guidance, and no Scientific Review Officer role exposed to applicants. NIJ's staff-directory URL I tried returned 404 (a tooling fact, not evidence that no directory exists — I could not locate one; web search budget was exhausted early in this session, so I could not search for an alternative).

THE THREE ROUTES THAT DO EXIST:
1. Programmatic — the optional Letter of Intent, to NIJDuboisResearch@usdoj.gov, addressed to the NIJ Director. Programme-specific and clearly monitored by programme staff; it is the only sanctioned pre-submission touch. It only exists while a solicitation is open.
2. Solicitation/eligibility questions — OJP Response Center, 800-851-3420 / grants@ncjrs.gov.
3. Mechanical — Grants.gov Customer Support 800-518-4726 / support@grants.gov (24/7 except federal holidays) for Step 1; JustGrants Service Desk 833-872-5175 / JustGrants.Support@usdoj.gov (7:00 a.m.-9:00 p.m. ET Mon-Fri, 9:00 a.m.-5:00 p.m. ET weekends and federal holidays) for Step 2.

PRACTICAL ADVICE THAT FOLLOWS: do not plan a Du Bois application around a conversation with a program officer, because there is no published person to have it with. The compensating move is to read the merit-review weights as a rubric (design and methods are 50% of the score), send the LOI, and get your intelligence from the funded-award record rather than from agency staff. Your institution's research office and a previously funded Du Bois PI are more accessible advisers here than NIJ is.

One named official is on record: NIJ Director Dr. Nancy La Vigne, as the LOI addressee in the FY24 NOFO (March 2024) and the person who "will make all final award decisions". Directors change; re-verify against any new NOFO before using the name.
result.resubmission_note:
FAR MORE PERMISSIVE THAN NIH — no single-resubmission rule, no A1 suffix, no 37-month window, no bar on concurrent overlapping applications, and no requirement that the resubmission return to the same solicitation.

The NOFO handles it through an optional narrative component, verbatim: "Resubmit Response (if applicable) (not counted against the proposal narrative page limit.) If an applicant is resubmitting an application presented previously to NIJ, under any prior NIJ solicitation but not funded, the applicant should indicate this. A statement should be provided, no more than two pages, addressing: (1) the title, submission date, and NIJ-assigned application number of the previous application; and (2) a brief summary of revisions to the application, including responses to previous feedback received from NIJ."

What that establishes:
- Scope is "any prior NIJ solicitation", not just a prior Du Bois competition — a proposal declined under, say, a Policing Practices solicitation can be reworked and resubmitted here.
- The response is capped at two pages and, unlike NIH's Introduction, does NOT consume narrative space — it sits outside the 30-page limit.
- It is framed as "should", and no cap on the number of attempts is stated anywhere in the NOFO.
- The requirement to give "responses to previous feedback received from NIJ" confirms that declined applicants get substantive critiques back; the NOFO does not say when or in what form.
- You need the NIJ-assigned application number from the earlier attempt, so keep it.

Given the programme's intermittent history (FY2000-2018, reinstituted FY2021, last run FY2024), the realistic resubmission path for a declined Du Bois application is often lateral — into whichever NIJ research solicitation is actually open that year — rather than waiting for this programme to return.
result.examples_or_samples:
NIJ publishes NO sample applications. There is no NIJ counterpart to NIAID's or NHGRI's funded-application libraries, and no counterpart to a summary statement being released publicly. What exists is a funded-award trail, which is genuinely usable if you know where to look.

1. THE PROGRAMME PAGE'S OWN AWARD TABLE — the best single starting point. https://nij.ojp.gov/funding/fellowships/web-du-bois-program carries a table of 40+ awards spanning 2000-2024 with researcher name, institution, project title and dollar amount. Project titles are hyperlinked: recent ones (e.g. the 2021 cohort) link to their NIJ award pages; older ones (2006-2008 era) link to OJP library publication pages carrying the resulting final research reports. That older half is the valuable part — you can read the actual delivered research from a funded Du Bois project end to end.

2. RECENT FUNDED AWARDS, for scale calibration. 2024: Vanessa Bouché / Life After Justice, "Incentivized Informants and Wrongful Convictions: Understanding the Risks and Mitigating the Effects", award 15PNIJ-24-GK-03091-MUMU, $1,133,976 — award page at https://nij.ojp.gov/funding/awards/15pnij-24-gk-03091-mumu, which names the FY24 Du Bois solicitation as its source, confirming the link between the programme page and the NOFO. 2023: Spencer Lawson $599,976; Clare Strange $730,834; S. Rebecca Neusteter $500,000. Note how far these sit above the Fellows $250,000 nominal minimum.

3. PUBLIC PROPOSAL ABSTRACTS. OJP requires a Proposal Abstract of "no more than 2,000 characters" and states it is made publicly available if awarded. These surface on NIJ award pages and are the closest thing to a successful abstract for this mechanism. (The specific 2024 award page I fetched showed metadata without the abstract body rendered, so coverage is uneven — check several.)

4. FINAL RESEARCH REPORTS. Every award must deliver a Final Research Report, and these are deposited in the OJP/NCJRS library, reachable from the older entries in the programme table. Reading a final report backwards against its award abstract is the nearest available substitute for reading an application beside its summary statement.

5. THE NOFO ITSELF AS A RUBRIC — https://nij.ojp.gov/funding/O-NIJ-2024-172018.pdf. It publishes the merit-review weights (Design and Implementation 50%, Capabilities 20%, Statement of the Problem 15%, Potential Impact 10%, Budget 5%), the exact required narrative sections, and the Priority Area 1 evidence checklist. NIH applicants get sample applications; NIJ applicants get the scoring sheet. Use it as one.

6. CRIMESOLUTIONS EVIDENCE STANDARDS — https://crimesolutions.ojp.gov/about/how-we-review-and-rate-program-start-finish. The NOFO directs applicants here "for further information on high-quality evaluation design elements", which makes it the de facto methodological standard your design will be judged against.

NOT FOUND: any route to a complete funded Du Bois application. This NOFO states no FOIA procedure for obtaining one (the FOIA route is an NIH practice and should not be assumed to transfer). Whether DOJ would release one on request is unresolved.
unresolved: WHETHER THE PROGRAMME WILL RUN AGAIN — the single most consequential gap. No Du Bois NOFO appears in NIJ's own expired-opportunity listings for FY25 or FY26, both of which carry otherwise complete NIJ research portfolios; /funding/current and /funding/forthcoming both return 'There are no results for your filter settings'; and the programme page carries no discontinuation, suspension or renaming notice and has not been modified since December 20, 2024. Two fiscal years without a competition is a fact; termination is NOT established and must not be recorded as one. The NOFO itself documents a prior lapse (FY2000-2018, then 'reinstituted... in FY 2021'), so intermittency is this programme's normal pattern. Recommend the row's status move from 'active' to something like 'active_not_currently_offered' or 'dormant', with the evidence being the absence from FY25/FY26 listings rather than any funder statement.

WHY the FY25/FY26 portfolios omit it — no NIJ or OJP statement was located explaining the omission. I deliberately did not infer a cause. Establishing this would need OJP press releases, NIJ annual program plans, or Federal Register notices, none of which I could reach this session.

WHETHER THE ELIGIBILITY ANCHORS RE-PEG EACH CYCLE — FY24 hard-coded 'December 31, 2023' (Fellows 7-year clock and the tenure bar) and 'September 30, 2024' (New Investigator 6-year clock). Only one recent NOFO was available to inspect, so I could not confirm the anchors shift by one year per competition, nor whether the 7-year and 6-year lengths are stable. Both must be re-read from any new NOFO.

CAREER-INTERRUPTION RELIEF — the FY24 NOFO states no extension to the 7-year Fellows clock, the 6-year New Investigator clock, or the tenure bar for parental leave, illness, caregiving or military service. Silence is not the same as refusal, but no provision was found and none should be assumed.

AWARD FEEDBACK TIMING — the resubmission section presupposes 'previous feedback received from NIJ', confirming critiques are returned to declined applicants, but the NOFO nowhere states when they arrive, what form they take, or whether peer reviewer comments are passed through verbatim.

SELECTIVITY — number of applications received and number funded are not published for any Du Bois cycle. FY24 set a $2,000,000 total pool against nominal minimums of $250,000 (Fellows) and $500,000 (Scholars), implying only a handful of awards, but no success rate could be established.

NAMED PROGRAM OFFICER — none is published for this mechanism. The NIJ staff-directory URL I tried (nij.ojp.gov/about/nij-staff) returned HTTP 404; that is a tooling fact, not evidence that NIJ publishes no directory. I could not locate an alternative directory route.

WHETHER NIJ ACCEPTS PROGRAMMATIC CONTACT OUTSIDE AN OPEN SOLICITATION — the NIJDuboisResearch@usdoj.gov inbox was established for FY24 letters of intent and there is no statement about whether it is monitored between competitions.
FULL FUNDED APPLICATIONS — no route found. Unlike NIH, this NOFO states no FOIA procedure for obtaining a copy of a funded application, and I did not verify whether DOJ would release one.

METHOD CAVEAT, per house rules: this session's WebSearch budget (200/200) was exhausted before my first search returned, so NO search index was used at any point. Every finding above came from direct fetches of nij.ojp.gov and ojp.gov, plus text extracted from NIJ's own solicitation PDF (O-NIJ-2024-172018.pdf, extracted locally with pdftotext after WebFetch returned it as binary). Nothing was cross-checked against Grants.gov's own listing, SAM.gov, or USAspending, so the FY25/FY26 absence rests on NIJ's site alone.

BRIEF MISMATCH, flagged for the corpus: the 'already established' machinery supplied with this task was NIH's (eRA Commons, ASSIST, SciENcv, ORCID mandate, standard due dates, study sections, council rounds, the single-A1 rule, the 5:00 p.m.-local deadline, the Application Viewing Window). NONE of it applies to NIJ, which is DOJ/OJP: Grants.gov + JustGrants, solicitation-specific paired deadlines, OJP peer review panels, and final decisions by the NIJ Director. If the workflow is injecting NIH machinery into non-NIH rows generically, other DOJ/NSF/NEH rows are likely receiving the same wrong baseline.

result.program_name: William T. Grant Scholars Program
result.next_deadline:

EXPECTED 2027 WINDOW (inference from three cycles, NOT a published date, do not cite as one): portal opens in the last week of March 2027; mentor/reference letters due ~10-12 June 2027; full application due in the last days of June or first days of July 2027 at 3 PM ET. The real date appears on the programme page in January 2027, when the 2027 Application Guidelines PDF is posted.

result.deadline_pattern:
Annual, single cycle, highly stable across 2024-2026. Guidelines PDF refreshed and dates posted each January → portal opens late March (3 PM ET) → mentor and reference letters due ~3 weeks before the application deadline, on the second or third Wednesday of June → full application due at the June/July turn, 3 PM ET → finalist interviews in New York City in February → Trustee decision by end of March → "Awards begin July 1 of the award year." Roughly 12 months from portal opening to money.

Consumer note for whoever writes this into the corpus: these dated values are currently routed OUT of data/mechanisms.csv by the project's own design docs, not by any funder constraint — docs/BRIEF.md specifies for `application_cadence` "(do NOT store specific dated deadlines here)" and sends dated calls to an unbuilt live layer (`live_opportunities_<country>.csv`, BRIEF §8); docs/SCHEMA.md says "No dated events"; DECISIONS.md line 18 repeats it. `application_cadence` = annual is still correct; the dates above need a home other than that column.
result.loi_deadline:
No LOI. FAQ verbatim: "Is a letter of inquiry part of the Scholars' application process? The Scholars Program does not require a letter of inquiry. Applicants must be nominated by their institutions before submitting any materials."

BUT two gates sit in front of the published deadline and both are easy to miss:

1. INSTITUTIONAL NOMINATION (limited submission). "Applicants must be nominated by their institutions. Major divisions of an institution (e.g., College of Arts and Sciences, Medical School) may nominate only one applicant each year." This forces an internal campus competition run by the dean/division chair and the research office, typically closing months before the funder deadline. The functional first deadline is your own institution's, and it is not published by the funder. If an institution nominates more than one person, a central administrative officer must file a "Letter of Independence of Multiple Applicants" confirming the nominees sit in distinct major divisions.

2. MENTOR AND REFERENCE LETTER DEADLINE — 20 days before the application deadline in the 2026 cycle (June 10 vs June 30) and it hard-blocks submission. Guide verbatim: "You may continue to other sections of the application while waiting for your mentors and references to submit their letters online, but you will not be able to submit your application until all letters are received." The Foundation adds: "We recommend beginning the online application early to give mentors and references ample time to complete their sections."

There is no separate pre-proposal document. The 6-page abstract is submitted inside the single application, but it functions as a screen: "Foundation staff use them to screen applications. In addition, Selection Committee members will review the abstracts of all finalists but will not read all the full applications."
result.review_to_award:
About 9 months submission → notification, about 12 months submission → money. Stages, from the 2026 Application Guidelines:

Submit end of June 2026 → (1) "Foundation staff screen abstracts, brief CVs, and, if warranted, full applications to determine whether they fit our research focus areas and potentially meet other Review Criteria" → (2) Scholars Selection Committee review, "Each application receives detailed reviews by two Committee members" → (3) "The Committee then chooses approximately 10 finalists, who will be invited to New York City for an interview in February 2027. Prior to the interview, finalists' proposals are reviewed by two external reviewers" → (4) interview, at which "finalists respond to Committee members' and external experts' reviews" → (5) "the Selection Committee chooses four to six William T. Grant Scholars to recommend to the Board of Trustees for approval. Applicants will be notified of the Trustees' decision by the end of March 2027" → (6) "Awards begin July 1 of the award year and are made to the applicant's institution."

Two practical consequences: the finalist interview is a live defence in New York, not a written rebuttal, and it lands ~8 months after submission; and an applicant must keep the 7-year eligibility clock in mind, since the window is measured at submission, not at award.

No funder-wide norm was researched for this funder, so this is the mechanism-specific timeline standing alone.
result.submission_requirements:
All through the Foundation's own online system; no Grants.gov, no federal forms. Formatting rule for every upload, verbatim: "12-point Times New Roman font, single-spaced text with a line space between each paragraph, numbered pages, and 1-inch margins on all sides."

Components and page limits (2026 Guidelines):
• Abstract — 6 pages maximum, on the Foundation's form. "Do not edit or delete instructions from the form." Used for staff screening and read by the Committee for all finalists.
• Full Research and Mentoring Plan — 40 pages maximum, comprising: five-year research plan 20 pages max; mentoring plan 4 pages max; bibliography 8 pages max; appendices 8 pages max.
• Publications 1 and 2 — 20 pages maximum each; journal articles, chapters or research reports, "published or in press."
• Abridged CV (Foundation form) and full CV.
• Budget — Foundation form, five years. "The total budget should be exactly $425,000 (including the combined direct and indirect costs for the full grant period). Indirect costs may not exceed 7.5 percent of total direct costs." Salary: "Requests to fund the recipient's salary must not exceed 50 percent of the total salary received from the sponsoring institution." Graduate students and study participants may be supported. Mentors "cannot be funded with monies from the award" but receive a $500 honorarium for annual reports. Budget justification form also required.
• Mentor letters — one to two proposed mentors for the first two years; "Two is typical and recommended." Each mentor submits a letter. "Mentor letters are not recommendations, and applicants should discourage cursory letters of support." Each must cover: assessment of the research plan and the applicant's potential; the current relationship and how the award adds value beyond it; the specific expertise to be acquired and the activities; a rationale that the time commitment fits the expertise; interaction mode and frequency; and confirmation of willingness to file annual reports.
• Reference letters — "Three letters of recommendation must be submitted from colleagues, supervisors, or the department/division chairperson who nominates the applicant... Proposed mentors may not submit recommendation letters." May come from another institution.
• Nominating Statement — from the dean or chairperson of the nominating division; must describe why the applicant was selected, assess the plan, state the applicant's current source and amount of salary, and give "a guarantee that 50 percent of the applicant's paid time will be devoted to research."
• Endorsement of Project — from the sponsored-research office or chief administrative officer, confirming institutional awareness of the submission.
• Letter of Independence of Multiple Applicants — if the institution nominates more than one.
• Resubmission Statement — if the applicant has applied before (see resubmission_note).

Deviation worth flagging: the mentoring plan is not a formality. The Guidelines carry a NOTE warning that applicants proposing to learn qualitative methods routinely under-specify the activities, and that reviewers expect "a combination of activities, such as taking courses; enrolling in summer workshops; getting continuous feedback... and consulting with an advisory committee, in addition to frequent and regular meetings with a mentor." It also advises against naming a former advisor: "Deepening a relationship with a casual colleague, or developing a new relationship, adds greater value... than proposing a former advisor or committee chair."
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
WHAT PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY (the half applicants usually get wrong here — this mechanism is unusually permissive):
• Holding a career development award, including an NIH K award, does NOT disqualify. FAQ verbatim: "Applicants can apply for the Scholars' award if they already have a career development award (e.g., K-awards). The Scholars' award must add significant value beyond what is supported by the other career development award." The only test is incremental value, not exclusivity.
• No exclusion for R01s, NSF awards, other foundation grants, or any research project funding appears anywhere in the 2024, 2025 or 2026 Application Guidelines or the FAQ. I searched all three guides and the FAQ for concurrent/overlap/other-award language and found none.
• Previously unsuccessful applicants may reapply. A "Resubmission Statement (if applicable)" is a standard listed component, present unchanged in all three guides; no cap on attempts is stated.
• Applicants outside the United States are eligible, provided the research "has compelling policy or practice implications for youth in the United States."
• Any discipline is eligible.
• Current Scholars may apply for an additional Foundation mentoring grant to mentor junior researchers of colour, so holding a Scholars award does not close off Foundation funding.

WHAT ACTUALLY DISQUALIFIES (none of it is prior funding — the gates are clock, position and nomination):
• More than seven years past the doctorate. "Applicants must have received their doctorate within seven years of submitting their application. We calculate this by adding seven to the year the doctorate was conferred... The month in which the degree was conferred or residency completed does not matter for this calculation." In medicine the clock runs from completion of the first residency. The month-insensitive rule can gain or cost an applicant a full cycle — check the conferral YEAR, not the date.
• Not in a career-ladder position. Students and postdocs are excluded: "This award is not intended for students or post-doctoral fellows" and "The award may not be used as a post-doctoral fellowship." The organisation must be "fiscally responsible for the applicant's position."
• Not nominated, or your division's single nomination went to someone else — one nominee per major division per year.
• Supplantation: "The award must not replace the institution's current support of the applicant's research." This is the nearest thing to a funding conflict in the whole mechanism, and it binds the INSTITUTION, not the applicant's other grants — the institution must still supply equipment, staff, facilities and the balance of salary, and guarantee ≥50% of paid time for research.
• Grants go only to tax-exempt organisations; "We do not make grants to individuals."

CAVEAT ON THE NEGATIVE FINDING: "no prior-funding exclusion found on the funder's published pages" is what I can establish. The online application system is behind a login and was not inspected, so a clause inside the form cannot be ruled out. Do not upgrade this to "no exclusion exists."

result.next_deadline:
STRUCTURAL FINDING FIRST: the Director's Fellowship has no deadline of its own, because you do not separately apply for it. It is a priced option period inside the base YFA proposal. Attachment C (Proposal Template Volume 1) opens: "The Technical and Management Volume must address the full 36-month program (base and option period)." The RA §I.D: "Proposals should also include a 12-month option period with a maximum funding level of $500,000... The 12-month option period, referred to as the 'Director's Fellowship,' will be reserved for a limited number of awardees who demonstrate exceptional YFA project performance over the 24-month base period." The Volume 1 cover sheet carries a separate "Total Proposed Cost — Base: $ / Option (if any): $ / Total: $" line. So the deadline that governs your access to the Fellowship is the base YFA deadline, three years earlier.

This is a live-check fact, not evidence of discontinuation. result.deadline_pattern:
Annual, dated, and the most calendar-able mechanism DARPA runs — this is Regime 3 in the funder-wide note, and the Director's Fellowship rides on it.

Recurring shape, anchored on the verified FY2026 cycle: RA posts late September/early October → executive summary due ~2 weeks later, 4:00 p.m. ET → question submittal closes ~11 days before proposals → full proposal due ~20 January, 4:00 p.m. ET → target award start the following August ("A target start date of August 2026 may be assumed for planning purposes"). Base period 24 months → Director's Fellowship nomination arises near the end of that base, ~2 years after award start.

Worked FY2026 intervals: posting→exec summary 15 days; exec summary→full proposal 97 days; questions close→full proposal 11 days; full proposal→target start ~7 months; award start→earliest DF decision ~24 months.

Time in ET and the hour is 4:00 p.m., not 5:00 p.m. — all four FY2026 milestones used 4:00 p.m. ET.

Backward-planning consequence for an ECR who wants a Director's Fellowship: the last decision point that affects it is the January full-proposal deadline of the base cycle. You must have priced the option year and written its technical content into the 8-page Volume 1 by then. There is no later opportunity to add it.

One-shot constraint on the pattern: the annual reissue does NOT give you a second try at YFA once you have held one. "Individuals who have previously received a YFA Award as a PI are not eligible to be a PI for this or any future YFA program." The Director's Fellowship is therefore the only route to a third year of YFA money, ever.
result.loi_required: yes — an executive summary stage exists and is strongly encouraged, but it is advisory, not a hard gate
result.loi_deadline:
FY2026 actual: "Executive Summary Due Date: October 15, 2025, 4:00 p.m." (ET) — 97 days before the 20 January 2026 full proposal, and 15 days after the RA posted. Expect the equivalent ~mid-October 2026 for the FY2027 cycle (pattern, not published).

WHAT IT IS AND ISN'T. Not mandatory, and not a gate: "Regardless of DARPA's response to an executive summary, proposers may submit a full proposal. DARPA will review all conforming full proposals using the published evaluation criteria (Section II) and without regard to any comments resulting from the review of an executive summary." But DARPA leans on it unusually hard: "Prior to submitting a full proposal, proposers are strongly encouraged to first submit an executive summary. As the YFA is considered a mentorship program, submission of a proposal is strongly discouraged if a proposal is not recommended for submission based on the executive summary." Read that as a soft gate with teeth.

FOUR DEVIATIONS FROM THE DARPA NORM, all easy to trip on:
1. IT IS BLIND-REVIEWED. This is the single biggest trap and has no analogue elsewhere at DARPA. "The executive summary will undergo a 'blind' review and must be completely anonymized: do not include identifying information of the PI, organization, or team members on the executive summary page (items 1 through 4)." Enforcement is a non-conformance gate: "If Institution or Key Personnel identifying information is found after the Executive Summary Cover Sheet, the executive summary may be deemed non-conforming and may not be reviewed." An academic's reflex — "building on my group's prior work at X" — kills the submission before it is read.
2. ONE PAGE. "Executive summaries shall not exceed a maximum of 1 page, excluding the cover sheet... Items 1 through 4 should not exceed 1 page." Figures, tables and charts sit inside that page. The cover sheet is separate and "may be expanded to 2 or more pages"; put a page break between them.
3. RESPONSE TIME IS ~45 DAYS, NOT THE 30-DAY DARPA ABSTRACT NORM. "Executive summaries submitted in response to this announcement may anticipate a response within approximately 45 calendar days." Sent by email to the Technical and/or Administrative POC on the cover sheet.
4. IT GOES TO A DIFFERENT PORTAL THAN THE PROPOSAL. Executive summary → BAAT, with "a separate announcement listing in BAAT (e.g. DARPARA2502-01, DARPARA2502-02, etc.)" per Topic Area. Full proposal → Grants.gov. Mandatory Attachment A template; .pdf, .odx, .doc or .docx.

Structure of the one page (maps onto the Heilmeier Catechism): Summary (1–2 sentences, minimal jargon) / Intro-Background (one paragraph: the problem, state of the art, its limits) / Impact (one short paragraph) / Methods-Approach (remainder of page: what is new, what are the advantages).

Limit: one executive summary per PI, against exactly one Topic Area. "Submitting more than one executive summary or full proposal may result in all of the PI's proposal submissions being determined non-conforming."
result.review_to_award:
THREE CLOCKS, and the one that matters for the Fellowship is the third.

1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY → RESPONSE: "approximately 45 calendar days" (RA §III). Deviates from the DARPA-wide 30-calendar-day abstract target in the BAA Guide. Output is a bare interest signal: DARPA "will respond to executive summaries with a statement as to whether DARPA is interested in the idea." FY2026: due 15 Oct 2025, so replies ~end of November — comfortably before the 20 Jan proposal deadline, which is the point of the 97-day gap.

2. FULL PROPOSAL → AWARD START: ~7 months. Proposals due 20 January 2026; "A target start date of August 2026 may be assumed for planning purposes." DARPA publishes no interim notification date for YFA, and there is no YFA equivalent of the SBIR/STTR "within 90 days of the closing date" commitment. Reviews are not comparative: "Proposals will not be evaluated against each other since they are not submitted in accordance with a common work statement." Award instrument is fixed — cooperative agreements only, "No award type other than cooperative agreements will be issued under this RA." Keep your proposal alive across that gap: "Proposal Validity Period (minimum 120 days)" on the cover sheet is shorter than the 180 days the funder-wide note cites for cost proposals, and shorter than the actual 7-month wait.

3. AWARD START → DIRECTOR'S FELLOWSHIP DECISION: ~24 months, i.e. roughly three years from the January you submitted. The option sits after "a 24-month base period", and qualification is judged on performance across it. Corroborated by the public record: the seven Director's Fellowships announced in 2026 went to the 2024 YFA class. For an FY2026 awardee starting August 2026, the base runs to ~August 2028 and the DF year to ~August 2029.

THE DEFERRAL CLAUSE — the timing subtlety that distinguishes this from an ordinary option exercise. "Director's Fellowship nominations by the DARPA PM Mentor may be deferred until measurable progress toward project objectives during the performance period have been achieved and required reasonable expenditure levels have been reached, provided that deferment not surpass the Cooperative Agreement PoP, to include any requested extensions." So the decision is not on a fixed date; your PM Mentor can hold it open until the evidence is there. Two practical consequences: (a) slow spending can delay or forfeit the nomination, not merely the science; (b) a base-period No-Cost Extension extends the window in which a nomination can still be made — "YFA recipients may request one No-Cost Extension (NCE) to the base PoP not to exceed 12 months."

DF period itself: 12 months, up to $500,000, and it too may be extended once — "Director's Fellowship recipients may request one NCE for the Director's Fellowship option PoP, not to exceed 12 months."
result.submission_requirements:
You are never filing a Director's Fellowship application. You are filing a base YFA proposal that must already contain the Fellowship year. Requirements below are the base-cycle ones, flagged where they deviate from the DARPA-wide norm.

THE DF-SPECIFIC REQUIREMENT — the one thing that decides whether you are ever eligible:
- "The Technical and Management Volume must address the full 36-month program (base and option period)" (Attachment C, opening line). Your 8 pages must cover 36 months, not 24.
- Price it: "Proposals should also include a 12-month option period with a maximum funding level of $500,000." Cover sheet has "Base: $ / Option (if any): $ / Total: $".
- Budget the extra travel: "please plan for 3 two-day meetings in the Washington, D.C., area over the course of the 24-month base period and one additional meeting over the course of the 12-month option period."
- SOW must "Separately define each year of the project" — so the option year needs its own tasks and measurable milestones.
- Interaction with the other option: "The U.S. Person Graduate Student option, if requested and exercised, will not extend into the Directors Fellowship option period." You cannot carry the student option into year three.

PAGE LIMITS — none appear in the RA body (only 3 instances of the word "page" in the whole RA, all incidental). They live in the mandatory templates, matching the DARPA-wide pattern:
- Volume 1 (Technical & Management): "shall not exceed a maximum of 8 pages."
- COUNTED against the 8: technical figures, tables, charts — AND "References, technical papers, resumes are included in the page limit so proposers may wish to include these as links in the bibliography." Resumes inside the page limit is harsher than most federal mechanisms and is the main reason YFA proposals run over.
- NOT counted: Cover Sheet, Table of Contents, Official transmittal letter, Summary Slide (Attachment B), Bibliography (optional).
- "The Government will not consider pages in excess of the page count limitations." Appendices are closed off: "Additional information not explicitly called for in the Technical and Management Volume must not be submitted with the proposal, but may be included as links in the bibliography. Such materials will be considered for the reviewers' convenience only and not evaluated as part of the proposal."
- Within Volume 1: key personnel bios "no more than one page per person" — and those pages count.
- Executive summary: 1 page excluding cover sheet (see LOI field).
- Formatting floor: 8.5x11, 1-inch margins, 12-point minimum, 8 or 10 point permitted for figures/tables/charts. Files in .pdf, .odx, .doc or .docx; summary slide in .ppt or .pptx.

MANDATORY TEMPLATES — use of each is a conformance condition ("Use of this template is mandatory. Failure to use this template or follow the instructions herein may result in the submission being determined non-conforming"):
- Attachment A: Executive Summary Template (required if submitting an executive summary)
- Attachment B: Proposal Summary Slide Template (required, one PowerPoint slide, separate file)
- Attachment C: Proposal Instructions and Volume I Template — Technical and Management (required)
- Attachment D: Proposal Instructions and Volume II Template — Administrative and National Policy Requirements (required)

INSTITUTIONAL SIGN-OFF — required, and it is the only letter YFA asks for:
- "Official Transmittal Letter: [Attach the official transmittal letter from the prime proposer organization. This is a brief, signed statement from an official at the submitter's organization (perhaps a Director of Research or Sponsored Programs) in support of the research proposed.]" It does not count against the 8 pages.
- NO letters of reference, NO mentor/sponsor statement, NO departmental commitment letter. Unlike an NIH K award, YFA asks for nothing from senior colleagues. The mentorship is DARPA's, supplied after award via the assigned PM Mentor.
- Self-certification on both cover sheets: "I certify that the PI is eligible per Section [III/IV] of the RA [Yes or No]."

REQUIRED CONTENT OF VOLUME 1 (fixed order): Official Transmittal Letter; Summary Slide; Executive Summary; Goals and Impact; Technical Plan; Management Plan; Personnel, Qualifications and Commitments; Capabilities; Statement of Work; Schedule and Milestones; Bibliography. The Executive Summary section is explicitly the Heilmeier Catechism ("What is the proposed work attempting to accomplish or do? How is it done today, and what are the limitations? Who or what will be affected and what will be the impact if the work is successful? How much will it cost, and how long will it take?").

DISCLOSURE FIELDS on the Volume 1 cover sheet — fill these honestly, they drive the eligibility check: "List all past DARPA awards" (office, solicitation #, title, amount, performance dates); "List all other past federal awards"; "Have you proposed to YFA before? [Yes or No] If yes what year"; "PI's Tenure Track Start Date (or Ph.D. date if at a Non-profit)"; "PI's Approved Leaves of Absence, if any" (type, start, finish); US citizenship and green-card status. Under Capabilities: "Identify any other solicitation(s) to which this concept has been proposed. If applicable, state whether funding or a positive funding decision has already been received, and from which agency."

ROUTE SPLIT — the classic YFA error:
- Executive summary → BAAT (baa.darpa.mil; returns 302 to a GET, live this pass), zip archive, separate BAAT listing per Topic Area.
- Full proposal → Grants.gov. "All proposals must be submitted through Grants.gov." Budget justification as Section L of the SF-424 R&R Budget. The DARPA-wide registration chain (UEI → SAM → Grants.gov) "can take up to four weeks"; SAM registration must be active and current "at all times throughout the award process."

OTHER DEVIATIONS WORTH KNOWING:
- One Topic Area only, named on the cover sheet: "Each submission (executive summary or full proposal) must specify ONE and only one TA... Executive summaries and full proposals that do not clearly address a specific TA may be deemed non-conforming." DARPA may reassign it.
- One proposal per PI, at each stage.
- "The PI must be from the Prime proposer's organization and must be identified as the sole Key Personnel in the proposal." Everyone else is Senior Personnel.
- Fundamental research only: "DARPA will not select proposals for negotiation of an award if the proposal is deemed to be Applied Research, or otherwise requires Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) restrictions." Publication costs "highly discouraged."
- Cost ceilings: base 24 months ≤$500,000 with "Each 12-month interval of the base period shall not exceed $250,000"; option ≤$500,000; optional concurrent U.S. Person Graduate Student ≤$350,000. Maximum lifetime value $1.35M.
- Green-card-in-process path has a hard deadline: "please email your USCIS Form I-797 to YFA2026@darpa.mil no later than the full proposal due date... If Attachment C reflects the individual is not a U.S. citizen or current U.S. Permanent Resident/Green Card holder, and DARPA has not received a USCIS Form I-797 via email by the full proposal due date, the proposal will be removed from consideration."
- Before award: WAWF registration, OCI disclosure and mitigation plan, affirmation regarding DARPA support. Patent reporting via i-Edison.
- Evaluation criteria, "in descending order of importance: Overall Scientific and Technical Merit; Potential Contribution and Relevance to the DARPA Mission; and Cost Realism."
result.prior_funding_conflicts:
Both halves below. The carve-outs matter as much as the bars, and DARPA writes them into the same sentences.

=== WHAT DISQUALIFIES YOU FROM THE BASE YFA (and therefore from ever reaching the Fellowship) ===

1. THE DOLLAR CEILINGS — the defining YFA bar. "A proposed PI who has received funding greater than $500,000 from DARPA or $1,250,000 from all DoD sources combined as either a prime or subawardee is not eligible to apply for the YFA program." Restated in §IV with the co-PI extension: "Individuals who have received funding greater than $500,000 from DARPA or $1,250,000 from all DoD sources combined as either a Prime or subawardee PI or co-PI are not eligible to be Key Personnel (i.e., PI) under the YFA program, but may serve as Senior Personnel." Note the thresholds are cumulative career totals of funding RECEIVED, and subawardee money counts.

2. ONE YFA PER LIFETIME — the constraint that makes the Director's Fellowship uniquely consequential. "Individuals who have previously received a YFA Award as a PI are not eligible to be a PI for this or any future YFA program, but may serve as Senior Personnel." There is no second YFA. Since the Fellowship is the only third year available, and it must be priced into the original proposal, a YFA applicant who omits the option period forfeits their only route to it permanently.

3. RANK / CLOCK. PI must be "in a current tenured track faculty position, tenured faculty within 3 years of their tenure date, or an equivalent at a non-profit research institution within 12 years of the receipt of their doctorate." Note the asymmetry: the academic path is rank-based with no years-since-PhD limit for the untenured; only the non-profit path uses a 12-year doctorate clock.

4. CATEGORICAL BARS, no exceptions offered. "Former DARPA PMs are not eligible to serve under this program in any capacity." "Researchers working at Federally Funded Research and Development Centers, University Affiliated Research Centers, National Laboratories, or other Government entities are not eligible to serve under this program in any capacity." "Non-U.S. organizations cannot participate in this announcement." All personnel "must be employed at a U.S. institution, which includes those in U.S. states and territories. Proposals from outside these regions will not be accepted."

5. NATIONALITY. "Proposed Key or Senior Personnel who are citizens of China, Cuba, Russia, Iran, Venezuela, and North Korea are not eligible for inclusion on a YFA proposal unless certain conditions are met."

=== WHAT EXPLICITLY PRESERVES ELIGIBILITY ===

1. SENIOR PERSONNEL IS ALWAYS OPEN. Both funding-based bars end with the same clause — "but may serve as Senior Personnel." Someone over the DARPA/DoD ceiling, and a past YFA PI, can both still join a colleague's YFA team. This is the carve-out most people miss, and it is the practical route for a mid-career collaborator.

2. HAVING APPLIED BEFORE AND LOST IS FINE. The cover sheet asks "Have you proposed to YFA before? [Yes or No] If yes what year" purely for information. There is no A1/A2 marking, no Introduction to Resubmission, no requirement to answer prior reviewers, and no cap on attempts. Only a prior AWARD as PI bars you.

3. LEAVES OF ABSENCE ARE ACCOMMODATED. Both cover sheets collect "PI's Approved Leaves of Absence, if any" with type, start date and finish date, alongside the tenure-track start date — the mechanism by which DARPA adjusts the eligibility clock for parental leave, medical leave and similar. Declare them; do not assume the raw dates disqualify you.

4. NON-U.S. INDIVIDUALS AT U.S. INSTITUTIONS CAN PARTICIPATE. "Non-U.S. individuals employed by U.S. institutions may participate to the extent that such participants comply with the citizenship and eligibility requirements under this RA, any necessary nondisclosure agreements, security regulations, export control laws, and other governing statutes." The restricted-nationality bar has three written exits: dual U.S. citizenship; U.S. Permanent Resident/Green Card holder; or "Individual is in the application process to become a U.S. Permanent Resident/Green Card holder" — with the I-797 emailed to the RA mailbox by the full proposal due date.

5. TENURE DOES NOT END YOU. "tenured faculty within 3 years of their tenure date" remain eligible — a recently promoted associate professor still qualifies.

6. A DISCOURAGING EXECUTIVE SUMMARY DOES NOT BAR THE PROPOSAL. "Regardless of DARPA's response to an executive summary, proposers may submit a full proposal." YFA is not an IPTO-style invitation-only gate.

7. CONCURRENT SUBMISSION ELSEWHERE IS PERMITTED, subject to disclosure — the template asks you to "Identify any other solicitation(s) to which this concept has been proposed" and whether funding "has already been received." Disclosure, not prohibition.

=== ELIGIBILITY FOR THE FELLOWSHIP ITSELF (once you hold a YFA) ===
Not competed against other people, and not dollar-gated. Two performance conditions plus a nomination:
- "To qualify for the Director's Fellowship option period, the effort's reports must demonstrate measurable progress toward project objectives during the performance period and show that a significant portion of the received funding has been expended." Underspending is a disqualifier in its own right — an unusual and easily overlooked condition.
- "Director's Fellowship nominations by the DARPA PM Mentor" — your assigned PM must put you forward.
- It is rationed: "reserved for a limited number of awardees who demonstrate exceptional YFA project performance." Seven from the 2024 class, against a programme that has "supported over 500 rising research stars from more than 60 universities" since 2006.

DRIFT WARNING: all dollar thresholds above are from DARPARA2502 (FY2026). The corpus row correctly notes these are RA-specific. Re-read them in the FY2027 RA when it posts; do not carry these figures forward as fixed.
result.program_officer_contact:
TWO DIFFERENT CONTACTS AT TWO DIFFERENT STAGES, and confusing them wastes the one that matters.

BEFORE AWARD — a mailbox, not a person, and the usual DARPA PM-courtship is deliberately throttled here.
- RA Coordinator: "Contact the RA Coordinator for this effort at: YFA2026@darpa.mil". Grants.gov lists the same address plus phone 571-218-4565, contact description "BAA Coordinator", under DARPA - Defense Sciences Office. Expect the mailbox to renumber with the cycle (YFA2027@darpa.mil).
- "Administrative, technical, and contractual questions should be emailed to YFA2026@darpa.mil. All questions must be in English and must include the name, email address, and the telephone number of a point of contact. DARPA will post an FAQ list on the DARPA webpage." Answers are public, so do not put your secret sauce in the question.
- Hard cut-off: "Question Submittal Closed: January 9, 2026, 4:00 p.m." — 11 days before the proposal deadline. The official channel shuts before you submit.
- BAAT technical support is separate and business-hours only: BAAT_Support@darpa.mil, cc the RA mailbox, "Monday – Friday, 9:00 a.m. – 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time."
- THE YFA EXCEPTION TO THE DARPA NORM: the funder-wide expectation that you court a PM before submitting is curtailed for YFA because of volume — per the brief, DARPA declines telecoms/meetings for executive-summary feedback and routes questions to the mailbox and public FAQ. The blind review of the executive summary is the structural expression of the same policy: at that stage DARPA does not want to know who you are. Pre-solicitation reading of PM interests is still worth doing; a pre-submission one-on-one is largely not on offer.

AFTER AWARD — a named person, and for the Director's Fellowship this is the ONLY person who matters.
- "Once awards are made, each YFA program performer will be assigned a DARPA Program Manager (PM) with interests closely related to their research topic. The PM will act as project manager and mentor to the YFA award recipients."
- That PM Mentor is the nominator: "Director's Fellowship nominations by the DARPA PM Mentor may be deferred until measurable progress toward project objectives during the performance period have been achieved and required reasonable expenditure levels have been reached."
- Practical reading for an awardee: your Fellowship depends on one person's judgement of your reports and your burn rate, over 24 months. The three two-day Washington DC meetings budgeted into the base period are where that relationship is actually built — treat them as evaluative, not administrative.
- Post-award, contract matters go to the Grants Officer (GO), not the PM: NCE requests and base-period extension justifications are "submitted to the Grants Officer (GO) for consideration."

HOW TO FIND THE RIGHT PM BEFORE YOU APPLY: the public YFA recipients list (below) names the PM Mentor against each recent awardee alongside their project title — e.g. Andrew Detor, Keith Whitener, Tabitha Dodson, Yannis Kevrekidis, Daniel Wallach, Derek Bernsen for 2025 awardees. Match your topic to the projects a PM already mentors, then read that office's page at darpa.mil/about/offices. Four offices participate in YFA: DSO, BTO, I2O and MTO.

Other routes: agency-level protests CMO_Protests@darpa.mil; general enquiries contact.darpa.mil.
result.resubmission_note:
No resubmission mechanism, consistent with the DARPA-wide position — no A1, no introduction page, no obligation to answer prior reviewers, no appeal. But YFA narrows the funder-wide picture in one decisive way and widens it in another.

NARROWER: the annual reissue is NOT a second bite once you have won. "Individuals who have previously received a YFA Award as a PI are not eligible to be a PI for this or any future YFA program." For every other DARPA mechanism the reissue is the resubmission route; for YFA a win closes the door permanently. This is precisely why the Director's Fellowship exists and why it must be priced into the original proposal — it is the sole continuation path.

WIDER: an unsuccessful applicant may come back freely. The cover sheet's "Have you proposed to YFA before? [Yes or No] If yes what year" is informational; nothing carries over, nothing is marked, and the next year's RA is a fresh evaluation. Watch eligibility drift rather than policy: the 3-years-post-tenure window closes, and — the trap specific to this mechanism — winning other DoD money in the interim can push you over the >$500,000 DARPA / >$1,250,000 DoD ceilings and disqualify you from a mechanism you were eligible for last year. Success elsewhere is the main way applicants age out.

WITHIN A CYCLE: a discouraging executive summary response does not preclude the full proposal ("Regardless of DARPA's response to an executive summary, proposers may submit a full proposal"), though DARPA "strongly discourage[s]" proceeding. YFA is not an invitation-only gate like IPTO. But you get one shot per stage: one executive summary, one full proposal, one Topic Area, and "Submitting more than one executive summary or full proposal may result in all of the PI's proposal submissions being determined non-conforming."

FOR THE FELLOWSHIP SPECIFICALLY: there is no resubmission concept at all, because there is no application. If your PM Mentor does not nominate you, there is nothing to re-file. The nearest thing to a second chance is the deferral clause — a nomination "may be deferred until measurable progress... have been achieved and required reasonable expenditure levels have been reached," and a base-period NCE of up to 12 months extends the window in which that can still happen. So a slow first year is recoverable; a slow whole base period is not.

HOW TO LEARN WHY YOU LOST: no summary statement exists. The DARPA-wide informal feedback session with the PM, available to selected and non-selected proposers on request after notification, is the substitute and is under-used. Note the tension with the YFA contact throttle: the throttle applies to executive-summary feedback during the competition, not to post-notification feedback.

CHEAPEST WAY TO LOSE, and the most avoidable: non-conformance. YFA supplies an unusual number of ways to fail before anyone reads the science — identifying information in a blind executive summary, more than one Topic Area, a missing mandatory template, exceeding 8 pages, a missing I-797, a second submission. A non-conforming submission "will receive no further consideration" and was never scientifically read.
result.examples_or_samples:
No funded YFA proposal text is published anywhere — that remains true and is recorded as unresolved. But this mechanism is unusually well served by three published artefacts that together do most of the work of a sample, and one of them is the best "who to talk to" resource DARPA publishes for any mechanism.

1. THE FULL RECIPIENT ROSTER, 2006–2025 — the strongest resource, and it is linked from the YFA page as "YFA awardees (2006-2025)". https://www.darpa.mil/sites/default/files/attachment/2026-06/darpa-yfa-recipients-2026.pdf — verified live this pass (HTTP 200, 546 KB, 39 pages, header "DARPA YFA Recipients (As of June 12, 2026)"). Columns for recent years: Principal Investigator | Institution | PM Mentor | Title. Two uses an ECR should make of it: (a) read 40–50 funded project titles in your area to calibrate ambition and register — this is the closest thing to reading successful abstracts; (b) identify the PM Mentor who funds work like yours, and identify recent awardees at institutions near you and email them. Past awardees are the people who will actually tell you how the process went, and unlike most funders' lists this one tells you which PM they were paired with. Sample 2025 rows: Sebastian Kube (Wisconsin, PM Andrew Detor); Renee Zhao and Sho Takatori (Stanford, PM Yannis Kevrekidis); Tuba Yavuz (Florida, PM Daniel Wallach).

2. THE MANDATORY TEMPLATES — free, published, and functionally an annotated sample, because every section carries DARPA's own bracketed instructional text telling you what to write. Downloadable from the archived FY2026 grants.gov record (opportunity DARPARA2502, id 360697, folder "DARPARA2502"), and re-posted with each cycle:
   - Attachment A — Executive Summary Template (the 1-page blind-review structure: Summary / Intro-Background / Impact / Methods-Approach)
   - Attachment B — Proposal Summary Slide Template (.pptx)
   - Attachment C — Proposal Template Volume 1, Technical and Management (the 8-page outline, 11 named sections, with prompts such as "Describe how the proposed project is revolutionary and how it significantly rises above the current state of the art")
   - Attachment D — Proposal Template Volume 2, Administrative and National Policy Requirements
   - Model Cooperative Agreement (shows the terms you will actually sign)
   Attachment download pattern: https://www.grants.gov/grantsws/rest/opportunity/att/download/<id> (redirects to apply07.grants.gov) — Attachment A id 349530, Attachment B 349531, Attachment C 349534, Attachment D 349532, base RA PDF 349529, Amendment 05 (consolidated) 349977.

3. THE DIRECTOR'S-FELLOWSHIP COHORT ITSELF — the only named DF recipients in the public record, seven from the 2024 class, with institutions and project titles (darpa.mil news, 20 years of YFA): Jairo Diaz Amaya (Rochester Institute of Technology, Osmotic Signalers for Functional Materials); Ognjen Ilic (Minnesota Twin Cities, Ultralightweight Nanophotonic Radiators for Adaptive and High-Power Heat Rejection); Yang Lin (Rhode Island, Precision in Miniature: Revolutionizing MPS with Digital Acoustofluidics and Nanoscale 3D Printing); Thirimadura Charith Mendis (Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Language and Hardware Adaptive Representations and Techniques for Compiling Heterogeneous Workloads); Samuel Oliveira (North Carolina A&T State University, Spatial-temporal Dynamics for Predictive Multiscale Models of Multi-cellular Circuit); Savio Poovathingal (Kentucky, Gas-surface scattering dynamics in very low Earth orbit); Carter Yagemann (Ohio State, End-to-End Modeling and Mitigation of Fault Injection Attacks). These seven are the only people who can describe the Fellowship nomination from the inside — a short, specific email to one working in your area is the highest-yield research an intending applicant can do.

4. THE HEILMEIER CATECHISM — https://www.darpa.mil/about/heilmeier-catechism (verified HTTP 200). The RA points proposers at it directly, and the Volume 1 Executive Summary section is simply four of its questions. Answer all eight in one page before you write anything else.

5. DOLLAR-LEVEL AWARD DATA — USAspending.gov, Assistance Listing 12.910 "Research and Technology Development", awarding agency Department of Defense, sub-agency Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. Tells you who holds DARPA money and how much; descriptions are administrative one-liners, not abstracts. DTIC's grant-abstract search (discover.dtic.mil/grant/) would be the better source but was offline when checked this pass.

WHAT DOES NOT EXIST for this mechanism: no sample-proposal page, no summary statements, no success-rate publication, no DF-specific FAQ or application form. The programme has "supported over 500 rising research stars from more than 60 universities" in 20 years; seven Fellowships in the 2024 class is the only selectivity datapoint available.
